1.1 Introduction

Welcome to Java—one of the world’s most popular and senior computer programming languages.1,2,3 This book provides an intensive, hands-on Java programming experience.

1. “TIOBE Index for February 2025.” Accessed February 18, 2025. https://tiobe.com/tiobe-index/.

2. “The Top Programming Languages 2024.” Accessed February 18, 2025. https://spectrum.ieee.org/top-programming-languages-2024.

3. “PYPL PopularitY of Programming Language.” Accessed February 18, 2025. https://pypl.github.io/PYPL.html.

The chapter introduces terminology and concepts that lay the groundwork for the Java programming capabilities you’ll learn, beginning in Chapter 2. Our intro to object orientation presents the terminology we use as we present Java object-oriented programming throughout this book. We introduce Java and discuss the Java Application Programming Interface (Java API) and various Java “open-source” libraries that help you avoid “reinventing the wheel.” We present a typical Java program-development environment in the context of the Java Development Kit (JDK), using it to test-drive a Java program (Section 1.7) to prepare you to run the book’s examples. You can also run our programs using one of the many Java integrated development environments (IDEs). We provide test-drives for several popular IDEs at

https://deitel.com/javafp5

We review the Internet, the web, the cloud and the Internet of Things (IoT) basics. We introduce the Metaverse and its related technologies, including blockchain, cryptocurrencies, NFTs, Web3, augmented reality, virtual reality and mixed reality. We briefly introduce several contemporary software-development technologies. Finally, we introduce big data, data science and artificial intelligence (AI) technologies—machine learning, deep learning and exciting generative AIs like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini and Anthropic’s Claude. You’ll use these and other genAIs throughout this book to leverage your Java learning experience and do some really cool stuff, beginning with this chapter’s Special Section: Generative AI Exercises!

 

This Book’s Architecture

Before you “dig in,” we recommend getting a “40,000-foot” view of the book’s architecture to understand where you’re headed as you prepare to learn and use the powerful Java programming language. To do so, review the following items:

  • In the Preface, the High-Level Overview presents the book’s modular architecture in a convenient condensed format. The Preface also contains a list of the book’s key features.

  • At https://deitel.com/javafp5, we provide testimonial comments from Java subject-matter experts and university professors who reviewed the prepublication manuscript.

  • The Preface presents the “soul of the book” and our approach to teaching modern Java programming. We introduce the early chapters’ “objects-natural approach,” in which you’ll use small numbers of simple Java statements to make objects of powerful preexisting classes perform significant tasks—long before you create your own custom Java classes in Chapter 8. Be sure to read the Preface’s Tour of the Book, which points out the key features of each chapter and enumerates the book’s more substantial case studies and generative AI exercises. You might also want to refer to the Preface’s High-Level Overview as you read the Tour.

Java Is Widely Used

There are billions of personal computers in use and an even larger number of mobile devices with computers at their core. Various estimates indicate that 7–9 million Java developers worldwide are writing Java code that runs on the 60 billion installed Java Virtual Machines (JVMs).4 In addition, the explosive growth of mobile devices is creating significant opportunities for programming mobile apps. The following table shows some device types that Java runs on:

4. Oracle. “Java.” Accessed November 26, 2024. https://www.oracle.com/java/.

Java Standard Edition (Java SE)

This fifth edition of Java for Programmers is based on the Java Standard Edition, which contains the capabilities needed to run desktop and server applications.5 Java supports several programming paradigms that we discuss in this book:

  • procedural programming (Chapters 2–7),

  • object-oriented programming (Chapters 8–10),

  • generic programming (Chapters 12 and 13),

  • functional programming (Chapter 14),

  • concurrent programming (Chapter 18) and

  • generative-AI-assisted programming (Chapter 19).

5. Oracle. “Java SE at a Glance.” November 26, 2024. https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/java-se-glance.html.

Jakarta EE

Java is used in such a broad spectrum of applications that it has two other editions. Jakarta EE—formerly called Java Enterprise Edition (Java EE)—is geared toward developing the kinds of large-scale, distributed networking and web-based applications that run major organizations.

Java Micro Edition

The Java Micro Edition (Java ME)—a subset of Java SE—is geared toward applications for resource-constrained embedded devices, such as smartwatches, medical devices, television set-top boxes, smart meters (e.g., for monitoring energy usage) and more.

1.2 Hardware

Computing costs are dropping dramatically due to rapid developments in hardware and software technologies. Computers that might have filled large rooms and cost millions of dollars decades ago are now inscribed on silicon computer chips smaller than a fingernail, many costing perhaps a few dollars each. Ironically, silicon is one of the most abundant materials on Earth—it’s an ingredient in ordinary sand. Silicon-chip technology has made computing so economical that computers and computerized devices have become commodities.

 

Moore’s Law, Multi-Core Processors and Concurrent Programming

Many of today’s personal computers can perform trillions of calculations in one second6,7—far more than a human can perform in a lifetime. You probably expect to pay at least a little more every year for most products and services. The opposite has been the case in the computer and communications fields, especially with regard to the hardware supporting these technologies. Over the years, hardware costs have fallen rapidly.

6. Tobias Mann, “Intel’s Lunar Lake Mobile Chips Boast 120 TOPS of AI Performance,” The Register, September 3, 2024. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://www.theregister.com/2024/09/03/intels_lunar_lake_mobile_chips/.

For decades, computer processing power approximately doubled inexpensively every couple of years. This remarkable trend is called Moore’s Law—named for Gordon Moore, co-founder of Intel and the person who identified the trend in the 1960s. Intel is a leading manufacturer of processors for today’s computers and embedded systems, such as smart home appliances, home security systems, robots, intelligent traffic intersections and more. Moore’s Law and related observations especially apply to:

  • the amount of memory that computers have for programs and data,

  • the amount of secondary storage they have to hold programs and data, and

  • their processor speeds—the speeds at which computers execute programs to do their work.

Key executives at computer-processor companies NVIDIA and ARM have indicated that Moore’s Law no longer applies. However, Intel’s CEO says it is “alive and well”—they are working on manufacturing advances that will enable more transistors on each chip.8 Computer processing power continues to increase but relies on new processor designs, such as multi-core processors.

8. Christian Hetzner, “Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger Dismisses Nvidia’s AI Chip Dominance: ‘Moore’s Law Is Alive and Well,’” Observer, June 2024. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://observer.com/2024/06/intel-ceo-pat-gelsinger-nvidia-ai-chip-rivalry/.

Multi-Core Processors and Performance

Most computers today have multi-core processors that economically implement multiple processors on a single integrated circuit chip. Intel has some processors with up to 128 cores.9 Our primary testing computer uses Apple’s M2 Max processor, which has a 12-core CPU, a 28-core GPU and a 16-core “neural engine” for AI tasks.10 Apple’s most recent M4 Max has up to a 16-core CPU, up to a 40-core GPU and a 16-core “neural engine” for AI tasks.11 AMD has processors with up to 192 cores.12 The number of cores will continue to grow. Today’s most powerful GPUs used in high-end gaming computers and artificial intelligence applications often have thousands of cores in their GPUs. For example, the NVIDIA RTX 5090 has 21,760 cores!13

In multi-core systems, the hardware can put multiple processors to work truly simultaneously on different parts of your task, enabling your program to complete faster. Taking full advantage of multi-core architecture requires writing multithreaded applications (Chapter 18). When a program’s task is split into separate threads, a multi-core system can run those threads in parallel when a sufficient number of cores is available.

Interest in multithreading is rising quickly with the proliferation of multi-core systems. Java has provided multithreading since its inception and has added higher-level capabilities over the years to simplify multithreaded application development. Chapter 18, Concurrency: Platform Threads to Virtual Threads, discusses creating and managing multi-threaded Java applications. It includes a detailed explanation with extensive code examples of the latest simplification technologies to emerge from Project Loom—virtual threads, structured concurrency and scoped values.

Computing Power Over the Years

Data is getting more massive, and so is the computing power needed to process it. Today’s processor performance is often measured in terms of FLOPS (floating-point operations per second). In the 1990s, the fastest supercomputer speeds were measured in gigaflops (109 FLOPS). By the late 1990s, Intel produced the first teraflop (1012 FLOPS) supercomputers. In 2008, IBM released the first petaflop (1015 FLOPS) supercomputer. Today’s fastest supercomputers can perform over one million trillion (a quintillion) instructions per second! As of November 2024, the USA’s El Capitan supercomputer (from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory) is the world’s fastest14—1.742 quintillion calculations per second (1.742 exaflops)!15 For perspective, it can perform in one second approximately 215 million calculations per person for everyone on the planet!16

The quantum computers now under development theoretically could operate at 18 quintillion (18,000,000,000,000,000,000) times the speed of today’s computers!17 This number is so extraordinary that in one second, a quantum computer could do staggeringly more calculations than the total that have been performed by all computing devices of any kind since the beginning of time. In December 2024, Google announced its new Willow quantum computing chip, which took five minutes to perform a task that would take a conventional computer 10 septillion (10,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000) years to complete.18 This almost unimaginable computing power could wreak havoc with blockchain-based cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin. Engineers are already rethinking blockchain19 and working on post-quantum cryptography to prepare for such massive increases in computing power.20

Computing power costs continue to decline, especially with advancements in processor architecture and cloud computing. People used to ask the question, “How much computing power do I need on my local system to deal with my peak processing needs?” Today, that thinking has shifted to “Can I quickly carve out in the cloud what I need temporarily for my most demanding computing workloads?” You pay for only what you use to accomplish a given task.

1.3 Java

The microprocessor revolution’s most significant contribution to date is that it enabled the development of personal computers and smartphones. Microprocessors also have profoundly impacted intelligent consumer-electronic devices, including the enormous number of devices in the Internet of Things (IoT). Recognizing this early on, Sun Microsystems in 1991 funded an internal corporate research project led by James Gosling, which resulted in a C++-based object-oriented programming language that Sun called Java.21 Using Java, which is among the world’s most senior and widely used high-level programming languages, you can write programs that will run on a great variety of computer systems and computer-controlled devices. This is sometimes called “write once, run anywhere (WORA).” This kind of portability is particularly powerful.

Java drew the business community’s attention because of the phenomenal interest in the Internet. It’s now used to develop large-scale enterprise applications, enhance the functionality of web servers, provide applications for consumer devices (cell phones, smart-phones, cable TV boxes and more), develop robotics software and for many other purposes. It was the original language for developing Android smartphone and tablet apps—it’s now one of two key Android development languages.22 Sun Microsystems was acquired by Oracle in 2010.

Java has been one of the most widely used general-purpose programming languages for three decades, so there is much existing Java code using older programming idioms—this is referred to as legacy code. We emphasize modern Java idioms in this book.

Java Release Cadence

Java follows a six-month release cadence that began with Java 9 in 2017. New versions are released every March and September, enabling faster delivery of new language and library features. A release is designated as a Long-Term Support (LTS) version every two years. These are geared toward enterprises requiring stability and extended support. Non-LTS releases encourage experimentation with evolving innovative new features but have shorter support cycles.

JEPs, JSRs and the JCP

Throughout the book, we encourage you to research various aspects of Java online. Some acronyms you’re likely to see are JEP, JSR and JCP.

Oracle uses JEPs (JDK Enhancement Proposals) to gather proposals from the Java community for changes to the Java language, APIs and tools, and to help create the road-maps for future Java Standard Edition (Java SE), Java Enterprise Edition (Java EE) and Java Micro Edition (Java ME) platform versions and the JSRs (Java Specification Requests) that define them. The complete list of JEPs can be found at

https://openjdk.org/jeps/0

JSRs (Java Specification Requests) are the formal descriptions of Java platform features’ technical specifications. Each new feature has a JSR that goes through a review and approval process before it’s added to Java. The complete list of JSRs can be found at

The JCP (Java Community Process) is responsible for developing JSRs. JCP expert groups create the JSRs and make them publicly available for review and feedback. You can learn more about the JCP at:

1.4 A Brief Review of Object Orientation

Building software quickly, correctly and economically remains an elusive goal at a time when demands for new and more powerful software are soaring. Objects, or more precisely—as we’ll see in Chapter 8—the classes objects come from, are essentially reusable software components. There are date objects, time objects, audio objects, video objects, automobile objects, people objects, etc. Almost any noun can be reasonably represented as a software object in terms of attributes (e.g., name, color and size) and behaviors (e.g., calculating, moving and communicating). Software developers have discovered that using a modular, object-oriented, design-and-implementation approach can make software development groups much more productive than was possible with earlier techniques—object-oriented programs are often easier to understand, test, debug, correct and evolve.

 

Automobile as an Object

Let’s begin with a simple analogy. Suppose you want to drive a car and make it go faster by pressing its accelerator pedal. What must happen before you can do this? Well, someone has to design the car before you can drive it. A car typically begins as engineering drawings, similar to the blueprints that describe a house’s design. These drawings include the design for an accelerator pedal. The pedal hides from the driver the complex mechanisms that make the car go faster, just as the brake pedal hides the mechanisms that slow the car, and the steering wheel hides the mechanisms that turn the car. This enables people with little or no knowledge of how engines, braking and steering mechanisms work to drive a car easily.

Before you can drive a car, it must be built from the engineering drawings that describe it. A completed car has an actual accelerator pedal to make the car go faster, but even that’s not enough—the car won’t accelerate on its own (hopefully!), so the driver must press the pedal to instruct the car to accelerate.

Methods and Classes

Let’s use our car example to introduce some key object-oriented programming concepts. Performing a task in a program requires a method. The method houses the program statements that perform its task. It hides these statements from its user, just as a car’s accelerator pedal hides from the driver the mechanisms that make the car go faster. In Java, we create a program unit called a class to hold the set of methods that perform the class’s tasks. For example, a class representing a bank account might contain a method to deposit money to an account, another to withdraw money from an account and a third to query the account’s current balance. A class is similar to a car’s engineering drawings, which house the design of an accelerator pedal, brake pedal, steering wheel, and so on.

Instantiation

Just as someone has to build a car from its engineering drawings before you can drive a car, you must build an object from a class before a program can perform the tasks defined by the class’s methods. The process of doing this is called instantiation, and an object is then referred to as an instance of its class.

Reuse

Just as a car’s engineering drawings can be reused many times to build many cars, you can reuse a class many times to build many objects of that class. Reusing existing classes when building new classes and programs saves time and effort. Reuse also helps you build more reliable and effective systems because existing classes and components often have been carefully tested, debugged and performance-tuned. Just as the notion of interchangeable parts was crucial to the Industrial Revolution, reusable classes are crucial to the software revolution spurred by object technology.

Messages and Method Calls

When you drive a car, pressing its gas pedal sends a message to the car to perform a task—that is, to “go faster.” Similarly, you send messages to an object. Each message is implemented as a method call that tells a method of the object to perform its task. For example, a program might call a particular bank account object’s deposit method to increase the account’s balance by the deposit amount.

Attributes and Instance Variables

Besides having capabilities to accomplish tasks, a car also has attributes, such as its color, number of doors, amount of gas in its tank, current speed and record of total miles driven (i.e., its odometer reading). Like its capabilities, the car’s attributes are represented as part of its design in its engineering diagrams (which, for example, include an odometer and a fuel gauge). As you drive a car, these attributes are “carried along” with the car. Every car maintains its own attributes. For example, each car knows how much gas is in its own gas tank but not how much is in the tanks of other cars.

An object, similarly, has attributes that it carries along as it’s used in a program. These attributes are specified as part of the object’s class. For example, a bank account object has a balance attribute representing the amount of money in the account. Each bank account object knows the balance in the account it represents but not the balances of the other accounts in the bank. Attributes are specified by the class’s instance variables.

Encapsulation and Information Hiding

Classes encapsulate (i.e., wrap) attributes and methods into objects created from those classes—an object’s attributes and methods are intimately related. Objects may communicate with one another, but they’re usually not allowed to know how other objects are implemented internally. Those details are hidden inside the objects. As we’ll see, this information hiding is crucial to good software engineering.

Inheritance

A new class of objects can be created quickly and conveniently by inheritance. The new class absorbs the characteristics of an existing class, possibly customizing them and adding unique characteristics of its own. In our car analogy, an object of the class “convertible” certainly is an object of the more general class “automobile,” but more specifically, the roof can be raised or lowered.

Interfaces

Java also supports interfaces—groups of method declarations that define what actions an object can perform without specifying how to perform them. In the car analogy, a “basic-driving-capabilities” interface consisting of a steering wheel, an accelerator pedal and a brake pedal would enable a driver to tell the car what to do. Once you know how to use this almost universal interface for turning, accelerating and braking, you can drive many types of cars, even though manufacturers may implement these systems differently.

A class implements zero or more interfaces, each of which can have methods, just as a car implements separate interfaces for basic driving functions, controlling the radio, controlling the heating and air conditioning systems, and the like. Just as car manufacturers implement capabilities differently, classes may implement an interface’s methods differently. For example, a software system may include a “backup” interface that offers the methods save and restore. Classes may implement those methods differently, depending on the types of things being backed up, such as programs, text, audios, videos, etc., and the types of devices where these items will be stored.

Object-Oriented Analysis and Design

Soon, you’ll write Java programs. How will you create the code for your programs? Perhaps you’ll turn on your computer and start entering code. This approach may work for small programs (like the ones we present in the book’s early chapters), but what if you were asked to create a software system to control thousands of automated teller machines for a major bank? Or suppose you were asked to work on a team of thousands of software developers building the next generation of the U.S. air traffic control system? For large and complex projects such as these, you should not simply start entering programs.

To create the best solutions, you should follow a detailed analysis process for determining your project’s requirements (i.e., defining what the system should do) and developing a design that satisfies them (i.e., deciding how the system should do it). Ideally, you’d go through this process and carefully review the design (and have it reviewed by others) before writing any code. If this process involves analyzing and designing your system from an object-oriented point of view, it’s called an object-oriented analysis and design (OOAD) process. Java has object-oriented programming (OOP) capabilities that enable you to implement object-oriented designs as secure, high-performance, robust, working systems.

The UML (Unified Modeling Language)

Although many different OOAD processes exist, a single graphical language for communicating the results of any OOAD process has come into wide use. The Unified Modeling Language (UML) is the most widely used graphical scheme for modeling object-oriented systems. We present our first UML diagrams in Chapters 3 and 4, then use them in our deeper treatment of object-oriented programming through Chapter 10.

1.5 Java Application Programming Interface (API) and Open-Source Libraries

You can create each class, interface and method you need from scratch to form your programs. Instead, most Java programmers take advantage of the rich collections of existing classes, interfaces and methods in the Java class libraries, also known as the Java API (Application Programming Interface). Thus, there are really two parts to learning Java programming:

  • learning the Java language itself, and

  • learning how to use the Java API’s classes, interfaces and methods and those in other publicly available open-source libraries.

Using Java API classes and methods instead of writing your own versions can improve program reliability and performance because they’re carefully written to work correctly and perform efficiently. This also shortens program development time.

 

Open Source Libraries

There are enormous numbers of open-source Java libraries that can help you perform significant tasks by writing only modest amounts of code. On GitHub, developers contribute to over 250,000 Java code repositories:

Click here to view code image

https://github.com/topics/java

In addition, pages such as

  • https://github.com/akullpp/awesome-java

  • https://github.com/Vedenin/useful-java-links

  • https://github.com/mhrimaz/AwesomeJavaFX

provide curated lists of popular Java libraries and resources—you’ll enjoy exploring these sites.

Building-Block Approach to Java Development

When programming in Java, you’ll typically mix your own code with the following preexisting building blocks:

  • Java API classes, interfaces and methods,

  • open-source Java library classes, interfaces and methods,

  • classes, interfaces and methods you create (after studying Chapters 8 and 9), and

  • classes, interfaces and methods others have created and made available to you.

The advantage of creating your own classes, interfaces and methods is knowing exactly how they work. The disadvantage is the time-consuming effort to design, develop, debug and performance-tune them. Throughout the book, we use the existing Java APIs and various open-source libraries to leverage your programming efforts and avoid “reinventing the wheel.” This is called software reuse and is a key part of our objects-natural teaching methodology.

1.6 Typical Java Program Development Environment

We now explain the steps to create and execute a Java program. Usually, there are five phases—edit, compile, load, verify and execute. We discuss them in the context of the Java Development Kit (JDK). See the Before You Begin that follows the Preface for information on downloading and installing the JDK on Windows and macOS.

 

Phase 1: Creating a Program

Phase 1 consists of editing a file with an editor program (or simply, an editor):

Using the editor, you type a Java program’s source code, make any necessary corrections and save it to your system. Java source code files are given a name ending with the .java extension, indicating that the file contains Java source code.

Windows and macOS provide the basic editors Notepad and TextEdit, respectively. Some more powerful editors available online include:

  • jEdit (https://jedit.org; cross-platform, written in Java),

  • Sublime (https://www.sublimetext.com; cross-platform)

  • Notepad++ (https://notepad-plus-plus.org; Windows-only) and

  • TextMate (https://textpad.com; macOS-only)

Integrated development environments (IDEs) provide tools that support the software development process, such as editors, debuggers for locating logic errors that cause programs to execute incorrectly, and more. The most popular Java IDEs are:

  • JetBrains’ IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition,

  • the Eclipse Foundation’s Eclipse IDE for Java Developers and

  • Microsoft’s Visual Studio Code cross-platform code editor—this is technically a powerful code editor but has plugins for Java development (and for many other programming languages).

We discuss installing each in the Before You Begin section. On the book’s website at

https://deitel.com/javafp5

we provide test-drives showing how to execute this book’s Java programs and how to develop new Java programs with these IDEs.

Phase 2: Compiling a Java Program into Bytecodes

In Phase 2, you use the javac command (the Java compiler) to compile a program:

For example, to compile a program called Welcome.java, you’d type

javac Welcome.java

in your system’s command window (Section 1.7). If the program compiles, the compiler produces a .class file called Welcome.class. IDEs typically do this for you. If the compiler detects errors, you must go back to Phase 1 and correct them. In Chapter 2, we’ll discuss the kinds of errors the compiler can detect.

When using javac, if you receive a message such as “bad command or filename,” “javac: command not found” or “'javac' is not recognized as an internal or external command, operable program or batch file,” your JDK is not installed correctly. Carefully review the installation instructions in the Before You Begin.

The Java compiler translates Java source code into bytecodes representing the tasks to execute in the execution phase (Phase 5). The Java Virtual Machine (JVM)—part of the JDK and the Java platform’s foundation—executes bytecodes.23 A virtual machine (VM) is software that simulates a computer but hides the underlying operating system and hardware from the programs that interact with it. If the same VM is implemented on many computer platforms, applications written for that type of VM can be used portably on all those platforms. The JVM is one of the most widely used virtual machines.

23. “Java virtual machine.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_virtual_machine#Bytecode_interpreter_and_just-in-time_compiler.

Unlike platform-dependent machine-language instructions, which are dependent on specific computer hardware, bytecode instructions are platform-independent. So, Java’s bytecodes are portable—without recompiling the source code, the same bytecode instructions can execute on any platform containing a JVM that understands the version of Java in which the bytecodes were compiled. The JVM is invoked by the java command. For example, to execute a Java program called Welcome, you’d type the command

java Welcome

in a command window to invoke the JVM, which would then initiate the steps necessary to execute the application. This begins Phase 3. IDEs typically provide a menu item, such as Run, that invokes the java command for you.

Phase 3: Loading a Program into Memory

In Phase 3, the JVM places the program in memory to execute it—this is known as loading:

The JVM’s class loader takes the .class files containing the program’s bytecodes and transfers them to primary memory. It also loads any of the .class files provided by Java that your program uses.

Phase 4: Bytecode Verification

In Phase 4, as the classes are loaded, the bytecode verifier examines their bytecodes to ensure that they’re valid and do not violate Java’s security restrictions:

Phase 5: Execution

In Phase 5, the JVM executes the bytecodes to perform the program’s specified actions:

In early Java versions, the JVM interpreted bytecodes. Most programs would execute slowly because the JVM would interpret and execute one bytecode at a time. Some modern computer architectures can execute several instructions in parallel. Today’s JVMs typically execute bytecodes using a combination of interpretation and just-in-time (JIT) compilation. In this process, the JVM analyzes the bytecodes as they’re interpreted, searching for hot spots—bytecodes that execute frequently. For these parts, a just-in-time (JIT) compiler, such as the OpenJDK’s HotSpot compiler, translates the bytecodes into the computer’s machine language. When the JVM encounters these compiled parts again, the faster machine-language code executes. Thus, programs actually go through two compilation phases—one in which Java code is translated into bytecodes (for portability across JVMs on different computer platforms) and a second in which, during execution, the bytecodes are translated into machine language for the computer on which the program executes.

Problems That May Occur at Execution Time

Programs might not work on the first try. Each preceding phase could fail due to various errors discussed throughout this book. For example, an executing program might try to divide by zero—an illegal operation for whole-number arithmetic in Java. This would cause the Java program to display an error message. If this occurred, you’d return to the edit phase, make the necessary corrections and proceed through the remaining phases again to determine whether the corrections fixed the problem(s).

Errors such as division by zero occur as a program runs, so they’re called runtime errors or execution-time errors. Fatal runtime errors cause programs to terminate immediately without successfully performing their jobs. Nonfatal runtime errors allow programs to run to completion, often producing incorrect results.

1.7 Test-Driving a Java Program with the Java Development Kit (JDK)

Before reading this test-drive, read the Before You Begin that follows the Preface to ensure you’ve placed the book’s examples in your user account’s Documents/examples folder and installed the JDK. In this section, you’ll use the JDK’s tools to compile and run your first Java program24—a guess-the-number game, which picks a random number from 1 to 1,000 and prompts you to guess it. If you guess the randomly selected number, the game ends. If you guess incorrectly, the program indicates whether your guess is higher or lower than the correct number. You keep guessing until you guess the number. There’s no limit on the number of guesses you can make, but it should not take more than 10 if you use the binary search technique.

24. We intentionally do not cover this Java program’s code here. This section’s purpose is to demonstrate compiling and running a program, so you can execute our examples in subsequent chapters.

1.7.1 Compiling and Running the Program with javac and java

We’ll show two ways to run the program. Here, we focus on the traditional approach in which you

  • use the javac command to compile the program, then

  • use the java command to run it.

IDEs typically provide a convenient way to perform both steps by pressing (or selecting) a button, selecting a menu item or using a keyboard shortcut.

Step 1: Changing to the ch01 Folder

First, open a terminal (command-line) window on your system:

  • On macOS, select Utilities in the Finder’s Go menu, then open the Terminal application.

  • On Windows, enter Terminal in your Windows taskbar’s Search field, then select Terminal in the search results to open a Windows PowerShell window.

Next, use the cd command to change to the ch01 subfolder of the book’s examples folder:

  • In the macOS Terminal window, enter the following command and press (or select) Enter:

    cd ~/Documents/examples/ch01

  • In the Windows PowerShell window, enter the following command and press (or select) Enter:

    cd ~\Documents\examples\ch01

In the remaining steps, we’ll show the macOS Terminal application’s prompts—the commands for compiling and running the program using the JDK’s command-line tools and your interactions with the program are identical between macOS and Windows.

Step 2: Compiling the Program

Before running the guess-the-number game, you must compile its Java source code with the javac command:

Click here to view code image

pauldeitel@MacBook-Pro ch01 % javac GuessTheNumberGame.java
pauldeitel@MacBook-Pro ch01 %

If the program compiles without errors, the javac command creates the .class file

GuessTheNumberGame.class

containing the program’s bytecodes.

Step 3: Running the Program

To run the program, use the java command followed by the name of the .class file without the .class extension:

Click here to view code image

(base) pauldeitel@MacBook-Pro ch01 % java GuessTheNumberGame
I have a number between 1 and 1000.
Can you guess my number?
Please enter your first guess.
?

The application displays "Please enter your first guess.", then displays a question mark (?) as a prompt on the next line.

Step 4: Entering Your First Guess

At the prompt, enter 500 and press (or select) Enter:

Click here to view code image

(base) pauldeitel@MacBook-Pro ch01 % java GuessTheNumberGame
I have a number between 1 and 1000.
Can you guess my number?
Please enter your first guess.
? 500
Too low. Try again.
?

The program displayed "Too low. Try again." because the value entered was less than the program’s chosen number.25

25. We wrote this program so it chooses the same “random” value each time it is run, so you’ll be able to use the same guesses we used.

Step 5: Entering Another Guess

At the next prompt, type 750 and press (or select) Enter:

Step 7: Playing the Game Again or Exiting the Program

After guessing the correct number, the application asks if you want to play again. Entering y causes the application to choose a new number and start a new game. Entering n terminates the application and returns you to the command-line prompt.

10 or Fewer Guesses

Guessing a number from 1 to 1000 should take at most 10 tries. When you start with 500 (assuming it is not the correct answer), you immediately eliminate half the numbers as your guess is either higher or lower than the correct answer. In the test-drive, 500 was too low, so we eliminated 1–500, leaving 500 values (501–1000) after one guess. Each guess should be the halfway point in the remaining range. On the next guess, 750 was too high, so we eliminated 750–1000, narrowing the potential range to 501–749, which is about half of the 500 remaining from the previous guess. If you repeatedly choose the halfway point in the remaining range, ten guesses would reduce the range to one value, which would be the correct answer. This halving technique is a property of the binary search algorithm.

1.7.2 Running the Program’s Source-Code File Directly with the java Command

You can run a single-source-file program—like Section 1.7.1’s guess-the-number game—directly using the java command, as in:26

When you execute the source code directly, the java command compiles the program in memory and immediately runs it. Unlike javac, the java command will not store a .class file containing the program’s bytecodes on your system.

You can even run multiple-source-file programs,27 like those you’ll begin building in Chapter 8, Real-World Modeling with Custom Classes. In this case, all the program’s source files are compiled in memory, then the program executes. These features make running a Java program more convenient for quick testing purposes.

1.8 Internet, World Wide Web, the Cloud and IoT

In the late 1960s, ARPA—the Advanced Research Projects Agency of the United States Department of Defense—rolled out plans for networking the main computer systems of approximately a dozen ARPA-funded universities and research institutions. The computers were to be connected with communications lines operating at speeds on the order of 50,000 bits per second, a stunning rate at a time when most people (of the few who even had networking access) were connecting over telephone lines to computers at a rate of 110 bits per second. Academic research was about to take a giant leap forward. ARPA implemented what quickly became known as the ARPANET, the precursor to the Internet. Today’s fastest consumer Internet speeds are on the order of billions of bits (gigabits) per second. The current Internet speed record holder is Japan’s National Institute of Information and Communications Technology, which achieved download speeds of 402 terabits (trillions of bits) per second—about 1.6 million times more than the average U.S. consumer’s 250 megabits per second broadband speed.28

28. Paulius Grinkevičius, “Japan Breaks Internet Speed Record, Hitting 402 Terabits per Second," CyberNews, July 4, 2024. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://cybernews.com/tech/internet-connection-speed-world-record.

Things worked out differently from the original plan. Although the ARPANET enabled researchers to network their computers, its main benefit proved to be the capability for quick and easy communication via what came to be known as electronic mail (e-mail). This is true even on today’s Internet, with e-mail, instant messaging, file transfer and social media, such as YouTube, Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, Reddit and X (formerly Twitter), enabling billions of people worldwide to communicate quickly and easily.

The protocol (set of rules) allowing computers to communicate with one another over the ARPANET became known as the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP). It ensured messages, consisting of sequentially numbered pieces called packets, were properly delivered from sender to receiver, arrived intact and reassembled in the correct order.

1.8.1 The Internet: A Network of Networks

In parallel with ARPANET’s evolution, organizations worldwide implemented their own networks for intra- and inter-organization communication. A huge variety of networking hardware and software appeared. One challenge was to enable these different networks to communicate with each other. ARPA accomplished this by developing the Internet Protocol (IP), which created a “network of networks,” the Internet’s current architecture. The combined set of protocols is now called TCP/IP. Each Internet-connected device has an IP address—a unique numerical identifier used by devices communicating via TCP/IP to locate one another on the Internet.

Companies rapidly realized that they could use the Internet to improve their operations and offer new and better client services. So, they spent large amounts of money developing and enhancing their Internet presence. This generated intense competition among communications carriers and hardware and software suppliers to meet the increased infrastructure demand. As a result, Internet bandwidth—the information-carrying capacity of communications lines—increased tremendously while hardware costs plummeted.

1.8.2 The World Wide Web: Making the Internet User-Friendly

The World Wide Web (or simply “the web”) is a collection of hardware and software associated with the Internet that allows computer users to locate and view documents (with various combinations of text, graphics, animations, audios and videos) on almost any subject. In 1989, Tim Berners-Lee of CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research) began developing the HyperText Markup Language (HTML)—the technology for sharing information via “hyperlinked” text documents. He also wrote communication protocols such as the HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP) to form the backbone of his new hypertext information system, which he called the World Wide Web.

In 1994, Berners-Lee founded the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C; w3.org), which is devoted to developing web technologies. A key W3C goal is to make the web universally accessible to everyone regardless of ability, language or culture.

1.8.3 The Cloud

More and more computing today happens “in the cloud” using software and data distributed across the Internet worldwide rather than locally on your computer or mobile device. Cloud computing allows you to increase or decrease computing resources to meet your needs at any given time, which is more cost-effective than purchasing your own hardware to provide enough storage and processing power to meet occasional peak demands. Cloud computing also saves money by shifting to the service provider the burden of managing computing resources (such as installing and upgrading the software, security, backups and disaster recovery capabilities).

The apps you use daily are heavily dependent on cloud-based services. These use massive clusters of computing resources (computers, processors, memory, storage, etc.) and databases that communicate over the Internet with each other and the apps you use. A service that provides access to itself over the Internet is known as a web service. As of November 2024, Amazon Web Services (AWS; 32% market share), Microsoft Azure (20%) and Google Cloud Platform (GCP; 12%) account for 64% of the cloud services market.29

29. Statista, “Worldwide Market Share of Leading Cloud Infrastructure Service Providers.” November 1, 2024. Accessed February 18, 2025, https://www.statista.com/chart/18819/worldwide-market-share-of-leading-cloud-infrastructure-service-providers/.

1.8.4 The Internet of Things (IoT)

The Internet is not just a network of computers—it’s an Internet of Things (IoT). A “thing” is any device with an IP address and the ability to send and sometimes receive data automatically over the Internet. Such “things” include:

  • cars with transponders for paying tolls and GPS for navigation,

  • autonomous robots,

  • monitors for parking space availability in a garage,

  • heart monitors implanted in humans,

  • smart sensors that monitor energy usage, weather, water quality and traffic,

  • smoke and carbon monoxide detectors,

  • radiation detectors,

  • item trackers in warehouses,

  • mobile apps that can track your movements,

  • thermostats that adjust room temperatures based on weather forecasts and activity in the home,

  • wearables like smartwatches, fitness trackers and smart glasses,

  • intelligent home appliances, lighting, doorbells and locks, and

  • many more.

There are expected to be 41.6 billion active IoT devices in 2025.30

30. Dell Technologies, “Internet of Things and Data Placement,” Edge to Core and the Internet of Things, Accessed February 18, 2025, https://infohub.delltechnologies.com/en-us/l/edge-to-core-and-the-internet-of-things-2/internet-of-things-and-data-placement/.

1.8.5 Edge Computing

Many IoT devices are used in edge computing,31 in which data processing, analysis and storage occur on or close to the devices that produce the data—that is, at the network’s edge. It “allows for faster processing and real-time decision-making, which is critical for applications requiring immediate responses, such as IoT devices and autonomous vehicles or edge computers.”32 For example, if a self-driving car loses its Internet connection, it must still make the decisions that enable it to drive safely. Edge computing is used in many fields, including healthcare, manufacturing, retail, clean energy, smart power grids, transportation, autonomous vehicles, smart cities and infrastructure, industrial automation and process control, defense, aerospace, agriculture, gaming, virtual reality, video surveillance and more.33,34

1.8.6 Mashups

The applications-development methodology of mashups enables you to rapidly develop powerful software by combining (often free) complementary web services and various forms of information feeds. One of the first mashups, housingmaps.com, combined the real-estate listings from craigslist.org with Google Maps to show the locations of homes for sale or rent in a given area.

A focus of this book’s object-natural approach is major software reuse beginning in Chapter 2—you’ll work with easy-to-use, powerful preexisting classes that do significant things. Similarly, before building your own web services, consider reusing the many powerful (and often free) preexisting services available across the Internet. Numerous online catalogs list dozens to thousands of existing web services:

  • GitHub’s Public APIs page (https://github.com/public-apis/public-apis) lists 51 categories containing hundreds of publicly available web services.

  • The Google APIs Explorer (https://developers.google.com/apis-explorer) lets you learn about and experiment with almost 300 Google web services without writing code.

  • The Free Public APIs page (https://www.freepublicapis.com/) lists hundreds of free public APIs.

  • Rapid (https://rapidapi.com35) claims to be the world’s largest API hub, listing thousands of free and paid APIs. Rapid also provides tools to help companies build and distribute their own APIs.

Section 1.13 presents artificial intelligence, which improves the Metaverse’s immersive nature by helping generate realistic digital avatars, environments, natural-language dialog and more.39

1.9.1 Virtual Reality (VR)

Virtual reality (VR) typically refers to simulated, three-dimensional (3D) environments that you interact with using:

  • non-immersive VR—in which the 3D environment is viewed in two-dimensional space using a computer’s screen,

  • semi-immersive VR—in which the 3D environment is viewed in two-dimensional space using large displays, such as big-screen TVs or video walls, or

  • fully immersive VR—in which users interact with the 3D environment via a head-mounted display (like a headset) and other devices (like hand-held controllers), making them feel like they’re part of the environment.

Some popular virtual reality devices include Meta Quest 3, Meta Quest Pro, Sony Play-Station VR2 and HTC Vive XR Elite.40

Augmented reality (AR) projects real-time computer-generated content—such as images, sound, video, animation and more—onto what is seen in the real world, typically via devices with built-in cameras, like smartphones, tablets and computerized glasses that enable both the real world and virtual content to be seen at the same time.41,42

A decade after its release, Niantic continues to find new ways to keep Pokemon Go players engaged.43

1.9.4 Blockchain

Accounting systems use ledgers to keep track of transactions. Blockchain50,51 is a software-based ledger distributed over nodes on the Internet. It maintains transaction data in cryptographically secured chunks—called blocks. These blocks are linked together, and new blocks are always added at the end. Once created, each block is immutable (not modifiable), so the blockchain maintains a permanent transaction record. The blockchain is decentralized, so no one person or group has control. This decentralization is the basis for the decentralized apps (dApps) that enable digital ownership in the Metaverse.

Blockchain is behind various digital technologies that have skyrocketed in popularity over the last several years, such as cryptocurrencies (Section 1.9.5) and non-fungible tokens (Section 1.9.7). It’s also used to implement many other kinds of applications,52 including

  • decentralized finance (DeFi) applications (lending, money transfer),

  • smart contracts,

  • safer Internet of Things (IoT) apps,

  • secure digital identities to help prevent fraud,

  • securing and sharing healthcare information,

  • business logistics, and

  • protecting intellectual property (IP).

1.11 Data Analytics and Data Science

We formed this section by asking genAIs to define data analytics and data science, then edited and used Gemini’s response as the basis for this section.75

75. Gemini response to “Consider the terms statistics, data analytics and data science. Precisely define the terms ‘data analytics’ and ‘data science’ and carefully explain the distinction between the two.” December 1, 2024. https://gemini.google.com. We edited the response.

 

Statistics

Statistics involves the study of collecting, organizing, analyzing, interpreting and presenting data. It provides the mathematical and theoretical framework for data analytics and data science.

Data Analytics

Data analytics is the process of examining existing datasets to uncover trends, patterns and insights. It focuses on understanding past data to inform present decisions, using techniques like descriptive statistics, data visualization and business intelligence. Essentially, data analytics aims to answer questions like “What happened?”, “Why did it happen?” and “What can be done to improve?” For example, analyzing website traffic data to understand user behavior and optimize website design falls under data analytics.

Data Science

Data science is a multidisciplinary field that uses scientific methods, algorithms, processes, and systems to extract knowledge and insights76 from both structured and unstructured data. It encompasses techniques such as machine learning, statistical modeling, data mining and predictive analytics. Data science aims to answer questions like “What might happen in the future?”, “How can we optimize outcomes?” and “What new discoveries can we make from this data?” It often involves building models to predict future outcomes and automate decision-making. For instance, data science might be used to develop a machine-learning model that predicts customer churn based on historical data.

76. Datamites Team, “How to Become a Data Scientist in Chandigarh,” DataMites (blog), September 8, 2023. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://datamites.com/blog/how-to-become-a-data-scientist-in-chandigarh/.

Distinction Between Data Analytics and Data Science

The primary distinction between data analytics and data science lies in their focus and methods:

  • Data analytics focuses on understanding past data using descriptive statistics and visualization.

  • Data science focuses on predicting future outcomes and discovering new insights by employing a broader range of techniques, including machine learning and predictive modeling.

In essence, data analytics is a subset of data science. Data science builds upon data analytics by incorporating more advanced techniques and focusing on prediction and discovery.

1.12 How Big Is Big Data?

The amount of data produced worldwide is enormous, and its growth is accelerating. Big data applications deal with massive amounts of data. The following table presents some common big-data byte measures:

For computer scientists and data scientists, understanding how to obtain, store, process and extract value from data is as crucial as writing effective programs, and possibly even more so with the booming interest in generative AI. In 2025, it’s expected that we’ll create 182 zettabytes of data—equivalent to approximately 182 sextillion bytes (182,000 exabytes; one exabyte is 1018 bytes) per day—and this is expected to more than double by 2028.77 The Internet is responsible for much of this data generation. Consider the following real-world examples of various popular data measures.

77. Statista, “Volume of Data/Information Created, Captured, Copied, and Consumed Worldwide from 2010 to 2023, with Forecasts from 2024 to 2028 (in Zettabytes).” Accessed February 18, 2025. https://www.statista.com/statistics/871513/worldwide-data-created/.

 

Megabytes

One megabyte (MB) is about one million (exactly 220) bytes. High-quality MP3-format audio files require from 1 to 2.4 MB per minute.78 JPEG-format photos taken on a digital camera can require 3 to 7 MB per photo. On one of our iPhones, the Camera settings app reports that 1080p video at 30 frames-per-second (FPS) requires 65 MB/minute, and 4K video at 60 FPS requires 440 MB/minute.

78. “Audio File Size Calculations.” Accessed February 18, 2025. https://www.audiomountain.com/tech/audio-file-size.html.

Gigabytes

One gigabyte (GB) is 1024 megabytes (230 bytes). A DVD can store up to 8.5 GB79, which could hold 141 hours of MP3 audio, hundreds of photos from a 16-megapixel camera, 7.7 minutes of 1080p video at 30 frames-per-second (FPS), or 2.33 minutes of 4K video at 60 FPS. The current highest-capacity Ultra HD Blu-ray discs can store up to 100 GB of video.80 Streaming a highly compressed 4K movie can use between 7 and 10 GB per hour.

79. “DVD.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD.

80. “Ultra HD Blu-ray.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra_HD_Blu-ray.

Terabytes

One terabyte (TB) is 1024 gigabytes (240 bytes). Recent disk drives for desktop computers come in sizes up to 36 TB,81 which could hold 50.4 years of MP3 audio, hundreds of thousands of photos from a 16-megapixel camera, 131.4 hours of 1080p video at 30 frames-per-second (FPS), or 39.7 hours of 4K video at 30 FPS.

81. “Hard disk drive.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified February 10, 2025. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_disk_drive.

Petabytes, Exabytes and Zettabytes

In 2021, there were almost five billion people online creating about 2.5 quintillion bytes of data each day82—that’s 2500 petabytes (each petabyte is 1024 terabytes) or 2.5 exabytes (each exabyte is 1024 petabytes). In 2025, there are expected to be 41.6 billion active IoT devices,83 and worldwide data produced is expected to reach 163 zettabytes—about 360 MB per minute for every person on the planet. That’s about 51.6 petabytes of new data per second, 3100 petabytes per minute, 186 exabytes per hour, or 446 exabytes (almost half a zettabyte) per day. That’s billions of hours of 4K video or trillions of photos every day!

Another enormous electricity consumer is the blockchain-based cryptocurrency Bit-coin. Processing just one Bitcoin transaction uses approximately the same amount of energy as powering the average American home for a week. The energy use comes from the process Bitcoin “miners” use to prove that transaction data is valid.87 This energy-consumption level is unsustainable, especially given the huge interest in blockchain-based applications, even beyond cryptocurrencies. The term “data analysis” was coined in the 1960s, though people have been analyzing data using statistics for thousands of years, going back to the ancient Egyptians.90 The term “big data” was coined around 1987.91

Consider four of the “V’s of big data”:92,93

  1. Volume—the data the world is producing is growing exponentially.

  2. Velocity—the speed at which data is produced, moves through organizations and changes are all growing quickly.94,95

  3. Variety—today’s data includes characters, digits, punctuation and special characters, as well as images, audios, videos and data from the rapidly growing number of Internet of Things sensors in our homes, businesses, vehicles, cities and more.

  4. Veracity—the validity of the data—is it complete and accurate? Can we trust that data when making crucial decisions? Is it real?

1.13 AI—at the Intersection of Computer Science and Data Science

When a baby first opens its eyes, does it “see” its parent’s faces? Does it understand any notion of a face or even a simple shape? Babies must “learn” the world around them. That’s what artificial intelligence (AI) technology called machine learning does. It observes massive amounts of data and learns from it. AI technologies are being used to play games, implement computer-vision applications, enable self-driving cars, enable robots to learn to perform new tasks, diagnose medical conditions, translate speech to other languages in near real-time, create chatbots that can respond smoothly and accurately to arbitrary questions after being trained on massive text databases called large language models, and much more. Who’d have guessed just a few years ago that artificially intelligent self-driving cars would be allowed on our roads—or even become common?

1.13.1 Artificial Intelligence (AI)

Two definitions of artificial intelligence (AI)99,100 are:

  • “a branch of computer science dealing with the simulation of intelligent behavior in computers” and

  • “the capability of a machine to imitate intelligent human behavior.”

99. “artificial intelligence.” Merriam-Webster.com. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/artificial%20intelligence.

100. “Artificial intelligence.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence.

The term AI was coined by John McCarthy in 1956. AI-based systems now permeate our daily lives. Examples include computer vision, speech recognition, natural language translation, recommender systems (such as Amazon recommending products you might like or Netflix recommending shows and movies you might like), automated game-playing systems, self-driving cars, and more recent remarkable tools like

  • chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude and Perplexity that converse almost indistinguishably from conversing with humans,

  • image generators like OpenAI’s Dall-E (now integrated into ChatGPT), Google’s Imagen (integrated into Gemini), Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, Adobe’s Firefly and many more that create original images from text descriptions, and

  • video generators like OpenAI’s Sora, Adobe’s Firefly Video, Google’s Veo 2, Meta’s MovieGen and Runway’s Gen-3 Alpha that create original video from text descriptions.

For many decades, AI has been a field with problems and no solutions. That’s because once a problem is solved, people say, “Well, that’s not intelligence; it’s just a computer program that tells the computer exactly what to do.” However, with AI techniques like machine learning (Section 1.13.4) and deep learning (Section 1.13.5), we’re not pre-programming solutions to specific problems. Instead, we’re having computers solve problems by learning from data—typically, lots of it. Many of the most interesting and challenging problems are being pursued with deep learning.

1.13.2 Artificial General Intelligence (AGI)

The ultimate goal of AI is artificial general intelligence (AGI)101 that, like a human, can understand, learn and apply knowledge across a wide range of tasks without needing extra training—basically, an AI that can “carry out any task that humans are capable of.”102 Experts disagree on when or if artificial general intelligence might become a reality—from 2025103 to the 2030s104 to 2300 or never.105

1.13.4 Machine Learning

Machine learning is “a subfield of artificial intelligence that gives computers the ability to learn without explicitly being programmed.”117 Machine learning typically uses predefined algorithms to build models that learn from training data. Those models can then be used to make predictions.118 For example, given labeled training data that contains legitimate e-mails and junk (also called spam) e-mails, a machine-learning model can learn from the training data, then be used to classify e-mails it has never “seen” as junk or not junk. E-mail apps like Microsoft’s Outlook and Google’s Gmail use techniques like this to move junk emails out of your inbox.

117. Sara Brown “Machine learning, explained.” April 21, 2021. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/machine-learning-explained.

118. “Machine learning.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_learning.

1.13.5 Deep Learning

Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that involves building artificial neural networks, which “attempt to simulate the network of neurons that make up a human brain so that the computer will be able to learn things and make decisions in a human-like manner.”119 The term “deep” comes from the number of software “layers” in an artificial neural network—the more layers, the deeper the network. The network learns more from its training data as it proceeds through the network layers.120 The availability of big data, significant processor power, faster Internet speeds and advancements in parallel computing hardware and software are making it possible for more organizations and individuals to pursue resource-intensive deep-learning solutions that are producing impressive results in computer vision, speech recognition, speech synthesis and newer generative AI applications (Section 1.14).

119. Jason Brownlee, “What is deep learning?” November 16, 2023. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://machinelearningmastery.com/what-is-deep-learning/.

120. “Deep learning.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_learning.

1.13.6 Reinforcement Learning

Reinforcement learning121,122 is a subset of machine learning in which algorithms learn from their environment, similar to how humans learn—for example, a video game enthusiast learning a new game or a baby learning to walk or recognize its parents. The algorithm implements an agent that learns by trying to perform a task, receiving feedback about success or failure, making adjustments then trying again. The goal is to maximize the reward. The agent receives a positive reward for doing something right and a negative reward (a punishment) for doing something wrong. The agent uses this information to determine the next action to perform and must try to maximize the reward.

1.14 Generative AI

 

Generative AI (genAI) describes algorithms that can generate new content—including text, images, audio and video—based on prompts provided by a user as input.123,124,125

123. “What Is Generative AI?” McKinsey & Company, April 2, 2024. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://www.mckinsey.com/featured-insights/mckinsey-explainers/what-is-generative-ai.

124. “Generative artificial intelligence.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence.

125. Hannah Wren, “A Beginner’s Guide to Generative AI for Business,” Zendesk, October 22, 2024. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://www.zendesk.com/blog/generative-ai-guide/.

GenAI Chatbots

OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude and Perplexity are AI-based chatbots you can converse with using natural language.126 For example, you could prompt it with text like:

  • “Tell me about the history of the Java programming language.”

  • “Who coined the term Metaverse?”

  • “Summarize the article at” followed by a link to the article.

126. “Introducing ChatGPT.” November 30, 2022. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://openai.com/blog/chatgpt.

Each chatbot then responds with answers that look and feel as if they were generated by a human.

Multimodal Chatbots

When genAIs were first introduced, they typically received a text prompt and generated a specific type of output, such as text or an image. Many genAI chatbots are now multi-modal, enabling them to understand text, images, audio and even video inputs and use them to generate outputs combining text, images, audio and video. For example, you can prompt genAIs with a speech audio file and instructions asking them to transcribe the speech to text, display the transcription, analyze its sentiment (positive, negative or neutral), translate it to another spoken language and synthesize speech in that other language—and even create images and videos from the generated text! These capabilities were out of reach even to the most sophisticated developers just a few years ago. Today, they’re available to the general public.

Turing Test

When you converse with ChatGPT and similar tools, it may seem like you’re chatting with another person. In 1950, Alan Turing proposed the imitation game—now known as the Turing test—as a way to determine whether a computer exhibits truly intelligent behavior.127 In it, three computer terminals would be hidden from one another, with two people operating terminals via text-based inputs and the third being computer-operated. One person would ask text-based questions that would be sent to the other two terminals. The second person and the computer would send text responses. If the person asking the questions could not determine whether the answers came from the other person or the computer, then the computer would be considered to have exhibited intelligent behavior.

127. “Turing test.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_test.

Things GenAIs Can Do

We prompted ChatGPT, asking for a list of all the types of things generative AIs can generate.128 We then asked it to summarize its lengthy response:

  • Text—Articles, essays, stories, poems, lyrics, code, summaries, marketing copy, academic writing, emails, and instructional guides.

  • Visual/images—Digital illustrations, concept art, character design, photo-realistic images, logos, branding elements, infographics and AI-enhanced graphics.

  • Audio—AI-composed music, sound effects, ambient audio, text-to-speech, narration, voice cloning and synthesized speech.

  • Video—AI-generated animations, explainer videos, video synthesis from text, deepfake videos and virtual characters.

  • 3D—3D models for games, simulations, virtual reality, digital sculptures, animations and special effects.

  • Code and software—Automated code generation, programming assistance, chat-bots, virtual assistants, automation scripts and machine-learning algorithms.

  • Interactive—Chatbot conversations, dynamic storytelling, personalized quizzes, surveys, interactive website and educational tools.

  • Data-related—AI-generated data analysis, reports, visualizations, graphs, charts, tables and synthetic datasets.

  • Educational—Study guides, lesson plans, quizzes, textbook sections, tutorials and interactive learning exercises.

  • Multimodal—AI-generated videos with narration and graphics, interactive simulations, and virtual environments combining text, visuals and user interaction.

  • Art and creative—Digital comics, graphic novels, mixed media art, style-transfer artwork, custom merchandise designs and AI-generated screenplays.

  • Miscellaneous—AI-generated recipes, fitness plans, daily affirmations, product names, slogans, personalized recommendations and legal document templates.

128. ChatGPT response to “Give me a list of all the types of things generative AIs can generate.” October 26, 2024. https://chatgpt.com. We edited the response.

These capabilities make content creation accessible to everyone.

Large Language Models (LLMs)

A large language model (LLM)129,130,131 is an AI that understands and can generate natural language. The term “large” comes from the fact that LLMs are implemented as artificial neural networks (or neural nets) with billions, and even trillions, of parameters. LLMs are trained on massive amounts of text—articles, books, the Internet, code and more. As neural nets learn, they tune parameters, attempting to produce better results. The parameters neural nets learn help LLMs understand and generate language patterns.

129. “Large Language Model.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_model.

130. Sean Michael Kerner, “Large Language Model (LLM),” TechTarget. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://www.techtarget.com/whatis/definition/large-language-model-LLM.

131. Adrian Tam, “What Are Large Language Models?” Machine Learning Mastery, July 20, 2023. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://machinelearningmastery.com/what-are-large-language-models/.

LLMs can generate text that’s indistinguishable from human writing. Some continue to learn and adapt, improving their effectiveness over time. They’re great at natural language tasks like translation, classification, summarization, answering questions, sentiment analysis, creative writing, and more. They’re also great at generating code, explaining code, finding errors in code, refactoring code and more.

Transformers

A transformer132,133,134 is a neural network that processes sequential data, like text. It can understand and recognize relationships between even distant words in a sentence. Transformers also recognize the relative importance of words. Many LLMs use generative pre-trained transformers (GPTs)135 that are trained on massive amounts of text using several artificial intelligence techniques.136 There are other techniques, like Google’s Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), which is geared to natural language understanding (NLU; introduced in Section 1.14).137
