Self-Attention

Self-attention138,139 is a key aspect of transformers, which are used in natural language processing. When trying to understand a word in a sentence, the context provided by surrounding words plays a significant role in determining its meaning. For example:

  • The word “good” typically is positive, but when preceded by “not,” the context becomes negative.

  • The word “bank” could refer to a financial institution or the side of a river, depending on whether it’s paired with words like “loan” or “river.”140 Instructors like to use books that are accompanied by a “test bank,” which helps them create quizzes.

  • Similarly, a phrase like “break the ice” shifts from its literal interpretation to a metaphorical one when used in contexts related to social interactions.140

138. Ashish Vaswani et al, “Attention Is All You Need,” arXiv preprint arXiv:1706.03762 (2017). Accessed February 18, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762.

139. “Attention (Machine Learning).” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_(machine_learning).

140. ChatGPT response to “Provide examples in which the context provided by surrounding words plays a significant role in determining a word’s meaning in a sentence.” October 26, 2024. https://chatgpt.com. We edited the response.

Transformers leverage self-attention to analyze each word in relation to the others around it. Since not all words contribute equally to the meaning of a sentence, self-attention assigns different weights to words, focusing more on the most relevant ones. Unlike humans, transformers can process and analyze vast numbers of words simultaneously, making connections between them to better grasp their overall meaning.

Tokens, Context and Context Windows

A token141 is the unit of processing in language models. Tokens can be words, parts of words or punctuation. Tokenization converts tokens to numerical values models can process. A token’s context is a sequence of tokens that comes before (and sometimes after) a word or phrase. Understanding the context helps models generate more accurate responses. A context window142 is the maximum number of tokens (input and output combined) a model can consider at once. The larger the context window is, the more context there is to your conversation with a genAI, the more relevant and coherent its responses will be, and the greater the cost to generate a useful response. This is why genAIs’ free tiers often have smaller context windows or allow fewer queries in a given time period.

141. Microsoft. “Understanding Tokens.” Microsoft Learn, May 20, 2024. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/ai/conceptual/understanding-tokens.

142. IBM Research. “Why Larger LLM Context Windows Are All the Rage.” IBM Research Blog, July 24, 2024. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://research.ibm.com/blog/larger-context-window.

GenAI chatbot context window sizes vary tremendously. For the four we use extensively—OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude and Perplexity—the context window sizes range from a low of 8,000 tokens for ChatGPT’s free version143 to a high of 1,000,000 tokens for Gemini’s paid version.144

143. ChatGPT response to “What’s your context window size?” February 15, 2025. https://chatgpt.com.

144. “Gemini Advanced.” Accessed February 18, 2025. https://gemini.google/advanced.

Prompts and Prompt Engineering

Prompt engineering is the process of designing prompts to obtain the best responses. Outside Chapter 19, many of the book’s sections end with Generative AI exercises in which we focus on prompt engineering to help you interact effectively with genAI tools. Think of this as learning a new and different type of programming language. With prompt engineering, you craft precise instructions or queries to guide genAIs in producing the required responses.

When you prompt genAIs, be sure to:

  • Include “Java” in your prompt when you ask genAIs to write Java code or answer questions about Java features. Also, ask them to write Java code using the latest Java idioms based on the Java version you’re using.

  • Keep track of your prompts and the quality of their results. This is crucial for learning what works and what doesn’t. This will also help you identify the nuances of different genAI platforms. You’ll build a repertoire of valuable prompts and anticipated results.

  • Experiment with multiple genAIs—including new ones as they appear—and compare the results to understand their varying capabilities.

  • Experiment with different prompting strategies to see which ones help you achieve your desired outcomes. Different programming challenges can require different prompting strategies.

  • Tune your prompt and try again if the genAIs’ results are not satisfactory. Better prompts produce better results. Some genAIs dig deeper into the subject matter.

When prompting some genAIs, pressing Enter (or Return) submits your prompt immediately. For others, you must explicitly press (or select) a button to submit the prompt. To move the cursor to a new line without submitting the prompt, use

Shift + Enter

or

Shift + Return

When we ask you to provide Java code to the genAIs as part of a prompt in Chapters 2 and higher, we recommend that you copy and paste the code from Java source-code files. Most genAIs also allow you to upload one or more files, but this is sometimes a feature provided only for paid subscribers.

It takes lots of experience to learn how to create great prompts. Various online guides to help you build better prompts, and you can even ask the genAIs themselves to tune your prompts. OpenAI provides a nice prompt engineering guide at

Click here to view code image

https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/prompt-engineering

and an extensive set of sample prompts at

Click here to view code image

https://platform.openai.com/docs/examples
Generative AI Anecdotes

During November and December of 2023, we would ask ChatGPT to perform tasks for which it previously generated detailed responses. Rather than detailed responses, it was lazy and provided steps telling us how to perform the tasks ourselves. Some researchers proposed the “winter break hypothesis,”145 speculating that ChatGPT learned to do less work at that time of year because people in the west tend to do less around the holiday season.

145. Edwards, Benj. “As ChatGPT gets “lazy,” people test “winter break hypothesis” as the cause." December 11, 2023. Accessed October 13, 2024. https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2023/12/is-chatgpt-becoming-lazier-because-its-december-people-run-tests-to-find-out/.

Though powerful, genAI chatbots sometimes make errors or even “hallucinate,”146 confidently presenting incorrect information as facts. As one example of an error, we asked several genAIs, “What do these Java statements output?” and fed them five simple statements that display the following three lines of asterisks:

****
*****
******

146. “Hallucination (artificial intelligence).” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallucination_(artificial_intelligence).

The typical genAI response was:

***************

or to display one asterisk per line vertically.

Around August 2024, someone discovered that asking ChatGPT’s voice mode, “How many R’s are in strawberry?” yielded the incorrect spoken response, “There are two R’s in strawberry.”147,148 Interestingly, entering the same question as a text prompt yielded the correct answer, “There are three R’s in strawberry.” On March 30, 2025, we repeated this experiment with ChatGPT’s voice mode, and it once again said, “There are two R’s in strawberry.” We said, “No. There are three R’s in strawberry.” The ChatGPT voice came back and said, “Let’s see: S-T-R-A-W-B-E-R-R-Y. You’re right, there are three R’s!”

147. Kit Eaton, “How Many R’s in Strawberry? This AI Can’t Tell You,” Inc., August 28, 2024. Accessed March 1, 2023. https://www.inc.com/kit-eaton/how-many-rs-in-strawberry-this-ai-cant-tell-you.html.

148. We tried this in March 2025, and ChatGPT voice mode still gives the wrong answer.

One example of hallucinating is that GenAIs have been known to make up court cases. You might research this with the following prompt, “Give me citations for court cases in which judges reprimanded lawyers for citing non-existent court cases generated by AIs.”

Another example of hallucinating comes from our experience in the early days of ChatGPT. We wanted to experiment with its ability to create text-based content. We asked it to write definitions of various computing terms and to provide four references for each—one of which we required to be Wikipedia. In general, it produced nice definitions and gave a direct link to the correct Wikipedia page. Without fail, however, the other three references we requested were completely fabricated—fake names, fake quotes, fake websites, and sometimes real websites but pages that did not exist. Though they are much better now than in their early days, you should always verify the information genAIs provide. Also, data on the Internet can have biases. When genAIs are trained, they might pick up those biases. We discuss these issues in Exercise 1.23 and in a section in Chapter 19.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Natural Language Understanding (NLU)149

149. Claude response to “Please write a paragraph explaining what natural language processing and natural language understanding are and how they’re fundamental to generative AI.” February 18, 2024. https://claude.ai. We edited the response.

Natural language processing (NLP) and natural language understanding (NLU) are two key technologies that enable genAIs to interact with human language. NLP focuses on how computers process and analyze human language—breaking down text into meaningful pieces like words, sentences and relationships between them.150 Think of NLP as the system that helps computers read and make sense of text, much like how you’re currently reading and processing these words.

150. The phrase “red brick factory” illustrates why natural language is such a challenging subject. Is a “red brick factory” a factory that makes red bricks? Is it a red factory that makes bricks of any color? Is it a factory built of red bricks that makes products of any type? In today’s music world, it could even be a rock band’s name or the name of a game on your smartphone.

NLU helps computers understand the meaning and context of language, not just the individual words. For example, when you ask a genAI, “What’s the weather like?” then ask, “Should I bring an umbrella?”, the genAI uses NLU to recognize that your second question is related to the weather and that you’re asking about rain protection.

NLP and NLU form the foundation for generative AI to understand your prompts and generate human-like responses. Without them, interacting with generative AI would be like trying to converse with someone who knows all the words in a language but doesn't understand how they fit together or what they actually mean.

1.15 Wrap-Up

This chapter introduced terminology and concepts that lay the groundwork for the Java programming capabilities you’ll learn throughout the book. We discussed Moore’s Law, noting that the steady stream of dramatic improvements it so accurately predicted for decades seems to be ending. As a result, hardware designers have shifted to multi-core architectures, which you’ll program with the multithreading techniques we discuss in Chapter 18, Concurrency: Platform Threads to Virtual Threads. We introduced Java and encouraged you to avoid reinventing the wheel when developing new software by using preexisting software components from the Java API and open-source Java libraries.

We briefly reviewed object orientation and the notions of classes, objects, interfaces, inheritance and polymorphism, providing the groundwork for the objects-natural case studies in Chapters 2–7 and 11 and our detailed treatment of object-oriented programming in Chapters 8–9.

We discussed a typical Java program-development environment in the context of the Java Development Kit (JDK) then used its tools to test-drive a Java program to prepare you to run the book’s example programs and original programs you’ll write. You can also run our programs with a Java integrated development environment (IDE)—we provide test-drives for several popular IDEs at https://deitel.com/javafp5.

We discussed the Internet, the web, the cloud and the Internet of Things (IoT). We introduced the Metaverse and key associated technologies—blockchain, cryptocurrencies, non-fungible tokens (NFTs), Web3, augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR) and mixed reality. We considered various software development technologies, including refactoring, design patterns, software development kits (SDKs), version control systems (VCS), agile software development, test-driven development (TDD), microservices and containerization.

We introduced big data analytics, then discussed big data and various data sizes, from megabytes to exabytes. Finally, we introduced artificial intelligence (AI)—an intersection between computer science and data science—presenting various AI milestones and brief overviews of several AI technologies, including artificial general intelligence (AGI), machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning and generative AI, which you’ll use throughout this book to leverage your Java learning experience. In this chapter’s end-of-chapter exercises, you’ll begin using generative AI to enhance your Java learning experience. In Chapter 2, you’ll begin programming in Java.

2.1 Introduction

 

This chapter introduces Java programming. We begin with simple programs that output messages on the screen. We then present a program that inputs (that is, reads) two numbers from a user, calculates their sum and displays the result. You’ll perform arithmetic calculations and save their results for later use. The last example demonstrates decision-making by comparing two numbers then displays messages showing the comparison results. Throughout the chapter, you’ll use generative AI to leverage your Java learning experience. You’ll use the JDK’s command-line tools to compile and run this chapter’s programs. If you prefer to use an integrated development environment (IDE), see our Test-Drives of popular IDEs at

https://deitel.com/javafp5
The “Objects-Natural” Learning Approach

In your programs throughout this book, you’ll create and use many objects of preexisting carefully developed and tested classes that enable you to perform significant tasks with minimal code, even in the book’s earliest chapters. These classes typically come from:

  • the Java Application Programming Interface (Java API), and

  • free third-party libraries created by the massive open-source communities that have developed around key programming languages.

To help you appreciate this programming style even in the book’s introductory chapters, you’ll conveniently create and use powerful objects of preexisting Java API classes without yet knowing how to create custom Java classes. We call this the objects-natural approach. In this chapter’s final example, you’ll begin by creating and using String objects. Then, in Chapters 8–9, you’ll craft valuable custom classes for your own use and for reuse by other programmers.

2.2 Your First Program in Java: Printing a Line of Text

 

Consider a simple program that displays a line of text. Figure 2.1 shows the program followed by a box that displays its output. We use line numbers for instructional purposes—they’re not part of the program. This example illustrates several important features. We’ll see that line 7 performs the program’s key action—displaying the text "Welcome to Java Programming!" on the screen.

Commenting Your Programs

We insert comments to document programs and improve their readability. The compiler ignores comments, so they do not cause the computer to perform any action when you run the program. By convention, we begin every program with a comment indicating the figure number and the program’s filename to help you find the file in the book’s examples folder (discussed in the Before You Begin section). The comment in line 1 indicates that you can find Welcome1.java in the examples/ch02/fig02_01 folder. This comment begins with //, indicating it’s an end-of-line comment that terminates at the end of the line. Such comments need not begin a line; they also can begin in the middle of a line and continue until the end (as in lines 5, 8 and 9). By our convention, line 2 is a comment describing the program’s purpose.

Java also has traditional comments that you can spread over several lines, as in

Click here to view code image

/* This is a traditional comment. It
   can be split over multiple lines */

These begin with the delimiter /* and end with */. The compiler ignores all text between the delimiters. Some organizations require programmers to start every source-code file with a multiline comment, including the program’s purpose, the programmer’s name, and the date and time the programmer last modified the program.

Javadoc Comments

A third comment type, called a Javadoc comment, is delimited by /** and */. The compiler ignores all text between the delimiters. Javadoc comments enable you to embed program documentation directly in your programs and are preferred in industry. The javadoc utility program1,2 (part of the JDK) reads Javadoc comments and uses them to prepare program documentation that’s viewed in a web browser. We use // comments throughout our code to save space.

1. “How to Write Doc Comments for the Javadoc Tool.” Accessed May 17, 2024. https://oracle.com/technical-resources/articles/java/javadoc-tool.html.

2. “The javadoc Command.” Accessed September 21, 2024. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/specs/man/javadoc.html.

Syntax Errors

Forgetting a comment delimiter is a syntax error—such errors occur when the compiler encounters code that violates Java’s language rules (that is, its syntax). These rules are similar to natural-language grammar rules specifying sentence structure, such as those in English, Spanish, Chinese, Hindi, etc. Syntax errors are also called compilation errors because they’re detected by the compiler. A program must compile without errors before you can execute it to perform its job.

Using Blank Lines

Blank lines (like line 3), space characters and tabs—known as whitespace—can make programs easier to read. The compiler ignores whitespace.

Declaring a Class

Line 4 begins class Welcome1’s class declaration. Every program consists of at least one class that you declare. The class keyword introduces a class declaration and is immediately followed by the class name (Welcome1). Keywords are reserved for use by Java. Each is spelled with all lowercase letters. Most classes we declare begin with the public keyword. You’ll learn more about public and non-public classes in Chapter 8. The following table shows the complete keywords list:

Filename for a public Class

A public class must be placed in a file with a filename of the form ClassName.java, so Welcome1 is stored in the file Welcome1.java. A compilation error occurs if a public class’s filename differs from the class name (in spelling or capitalization) followed by .java.

Class Names and Identifiers

By convention, every word in a class-name identifier begins with an uppercase letter. For example, the name DollarAmount starts its first word (Dollar) with an uppercase D and its second word (Amount) with an uppercase A. This naming convention is known as camel case because the uppercase letters stand out like a camel’s humps.

A class name is an identifier—a series of characters consisting of letters, digits, underscores (_) and dollar signs ($) that does not begin with a digit and does not contain spaces. Some valid identifiers are Welcome1, $value, _value, m_inputField1 and button7. The name 7button is invalid because it begins with a digit, and the name input field is invalid because it contains a space. Java is case sensitive—uppercase and lowercase letters are distinct—so value and Value are different valid identifiers.

Class Body

A left brace ({ at the end of line 4) begins the class declaration body. A corresponding right brace (} at line 9) must end each class declaration.

Lines 5–8 are indented. You should indent the entire body of each class declaration one “level” between the braces. This convention emphasizes the class’s structure and makes it easier to read. We use three spaces to form an indent level—many programmers prefer two or four spaces. Whatever you choose, use it consistently. IDEs typically indent code for you, using four-space indents by default. The Tab key may also be used to indent code. You can configure each IDE to specify the number of spaces inserted when you press Tab.

It’s a syntax error if braces do not occur in matching pairs. To prevent this error, when you enter an opening left brace ({), immediately enter the closing right brace (}). Then, put the cursor between the braces and indent to begin entering the body. In most IDEs, when you enter the opening left brace ({), the IDE adds the closing brace, moves the cursor between the braces and indents for you.

Declaring a Method

Line 6 is the starting point of every program. The parentheses after the identifier main indicate that it’s a program building block called a method. Class declarations normally contain one or more methods. One method must be called main and must be defined as in line 6; otherwise, the program will not execute.3

3. At the time of this writing, a preview feature called “instance main” simplifies line 6 to void main() {.

Methods perform tasks and can return information when they complete their tasks. We’ll explain the purpose of keyword static in Section 8.2.5. The void keyword indicates that this method will not return any information. Later, we’ll see methods that return information. For now, mimic main’s first line in your programs. Chapter 6 discusses the String[] args in parentheses.

The method’s left brace (end of line 6) begins the method body. A corresponding right brace (line 8) ends it. You should indent each method’s body one “level” between the braces, as in line 7. This emphasizes the method’s structure and makes it easier to read.

Performing Output with System.out.println

Line 7 displays the characters between the double quotation (") marks. The quotation marks are not displayed. Together, the quotation marks and the characters between them are called a string, a character string or a string literal. The compiler does not ignore whitespace characters in strings. Strings in double quotation (") marks may not span multiple lines of code.4

4. Later, we’ll discuss text blocks for forming multiline strings.

System.out is the standard output object, which is predefined for you. It allows programs to display text in the command window where you execute the program:

  • a Command Prompt or Windows PowerShell on Microsoft Windows, or

  • a terminal or a shell in Linux/macOS.

Many programmers call the command window simply the command line.

The System.out.println method displays a line of text. The string in the parentheses in line 7 is the method’s argument. When System.out.println completes its task, it moves the output cursor (the location where the next character will display) to the beginning of the next line. This is similar to pressing the Enter key while entering text in an editor—the cursor moves to the beginning of the next line in the document.

The entire line 7, including the semicolon (;), is called a statement. A method typically contains statements that perform its task. Most statements end with a semicolon.

Using End-of-Line Comments on Right Braces for Readability

For now, we include an end-of-line comment after a closing brace that ends a method declaration and after a closing brace that ends a class declaration. For example, line 8 indicates the closing brace of the main method, and line 9 indicates the closing brace of the Welcome1 class. We’ll omit such ending comments after this chapter.

System.out.println("*");
System.out.println("*****");
System.out.println("**");

Compare the results to the following output:

*
*****

2.2.1 Compiling the Program

You can now compile and execute the program. Here, we’ll use the Java Development Kit’s command-line tools. We assume the book’s examples are in your user account’s Documents folder in a subfolder named examples as discussed in the Before You Begin section.

Change to the Correct Folder

First, open a command window (see Section 1.7) and change to the folder where the program is stored. Operating systems typically use the command cd to change folders. On Windows, change to the fig02_01 folder by entering the following command and pressing the Enter (or Return) key:

Click here to view code image

cd %userprofile%\Documents\examples\ch02\fig02_01

On Linux/macOS, use the following command instead:

Click here to view code image

cd ~/Documents/examples/ch02/fig02_01
Compile the .java File

To compile the program, enter the following command and press Enter:

javac Welcome1.java

If the program does not contain compilation errors, this command creates Welcome1’s class file (Welcome1.class) containing the platform-independent bytecodes representing the program. When we use the java command to execute the program on a given platform, the JVM will translate these bytecodes into instructions understood by the underlying operating system and hardware.

Error Messages

When compiling, if you receive the error message “class Welcome1 is public, should be declared in a file named Welcome1.java,” either

  • your filename does not match the file’s public class name or

  • you misspelled the class name in the compilation command.

Sometimes, it’s helpful to “break” a working program to become familiar with the compiler’s error messages. Though error messages generally give you an idea of what caused them, they do not always state the exact problems in the code. Try removing a semicolon or brace from the program of Fig. 2.1, then recompiling to produce the error messages generated by the omission.

If the compiler reports a syntax error, it may not be on the line that the error message indicates. First, check the line reported in the error message. If you don’t find an error on that line, check several preceding lines. Each compilation error message contains the filename and line number where the error occurred. For example, Welcome1.java:6 would indicate that an error occurred at line 6 in Welcome1.java. The rest of the message would provide information about the error.

2.2.2 Executing the Program

Execute the Welcome1 program by entering the following command and pressing Enter:

java Welcome1

Notice that you do not include the.class filename extension when running the program. The JVM launches and loads the Welcome1.class file, then calls Welcome1’s main method. Next, line 7 in main displays

Welcome to Java Programming!

2.3 Modifying Your First Program

 

In this section, we modify Fig. 2.1’s example to print text on one line using multiple statements and to print text on several lines using one statement.

Displaying a Single Line of Text with Multiple Statements

Class Welcome2 (Fig. 2.2) uses two statements (lines 7–8) to produce the output in Fig. 2.1.

The program is similar to Fig. 2.1, so we discuss only the changes here. Line 2 is an end-of-line comment stating the purpose of the program. Line 4 begins the Welcome2 class declaration. Lines 7–8 in the main method display one line of text. The first statement uses the System.out.print method to display a string. Each print or println statement resumes displaying characters from where the last statement stopped. Unlike println, after displaying its argument, print does not position the output cursor at the beginning of the next line—the next character the program displays will appear immediately after the last character that print displays. So, line 8 positions the first character in its argument (the letter “J”) immediately after the last character that line 7 displays (the space character before the string’s closing double-quote character).

Displaying Multiple Lines of Text with a Single Statement

A single statement can display multiple lines using newline characters (\n), which position the output cursor at the beginning of the next line. The program in Fig. 2.3 outputs four lines of text. Most of the program is identical to those in Figs. 2.1 and 2.2.

Line 7 displays four lines of text. Normally, each character in a string displays as it appears in the double quotes. However, the paired characters \ and n (repeated three times in the statement) do not appear on the screen. The backslash (\) is an escape character, which has special meaning to System.out’s print and println methods. When a backslash appears in a string, it’s combined with the next character to form an escape sequence—the \n escape sequence represents the newline character. When \n is encountered in a string being output, the output cursor moves to the beginning of the next line.

The following table describes several escape sequences—for the complete list, refer to the Java Language Specification, Section 3.10.7, Escape Sequences:5

2.4 Displaying Text with printf

The System.out.printf method displays formatted data—the “f” in printf means “formatted.” Figure 2.4 uses printf to output "Welcome to" and "Java Programming!" on separate lines.

Line 7 calls System.out.printf to display the program’s output. The method call specifies three arguments. When a method requires two or more arguments, you place them in a comma-separated list with a space after each comma (,) for readability.

Method printf’s first argument is a format string that may consist of fixed text and format specifiers. Fixed text is output by printf just as it would be by print or println. Each format specifier is a placeholder for a value and specifies the type of data to output.

Format specifiers begin with a percent sign (%) followed by a character representing the data type. The %s format specifier is a placeholder for a string. The format string in line 7 specifies that printf should output two strings, each followed by a newline character. This example substitutes "Welcome to" for the first %s and "Java Programming!" for the second %s. The output shows that two lines of text are displayed.

Notice that instead of the newline escape sequence \n, which we’ve been using with System.out.print and System.out.println, we used the %n format specifier, which may appear only in format strings. In later chapters, we’ll present additional details of formatting output with printf, and Appendix B covers print formatting in more depth.

2.5 Another Program: Adding Integers

 

The program in Fig. 2.5 reads (or inputs) two integers (whole numbers, such as –22, 7, 0 and 1024) entered by a user, stores them in variables, computes their sum and displays it. In our program outputs, we use bold text to identify user inputs (45 and 72 in this example).

import Declarations

A great strength of Java is its rich set of predefined classes that you can reuse rather than “reinventing the wheel.” These classes are grouped into packages—named groups of related classes—collectively called the Java Application Programming Interface (Java API).

Line 3 is an import declaration that helps the compiler locate a class used in this program. It indicates that the program uses the predefined Scanner class (discussed shortly) from the java.util package. The compiler then ensures that you use the class correctly.

All import declarations must appear before you declare a class in the file. Placing an import declaration inside or after a class declaration is a syntax error. Forgetting to include an import declaration for a class that must be imported results in a compilation error containing a message such as “cannot find symbol.” When this occurs, check that you provided the proper import declarations and that the names in them are correct, including proper capitalization.

Declaring and Creating a Scanner to Obtain User Input

You must declare each variable with a name and a type before using it. A variable’s name enables the program to access the variable’s value in memory. By convention, variable-name identifiers use the camel-case naming convention with a lowercase first letter—for example, firstNumber. A variable name can be any valid identifier—again, a series of characters consisting of letters, digits, underscores (_) and dollar signs ($) that does not begin with a digit and does not contain spaces. A variable’s type specifies what kind of information is stored at that location in memory. Like other statements, declaration statements end with a semicolon (;).

Line 9 of main is a variable declaration statement that specifies the name (input) and type (Scanner) of a variable used in this program. A Scanner (package java.util) enables a program to read data (such as, numbers and strings) for use in a program. The data can come from many sources, such as the user or a file on disk. Before using a Scanner, you must create it and specify the source of the data.

The = in line 9’s declaration indicates that Scanner variable input should be initialized to prepare it for use in the program. The initial value is the result of the expression to the right of the equals sign—new Scanner(System.in). This expression uses the new keyword to create a Scanner object that reads characters entered by the user. The System.in standard input object enables programs to read bytes entered by the user. The Scanner translates these bytes into types (like int) the program can use.

Prompting the User for Input

Line 11 uses System.out.print to display "Enter first integer: ". This prompt message directs the user to take a specific action. We use print here rather than println so that the user’s input appears on the same line as the prompt—the space after the prompt’s colon (:) makes the program’s output more readable. Recall from Section 2.2 that identifiers starting with capital letters typically represent class names. The System class is part of the java.lang package, which Java automatically imports into every program. The java.lang classes are the only Java API classes that do not require an import declaration.

Declaring a Variable to Store an Integer and Obtaining One from the User

The variable declaration statement in line 12 declares that number1 holds data of type int—that is, integer (whole number) values, such as 72, –1127 and 0. The value range for an int is –2,147,483,648 to +2,147,483,647. A program’s int values may not contain commas because Java uses them to separate items in lists, such as the arguments to method System.out.printf in line 19 of this program. For readability, you can group digits with underscores as a digit separator—so 60_000_000 represents the value 60,000,000.

Types float and double hold real numbers, and type char holds character data. Real numbers contain decimal points, such as 3.4, 0.0 and –11.19. Variables of type char represent individual characters, such as

  • a letter (e.g., A or z),

  • a digit (0–9),

  • a special character (e.g., * or %) or

  • an escape sequence (e.g., \t for a tab or \n for a newline).

The types int, float, double and char are primitive types. Their names are keywords and must appear in all lowercase letters. The other primitive types are boolean, byte, short and long. For a summary of the numeric primitive types’ value ranges, visit the Java Language Specification Section 4.2, “Primitive Types and Values.”6

6. The Java Language Specification, Java SE 22 Edition. Section 4.2, “Primitive Types and Values” Accessed May 30, 2024. https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-4.html#jls-4.2.

The = in line 12 indicates that int variable number1 should be initialized in its declaration with the result of input.nextInt(). This uses the Scanner object input’s nextInt method to obtain an integer from the user. At this point, the program waits for the user to enter a number and press the Enter key to submit it to the program.

Our program assumes that the user enters a valid integer value. If not, a logic error will occur, and the program will terminate. Chapter 10, Exception Handling: A Deeper Look, discusses how to make your programs more robust by enabling them to handle such errors. This helps make your program fault-tolerant.

Obtaining a Second Integer

Line 14 prompts the user to enter the second integer. Line 15 declares the int variable number2 and initializes it with a second integer read from the user.

Using Variables in a Calculation

Line 17 declares the int variable sum and initializes it with the result of the calculation number1 + number2. The + operator is a binary operator because it has two operands—number1 and number2. Portions of statements that contain calculations are called expressions. In fact, an expression is any portion of a statement that has a value. The value of the expression number1 + number2 is their sum. Similarly, the value of the expression input.nextInt() (lines 12 and 15) is the integer entered by the user. Place spaces on either side of a binary operator for readability.

Displaying the Calculation Result

After the calculation has been performed, line 19 uses method System.out.printf to display sum’s value. The %d format specifier is a placeholder for an int value (sum)—the letter d stands for “decimal (base 10) integer.” The remaining characters in the format string are all fixed text. So, method printf displays "Sum is ", followed by sum’s value—which replaces %d—and a newline.

We could have combined lines 17 and 19 into the single statement

Click here to view code image

System.out.printf("Sum is %d%n", (number1 + number2));

The parentheses around the expression number1 + number2 are redundant—they’re included to emphasize that the value of the entire expression is output in the position of the %d format specifier.

Declaring and Initializing Variables in Separate Statements

Each variable must have a value before you use it in a calculation (or other expression). The variable declaration statement in line 12 declares number1 and initializes it with a value the user enters. Sometimes, you declare a variable in one statement then give it a value in another. For example, line 12 could have been written in two statements as

Click here to view code image

int number1; // declare the int variable number1
number1 = input.nextInt(); // assign the user's input to number1

The first statement declares number1 but does not initialize it. The second statement uses the assignment operator (=) to assign number1 the integer entered by the user. You can read this statement as “number1 gets the value of input.nextInt().” Everything to the right of the = is evaluated before the assignment stores the result.

2.6 Arithmetic

 

Many programs perform arithmetic calculations using the arithmetic operators summarized in the following table:

Note the use of various special symbols not used in algebra. The asterisk (*) indicates multiplication, and the percent sign (%) is the remainder operator, which we’ll discuss shortly. The arithmetic operators in the table are binary operators—each operates on two operands—e.g., the expression f + 7 contains the binary operator + and the two operands f and 7.

Integer Division

Integer division yields an integer quotient. For example, the expression 7 / 4 evaluates to 1, and the expression 17 / 5 evaluates to 3. Any fractional part in integer division is truncated (that is, discarded)—no rounding occurs.

Remainder Operator (%)

The remainder operator, %, yields the remainder after division—x % y yields the remainder after dividing x by y. Thus, 7 % 4 yields 3, and 17 % 5 yields 2. This operator is most commonly used with integer operands but also can be used with other arithmetic types. Popular uses of this operator are to determine whether an integer is even or odd, or whether one number is a multiple of another.

Arithmetic Expressions in Straight-Line Form

Arithmetic expressions must be written in straight-line form to facilitate entering programs into computers. Thus, expressions such as “a divided by b” must be written as a/b so all constants, variables and operators appear in a straight line. The following algebraic notation is generally not acceptable to compilers:

$\frac{a}{b}$

Parentheses for Grouping Subexpressions

Parentheses group terms in Java expressions in the same manner as in algebraic expressions. For example, to multiply a times the quantity b + c, we write

a * (b + c)

If an expression contains nested parentheses, such as

(a * (b + c))

the expression in the innermost set of parentheses—b + c in this case—evaluates first.

Rules of Operator Precedence

Java applies the arithmetic operators in a precise sequence determined by the rules of operator precedence, which are generally the same as those followed in algebra:

  1. Multiplication, division and remainder operations are applied first. If an expression contains several such operations, they’re applied from left to right. Multiplication, division and remainder operators have the same level of precedence.

  2. Addition and subtraction operations are applied next. If an expression contains several such operations, the operators are applied from left to right. Addition and subtraction operators have the same level of precedence.

  3. The assignment operator is applied last.

These rules enable Java to apply operators in the correct order.7 When we say operators are applied from left to right, we’re referring to their grouping. Some group from right to left. The following table summarizes these rules of operator precedence:

7. We use simple examples to explain the order of evaluation. Subtle order-of-evaluation issues can occur in more complex expressions. For more information, refer to Chapter 15 of The Java™ Language Specification (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-15.html).

2.7 Decision Making: Equality and Relational Operators

 

A condition is an expression that can be true or false. The if statement makes a decision based on a condition’s value. You form conditions in if statements using the equality operators (== and !=) and relational operators (>, <, >= and <=) summarized below:

Both equality operators have the same precedence level, which is lower than that of the relational operators. The equality operators group from left to right. The relational operators all have the same precedence level and also group from left to right.

Using the if Statement

Figure 2.6 uses six if statements to compare two integers input by the user. If the condition in any of these is true, the corresponding body statement executes; otherwise, it is skipped. We use a Scanner to input the integers from the user and store them in variables number1 and number2. The program compares the numbers with all six relational and equality operators and displays the results of the comparisons that are true. We show three sample outputs for different pairs of values entered by the user.

Line 10 in class Comparison’s main method sets up a Scanner for reading data from the user. Lines 12–13 prompt the user to enter the first integer, then input the value and store it in the int variable number1. Lines 15–16 prompt the user to enter the second integer, then input the value and store it in the int variable number2. Lines 18–20 compare the number1 and number2 values to determine whether they’re equal. If so, line 19 displays the numbers separated by ==. The if statements starting in lines 22, 26, 30, 34 and 38 compare number1 and number2 using the operators !=, <, >, <= and >=. For those if statements in which the conditions are true, the corresponding body statement displays an appropriate line of text showing the condition that evaluated to true.

Blocks

Each if statement in Fig. 2.6 contains one body statement that’s indented to enhance readability. IDEs typically do this indentation for you. Also, notice that we’ve enclosed each body statement in a pair of braces, { }, creating a block.

You don’t need to use braces around single-statement bodies, but you must include the braces around multiple-statement bodies. You’ll see later that forgetting to enclose multiple-statement bodies in braces leads to errors. To avoid such errors, always enclose an if statement’s body statement(s) in braces.

Placing a semicolon immediately after the right parenthesis after the condition in an if statement is often a logic error (although not a syntax error). The semicolon (;) acts as an empty statement (i.e., a statement that does nothing). In this case, the if statement performs no action, regardless of whether the condition is true. Worse yet, the indented statement that appears to be in the if statement’s body always executes—a logic error that typically causes the program to produce incorrect results.

Whitespace

Note the use of whitespace in Fig. 2.6. The compiler ignores most whitespace, so statements may be split over several lines and spaced according to your preferences without affecting a program’s meaning. Identifiers and strings may not be split. Ideally, statements should be kept small, but this is not always possible.

If you spread a statement over several lines, choose natural breaking points, such as after a comma in a comma-separated list or after an operator in a lengthy expression. When a statement is split across two or more lines, indent all lines after the first by the same amount until the end of the statement.

2.8 Objects-Natural Case Study: Creating and Using Objects of the Java API’s String Class

 

Throughout this book, we emphasize using valuable preexisting classes from the Java API and various libraries from the Java open-source community. You’ll focus on knowing what libraries are out there, choosing the ones you’ll need for your applications, creating objects from existing library classes and making those objects exercise their capabilities. By “objects natural,” we mean that you’ll be able to conveniently create and program with powerful objects even before you learn to create your own custom classes in Chapter 8.

You’ve already worked with Java objects. You used the System.out object to display a program’s output, and you used Scanner objects with the System.in object to obtain inputs from the user. These encapsulate the mechanisms for output and input. The System.out and System.in objects are created for you by the System class, and you created the Scanner objects with the new operator. In this section, you’ll create and interact with objects of the Java API’s String class.8

8. You’ll learn additional String capabilities in subsequent chapters. Chapter 7 discusses class String in detail, test-driving many more of its methods.

Test-Driving Class String

Classes cannot execute by themselves. A Person object can drive a Car object by telling it what to do (go faster, go slower, turn left, turn right, etc.) without knowing how the car’s internal mechanisms work. Similarly, the main method can “drive” String objects by calling their methods—without knowing how the class is implemented. In this sense, main in the following program is referred to as a driver program. Figure 2.7’s main method test-drives several String objects.

Creating String Objects

For each string literal, the Java compiler creates an object of the Java API’s String class and initializes it with the literal’s characters.9 So, lines 5–7 create three String objects: s1 contains "happy", s2 contains " birthday", and s3 contains the empty string (""). When we declare int variables, as we did earlier, the compiler knows what int is—it’s a primitive type built into Java. Similarly, the compiler understands aspects of the Java API’s String class, such as how to create a String object from a string literal.

9. For most classes, you must create objects of the class using new, as you did with class Scanner in Figs. 2.5 and 2.6.

Like the System class, the String class is part of the java.lang package, so it’s imported into every program. When packaged properly, classes can be reused by other programmers. This is one of the most significant benefits of working with languages like Java that support object-oriented programming. Such languages have rich libraries of powerful prebuilt classes. For example, you can reuse the Java API’s classes in any program simply by importing them, as we did with the Scanner class in Figs. 2.5 and 2.6.

String Method length

Lines 10–12 output each String and its length. The String class’s length method returns the number of characters stored in a particular String object. To call this method for a specific object, you specify the object’s name (s1), followed by the dot operator (.), then the method name (length) and a set of parentheses. Empty parentheses indicate that length does not require additional arguments to perform its task.

Comparing String Objects

Strings can be compared with one another for equality using the String class’s equals method, which returns true or false:10

  • Line 16 compares s1’s contents to the contents of the string literal "happy"—these Strings contain the same characters, so equals returns true.

  • Line 17 compares s2’s contents to s1’s contents—these Strings do not contain the same characters so equals returns false.

10. Note that operator == cannot be used to compare the contents of String objects. We’ll explain why in the object-oriented programming chapters.

String comparisons are case-sensitive.11 The printf calls in lines 16 and 17 use the %b format specifier, which is a placeholder for the value of a condition. This format specifier causes printf to display a condition’s value as the word "true" or the word "false".

11. In Chapter 7, you’ll see that Strings perform “lexicographical” comparisons using the numerical values of the characters in each String.

String Method isEmpty

Line 22 calls String’s isEmpty method, which returns true if the String is empty—i.e., its length is 0. The object s3 was initialized to the empty string (""), so it is indeed empty, and the body of the if statement will execute.

String Concatenation

Line 24 assigns a new value to s3 produced by “adding” the Strings s1 and s2 using the + operator—known as String concatenation. After the assignment, s3 contains the characters of s1 followed by the characters of s2—that is, "happy birthday". Line 25 outputs s3’s contents and length to demonstrate that the String concatenation worked correctly.

String Methods startsWith and endsWith

Lines 29–34 demonstrate String’s startsWith method and endsWith method, which return true if the String starts with or ends with a specified substring, respectively; otherwise, they return false. These String comparisons are also case-sensitive. Lines 30 and 32 show that s1 starts with the substring "ha", but s2 does not. Lines 33 and 34 show that s1 does not end with "ay" but s2 does.

In this chapter, you created basic Java programs. We started with programs that displayed messages on the screen using System.out’s print, println and printf methods. 3.1 Introduction

In this chapter and the next, we present the theory and principles of structured programming. As you’ll see in later chapters, the concepts presented here will be crucial in building classes and manipulating objects.

We discuss the if statement in more detail and introduce the if…else and while statements. We introduce the compound assignment operators and the increment and decrement operators. We also consider the portability of Java’s primitive types. Finally, we continue our objects-natural approach with a case study on creating and manipulating super-sized integers that can represent values beyond the limited integer ranges supported by Java’s integer primitive types.

3.2 Control Structures

Statements in a program typically execute one after the other in the order they’re written, as you saw in Chapter 2. This process is called sequential execution. Various Java statements enable you to specify that the next statement to execute is not necessarily the next one in sequence. This is called transfer of control.

During the 1960s, it became clear that the indiscriminate use of transfers of control was the root of much difficulty experienced by software development groups. The blame was pointed at the goto statement (used in most programming languages of the time), which allowed you to specify a transfer of control to one of a wide range of destinations in a program.1

1. Java does not have a goto statement; however, goto is reserved by Java and should not be used as an identifier in programs. Using it causes a compilation error.

The research of Bohm and Jacopini2 demonstrated that programs could be written without any goto statements. The challenge for the era’s programmers was to shift their styles to “goto-less programming.” The term structured programming became almost synonymous with “goto elimination.” Not until the 1970s did most programmers start taking structured programming seriously. The results were impressive. Software development groups reported shorter development times, more frequent on-time delivery of systems and more frequent within-budget completion of software projects. The key to these successes was that structured programs were clearer, easier to debug and modify, and more likely to be bug-free in the first place.

2. C. Bohm and G. Jacopini, “Flow Diagrams, Turing Machines, and Languages with Only Two Formation Rules,” Communications of the ACM, Vol. 9, No. 5, May 1966, pp. 366–371.

Bohm and Jacopini’s work demonstrated that all programs could be written in terms of only three control structures—the sequence structure, the selection structure and the iteration structure. When we introduce Java’s control-structure implementations, we’ll refer to them in the terminology of the Java Language Specification as “control statements.”

3.2.1 Sequence Structure

The sequence structure is built into Java. Unless directed otherwise, the computer executes Java statements one after the other in the order they’re written—that is, in sequence. The following UML activity diagram illustrates a typical sequence structure in which two calculations are performed in order:

Java lets you have as many actions as you want in sequence. As we’ll soon see, anywhere a single action may be placed, we may place several actions in sequence.

A UML activity diagram models the workflow (also called the activity) of a portion of a software system. Such workflows may include a portion of an algorithm, like the sequence structure above. Activity diagrams are composed of symbols, such as action-state symbols (rectangles with their left and right sides replaced with outward arcs), diamonds and small circles. These symbols are connected by transition arrows, which represent the flow of the activity—that is, the order in which the actions should occur.

Activity diagrams help you develop and represent algorithms. They clearly show how control structures operate. In Chapters 3 and 4, we use the UML to show each control statement’s workflow—also called its flow of control.

The preceding activity diagram includes two action states, each containing an action expression specifying a particular action to perform—“add grade to total” or “add 1 to counter.” Other actions might include calculations or input/output operations. The arrows represent transitions, indicating the order in which the actions described by the action states occur. The program that implements the preceding diagram’s activities first adds grade to total, then adds 1 to counter.

The solid circle at the top of the activity diagram represents the initial state—the beginning of the workflow before the program performs the modeled actions. The solid circle surrounded by a hollow circle at the bottom of the diagram represents the final state—the end of the workflow after the program performs the modeled actions.

The diagram also includes rectangles with the upper-right corners folded over. These optional UML notes (like comments in Java) are explanatory remarks describing the purpose of the diagram’s symbols. Our notes show the Java code associated with each action state. A dotted line connects each note with the element it describes. Activity diagrams usually do not show the corresponding Java code. We show it here to illustrate how the diagram relates to Java code. For more information on the UML, visit https://uml.org.

3.2.2 Selection Statements

Java has three types of selection statements (discussed in this chapter and Chapter 4). The if statement (Section 3.3) either performs (selects) an action if a condition is true or skips it if the condition is false. The if…else statement (Section 3.4) performs an action if a condition is true and performs a different action if the condition is false. The switch statement (Section 4.8) performs one of several actions depending on the value of an expression.

The if statement is called a single-selection statement because it selects or ignores a single action (or, as we’ll soon see, a single group of actions). The if…else statement is called a double-selection statement because it selects between two different actions (or groups of actions). The switch statement is called a multiple-selection statement because it selects among many different actions (or groups of actions).

3.2.3 Iteration Statements

Java provides four iteration statements—also called repetition or looping statements—for performing statements repeatedly while a loop-continuation condition is true. The iteration statements are while (Section 3.5), for (Section 4.3), do…while (Section 4.7), and enhanced for (Section 6.13). The while and for statements perform the action (or group of actions) in their bodies zero or more times—if the loop-continuation condition is initially false, the action (or group of actions) will not execute. The do…while statement performs the action (or group of actions) in its body one or more times.

Keywords

The words if, else, switch, while, do and for are Java keywords. We showed the complete list of Java keywords in Section 2.2. You can also find them in the Java Language Specification, Section 3.9, “Keywords.”3

3. The Java Language Specification, Java SE 22 Edition. Section 3.9, “Keywords.” Accessed May 21, 2024. https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-3.html#jls-3.9.

3.2.4 Summary of Control Statements

Java has only three kinds of control structures, which we refer to as control statements from this point forward:

  • the sequence statement,

  • selection statements (three types) and

  • iteration statements (four types).

We can model each control statement as an activity diagram containing initial and final states representing a control statement’s entry and exit points. Single-entry/single-exit control statements make it easy to build programs by connecting the exit point of one to the entry point of the next—that is, control-statement stacking. The only one other way in which control statements may be connected is control-statement nesting in which one control statement appears inside another.

3.3 if Single-Selection Statement

 

We briefly introduced if single-selection statement in Section 2.7. Programs use selection statements to choose among alternative courses of action. For example, suppose a passing grade on an exam is 60. The following if statement determines whether the condition grade >= 60 is true:

Click here to view code image

if (grade >= 60) {
   System.out.println("Passed");
}

If so, the statement prints "Passed"; otherwise, the condition is false, and the output statement is ignored and the next statement in sequence (if any) executes. Indenting the second line is optional but recommended for clarity.

boolean Primitive Type

In Section 2.7, you created conditions using the relational and equality operators. A Java condition must evaluate to true or false—each is a Java keyword. Java provides the boolean primitive type for variables that can store only true or false values.

UML Activity Diagram for an if Statement

The following diagram illustrates the single-selection if statement’s flow of control:

This figure contains an activity diagram’s most important symbol—the diamond, or decision symbol, which indicates a decision is to be made. The workflow continues along a path determined by the symbol’s associated guard conditions, which can be true or false. Each transition arrow emerging from a decision symbol has a guard condition specified in square brackets next to the arrow. If a guard condition is true, the workflow enters the action state to which the transition arrow points. In this diagram, if the grade is greater than or equal to 60, the program prints “Passed,” then transitions to the activity’s final state. If the grade is less than 60, the program transitions to the final state without printing a message. The if statement is a single-entry/single-exit control statement.

3.4 if…else Double-Selection Statement

 

The if single-selection statement performs an indicated action only when the condition is true. The if…else double-selection statement allows you to specify an action to perform when the condition is true and another action when the condition is false. For example, the following if…else statement prints "Passed" if the student’s grade is greater than or equal to 60; otherwise, it prints "Failed":

Click here to view code image

if (grade >= 60) {
   System.out.println("Passed");
}
else {
   System.out.println("Failed");
}

In either case, after printing occurs, the next statement in sequence (if any) executes. The if and else bodies are both indented equally. For readability, you should consistently apply your indentation convention throughout your programs. If there are several indentation levels, each should be indented with the same additional amount of space. We prefer three-space indents. IDEs typically auto-indent the code for you.

UML Activity Diagram for an if…else Statement

The following diagram illustrates the flow of control in the preceding if…else statement:

Once again, the UML activity diagram begins with the initial state, contains transition arrows, a decision and action states, and ends with a final state.

if (count > 10) {
   System.out.println("count is greater than 10");
}
else
   System.out.println("count is less than or equal to 10");

3.4.1 Nested if…else Statements

You can test multiple cases by placing if…else statements inside if…else statements to create nested if…else statements. The following nested if…else prints A for grades greater than or equal to 90, B for grades 80 to 89, C for grades 70 to 79, D for grades 60 to 69 and F for all other grades. We use shading to highlight the nesting:

Click here to view code image

 if (grade >= 90) {                         
    System.out.println("A");                
 }                                          
 else {                                     
    if (grade >= 80) {                      
       System.out.println("B");             
    }                                       
    else {                                  
       if (grade >= 70) {                   
          System.out.println("C");          
       }                                    
       else {                               
          if (grade >= 60) {                
             System.out.println("D");       
          }                                 
          else {                            
             System.out.println("F");       
          }                                 
       }                                    
    }                                       
 }

If grade is greater than or equal to 90, the first four conditions in the nested if…else statement are true. However, only the first if part’s statement executes—the else part of the “outermost” if…else statement is skipped.

Most programmers prefer to write the preceding nested if…else statement as

if (grade >= 90) {
   System.out.println("A");
}
else if (grade >= 80) {
   System.out.println("B");
}
else if (grade >= 70) {
   System.out.println("C");
}
else if (grade >= 60) {
   System.out.println("D");
}
else {
   System.out.println("F");
}

The latter form avoids deep indentation to the right, which often leaves little room on a line of source code, forcing lines to be split and making the code less readable. In a nested if…else statement, ensure that you test for all possible cases.

3.4.2 Blocks

The if statement expects only one statement in its body. To include several statements in an if’s or else’s body, you must enclose the statements in braces ({ and }). Recall from Section 2.7 that statements in braces form a block. You can place a block anywhere in a method where you can place a single statement. We always enclose control statement bodies in braces. This avoids a logic error called the “dangling-else” problem.

The following example includes a multi-statement block in an if…else statement’s else part:

Click here to view code image

if (grade >= 60) {
   System.out.println("Passed");
}
else {
   System.out.println("Failed");
   System.out.println("You must take this course again");
}

If grade is less than 60, both statements in the else’s body execute, displaying:

Click here to view code image

Failed
You must take this course again

The braces surrounding the two statements in the else clause are important. Without the braces, the statement

Click here to view code image

System.out.println("You must take this course again");

would be outside the else’s body and "You must take this course again" would print even for passing grades—a logic error.

Syntax Errors and Logic Errors

The compiler catches syntax errors, such as when one brace in a block is left out of the program. A logic error, such as an incorrect calculation, has its effect at execution time. A fatal logic error causes a program to fail and terminate prematurely. A nonfatal logic error allows a program to continue executing but causes it to produce incorrect results.

Empty Statement

Just as a block can be placed anywhere a single statement can be placed, it’s also possible to have an empty statement. Recall from Section 2.7 that the empty statement is represented by placing a semicolon (;) where a statement would normally be.

Placing a semicolon after the condition in an if or if…else statement leads to a logic error in single-selection if statements and a syntax error in double-selection if…else statements (when the if-part contains an actual body statement).

3.4.3 Conditional Operator (?:)

The conditional operator (?:) can be used in place of simple if…else statements. The conditional operator is the only ternary operator—it takes three operands. Together, the operands and the ?: symbol form a conditional expression. For example, the following statement prints the value of println’s conditional-expression argument:

Click here to view code image

System.out.println(grade >= 60 ? "Passed" : "Failed");

  • The operand to the left of the question mark (?)—grade >= 60—is a condition that evaluates to true or false.

  • The operand between the question mark (?) and the colon (:)—"Passed"—is the conditional expression’s value if the condition is true.

  • The operand after the colon (:)—"Failed"—is the conditional expression’s value if the condition is false.

The conditional expression in this statement evaluates to "Passed" if grade >= 60 is true or "Failed" if it’s false. Thus, this statement with the conditional operator is essentially the same as the if…else statement shown at the beginning of Section 3.4. The conditional operator’s precedence is low, so it’s usually placed in parentheses.

1 Prompt genAIs to write a single System.out.printf statement that determines whether the int variable number’s value is odd or even and prints the result. Tell the genAIs to assume number exists and contains 7. Compare their generated code to the following statement and confirm their code produces the same result:

Click here to view code image

System.out.printf("%d is %s%n",
   number, number % 2 == 0 ? "even" : "odd");
7 is odd

3.5 while Iteration Statement

 

An iteration statement specifies that a program should repeat an action while some condition remains true. Consider a program segment that uses the while iteration statement to find the first power of 3 larger than 50. After this code executes, product contains the result:

int product = 3;
while (product <= 50) {
   product = 3 * product;
}

First, we initialize product to 3. Then, the while statement executes as follows:

  1. The program tests the condition product <= 50, which is true because product is 3. The body statement multiplies product by 3 and assigns the result (9) to product. The loop’s first iteration is now complete.

  2. The program tests the condition again—it’s true because product is now 9. The body sets product to 27. The loop’s second iteration is now complete.

  3. The program tests the condition again—it’s true because product is now 27. The body sets product to 81. The loop’s third iteration is now complete.

  4. The program tests the condition again—it’s finally false because product is now 81, which is not less than or equal to 50, so the loop terminates.

Variable product now contains 81—the first power of 3 greater than 50. The while statement’s body may be a single statement or a block.

UML Activity Diagram for a while Statement

The following UML activity diagram illustrates the preceding while’s flow of control:

This diagram introduces the UML’s merge symbol. The UML represents both the merge symbol and the decision symbol as diamonds. The merge symbol joins two flows of activity into one. In this diagram, the merge symbol joins the transitions from the initial state and from the action state, so they both flow into the decision that determines whether the loop should begin (or continue) executing.

The decision and merge symbols can be distinguished by the number of “incoming” and “outgoing” transition arrows:

  • A decision symbol has one transition arrow pointing to the diamond and two or more pointing from it to indicate possible transitions. Each transition arrow pointing from a decision symbol has a guard condition next to it.

  • A merge symbol has two or more transition arrows pointing to the diamond and only one pointing from it to indicate multiple activity flows merging to continue the activity. A merge’s transition arrows do not have guard conditions.

The diagram clearly shows the while statement’s iteration. The transition arrow emerging from the action state points back to the merge, from which program flow transitions back to the decision tested at the beginning of each iteration. The while statement executes until the guard condition “product <= 50” becomes false, and thus the guard condition “product > 50” becomes true. Then, the while statement reaches its final state, and the program continues with the next statement in sequence.

3.6 Counter-Controlled Iteration

Let’s solve two variations of a problem that averages student grades. Consider the following problem statement:

A class of ten students took a quiz. The grades (integers in the range 0–100) for this quiz are available to you. Determine the class average on the quiz.

The class average is the sum of the grades divided by the number of students. The program for solving this problem must input each grade, keep track of the total of all grades input, perform the averaging calculation and print the result. We use counter-controlled iteration to input the grades one at a time. This technique uses a variable called a counter (or control variable) to control the number of times statements will execute. Counter-controlled iteration is also called definite iteration because the number of iterations is known before the loop executes. In this example, iteration terminates when the counter exceeds 10. This section presents the Java program (Fig. 3.1) to implement the algorithm.

3.6.1 Implementing the Algorithm

In Fig. 3.1, class ClassAverage’s main method allows the user to enter 10 grades, then calculates and displays the average.

Local Variables in Method main

Line 8 declares and initializes Scanner variable input, which is used to read values entered by the user. Lines 11, 12, 17 and 23 declare the local int variables total, gradeCounter, grade and average. Variable grade stores the user input.

These declarations appear in main’s body. Variables declared in a method body are local variables. They can be used only from the line of their declaration to the method’s closing right brace. A local variable’s declaration must appear before the variable is used in that method. A local variable cannot be accessed outside the method in which it’s declared. Variable grade, declared in the while loop’s body, can be used only in that block.

Initialization Phase: Initializing Variables total and gradeCounter

The assignments (in lines 11–12) initialize total to 0 and gradeCounter to 1. These initializations occur before the variables are used in calculations.

All local variables must be initialized before their values are used in expressions; otherwise, compilation errors occur. Totals are generally initialized to 0. Counters are generally initialized to 0 or 1, depending on how they’re used. Throughout the book, we’ll show examples of when to use 0 and when to use 1.

Processing Phase: Reading 10 Grades from the User

Line 15 indicates that the while statement should continue looping (also called iterating) as long as gradeCounter’s value is less than or equal to 10. While this condition remains true, the while statement repeatedly executes the statements in lines 16–19:

  • Line 16 displays the prompt "Enter grade: ".

  • Line 17 reads the grade entered by the user and assigns it to variable grade.

  • Line 18 adds the new grade into the total, replacing its previous value.

  • Line 19 adds 1 to gradeCounter (replacing its previous value) to indicate that the program processed a grade and is ready to input the next grade from the user.

Incrementing gradeCounter eventually causes it to exceed 10. Then, the loop terminates because its condition (line 15) becomes false.

Termination Phase: Calculating and Displaying the Class Average

When the loop terminates:

  • Line 23 calculates the average and assigns the result to the variable average.

  • Line 26 uses System.out’s printf method to display the text "Total of all 10 grades is " followed by total’s value.

  • Line 27 uses printf to display the text "Class average is " followed by the average’s value.

When execution reaches line 28, the program terminates.

3.6.2 Integer Division and Truncation

Line 23’s averaging calculation produces an integer result. In the sample output, the sum of the grades is 846, which, when divided by 10, should yield 84.6. This is a floating-point number—a number with a decimal point. In line 23, however, the result of total / 10 is the integer 84 because total and 10 are both integers. Dividing two integers results in integer division—any fractional part of the calculation is truncated (i.e., lost). In the next section, we’ll see how to obtain a floating-point result from the averaging calculation. Assuming that integer division rounds (rather than truncates) can lead to incorrect results.

3.6.3 Arithmetic Overflow

In Fig. 3.1, line 18 adds each grade entered by the user to the total:

Click here to view code image

total = total + grade; // add grade to total

Even this simple statement has a potential problem—adding the integers could result in a value too large to store in an int variable. This is known as arithmetic overflow and causes undefined behavior, which can lead to unintended results.4 Figure 2.5’s Addition program had the same issue in line 17, which calculated the sum of two int values entered by the user:

4. “Integer Overflow.” Wikipedia, last modified May 18, 2024. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_overflow#Security_ramifications. [Discusses potential problems associated with integer overflow.]

Click here to view code image

int sum = number1 + number2; // add numbers, then store total in sum

The constants Integer.MIN_VALUE and Integer.MAX_VALUE represent the minimum and maximum values an int variable can store. There are similar constants for the other numeric primitive types. You can find the values of these constants in each class’s online documentation. Integer’s documentation is located at:

Click here to view code image

https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/
   lang/Integer.html

3.6.4 Input Validation

Whenever a program receives input from the user, various problems might occur. For example, line 17 of Fig. 3.1

Click here to view code image

int grade = input.nextInt(); // input next grade

assumes the user will enter an integer grade in the range 0 to 100, but the user could enter:

  • an integer less than 0,

  • an integer greater than 100,

  • an integer outside the range of values that can be stored in an int variable,

  • a number containing a decimal point or

  • a value containing letters or special symbols that do not even represent a number.

Industrial-strength programs must test for all possible erroneous cases to ensure valid inputs. A program that inputs grades should validate them using range checking to ensure they are values from 0 to 100. You can then ask the user to re-enter any out-of-range value. If a program requires inputs from a specific set of values (such as non-sequential product codes), you should ensure that each input matches a value in the set.
