3.7 Sentinel-Controlled Iteration

Let’s generalize Section 3.6’s class-average problem. Consider the following problem:

Develop a class-averaging program that processes grades for an arbitrary number of students each time it is run.

In the previous class-average example, the number of grades (10) was known in advance. For this problem, we do not know how many grades the user will enter during the program’s execution. The program must process an arbitrary number of grades.

One way to solve this problem is to use a sentinel value (also called a signal value or a flag value) indicating the end of data entry. After entering all the legitimate grades, the user enters the sentinel value to indicate that no more grades will be entered.

You must choose a sentinel value that cannot be confused with an acceptable input value. Grades on a quiz are nonnegative integers, so –1 is an acceptable sentinel value for this problem. Thus, a run of the class-averaging program might process a stream of inputs such as 95, 96, 75, 74, 89 and –1. The program would then compute and print the class average for the five grades, excluding –1, because it’s the sentinel value and should not enter into the averaging calculation.

3.7.1 Implementing Sentinel-Controlled Iteration

Figure 3.2 implements sentinel-controlled iteration. Much of Fig. 3.2 is identical to Fig. 3.1, so we concentrate on the new content here. Although each grade the user enters is an integer, the average calculation will likely produce a floating-point number like 84.6, which an int cannot represent. You store floating-point numbers using the types float and double:

  • Variables of the float primitive type represent single-precision floating-point numbers. They have up to seven significant digits to the right of the decimal point.

  • Variables of the double primitive type represent double-precision floating-point numbers. These require twice as much memory as float variables. They have up to 15 significant digits—about twice a float variable’s precision.

Most programmers use type double because all floating-point numbers in a program’s source code, such as 7.33 and 0.0975, are represented as type double by default. Such values are known as floating-point literals. For the precise ranges of Java’s floating-point types, visit the Java Language Specification Section 4.2, “Primitive Types and Values.”5

5. The Java Language Specification, Java SE 22 Edition. “4.2. Primitive Types and Values.” Accessed May 21, 2024. https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-4.html#jls-4.2.

Program Logic for Sentinel-Controlled Iteration vs. Counter-Controlled Iteration

Line 12 initializes gradeCounter to 0 because no grades have been entered yet. Remember that we’re using sentinel-controlled iteration to input the grades, so we increment the variable gradeCounter only when the user enters a valid grade. Line 33 declares the double variable average, which stores the class average as a floating-point number.

Compare this program’s logic for sentinel-controlled iteration with Fig. 3.1’s counter-controlled iteration:

  • In counter-controlled iteration, each loop iteration (lines 15–20 of Fig. 3.1) reads a value from the user for the specified number of iterations.

  • In sentinel-controlled iteration, lines 16–17 of Fig. 3.2 prompt for and input the first value before reaching the while. This value determines whether the flow of control should enter the while’s body. If the condition is false, the user entered the sentinel value—no grades were entered, so the while’s body does not execute. If the condition is true, the body adds the grade to the total and increments the gradeCounter. Then, lines 25–26 prompt for and input the next grade. At this point, program control reaches the loop’s closing right brace (line 27). Execution continues by testing the while’s condition (line 20), using the most recently entered grade to determine whether the loop body should execute again.

Notice that the next grade is always input from the user immediately before the program tests the while statement’s condition. This allows the program to determine whether the value just input is the sentinel value before processing it (i.e., adding it to the total). If grade contains the sentinel value, the loop terminates without adding –1 to the total. In a sentinel-controlled loop, prompts should remind the user of the sentinel.

After the loop terminates, the if…else statement in lines 31–42 executes. The condition (line 31) determines whether any grades were input. If none were input, the else part displays "No grades were entered". After the if…else executes, the program terminates.

3.7.2 Explicitly and Implicitly Converting Between Primitive Types

If at least one grade was entered, line 33 calculates the average of the grades. Recall from Fig. 3.1 that integer division yields an integer result. Even though variable average is declared as a double, if we had written the averaging calculation as

Click here to view code image

double average = total / gradeCounter;

it would lose the fractional part of the quotient before the result is assigned to average. This occurs because total and gradeCounter are both integers, and integer division yields an integer result.

Most averages are floating-point numbers. To perform a floating-point calculation with integer values, we must temporarily treat these values as floating-point numbers. The unary cast operator accomplishes this task. Line 33 of Fig. 3.2 uses the (double) cast operator to create a temporary floating-point copy of its operand total (which appears to the operator’s right). Using a cast operator in this manner is called explicit conversion or type casting. The value stored in total is still an integer.

The calculation now consists of a floating-point value (the temporary double copy of total) divided by the integer gradeCounter. In mixed-type arithmetic expressions, Java performs an operation called promotion (or implicit conversion) on selected operands. In an arithmetic expression containing int and double values, copies of the int values are promoted to double values for use in the expression. In this example, gradeCounter’s value is promoted to type double, then floating-point division is performed, and the calculation’s result is assigned to average. Later in this chapter, we discuss all the primitive types. You’ll learn more about the promotion rules in Section 5.11.

3.7.3 Formatting Floating-Point Numbers

Lines 36–37 display gradeCounter’s and total’s values. Line 38 displays the double variable average’s value. Method printf uses the %f format specifier to format floating-point numbers. By default, %f formats doubles with six digits of precision to the right of the decimal point, but you can specify a custom precision between the % and the f. The average of the three grades in the sample execution was 85.666666…, with the sequence of 6s repeating infinitely. In the format specifier %.2f, the .2 is the custom precision. This rounds the average to the hundredths position, producing 85.67 with 2 digits to the right of the decimal point.

A Note Regarding Floating-Point Number Precision

Floating-point numbers are not always 100% precise, but they have numerous applications. For example, when we speak of a “normal” body temperature of 98.6 °F, we do not need to be precise to many digits. When we read the temperature on a thermometer as 98.6, it may actually be 98.5999473210643. Calling this number simply 98.6 is fine for most applications involving body temperatures.

Floating-point numbers often arise from division, as in this example’s class-average calculation. In conventional arithmetic, when we divide 10 by 3, the result is 3.3333333…, with the 3s repeating infinitely. The computer allocates only a fixed amount of space to hold such a value, so the stored floating-point value can be only an approximation.

Due to the imprecise nature of floating-point numbers, type double is preferred to float because double variables can represent floating-point numbers more accurately. So, we primarily use type double throughout the book. Assuming floating-point numbers are represented precisely can lead to incorrect results. In some cases, the precision of float and double variables will be inadequate. For precise floating-point numbers (such as those required by monetary calculations), Java provides class BigDecimal (package java.math), which we’ll discuss in Section 4.11’s Objects-Natural Case Study.

3.8 Nested Control Statements

We’ve seen that control statements can be stacked on top of one another (in sequence). In this case study, we examine the only other structured way control statements can be connected—namely, by nesting one control statement within another.

3.8.1 Problem Statement

Consider the following problem statement:

A college offers a course that prepares students for the state licensing exam for real-estate brokers. Last year, ten of the students who completed this course took the exam. The college wants to know how well its students did on the exam. You’ve been asked to write a program to summarize the results.

You’ve been given a list of these 10 students. Next to each name is written a 1 if the student passed the exam or a 2 if the student failed.

Your program should analyze the results of the exam as follows:

  1. Input each test result (i.e., a 1 or a 2). Display “Enter result” each time the program requests another test result.

  2. Count the number of test results of each type.

  3. Display a summary of the test results, indicating the number of students who passed and the number who failed.

  4. If more than eight students passed, print “Bonus to instructor!”

Problem Statement Observations

After reading the problem statement carefully, we make the following observations:

  • The program must process test results for 10 students. A counter-controlled loop can be used because the number of test results is known in advance.

  • Each test result is either a 1 or a 2. As the program reads each result, it must determine whether it’s a 1 or a 2. We test for a 1 in our algorithm. If the number is not a 1, we assume it’s a 2.

  • Two counters are used to keep track of the exam results—one to count the number of students who passed the exam and one to count the number who failed.

  • After the program has processed all the results, it must decide whether more than eight students passed the exam.

3.8.2 Implementing the Program

Figure 3.3 implements the program with counter-controlled iteration and shows two sample executions. Lines 11–13 and 19 declare the variables we use to process the examination results. Initializing local variables when they’re declared helps you avoid compilation errors from attempts to use uninitialized variables. While Java does not require that local-variable initializations be incorporated into declarations, it does require that local variables have values before they’re used in an expression; otherwise, compilation errors occur.

The while statement (lines 16–31) loops 10 times. During each iteration, it inputs and processes one exam result. The if…else statement (lines 22–27) for processing each result is nested in the while statement. If the result is 1, the if…else statement increments passes; otherwise, it assumes the result is 2 and increments failures. Line 30 increments studentCounter before the loop condition is tested again at line 16. After 10 values have been input, the loop terminates, and line 34 displays the number of passes and failures. The if statement at lines 37–39 determines whether more than eight students passed the exam and, if so, outputs the message "Bonus to instructor!".

Figure 3.3 shows the input and output from two sample executions of the program. During the first, the condition at line 37 is true—more than eight students passed the exam, so the program outputs a message to bonus the instructor.

3.9 Compound Assignment Operators

The compound assignment operators enable you to abbreviate assignment expressions. You can abbreviate the statement

c = c + 3; // adds 3 to c

with the addition compound assignment operator, +=, as

Click here to view code image

c += 3; // adds 3 to c more concisely

The += operator adds its right operand’s value to the left-side variable’s value then stores the result in the left-side variable. Thus, the assignment expression c+=3 adds 3 to c. Compound assignment operators perform an implicit conversion on the right-hand expression’s value to match the type of the variable on the operator’s left side. So, if the left-side variable is an int and the right-side expression results in a double, the double value’s floating-point part will be truncated.6 The following table shows the arithmetic compound assignment operators, sample expressions and explanations of what the operators do:

6. The Java Language Specification, Java SE 22 Edition. Section 15.26.2, “Compound Assignment Operators.” Accessed August 28, 2024. https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-15.html#jls-15.26.2.

y += 3.3;

Confirm that the genAIs indicate y is 8. You might expect a compilation error from the assignment statement. Compound assignment operators implicitly convert the right-hand expression’s value to match the type of the variable on the operator’s left side. So, 3.3 is truncated to 3.

3.10 Increment and Decrement Operators

 

The following table summarizes the unary operators for adding 1 to or subtracting 1 from the value of a numeric variable—these are the unary increment operator, ++, and the unary decrement operator, --. Unlike binary operators, the unary increment and decrement operators, by convention, should be placed next to their operands with no intervening spaces:

Prefix Increment vs. Postfix Increment

Figure 3.4 demonstrates the difference between the prefix increment and postfix increment versions of the ++ increment operator. The decrement operator (--) works similarly.

Line 7 initializes the variable c to 5, and line 8 outputs c’s initial value. Line 9 outputs the value of the expression c++. This expression postincrements the variable c, so the statement outputs c’s original value (5) again, then c’s value is incremented (to 6). Line 10 outputs c’s new value (6) to prove that the variable’s value was indeed incremented in line 9.

Line 15 resets c’s value to 5, and line 16 outputs c’s value. Line 17 outputs the value of the expression ++c, which preincrements c, so the statement outputs c’s new value (6). Line 18 outputs c’s value again to show that the value of c is still 6 after line 17 executes.

Simplifying Increment Statements

The arithmetic compound assignment operators and the increment and decrement operators can be used to simplify program statements. For example, the three assignment statements in Fig. 3.3 (lines 23, 26 and 30)

Click here to view code image

passes = passes + 1;
failures = failures + 1;
studentCounter = studentCounter + 1;

can be written more concisely with compound assignment operators as

passes += 1;
failures += 1;
studentCounter += 1;

with prefix increment operators as

++passes;
++failures;
++studentCounter;

or with postfix increment operators as

passes++;
failures++;
studentCounter++;

When incrementing or decrementing a variable in a statement by itself, the prefix increment and postfix increment forms have the same effect, and the prefix decrement and postfix decrement forms have the same effect. It’s only when a variable appears in the context of a larger expression that preincrementing and postincrementing the variable have different effects (and similarly for predecrementing and postdecrementing).

3.11 Primitive Types

Java requires all variables to have a type.7 In C and C++, programmers frequently have to write separate versions of programs to support different computer platforms because the primitive types are not guaranteed to be identical among computers. For example, an int on one machine might be represented by 16 bits (2 bytes) of memory, on another machine by 32 bits (4 bytes), and on another by 64 bits (8 bytes). In Java, int values are always 32 bits (4 bytes). The eight primitive types in Java—boolean, byte, char, double, float, int, long and short—are portable across all computer platforms that support Java. For a summary of these types’ value ranges, visit the Java Language Specification Section 4.2, Primitive Types and Values.8 Because the designers of Java want to ensure portability, they use internationally recognized standards for character formats (Unicode; https://unicode.org) and floating-point numbers (IEEE 754; https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/754/6210/).

7. We’ll see an exception to this with lambdas in Chapter 14, Functional Programming with Lambdas & Streams.

3.12 Objects-Natural Case Study: Super-Sized Integers

 

The explosive growth of Internet communications and data storage on Internet-connected devices has dramatically increased the importance of privacy and security. Cryptography has been used for thousands of years to encode data, making it difficult (and hopefully impossible) for unauthorized users to read,9,10 which is critically important in today’s connected world. Most websites (including deitel.com) use HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) to encrypt and decrypt your Internet interactions.

9. “Cryptography.” Accessed June 1, 2024. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptography#History.

10. Binance Academy, “History of Cryptography.” Accessed June 1, 2024. https://www.binance.vision/security/history-of-cryptography.

Some Applications Need Integers Outside a long Integer’s Range

Java’s primitive type long can store values in the range –9,223,372,036,854,775,808 to 9,223,372,036,854,775,807—a maximum of 19 decimal digits, which can represent integers in the low quintillions. Many cryptography algorithms perform calculations with integers far larger than we can store in a long.

One of the most popular encryption/decryption schemes is RSA Public-Key Cryptography, commonly used to secure data transmitted over the Internet.11,12,13 Industrial-strength RSA implementations work with enormous prime numbers consisting of hundreds of digits, far more than primitive type long can hold.

11. “RSA (Cryptosystem).” Accessed June 1, 2024. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem).

12. “RSA Algorithm.” Accessed June 1, 2024. https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_algorithm.

13. K. Moriarty, B. Kaliski, J. Jonsson and A. Rusch, “PKCS #1: RSA Cryptography Specifications Version 2.2,” November 2016. Accessed June 1, 2024. https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8017.

A key reason RSA is so secure is the sheer amount of time required to factor the product of those primes, even for today’s most powerful supercomputers. Public-key cryptography is also used to secure the blockchain technology behind cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin.14 Later in the book, we’ll discuss public-key cryptography.

14. Sarah Rothrie, “How Blockchain Cryptography Is Fighting the Rise of Quantum Machines,” December 28, 2018. Accessed June 1, 2024. https://coincentral.com/blockchain-cryptography-quantum-machines/.

Integers Outside long’s Range Require Custom Programming

So, how can we manipulate huge integers with arbitrary numbers of digits? Applications requiring integers outside long’s range require custom programming. We could use the Java class mechanism (mentioned in Section 1.4 and covered in detail in Chapter 8) to develop a custom class that handles huge-integer arithmetic—but that could take months of effort. The objects-natural approach encourages us to check first for classes in the Java API or in free, open-source class libraries to determine if such a “huge-integer” class already exists.

Huge Integers with the Java API’s java.math.BigInteger Class

There are preexisting classes for creating and manipulating huge integers. For this example, we’ll demonstrate the BigInteger class from the Java API’s java.math package:

   math/BigInteger.html

15. If you drive a car, you use it effectively without having to understand how car engines, steering, brakes and transmission systems work internally. After you get deeper into Java, you might want to study BigInteger’s source code (approximately 5,000 lines, including extensive Javadoc comments) to learn how it’s implemented. You might say, “I insist on knowing how everything I use in Java is implemented.” Reflect for a moment on the fact that you’re using a Java compiler to translate your Java programs into the bytecodes that the Java Virtual Machine then translates into your computer’s machine language. Do you know how the compiler is implemented? Are you sure that it correctly translates each of your Java programs so they’ll run properly and produce correct results?

Largest Value of a long

Line 9 displays Long.MAX_VALUE—a constant representing the maximum value a long variable can store (9,223,372,036,854,775,807). As you’ll see, each BigInteger calculation in this example results in a value greater than Long.MAX_VALUE. Each primitive type (e.g., long) has a corresponding class (e.g., the Long class) in the java.lang package. These classes provide the constants MIN_VALUE and MAX_VALUE, representing the smallest and largest values the corresponding primitive types can store.

Initializing a BigInteger with a String

If a BigInteger’s initial value exceeds the maximum integer value Java supports, you can initialize a new BigInteger object with a string representing the integer value, as we did with the 30-digit integer in lines 12–13.

Initializing a BigInteger with an Integer

Lines 14–15 ask the BigInteger class to create new BigInteger objects and initialize them with primitive-type integer values. Classes provide methods to perform tasks. Each method we’ve used so far was called on an object. For example, to display text, Fig. 3.5 calls the printf and println methods on the System.out object. Some classes provide methods you call directly on the class rather than on an object of the class. These are called static methods. You call a static method by specifying the class name followed by a dot (.) separator and the method name, as in

ClassName.methodName(arguments)

Class BigDecimal’s static valueOf method creates and returns a new BigInteger object initialized with valueOf’s primitive-type integer argument:

  • Line 14 initializes value2 with a BigInteger containing a long’s maximum value. The L (“el”) suffix at the end of 9_223_372_036_854_775_807L indicates that the value is a long integer. Without the L, the Java compiler treats whole numbers in code as int values—in this case, line 14 would cause a compilation error because this value is much larger than an int’s maximum positive value (2,147,483,647).17

    17. We could have used Long.MAX_VALUE in line 14 rather than 9_223_372_036_854_775_807L.

  • Line 15 initializes value3 with a BigInteger containing the int value 17.

Lines 18–20 display the initial values of the BigIntegers value1, value2 and value3.

How Does printf’s String Specifier %s Understand a BigInteger Object?

Every Java primitive-type value and object has a string representation. When you format any value or object using printf with the %s specifier, Java converts that value or object to a string. For an object, Java does this by calling the object’s toString method, which we’ll discuss in later chapters. The toString method is also called when you display an object with System.out’s print and println methods.

Performing BigInteger Arithmetic

Class BigInteger provides various methods for common arithmetic operations. Lines 23–30 demonstrate the BigInteger methods add, subtract and multiply. BigInteger correctly handles integers of any number of digits. Each result is a value with more digits than can be represented by Java’s integer primitive types. The multiplication in line 28, for example, produces a 48-digit integer. Though a BigInteger can represent any integer value, it does not use the primitive types understood by the Java virtual machine. So calculations with BigInteger run (possibly much) slower than those with primitive types.18

4.1 Introduction

This chapter introduces all but one of Java’s remaining control statements. We demonstrate the for, do…while and switch statements. We explore the essentials of counter-controlled iteration using while and for. We use a switch statement to count the number of A, B, C, D and F grade equivalents in a set of numeric grades entered by the user. We introduce the break and continue program-control statements. We discuss the logical operators, which enable you to use more complex conditional expressions in control statements. Throughout the chapter, you’ll use generative AI to leverage your Java learning experience. We discuss the challenges of processing monetary amounts with floating-point types like double. Then, in Section 4.11’s Objects-Natural Case Study, we represent and manipulate monetary amounts precisely using objects of the Java API class BigDecimal.

4.2 Essentials of Counter-Controlled Iteration

Let’s use the while iteration statement (Section 3.5) to formalize the elements of counter-controlled iteration:

  1. a control variable (or loop counter),

  2. the initial value of the control variable,

  3. the increment by which the control variable is modified each time through the loop (also known as each iteration of the loop), and

  4. the loop-continuation condition that determines if looping should continue.

Consider the program of Fig. 4.1, which uses a loop to display 1–10. Lines 6, 8 and 10 define the elements of counter-controlled iteration. Line 6 declares the control variable (counter) as an int, reserves space for it in memory and sets its initial value to 1. The while statement’s loop-continuation condition (line 8) tests whether the control variable’s value is less than or equal to 10 (the final value for which the condition is true). The program performs this while statement’s body even when the control variable is 10. The loop terminates when the control variable exceeds 10 (that is, counter becomes 11). Line 9 displays counter’s value during each iteration. Line 10 increments the control variable by 1 at the end of each iteration to prepare to process the next value.

You should always control counting loops with integers. Recall that floating-point values are approximate. So, controlling counting loops with floating-point variables can result in imprecise counter values and inaccurate termination tests that could cause an infinite loop.

Generative AI

1 Prompt genAIs, asking them to find and correct the error in the following code, which should print the values 1–5:

int n = 1;

while (n < 5) {
   System.out.println(n++);
}

Confirm that the genAIs point out the loop currently prints the values 1–4 and, to print 1–5, the loop-continuation condition should use <= rather than < or use the final value 6 rather than 5.

4.3 for Iteration Statement

 

The for iteration statement specifies the counter-controlled-iteration details in a single line of code. Typically, you use for statements for counter-controlled iteration and while statements for sentinel-controlled iteration, but each can be used for either iteration type. Figure 4.2 reimplements the program of Fig. 4.1 using a for statement.

The for statement (lines 8–10) declares the control variable counter and initializes it to 1. Next, the statement tests the loop-continuation condition (counter <= 10) between the two required semicolons. The condition is true because counter’s initial value is 1, so line 9 displays counter’s value (1). Next, ++counter increments counter by 1. Then, the loop-continuation condition is tested again to determine whether to proceed with the loop’s next iteration. At this point, counter’s value is 2, so the condition is still true, and the program executes line 9. This process continues until the loop displays 1–10. When counter’s value becomes 11, the loop-continuation condition is false, so iteration terminates, and the program continues with the first statement after the loop (line 12).

Off-By-One Errors

If you incorrectly specified the loop-continuation condition in Fig. 4.2 as counter < 10, the loop would iterate only nine times—a common logic error called an off-by-one error. An incorrect final value in a loop-continuation condition can also cause an off-by-one error. In a loop that counts from 1 through 10, the condition should be counter <= 10 or counter < 11. Many programmers prefer zero-based counting in which to count 10 times, counter would be initialized to 0, and the loop-continuation test would be counter < 10.1

1. In Chapter 6, we’ll see examples of zero-based counting.

A Closer Look at the for Statement’s Header

Let’s take a closer look at the for statement in Fig. 4.2:

This line—including the keyword for and everything in the parentheses after for (line 8 in Fig. 4.2)—is sometimes called the for statement header.

General Format of a for Statement

The general format of the for statement is

Click here to view code image

for (initialization; loopContinuationCondition; increment) {
   statement(s)
}

where

  • initialization declares the loop’s control variable and provides its initial value,

  • loopContinuationCondition—between the two required semicolons—determines whether the loop should continue executing, and

  • increment modifies the control variable’s value after the loop body executes, so the loop-continuation condition eventually becomes false.

If the loopContinuationCondition is initially false, the for statement’s body does not execute—execution continues after the for with the next statement in sequence. The initialization and increment expressions can be comma-separated lists of initialization expressions or increment expressions—the expressions in each evaluate left to right.

Placing a semicolon immediately after the right parenthesis of a for header makes that for’s body an empty statement. This usually is a logic error.

Infinite loops occur when an iteration statement’s loopContinuationCondition never becomes false. To prevent this in a counter-controlled loop, modify the control variable during each loop iteration so the loop-continuation condition eventually becomes false.

Scope of a for Statement’s Control Variable

If the initialization expression declares the control variable, it can be used only in that for statement—not beyond it. This restricted use is the variable’s scope, which defines its lifetime and where it can be used in a program. For example, a variable’s scope is from its declaration point in a block to the right brace that closes the block. As you’ll see in Chapter 5, Methods, it’s good practice to limit each variable’s scope to only where it’s needed.

Expressions in a for Statement’s Header Are Optional

A for header’s three expressions are optional:

  • If you omit the loopContinuationCondition, the condition is always true, creating an infinite loop. We’ll see later that this is sometimes useful.

  • You might omit the initialization expression if the program initializes the control variable before the loop.

  • You might omit the increment expression if the program calculates the increment in the loop’s body or if no increment is needed.

The increment expression in a for acts like a standalone statement at the end of the for’s body. Therefore, the following increment expressions are equivalent in a for:

counter = counter + 1
counter += 1
++counter
counter++

The increment expression does not appear in a larger expression, so preincrementing and postincrementing have the same effect. We prefer preincrement.2 The increment may also be negative, in which case it’s a decrement, and the loop counts downward.

2. This preincrement preference comes from our experience with C++, where preincrement sometimes performs better than postincrement. In Java, for a standalone counter increment, such as in a for’s increment expression, there’s no performance advantage of preincrement over postincrement, so the compiler produces the same code. Many Java programmers prefer postincrement. Be careful when using preincrement and postincrement in more complex expressions where they operate differently.

Using a for Statement’s Control Variable in the Statement’s Body

Programs frequently display the control variable’s value or use it in calculations in the for loop’s body, but this is not required. You can change the control variable’s value in the loop’s body, but this can lead to subtle errors. If you must modify the control variable’s value in the loop’s body, prefer while to for.

The following UML activity diagram of Fig. 4.2’s for statement shows that initialization occurs once before the statement tests the loop-continuation condition the first time. Incrementing occurs after the body statement executes:

4.4 Examples Using the for Statement

The following examples show techniques for varying the control variable in a for statement. In each case, we write only the appropriate for header. Note the change in the relational operator for the loops that decrement the control variable.

  1. Vary the control variable from 1 to 100 in increments of 1.

    Click here to view code image

    for (int i = 1; i <= 100; ++i)

  2. Vary the control variable from 100 to 1 in decrements of 1.

    Click here to view code image

    for (int i = 100; i >= 1; --i)

  3. Vary the control variable from 7 to 77 in increments of 7.

    Click here to view code image

    for (int i = 7; i <= 77; i += 7)

  4. Vary the control variable from 20 to 2 in decrements of 2.

    Click here to view code image

    for (int i = 20; i >= 2; i -= 2)

  5. Vary the control variable over the values 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20.

    Click here to view code image

    for (int i = 2; i <= 20; i += 3)

  6. Vary the control variable over the values 99, 88, 77, 66, 55, 44, 33, 22, 11, 0.

    Click here to view code image

    for (int i = 99; i >= 0; i -= 11)

Do not use equality operators (!= or ==) in a loop-continuation condition if the loop’s control variable increments or decrements by more than 1. For example, in the following for header, counter != 10 never becomes false, resulting in an infinite loop because counter increments by 2 after each iteration, producing the odd values 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, …:

Click here to view code image

for (int counter = 1; counter != 10; counter += 2)

A common logic error in a loop that counts downward is using an incorrect relational operator in the loop-continuation condition—for example, i<= 1 instead of i>= 1 in a loop counting down to 1. Counting loops are error-prone. In subsequent chapters, we’ll introduce lambdas and streams technologies that you can use to eliminate such errors.

4.6 Calculating Compound Interest with the for Statement

 

Let’s use a for statement to calculate compound interest. Consider the following problem:

A person invests $1,000 in a savings account yielding 5% interest. Assuming all the interest is left on deposit, calculate and print the amount of money in the account at the end of each year for 10 years. Use the following formula to determine the amounts:

a = p (1 + r)n

where

p is the original principal amount invested

r is the annual interest rate (e.g., use 0.05 for 5%)

n is the number of years

a is the amount on deposit at the end of the nth year.

Figure 4.4 uses a loop to perform the compound-interest calculation for each of the 10 years the money remains on deposit. Lines 6, 7 and 15 declare the double variables principal, rate and amount. Lines 6–7 initialize principal to 1000.00 and rate to 0.05 (5%). Line 15 initializes amount to the compound-interest calculation’s result.

Formatting Strings with Field Widths and Alignment

Line 10 displays headers for two columns of output—the year and the amount on deposit at the end of that year. We use the format specifier %20s to output the String "Amount on Deposit". The integer 20 between the % and the conversion character s indicates that the value should be displayed with a field width of 20—that is, printf displays the value with at least 20 character positions. If the value to display has fewer than 20 characters (17 in this example), the value is right aligned in the field by default. If the value to display had more than 20 characters, the field width would be extended to the right to accommodate the entire value—this would typically upset our tabular output’s neat columns. To display values left aligned, use the minus sign (–) formatting flag, as in %-20s.

Performing the Interest Calculations with static Method pow of Class Math

The for statement (lines 13–19) executes its body 10 times, varying the control variable year from 1 to 10 in increments of 1. This loop terminates when year becomes 11. Java does not include an exponentiation operator, but the Math class has the static pow method for raising a value to a power. Recall from Section 3.12 that you can call a static method by specifying the class name followed by a dot (.) and the method name. Line 15 implements the formula from the problem statement. The expression

Math.pow(1.0 + rate, year)

calculates 1.0 + rate raised to the year power. The method receives two double arguments and returns a double result. Class Math is defined in the package java.lang, so you do not need to import Math to use it. In Chapter 5, you’ll learn how to implement custom static methods.

The calculation 1.0 + rate in the Math.pow call’s first argument produces the same result during each iteration of the loop, so repeating it in every iteration is wasteful. Generally, you should put such calculations outside the loop. However, today’s sophisticated optimizing compilers typically do this when they compile the code.

Formatting Floating-Point Numbers

After each calculation, line 18 outputs the year and the amount on deposit at the end of that year. The year is output in a field width of four characters, as specified by %4d. The amount is output as a floating-point number with the format specifier %,20.2f:3

  • The comma (,) formatting flag indicates that the floating-point value should be output with a grouping separator. The separator is specific to the user’s locale (i.e., country). For example, in the United States, the number will be output using commas to separate every three digits and a decimal point to separate the fractional part of the number, as in 1,050.00.

  • The number 20 in the format specification indicates that the value should be right aligned in a field width of 20 characters.

  • The precision .2 tells printf to round amount to the nearest hundredth and displays it with two digits to the right of the decimal point.

3. Method printf uses class Formatter to perform its formatting. Class Formatter’s documentation provides lists all the formatting capabilities. “Class Formatter.” Accessed September 21, 2024. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/util/Formatter.html.

Floating-Point Numbers Are Approximations

Recall from Section 3.7.3 that floating-point numbers often arise in arithmetic as a result of division. For example, when dividing 10 by 3, the result is 3.3333333…, with the sequence of 3s repeating infinitely. The computer allocates a fixed amount of space to hold such a value, so the stored value can be only an approximation. Floating-point types like double suffer from what is referred to as representational error. Assuming that floating-point numbers are represented exactly can lead to incorrect results.

A Warning about Displaying Rounded Values

In this example, we declared the double variables amount, principal and rate. We’re dealing with fractional parts of dollars and thus need a type that allows decimal points in its values. Unfortunately, floating-point numbers can cause trouble. Here’s a simple explanation of what can go wrong when using double (or float) to represent dollar amounts, assuming that dollar amounts are displayed with two digits to the right of the decimal point: Two double dollar amounts stored in the machine could be 14.234, which would typically be rounded to 14.23 for display purposes, and 18.673, which would typically be rounded to 18.67 for display purposes. When these amounts are added, they produce the internal sum 32.907, which would typically be rounded to 32.91 for display purposes. Thus, your output could appear as

$\frac{\begin{array}{r} {14.23} \\ {+ ~~18.67} \end{array}}{~~~~~32.91}$

but a person adding the individual numbers as displayed would expect the sum to be 32.90. You’ve been warned!

Monetary Calculations

Do not use double (or float) variables for monetary calculations. The imprecision of floating-point numbers can lead to errors. The Java API provides class BigDecimal (package java.math) for this purpose, which we demonstrate in Section 4.11’s Objects-Natural Case Study.

In a global economy, dealing with currencies, monetary amounts, conversions, rounding and formatting is complex. JavaMoney (https://javamoney.github.io), which is not part of the core Java API, was developed to meet these challenges.

4.7 do…while Iteration Statement

 

The do…while iteration statement is similar to the while statement:

  • The while statement tests its loop-continuation condition before executing the loop’s body. If the condition is false, the body never executes.

  • A do…while tests its loop-continuation condition after executing the loop’s body. Therefore, the body always executes at least once.

Figure 4.5 uses a do…while to output the numbers 1–10. Line 6 declares and initializes the control variable counter. Upon entering the do…while statement, line 9 displays counter’s value, and line 10 increments counter. Then, the program evaluates the loop-continuation test at line 11. If the condition is true, lines 9 and 10 execute again. If the condition is false, the loop terminates, and the program continues with the next statement in sequence (line 13).

UML Activity Diagram for the do…while Iteration Statement

The do…while statement’s UML activity diagram makes it clear that a do…while does not evaluate its loop-continuation condition until after its body executes at least once. Compare this activity diagram with that of the while statement shown in Section 3.5.

4.8 switch Multiple-Selection Statement

 

The switch multiple-selection statement performs different actions based on the possible values of a constant integral expression of type byte, short, int or char (but not long), or based on the value of a String. You’ll see in later chapters that these restrictions have been eased considerably in recent Java versions.

Using a switch Statement to Count A, B, C, D and F Grades

Figure 4.6 calculates the class average of a set of user-entered numeric grades. The program’s switch statement determines whether each grade is the equivalent of an A, B, C, D or F and increments the appropriate grade counter. Then, the program displays a summary showing the number of students who received each grade. Like earlier versions of the class-average program, Fig. 4.6 declares local variables total (line 7) and gradeCounter (line 8) to keep track of the sum of the grades entered by the user and the number of grades entered. Lines 9–13 declare counter variables for each grade category. Note that the variables in lines 7–13 are explicitly initialized to 0.

Method main has two key parts. Lines 24–48 read an arbitrary number of integer grades from the user using sentinel-controlled iteration, update instance variables total and gradeCounter, and increment an appropriate letter-grade counter for each grade entered. Lines 51–69 output a report containing the total of all grades entered, the average of the grades and the number of students who received each letter grade. If no grades were entered, line 71 displays an appropriate message. Let’s examine these parts in more detail.

Reading Grades from the User

Lines 17–21 prompt the user to enter integer grades and to enter the end-of-file indicator to terminate the input. Here, we specify the instructions using a relatively new Java feature called a text block—a convenient way to represent a multiline string. Each text block begins with the delimiter """ on a line by itself, followed by any number of lines of text and a terminating """ delimiter. Each line of text (except the one with the terminating """) ends with an implicit newline.

The end-of-file indicator is a system-dependent keystroke combination the user enters to indicate there’s no more data to input. On macOS and Linux systems, you can enter end-of-file by inputting the following sequence on a line by itself:

<Ctrl> d

This notation means to simultaneously press both the Ctrl key and the d key. On Windows systems, you can enter end-of-file by inputting

<Ctrl> z

On some systems, you must press Enter after inputting the end-of-file key sequence. Also, Windows typically displays the characters ^Z on the screen when the end-of-file indicator is entered, as shown in Fig. 4.6’s sample output.

The while statement (lines 24–48) obtains the user input. The condition at line 24 calls Scanner’s hasNext method to determine whether there’s more data to input. This method returns true if there’s more data in the input stream; otherwise, it returns false. The returned value is then used as the while statement’s condition. When using hasNext with the standard-input stream, line 24 waits for the user to enter a value or the end-of-file indicator, then the program continues accordingly. The hasNext method returns false once the user enters the end-of-file indicator.

Line 25 inputs a grade from the user. Line 26 adds grade to total. Line 27 increments gradeCounter. These variables are used to compute the average of the grades.

Processing the Grades

The switch statement (lines 30–47) determines which letter-grade counter to increment based on the numeric grade entered. We assume that the user enters a valid grade in the range 0–100 where 90–100 represents A, 80–89 represents B, 70–79 represents C, 60–69 represents D, and 0–59 represents F. The switch statement’s block contains a sequence of case labels and an optional default case, which can appear anywhere in the switch but typically appears last. When the flow of control reaches the switch, the program evaluates the controlling expression in the parentheses following switch

grade / 10

then compares this value with each case label.

Controlling Expression Produces Integer Values

Line 30’s controlling expression performs integer division, which truncates the result’s fractional part. When we divide an int value from 0 to 100 by 10, the result is always an int value from 0 to 10. We test several of these values in our case labels. If the user enters the integer 85, the controlling expression evaluates to 8. The switch compares 8 with each case label. If a match occurs (case 8: at line 35), that case’s statements execute. For 8, line 36 increments bCount, because a grade in the 80s is a B. The break statement (line 37) exits the switch, then the next statement in sequence executes. In this program, we reach the end of the while loop, so control returns to its loop-continuation condition in line 24 to determine whether the loop should continue executing.

Performing the Same Statements for Multiple cases

Our switch statement’s cases explicitly test for the values 10, 9, 8, 7 and 6. The cases in lines 31–32 test for the values 10 and 9, which both represent the grade A. Listing cases consecutively with no statements between them enables them to perform the same set of statements. So, when the controlling expression evaluates to 10 or 9, the statements in lines 33–34 execute. The switch statement does not provide a mechanism for testing ranges of values—every value you need to test must be listed in a separate case label.4 The switch statement differs from other control statements in that it does not require braces around multiple statements in a case.

4. In Chapter 5, we introduce switch expressions, which can specify in each case a comma-delimited list of values to match.

The default Case

If the controlling expression’s value does not match any of the case labels, the default case (lines 44–46) executes. In this example, the default case processes all controlling-expression values less than 6—that is, all failing grades. If no match occurs and the switch does not contain a default case, program control simply continues with the first statement after the switch. In a switch, it’s good practice to test all possible values of the controlling expression. Also, providing a default case focuses you on the need to process exceptional conditions.

Displaying the Grade Report

Lines 51–69 output a report based on the grades entered (as shown in the input/output window in Fig. 4.6). Line 54 determines whether the user entered at least one grade—this helps us avoid dividing by zero. If so, line 56 calculates the class average. Lines 59–68 then output the total of all the grades, the class average and the number of students who received each letter grade. If no grades were entered, line 71 outputs an appropriate message.

case without a break Statement

Without break statements, each time a match occurs in the switch, the statements for that case and subsequent cases execute until a break statement or the end of the switch is reached. This is referred to as “falling through” to the statements in subsequent cases. Forgetting a break statement when one is needed in a switch is a logic error.

switch Statement UML Activity Diagram

The following is the UML activity diagram for the general switch statement with breaks:

Most switch statements use a break in each case to terminate the switch statement. The diagram emphasizes this by including break statements and showing that the break statement at the end of a case causes control to exit the switch statement immediately. A break is not required for the switch’s last case (or the optional default case when it appears last)—execution simply continues with the next statement after the switch.

Notes on the Expression in Each case of a switch

In a switch, each case must contain a String or a constant integral expression—that is, any combination of integer constants that evaluates to a constant integer value (e.g., –7, 0 or 221) of type byte, char, short or int. An integer constant is simply an integer value. In addition, you can use character constants (of type char), which are specific characters in single quotes, such as 'A', '7' or '$'. These represent the characters’ integer values in the Unicode character set.5 You can view the integer values of many Unicode characters at

Click here to view code image

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Unicode_characters

5. “Unicode.” Accessed May 26, 2024. https://home.unicode.org/.

The expression in each case can also be a constant variable or an enum constant:

  • A constant variable (or simply a constant) is declared final (discussed in Chapter 5) and contains a value that does not change throughout the program.

  • Java also has a feature called enum types (discussed in Chapter 5) that define constants. An enum’s constants may be used in case labels.

In Chapter 9, Real-World Modeling with Inheritance, Polymorphism & Interfaces, we present a more elegant way to implement switch logic. We use a technique called polymorphism to create programs that often are clearer, easier to maintain and easier to extend than programs using switch logic.

4.9 break and continue Statements

 

In addition to selection and iteration statements, Java provides the break and continue statements to alter the flow of control.6

6. Java also has labeled break and continue statements. See the book’s webpage at https://deitel.com/javafp5.

break Statement

In the preceding section, we used break to terminate a switch statement’s execution. Executing a break in a while, for or do…while immediately exits that statement—execution continues with the next statement in sequence. Figure 4.7 demonstrates break exiting a for. When the nested if statement (lines 8–10) detects that count is 5, the break statement (line 9) terminates the enclosing loop, then the program proceeds to line 15, which displays a message indicating the control variable’s value when the loop terminated. The loop fully executes its body only four times instead of the 10 specified in the for header (line 7). Line 15 can access the control variable count after the loop because we declared count before the loop (line 5) rather than in the for header’s initialization section (line 7).

continue Statement

When you execute the continue statement in a loop, it skips the remaining statements in the loop’s body and proceeds with the loop’s next iteration:

  • In a while or do…while statement, the program evaluates the loop-continuation test immediately after continue executes.

  • In a for statement, the increment expression executes, then the program evaluates the loop-continuation test.

Figure 4.8 uses continue (line 7) to skip the statement at line 10 when the nested if determines that count’s value is 5. When the continue executes, program control continues with the ++count increment expression in the for statement’s header (line 5).

Some programmers feel that the break and continue statements violate structured programming. The same effects are achievable with structured-programming techniques, so these programmers do not use break or continue.

There’s a tension between achieving quality software engineering and achieving the best-performing software. Sometimes, one goal is achieved at the expense of the other. For all but the most performance-intensive situations, apply the following guidelines: First, make your code simple and correct; then make it fast and small, but only if necessary.

4.10 Logical Operators

The if, if…else, while, do…while and for statements each require a condition to determine how to continue a program’s flow of control. So far, we’ve studied only simple conditions, such as count <= 10 and total > 1000. Simple conditions test only one condition and are expressed in terms of the relational operators >, <, >= and <= and the equality operators == and !=. To test multiple conditions when making a decision, we performed these tests in separate statements or in nested if or if…else statements. Sometimes, control statements require more complex conditions to determine a program’s flow of control.

The logical operators

  • && (conditional AND),

  • || (conditional OR),

  • & (boolean logical AND),

  • | (boolean logical inclusive OR),

  • ^ (boolean logical exclusive OR) and

  • ! (logical complement)

enable you to combine two or more simple conditions to form compound conditions. The &, | and ^ operators are also bitwise operators when they’re applied to integer operands.7

7. See the book’s webpage at https://deitel.com/javafp5 for a discussion of bitwise operators.

4.10.1 Conditional AND (&&) Operator

In 2023, after three years of the Covid pandemic, the United States experienced a pilot shortage that snarled air traffic. To alleviate the pilot shortage, the government considered raising the mandatory pilot retirement age from 65 to 67 so veteran pilots in good health could continue flying for two more years.

Let’s assume an airline wanted to ask each veteran pilot aged 63 or older whether they’d like to apply to keep flying until age 67 rather than retiring at age 65, and the airline needed to know how many pilots fit into this age category. The airline could write a program to search their employee records and determine the number of 63-years-of-age-or-older veteran pilots. The program might contain the statement:

Click here to view code image

if (employeeType == PILOT && age >= 63) {
   ++veteranPilots;
}

Assume PILOT is a constant. The if statement contains two simple conditions separated by the && (conditional AND) operator:

  • employeeType == PILOT determines whether an employee is a pilot.

  • age >= 63 determines whether an employee is nearing retirement age.

The if statement considers the combined condition, which is true only if both simple conditions are true. If so, the if statement’s body increments veteranPilots by 1; otherwise, the program skips the increment. Some programmers find that the combined condition is more readable with redundant parentheses, as in

Click here to view code image

if ((employeeType == PILOT) && (age >= 63)) {
   ++veteranPilots;
}

The following truth table summarizes the && operator, showing all possible combinations of false and true values for expression1 and expression2. Java evaluates to false or true all expressions that include relational operators, equality operators or logical operators:

4.10.2 Conditional OR (||) Operator

Suppose we wish to ensure that either or both of two conditions are true before choosing a path of execution. In this case, we use the || (conditional OR) operator, as in the following program segment:

Click here to view code image

if ((semesterAverage >= 90) || (finalExam >= 90)) {
   System.out.println ("Student grade is A");
}

This statement also contains two simple conditions:

  • semesterAverage >= 90 determines whether the student deserves an A in the course for a solid performance throughout the semester.

  • finalExam >= 90 determines whether the student deserves an A in the course for outstanding performance on the final exam.

The if statement then considers the combined condition

Click here to view code image

(semesterAverage >= 90) || (finalExam >= 90)

and awards the student an A if either or both of the simple conditions are true. The only time this would not print "Student grade is A" is if both simple conditions are false. The following is a truth table for the conditional OR (||) operator.

The && operator has a higher precedence than ||. Both group from left to right.

4.10.3 Short-Circuit Evaluation of Complex Conditions

The parts of an expression containing && or || operators are evaluated only until it’s known whether the condition is true or false. Thus, the evaluation of the condition

Click here to view code image

(employeeType == PILOT) && (age >= 63)

stops immediately if employeeType is not equal to PILOT (i.e., the entire expression is false) but continues if employeeType is equal to PILOT (i.e., the entire expression might still be true if age >= 63 is true). This short-circuit evaluation is a performance feature of && and || expressions.

In expressions using &&, a condition—we’ll call this the dependent condition—may require another condition to be true for the evaluation of the dependent condition to be meaningful. In this case, the dependent condition should be placed after the && operator to prevent errors. Consider the following condition:

(i != 0) && (10 / i == 2)

The dependent condition (10/i==2) must appear after the && operator to prevent the possibility of division by zero.

4.10.4 Boolean Logical AND (&) and Inclusive OR (|) Operators

The boolean logical AND (&) operator and boolean logical inclusive OR (|) operator are identical to the && and || operators, except that the & and | operators always evaluate both operands—they do not perform short-circuit evaluation. This is useful if the right operand has a required side effect—a modification of a variable’s value. For example,

Click here to view code image

(birthday == true) | (++age >= 65)

guarantees that the condition ++age >= 65 will be evaluated. Thus, the variable age is incremented, regardless of whether the overall condition is true or false. For clarity, avoid expressions with side effects (such as increments) in conditions. They can make code harder to understand and can lead to subtle logic errors.

Assignment (=) expressions generally should not be used in conditions. Every condition must result in a boolean value; otherwise, a compilation error occurs. In a condition, an assignment will compile only if a boolean expression is assigned to a boolean variable.

4.10.5 Boolean Logical Exclusive OR (^) Operator

A simple condition containing the boolean logical exclusive OR (^) operator is true only if one of its operands is true and the other is false. If both are true or both are false, the condition is false. This operator is guaranteed to evaluate both of its operands. The following is a truth table for the boolean logical exclusive OR (^) operator.

4.10.6 Logical Complement (!) Operator

The logical complement (!) operator—also called the logical negation operator or logical NOT operator—“reverses” the meaning of a condition. Unlike the logical operators &&, ||, &, | and ^, which are binary operators that combine two conditions, the logical negation operator is a unary operator with only one condition as an operand. The operator is placed before a condition to choose a path of execution if the original condition (without the logical negation operator) is false, as in the program segment

Click here to view code image

if (!(grade == sentinelValue)) {
   System.out.printf("The next grade is %d%n", grade);
}

which executes the printf call only if grade is not equal to sentinelValue. The parentheses around the condition grade == sentinelValue are needed because the logical negation operator has a higher precedence than the equality operator.

In most cases, you can avoid using logical negation by expressing the condition differently with an appropriate relational or equality operator. For example, the previous statement also may be written as follows:

Click here to view code image

if (grade != sentinelValue) {
   System.out.printf("The next grade is %d%n", grade);
}

This flexibility can help you express a condition more conveniently. The following is a truth table for the logical negation operator.

4.10.7 Example: Generating Logical-Operator Truth Tables

Figure 4.9 uses logical operators to produce the truth tables discussed in this section. The output shows each boolean expression and its result. We used the %b (boolean) format specifier to display the word “true” or the word “false” based on a boolean expression’s value. Lines 7–11 produce the truth table for &&. Lines 14–18 produce the truth table for ||. Lines 21–25 produce the truth table for &. Lines 28–33 produce the truth table for |. Lines 36–41 produce the truth table for ^. Lines 44–45 produce the truth table for !.

4.11 Objects-Natural Case Study: Precise Monetary Calculations with Java API Class BigDecimal

 

Many applications require precise representations of numbers with decimal points. Institutions like banks that deal with millions or even billions of transactions daily must tie out their monetary transactions “to the penny.” We mentioned earlier that using double values to process monetary amounts, as in Fig. 4.4’s compound-interest example, introduces representational error and rounding issues that could prevent “to the penny” accuracy:

  1. There were representational errors because we stored precise decimal monetary amounts and interest rates as doubles, which are only approximations.

  2. The floating-point values were rounded because the interest calculations often result in fractional pennies, which must be rounded to the hundredths place to represent cents. Rounding can be unpredictable in situations with floating-point representational errors.

There are many points in monetary calculations in which rounding may occur. For example, on a restaurant bill, the tax could be calculated on each item, resulting in separate rounding operations, or it could be calculated only once on the total bill amount. These alternate approaches could yield different results.

Custom Types for Precise Monetary Calculations

You’ll see in Chapter 8 that Java is an extensible language. So, we could create a custom class for monetary calculations and other applications that require precise representation and manipulation of numbers with decimal points. However, getting it right might take significant time and effort. Rather than “reinventing the wheel,” we can use preexisting classes from the Java API (or other libraries) that provide types for to-the-penny precision. In this Objects-Natural Case Study, we’ll create objects of the Java API’s BigDecimal class and use its methods to perform precise monetary calculations.

Representing and Calculating with Monetary Amounts Is a Complex Issue

Processing monetary amounts can be far more complex than what we show here. Banks have to deal with issues such as using a “fair rounding algorithm” when calculating daily interest on their accounts. Rounding rules can vary by currency, government, company, etc. Also, there are a great many currencies worldwide with different conventions for thousands separators, decimal separators, currency symbols, and more. Various Java libraries (including ones that are not part of the core Java API, such as JavaMoney) deal with issues like these.

BigDecimal Objects Require More Memory than Primitive Type Variables

BigDecimal can represent exact monetary amounts like 123.02 and perform to-the-penny arithmetic without representational error. To do this, BigDecimal’s internal coding scheme uses extra memory to store values with arbitrary precision. A BigDecimal’s precision includes all the significant digits to the left and right of the decimal point. By default, BigDecimal calculations are exact—they do not round their results. As you’ll see, you can specify a rounding policy, which financial institutions typically require for monetary calculations.

The following statement creates the BigDecimal variable monetaryAmount and initializes it with the double value 123.02 that we mentioned above:

Click here to view code image

BigDecimal monetaryAmount = new BigDecimal(123.02);

If you print monetaryAmount, you’ll see that this BigDecimal number is actually initialized from the following double value “under the hood:”

Click here to view code image

123.0199999999999960209606797434389591217041015625

This clearly shows this double’s representational error—monetaryAmount is initialized to slightly less than 123.02. To represent 123.02 precisely, initialize monetaryAmount with a String, as in:

Click here to view code image

BigDecimal monetaryAmount = new BigDecimal("123.02");
Demonstrating the Java API’s BigDecimal Class

Figure 4.10 reimplements the compound interest calculation in Fig. 4.4 using BigDecimal objects to represent monetary amounts and interest rates precisely and perform precise arithmetic using them. Lines 3–4 import the java.math package classes we’ll use in this example. Like Fig. 4.4, the first two output columns in Fig. 4.10 display the year and the rounded amount on deposit at the end of each year. This example also displays a third column showing the exact stored value. You can use this for comparison purposes when we discuss how rounding works. Specifying a rounding policy causes a slight difference in the second column’s displayed values vs. those displayed in Fig. 4.4.

Initializing BigDecimal Objects

Due to the representational error with floating-point numbers, you typically create a Big-Decimal object from

  • an integer value, which is represented exactly by Java, or

  • a string containing the exact digits you wish to represent to the left and right of the decimal point.

Lines 9 and 10 initialize the BigDecimals principal and rate with the strings "1000.00" and "0.05", respectively.

Formatting BigDecimal Objects for Output

BigDecimals are converted to strings for display purposes. By default, the digits of their exact values are displayed. Lines 12–13 use the %7s format specifier to right-align the principal and rate in fields that are seven characters wide. The principal and rate decimal points align vertically because each has two digits to the right of the decimal point.

Performing the Interest Calculations with BigDecimal

Lines 21–22

Click here to view code image

BigDecimal amount = principal.multiply(
   BigDecimal.ONE.add(rate).pow(year));

perform the interest calculation using BigDecimal’s multiply, add and pow methods. The expression evaluates as follows:

  1. First, the expression BigDecimal.ONE.add(rate) adds 1 to the rate to produce a BigDecimal containing 1.05—equivalent to 1.0 + rate in line 15 of Fig. 4.4. BigDecimal.ONE is a predefined BigDecimal object representing the value 1. Big-Decimal also predefines BigDecimal.ZERO (0), BigDecimal.TWO (2) and BigDecimal.TEN (10). These values are used frequently in BigDecimal calculations and help programmers avoid the overhead of creating them repeatedly.

  2. Next, we call BigDecimal method pow—which receives an int argument—on the preceding result to raise 1.05 to the power year. This is equivalent to passing 1.0 + rate and year to method Math.pow in line 15 of Fig. 4.4.

  3. Finally, we call BigDecimal method multiply on the principal object, passing the preceding result as the argument. This returns a BigDecimal representing the amount on deposit at the end of the specified year.

Lines 23–24 display the year, the rounded amount on deposit at the end of each year and, for comparison purposes, the unrounded amount, which in year 10 already contains much more precision than double offers. We discuss the rounding below.

A Policy Issue: Half-Up Rounding vs. Banker’s Rounding

Compare Fig. 4.4’s and Fig. 4.10’s outputs. Year 3 has a slightly different output—1157.63 in Fig. 4.4 vs. 1157.62 in Fig. 4.10. This is due to the different rounding algorithms used for doubles vs. the BigDecimals in this example and could also be due to representational errors when calculating with doubles. In Fig. 4.4’s calculation for year 3,

1000.00 * pow(1 + 0.05, 3)

pow returns 1.157625 (that is, 1.053), so the preceding calculation yields 1157.625. By default, double amounts use half-up rounding—for two digits to the right of the decimal point, if the third digit is 5 or higher, we round the previous digit up; otherwise, we round it down. So in Fig. 4.4, 1157.625 rounded up to 1157.63.

Banker’s Rounding

Unfortunately, the commonly used half-up rounding is a biased technique:

  • For the four digits 1, 2, 3 and 4, we round the preceding digit down.

  • For the five digits 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9, we round the preceding digit up.

More values round up than down, leading to possible discrepancies in monetary calculations. To fix this bias, the expression

Click here to view code image

amount.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)

in line 24 uses BigDecimal’s setScale method to round amount to two digits to the right of the decimal point using banker’s rounding8 (also called round half to even or simply half even)—specified by setScale’s second argument, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN.

8. “Rounding,” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed June 7, 2024. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rounding.

With banker’s rounding, when the digit used to determine rounding is 5 (the third digit in this example), this algorithm rounds the previous digit (the second digit in this example) to the nearest even integer. So, when rounding the BigDecimal amount, the value

  • 1157.625 rounds down to 1157.62. Similarly,

  • 1157.635 would round up to 1157.64,

  • 1157.645 would round down to 1157.64,

  • 1157.655 would round up to 1157.66,

  • 1157.665 would round down to 1157.66,

  • etc.

4.12 Wrap-Up

We’ve now introduced most of Java’s control statements, which enable you to control the flow of execution in functions. Chapter 3 discussed if, if…else and while. This chapter demonstrated for, do…while and switch. In Chapter 6, we’ll introduce the enhanced for statement.

You used the break statement to exit a switch statement and to terminate a loop immediately. You used the continue statement to terminate a loop’s current iteration and proceed with the loop’s next iteration. We mentioned that while and do…while loops proceed immediately to their loop-continuation conditions, whereas for loops proceed to their increments first. We introduced the logical operators for creating more complex conditional expressions in control statements. You also continued using generative AI to leverage your Java learning experience.

In our first compound-interest example, we discussed the representational errors associated with floating-point types. Then, in the Objects-Natural Case Study, we performed precise monetary calculations using the Java API’s BigDecimal class to represent floating-point numbers exactly and perform “to-the-penny” arithmetic. We showed that primitive type double uses the biased half-up rounding algorithm and that BigDecimal eliminates that bias by using banker’s rounding.

In Chapter 5, you’ll create your own custom methods, understand how the method-call-and-return mechanism works, learn simulation techniques with random-number generation, and define overloaded methods—that is, methods with the same name that perform the same jobs but with different types and/or numbers of arguments.
