5.1 Introduction

In this chapter, we introduce creating and calling custom methods. We’ll use simulation techniques with random-number generation to program a version of a popular dice game that employs most of the programming techniques you’ve used to this point.

We’ll demonstrate Java’s switch enhancements. First, we’ll use a standalone switch statement with more concise case labels. Then, we’ll show switch expressions that yield values—these simplify code that declares a variable then uses a switch statement to assign a value to that variable.

We’ll discuss scope, which determines where you can use the identifiers you’ve declared in a program. You’ll see that classes can have multiple “overloaded” methods of the same name that perform similar tasks for different types and/or numbers of arguments.

We’ll distinguish between methods you call on objects—such as printf on the System.out object—and static methods you call on a class rather than an object. We’ll overview various packages from the Java API. You’ll see how Java keeps track of which method is executing, how methods’ local variables are maintained in memory, and how a method knows where to return after it completes execution. We discuss argument promotion—automatically converting an argument’s value, if possible, to the type a method expects to receive in its corresponding parameter—and casting, in which you explicitly force a conversion between types.

You’ll continue using generative AI to leverage your Java learning experience. In the Objects-Natural Case Study, you’ll use the Java Date/Time API to perform common date and time manipulations in an application that inputs your birth date and time (or approximations if you wish), then determines the day of the week on which you were born and how long you’ve been alive in years, months, days, hours, minutes and seconds.

5.2 Declaring Methods

 

So far, each class we declared contained one method named main and used various Java API features. Here, you’ll declare then call your first custom method.

Class MaximumFinder (Fig. 5.1) has two methods—main (lines 6–22) and maximum (lines 25–39). The maximum method determines and returns the largest of three double values. Recall that the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) automatically calls main when you execute a program. Most methods do not get called automatically. You must call the maximum method explicitly to tell it to perform its task.

The public and static Keywords

Method maximum’s declaration (lines 25–39) begins with the public keyword to indicate that the method is “available to the public”—that is, it can be called from methods of other classes. The static keyword enables the main method (another static method) to call maximum, as shown in line 18, without qualifying the method name with the class name MaximumFinder—static methods in the same class can call each other directly. Any other class that uses maximum must fully qualify the method name, as in

Click here to view code image

MaximumFinder.maximum(10, 30, 20)

Many of our examples begin every method declaration with the public and static keywords. You’ll learn about non-public and non-static methods in Chapter 8.

The Return Type

After public and static and before the method name is the method’s return type, which specifies the type of data the method returns (that is, gives back to its caller) after performing its task. For example, when you go to an automated teller machine (ATM) and request your account balance, you expect the ATM to return your balance value. Similarly, when a statement calls method maximum in this example, the statement expects to receive back the largest of the three values. The return type double indicates that this method will perform a task then return a double value to the calling method—main in this example. You’ve already used methods that return information. For example, Scanner’s nextInt method inputs an integer entered by the user then returns that integer for use in the program. Sometimes, you’ll define methods that perform a task but do not return any information. Such methods use the return type void (as in line 6 of main).

The Method Name and Parameters

The method name, maximum, follows the return type. Class names, method names and variable names are all identifiers. By convention, they use the camel-case naming scheme discussed in Chapter 2. Also, by convention, class names begin with an initial uppercase letter, and method and variable names begin with an initial lowercase letter.

The parentheses after the method name are required. A method that needs additional information to perform its task can specify one or more parameters to receive that information. Empty parentheses indicate that a method does not require additional information to perform its task.

You declare parameters as a comma-separated parameter list in the parentheses following the method name. Each parameter must specify a type and an identifier. The method maximum requires three double parameters named x, y and z.

Variables declared in a particular method’s parameter list (such as x, y and z) and body (such as maximumValue) are local variables—they can be used only in that method. Each method can access its own local variables but not those of other methods. Collectively, the elements in line 25 are often referred to as the method header.

Method maximum’s Body

The method header is always followed by the method’s body, which is delimited by left and right braces, as in lines 25 and 39. A method’s body contains one or more statements that perform the method’s task.

We determine the maximum value as follows:

  • Initially, we assume that parameter x contains the largest value, so line 26 declares the local variable maximumValue and initializes it with parameter x’s value.

  • Of course, y or z may contain the largest value, so we must compare each with maximumValue. Lines 29–31 determine whether y is greater than maximumValue. If so, line 30 assigns y to maximumValue.

  • Lines 34–36 determine whether z is greater than maximumValue. If so, line 35 assigns z to maximumValue.

At this point, maximumValue contains the largest value, so line 38 uses the return statement to return that value to line 18, where maximum was called. When a method returns to its caller, its local variables no longer exist in memory.

Local-Variable Type Inference

Line 8 in main introduces the var keyword for local-variable type inference. When you initialize a local variable in its declaration, the var keyword tells the compiler to infer (that is, determine) the variable’s type from the type of its initializer. In line 8, we initialize input with a new Scanner object, so the compiler infers that input’s type is Scanner. This simplifies statements like

Click here to view code image

Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);

that show the type on both sides of a variable declaration statement.

Getting the User Input and Calling Method maximum

Lines 11–15 in main prompt the user to enter three double values, then read them using Scanner’s nextDouble method, which returns the user’s input as a double value. A method call supplies values—called arguments—for each of the method’s parameters. For example, the argument to method System.out.println specifies the data to display. When we call maximum at line 18, its x, y and z parameters are initialized with copies of number1’s, number2’s and number3’s values, respectively. There must be one argument in the method call for each parameter in the method declaration. Also, each argument’s type must be consistent with the corresponding parameter’s type. For example, a parameter of type double can receive values like 7.35, 22 or –0.03456, but not Strings like "hello" nor the boolean values true or false. Section 5.11 discusses the argument types you can provide in a method call for each primitive-type parameter. Line 21 displays the result.

Implementing Method maximum by Reusing Method Math.max

The entire body of our maximum method could be implemented concisely with two calls to Math.max, as follows:

Click here to view code image

return Math.max(x, Math.max(y, z));

The arguments to the first Math.max call are x and Math.max(y, z). Before any method can be called, its arguments must be evaluated to determine their values. If an argument is a method call, the method call must be performed to determine its return value. So, in the preceding statement, Math.max(y, z) is evaluated first to determine the maximum of y and z. Then, that result is passed as the second argument to the other Math.max call, which returns the larger of its two arguments. This is a nice example of software reuse—we find the largest of three values by reusing Math.max, which finds the larger of two values.

Separating Programs into Smaller, More Manageable Pieces

Methods and classes allow you to separate a program’s tasks into small self-contained units. Motivations for using methods and classes to create program components include:

  • Software reuse. For example, in earlier programs, we did not have to define how to create and manipulate strings or read inputs from the user. Java provides these capabilities via the String and Scanner classes and their methods.

  • Avoiding code repetition.

  • Hiding complexity.

  • Easier testing, debugging and maintenance.

To promote reusability, every method should perform a single, well-defined task, and the method’s name should express that task effectively. We’ll say lots more about software reusability in our treatment of object-oriented programming.

Generative AI

1 Prompt genAIs, asking them to find and correct the error(s) in the following code, which should return the result of adding the values of parameters x and y:

int sum(int x, int y) {
   int result = x + y;
}

Compare their responses with the following: The method is supposed to return an int but does not. To fix this, delete the variable result and place the statement

return x + y;

in the method, or add the following statement at the end of the method body:

return result;

5.3 Notes on Declaring and Using Methods

 

Calling Methods

There are three ways to call a method:

  1. Use a method name by itself to call another method of the same class—such as maximum(number1, number2, number3) in line 18 of Fig. 5.1.

  2. Use an object’s name, followed by a dot (.) and the method name to call a non-static method of an object—such as input.nextDouble() in line 13 of Fig. 5.1, which calls a Scanner method from MaximumFinder’s main method. Non-static methods are typically called instance methods.

  3. Use the class name and a dot (.) to call a static method of a class—such as Math.pow(1.0 + rate, year) in Fig. 4.4.

Returning from Methods

There are three ways to immediately return control to the statement that calls a method:

  • When the method-ending right brace is reached in a method with return type void.

  • When the following statement executes in a method with return type void

    return;

  • When a method returns a result with a statement of the following form in which the expression is evaluated and its result (and control) are returned to the caller:

    return expression;

Forgetting to return a value from a method that should return a value is a compilation error. If a method specifies a return type other than void, the method must contain a return statement that returns a value consistent with the method’s return type. Returning a value from a method with a void return type is a compilation error.

5.4 Case Study: Die Rolling Simulation with Random-Number Generation

 

Let’s take a brief diversion into simulation and game-playing. Here and in Section 5.5, we’ll develop a game-playing program with multiple methods. As you’ll see, the program uses most of the control statements presented thus far in the book and introduces several new programming concepts.

You can introduce the element of chance into a program via RandomGenerator objects from the java.util.random package. Such objects can produce random boolean, byte, float, double, int, long and other values using one of 13 random-number-generation algorithms listed at:

Click here to view code image

https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/
   util/random/package-summary.html
Creating a RandomGenerator Object

In the next several examples, we use RandomGenerator objects to produce random values using the default algorithm in the JDK.1 The following statement uses RandomGenator static method getDefault to create a new RandomGenerator object:

Click here to view code image

RandomGenerator randomNumbers = RandomGenerator.getDefault()

1. L32X64MixRandom is the default algorithm used by the RandomGenerator object returned from get-Default. This could change in the future as random-number-generation algorithms improve. “Interface RandomGenerator.” Accessed September 21, 2024. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/util/random/RandomGenerator.html.

It can then be used to generate random values—we discuss only random int values here. For information on generating other random values, refer to

Click here to view code image

https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/
   util/random/RandomGenerator.html
Obtaining a Random int Value

Consider the following statement:

Click here to view code image

int randomValue = randomNumbers.nextInt();

RandomGenerator method nextInt generates a random int value from -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647. If it truly produces values at random, then every value in that range should have an equal chance (or probability) of being chosen each time nextInt is called.

Changing the Range of Values Produced By nextInt

The range nextInt produces generally differs from the range a given Java program requires. For example, a program that simulates coin tossing might require only 0 for “heads” and 1 for “tails.” A program that simulates the rolling a six-sided die might require random integers in the range 1–6. A program that randomly predicts the next type of spaceship (out of four possibilities) that will fly across the horizon in a video game might require random integers in the range 1–4. For cases like these, RandomGenerator provides other versions of nextInt:

  • nextInt with one int argument returns a value from 0 up to, but not including, the argument’s value. For example, to simulate a coin toss, the following statement returns 0 or 1:

    Click here to view code image

    int randomValue = randomNumbers.nextInt(2);

  • nextInt with two int arguments returns a value from the first argument’s value up to, but not including, the second argument’s value. For example, to simulate rolling a six-sided die, the following statement returns a value in the range 1–6:

    Click here to view code image

    int randomValue = randomNumbers.nextInt(1, 7);
Rolling a Six-Sided Die 10 Times

Figure 5.2 shows two sample outputs confirming that the results of the preceding nextInt call are integers in the range 1–6 and that each run produces different numbers. Line 3 imports RandomGenerator. Line 8 creates the RandomGenerator object randomNumbers to produce random values. Line 13 executes 10 times in a loop to roll the die.

Rolling a Six-Sided Die 60,000,000 Times

The numbers produced by nextInt occur with approximately equal likelihood. So, when simulating a six-sided die, we expect each face to occur about 16.667% (1/6th) of the time. For small numbers of die rolls, this is unlikely. For example, Fig. 5.2’s second sample output contained no 1s. As we continue rolling a die many times, the “law of large numbers” says that each face’s frequency should converge on 16.667% of the total die rolls. Let’s demonstrate this by simulating 60,000,000 rolls of a die (Fig. 5.3).2 Each face should appear approximately 10,000,000 times. Line 18 uses the _ digit separator (Section 2.5) to make the int value 60_000_000 more readable.

2. When co-author Harvey Deitel first implemented this example in another language for his classes in 1976, he performed only 600 die rolls—6000 would have taken too long. On our current laptop test system, this program took about 1.33 seconds to complete 60,000,000 die rolls. 600,000,000 die rolls took 8.03 seconds. The die rolls occur sequentially. Chapter 18, Concurrency: Platform Threads to Virtual Threads, explores how to parallelize applications to take advantage of today’s multi-core computers.

As the sample outputs show, the values produced by nextInt enable the program to simulate rolling a six-sided die. The program uses nested control statements (a switch is nested inside the for) to determine the number of times each side of the die appears. The for statement (lines 18–30) iterates 60,000,000 times. During each iteration, line 19 produces a random value from 1 to 6. That value is then used as the controlling expression (line 22) in a switch statement that uses the new, more concise case label format (lines 22–29)—we’ll discuss this in more detail momentarily. Based on the face value, the switch increments one of the six counter variables during each loop iteration. Run the program a couple of times and observe the different results during each run.

When we study arrays in Chapter 6, we’ll show an elegant way to replace the entire switch in this program with a single statement. Then, when we study functional programming in Chapter 14, we’ll show how to replace the loop that rolls the dice, the switch and the statement that displays the results with a single statement!

Introducing switch Statements with More Concise case Labels

The switch statement (introduced in Section 4.8) has several limitations:

  • Its cases support only integer-type, String and enum constants. (We’ll introduce enums in Fig. 5.4).

  • Each case label may specify only one value.

  • If you do not include break statements, once a match occurs, cases fall through and continue executing subsequent cases until the switch terminates—a possible logic error.

  • The default case is optional—forgetting to include it could lead to logic errors.

Java enhanced switch statements and introduced switch expressions to improve on these limitations and provide additional capabilities. We present some of those improvements here and in Section 5.5, then show several more advanced features in Chapter 8.

A switch has several forms—we’ll show two in this chapter:

  • In this example, we use a switch statement (lines 22–29) with the new, more concise case labels.

  • At the end of Section 5.5, we show a switch expression that yields a value, which can assign a value to a variable for use later in a program.

The switch statement in lines 22–29 differs from a traditional switch statement as follows:

  • Rather than a case label that ends with a colon (:), the value tested in each case is followed by an arrow (->) symbol that points to the case’s body. By default, the body is one statement, but cases may contain a block of several statements in braces.

  • After a case executes, the switch expression terminates immediately—no break statements are required.

Generalized Scaling and Shifting of Random Numbers

You can choose integers randomly from sets of values other than ranges of consecutive integers. For example, to obtain a random value from the sequence 2, 5, 8, 11 and 14, you could use the statement

Click here to view code image

int number = 2 + 3 * randomNumbers.nextInt(5);

In this case, randomNumbers.nextInt(5) produces values in the range 0–4. Each value produced is multiplied by 3 to produce a number in the sequence 0, 3, 6, 9 and 12. We add 2 to that value to shift the range of values and obtain a value from the sequence 2, 5, 8, 11 and 14. We can generalize this result as

Click here to view code image

int number = shiftingValue +
   differenceBetweenValues * randomNumbers.nextInt(scalingFactor);

where

  • shiftingValue specifies the first number in the desired range of values,

  • differenceBetweenValues represents the constant difference between consecutive numbers in the sequence and

  • scalingFactor specifies how many numbers are in the range.

Secure Random Numbers

Some random-number-generation algorithms produce deterministic random numbers—that is, values that can be predicted by malicious programmers. Objects of the SecureRandom class (java.security package) produce nondeterministic random numbers that cannot be predicted. Deterministic random numbers have been the source of many software security breaches.3 Most programming languages now have library features similar to SecureRandom for producing nondeterministic random numbers to help prevent such problems.

3. “Random number generator attack,” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed August 30, 2024. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_number_generator_attack.

You can create a secure random-number generator object as follows:

Click here to view code image

var randomNumbers = new SecureRandom();

SecureRandom has many of the same method names as RandomGenerator. Using Secure-Random instead of RandomGenerator to achieve higher levels of security incurs a significant performance penalty. For “casual” programs, prefer class RandomGenerator.

5.5 Case Study: A Game of Chance; Introducing enums

 

A popular game of chance is the dice game known as craps, which is played in casinos and back alleys throughout the world. The rules of the game are straightforward:

You roll two dice. Each die has six faces containing one, two, three, four, five and six spots, respectively. After the dice have come to rest, the sum of the spots on the two upward faces is calculated. You win if the sum is 7 or 11 on the first throw. You lose (i.e., the “house” wins) if the sum is 2, 3 or 12 on the first throw (called “craps”). If the sum is 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 or 10 on the first throw, that sum becomes your “point.” To win, you must continue rolling the dice until you “make your point” (i.e., roll that same point value). You lose by rolling a 7 before making your point.

Figure 5.4 simulates the game of craps, using methods to implement the game’s logic. The main method (lines 14–60) calls the rollDice method (lines 63–74) as necessary to roll the two dice and compute their sum. The four sample outputs show winning and losing on the first roll, and winning and losing on a subsequent roll.

Method rollDice

In the rules of the game, the player must roll two dice on each roll. The method rollDice (lines 63–74) rolls the two dice, computes and prints their sum, and returns their sum. The method is declared once, but called from lines 18 and 40 in main, which contains the logic for one complete game of craps. Method rollDice takes no arguments, so it has an empty parameter list. Each time it’s called, rollDice returns the sum of the dice, so the return type int is indicated in the method header (line 63). Although lines 65 and 66 look like the perform the same task, they do not necessarily produce the same result. Each statement produces a random value in the range 1–6. The variable randomNumbers (used in lines 65 and 66) is declared as a private static final variable of the class and initialized with a RandomGenerator object in lines 7–8:

  • Making it private indicates it will be used only in class Craps.

  • Making it a static class variable enables the class’s static methods (like roll-Dice) to use it without having to create an object of the class.

  • Making it final indicates that randomNumbers does not change after it’s initialized. It’s good practice to declare such variables final to prevent accidental changes.

Method main’s Local Variables

The game is reasonably involved. The player may win or lose on the first roll, or may win or lose on any subsequent roll. Method main (lines 14–60) uses

  • local variable myPoint (line 15) to store the “point” if the player doesn’t win or lose on the first roll,

  • local variable gameStatus (line 16) to keep track of the overall game status and

  • local variable sumOfDice (line 18) to store the most recent roll’s sum of the dice.

Variable myPoint is initialized to 0 to ensure that the program will compile. If you do not initialize it, the compiler issues an error, because it is not assigned a value in every case of the switch statement—thus, the program could try to use myPoint before it’s assigned a value. By contrast, gameStatus is assigned a value in every case and the default case of the switch statement—thus, it’s guaranteed to be initialized before it’s used. So, we do not need to initialize gameStatus in line 16.

enum Type Status

Local variable gameStatus (line 16) is declared to be of a new type called Status (declared at line 11). Type Status is a private member of the Craps class because Status will be used only in that class. Status is an enum type, which, in its simplest form, declares a set of constants represented by identifiers—that is, named constants. An enum type is a special class type that’s introduced by the enum keyword and a type name (Status). Braces delimit an enum declaration’s body. Inside the braces is a comma-separated list of enum constants, each representing a unique value. The identifiers in an enum must be unique and, by convention, use all uppercase letters. Using enum constants (like Status.WON, Status.LOST and Status.CONTINUE) rather than literal values (such as 0, 1 and 2) makes programs easier to read and maintain. You’ll learn more about enum types in Chapter 8.

Status variables can be assigned only the three constants declared in the enum (line 11) or a compilation error will occur. When the game is won, the program sets local variable gameStatus to Status.WON (lines 24 and 44). When the game is lost, the program sets local variable gameStatus to Status.LOST (lines 29 and 48). Otherwise, the program sets local variable gameStatus to Status.CONTINUE (line 32) to indicate that the game is not over, and the dice must be rolled again.

Logic of the main Method

Line 18 in main calls rollDice, which picks two random values from 1 to 6, displays the values of the first die, the second die and their sum, and returns the sum. Method main next enters the switch statement (lines 21–36), which uses the sumOfDice value to determine whether the game has been won or lost or should continue with another roll. Lines 22–25 determine whether the player won on the first roll with 7 or 11. Lines 26–30 determine whether the player lost on the first roll with 2, 3 or 12. After the first roll, if the game is not over, the default case (lines 31–35) sets gameStatus to Status.CONTINUE, saves sumOfDice in myPoint and displays the point.

If we’re still trying to “make our point” (i.e., the game is continuing from a prior roll), lines 39–51 execute. Line 40 rolls the dice again. If sumOfDice matches myPoint (line 43), line 44 sets gameStatus to Status.WON, then the loop terminates because the game is complete. If sumOfDice is 7 (line 47), line 48 sets gameStatus to Status.LOST, and the loop terminates because the game is complete. When the game completes, lines 54–59 display a message indicating whether the player won or lost, and the program terminates.

The program uses the various program-control mechanisms we’ve discussed. The Craps class uses two methods—main and rollDice (called twice from main)—and the switch, while, if…else and nested if control statements. Also, note the use of multiple case labels in the switch statement to execute the same statements for sums of 7 and 11 (lines 22–23) and for sums of 2, 3 and 12 (lines 26–28).

switch Expressions Yield Values

Line 16’s gameStatus declaration and the switch statement at lines 21–36 demonstrate a common Java code pattern: Declare a variable followed by a switch statement in which every branch assigns a value to that variable for use later in the code. A switch expression that yields a value simplifies this code pattern.

We can replace lines 16 and 21–36 with the following statement that initializes gameStatus with the result of a switch expression:

Click here to view code image

Status gameStatus = switch (sumOfDice) {
   case 7, 11 -> Status.WON;
   case 2, 3, 12 -> Status.LOST;
   default -> {
      myPoint = sumOfDice; // remember the point
      System.out.printf("Point is %d%n", myPoint);
      yield Status.CONTINUE; // game is not over
   }
}; // required semicolon to terminate the statement

In switch expressions, every branch must yield a value, you must have a default case and the statement in which the switch expression appears must end with a semicolon (;). The value each branch yields is specified to the right its arrow (->) symbol. This switch expression compares sumOfDice to each case. The first two cases

case 7, 11 -> Status.WON;
case 2, 3, 12 -> Status.LOST;

show that switch expressions can specify comma-separated lists of values:

  • If the dice total 7 or 11, the expression yields Status.WON.

  • If the dice total 2, 3 or 12, the expression yields Status.LOST.

For all other sums, the default case executes a block of code, which

  • assigns sumOfDice to myPoint,

  • prints the point and

  • yields the value Status.CONTINUE to initialize gameStatus.

When the code to the right of any branch’s arrow (->) symbol is a block in braces (as in the default case), the block’s last statement must be an explicit yield statement containing the value to yield. You may not use return statements in switch expressions.

We can also replace lines 43–50 in Fig. 5.4 with a switch expression that yields a value to update gameStatus’s value after subsequent die rolls:

Click here to view code image

// determine game status
gameStatus = switch (sumOfDice) {
   case 7 -> Status.LOST;
   default -> sumOfDice == myPoint ?
      Status.WON : Status.CONTINUE;
};

If sumOfDice is 7, the switch expression yields Status.LOST as the new gameStatus value. For all other roll values, the default case uses a conditional expression to determine whether the sum of the dice is equal to myPoint. If so, the default case yields Status.WON; otherwise, it yields Status.CONTINUE. This default case does not require a yield statement because the code to the right of -> is not a block of statements in braces.

For an invalid value, print a string containing the value and "is invalid", then yield the empty string. Compare the Java code they generate to the following code:

5.6 Scope of Declarations

 

You’ve seen declarations of various Java entities, such as classes, methods, variables and parameters. Declarations introduce names that can be used to refer to such Java entities. The scope of a declaration is the portion of the program that can refer to the declared entity by its name. Such an entity is said to be “in scope” for that portion of the program. This section introduces several important scope issues. The basic scope rules are as follows:

  1. The scope of a parameter declaration is the body of the method in which the declaration appears.

  2. The scope of a local variable declaration is from the point at which the declaration appears to the end of that block.

  3. The scope of a local variable declaration in a for statement’s header is the body of the for statement and the other expressions in the header.

  4. A method or field’s scope is the entire body of the class.

Any block may contain variable declarations. If a local variable or parameter in a method has the same name as a field of the class, the field is hidden until the block terminates execution—this is called shadowing. Although you can access a shadowed static class variable by preceding its name with the class’s name and a dot (.), as in ClassName.x, avoiding shadowing can prevent subtle errors. It’s a compilation error if multiple local variables have the same name in the same method.

Figure 5.5 demonstrates field and local-variable scopes. Line 6 declares and initializes the field x to 1. This field is shadowed in any block (or method) that declares a local variable named x. Method main declares a local variable x (line 11) and initializes it to 5. Line 13 outputs this local variable’s value to show that the field x (whose value is 1) is shadowed in main.

The program declares two other methods—useLocalVariable (lines 24–32) and useField (lines 35–41)—that take no arguments and return no results. Method main calls each method twice (lines 15–18). Method useLocalVariable declares local variable x (line 25). When useLocalVariable is first called (line 15), it creates local variable x and initializes it to 25, outputs the value of x (lines 27–28), increments x (line 29) and outputs the value of x again (lines 30–31). When uselLocalVariable is called a second time (line 17), it recreates local variable x and reinitializes it to 25, so the output of each useLocalVariable call is identical.

Method useField does not declare any local variables. Therefore, when it refers to x, the class’s field x (line 6) is used. When method useField is first called (line 16), it outputs the value (1) of field x (lines 36–37), multiplies the field x by 10 (line 38) and outputs the value (10) of field x again (lines 39–40) before returning. The next time method useField is called (line 18), the field has its modified value (10), so the method outputs 10, then 100.

Finally, in method main, the program outputs the value of local variable x again (line 20) to show that none of the method calls modified main’s local variable x, because the methods all referred to variables named x in other scopes.

Principle of Least Privilege

In a general sense, the principle of least privilege says that “things” should have the capabilities they need to get their job done, but no more. An example is the scope of a variable. A variable should not be visible when it’s not needed. Declare variables as close to where they’re first used as possible.

5.7 Method Overloading

 

Methods of the same name can be declared in the same class if they have different sets of parameters (determined by the number, types and order of the parameters). This is called method overloading. When an overloaded method is called, the compiler selects the appropriate method based on the number, types and order of the arguments in the call. Method overloading is commonly used to create several methods with the same name that perform the same or similar tasks but on different types and/or different numbers of arguments. For example, the Math class provides method min that is overloaded with four versions each:

  1. One that returns the smaller of two double parameters.

  2. One that returns the smaller of two float parameters.

  3. One that returns the smaller of two int parameters.

  4. One that returns the smaller of two long parameters.

Our next example demonstrates declaring and invoking overloaded methods.

Declaring Overloaded Methods

Class MethodOverload (Fig. 5.6) declares overloaded square methods—one calculates the square of an int (and returns an int), and one calculates the square of a double (and returns a double). Although these methods have the same name and similar parameter lists and bodies, it may help to think of them as different methods named “square of int” and “square of double,” respectively.

Line 7 invokes method square with the argument 7. Literal integer values are treated as type int, so the method call in line 7 invokes the version of square at lines 12–16 that specifies an int parameter. Similarly, line 8 invokes method square with the argument 7.5. Literal floating-point values are treated as type double, so the method call in line 8 invokes the version of square at lines 19–23 that specifies a double parameter. Each method first outputs a line of text to show that the proper method was called in each case. The values in lines 8 and 20 are displayed with the %f format specifier, which outputs values of type float or double with six digits of precision to the right of the decimal point by default.

Distinguishing Between Overloaded Methods

The compiler distinguishes overloaded methods by their signatures—a combination of the method’s name and the number, types and order of its parameters, but not its return type. If the compiler looked only at method names during compilation, the code in Fig. 5.6 would be ambiguous—the compiler would not know how to distinguish between the two square methods. Internally, the compiler uses longer method names that include the original method name, the types of each parameter and the exact order of the parameters to determine whether the methods in a class are unique in that class.

For example, in Fig. 5.6, the compiler might (internally) use the logical name “square of int” for the square method that specifies an int parameter and “square of double” for the square method that specifies a double parameter—the actual names the compiler uses are messier. If method1’s declaration begins as

void method1(int a, float b)

then the compiler might use the logical name “method1 of int and float.” If the parameters are specified as

void method1(float a, int b)

then the compiler might use the logical name “method1 of float and int.” The order of the parameter types is important—the compiler considers the preceding two method1 headers to be distinct.

Return Types of Overloaded Methods

In discussing the logical names of methods used by the compiler, we did not mention return types. Method calls cannot be distinguished only by return type. When two methods have the same signature and different return types, the compiler issues an error message indicating that the method is already defined in the class. Overloaded methods can have different return types if the methods have different parameter lists. Also, overloaded methods need not have the same number of parameters. Declaring overloaded methods with identical parameter lists is a compilation error.

5.8 Class Math: static Methods and Variables

 

Section 3.12 discussed that most methods are called on specific objects and that some classes contain convenient static methods to perform common tasks. Such methods are also known as class methods. Recall that we used class Math’s static method pow to raise a value to a power in Fig. 4.4. For any class with static methods that’s imported into your program, you can call the static methods by specifying the class’s name, followed by a dot (.) and the method name, as in

ClassName.methodName(arguments)
Math Class Methods

We use Math class methods here to present the concept of static methods. Recall that Math is part of the java.lang package, which is implicitly imported by the compiler, so can use class Math’s methods without explicitly importing the class.

Class Math provides static methods that perform common mathematical calculations. For example, you can calculate the square root of 900.0 with the static method call

Math.sqrt(900.0)

This expression evaluates to 30.0. Method sqrt takes an argument of type double and returns a result of type double. To output the value of the preceding method call, you might write the statement

Click here to view code image

System.out.println(Math.sqrt(900.0));

Here, the value sqrt returns becomes the argument to println. The Math class’s methods are all static, so you do not need to create a Math object to call sqrt. You call each Math method by preceding its name with the class name Math and the dot (.) separator.

Method arguments may be constants, variables or expressions. If c = 13.0, d = 3.0 and f = 4.0, then the statement

Click here to view code image

System.out.println(Math.sqrt(c + d * f));

calculates and prints the square root of 13.0 + 3.0 * 4.0 = 25.0—namely, 5.0. The following table summarizes some Math class static methods—x and y in the table have type double. Methods abs, max and min are overloaded for double, float, long or int parameters.

Class Variables and Math Class static Constants PI and E

Just as a class may contain static methods, a class also may contain static variables that belong to the class, not to specific objects of the class. Such variables are also known as class variables. Class Math declares the constants Math.PI and Math.E. Each is a double approximation of a commonly used mathematical constant with 15 digits to the right of the decimal point:

  • Math.PI (3.141592653589793) is the ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter.

  • Math.E (2.718281828459045) is the base value for natural logarithms (calculated with class Math’s static method log).

These constants are declared in class Math with the modifiers public, final and static:

  • Making them public allows you to use them in your own classes.

  • Any variable declared with the final keyword is constant—its value cannot change after the variable is initialized.

  • Making these variables static allows them to be accessed via the class name Math and a dot (.) separator, just as class Math’s methods are.

A class’s variables are sometimes called fields. Section 8.16 says more about static fields.

Why Is Method main Declared static?

When you execute the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) with the java command, the JVM attempts to invoke the main method of the class you specify. Declaring main as static allows the JVM to invoke main without creating an object of the class. When you execute your program, you specify its class name as an argument to the java command, as in

Click here to view code image

java ClassName argument1 argument2 …

The JVM loads the class specified by ClassName and uses that class name to invoke the main method. In the preceding command, ClassName is an argument to the JVM that tells it which class to execute. Following the ClassName, you can also specify a list of Strings (separated by spaces) as arguments that the JVM will pass to your program—these are known as command-line arguments. Such arguments might specify options required to run the program, such as the name of a file a program should process. Every class may contain main—only the main of the class used to execute the program is called. As you’ll learn in Chapter 6, Arrays and ArrayLists, your program can access those command-line arguments and use them to customize the program.

5.10 Method-Call Stack and Activation Records

 

To understand how Java performs method calls, we first consider a data structure (i.e., collection of related data items) known as a stack. Think of a stack as analogous to a pile of dishes. When a dish is placed on the pile, it’s placed at the top—referred to as pushing the dish onto the stack. Similarly, when a dish is removed from the pile, it’s removed from the top—referred to as popping the dish off the stack. Stacks are known as last-in, first-out (LIFO) data structures—the last item pushed (inserted) on the stack is the first item popped (removed) from the stack.

Method-Call Stack

The method-call stack (also known as the program-execution stack) supports the method call/return mechanism. It also supports the creation, maintenance and destruction of each called method’s local variables. As we’ll see in this section’s diagrams, last-in, first-out (LIFO) behavior is precisely what a method needs to return to its caller.

Stack Frames

As each method is called, it may, in turn, call other methods, which may, in turn, call other methods—all before any of the methods return. Each method eventually must return control to the method that called it. So, somehow, the system must keep track of the return addresses. The method-call stack is the perfect data structure for handling this information. When a method calls another method, an entry is pushed onto the stack. This entry—called a stack frame or an activation record—contains the return address that the called method needs to return to the calling method. It also includes some additional information we’ll soon discuss. When the called method returns to its calling method, the stack frame for the called method is popped, and control transfers to the return address in the popped stack frame.

The beauty of the call stack is that each called method always finds at the top of the call stack the information it needs to return to its caller. If a method calls another method, a stack frame for the new method call is simply pushed onto the call stack. Thus, the return address required by the newly called method to return to its caller is now at the top of the stack.

Local Variables and Stack Frames

The stack frames have another important responsibility. Most methods have local variables, which include the parameters and any local variables the method declares. Non-static local variables need to exist while a method is executing. They must remain active if the method makes calls to other methods. But when a called method returns to its caller, the called method’s local variables need to “go away.” The called method’s stack frame is a perfect place to reserve the memory for the called method’s local variables. That stack frame exists as long as the called method is active. When that method returns, its stack frame is popped from the stack, and its local variables no longer exist.

Stack Overflow

Of course, a computer’s memory is finite, so only a certain amount of memory can be used to store activation records on the method-call stack. If more method calls occur than can have their activation records stored on the method-call stack, a fatal error known as stack overflow occurs.5

5. This is how the website stackoverflow.com got its name. This is an excellent website for getting answers to your programming questions.

Method-Call Stack in Action

Now, let’s consider how the call stack supports the operation of a square method (lines 13–15) called by main (lines 6–10 of Fig. 5.7).

Step 1: Java Virtual Machine Invokes main to Execute the Application

First, the JVM calls main. This pushes a stack frame onto the stack, as shown in the following diagram. The stack frame tells main how to return to the JVM (that is, transfer to return address R1) and contains the space for main’s local variable y, which is initialized to 10, and local variable result, which is not yet initialized. (To keep these diagrams concise, we do not show the public and static keywords for each method in this example.)

Step 2: main Invokes Method square to Perform the Calculation

Before returning to the JVM, main calls method square in line 9 of Fig. 5.7. This pushes a stack frame for square (lines 13–15) onto the method-call stack:

This stack frame contains the address R2 that square needs to return to main and the memory for square’s parameter x.

Step 3: square Returns Its Result to main

After square calculates the square of its argument, it needs to return to main—and no longer needs the memory for its variable x. So the stack is popped, giving square the return location R2 in main and losing square’s local variable. The following diagram shows the method-call stack after square’s stack frame has been popped and square’s return value has been stored in main’s local variable result:

Reaching the closing right brace of main (line 10 of Fig. 5.7) pops its stack frame from the stack. This gives main the address it needs to return to the JVM (R1 in the first diagram). At this point, main’s local variables, y and result, are no longer available.6

5.11 Argument Promotion and Casting

Another important feature of method calls is argument promotion—converting an argument’s value, if possible, to the type the method expects to receive in its corresponding parameter. For example, a program can call Math method sqrt with an int argument even though a double argument is expected. The statement

Click here to view code image

System.out.println(Math.sqrt(4));

correctly evaluates Math.sqrt(4) and prints the value 2.0. The method declaration’s parameter list causes a copy of the int value 4 to be converted to the double value 4.0 before the value is passed to method sqrt. Conversions that do not adhere to Java’s promotion rules may lead to compilation errors. These rules specify which conversions are allowed and can be performed without losing data. In the sqrt example above, an int is converted to a double without changing its value. However, converting a double to an int truncates the fractional part of the double value. Thus, part of the value is lost. Converting large integer types to small integer types (for example, long to int or int to short) may also change values.

The promotion rules apply to expressions containing values of two or more primitive types and primitive-type values passed to methods. A temporary copy of each value is promoted to the “highest” type—the types of the original values remain unchanged. The following table lists the primitive types and the types to which each can be promoted:

The valid promotions for a given type are always to a type higher in the table. For example, an int can be promoted to the higher types long, float or double.

Converting values to types lower in the preceding table will result in different values if the lower type cannot represent the value of the higher type (for example, the int value 2000000 cannot be represented as a short, and any floating-point number with digits after its decimal point cannot be represented in an integer type such as long, int or short). Therefore, in cases where information could be lost due to conversion, the compiler requires you to use a cast operator (introduced in Section 3.7) to explicitly force the conversion to occur—otherwise, a compilation error occurs. This enables you to “take control” from the compiler. You essentially say, “I know this conversion might cause a loss of information, but for my purposes here, that’s fine.”

Casting a primitive-type value to another primitive type may change the value if the new type is not a valid promotion. For example, casting a floating-point value to an integer value may introduce truncation errors (loss of the fractional part) into the result.

Suppose method square calculates the square of an integer and thus requires an int argument. To call square with a double argument named doubleValue, we would be required to write the method call as

square((int) doubleValue)

This method call explicitly casts doubleValue’s value to a a temporary int for use in square. So, if doubleValue’s value is 4.5, the method receives 4 and returns 16, not 20.25.

5.12 Objects-Natural Case Study: Java Date/Time API

Let’s introduce features of the Java Date/Time API, which provides robust capabilities for

  • conveniently managing date and time information,

  • performing date and time calculations and

  • presenting dates and times using locale-specific formatting that considers the user’s spoken (or written) language, country and time zone (that is, the user’s locale).

We’ll build a program that inputs a user’s birth date and time (or approximations if they wish), then determines and displays

  • the day of the week the user was born,

  • the number of years, months and days the user has been alive, and

  • the total months, days, hours, minutes and seconds the user has been alive.

Here is a sample output for a person born July 20, 1969, at 10:56 PM Eastern Time—your output will differ since you did not run the program on the same date and time as we did:7

Click here to view code image

Enter your birthday (yyyy-MM-dd): 1969-07-20
Enter your birth time (HH:mm): 22:56

Birth date/time: Jul 20, 1969, 10:56:00 PM
Current date/time: Jun 15, 2024, 12:40:56 PM

You were born on a Sunday
You have been alive for 54 years, 10 months, and 26 days

Total days:    20,054

In Section 5.12.2, we’ll show how to run the program with command-line arguments that specify spoken (or written) languages and locales so you can obtain locale-specific formatting of the dates, times and numeric values displayed in the preceding output. For simplicity, we will not translate the other English text in this example.

Some key Date/Time API types we’ll use in this case study include:

  • The LocalDate class, LocalTime class, and LocalDateTime class (each from the java.time package8) represent dates, times and combined date-time values based on the user’s local date and time.

    8. “Package java.time,” Accessed September 21, 2024. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/time/package-summary.html.

  • The Period class and Duration class (each from the java.time package) represent periods of time. A Period is date-based, storing years, months and days. A Duration is time-based, storing hours, minutes and seconds.

  • The DateTimeFormatter class, FormatStyle enum and TextStyle enum (each from the java.time.format package9) enable precise date and time formatting.

    9. “Package java.time.format,” Accessed September 21, 2024. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/time/format/package-summary.html.

  • The ChronoUnit enum (from the java.time.temporal package10) provides constants for specifying the units of values returned by various Date/Time classes’ calculation methods.

    10. “Package java.time.temporal,” Accessed September 21, 2024. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/time/temporal/package-summary.html.

The beauty of the objects-natural approach is that the types discussed here consist of nearly 4000 source-code lines (not including comments). Implementing these types yourself would take significant time to write, test, debug and prove them correct. But, you can benefit from their powerful capabilities simply by writing small numbers of statements that manipulate objects of these types and call their methods.

5.12.1 Data/Time Manipulations

Figure 5.8 implements the application using various Date/Time API features. We’ve split the program into parts for discussion purposes.

Importing the Java API Classes and enums

Lines 4–14 import the classes and enums used in this program.

Inputting the Birthday and Birth Time from the User

Lines 21–26 prompt for and input the user’s birthday and birth time:

Click here to view code image

16   public class AgeCalculator {
17      public static void main(String[] args) {
18         var input = new Scanner(System.in);
19
20         // input user's birthday and convert it to a LocalDate
21         System.out.print("Enter your birthday (yyyy-MM-dd): ");
22         var birthday = LocalDate.parse(input.nextLine());
23
24         // input user's birth time and convert it to a LocalTime
25         System.out.print("Enter your birth time (HH:mm): ");
26         var birthTime = LocalTime.parse(input.nextLine());
27
Enter your birthday (yyyy-MM-dd): 1969-07-20
Enter your birth time (HH:mm): 22:56

The code operates as follows:

  • Line 21 specifies that the birthday should be input in the format yyyy-MM-dd, which represents a four-digit year (e.g., 1969), a two-digit month (e.g., 07) and a two-digit day (e.g., 20), each separate from the next by a dash (-). The Date/Time API uses capital M’s to represent months and lowercase m’s to represent minutes. The DateTimeFormatter class’s documentation contains a table explaining the letters used in date and time formats.11

    11. “Class DateTimeFormatter,” Accessed September 21, 2024. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/time/format/DateTimeFormatter.html.

  • Line 22 uses the Scanner class’s nextLine method to read a line of text as a string. It then passes the string to the LocalDate class’s parse method, which converts the date to a LocalDate object that we store in birthday.

  • Line 25 specifies that the birth time should be input in the HH:mm format, representing a two-digit hour and a two-digit minute, separated by a colon (:). The Date/Time API uses capital H’s to represent hours in 24-hour clock format, whereas lowercase h’s represent 12-hour clock format.

  • Line 26 reads a line of text as a string and passes it to the LocalTime class’s parse method to convert the time to a LocalTime object, then stores it in birthTime.

Creating LocalDateTime Objects for the Birthday and Birth Time and the Current Date and Time

To prepare for date/time calculations, line 29 converts the birthday and birthTime objects into a LocalDateTime object by calling the LocalDateTime class’s of method and storing the result in birthDateTime. We’ll calculate differences between the current date and time and birthDateTime, so line 32 calls the LocalDateTime class’s now method to get the current date and time on the user’s system and store it in now. Line 35 calls our displayDatesAndTimes method (discussed shortly) to display the LocalDateTime objects birthDateTime and now in the default format for the user’s locale.

Click here to view code image

28         // combine the birthday and birthTime into a LocalDateTime object
29         var birthDateTime = LocalDateTime.of(birthday, birthTime);
30
31         // get the current date and time as a LocalDateTime object
32         var now = LocalDateTime.now();
33
34         // show the dates/times
35         displayDatesAndTimes(birthDateTime, now);
36
Birth date/time: Jul 20, 1969, 10:56:00 AM
Current date/time: Jun 15, 2024, 11:40:59 AM
Calculating the Period and Duration Between the LocalDateTime Objects

Lines 38 and 41 calculate the difference between the birth date/time and the current date/time in years, months and days, then hours, minutes, and seconds:

Click here to view code image

37         // calculate date/time difference in years, months and days
38         var period = Period.between(birthday, now.toLocalDate());
39
40         // calculate date/time difference in hours, minutes and seconds
41         var duration = Duration.between(birthDateTime, now);
42

Lines 38 and 41 use methods of the Period and Duration classes:

  • The Period class’s static method between (line 38) returns a Period object representing the difference between two LocalDate objects in years, months and days. Here, we pass the birthday object created in line 22 and the now object’s LocalDate representation returned by the LocalDateTime class’s static toLocalDate method. This method ignores a LocalDateTime’s time part.

  • Duration class’s static method between (line 41) returns a Duration object representing the difference between two LocalDateTime objects (birthDateTime and now) in hours, minutes and seconds. This calculation uses the full dates and times.

Determining a Date’s Day of the Week

Lines 44–46 display the day of the week on which the user was born:

Click here to view code image

43         // display day of the week the user was born
44         System.out.printf("You were born on a %s%n%n",
45            birthday.getDayOfWeek().getDisplayName(
46               TextStyle.FULL, Locale.getDefault()));
47
You were born on a Sunday

The LocalDate class’s getDayOfWeek method (line 45) returns a constant from the DayOfWeek enum, which contains constants for all seven days. Each day has a human-readable, locale-specific string representation returned by the DayOfWeek enum’s getDisplayName method, which has two arguments:

  • The TextStyle.FULL12 constant (line 46) specifies that the full name of the day should be returned (e.g., “Monday”, “Tuesday”).

    12. “Enum Class TextStyle,” Accessed September 21, 2024. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/time/format/TextStyle.html.

  • The second argument specifies the locale to use for formatting. The Locale class’s static getDefault method (line 46) returns the default Locale object with settings specific to the user’s system.

Displaying How Long the User Has Been Alive

Lines 49–61 display how long the user has been alive in years, months and days, then in total months, days, hours, minutes and seconds—here we define printf’s format string as a text block that specifies the output’s line-by-line layout:

  • Line 58 calls the Period class’s getYears, getMonths and getDays methods to get the number of years, months and days between the birth date and time and the current date and time.

  • Line 59 calls the Period class’s toTotalMonths method to determine the total number of months in the Period.

  • Line 60 calls the LocalDate class’s until method to determine the difference between the LocalDate birthday and its first argument—the date part of the now returned by now.toLocalDate(). Method until’s second argument specifies the units in which the difference is returned. ChronoUnit.DAYS indicates the difference should be converted to days.

  • Line 61 calls the Duration enum’s toHours, toMinutes and toSeconds methods to get the number of hours, minutes and seconds between the birth date and time and the current date and time.

53                  Total days: %,d

Jul 20, 1969, 10:56:00 PM

Lines 74 and 76 convert the LocalDateTime objects to strings for display by calling the LocalDateTime class’s format method. The argument is the DateTimeFormatter object (formatter, line 69) that specifies the formatting. The Date/Time API also provides extensive support for specifying custom locales, rather than simply working with the system’s default locale.

5.12.2 Running the Program for a Different Locale Than Your Own

You can customize the Java runtime by passing -D options to the java command, as you’ll see below. Each option is specified as -D flag followed immediately by a system property’s name. For dates, times and numeric locale-specific formatting in other languages, countries and time zones, you can run the AgeCalculator program with the following options:

  • -Duser.language specifies a language code.

  • -Duser.country specifies a country code.

  • -Duser.timezone specifies a timezone code.

For example, to set the language to Spanish, the country to Spain, and the time zone to Europe/Madrid, you can execute the program as follows:

5.13 Wrap-Up

In this chapter, you created your first custom method declarations. You declared named constants using enum types. You used the class RandomGenerator to generate random numbers for simulations and game-playing. You learned that some applications require secure random numbers for which you can use class SecureRandom.

We introduced the switch enhancements and showed that they can more concisely represent switch logic. We also showed switch expressions that yield values—these simplify the code pattern in which a variable declaration is followed by a switch statement that assigns a value to the variable in every branch.

You learned about the scope of fields and local variables in a class. We showed that multiple methods in a class can be overloaded by providing methods with the same name and different signatures—such methods typically perform the same or similar tasks using different types and/or numbers of parameters.

We used the Math class to introduce static class members, then discussed why main is static. You learned about some of the commonly used packages in the Java API. You saw how the method-call stack and stack frames keep track of the methods that have been called and where each method must return to when it completes its task. We also discussed Java’s promotion rules for converting implicitly between primitive types and how to perform explicit conversions with cast operators.

You continued using generative AI to leverage your Java learning experience. In the Objects-Natural Case Study, you used capabilities of the Java Date/Time API to perform common date and time manipulations in an application that input your birth date and birth time, then determined how long you’ve been alive in years, months, days, hours, minutes and seconds, and on what day of the week you were born.

We’ll discuss more details of methods in Chapter 8, Real-World Modeling with Custom Classes—where you’ll declare your own classes, create objects of those classes and invoke their methods—and Chapter 22, Recursion and Big O.

In Chapter 6, you’ll learn how to maintain lists and tables of data in arrays. You’ll see a more elegant implementation of the program that rolls a die 60,000,000 times. You’ll also learn how to access a program’s command-line arguments that the JVM passes to method main when a program begins execution.

6.1 Introduction

This chapter introduces data structures, which enable you to store collections of related data items. Array objects are data structures containing data items of the same type and make it convenient to process related groups of values. In this chapter, we:

  • Examine the differences between primitive types and reference types and show that arrays can be used to store both.

  • Discuss how to declare, create and initialize arrays, and demonstrate common array manipulations, such as calculating array-element values, totaling array elements, visualizing array data and using array elements as counters.

  • Introduce Java’s exception-handling mechanism, using it to process an error that occurs when a program attempts to access a non-existent array element.

  • Demonstrate the enhanced for statement for processing an array’s data more conveniently and with fewer potential errors than with the counter-controlled for statement.

  • Introduce two-dimensional arrays for representing tables containing rows and columns of data.

  • Declare and manipulate several two-dimensional arrays, iterating through them using nested counting for loops and nested enhanced for loops.

  • Create methods that can be called with varying numbers of arguments and show how to manipulate the main method’s command-line arguments via its args parameter.

  • Use array manipulation methods from class Arrays (package java.util) to avoid “reinventing the wheel.”

You’ll continue using generative AI to leverage your Java learning experience. This chapter’s Objects-Natural Case Study introduces the ArrayList collection class—a reusable, reliable, powerful and efficient data structure that is similar to an array but is dynamically resizable to accommodate more or fewer elements.

6.2 Primitive Types vs. Reference Types

 

Java’s types are either primitive types or reference types. The eight primitive types are boolean, byte, char, short, int, long, float and double—you’ve created variables of types int and double. You’ve also worked with objects of reference types including Scanner, String, BigInteger, BigDecimal, RandomGenerator and various types from the Java Date/Time API. All nonprimitive types are reference types.

Primitive-Type Variables Store Values

A primitive-type variable holds exactly one value of its declared type at a time. Consider the following int variable declaration:

int number = 7;

After this statement executes, number contains the value 7, as in the following diagram:

When you assign a new value to number, the new value replaces 7, and the previous value is lost.

Reference-Type Variables Store the Locations of Objects

Reference-type variables store references to objects that are located elsewhere in memory. For example, given the following declaration

String name = "Paul";

the variable name refers to a String object somewhere in memory containing "Paul", as in the following diagram:

You use the variable name to refer to String object and call its methods. For example, the following statement calls the String object’s length method and stores the result in the int primitive variable length:

int length = name.length();

You can invoke methods via reference-type variables, which refer to objects, but not via primitive-type variables.

6.3 Arrays

An array is a group of variables (called elements) containing data of the same type. Arrays are objects, so they’re reference types—an array variable contains a reference to an array object in memory. The elements of an array can be primitive types or reference types (including other arrays, as shown in Section 6.16). To refer to a particular element in an array, we specify the name of the reference to the array and the index (that is, position number) of the element in the array.

The following diagram shows a visual representation of an int array named c:

Array names follow the same conventions as other variable names. This array contains five elements. A program refers to any one of these elements with an array-access expression that includes the name of the array followed by the index of the particular element in square brackets, [ ]—e.g., c[0]. The first element in every array has index 0. Thus, the elements of the array c are c[0] (pronounced “c sub zero”) through c[4]. The value of c[0] is -45, c[2] is 0 and c[4] is 1543. An array-access expression can be used on the left side of an assignment to place a new value into an array element. For example, the following statement replaces c[4]’s value:

c[4] = 87;

An index must be a nonnegative integer expression. The highest index (in this case, 4) is always one less than the array’s size (in this case, 5). Each array knows its own size (number of elements), which you can access via its length instance variable, as in

c.length

An array’s length cannot be changed after it’s created.

6.4 Declaring and Creating Arrays

 

An array object’s elements occupy contiguous space in memory, enabling efficient access to the elements by their indices. To create an array object, you use an array-creation expression consisting of new followed by the array’s element type and square brackets specifying the number of elements. Such an expression returns a reference that can be stored in an array variable. The following declaration and array-creation expression create an array object containing five int elements and store the array’s reference in the array variable named c:

int[] c = new int[5];

When you create an array, each element receives a default value—zero for numeric primitive-type elements, false for boolean elements and null for reference-type elements. The value null indicates that a reference-type variable does not currently refer to an object. You’ll soon see that you can provide non-default element values when you create an array.

Declaring an Array Variable and Creating an Array in Separate Statements

Creating an array can also be performed in two steps as follows:

Click here to view code image

int[] c; // declare the array variable
c = new int[5]; // create the array; assign to array variable

In the declaration, the square brackets following the type indicate that c is a variable that will refer to an array—the declaration does not reserve any memory for the array’s elements. In the assignment statement, the array variable c receives the reference to a new array of five int elements.

Creating Multiple Arrays in One Statement

A program can create several arrays in a single declaration. The following declaration reserves 100 elements for b and 27 elements for x:

Click here to view code image

String[] b = new String[100], x = new String[27];

When the array’s element type and the square brackets are combined at the beginning of the declaration, all the identifiers in the declaration are array variables. In this case, variables b and x refer to String arrays. For readability and clarity, declare only one variable per declaration. The preceding declaration is equivalent to:

Click here to view code image

String[] b = new String[100]; // create array b
String[] x = new String[27]; // create array x
Placement of the Square Brackets in Array Variable Declarations

Declaring multiple array variables in a single declaration can lead to subtle errors. Consider the declaration

int[] a, b, c;

This declares a, b and c as array variables. Again, placing square brackets directly following the type indicates that all the identifiers in the declaration are array variables. However, if only a is intended to be an array variable, and b and c are intended to be individual int variables, then the declaration should be

int a[], b, c;

In this declaration, int distributes to each variable, but the square brackets apply only to the variable a. So, a can store a reference to an array of ints, and b and c can store individual int values. Declaring each variable in a separate variable-declaration statement eliminates this confusion.

Primitive-Type vs. Reference-Type Elements

A program can declare arrays with elements of any type:

  • Every element of a primitive-type array is a variable that contains a value of the array’s declared element type. For example, every int array element is a variable that stores an int value.

  • Every element of a reference-type array is a variable that can refer to an object of the array’s declared element type. For example, every String array element is a variable that can refer to a String object.

6.5 Creating and Initializing an Array

The program of Fig. 6.1 uses the keyword new to create an array of five int elements, which are initially zero—the default initial value for int array elements. Line 7 declares array—a reference-type variable capable of referring to an array of int elements—then initializes it with a reference to an array object containing five int elements. Line 9 outputs the column headings. The first column contains each array element’s index (0–4), and the second column contains each array element’s default initial value (0).

The for statement (lines 12–14) outputs the index (represented by counter) and value of each array element (represented by array[counter]). The control variable counter is initially 0 because index values start at 0. Using zero-based counting allows the loop to access every element. The for’s loop-continuation condition uses the expression array.length (line 12) to determine the array’s length. In this example, the length is five, so the loop continues executing as long as counter’s value is less than 5. A five-element array’s highest index value is 4, so using the less-than operator in the loop-continuation condition ensures the loop does not attempt to access an element beyond the end of the array—during the loop’s final iteration, counter is 4. We’ll soon see what Java does when encountering an out-of-range index at execution time.

Generative AI

1 Prompt genAIs to find and correct the error(s) in the following code:

Click here to view code image

int[] values = new int[10];

for (int i = 0; i <= values.length; ++i) {
   System.out.println(values[i]);
}

Confirm that their responses indicate the loop-continuation test causes the code to reference an out-of-bounds array element (values[10]) and change the <= operator to <.

6.6 Array Initializers

You can create an array and initialize its elements with an array initializer—a comma-separated list of expressions enclosed in braces. In this case, the array length is determined by the number of elements in the array initializer. For example,

Click here to view code image

int[] n = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};

creates a five-element array with index values 0–4. Element n[0] is initialized to 10, n[1] to 20, etc. When the compiler encounters an array declaration that includes an array initializer, it counts the number of initializers in the list to determine the array’s size and creates a new array of that size for you.

Figure 6.2 initializes an integer array with five values (line 7) and displays the array in tabular format. The code for displaying the array elements (lines 12–14) is identical to that in Fig. 6.1 (lines 12–14).

Rather than using array initializers, as in line 7, array element values are often read into a program. For example, you could input the values from a user or a file on disk, as discussed in Chapter 11, Files, I/O Streams, JSON Serialization & CSV Files. Reading the data into a program (rather than “hand coding” it into the program) makes the program more reusable because it can be used with different data sets.

6.7 Calculating Array Element Values

Figure 6.3 creates a five-element array, assigns an even integer from 2 through 10 to each element, then displays the array in tabular format. The for statement in lines 10–12 calculates an array element’s value by multiplying the current value of the control variable counter by 2, then adding 2. Lines 17–19 display each array element’s index and value.

We specified the array’s size using the ARRAY_LENGTH constant variable (line 6) declared with the final modifier and initialized to 5. Constant variables must be initialized before use and cannot be modified thereafter. Attempting to modify a final variable after it’s initialized causes a compilation error. Like enum constants, constant variables are named constants. They often make programs more readable. A named constant such as ARRAY_LENGTH clearly indicates its purpose, whereas a literal value such as 5 could have different meanings based on its context. Constant variables use all uppercase letters by convention, and multiword names should separate each word from the next with an underscore (_) as in ARRAY_LENGTH.

6.8 Totaling Array Elements

Array elements often stored values for use in calculations. For example, if an array’s elements represent exam grades, a professor may wish to total them and use the sum to calculate the class average. Lines 10–12 in Fig. 6.4 sum the values in the 10-element int array grades (created and initialized at line 6).
