8.7 Case Study: Time Class

 

Our next example consists of classes Time1 (Fig. 8.10) and Time1Test (Fig. 8.11). Class Time1 represents the time of day. Class Time1Test’s main method creates one Time1 object and invokes its methods. The program’s output appears in Fig. 8.11.

Time1 Class Declaration

Class Time1’s private int instance variables hour, minute and second (Fig. 8.10, lines 5–7) represent the time in universal-time format (24-hour clock format in which hours are in the range 0–23, and minutes and seconds are each in the range 0–59). Time1 contains public methods setTime (lines 11–22), toUniversalString (lines 25–27) and toString (lines 30–34). These methods are the public services or the public interface the class provides to its clients.

Default Constructor

Class Time1 does not declare a constructor, so the compiler supplies a default constructor. Each instance variable implicitly receives the default int value (0).

Method setTime and Throwing Exceptions

Method setTime (lines 11–22) is a public method with three int parameters used to set the time. Lines 13–14 test each argument to determine whether the value is outside the proper range. The hour value must be greater than or equal to 0 and less than 24 because the universal-time format represents hours as integers from 0 to 23 (e.g., 1 PM is hour 13, 11 PM is hour 23, midnight is hour 0, and noon is hour 12). Similarly, both minute and second values must be greater than or equal to 0 and less than 60. If the argument values are valid, lines 19–21 assign them to the hour, minute and second instance variables. You should modify an object’s instance variables only if a method’s arguments are all valid.

For invalid values, setTime throws an IllegalArgumentException (lines 15–16) to notify the client code of the problem. Line 15 creates a new IllegalArgumentException object and calls its constructor that receives a custom error message. Next, the throw statement immediately terminates setTime and returns the exception to the calling method. Then, the client code can handle the exception using try...catch (Section 6.12).

Method toUniversalString

Method toUniversalString (lines 25–27) takes no arguments and returns a String in universal-time format, consisting of two digits each for the hour, minute and second—recall that you can use the 0 flag in a printf format specification (e.g., "%02d") to display leading zeros for a value that doesn’t use all the character positions in the specified field width. For example, if the time were 1:30:07 PM, the method would return 13:30:07. Line 26 uses static String method format to return a String containing the formatted hour, minute and second values, each with two digits and possibly a leading 0 (specified with the 0 flag). The format method is similar to printf, but returns a formatted String rather than displaying it.

Method toString

Method toString (lines 30–34) takes no arguments and returns a String in 12-hour format, consisting of the hour, minute and second values separated by colons and followed by AM or PM (e.g., 11:30:17 AM or 1:27:06 PM). Like toUniversalString, toString uses static String method format to format the minute and second as two-digit values, with leading zeros if necessary. Line 32 uses a conditional operator (?:) to determine the hour value in the String. If the hour is 0 or 12 (AM or PM), it appears as 12; otherwise, it appears as a value from 1 to 11. The conditional operator in line 33 determines whether AM or PM will be returned as part of the String.

Using Class Time1

Class Time1Test (Fig. 8.11) uses class Time1. Line 7 declares the Time1 variable time and initializes it with a new Time1 object. Operator new implicitly invokes class Time1’s default constructor because Time1 does not declare any constructors. To confirm that the Time1 object was initialized properly, line 10 calls the private method displayTime (lines 31–34), which, in turn, calls the Time1 object’s toUniversalString and toString methods to output the time in universal-time format and standard-time format, respectively. Note that toString could have been called implicitly here rather than explicitly. Next, line 14 calls the time object’s setTime method to change the time. Then, line 15 outputs the time in both formats again to confirm the time was set correctly.

Methods declared private, such as displayTime, can be called only by other methods of the same class. Such methods are utility methods or helper methods because that support the operation of the class’s other methods.

Calling Time1 Method setTime with Invalid Values

To illustrate that method setTime validates its arguments, line 20 calls method setTime with invalid arguments of 99 for the hour, minute and second. This statement is placed in a try block (lines 19–21) in case setTime throws an IllegalArgumentException, which it will do since the arguments are all invalid. When this occurs, the exception is caught at lines 22–24, and line 23 displays the exception’s error message by calling its getMessage method. Line 27 outputs the time again in both formats to confirm that setTime did not change the time when invalid arguments were supplied.

Software Engineering of the Time1 Class Declaration

Consider class Time1’s design. Instance variables hour, minute and second are private. The data representation used in the class is of no concern to the class’s clients. For example, it would be reasonable for Time1 to represent the time internally as the number of seconds since midnight or the number of minutes and seconds since midnight. Clients could use the same public methods and get the same results without being aware of this change. You’ll ask generative AIs to make this change in Generative AI question 1.

Classes simplify programming because the client can use only a class’s public methods. Such methods are client-oriented rather than implementation-oriented. Clients are neither aware of nor involved in a class’s implementation. Clients generally care about what the class does, not how the class does it.

Interfaces change less frequently than implementations. When an implementation changes, implementation-dependent code must change accordingly. Hiding the implementation reduces the possibility that other program parts will become dependent on a class’s implementation details.

Java Date/Time API

This section’s example and several of this chapter’s later examples demonstrate various class-implementation concepts in classes that represent dates and times. In professional Java development, you should use the Java Date/Time API’s features, like those we introduced in Section 5.12, rather than building your own date and time classes. We use some additional Date/Time API features in Chapter 18.

8.8 Controlling Access to Members

The access modifiers public and private control access to a class’s variables and methods. In Chapter 9, we’ll introduce the additional access modifier protected. The primary purpose of public methods is to present to the class’s clients a view of the class’s services—the class’s public interface.

Figure 8.12 demonstrates that private class members are not accessible outside the class. Lines 7–9 attempt to access the private instance variables hour, minute and second of the Time1 object time. When this program is compiled, the compiler generates error messages indicating these private members are inaccessible. This program assumes that the Time1 class from Fig. 8.10 is used. An attempt by a method that’s not a member of a class to access a private member of that class generates a compilation error.

8.9 Referring to the Current Object’s Members with the this Reference

Every object can access a reference to itself with keyword this. When an instance method is called for a particular object, the method’s body implicitly uses “this.” to refer to the object’s instance variables and other methods, enabling the class’s code to know which object to manipulate. As you’ll see in Fig. 8.13, you can also use “this.” explicitly in an instance method’s body. Section 8.10 shows another interesting use of the this keyword. Section 8.16 explains why “this.” cannot be used in a static method.

Figure 8.13 demonstrates implicit and explicit use of the this reference. This example is the first in which we declare two classes in one file—class ThisTest is declared in lines 4–9, and class SimpleTime in lines 12–41. When you compile a source-code (.java) file, the compiler produces a separate .class file for every class in that file. In this case, two files are produced—SimpleTime.class and ThisTest.class. The compiler places these files in the same folder. Note also in Fig. 8.13 that only class ThisTest is declared public. A source-code (.java) file may contain only one public class—recall that every public class must be declared in a file that has the class’s name followed by the .java filename extension. Non-public classes can be used only by other classes in the same package, and classes compiled into the same folder are in the same package. So, SimpleTime can be used only in class ThisTest.

Class SimpleTime (lines 12–41) declares three private instance variables—hour, minute and second (lines 13–15). The class’s constructor (lines 20–24) receives three int arguments to initialize a SimpleTime object. Once again, we used parameter names for the constructor that are identical to the class’s instance-variable names (lines 13–15), so we use “this.” to refer to the instance variables in lines 21–23. Most IDEs will issue a warning if you say x = x; instead of this.x = x;. The statement x = x; is often called a no-op (no operation)—in this case, the statement would assign x to itself, which does not modify x.

Method buildString (lines 27–31) returns a String created by a statement that uses the this reference to call toUniversalString explicitly (line 29) and implicitly (line 30). Both lines perform the same operation. You typically will not use this explicitly to reference other methods within the current object. Also, line 39 in toUniversalString explicitly uses “this.” to access each instance variable, though this is not required because the method has no local variables that shadow the class’s instance variables.

There’s only one copy of each method per class—every object of the class shares the method’s code. On the other hand, each object has its own copy of the class’s instance variables. The class’s non-static methods implicitly use this to determine the specific object of the class to manipulate.

Class ThisTest’s main method (lines 5–8) demonstrates class SimpleTime. Line 6 creates a SimpleTime object and invokes its constructor. Line 7 invokes the object’s build-String method then displays the results.

8.10 Case Study: Time Class Overloaded Constructors

 

Next, we demonstrate a class with overloaded constructors, enabling objects of our class to be initialized various ways. Like overloaded methods (Section 5.7), you overload constructors by providing multiple constructor declarations with different signatures.

Class Time2 with Overloaded Constructors

The Time1 class’s default constructor in Fig. 8.10 initialized hour, minute and second to their default 0 values (i.e., midnight in universal time). To initialize objects with non-default values, you must provide custom constructors. Class Time2 (Fig. 8.14) contains five overloaded constructors that enable flexible initialization of Time2 objects by passing different arguments. We broke this class into parts for discussion purposes. Lines 5–7 declare the class’s hour, minute and second instance variables.

Class Time2’s Constructors—Calling One Constructor from Another via this

Each constructor accomplishes the same basic job—initialize a Time2 object’s instance variables. Portions of that work are identical for each constructor, so we’ll share validation and initialization code by having four of them invoke a fifth that, in turn, ensures the hour is in the range 0–23, the minute and second are each in the range 0–59, then initializes them. As with overloaded functions, the compiler invokes the appropriate constructor by matching the number, types and order of a constructor call’s argument types with the number, types and order of the parameter types specified in each constructor declaration. Class Time2 also provides set and get methods for each instance variable.

Time2 Constructor with No Arguments

Lines 11–13 declare a no-argument constructor. Once you declare any constructors in a class, the compiler will not provide a default constructor. This no-argument constructor ensures that class Time2’s clients can create Time2 objects with default values.

13      }

Line 12 uses this to invoke the Time2 constructor that takes three parameters (lines 26–42) with 0 for the hour, minute and second. Using the this keyword as shown here must be the constructor’s first statement and is a common way to avoid duplicate initialization code. A constructor that entrusts its work to another constructor in the same class is a delegating constructor. We use this syntax in four of the five Time2 constructors to make the class easier to maintain and modify—we’ll say more about this momentarily.

Notes Regarding Class Time2’s Set and Get Methods and Constructors

Methods toUniversalString and toString call Time2’s get methods in line 111 and lines 117–118, respectively. These methods could have accessed Time2’s private data directly without calling the get methods but there’s a software-engineering benefit to calling them.

Our internal time representation uses three ints, requiring 12 bytes of memory. Consider changing this to the total seconds since midnight—a single int requiring only four bytes. If we make this change, only the methods that access private data directly need to change. In this case, we’d modify the three-argument constructor, the setTime method and the individual set and get methods for the hour, minute and second. There would be no need to modify toUniversalString and toString because they do not access the data directly. Designing the class in this manner reduces the likelihood of programming errors when altering the class’s implementation.

Similarly, each Time2 delegating constructor could have included a copy of the appropriate statements from the three-argument constructor. This might be slightly more efficient because it would eliminate extra constructor calls. However, duplicating statements makes changing the class’s internal data representation more difficult.6 Having the Time2 delegating constructors call the constructor with three arguments requires making changes only to the three-argument constructor’s implementation. Also, the compiler can optimize programs by removing calls to simple methods and replacing them with the expanded code of their declarations—a technique known as inlining the code, which improves program performance.

6. In Chapter 9, we’ll explain why we chose to duplicate code between class Time2’s constructor and setTime methods.

8.11 Default and No-Argument Constructors

Every class must have at least one constructor. The compiler creates a default constructor with no arguments in a class that does not contain custom constructors. The default constructor initializes the instance variables to the initial values specified in the instance variables’ declarations; otherwise, it uses default values (zero for primitive numeric types, false for boolean values and null for references).

The compiler will not create a default constructor if your class declares constructors. In this case, you must declare a no-argument constructor if default initialization is required. Like a default constructor, a no-argument constructor is invoked with empty parentheses. The Time2 no-argument constructor (lines 11–13 of Fig. 8.14) explicitly initializes a Time2 object by passing to the three-argument constructor 0 for each parameter. Since 0 is the default value for int instance variables, the no-argument constructor in Time2 could be declared with an empty body. In this case, each instance variable would receive its default value when the no-argument constructor is called. If we omit the no-argument constructor, clients of this class would not be able to create a Time2 object with the expression new Time2().

Ensure that you do not include a return type in a constructor definition. Java allows other methods of the class besides its constructors to have the same name as the class and specify return types. Such methods are not constructors and will not be called when an object of the class is instantiated.

8.12 Notes on Set and Get Methods

 

As you know, client code can manipulate a class’s private fields only through the class’s methods. Set methods are commonly called mutator methods because they change an object’s state—i.e., modify the values of instance variables.7 Get methods are commonly called accessor methods or query methods.

7. Other methods besides set methods can also be mutator methods.

Set and Get Methods vs. public Data

It would seem that providing set and get capabilities is essentially the same as making a class’s instance variables public. This is one of the subtleties that makes Java desirable for software engineering.

A public non-final instance variable can be read or written by any method that has a reference to an object containing that variable. A public get method certainly allows client-code methods to access a private instance variable, but the get method can control how the client “sees” the data. For example, a get method might format the data it returns, shielding the client code from the actual data representation. A public set method can—and should—carefully scrutinize attempts to modify the variable’s value and throw an exception if necessary. For example, attempts to set the day of the month to 37 or a person’s weight to a negative value should be rejected. Thus, although set and get methods provide access to private data, the access can be carefully restricted by the method implementations, promoting good software engineering.

Classes should never have public non-constant data. Declaring data public static final enables lets you make constants available to your class’s clients. For example, class Math offers public static final constants Math.PI and Math.E.

Validity Checking in Set Methods

The benefits of data integrity do not follow automatically simply because instance variables are declared private—you must provide validity checking. A class’s set methods could prevent attempts to assign invalid data to objects of the class. Typically, set methods have the void return type and use exception handling to indicate attempts to assign invalid data. We discuss exception handling in detail in Chapter 10.

When appropriate, provide public methods to access private instance variables. This architecture helps hide the implementation of a class from its clients, which improves program modifiability. Using set and get methods helps you create classes that are easier to debug and maintain. If only one method performs a particular operation, such as setting an instance variable in an object, it’s easier to debug and maintain the class. If the instance variable is not being set correctly, the code that actually modifies the instance variable is localized to one set method. Your debugging efforts can be focused on that one method.

Predicate Methods

Another common use for accessor methods is to test whether a condition is true or false—such methods are often called predicate methods. An example is class ArrayList’s isEmpty method, which returns true if the ArrayList is empty and false otherwise. A program might test isEmpty before attempting to read another item from an ArrayList. By convention, predicate method names begin with is rather than get.

8.13 Composition

 

A class can have references to objects of other classes as members. This is called composition and is sometimes referred to as a has-a relationship. For example, an AlarmClock object needs to know the current time and when it’s supposed to sound its alarm, so it’s reasonable to include two references to Time objects in an AlarmClock object. A car has-a steering wheel, a brake pedal, an accelerator pedal and more.

Class Date

This composition example contains classes Date (Fig. 8.16), Employee (Fig. 8.17) and EmployeeTest (Fig. 8.18). Class Date declares instance variables month, day and year (lines 5–7) to represent a date. The constructor receives three int parameters. Lines 15–18 validate the month—if it’s out-of-range, lines 16–17 throw an exception. Lines 21–25 validate the day. If the day is incorrect based on the number of days in the particular month—except February 29th which requires special leap-year testing—lines 23–24 throw an exception. Lines 28–29 perform the leap-year testing for February. If the month is February, the day is 29 and the year is not a leap year, lines 30–31 throw an exception. If no exceptions are thrown, then lines 34–36 initialize the Date’s instance variables and line 38 outputs the this reference as a String. Since this refers to the current Date object, the object’s toString method (lines 42–44) is called implicitly to get the object’s String representation. In this example, we assume that the year value is correct—an industrial-strength Date class should also validate the year.

Class Employee

Class Employee (Fig. 8.17) has reference-type instance variables firstName (String), lastName (String), birthDate (Date) and hireDate (Date), showing that a class can have as instance variables references to objects of other classes. The Employee constructor (lines 11–17) takes four parameters, representing the first name, last name, birth date and hire date. The objects referenced by the parameters are assigned to an Employee object’s instance variables. When Employee’s toString method is called, it returns a String containing the employee’s name and the String representations of the two Date objects. Each String is obtained with an implicit call to the Date class’s toString method.

Class EmployeeTest

Class EmployeeTest (Fig. 8.18) creates two Date objects representing an Employee’s birthday and hire date. Line 8 creates an Employee and initializes its instance variables by passing to the constructor two Strings (representing the Employee’s first and last names) and two Date objects (representing the birthday and hire date). Line 10 implicitly invokes the Employee’s toString method to display the values of its instance variables and demonstrate that the object was correctly initialized.

8.14 enum Types

 

In Fig. 5.4, we introduced the basic enum type, which defines a set of constants represented as unique identifiers. In that program, the enum constants represented the game’s status. In this section, we discuss the relationship between enum types and classes. Like classes, all enum types are reference types. An enum declaration creates an enum type containing a comma-separated list of enum constants. The declaration may optionally include other components of traditional classes, such as constructors, fields and methods (as you’ll see momentarily). Each enum declaration declares an enum class with the following restrictions:

  1. enum constants are implicitly final because constants cannot be modified.

  2. enum constants are implicitly static—since they can’t be modified, only one copy of the constant is needed.

Any attempt to create an object of an enum type with operator new results in a compilation error. The enum constants can be used anywhere constants can be used, such as in the case labels of switch statements and to control enhanced for statements.

Declaring Instance Variables, a Constructor and Methods in an enum Type

Figure 8.19 demonstrates instance variables, a constructor and methods in an enum type. The enum declaration contains two parts—the enum constants and the other members of the enum type.

Lines 7–12 declare six constants. Each is optionally followed by arguments that are passed to the enum Book’s constructor (lines 19–22). Like the constructors in classes, an enum constructor can specify any number of parameters and can be overloaded. In this example, the enum constructor requires two String parameters, specifying the book’s title and copyright year. To properly initialize each enum constant, we follow it with parentheses containing two String arguments. In an enum declaration, the enum constants must be declared before the enum’s constructors, fields and methods.

The second part (lines 15–32) declares the enum’s other members—instance variables title and copyrightYear (lines 15–16), a constructor (lines 19–22) and two methods (lines 25–27 and 30–32) that return the book title and copyright year, respectively. Each constant in type Book is an object of type Book that has its own copy of instance variables.

Using enum type Book

Figure 8.20 tests the Book enum and illustrates how to iterate through a range of its constants. For every enum, the compiler generates the static method values (called in line 10), which returns an array of the enum’s constants in their declaration order. Lines 10–13 display the constants. Line 12 invokes the enum Book’s getTitle and getCopyrightYear methods to get the title and copyright year associated with the constant. When an enum constant is implicitly converted to a String (e.g., book in line 11), the constant’s identifier is used as the String representation (e.g., JHTP for the first enum constant).

Lines 18–21 use the static method range of class EnumSet (package java.util) to display a range of the enum Book’s constants. Method range takes two parameters—the first and the last enum constants in the range—and returns an EnumSet that contains all the constants between these two constants, inclusive. For example, the expression EnumSet.range(Book.JHTP, Book.CPPHTP) returns an EnumSet containing Book.JHTP, Book.CHTP, Book.CPP20FP and Book.CPPHTP. The enhanced for statement can be used with an EnumSet just as it can with an array. Lines 18–21 use it to display the title and copyright year of every book in the EnumSet. Class EnumSet provides several other static methods for creating sets of enum constants from the same enum type.

8.15 Garbage Collection

Every object uses system resources, such as memory. We need a disciplined way to give resources back to the system when they’re no longer needed; otherwise, “resource leaks” might occur that would prevent resources from being reused by your program or others. The JVM performs automatic garbage collection to reclaim the memory occupied by objects that are no longer used.

If there are no more references to an object, the object is eligible to be collected when the JVM executes its garbage collector. This might not occur right away. If a program terminates before garbage collection occurs, all of its memory is returned to the system. So, memory leaks common in other languages like C and C++ (because they do not automatically reclaim memory) are less likely in Java. However, some can still happen in subtle ways.

Resource leaks other than memory leaks can also occur. For example, a program may open a file on secondary storage to modify its contents. If the program does not close the file, it must terminate before another program can use the file.

Many Java API classes (e.g., class Scanner and classes that read from or write to files) provide close or dispose methods that can release resources when they’re no longer needed in a program.

8.16 static Class Members

 

Every object has its own copy of its class’s instance variables. Sometimes, one variable should be shared by all objects of a class. A static field—called a class variable—represents classwide information. All objects of the class share the class’s static fields.

Motivating static

Let’s motivate static data with an example. Suppose we have a video game with Martians and other space creatures. Each Martian tends to be brave and willing to attack other space creatures when the Martian is aware that at least four other Martians are present. If fewer than five Martians are present, each becomes cowardly. Thus, each Martian needs to know the martianCount. We could endow class Martian with martianCount as an instance variable. Then, every Martian would have a separate copy of the instance variable, and every time we create a new Martian or destroy an existing one, we’d have to update the martianCount in every Martian object. This wastes space with the redundant copies, wastes time updating the separate copies and is error-prone. Instead, we declare martianCount to be static, making martianCount classwide data so every Martian can access it. This saves space. The Martian constructor would increment the static martianCount as each new Martian is created. Since there’s only one copy, we do not have to increment separate copies for each Martian object. Similarly, when a Martian is destroyed, a method of the class would be called to decrement the martianCount.

Class Scope

A class’s static variables have class scope—they can be used in all of the class’s methods. We can access a class’s public static members through a reference to any object of the class or by qualifying the member name with the class name and a dot (.), as in Math.sqrt(2). A class’s private static class members can be accessed by client code only through the class’s methods. The static class members exist even when no objects of the class exist—they’re available as soon as the class is loaded into memory at execution time. To access a public static member when no objects of the class exist (and when they do), prefix the class name and a dot (.) to the static member, as in Math.PI. To access a private static member when no objects of the class exist, provide a public static method and call it by qualifying its name with the class name and a dot.

static Methods Cannot Directly Access Instance Variables and Instance Methods

A static method cannot directly access a class’s instance variables and instance methods because a static method can be called even when no objects of the class have been instantiated. So, “this.” cannot be used in a static method. Java creates the this reference only in instance methods because it must refer to a specific object of the class. When a static method is called, there might not be any objects of its class in memory.

Tracking the Number of Employee Objects That Have Been Created

Our next program declares two classes—Employee (Fig. 8.21) and EmployeeTest (Fig. 8.22). Class Employee declares private static variable count (Fig. 8.21, line 6) and public static method getCount (lines 32–34). The static variable count maintains a count of the number of Employee objects created so far. This class variable is initialized to 0 in line 6. If a static variable is not initialized, the compiler assigns it a default value—in this case, 0, the default value for type int.

When Employee objects exist, the variable count can be used in any method of an Employee object. This example increments count in the constructor (line 16). The public static method getCount (lines 32–34) returns the number of Employee objects created so far. When no objects of class Employee exist, client code can access variable count by calling method getCount via the class name, as in Employee.getCount(). Invoke every static method using the class name and a dot (.) to emphasize that the method is static.

Class EmployeeTest

EmployeeTest method main (Fig. 8.22) instantiates two Employee objects (lines 11–12). When each Employee object’s constructor is invoked, it initializes the Employee’s instance variables firstName and lastName, then adds one to the Employee static variable count.

When main terminates, local variables e1 and e2 are discarded—remember that a local variable exists only until the block in which it’s declared completes execution. Because e1 and e2 were the only references to the Employee objects created in lines 11–12 (Fig. 8.22), these objects become “eligible for garbage collection” as main terminates.

In a typical app, the garbage collector might eventually reclaim the memory for any objects that are eligible for collection. If any objects are not reclaimed before the program terminates, the operating system will reclaim the memory used by the program. The JVM does not guarantee when, or even if, the garbage collector will execute. When it does, it’s possible that no objects or a subset of the eligible objects will be collected.

8.17 static Import

 

In Section 5.8, you learned about the static fields and methods of class Math—we access these by preceding each with the class name Math and a dot (.). A static import declaration enables you to import a class’s static members so you can access them via their unqualified names in your class—without the class name and a dot (.).

static Import Forms

A static import declaration has two forms that are listed in the Java Language Specification’s language grammar as SingleStaticImportDeclaration and StaticImportOnDemand-Declaration:

  • A SingleStaticImportDeclaration imports a specific static member.

  • A StaticImportOnDemandDeclaration imports all static members of a class.

A SingleStaticImportDeclaration consists of a package name (e.g., java.lang), a class name and the name of a static method or field, as in:

Click here to view code image

import static packageName.ClassName.staticMemberName;

A StaticImportOnDemandDeclaration consists of a package name (e.g., java.lang), a class name and an asterisk (*) indicating that all static members of the class should be available for use in the file, as in:

Click here to view code image

import static packageName.ClassName.*;

Such declarations import only static class members. Regular import statements should be used to specify the classes used in a program.

Demonstrating static Import

Figure 8.23 demonstrates a static import. Line 3 is a StaticImportOnDemandDeclaration, which imports all of class Math’s static fields and methods. Lines 7–10 access the Math class’s static methods sqrt (line 7) and ceil (line 8) and its static fields E (line 9) and PI (line 10) without qualifying their names with class name Math and a dot.

8.18 final Instance Variables

The principle of least privilege is fundamental to good software engineering. In the context of an app’s code, it states that code should be granted only the amount of privilege and access needed to accomplish its designated operation, but no more. This makes your programs more robust by preventing code from accidentally (or maliciously) modifying variable values and calling methods that should not be accessible.

Let’s see how this principle applies to instance variables. Some should be modifiable, and some should not. You can use the keyword final to specify that a variable is not modifiable (i.e., it’s a constant) and that any attempt to modify it is an error. For example,

private final int INCREMENT;

declares a final (constant) int instance variable INCREMENT. Such variables can be initialized when they’re declared. If they’re not, they must be initialized in every constructor and cannot be changed after the object is constructed. Initializing constants in constructors enables each object of the class to have a different value for the constant. A compilation error occurs if a final variable is not initialized in its declaration or in every constructor. By convention, identifiers for constants use all capital letters with words separated by underscores (_).

Attempting to modify a final instance variable after it’s initialized is a compilation error caught at compilation time rather than execution time. It’s always preferable to get bugs out at compilation time, if possible, rather than at execution time (where experience has shown that repair is often far more costly).

Declaring an instance variable as final helps enforce the principle of least privilege. If an instance variable should not be modified, declare it final to prevent modification. For example, in Fig. 8.17, the instance variables firstName, lastName, birthDate and hireDate are never modified after initialization, so they should be declared final. Testing, debugging and maintaining programs is easier when every variable that can be final is, in fact, final. You’ll see additional benefits of final in Chapter 18, Concurrency: Platform Threads to Virtual Threads.

A final field should be static if it’s initialized in its declaration to a value that’s the same for all objects of the class. Making the field static enables all objects of the class to share the final field.

8.19 Package Access

If a method or field of a class is not declared with an access modifier, it has package access by default. In a program with one class, this has no effect. In a program with multiple classes in the same package, the classes can access each other’s package-access members directly through references to objects of those classes or through the class name for static members. Package access is rarely used.

Figure 8.24 demonstrates package access. The program contains two classes in one source-code file—class PackageDataTest (lines 5–19) and class PackageData (lines 22–30). Classes in the same source file are part of the same package. So, PackageDataTest is allowed to modify the package-access data of PackageData objects. In the PackageData class declaration, lines 23–24 declare the instance variables number and string with no access modifiers—so, these are package-access instance variables. Class PackageDataTest’s main method creates a PackageData object (line 7) then modifies the PackageData instance variables directly (lines 13–14). When you compile this program, the compiler produces the files PackageDataTest.class and PackageData.class and places them in the same folder.

8.20 record Classes

 

Some programming languages provide a fixed-size, immutable data structure called a tuple that simply groups related data items. In those languages, you can pass tuple objects to methods, return them from methods and conveniently access their data items. They basically carry data from one portion of a program to another. Java’s record classes8 provide a compact syntax for declaring data-carrier classes that enable you to create objects and use them similarly to tuples.

8. “JEP 395: Records.” Accessed July 12, 2024. https://openjdk.org/jeps/395.

When declaring a record class, you specify its instance variable names and types, and the Java compiler conveniently autogenerates “boilerplate” code for you, including:

  • a private final instance variable for each of the related data items you specify—a record’s instance variables are immutable,9

    9. In Chapter 18, Concurrency: Platform Threads to Virtual Threads, we’ll discuss various benefits of immutable objects in programs that perform operations concurrently.

  • a public constructor with arguments to initialize each instance variable—this constructor does not validate its arguments, but you can provide validation code,

  • get methods with the same names as the instance variables—each returns its corresponding instance variable’s value,

  • a toString method that returns a record’s String representation in the following form, where variable1, variable2, … are the instance variable names:

    Click here to view code image

    TypeName[variable1=value1,  variable2=value2,  …]

  • an equals method that returns true or false, based on whether the contents of two record objects of the same type have the same contents, and

  • a hashCode method—we discuss this method and the data structures concept known as “hashing” in Section 12.10.

Defining a record Class

Figure 8.25 defines the record class Employee (lines 3–15), representing an employee’s first name (a String), last name (a String), salary (a double for simplicity in this example) and department (a String). We broke the program into pieces for discussion purposes. A record class begins with the record keyword and a type name followed by parentheses containing the class’s instance variables. After the parentheses, the record class’s body is delimited by braces ({ and }). The body’s braces will be empty for record classes that require only the default compiler-generated code.

You can customize the compiler-generated constructor and methods. For the constructor, records use a shorthand notation (lines 10–14) consisting of the record class’s name followed immediately by braces containing the constructor’s data validation code—this code is added to the autogenerated constructor. If the data validation does not throw an exception, the constructor automatically assigns each constructor argument to the corresponding instance variable.

Creating Employee record Objects and Getting Their String Representations

Lines 19–21 create three new Employee objects. As with objects of regular classes, these statements use the record class’s constructor to initialize each object’s data. Line 24 displays the autogenerated String representation of each Employee object—converting any object to a String (%s) in a printf call implicitly calls the object’s toString method.

Java records can also declare static data, static methods and instance methods, and can implement interfaces (Chapter 9). 8.20.1 Pattern Matching for switch Expressions

Since switch expressions were introduced in Java 14, they’ve been enhanced with reference-type pattern-matching capabilities in Java 21.10 Each case can specify a reference type and a variable name to which the controlling-expression object is assigned if its type matches the type in a given case. That case can then manipulate the object via the variable. Figure 8.26 defines record classes for a Rectangle (line 6) with instance variables length and width, and a Circle (line 7) with instance variable radius. We use these with the getPerimeter method (lines 20–26) to calculate a Rectangle’s and a Circle’s perimeters. Lines 10–11 in main create and initialize a Rectangle and a Circle. Lines 12–15 display each object’s String representation and perimeter.

10. “JEP 441: Pattern Matching for switch.” Accessed July 18, 2024. https://openjdk.org/jeps/441.

Method getPerimeter (lines 20–26) receives an Object and returns the calculation result as a double. The parameter type Object indicates that the method can receive any reference-type object as an argument. The pattern-matching switch (lines 21–25) determines the type of the object in its controlling expression:

  • If its type matches a case, the switch stores the object in that case’s variable.

  • Then, the expression to the right of the matching case’s -> uses the variable to get the record object’s data and perform the appropriate perimeter calculation.

The default case executes for any type the switch does not recognize. This example throws an IllegalArgumentException for anything that is not a Rectangle or a Circle.

8.20.2 Decomposing records in switch Expressions

In pattern-matching switch expressions, you can use a record pattern11 to automatically assign the values in a record object to variables used in the case. This is known as decomposing records, and it enables you to access the data items without having to call the record’s get methods. Figure 8.27 modifies Fig. 8.26, using record patterns (lines 23–24) to decompose the Rectangle and Circle objects. You define a record pattern as the record class name followed by parentheses containing the variables in which to place a matching object’s values. The pattern’s variable names need not match the record’s instance variable names. The case can then process the matching object’s data using the pattern’s variables. We used local-variable type inference (var) here to infer the pattern’s variable types from the record classes’ instance variables. Figure 8.27 produces the same results as Fig. 8.26.

11. “JEP 440: Record Patterns.” Accessed March 24, 2024. https://openjdk.org/jeps/440.

8.21 Wrap-Up

In this chapter, you declared custom classes, created objects of those classes and called their methods to perform useful actions. You declared instance variables to maintain data for each object and methods to operate on that data. We discussed the difference between a method’s local variables and a class’s instance variables, and you saw that instance variables are initialized automatically to default values. You used constructors to specify initial values for an object’s instance variables.

We presented a card-shuffling-and-dealing simulation. The Time class case study showed a complete class declaration consisting of private data, overloaded public constructors for initialization flexibility, set and get methods for manipulating the class’s data, and methods that returned String representations of a Time object in standard time and universal time formats. You saw that a class’s toString method returns an object’s String representation and can be called explicitly or implicitly when an object is used where a String is expected. We showed how to throw an exception to indicate that a problem has occurred.

You learned that the this reference is used implicitly in a class’s instance methods to access the class’s instance variables and other instance methods. You also saw explicit uses of this to access the class’s members (including shadowed fields) and, from a constructor, to call another constructor of the same class.

We discussed the differences between default constructors provided by the compiler and no-argument constructors provided by the programmer. You saw that with composition, a class can have references to objects of other classes as members. We discussed more features of enum types. We mentioned Java’s garbage-collection capability and how it (unpredictably) reclaims the memory of objects that are no longer used. We motivated static fields, and demonstrated how to declare and use static fields and methods. You also saw how to declare and initialize final fields.

We discussed package access for fields and methods without an access modifier. You saw the relationship between classes in the same package that allows each class to access the package-access members of other classes in the package.

We introduced record classes and showed that the Java compiler autogenerates various common methods for them. We also showed how record objects can be used with switch expressions to perform different operations based on record class types. Finally, you used record patterns to decompose record objects into their individual data items.

We’ve now introduced the basic concepts of control statements, methods, arrays, collections, classes and objects. The next chapter discusses a core aspect of object-oriented programming in Java—inheritance. You’ll see that all classes in Java are related by inheritance, directly or indirectly, to the class called Object. You’ll explore how the relationships among classes enable you to build powerful applications.

9.1 Introduction

 

In Chapter 1, we introduced the basics of object-oriented programming (OOP) in the context of real-world things—automobiles. With the objects-natural approach, you've been creating objects from preexisting classes and conveniently getting them to perform powerful operations without having to know how they’re built on the inside. This is much like driving an automobile without knowing how to build one.

In Chapter 8, you started building custom classes, which are software models of real-world things. Here in Chapter 9, you'll study the key object-oriented technologies of inheritance, polymorphism and interfaces, which enable you to model the relationships and interactions among real-world objects.

Inheritance

With inheritance, you can base new classes on existing proven software—a new class is created by acquiring an existing class’s capabilities and possibly modifying them or adding new ones. As you’ll see, this is done without copying and pasting source code.

When creating a class, rather than declaring completely new members, you can specify that the new class should inherit the members of an existing one. The existing class is the superclass, and the new class is the subclass. A subclass can add its own fields and methods, making it more specialized than its superclass. The subclass exhibits the behaviors of its superclass. It can override them to operate appropriately for the subclass, so inheritance is sometimes called specialization. A subclass can become a superclass for future subclasses.

We distinguish between the inheritance is-a relationship and composition’s has-a relationship. In an is-a relationship, an object of a subclass can also be treated as an object of its superclass. For example, a car is a vehicle, and a square is a shape. In a has-a relation-ship, an object contains as members references to other objects. For example, a car has a steering wheel (and a car object has a reference to a steering-wheel object).

New classes can inherit from abundant classes in class libraries. Organizations develop their own class libraries and can use others (mostly open-source) available worldwide. This facilitates the rapid development of more powerful, proven and economical software.

Polymorphism

We demonstrate polymorphism with inheritance hierarchies, which enables you to conveniently “program in the general” rather than “program in the specific.” You can write programs with objects that share the same superclass, either directly or indirectly, as if they were all objects of that superclass—this can simplify programming. Polymorphism’s key concept is relying on each object to “do the right thing”—i.e., what’s appropriate for that type of object in response to the same method call. Thus, the same message sent to various types of objects can have many forms of results, hence the term polymorphism.

With polymorphism, we can design and implement systems that are easily extensible—new classes can be added with little or no modification to the general portions of the program. The new classes simply “plug right in.”

Occasionally, when performing polymorphic processing, we might want to “program in the specific.” We’ll see that a program can determine the type of an object at execution time and act on that object accordingly.

Interfaces

We introduce interfaces, which are particularly useful for assigning common functionality to possibly unrelated classes, enabling objects of these classes to be processed polymorphically. Objects of classes that implement the same interface can respond to all of that inter-face’s method calls.

Interfaces define and standardize how things, such as people and systems, can interact. For example, a radio’s controls serve as an interface between radio users and the radio’s internal components. The controls allow users to perform a common set of operations (e.g., turn the radio on or off, change the station, adjust the volume and choose between AM and FM). Radios may implement the controls differently (e.g., push buttons, dials and voice commands). The interface specifies what operations a radio must permit users to perform but does not specify how the operations are performed.1

1. You’ll see later in this chapter that Java interfaces may define default methods that specify how operations are performed by default.

9.2 Superclasses and Subclasses

 

Often, an object of one class is an object of another class as well—e.g., a CarLoan is a Loan, as are HomeImprovementLoans and MortgageLoans. Thus, CarLoan can be said to inherit from Loan. In this context, Loan is a superclass, and CarLoan is a subclass. A CarLoan is a Loan type, but it’s incorrect to claim that every Loan is a CarLoan—it could be any loan type.

Examples of Superclasses and Subclasses

The following table lists several simple examples of superclasses and subclasses. Super-classes tend to be “more general” and subclasses “more specific:”

Because every subclass object is an object of its superclass, and one superclass can have many subclasses, the set of objects a superclass represents is often larger than the set of objects any of its subclasses represent. For example, the superclass Vehicle represents all vehicles, including Cars, Trucks, Airplanes, Boats, etc. By contrast, subclass Car rep-resents a smaller, more specific subset of Vehicles.

University Community Member Class Hierarchy

Inheritance relationships form treelike hierarchical structures—a superclass exists in a hierarchical relationship with its subclasses. Let’s consider a sample class hierarchy—also called an inheritance hierarchy. A university community can have thousands of members, including employees, students and alumni, as shown in the following UML class diagram. Every class hierarchy begins with class Object (in package java.lang), which every class directly or indirectly extends (or “inherits from”). For just this first diagram, we explicitly show class Object at the top of the hierarchy, as all Java classes inherit from it:

Employees are either Faculty or Staff members. Faculty are either Administrators (e.g., deans and department chairpersons) or Teachers. The hierarchy could contain many other classes. For example, Students can be Graduate or Undergraduate students. Undergraduate students can be Freshmen, Sophomores, Juniors or Seniors, and so on.

Each upward-pointing arrow in this class hierarchy represents an is-a relationship. As we follow the arrows, we can state, for example, that “an Employee is a CommunityMember” and “a Teacher is a Faculty member.” The direct superclass is the superclass from which the subclass explicitly inherits. CommunityMember is the direct superclass of the classes Employee, Student and Alum. An indirect superclass is any class above the direct superclass in the class hierarchy, which defines the inheritance relationships among classes. CommunityMember is the indirect superclass of all the classes below Employee in the diagram. Starting from the bottom, you can follow the arrows upward and apply the is-a relation-ship to the topmost superclass. For example, an Administrator is a Faculty member, is an Employee, is a CommunityMember and, of course, is an Object. Section 9.4 discusses class Object in detail.

Java supports single inheritance, in which each class derives from one direct super-class. Java does not support multiple inheritance in which a class derives from more than one direct superclass. Later in the chapter, we explain how to use Java interfaces to realize the benefits of multiple inheritance while avoiding associated problems.

Shape Hierarchy

Now consider the following Shape inheritance hierarchy:

The hierarchy begins with superclass Shape. Shapes are either TwoDimensionalShapes or ThreeDimensionalShapes—the direct subclasses of Shape. The hierarchy’s third level contains specific TwoDimensionalShape and ThreeDimensionalShape types. Again, we can follow the arrows from the bottom of the diagram upward to the topmost superclass in this class hierarchy to identify several is-a relationships. For example, a Triangle is a TwoDimensionalShape and is a Shape, while a Sphere is a ThreeDimensionalShape and is a Shape. This hierarchy could contain many other classes. For example, Ellipses and Trapezoids are also TwoDimensionalShapes and a Cylinder is a ThreeDimensionalShape.

Not every class relationship is an inheritance relationship. For example, Chapter 8 discussed the has-a (composition) relationship, in which classes have instance variables that reference objects of other classes. Given Employee, BirthDate and TelephoneNumber classes, it’s improper to say that an Employee is a BirthDate or that an Employee is a TelephoneNumber. However, it is proper to say that an Employee has a BirthDate, and an Employee has a TelephoneNumber.

It’s possible to treat superclass and subclass objects similarly—their commonalities are expressed in the superclass’s members. Objects of all classes that extend (i.e., inherit from) a common superclass can be treated as objects of that superclass—such objects have an isa relationship with the superclass.

A subclass can customize the methods it inherits from its superclass. To do this, the subclass method overrides (redefines) the superclass method with an implementation appropriate for the subclass.

9.3 Relationship Between Superclasses and Subclasses

We now use an inheritance hierarchy of employee types in a company’s payroll application to demonstrate the relationship between superclasses and subclasses:

  • The superclass SalariedEmployees are paid a fixed weekly salary.

  • The subclass SalariedCommissionEmployees receive a weekly salary plus a percentage of their sales.

We divide our discussion of the relationship between these classes into two examples. The first declares class SalariedEmployee, which directly inherits from class Object and contains the private instance variables name and salary. The second example declares class SalariedCommissionEmployee, which directly inherits from SalariedEmployee and adds private instance variables grossSales and commissionRate and corresponding methods. It also customizes (i.e., overrides) two inherited SalariedEmployee methods. The software reuse provided by inheritance lets us write less code when developing the new subclass than if we had to write it from scratch. Then, we show how a SalariedCommissionEmployee object can use the inherited SalariedEmployee public methods to manipulate (in a controlled manner) the private instance variables inherited from SalariedEmployee.

9.3.1 Creating and Using a SalariedEmployee Class

Let’s examine class SalariedEmployee (Fig. 9.1). Line 5 begins the class declaration and indicates that the class extends (i.e., inherits from) class Object (from package java.lang). This causes class SalariedEmployee to inherit Object’s methods—it does not have any fields. If you don’t specify which class a new class extends, it implicitly extends Object. For this reason, you typically will not include “extends Object” in your code—we do so in this one example for demonstration purposes.

Overview of Class SalariedEmployee’s Methods and Instance Variables

The class declares its instance variables as private (lines 6–7), so objects of other classes cannot directly access these variables. Class SalariedEmployee’s public services include:

  • a constructor (lines 10–20),

  • a public getName method (line 23) to get the value of the final instance variable name (line 6),

  • public methods setSalary and getSalary (lines 26–35) to set and get the instance variable salary (line 7),

  • method calculateEarnings (line 38) to calculate a SalariedEmployee’s earnings, and

  • method toString (lines 41–45) to create a SalariedEmployee’s String representation.

The constructor and setSalary each validate their salary arguments to ensure they’re greater than or equal to 0 before modifying the instance variable salary.

Class SalariedEmployee’s Constructor

A superclass’s constructors are not inherited, but can be called by subclasses. In fact, Java requires each subclass constructor to call its direct superclass’s constructor explicitly or implicitly to initialize the inherited superclass instance variables. We discuss the syntax for calling a superclass constructor explicitly in Section 9.3.2.

In this example, SalariedEmployee’s constructor implicitly calls class Object’s constructor. If the code does not include an explicit call to the superclass constructor, Java implicitly calls the superclass’s default or no-argument constructor. The comment in line 11 indicates where Java implicitly calls the superclass Object’s default constructor. Even if a class does not have constructors, the default constructor that the compiler implicitly declares for the class will call the superclass’s default or no-argument constructor.

We did not validate the name argument before assigning it to the name instance variable (line 18). We could validate it—perhaps to ensure that the name has a reasonable length.

SalariedEmployee Member Function calculateEarnings

Method calculateEarnings (line 38) calls getSalary and returns the result. You may wonder why we bother to provide calculateEarnings given that we can call getSalary directly and get the same result. As you’ll see in Section 9.3.2, class SalariedCommission-Employee will override calculateEarnings to customize how to calculate the earnings for objects of that class. Then, in Section 9.6, we’ll show that polymorphism requires methods in each class that have the same signature.

SalariedEmployee Member Function toString

Method toString (lines 41–45) returns a String containing a SalariedEmployee object’s information, which we obtain by calling the class’s get methods. Method toString is one of the methods that every class inherits directly or indirectly from class Object (summarized in Section 9.4). As you’ve seen, the JVM calls toString implicitly when an object must be converted to a String representation, such as when you output an object as a String with printf or format an object as a String with String method format. Class Object’s toString method returns a String that includes the object’s class name and the object’s hashcode (see Section 9.4). This toString is primarily a placeholder a subclass can override to specify an appropriate String representation for a subclass object’s data.

SalariedEmployee’s toString method (lines 41–45) overrides (redefines) the inherited Object version. To override a superclass method, a subclass must declare a method with the same signature (method name, number of parameters, parameter types and order of parameter types) as the superclass method. Object’s toString method takes no parameters, so SalariedEmployee declares toString with no parameters.

@Override Annotation

Line 41 uses the optional @Overrideannotation to indicate that the following method declaration (i.e., toString) should override an existing superclass method. This annotation helps the compiler catch a few common errors. In this example, we intend to override superclass method toString, which is spelled with a lowercase “t” and an uppercase “S.” If you inadvertently use a lowercase “s,” the compiler will flag this as an error because the superclass does not contain a method named tostring with a lowercase “s.” If you didn’t use the @Override annotation, tostring would be an entirely different method that would not be called if a SalariedEmployee object were used where a String was needed.

Another common overriding error is declaring the wrong number or types of parameters in the subclass method’s parameter list. This creates an unintentional overload of the superclass method rather than overriding the existing method. If you then attempt to call the method (with the correct number and types of parameters) on a subclass object, the superclass’s version is invoked—potentially leading to subtle logic errors. When the compiler encounters a method declared with @Override, it compares the method’s signature with the superclass’s method signatures. If there isn’t an exact match, the compiler issues an error message, such as “method does not override or implement a method from a super-type.” You can then correct your method’s signature so that it matches one in the super-class.

Though @Override is optional, declare overridden methods with it so the compiler can ensure that you defined their signatures correctly. It’s always better to find errors at compile time rather than at runtime. For this reason, the toString methods in Chapter 8’s examples should have been declared with @Override as well.

You Cannot Reduce a Method’s Visibility in a Subclass

A public superclass method must be public in each of that class’s direct and indirect subclass. It’s a compilation error to override a method with a more restricted access modifier:

  • a public superclass method cannot be protected2 or private in a subclass and

  • a protected superclass method cannot be private in a subclass.

2. We discuss protected in Section 9.16.

Doing so would break the is-a relationship, which requires that all subclass objects be able to respond to method calls made to public methods declared in the superclass. If a public method could be overridden as a private method, the subclass objects would not be able to respond to the same method calls as superclass objects.

Class SalariedEmployeeTest

Figure 9.2 tests class SalariedEmployee. Lines 9–10 instantiate a SalariedEmployee object. Lines 14–15 use SalariedEmployee’s get methods to retrieve the object’s instance-variable values for output. Line 17 invokes the object’s setSalary method to change the salary. Lines 20–23 output the updated SalariedEmployee’s String representation and earnings. Again, when you output an object using the %s format specifier, the JVM implicitly invokes the object’s toString method to obtain its String representation.

9.3.2 Creating a SalariedEmployee/SalariedCommissionEmployee Inheritance Hierarchy

Now, let’s create a SalariedCommissionEmployee class (Fig. 9.3) that inherits from class SalariedEmployee (Fig. 9.1). A SalariedCommissionEmployee object is a SalariedEmployee, as indicated by line 6’s extends clause. Inheritance passes on SalariedEmployee’s capabilities to the subclass. A SalariedCommissionEmployee also has BigDecimal gross-Sales and commissionRate instance variables (Fig. 9.3, lines 7–8), which we’ll multiply to calculate the commission earned.

Inheritance

SalariedCommissionEmployee inherits all of SalariedEmployee’s members, except its constructor, which is specific to the SalariedEmployee superclass. Only the superclass’s public and protected3 members are directly accessible in the subclass. In inheritance, public superclass members remain public in the subclass, and protected ones remain protected. There’s only one copy of the inherited members. This makes the code easier to maintain, modify and debug because the code related to a SalariedEmployee exists only in that class.

3. We discuss protected in Section 9.16. There are no protected members in this class.

SalariedCommissionEmployee Services Provided to Client Code

Class SalariedCommissionEmployee’s public services (Fig. 9.3) include:

  • its own constructor (lines 11–30),

  • the methods setGrossSales, getGrossSales, setCommissionRate, getCommissionRate, calculateEarnings and toString (lines 33–70), and

  • the public methods inherited from SalariedEmployee.

The setGrossSales (lines 33–39) and setCommissionRate (lines 45–53) methods validate their arguments before modifying the instance variables grossSales and commissionRate:

  • setGrossSales ensures that the grossSales value is greater than 0, and

  • setCommissionRate ensures that the commissionRate value is greater than 0 and less than 1.

Recall that BigDecimal’s compareTo method returns a negative value, zero or a positive value if the method’s caller is less than, equal to or greater than the method’s argument. We compare these return values to 0 to determine whether the grossSales are negative (lines 17 and 34) and whether the commissionRate is less than or equal to 0 or greater than or equal to 1 (lines 22–23 and 46–47).

Although SalariedCommissionEmployee’s source code does not contain the inherited SalariedEmployee members, they’re nevertheless a part of the subclass. A SalariedCommissionEmployee object also contains SalariedEmployee’s private instance variables, but they’re not directly accessible within the subclass. You can access them only via the inherited SalariedEmployee public methods (or protected methods if there were any).

SalariedCommissionEmployee’s Constructor

Each subclass constructor must call a constructor in its direct superclass to initialize the instance variables inherited from that superclass. So, instantiating a subclass object begins a chain of constructor calls. For each new object you create, class Object’s constructor is always the last constructor called in the chain.

The constructor (lines 11–30) does this explicitly via superclass constructor call syntax (line 14), which consists of keyword super, followed by a set of parentheses containing the superclass constructor arguments—this initializes the inherited superclass instance variables name and salary. The explicit superclass constructor call must be the first statement in the constructor’s body—this requirement will be relaxed in a future Java version.4

4. Java 23’s “JEP 482: Flexible Constructor Bodies (Second Preview)” proposes changing this requirement so a subclass constructor can validate its arguments before calling the superclass constructor. This will enable you to prevent unnecessary work in the event that the subclass constructor throws an exception for an invalid argument. See the book’s webpage at https://deitel.com/javafp5 for an example. Accessed September 19, 2024. https://openjdk.org/jeps/482.

After calling the superclass constructor, the SalariedCommissionEmployee constructor validates the grossSales and commissionRate arguments and, if valid, assigns them to the corresponding instance variables. When a superclass contains a no-argument constructor, you can use super() to call that constructor explicitly, but this is rarely done.

We mentioned in Chapter 8 that you should not call a class’s instance methods from its constructor(s). If you follow this advice, you’ll avoid subtle problems caused by calling the class’s overridable methods either directly or indirectly, which can lead to runtime errors—see Section 9.10 for additional details.

SalariedCommissionEmployee Method calculateEarnings

SalariedCommissionEmployee’s calculateEarnings method (lines 59–63) overrides SalariedEmployee’s version to calculate a SalariedCommissionEmployee’s earnings. Line 61 uses the expression

super.calculateEarnings()

to calculate the portion of the earnings based on salary. The method then adds that value to the commission and returns the total earnings.

Note the syntax used to invoke an overridden superclass method from a subclass—you place the keyword super and a dot (.) separator before the superclass method name. This method invocation is a good software engineering practice—if a method performs all or some of the actions needed by another method, call that method rather than duplicate its code. This reduces code-maintenance problems.5

5. A downside is that this creates tight coupling between superclass and subclasses that can make large-scale systems difficult to modify. We discuss this further in Section 9.13.

When a subclass overrides a superclass method, the subclass version often calls the superclass version to do a portion of the work. Failure to prefix the superclass method name with the keyword super and the dot (.) separator when calling the superclass’s method causes the subclass method to call itself, potentially creating an error called infinite recursion, which would eventually cause the method-call stack to overflow—a fatal runtime error. Recursion, used correctly, is a powerful capability discussed in Chapter 22, Recursion and Big O.

SalariedCommissionEmployee Method toString

Similarly, SalariedCommissionEmployee’s toString method (Fig. 9.3, lines 66–70) overrides SalariedEmployee’s toString method. The new version returns a String containing SalariedEmployee’s String representation obtained by the expression in line 69:

super.toString()

followed by the SalariedCommissionEmployee’s grossSales and commissionRate.

Testing Class SalariedCommissionEmployee

Figure 9.4 creates the SalariedCommissionEmployee object employee (lines 9–11). Lines 14–21 output the employee’s data by calling its get methods to retrieve the object’s instance variable values. Lines 24–25 use setGrossSales and setCommissionRate to change the employee’s grossSales and commissionRate values, respectively. Then, lines 28–31 display the employee’s updated information and earnings, calling toString (implicitly) to get the employee’s String representation and calculateEarnings to get the employee’s earnings.

Notes on Class SalariedCommissionEmployee

We could have copied code from class SalariedEmployee and pasted it into class SalariedCommissionEmployee, then modified class SalariedCommissionEmployee to include grossSales and commissionRate instance variables and methods to manipulate them. This “copy-and-paste” approach would be error-prone and time-consuming. Worse yet, it spreads copies of the same code throughout a system, creating code-maintenance problems—changes to the duplicated code would need to be made in multiple classes.

With inheritance, the instance variables and methods that are the same for all the classes in the hierarchy are declared in a superclass. Changes made to these common features in the superclass are inherited by the subclasses. Without inheritance, changes would need to be made to all the source-code files that contain a copy of the code in question. By using inheritance and by calling superclass methods that hide the superclass’s private data and ensure its consistency, we’ve efficiently and effectively constructed a well-engineered subclass. But can we do better?

Class Design

At the design stage in an object-oriented system, you’ll often find that classes share common characteristics. You can identify and “factor out” the common instance variables and methods and place them in a superclass. Then, you can use inheritance to create subclasses that extend these shared characteristics with additional specialized capabilities. Declaring a subclass does not affect its superclass’s source code. While inheritance is a powerful tool, experience has shown that it has weaknesses. Section 9.13 discusses why you might prefer composition and interfaces to inheritance.

9.5 Intro to Polymorphism: Polymorphic Video Game

 

Suppose we’re designing a video game containing Martians, Venusians, Plutonians, SpaceShips and LaserBeams. Each inherits from a SpaceObject superclass with the method draw and implements this method appropriately for that subclass.

Screen Manager

A screen-manager program maintains an ArrayList of SpaceObject references to objects of the various classes. The screen manager periodically sends each object the same draw message to refresh the screen. Each object responds in its unique way. For example,

  • a Martian might draw itself in red with the appropriate number of antennae,

  • a SpaceShip might draw itself as a silver flying saucer and

  • a LaserBeam might draw itself as a bright red beam across the screen.

The same draw message has many forms of results—hence the term polymorphism.

Adding New Classes to the System

A polymorphic screen manager facilitates adding new classes to a system with minimal code modifications. Suppose we want to add Mercurian objects to our game. We build a class Mercurian that inherits from SpaceObject and defines method draw, then add the object’s reference to the ArrayList of SpaceObjects. The screen-manager code invokes draw the same way for every object the ArrayList refers to, regardless of the object’s type. So, the new Mercurian objects just “plug right in.”

Polymorphism enables you to deal in generalities and let the execution-time environment concern itself with the specifics. You can direct objects to behave appropriately without knowing their types as long as they belong to the same class hierarchy and are accessed via a superclass variable.

Polymorphism enhances extensibility by allowing software to operate independently of specific object types. New object types can be integrated into a system without altering its core functionality, as long as they can respond to existing messages. Only code that instantiates new objects must be modified to accommodate new types.
