9.6 Demonstrating Polymorphic Behavior

 

Section 9.3 created a class hierarchy, in which SalariedCommissionEmployee inherited from SalariedEmployee. The examples in that section manipulated SalariedEmployee and SalariedCommissionEmployee objects by using references to them to invoke their methods. We aimed a superclass variable at a superclass object and a subclass variable at a subclass object. These assignments are natural and straightforward, as superclass variables are intended to refer to superclass objects, and subclass variables are intended to refer to subclass objects. Other assignments are possible.

In the next example, we aim a superclass reference at a subclass object. We then show how invoking a method on a subclass object via a superclass reference invokes the subclass functionality. The referenced object’s type, not the variable’s type, determines which method is called. This example demonstrates that an object of a subclass can be treated as an object of its superclass, enabling various interesting manipulations. For example, a program can create an array of superclass variables that refer to objects of many subclass types. This is allowed because each subclass object is an object of its superclass. We can assign the reference of a SalariedCommissionEmployee object to a superclass SalariedEmployee variable because a SalariedCommissionEmployee is a SalariedEmployee.

The example in Fig. 9.5 demonstrates three ways to use superclass and subclass variables to store references to superclass and subclass objects. The first two are straightforward—we assign a superclass reference to a superclass variable and a subclass reference to a subclass variable. Then, we demonstrate the relationship between subclasses and super-classes (i.e., the is-a relationship) by assigning a subclass reference to a superclass variable. This program uses classes SalariedEmployee and SalariedCommissionEmployee from Figs. 9.1 and 9.3.

Creating Superclass and Subclass Objects

Lines 10–11 create a SalariedEmployee object and assign its reference to a variable of type SalariedEmployee. Lines 14–16 create a SalariedCommissionEmployee object and assign its reference to a SalariedCommissionEmployee variable. These assignments are natural—for example, a SalariedEmployee variable’s primary purpose is to hold a reference to a SalariedEmployee object.

Calling Superclass Methods Via a Superclass Variable

Lines 19–25 use the superclass variable salariedEmployee to invoke SalariedEmployee methods toString (line 23) and calculateEarnings (line 24). Because the variable refers to a SalariedEmployee superclass object, the superclass versions of both methods are called.

Calling Subclass Methods Via a Subclass Variable

Similarly, lines 28–34 use the subclass variable salariedCommissionEmployee to invoke SalariedCommissionEmployee methods toString (line 32) and calculateEarnings (line 33). Because salariedCommissionEmployee refers to a SalariedCommissionEmployee subclass object, the subclass versions of both methods are called.

Calling Subclass Methods Via a Superclass Variable

Line 37 assigns the SalariedCommissionEmployee subclass object referenced by salaried-CommissionEmployee to the superclass SalariedEmployee variable salariedEmployee2. Lines 38–44 use this superclass variable to invoke SalariedCommissionEmployee subclass methods toString (line 42) and calculateEarnings (line 43). When a superclass variable refers to a subclass object and is used to call a method, the subclass version of the method is called. Hence, lines 42–43 call class SalariedCommissionEmployee’s methods toString and calculateEarnings. The Java compiler allows assigning a subclass object to a superclass variable because an object of a subclass is an object of its superclass (but not vice versa).

When the compiler encounters a method call made through a variable, the compiler determines if the method can be called by checking the variable’s class type. The call is compiled if that class contains the proper method declaration (or inherits one). At execution time, the type of the object to which the variable refers determines the actual method to use. This process—called dynamic binding—enables polymorphic behavior.

9.7 abstract Classes and Methods

 

Sometimes, it’s useful to declare abstract classes for which you never intend to create objects. We refer to them as abstract superclasses becausethey’re used only as superclasses in inheritance hierarchies. As we’ll soon see, these classes cannot be used to instantiate objects because they’re incomplete. We demonstrate an abstract class in Section 9.8’s code example.

Purpose of abstract Classes

An abstract class provides a superclass from which other classes can inherit and thus share a common design. In Section 9.2’s Shape hierarchy, for example, subclasses inherit the notion of what it means to be a Shape—perhaps common attributes such as location, fillPattern, color and borderThickness, and behaviors such as draw, move, resize, rotate and setColor.

Classes used to instantiate objects are called concrete classes. Such classes implement every method they declare (some implementations might be inherited). For example, we could derive concrete classes Circle, Square and Triangle from the abstract superclass TwoDimensionalShape. Similarly, we could derive concrete classes Sphere, Cube and Tetrahedron from the abstract superclass ThreeDimensionalShape.

abstract superclasses are too general to instantiate real objects—they specify only commonality among subclasses. We need to be more specific before we can instantiate objects. For example, if you send the draw message to abstract class TwoDimensionalShape, the class knows that two-dimensional shapes should be drawable, but it does not know what specific shape to draw, so it cannot implement a real draw method. Concrete classes provide the specifics that make it possible to instantiate objects.

Not all hierarchies contain abstract classes. However, you’ll often write client code that uses only variables of abstract superclass types to reduce the client code’s dependencies on a range of subclass types. For example, you can write a method that receives an abstract superclass type parameter. When called, such a method can receive an object of any concrete class that directly or indirectly extends that superclass.

abstract classes sometimes constitute several levels of a hierarchy. For example, In Section 9.2’s Shape hierarchy, class Shape and its direct subclasses TwoDimensionalShape and ThreeDimensionalShape would each be abstract because they are not specific enough to determine the actual shape. The hierarchy’s third level declares concrete TwoDimensionalShapes(Circle, Square and Triangle) and ThreeDimensionalShapes (Sphere, Cube and Tetrahedron).

Declaring an abstract Class and abstract Methods

You declare a class abstract by placing the abstract keyword before the class keyword. An abstract class declares common attributes and behaviors (abstract and concrete) for the classes in a class hierarchy. An abstract class’s instance variables and concrete methods are subject to the standard rules of inheritance.

An abstract class normally contains one or more abstractmethods, but this is not required. An abstract method is an instance method declared abstract, as in

Click here to view code image

public abstract void draw(); // abstract method

abstract methods do not provide implementations. A class containing any abstract methods must be explicitly declared abstract. Subclasses must declare the “missing piece(s),” if any, to become concrete classes from which you can instantiate objects. So, a concrete subclass of an abstract class must provide a concrete implementation for each abstract method. Otherwise, the subclass must be declared abstract.

Some Methods Cannot Be abstract

Constructors and static methods cannot be abstract. Constructors are not inherited, so an abstract constructor could never be implemented. Though non-private static methods are inherited, they cannot be overridden. An abstract method is meant to be overridden for polymorphic processing of objects. A static method is associated with a class, not specific objects, so declaring a static method abstract would not make sense.

Using abstract Classes to Declare Variables

Although we cannot instantiate objects of abstract superclasses, you’ll soon see that we can use an abstract superclass to declare variables that can refer to objects of any concrete class derived from that superclass. We’ll use such variables to manipulate subclass objects polymorphically. You can also use abstract superclass names to invoke static methods declared in those abstract superclasses.

Layered Software Systems

Polymorphism is particularly effective for implementing so-called layered software systems. In operating systems, for example, each physical device type could operate quite differently. Even so, commands to read or write data from and to devices may have a certain uniformity. For each device, the operating system uses software called a device driver to control all communication between the system and the device. The write message sent to a device-driver object needs to be interpreted specifically in the context of that driver and how it manipulates devices of a specific type. However, the write call to one device is no different from the write to any other device in the system—place some number of bytes from memory onto that device.

An object-oriented operating system might use an abstract superclass to provide a common “interface” appropriate for all device drivers. Then, subclasses that behave similarly are formed through inheritance from that abstract superclass. The device-driver methods are declared as abstract methods in the superclass. The implementations of these abstract methods are provided in the concrete subclasses that correspond to the specific types of device drivers. New devices are constantly being developed, often long after the operating system has been released. When you buy a new device, it comes with a device driver provided by the device vendor. The device is immediately operational after you install the driver and connect the device to your computer. The new devices and their drivers “plug right in.” This is another elegant example of how polymorphism makes systems extensible.

1 Prompt genAIs, asking why we would want to declare a Java class abstract even if it has no abstract methods.

9.8 Case Study: Payroll System Using Polymorphism

 

Let’s use an abstract class and polymorphism to calculate payroll for two employee types. We create an Employee hierarchy to solve the following problem:

A company pays its employees weekly. The employees are of two types:

  1. Salaried employees receive a fixed salary regardless of their hours worked.

  2. Commission employees receive a percentage of their sales.

For the current pay period, the company has decided to reward salaried employees by raising their salaries by 10%. The company wants to implement a program that performs its payroll calculations polymorphically.

Employee Hierarchy

We use the abstract class Employee to represent the general concept of an employee and define the “interface” to the hierarchy—that is, the methods all Employee subclasses must have so a program can invoke those methods on all Employee objects. Classes SalariedEmployee and CommissionEmployee inherit directly from Employee. The following UML class diagram shows our polymorphic payroll application’s inheritance hierarchy. The abstract class name Employee is italicized, per UML convention.

The abstract superclass Employee declares the “interface” to the hierarchy—that is, the methods that a program can invoke on all Employee objects throughout the hierarchy. We use the term “interface” here in a general sense to refer to the various ways programs can communicate with objects of any Employee subclass. Be careful not to confuse the general notion of an “interface” with the formal notion of a Java interface (Section 9.11). Each employee, regardless of how their earnings are calculated, has a name, so we’ll declare the private instance variable name in the abstract superclass Employee.

The following diagram shows each class in the hierarchy down the left side and methods calculateEarnings and toString across the top. For each class, the diagram shows the desired results of each method. We do not list superclass Employee’s getName method because it’s not overridden by any subclasses—it’s inherited and used “as is.”

The following sections implement the Employee class hierarchy. The first declares abstract superclass Employee. Each of the next two sections implements one of the concrete subclasses. The last section implements a test program that builds objects of all these classes and processes them polymorphically.

9.8.1 abstract Superclass Employee

Class Employee (Fig. 9.6) provides methods getName, toString and calculateEarnings.

Class Employee’s declaration (Fig. 9.6) includes:

  • a constructor (line 9) that receives a String to initialize the final instance variable name (declared at line 6)—the constructor does not validate its parameters in this example,

  • a getName method to return the name (line 12),

  • a toString method (lines 15–16) to return the String representation of an Employee, and

  • an abstract method calculateEarnings (line 19)—this will be overridden by each concrete Employee subclass.

Each Employee subclass will override toString to create a String representation that contains all of the employee’s information.

abstract Method calculateEarnings

Why did we declare calculateEarnings as an abstract method? Calculating earnings certainly applies to all employees. However, we cannot calculate the earnings for the general notion of an Employee—we first must know the specific Employee. Declaring this method abstract indicates that each concrete subclass must override calculateEarnings with an appropriate implementation.

You cannot create Employee objects directly because Employee is an abstract class. However, due to inheritance, every object of any Employee subclass is an Employee and thus is guaranteed to provide method calculateEarnings. So, a program can invoke the method polymorphically on any object that is an Employee via a superclass Employee variable.

In Section 9.8.4, we’ll create an array of superclass Employee variables, each referencing a subclass object that is an Employee. The program will iterate through the array, polymorphically calling calculateEarnings on each object. The compiler allows calls to method calculateEarnings via Employee variables because it’s declared in class Employee—again, the variable’s type determines which methods a program can call using that variable.

9.8.2 Concrete Subclass SalariedEmployee

Class SalariedEmployee (Fig. 9.7) extends class Employee (line 5) and overrides abstract method calculateEarnings (lines 33–34), which makes SalariedEmployee a concrete class. The class includes:

  • a constructor (lines 9–18) that receives a name and a salary and passes the name to superclass Employee’s constructor (line 10) to initialize Employee’s private instance variable;

  • a setSalary method to assign a new nonnegative value to the salary instance variable (lines 21–27),

  • a getSalary method to return salary’s value (line 30),

  • a calculateEarnings method (lines 33–34) that overrides the superclass version to calculate a SalariedEmployee’s earnings and

  • a toString method (lines 37–41) that overrides the superclass version to return a String including the information returned by superclass Employee’s toString and SalariedEmployee’s getSalary methods.

Method calculateEarnings overrides Employee’s abstract method to provide a concrete implementation that returns the SalariedEmployee’s salary. If we do not implement calculateEarnings, class SalariedEmployee must be declared abstract. Of course, we want class SalariedEmployee to be concrete in this example.

Method toString (lines 37–41) overrides Employee’s toString. If class SalariedEmployee did not override toString, it would inherit Employee’s version. In that case, class SalariedEmployee’s toString method would return only the name, which does not adequately represent a SalariedEmployee.

9.8.3 Concrete Subclass CommissionEmployee

Class CommissionEmployee (Fig. 9.8) extends class Employee (line 5). The class includes:

  • a constructor (lines 10–28) that receives a name, a gross sales amount and a commission rate and passes the name to superclass Employee’s constructor (line 12) to initialize Employee’s private instance variable;

  • set methods (lines 31–37 and 43–51) to assign valid new values to instance variables grossSales and commissionRate;

  • get methods (lines 40 and 54) to return the values of grossSales and commissionRate;

  • a calculateEarnings method (lines 57–60) that overrides the superclass version to calculate a CommissionEmployee’s earnings; and

  • a toString method (lines 63–67) that overrides the superclass version to return a String including the information returned by superclass Employee’s toString and CommissionEmployee’s getGrossSales and getCommissionRate methods.

9.8.4 Polymorphic Processing, Operator instanceof and Downcasting

Figure 9.9 tests our Employee hierarchy. Lines 9–12 create a SalariedEmployee object and a CommissionEmployee object. The program manipulates these objects non-polymorphically, via variables of each object’s own type, then polymorphically, using an array of Employee variables. While processing the objects polymorphically, the program increases the salary of each SalariedEmployee by 10%—this requires determining the object’s type at execution time. Finally, the program polymorphically determines and outputs the type of each object in the Employee array. Lines 14–21 output each object’s String representation and earnings non-polymorphically, using the salariedEmployee variable to call the SalariedEmployee methods and the commissionEmployee variable to call the Commission-Employee methods. Each object’s toString method is called implicitly by printf when the object is output as a String with the %s format specifier (lines 16 and 19).

Creating the Array of Employees

Line 24 creates the array employees and initializes it with the references stored in variables salariedEmployee and commissionEmployee—the compiler assigns these to employees elements 0 and 1, respectively. These assignments are allowed, because a SalariedEmployee is an Employee, and a CommissionEmployee is an Employee. Even though Employee is an abstract class, we can assign SalariedEmployee and CommissionEmployee references to superclass Employee variables (in this case, the array elements).

Polymorphically Processing Employees

Lines 29–45 iterate through array employees and invoke methods toString (implicitly; line 30) and calculateEarnings (line 43) with Employee variable currentEmployee, which represents a different Employee in the array on each iteration. The output illustrates that a superclass reference can be used to invoke methods of the superclass, but the subclass-specific method implementations are indeed invoked.

The JVM once again uses dynamic binding (also called late binding) to resolve all calls to toString and calculateEarnings at execution time, based on the type of the object to which currentEmployee refers. Only the methods of class Employee can be called via an Employee variable. Employee, of course, inherits class Object’s methods, so we can also call Object methods (like toString) via Employee variables.

Performing Type-Specific Operations on CommissionEmployees

We perform special processing on SalariedEmployee objects. As we encounter these objects at execution time, we increase their salary by 10%. When processing objects polymorphically, we typically do not need to worry about specifics like this. However, to adjust the salary, we must determine the specific type of Employee object at execution time.

Line 33 uses the pattern-matching instanceof operator (Java 16) to determine whether a particular Employee is a SalariedEmployee. The condition in line 33 is true if currentEmployee refers to an object that is a SalariedEmployee—this includes SalariedEmployee subclass objects because of the is-a relationship a subclass has with its superclass. If the condition is true, the pattern-matching instanceof expression automatically converts the reference in currentEmployee down from the superclass type Employee to the subclass type SalariedEmployee, then assigns the reference to the subclass variable employee. This conversion is known as a downcast and is allowed only if the object currentEmployee is-a SalariedEmployee. The condition at line 33 ensures this is the case. This downcast is required if we’re to invoke subclass SalariedEmployee methods getSalary and setSalary on the current Employee object—attempting to invoke a subclass-only method directly on a superclass reference is a compilation error.

If the instanceof expression in line 33 is true, lines 34–39 perform the special processing required for the SalariedEmployee object. Using SalariedEmployee variable employee, lines 34–35 invoke subclass-only methods getSalary and setSalary to retrieve and update the employee’s salary with the 10% raise. Then, lines 37–39 use get-Salary to get the new salary and display it.

Calling calculateEarnings Polymorphically

Line 43 invokes method calculateEarnings on currentEmployee, which polymorphically calls the current subclass object’s appropriate calculateEarnings method. Obtaining the earnings of the CommissionEmployee polymorphically produces the same results as obtaining it in line 20. The earnings amount obtained for the SalariedEmployee is higher than that in line 17, due to the 10% increase in its base salary.

Getting Each Employee’s Class Name

To show that every object knows its own class, lines 48–51 display each Employee’s type as a String. Every object can access its class’s information via the inherited Objectmethod getClass. Method getClass returns a reference to an object of type Class (from package java.lang), which contains information about the object’s type, such as its class name. Line 50 invokes getClass on the current object to get its class. Then, it uses the reference returned by getClass to invoke the Classmethod getName to get the object’s class name.

Avoiding Compilation Errors with Downcasting

In this example, we avoided several compilation errors by downcasting an Employee variable to a SalariedEmployee variable via the pattern-matching instanceof expression in line 33. If you attempt to assign the Employee variable currentEmployee directly to a SalariedEmployee variable, you’ll receive an “incompatible types” compilation error. Assigning the reference stored in a superclass variable to a subclass variable is not allowed because an Employee is not a SalariedEmployee—the is-arelationship applies only between the subclass and its superclasses, not vice versa.

Similarly, if lines 35 and 39 were to use superclass variable currentEmployee to invoke subclass-only methods getSalary and setSalary, we’d receive “cannot find symbol” compilation errors at these lines. Attempting to invoke subclass-only methods via a super-class variable is not allowed—even though lines 35 and 39 execute only if instanceof in line 33 returns true to indicate that currentEmployee holds a reference to a SalariedEmployee object. Using a superclass Employee variable, we can invoke only the methods in class Employee—getName, calculateEarnings and toString. Although the actual method called depends on the object’s type, a variable can be used to invoke only those methods that are members of that variable’s type, which the compiler verifies.

instanceof Before Java 16

The pattern-matching instanceof operator was finalized in Java 16. Prior to that, line 33’s if header would have been implemented as follows:

Click here to view code image

if (currentEmployee instanceof SalariedEmployee) {
   // downcast Employee reference to SalariedEmployee reference
   SalariedEmployee employee = (SalariedEmployee) currentEmployee;

   // rest of if statement body
}

The if’s first body statement uses the cast operator—(SalariedEmployee)—to convert the superclass Employee reference in currentEmployee to the subclass variable employee. That statement will not execute, however, unless we already know that currentEmployee refers to a SalariedEmployee object—that is, the if’s instanceof condition is true. This prevents a ClassCastException, which occurs when downcasting if the referenced object does not have an is-a relationship with the type specified in the cast. Although it’s allowed, you should generally avoid downcasting.

9.9 final Methods and Classes

 

You’ve seen that variables can be declared final to indicate that they cannot be modified after they’re initialized—such variables represent constant values. It’s also possible to declare methods and classes with the final modifier.

Final Methods Cannot Be Overridden

A finalmethod in a superclass cannot be overridden in a subclass—this guarantees that the final method implementation will be used by all direct and indirect subclasses in the hierarchy. Methods declared private are implicitly final—the subclass cannot access its superclass’s private members, so it’s not possible to override them. Methods declared static are also implicitly final because only non-static instance methods can be overridden. Since a final method’s declaration can never change, calls to final methods are resolved at compile time—known as static binding.

Final Classes Cannot Be Superclasses

A finalclass cannot be extended, so its methods are implicitly final. String is a final class. If you were allowed to extend String, objects of that subclass could be used wherever Strings are expected. Since it cannot be extended, programs that use Strings can rely on the functionality of String objects as specified in the Java API. Making the class final also prevents programmers from creating subclasses that might bypass security restrictions.

record Classes

A record class is implicitly a final class, so its methods are implicitly final. A record class’s instance variables are also final.

If It Can Be Final, It Should Be

In general, if a variable, method or class can be final, it should be final. This is another example of the principle of least privilege. When we study concurrency in Chapter 18, you’ll see that final variables make it easier to parallelize your programs for use on today’s multi-core processors for improved performance.

Sometimes, declaring classes final is important—typically for security reasons. Unless you carefully design a class for extension, you should declare the class as final to avoid (often subtle) errors. Like any class, you can reuse a final class via composition—for example, our Employee class composed a reference to a String object, and String is a final class. For more insights on using final, visit

Click here to view code image

https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/IandI/final.html

9.10 Issues with Constructors Calling Instance Methods

In Section 8.10, we chose to duplicate code between class Time2’s constructor and set-Time methods. We did this because you should not call a class’s non-static methods from its constructors. To understand why, recall that when you construct a subclass object, the subclass constructor calls a constructor in its direct superclass before the subclass instance-variable initialization code executes. If the superclass constructor then calls a method that the subclass overrides, the subclass’s version executes before the subclass constructor finishes initializing the subclass object’s data. If the subclass method uses instance variables that have not yet been initialized this could lead to subtle, difficult-to-detect errors.

Let’s assume that a constructor and a set method perform the same validation for a particular instance variable. How should you handle the common code?

  • Duplicating brief validation code in the constructor and the set method is a simple way to eliminate the problem we’re considering here.

  • For lengthier validation code, you can define a static validation method—typically a private static helper method—then call it from the constructor and the set method. It’s acceptable to call a static method from a constructor because it is not overridable.

It’s also acceptable for a constructor to call a final or private instance method if it does not directly or indirectly call any overridable instance methods.

9.11 Creating and Using Interfaces

 

Our next example (Figs. 9.10–9.13) reexamines Section 9.8’s payroll system. Suppose the company wishes to perform several accounting operations in a single accounts-payable application. In addition to calculating each employee’s earnings, the company must also calculate the payments due for invoices (i.e., bills for goods purchased). Though applied to unrelated things—employees and invoices—both operations obtain payment amounts:

  • For an employee, the payment amount is the employee’s earnings.

  • For an invoice, the payment amount is the total cost of the invoice’s listed goods.

Can we polymorphically calculate such different things as the payments due for employees and invoices in a single application? Does Java allow unrelated classes to implement a set of common methods (e.g., a method that calculates a payment amount)? Java interfaces offer this capability.

Standardizing Interactions

In our car analogy from Section 1.4, a “basic-driving-capabilities” interface consisting of a steering wheel, an accelerator pedal and a brake pedal would enable a driver to tell the car what to do. Once you know how to use this interface for turning, accelerating and braking, you can drive many different cars, even though manufacturers may implement these systems differently. For example, there are many types of braking systems—disc brakes, drum brakes, antilock brakes and more. When you press the brake pedal, your car’s brake system type is irrelevant—what matters is that the car slows down.

Software Objects Communicate Via Interfaces

Software objects also communicate via interfaces. A Java interface describes a set of methods that can be called on an object to tell it, for example, to perform some task or return some information. The next example introduces an interface named Payable to describe the functionality of any object that must be “capable of being paid” and thus must offer a method to determine the payment amount due.

Using an Interface

To use an interface, a concrete class must

  • specify that it implements the interface and

  • provide a concrete implementation of each abstract method in the interface.

To specify that a class implements an interface, add the implements keyword and the name of the interface to the end of your class declaration’s first line, as in:

Click here to view code image

public class ClassName extends SuperclassName implements InterfaceName

or

Click here to view code image

public class ClassName implements InterfaceName

InterfaceName may be a comma-separated list of interfaces. Implementing an interface is like signing a contract with the compiler that states, “I will declare all the abstract methods specified by the interface, or I will declare my class abstract;” otherwise, a compilation error occurs.

Tagging Interfaces

A tagging (ormarker)interface is an empty interface with no methods or constant values. They’re used to add is-a relationships to classes. For example, Java has a mechanism called serialization, which can convert objects to byte representations (e.g., for storing objects in files or sending them over networks) and can convert those byte representations back to objects (called deserialization), using classes ObjectOutputStream and ObjectInput-Stream. To enable this mechanism to work with your objects, tag them as Serializable by adding implements Serializable to the end of your class declaration’s first line. Then, all the objects of your class have the is-a relationship with Serializable.

9.11.1 Developing a Payable Hierarchy

To build an application that can determine payments for employees and invoices alike, we first create interface Payable, which contains the method calculatePayment that returns a BigDecimal representing the amount to pay for an object of any class that implements the interface. Method calculatePayment is a general-purpose method that can be applied to a broad range of possibly unrelated objects. When declaring a method in an interface, you should choose a method name that describes the method’s purpose in a general manner because the method may be implemented by unrelated classes.

After declaring Payable, we introduce class Invoice, which implements Payable. We then modify class Employee so it, too, implements Payable. Then, our program can polymorphically call calculatePayment on Invoice and Employee objects, enabling the required processing of Invoices and Employees for the accounts payable application.

UML Diagram Containing an Interface

The following UML class diagram shows the interface and class hierarchy:

The hierarchy begins with interface Payable. The UML distinguishes an interface from classes by placing the word “interface” in guillemets (« and ») above the interface name. The UML expresses the relationship between a class and an interface through a relationship known as realization. A class is said to realize (implement) the methods of an interface. A class diagram models a realization as a dashed arrow with a hollow arrowhead pointing from the implementing class to the interface. The preceding diagram indicates that classes Invoice and Employee each realize interface Payable. Class Employee appears in italics, indicating that it’s an abstract class. Concrete class SalariedEmployee extends Employee, inheriting its superclass’s realization relationship with interface Payable.

1 Prompt genAIs to list the most frequently used interfaces in the Java API and give a brief explanation of each.

9.11.2 Interface Payable

Interfaces are typically public types. Like a public class, a public interface must be declared in a file with the same name as the interface and the .java filename extension (e.g., Payable.java). The keyword interface (line 5 of Fig. 9.10) begins an interface declaration. This interface contains the public abstract method calculatePayment. The method has no parameters, but interface methods can have parameters. Interfaces can also have any number of methods.

Originally, an interface could contain only constants and public abstract methods without implementations. Java 8 and 9 enhanced interfaces to allow method implementations (Section 9.12). Any interface methods you declare without bodies are implicitly public and abstract, but declaring them public and abstract explicitly clarifies your intentions—this differentiates the interface’s abstract methods from the other kinds of interface methods. All fields in an interface are implicitly public, static and final.

9.11.3 Class Invoice

Class Invoice (Fig. 9.11) represents an invoice for one kind of part. The class declares private instance variables partNumber, partDescription, quantity and pricePerItem (in lines 6–9). Class Invoice also contains a constructor (lines 12–28), get methods (lines 31–34) and a toString method (lines 37–42) that returns a String representation of an Invoice object.

Line 5 indicates that Invoice implements interface Payable. Like all classes, Invoice also implicitly extends Object. Class Invoice implements the one abstract method in interface Payable—method calculatePayment in lines 45–49. The method calculates and returns the invoice amount—the product of quantity and pricePerItem, obtained through the appropriate get methods. This method satisfies the implementation requirement for this method in interface Payable, so we’ve fulfilled the interface contract with the compiler.

9.11.4 Modifying Class Employee to Implement Interface Payable

We now modify Fig. 9.6’s Employee class to implement interface Payable (Fig. 9.12). This class declaration is identical to that of Fig. 9.6 with two exceptions:

  • Line 5 of Fig. 9.12 indicates that class Employee now implements Payable.

  • Lines 23–24 implements interface Payable’s calculatePayment method.

Method calculatePayment simply calls Employee’s abstract calculateEarnings method. This might seem strange given that calculateEarnings does not have an implementation. However, when we call calculatePayment at execution time, it will be for an object of a concrete Employee subclass. So, line 24 will polymorphically call that subclass’s concrete calculateEarnings method, which knows how to calculate earnings for objects of that subclass type.

Subclasses of Employee and Interface Payable

When a class implements an interface, the same is-a relationship as inheritance applies. Class Employee implements Payable, so an Employee is a Payable. Thus, any object of an Employee subclass also is a Payable. So, if we update the class hierarchy in Section 9.8 with the new Employee superclass in Fig. 9.12, then all objects of the Employee subclasses SalariedEmployee and CommissionEmployee would be Payable objects.

Just as we can assign the reference of a SalariedEmployee subclass object to a super-class Employee variable, we can assign the reference of a SalariedEmployee object (or any other Employee derived-class object) to a Payable variable. Invoice implements Payable, so an Invoice object also is a Payable object, and we can assign the reference of an Invoice object to a Payable variable.

The is-a relationship between superclasses and subclasses, and between interfaces and the classes that implement them, holds when passing an object to a method. When a method parameter receives an argument of a superclass or interface type, the method polymorphically processes the object it receives as an argument.

Using a superclass reference, we can polymorphically invoke any method declared in the superclass and its superclasses (e.g., class Object). Using an interface reference, we can polymorphically invoke any method declared in the interface, its superinterfaces (one interface can extend another) and in class Object. Calling methods of class Object is allowed via an interface variable because the variable must refer to an object to call a method, and all objects have class Object’s methods.

PayableInterfaceTest (Fig. 9.13) illustrates that interface Payable can be used to process a set of Invoices and Employees polymorphically in a single application. Lines 10–15 declare and initialize the four-element array payableObjects. Lines 11–12 place the references of Invoice objects in payableObjects’ first two elements. Lines 13–14 place the references of SalariedEmployee objects in payableObjects’ last two elements. The elements can be initialized with Invoices and SalariedEmployees because an Invoice is a Payable, a SalariedEmployee is an Employee and an Employee is a Payable.

9.12 Other Interface Features

This section introduces other interface features that you’ll see again in later chapters.

9.12.1 default Interface Methods

As we mentioned, interface methods originally could be only public abstract methods. This meant that an interface specified what operations an implementing class must perform but not how the class should perform them.

Java 8 enabled interfaces to include public default methods with concrete default implementations that specify how operations are performed. If a class implements such an interface, the class receives the interface’s default implementations. The implementing class can override the interface’s default methods if necessary, but that’s not required. To declare a default method, place the keyword default between public and the method’s return type and provide a concrete method implementation:

Click here to view code image

public default returnType methodName(parameters) {
   statement(s)
}
Adding Methods to Existing Interfaces

Before default methods, adding methods to an interface would break implementing classes that did not define the new methods—you must declare your class abstract if you do not define each of an interface’s abstract methods. Any class that implements an interface will not break when a default method is added. You must recompile the interface when you modify it, but an implementing class simply receives the new default method’s implementation. So, default methods enable you to evolve an existing interface by adding new methods to it without breaking the classes that implement it.

9.12.2 static Interface Methods

Chapter 12 introduces the Collections class, which contains many static helper methods for processing objects that implement Java Collections API interfaces Collection, List, Map, Set and more. For example, the Collections method sort can sort the elements of any object that is a List—that is, the object’s class implements the List inter-face. With static interface methods (also added in Java 8), such helper methods can be declared directly in interfaces rather than separate classes.

9.12.3 Functional Interfaces

Any interface containing only one abstract method is a functional interface.6 Functional interfaces are used extensively with Java’s lambda capabilities, which we introduce in Chapter 14, Functional Programming with Lambdas & Streams. Lambdas provide a shorthand notation for implementing functional interfaces. Some functional interfaces that you’ll use in this book include:

6. Some people call these SAM (single abstract method) interfaces.

  • Comparator (Chapter 12, Generic Collections)—You’ll implement this interface to define a method that compares two objects of a given type to determine whether the first object is less than, equal to or greater than the second.

  • ChangeListener (Chapter 15, JavaFX Graphical User Interfaces: Part 1)—You’ll implement this interface to define a method that’s called when the user interacts with a slider graphical user interface control.

  • Runnable (Chapter 18, Concurrency: Platform Threads to Virtual Threads)—You’ll implement this interface to define a task that may run in parallel with other parts of your program.

9.12.4 private Interface Methods

As you know, a class’s private helper methods may be called only by the class’s other methods. You can declare private interface methods, enabling you to define methods with common code used only by the interface’s other concrete methods. An interface’s private instance methods can be called directly (i.e., without an object reference) only by the inter-face’s other instance methods. An interface’s private static methods can be called by any of the interface’s instance or static methods. Including the default keyword in a private interface method’s declaration is a compilation error—default methods must be public.

9.13 Program to an Interface, Not an Implementation7

 

7. The concepts we present in this section are widely discussed in the software engineering community and derived from many sources. “Program to an Interface, Not an Implementation” is defined in Gamma, Erich et al. Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1995, 17–18, and further emphasized and discussed in Bloch, Joshua. Effective Java, Third Edition. Upper Saddle River, NJ: Addison-Wesley, 2018.

There’s much discussion in the software engineering community about the relative merits of composition and inheritance. Many professionals believe inheritance is overused and composition often is more appropriate. This section compares these approaches, then refactors Section 9.8’s Employee hierarchy using composition and interfaces.

Inheritance-Based Designs

Implementation inheritance in which a subclass extends a superclass is primarily used to define closely related classes with many of the same instance variables and method implementations. This kind of inheritance creates tightly coupled classes in which the super-class’s instance variables and methods are inherited into subclasses. Changes to a superclass directly affect all corresponding subclasses.

Tight coupling can make modifying class hierarchies difficult. Consider modifying Section 9.8’s Employee hierarchy to support retirement plans. There are many retirement plan types, including 401(k)s and IRAs. We might add an abstract makeRetirementDe-posit method to the superclass Employee. Then we’d define various subclasses such as SalariedEmployeeWith401k, SalariedEmployeeWithIRA, CommissionEmployeeWith-401k, CommissionEmployeeWithIRA, etc., each with an overridden makeRetirementDe-posit implementation. This approach quickly proliferates subclasses, making the hierarchy more challenging to implement and maintain.

Rethinking the Employee Hierarchy: Composition and Dependency Injection

Over the years, programmers have written numerous papers, articles and blog posts about the problems with tightly coupled class hierarchies like Section 9.8’s Employee hierarchy. In this example, we’ll refactor our Employee hierarchy so that the Employee’s compensation model is not “hardwired” into the class hierarchy.8

8. We’d like to thank Brian Goetz, Oracle’s Java Language Architect, for suggesting the class architecture we use in this section when he reviewed an earlier edition of Java How to Program.

To do so, we’ll use composition and dependency injection in which a class contains a reference to an object that provides a behavior required by objects of the class.9 In our Employee payroll example, that behavior calculates each Employee’s earnings. We’ll reimplement the Employee class using composition—in this example, an Employee has a reference to a CompensationModel object. As you’ll see, you can “inject” compensation functionality into an Employee object by initializing an Employee’s CompensationModel reference as you construct the Employee or even by setting a new CompensationModel at a later time. Composing a CompensationModel reference creates a loosely coupled relation-ship between an Employee and its CompensationModel, making it easy to change CompensationModels dynamically without needing to recompile class hierarchies.

9. “Dependency Injection.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed September 19, 2024. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dependency_injection.

Interfaces Are Best for Flexibility

In this example, we’ll declare CompensationModel as an interface with an abstract method calculateEarnings, then declare implementations of CompensationModel that specify the ways in which an Employee gets paid:

  • Class Salaried implements CompensationModel for an employee who gets paid a fixed salary.

  • Class Commission implements CompensationModel for an employee who gets paid a commission based on gross sales.

Class Employee’s calculateEarnings method will call its composed Compensation-Model’s calculateEarnings method to determine the Employee’s earnings. The new Employee class will not be a superclass—to emphasize that, we’ll make it final.

Generative AI

1 Prompt genAIs, asking why Java implementation inheritance creates tightly coupled classes.

9.13.1 CompensationModel Interface

Figure 9.14 defines the CompensationModel interface containing the abstract method calculateEarnings (line 6). Each class that implements this interface will define the instance variable(s) necessary to calculate an employee’s compensation and will override CompensationModel’s calculateEarnings method to perform the appropriate calculation. An object of any class that implements this interface is a CompensationModel.

9.13.2 An Employee Has a CompensationModel—Composition and Dependency Injection

Figure 9.15 defines class Employee. This class is declared final, so it cannot be a super-class. Each Employee has a reference to its CompensationModel implementation (line 7).

Class Employee provides the following constructor and methods:

  • The constructor (lines 11–14) initializes the Employee’s name and aims its model reference at an object that implements the CompensationModel interface. This is a form of dependency injection known as constructor injection. The constructor receives a reference to another object and stores it in (i.e., injects it into) the object being constructed.

  • The setCompensationModel method (lines 18–20) enables the client code to change an Employee’s CompensationModel. This is a form of dependency injection known as property injection. In Java, a property is the term used to describe a pair of set and get methods that provide controlled access to an instance variable.

  • The getCompensationModel method (line 23) returns an Employee’s current CompensationModel.

  • The calculateEarnings method (lines 26–28) determines the Employee’s earnings by calling its CompensationModel’s calculateEarnings method via the model reference.

  • The overridden toString method (lines 31–34) creates an Employee’s String representation consisting of the Employee’s name, followed by the compensation information we get by calling the CompensationModel implementation’s toString method via the model reference.

9.13.3 CompensationModel Implementations

Next, let’s define our CompensationModel implementations. Objects of these classes will be injected into Employee objects to specify how to calculate their earnings.

Salaried Class That Implements CompensationModel

A Salaried compensation model (Fig. 9.16) defines how to pay an Employee who receives a fixed salary. The class implements the CompensationModel interface (line 5) and provides:

  • instance variable salary (line 6) to store the weekly salary,

  • a constructor (lines 9–16) to validate and initialize the salary,

  • a getSalary method (line 19) to return the salary value,

  • a calculateEarnings method (lines 22–23) that overrides the superclass version to return the salary and

  • a toString method (lines 26–29) that overrides the superclass version to return a String representation of a Salaried object for use in this program’s outputs.

Salaried is declared final (line 5) so it may not be used as a superclass.

Commission Class That Implements CompensationModel

A Commission compensation model (Fig. 9.17) defines how to pay an Employee commission based on gross sales. The class implements CompensationModel (line 5) and provides:

  • instance variables grossSales (line 6) and commissionRate (line 7) to store the data required to calculate an employee’s commission,

  • a constructor (lines 10–25) to validate and initialize the instance variables,

  • get methods (lines 28 and 31) to return the instance variable values,

  • a calculateEarnings method (lines 34–37) that overrides the superclass version to return the grossSales times the commissionRate and

  • a toString method (lines 40–44) that overrides the superclass version to return a String representation of a Commission object for use in this program’s outputs.

Commission is declared final (line 5) so it may not be used as a superclass.

9.13.4 Testing the CompensationModel Hierarchy

Next, let’s create Employee objects and initialize each with an appropriate concrete CompensationModel implementation (Fig. 9.18).

The main method operates as follows:

  • Line 9 creates a Salaried CompensationModel object (salaried).

  • Line 10 creates the Employee salariedEmployee and injects its Compensation-Model, passing salaried as the second constructor argument.

  • Lines 12–13 create a Commission CompensationModel object (commission).

  • Line 14 creates the Employee commissionEmployee and inject its Compensation-Model, passing commission as the second constructor argument.

  • Line 17 creates an array of Employees and initializes it with salariedEmployee

    and commissionEmployee.

  • Lines 20–34 calculate each Employee’s earnings polymorphically. A requirement of this application is to give a 10% raise to employees who are paid a fixed weekly salary before calculating their earnings. Lines 22–29 use the pattern-matching instanceof operator to determine whether the current Employee’s Compensation-Model is a Salaried object. If so, line 22 converts the CompensationModel reference to a Salaried reference and assigns it to the variable named s in the condition. Lines 23–24 use the variable s in the if’s body to invoke Salaried-specific method getSalary to get the current Employee’s salary then increase it by 10%. Lines 27–28 use the new salary to initialize a new Salaried CompensationModel, calling setCompensationModel to inject the new Salaried object into the current Employee. Finally, lines 31–33 display the current Employee’s String representation and (possibly updated) earnings. Note in the output window that the salariedEmployee’s earnings are indeed 10% higher than its initial value in line 9.

9.13.5 Dependency Injection Design Benefits10

10. For more information on dependency injection, see the seminal book: Mark Seemann and Steven van Deursen, Dependency Injection Principles, Practices, and Patterns (Manning Publications, 2019).

Flexibility If CompensationModels Change

Declaring the CompensationModels as separate classes that implement the same interface provides flexibility for future changes. Suppose a company adds new ways to pay employees. We can simply define a new class that implements CompensationModel and overrides calculateEarnings appropriately.

Flexibility If Employees Are Promoted

The interface-based, composition-and-dependency-injection approach used in this example is more flexible than Section 9.8’s class hierarchy. In Section 9.8, if an Employee were promoted, you’d need to change its object type by creating a new object of the appropriate Employee subclass, then moving data into the new object. Using dependency injection, you can simply call Employee’s setCompensationModel method and inject a reference to a different CompensationModel that replaces the existing one. Inheritance is done at compile time, so it does not provide this flexibility.

Flexibility If Employees Acquire New Capabilities

The interface-based composition and dependency-injection approach is also more flexible for enhancing class Employee. If we decide to support retirement plans (such as 401(k)s and IRAs), we could say that every Employee has a RetirementPlan. First, we’d define the RetirementPlan interface with a makeRetirementDeposit method and provide appropriate subclass implementations.

Using interface-based composition and dependency injection, as in this example, requires only small changes to class Employee to support RetirementPlans:

  • an instance variable that refers to a RetirementPlan,

  • one more constructor argument to initialize the RetirementPlan reference and

  • a setRetirementPlan method we can call if we ever need to inject a different Employee RetirementPlan.

9.13.6 interfaces vs. abstract Classes

Interface inheritance may require more work than implementation inheritance because concrete classes must provide both data and implementations of the interface’s abstract methods, even if they’re similar or identical among classes. As you’ve seen, this approach gives you additional flexibility by eliminating the tight coupling between classes.

interfaces Are More Flexible Than abstract Classes

Given that interfaces may contain instance methods and static methods with implementations, interfaces are appropriate for almost all cases in which you would have used abstract classes previously. With the exception of instance variables, you get the benefits that abstract classes provide. Also, a new class can implement any number of interfaces but can extend only one class (abstract or concrete).

interfaces Change Less Frequently Than Implementations

Just as superclasses can change, so can interfaces. If the signature of an interface method changes, all corresponding classes would require modification. Experience has shown that interfaces change much less frequently than implementations.

9.14 sealed Classes and Interfaces

 

Java 17 introduced sealed classes and sealed interfaces11 that enable developers to strictly control

11. “JEP 409: Sealed Classes.” Accessed September 19, 2024. https://openjdk.org/jeps/409.

  • the classes that are allowed to extend a sealed class,

  • the classes that are allowed to implement a sealed interface and

  • the interfaces that are allowed to extend a sealed interface.

The sealed keyword gives class and interface hierarchy designers complete control over the allowed direct subtypes and prevents other developers from extending a hierarchy unless an allowed subtype is explicitly declared non-sealed. sealed also simplifies code maintenance because the hierarchy is not prone to the errors introduced by incorrectly extending it with new classes or interfaces. In addition, sealed classes and interfaces streamline pattern-matching switch expressions by eliminating the default case that typically handles unexpected types. All classes in a sealed hierarchy are known in advance, so you simply provide a case for each class in the hierarchy.

For this demo, we’ll modify the CompensationModel hierarchy from Section 9.13 to use a sealed interface. Classes Employee, Salaried and Commission are identical, so we do not repeat them here.

Sealing the CompensationModel Hierarchy

Figure 9.19 declares the CompensationModel interface as sealed (line 5). The only classes that can implement this interface are listed in its permits clause’s comma-separated list (line 5). If we wish to support additional CompensationModels in the future, we must add them to this permits clause and recompile. For a sealed class, you place the sealed key-word before the class keyword and follow the class name with a permits clause.

We mentioned that an interface can extend another interface—this enables you to create an interface that enhances the functionality described by an existing interface. In a sealed interface that extends another interface, the permits clause listing the classes that are allowed to implement the interface must appear after the extends clause, as in:

Click here to view code image

public sealed interface NewInterface extends SuperInterface
      permits ListOfImplementingClasses {
      // interface members
}

In a sealed class, the permits clause listing the classes that are allowed to extend the class must appear after any extends or implements clauses, as in:

Click here to view code image

public sealed class NewClass extends Superclass implements ListOfInterfaces
   permits ListOfSubclasses {
   // class members
}
Note Regarding the Salaried and Commission Classes

Classes that extend sealed classes or implement sealed interfaces must be declared

  • final so they cannot be extended,

  • sealed and specify a permits clause indicating specific allowed subclasses, or

  • non-sealed to allow them to be extended without restrictions.

In Figs. 9.16 and 9.17, we declared the Salaried and Commission classes final, so they do not require any modifications for this example.

switch Expression in main

For this example, we replaced Fig. 9.18’s use of an if statement and the pattern-matching instanceof operator with a pattern-matching switch expression that yields a value (Fig. 9.20, lines 23–34) to demonstrate pattern matching with a sealed hierarchy. Recall that we introduced pattern-matching switch expressions that yield values in Section 5.5. Lines 24 and 33 specify cases for each of the sealed hierarchy’s allowed types. This switch expression does not require a default case, as a sealed hierarchy cannot have unexpected types. You’ll get compilation errors if you expand the sealed hierarchy and forget to add appropriate cases for new types. Note in the output window that the salariedEmployee’s earnings are indeed 10% higher than its initial value in line 9.

9.15 private Constructors

 

We mentioned previously that constructors are typically declared public. Sometimes, it’s useful to declare one or more private constructors in a class.

Preventing Object Instantiation

You can prevent client code from creating objects of a class by making the class’s constructors private. For example, consider class Math, which contains only public static constants and public static methods. Since there’s no need to create a Math object to use the class’s constants and methods, its constructor is private.

Sharing Initialization Code in Constructors

One use of a private constructor is sharing initialization code among a class’s other constructors. You can use delegating constructors (introduced in Section 8.10) to call the private constructor with the shared initialization code.

Factory Methods

Another common use of private constructors is to force client code to use “factory methods” to create objects. A factory method is a public static method that creates and initializes an object of a specified type (possibly of the same class), then returns a reference to it. A benefit of this architecture is that the method’s return type can be an interface or a superclass (abstract or concrete).

9.16 protected Members

 

Chapter 8 discussed access modifiers public and private:

  • A class’s public members are accessible wherever the program has a reference to an object of that class or one of its subclasses.

  • A class’s private members are accessible only within the class itself.

Access modifier protected offers an intermediate access level between public and private:

  • A superclass’s protected members can be accessed directly by members of that superclass, by members of its subclasses and by members of other classes in the same package.

  • A superclass’s protected members also have package access. Recall from Section 8.19 that in a program with multiple classes in the same package, the classes can access each other’s package-access members directly through references to objects of those classes or through the class name for static members.

So, from most to least restrictive, Java’s access modifiers for class members are:

  • private

  • package access (the default when no access specifier is listed)

  • protected

  • public

A superclass’s public and protected members retain their access modifiers when they become members of the subclass:

  • public superclass members become public subclass members, and

  • protected superclass members become protected superclass members.

A superclass’s private members are hidden from subclasses and can be manipulated by the subclass only through the public or protected methods inherited from the super-class. Subclass methods can refer to public and protected members inherited from the superclass simply by using the member names.

Declaring private instance variables helps you test, debug and correctly modify systems. If a subclass could access its superclass’s private instance variables, classes that inherit from that subclass could also access them. This would eliminate the benefits of information hiding.

Notes on Using protected Instance Variables

Inheriting protected instance variables enables subclasses to access the variables directly. In most cases, however, you should use private instance variables to encourage proper software engineering. Your code will be easier to maintain, modify and debug.

Using protected instance variables creates several potential problems. First, the subclass object can set an inherited variable’s value directly without using a set method. Therefore, a subclass object can assign an invalid value to the variable, possibly leaving the object in an inconsistent state.

Another problem with protected instance variables is that subclass methods are more likely to depend on the superclass’s data implementation. In practice, subclasses should depend only on the superclass services (i.e., non-private methods) and not the super-class’s data implementation. With protected instance variables in the superclass, we may need to modify all the subclasses of the superclass if the superclass implementation changes. Such a class is considered to be fragile or brittle because a change in the superclass can “break” subclass implementation. You should be able to change the superclass implementation while still providing the same services to the subclasses. Of course, if the superclass services change, we must reimplement its subclasses.

A third problem is that a class’s protected members are visible to all classes in the same package as the class containing the protected members—this is not always desirable. Declaring superclass instance variables private (as opposed to protected) enables the superclass implementation of these instance variables to change without affecting subclass implementations.

Use the protected access modifier when a superclass should provide a method only to its subclasses and other classes in the same package but not to other clients. Avoid protected instance variables. Instead, include non-private methods that access private instance variables.

9.17 Wrap-Up

This chapter introduced inheritance—the ability to create classes by acquiring an existing class’s members (without copying and pasting the code) and having the ability to embellish them with new capabilities. You learned the notions of superclasses and subclasses and used keyword extends to create a subclass that inherits members from a superclass.

We showed how to use the @Override annotation to prevent unintended overloading by indicating that a method overrides a superclass method. You used super to access overridden superclass members. You saw how constructors are used in inheritance hierarchies. You studied the methods of class Object, the direct or indirect superclass of all Java classes. We discussed the merits of designing classes with composition vs. inheritance.

We introduced polymorphism—the ability to process objects that share the same superclass in a class hierarchy as if they were all objects of the superclass. We discussed how polymorphism makes systems extensible and maintainable, then demonstrated how to use overridden methods to effect polymorphic behavior.

We introduced abstract classes, which allow you to provide an appropriate super-class from which other classes can inherit. You learned that an abstract class can declare abstract methods that each concrete subclass must implement and that a program can use variables of an abstract class to invoke the subclasses’ implementations of abstract methods polymorphically. You saw how to determine an object’s type at execution time.

We explained the notions of final methods and classes. The chapter discussed declaring and implementing an interface as a way for possibly disparate classes to implement common functionality, enabling objects of those classes to be processed polymorphically. We discussed why constructors should not call overridable methods and that it’s OK to call final, static and private methods from constructors.

We introduced default, static and private interface methods. We discussed the purpose of private constructors. We introduced the access modifier protected and mentioned that subclass methods can directly access inherited protected superclass members.

We initially focused on implementation inheritance, then pointed out that decades of experience have shown it can be difficult to maintain and modify tightly coupled implementation-inheritance hierarchies. So, we refactored our Employee payroll example to use interface inheritance. In that example, we introduced the composition-and-dependency-injection approach in which a class contains a reference to an object that provides behaviors required by objects of the class. Then, we discussed how this interface-based approach makes the example easier to modify and evolve. Finally, we discussed sealed classes and interfaces for controlling which classes can extend a class or implement an interface.

You’ve now studied classes, objects, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and interfaces—the essential aspects of object-oriented programming. In the next chapter, we’ll discuss exceptions in more depth—exception handling enables more robust programs.

Exception Handling: A Deeper Look

Objectives

In this chapter, you’ll:

  • Learn why exception handling is an effective mechanism for responding to runtime problems.

  • Use try blocks to delimit code in which exceptions might occur.

  • Use throw to indicate that a problem occurred.

  • Use catch blocks to specify exception handlers.

  • Learn when to use exception handling.

  • Understand the exception class hierarchy.

  • Use the finally block to release resources to prevent resource leaks.

  • Chain exceptions by catching one exception and throwing another.

  • Create custom exceptions.

  • Use the debugging feature assert to test that a condition is true at a particular point in a method.

  • Learn how a try-with-resources statement can automatically deallocate a resource when a try block terminates.

Outline

Special Section: Generative AI Exercises

10.1 Introduction

 

As you’ve learned in earlier chapters, an exception indicates a problem during a program’s execution. Exception handling enables applications to resolve (or handle) exceptions. The features presented in this chapter help you write robust and fault-tolerant programs that can deal with problems and continue executing or terminate gracefully.1

1. Java exception handling is based in part on the work of Andrew Koenig and Bjarne Stroustrup—A. Koenig and B. Stroustrup, “Exception Handling for C++ (revised),” Proceedings of the Usenix C++ Conference, pp. 149–176, San Francisco, April 1990.

First, we handle an exception that occurs when a method attempts to divide an integer by zero. We discuss when to use exception handling and present a portion of the exception-handling class hierarchy. You’ll learn that only subclasses of Throwable can be used with exception handling. We introduce the try statement’s finally block, which executes whether or not an exception occurs. We then demonstrate how to use chained exceptions to add application-specific information to an exception and how to create your own exception types. Next, we introduce preconditions and postconditions, which must be true when your methods are called and when they return, respectively. We then present assertions, which help you debug your code during development. We also discuss catching multiple exceptions with one catch handler and the try-with-resources statement that automatically releases a resource after it’s used in a try block.

Exceptions Used Throughout This Book

This chapter focuses on the exception-handling concepts and presents mechanical examples demonstrating key features. Many Java API methods throw exceptions that we handle in our code. The following table shows some of the exception types we’ve covered, as well as others we’ll discuss in later chapters.

In industry, organizations develop their own design, coding, testing, debugging and maintenance standards. Companies often have exception-handling standards based on the types of applications they develop, such as real-time systems, high-performance mathematical calculations, big data, network-based distributed systems, artificial intelligence applications, etc.

When to Use Exception Handling

Exception handling is designed to process synchronous errors—these occur in a program’s regular flow of control as statements execute. Common examples are division by zero, outof-range array indices, arithmetic overflow (i.e., a value outside the representable range of values) and invalid method parameters.

Exception handling provides a single, uniform technique for documenting, detecting and recovering from errors. This helps developers working on large projects understand each other’s error-processing code. Exception handling is not meant as an alternate way to specify a program’s flow of control or for issues that can be prevented simply by testing a condition before performing a task. Sometimes, you can prevent an exception by validating data first. For example, before you perform integer division, you can ensure that the denominator is not zero, which prevents the ArithmeticException that occurs when you divide by zero. Exception handling is not designed to process problems associated with asynchronous events (e.g., network message arrivals, mouse clicks and keystrokes), which occur in parallel with and independent of the program’s flow of control.

You should incorporate your exception-handling and error-recovery strategy into your system from the inception of the design process. Including these after a system has been implemented can be difficult.

10.2 Example: Divide by Zero without Exception Handling

 

First, let’s demonstrate what happens when exceptions arise in a program that does not use exception handling. Figure 10.1 prompts the user for two integers and passes them to the quotient method, which calculates the integer quotient and returns an int result. In this example, you’ll learn that exceptions are thrown (i.e., the exception occurs) by a method when it detects a problem and cannot handle it. The first sample execution in Fig. 10.1 shows a successful integer division.

Stack Trace

In the second execution, the user enters 0 as the denominator. Several lines of information are displayed in response to this invalid input. This stack trace includes the exception’s package and class name (java.lang.ArithmeticException) in a descriptive message that indicates the problem, the line where it occurred and the method-call stack (i.e., the call chain) when the problem occurred. The stack trace shows the path of execution that led to the exception method by method. This helps you debug the program. Even if a problem has not occurred, you can print a stack trace at any time by calling Thread.dumpStack().

Stack Trace for an ArithmeticException

The first line specifies that an ArithmeticException occurred. The text /byzero after the class name indicates that this exception happened due to an attempt to divide (/) by zero. Java does not allow division by zero in integer arithmetic. When this occurs, Java throws an ArithmeticException. Such exceptions can arise from several arithmetic problems, so the text /byzero provides specific information about the exception’s cause to help you understand the problem.

Starting from the stack trace’s last line, note that the exception was detected in line 19. Each line of the stack trace contains the class and method names separated by a dot (e.g., DivideByZeroNoExceptionHandling.main) followed by the filename and line number (e.g., DivideByZeroNoExceptionHandling.java:19) where the problem occurred in that method. Moving up the stack trace, note that method main called method quotient where the exception occurred in line 8. The stack trace’s top line number indicates the exception’s throw point—the initial point at which the exception occurred.

Side Note Regarding Floating-Point Arithmetic

Java allows division by zero with floating-point values, resulting in positive or negative infinity, which is displayed as "Infinity" or "-Infinity". If you divide 0.0 by 0.0, the result is NaN (not a number)—a floating-point value displayed as "NaN". To compare a floating-point value to NaN, use Float.isNaN(floatValue) or Double.isNaN(doubleValue). Each returns a boolean value indicating whether the argument value is NaN. Classes Float and Double are in package java.lang.

Stack Trace for an InputMismatchException

In Fig. 10.1’s third execution, the user entered "hello" as the numerator, resulting in an InputMismatchException (package java.util). Our prior examples that input numeric values assumed the user would enter a proper integer value. Users sometimes enter erroneous noninteger values. An InputMismatchException occurs when Scanner method nextInt receives a String that does not represent a valid integer. Starting from the end of the stack trace, note that the exception was detected in line 15. Moving up the stack trace, we notice that the exception occurred in Scanner’s method nextInt.

Program Termination

In Fig. 10.1, when exceptions occur and Java displays stack traces, the program exits. This does not always happen—sometimes, a program can continue executing. In such cases, the program may produce unexpected results. For example, a graphical user interface (GUI) application will often continue executing. In Fig. 10.1, two exception types were detected in main. In the next example, we’ll handle these exceptions so that you can enable the program to run to normal completion.
