10.3 Example: Handling ArithmeticExceptions and InputMismatchExceptions

 

Figure 10.2 modifies the previous program, using exception handling to deal with any ArithmeticExceptions and InputMismatchExceptions that arise. The program still prompts the user to enter two integers and passes them to method quotient, which calculates the quotient and returns an int result. If the user makes an input mistake, this program catches and handles the exception, allowing the user to re-enter the input.

Lines 17–41 repeatedly ask the user for input until valid inputs are received. In the sample execution:

  • First, the user enters "hello" when an integer is expected. An InputMismatch-Exception occurs, and the program asks the user to try again.

  • Next, the user enters a valid numerator (100) but a denominator of 0. An ArithmeticException exception occurs, and the program asks the user to try again.

  • Finally, the user enters a proper numerator and a non-zero denominator, so the program performs the division, displays the result and completes successfully.

Enclosing Code in a try Block

Lines 18–28 contain a try block, which encloses the code that might throw an exception and the code that should not execute if an exception occurs—if an exception occurs, the remaining code in the try block will be skipped. A try block consists of the keyword try followed by a block of code enclosed in curly braces. The statements that read the integers from the keyboard (lines 20 and 22) each use method nextInt, which throws an Input-MismatchException if the value read in is not an integer.

The division that can cause an ArithmeticException is not performed in the try block. Rather, the call to method quotient (line 24) in the try block invokes the code that attempts the division (line 10), and the JVM throws an ArithmeticException object when the denominator is zero. Exceptions may surface from

  • code in a try block,

  • method calls initiated by code in a try block or

  • the Java Virtual Machine as it executes Java bytecodes.

Catching Exceptions

This example’s try block is followed by two catch blocks:

  • one handles an InputMismatchException (lines 29–35) and

  • one handles an ArithmeticException (lines 36–40).

A catch block (also called a catch clause or exception handler) catches and handles an exception thrown from the corresponding try. The catch keyword is followed by

  • required parentheses containing an exception parameter identifying the exception type the handler can process and

  • a block of code enclosed in curly braces.

At least one catch block—or a finally block (Section 10.6)—must immediately follow the try block. We prefer to name our exception parameters (inputMismatchException and arithmeticException) based on their types. Many Java programmers use the letter e as the name of their exception parameters.

When an exception occurs in a try block, the first catch whose type matches the thrown exception’s type executes. The catch’s type matches if it is the thrown exception’s type or is a direct or indirect superclass of it. The exception parameter’s name enables the catch block to interact with a caught exception object (as in lines 30–31 and 37). We used the System.err (standard error stream) object here to output error messages. Like System.out, System.err’s print methods display data to the command prompt by default.

If lines 20 or 22 cause an InputMismatchException, the try block terminates (so method quotient is not called), and execution continues with the catch block at lines 29–35. Because an InputMismatchException occurred, the call to method nextInt never successfully read the user’s invalid input—so line 32 reads and discards that input with a call to Scanner method nextLine. Then, lines 33–34 display an error message and ask the user to try again. We’ll discuss the catch block for ArithmeticExceptions shortly.

When either catch block terminates, main continues after the last catch block, returning to the top of the loop to re-prompt the user for input. We’ll soon take a deeper look at how this flow of control works in exception handling.

Multi-catch

It’s common for a try block to be followed by several catch blocks to handle various exceptions. If several catch blocks’ bodies are identical and there are no is-a relationships among the exceptions being caught, you can use the multi-catch feature to catch those exceptions in a single catch handler and perform the same task. The syntax for a multi-catch is:

Click here to view code image

catch (Type1 | Type2 | Type3 e)

Each exception type is separated from the next with a vertical bar (|). The preceding line of code indicates that any of the types (or their subclasses) can be caught in the exception handler. Any number of exception types can be specified in a multi-catch.

Uncaught Exceptions

An uncaught exception is one for which there are no matching catch blocks. There were uncaught exceptions in the second and third outputs of Fig. 10.1. Recall that when exceptions occurred in that example, the program terminated immediately after displaying the exception’s stack trace.

Uncaught exceptions do not always result in program termination. Java uses a “multithreaded” model of program execution—each thread is a concurrent activity. One program can have many threads. If a program has only one thread, an uncaught exception will cause the program to terminate. If a program has multiple threads, an uncaught exception will terminate only the thread in which the exception occurred. Some threads may rely on others. If one thread terminates due to an uncaught exception, there may be adverse effects on the program’s other threads. Chapter 18, Concurrency: Platform Threads to Virtual Threads, discusses these issues in depth.

Termination Model of Exception Handling

In Fig. 10.2, the first catch block catches InputMismatchExceptions, and the second catch block catches ArithmeticExceptions. After an exception is handled, program control does not return to the throw point because the try block has expired. Rather, control resumes after the last catch. This is known as the termination model of exception handling. Some languages use the resumption model of exception handling, in which, after an exception is handled, control resumes just after the throw point.

After executing a catch block, this program’s flow of control proceeds to the first statement after the last catch block (line 41). In this case, the program reaches the while loop’s closing brace, so control returns to the loop’s condition. The condition is still true, so the program prompts the user for input again. This loop executes until valid input is entered. At that point, line 27 assigns false to continueLoop, then the try block terminates. When no exceptions are thrown in the try block, Java skips the catch blocks and control continues with the first statement after the catch blocks.2 Now the loop’s condition is false, and main ends.

2. We’ll present another possibility when we discuss the finally block in Section 10.6.

The try block and its corresponding catch and/or finally blocks form a try statement. Do not confuse the terms “try block” and “try statement”—the latter includes the try block and the following catch blocks and/or finally block.

As with any other block of code, when a try block terminates, local variables declared in the block go out of scope and are no longer accessible; thus, a try block’s local variables are not accessible in the corresponding catch blocks. When a catch block terminates, local variables declared within that block (including its exception parameter) also go out of scope.

throws Clause

In method quotient (lines 8–11), the throws clause (line 9) specifies the exceptions the method might throw if problems occur. This clause, which must appear after the method’s parameter list and before the body, contains a comma-separated list of exception types. Such exceptions might be thrown by statements in the method’s body or methods called from there. We’ve added the throws clause to this method to indicate to its callers that this method might throw an ArithmeticException. Some exception types, such as ArithmeticException, are not required to be listed in the throws clause. For those that are, the method can throw exceptions that have the is-a relationship with the classes listed in the throws clause. You’ll learn more about this in Section 10.4.

Read a method’s online API documentation before using it in a program. The documentation specifies exceptions thrown by the method (if any) and indicates why such exceptions might occur. Next, read the online API documentation for the specified exception classes, which typically lists why such exceptions occur. Finally, handle those exceptions in your program.

Method quotient Failing Due to Division By Zero

When line 10 executes, if the denominator is zero, the JVM throws an ArithmeticException object. This object will be caught by the catch block at lines 36–40, which displays the exception’s basic information returned by its toString method. Then, the program asks the user to try again.

When quotient throws an ArithmeticException, it terminates immediately and does not return a value. Its local variables go out of scope. If quotient contained local variables that were references to objects and there were no other references to those objects, the objects would be marked for garbage collection. In this program, when an Arithmetic-Exception occurs, the try block from which quotient was called terminates before lines 25–27 can execute. Here, too, the try block’s local variables go out of scope.

Method quotient Successfully Executing

If the denominator is not zero, quotient performs the division and returns the result to the line in the try block that called quotient (line 24). Lines 25–26 display the result, and line 27 sets continueLoop to false. In this case, the try block completes successfully, so the program skips the catch blocks, the condition at line 17 fails and main completes execution normally.

10.4 Java Exception Hierarchy

 

All Java exception classes inherit directly or indirectly from class Exception, forming an inheritance hierarchy. You can extend this hierarchy with your own exception classes.

The following UML class diagram shows a small portion of the inheritance hierarchy for class Throwable (a subclass of Object), which is the superclass of class Exception—only Throwable objects can be used with the exception-handling mechanism:

Class Throwable has two direct subclasses—Exception and Error:

  • Class Exception and its subclasses—for example, RuntimeException (package java.lang) and IOException (package java.io)—represent exceptional situations that can occur in a Java program and that can be caught by the application.

  • Class Error and its subclasses represent abnormal situations that happen in the JVM. Most Errors happen infrequently and should not be caught by applications—it’s usually not possible for applications to recover from them.

The Java exception hierarchy contains hundreds of classes. Information about them can be found throughout the Java API. You can view Throwable’s documentation at

Click here to view code image

https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/
   lang/Throwable.html

From there, you can look at this class’s subclasses for more information about Java’s Exceptions and Errors.

Catching Subclass Exceptions

If a catch handler is written to catch superclass exception objects, it will also catch all objects of that exception class’s subclasses. This enables a catch block to handle related exceptions polymorphically. You should catch each subclass individually if they require different processing.

Only the First Matching catch Executes

If multiple catch blocks match a particular exception type—e.g., one catches a specific exception class, and another catches its superclass—only the first matching catch block executes. For example, we could follow a catch block for ArithmeticException with a catch block for Exception—both match ArithmeticExceptions, but only the first matching catch would execute. Placing a catch block for a superclass exception type before other catch blocks that catch subclass exception types would prevent those catch blocks from executing, so a compilation error occurs.

Catching subclass types individually is subject to error if you forget to test for one or more of the subclass types explicitly. Catching the superclass guarantees that objects of all subclasses will be caught. Positioning a catch block for the superclass type after all other subclass catch blocks ensures that all subclass exceptions are eventually caught.

In industry, throwing or catching type Exception is discouraged—we use it in this chapter to demonstrate exception-handling mechanics. In subsequent chapters, we generally throw and catch more specific exception types.

10.5 Checked vs. Unchecked Exceptions

 

Java distinguishes between two categories of exceptions—checked and unchecked. Understanding the distinction between them will help you write more robust code. The Java compiler enforces special requirements for checked exceptions.

RuntimeExceptions Are Unchecked Exceptions

An exception class’s location in the Java Exception class hierarchy (Section 10.4) determines whether it’s checked or unchecked. Every direct or indirect subclass of RuntimeException (package java.lang) is an unchecked exception. These are typically caused by programming errors. Several common unchecked exceptions include:

  • ArithmeticExceptions (shown in Figs. 10.1 and 10.2) occur when you attempt to divide by zero in integer arithmetic. To avoid these, ensure that the denominator is not zero before the calculation.

  • ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsExceptions (Chapter 6) occur when you try to access array elements outside the array’s bounds. To avoid these, ensure that array indices are greater than or equal to 0 and less than the array’s length.

  • IllegalArgumentExceptions are often thrown by constructors and methods when they receive incorrect arguments (as we did in Chapters 8 and 9). You can avoid these by ensuring you pass correct arguments to methods.

  • NullPointerExceptions occur when you attempt to call a method via a variable that contains null—that is, the variable does not refer to an object. You can avoid these by ensuring that a reference is not null before you use it to call a method.

  • StringIndexOutOfBoundsExceptions occur when you try to access a character outside a String’s bounds. You can avoid these by ensuring that your indices are always greater than or equal to 0 and less than the value returned by String’s length method.

Errors are Unchecked

Direct and indirect subclasses of Error are unchecked by the compiler—they represent critical errors from which programs cannot recover. For example, VirtualMachineError’s documentation3 says this error is “thrown to indicate that the Java Virtual Machine is broken or has run out of resources necessary for it to continue operating.” If this error occurs, there’s nothing your program can do, so you should not catch it.

3. “Class VirtualMachineError.” Accessed September 22, 2024. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/VirtualMachineError.html.

Checked Exceptions

All classes that inherit directly or indirectly from Exception but not RuntimeException are checked exceptions. These are typically caused by conditions not controlled by the program. For example, in file processing (Chapter 11), if a Java program attempts to open a file that does not exist, a checked FileNotFoundException occurs.

The Compiler and Checked Exceptions

The compiler enforces a catch-or-declare requirement for checked exceptions. If a method’s code might throw a checked exception, the method must either

  • catch the exception by wrapping the code in a try block followed by a catch handler that deals with the checked-exception type (or one of its superclasses) or

  • declare the exception to the method’s callers by placing the exception type in a throws clause between the method’s parameter list and body.

If the code does not satisfy these requirements, a compilation error occurs. This forces you to think about and deal with potential problems, producing more robust code. If an exception can be handled meaningfully in a method, the method should catch the exception rather than declare it.

The Compiler and Unchecked Exceptions

The compiler does not enforce the catch-or-declare requirement for unchecked exceptions, which typically represent preventable coding errors. Ideally, you should fix such errors during program development. However, providing appropriate exception handling code for unchecked exceptions can make your programs more robust. Unchecked exceptions are not required to be listed in a method’s throws clause.

throws Clauses in Overridden Methods

If a subclass method overrides a superclass method, it’s an error for the subclass method to list more exceptions in its throws clause than the superclass method does. However, a subclass’s throws clause may list a subset of the types in a superclass’s throws clause.

10.6 finally Block

 

Programs often accomplish their tasks by using system resources, such as memory, files, network connections and database connections. When a program no longer needs a resource, the program should immediately return it to the system to avoid a resource leak, which can prevent other programs from using it.

In programming languages such as C and C++, the most common resource leak is a memory leak. Java’s automatic garbage collection prevents most memory leaks, but Java will not garbage-collect an object until there are no remaining references to it. So, memory leaks can still occur if a program erroneously keeps references to unneeded objects. Other resources must be explicitly released to ensure they’re available for future use.

finally Block Placement

A try statement’s finally block (also called the finally clause) consists of the finally keyword, followed by code enclosed in curly braces:

  • If a try statement has one or more catch blocks, the finally block is optional and is placed after the last catch block.

  • If a try statement has no catch blocks, the finally block is required and immediately follows the try block.

When the finally Block Executes

If present, a finally block always executes when its corresponding try block terminates, regardless of whether an exception occurs. The only case in which a finally block does not execute is if the try block calls the System class’s exit method, which immediate terminates the program. If an exception occurs but is not caught by the catch handlers or if a catch block throws an exception, control proceeds to the finally block before the program passes the exception to the next enclosing try block, typically in a calling method. Because a finally block always executes, it’s an ideal location for resource-release code that returns files, network connections, database connections and other resources to the system.

Demonstrating the finally Block

Figure 10.3 mechanically demonstrates that the finally block executes whether or not an exception is thrown in the corresponding try block. The program contains static methods main (lines 5–14), throwException (lines 17–35) and doesNotThrowException (lines 38–50). Methods throwException and doesNotThrowException are declared static, so main can call them directly.

Throwing Exceptions Using the throw Statement

Method main (Fig. 10.3) begins executing, enters its try block and line 7 immediately calls method throwException (lines 17–35). The throw statement in line 20 throws an Exception to immediately terminate the try block. The object in a throw statement must be of a class that directly or indirectly inherits from Throwable.

Rethrowing Exceptions

The Exception from line 20 is caught at line 22. Then, line 25 rethrows the exception. Exceptions typically are rethrown when a catch block, upon receiving an exception, can only partially process it. Rethrowing an exception defers the exception handling (or perhaps a portion of it) to another catch block associated with an enclosing try statement. You rethrow an exception by using throw, followed by the exception parameter name, which refers to the exception object that was just caught.

When a rethrow occurs, the next enclosing try block gets an opportunity to detect and handle the exception. In this case, the next enclosing try block is in lines 6–8 in method main. However, before the rethrown exception is returned to line 7 in main, the finally block in lines 30–32 executes. Then, method throwException terminates, main detects the rethrown exception in the try block and handles it in the catch block (lines 9–11).

finally Also Executes When No Exceptions Occur

Next, line 13 in main calls method doesNotThrowException (lines 38–50). No exception is thrown in doesNotThrowException’s try block (lines 39–41), so the program skips the catch block (lines 42–44), but the finally block (lines 45–47) nevertheless executes. Then, control proceeds to the statement after the finally block (line 49), the function returns to main, and the program terminates.

Do Not Throw Exceptions from finally Blocks

Do not write code in a finally block that can throw an exception. If such code is required, enclose it in a try…catch within the finally block to prevent the finally from throwing the exception. When a finally block throws a new exception while one is still being processed, the first exception is lost.

Do Not Overuse try Statements

The try statement removes error-processing code from a program’s logic, improving program clarity. Do not wrap each statement that might throw in a separate try statement, which decreases readability. Instead, place significant portions of your code in a try block, followed by the necessary catch blocks and, if needed, a finally block (if one is required).

10.7 Stack Unwinding and Obtaining Information from an Exception

 

When an exception is thrown but not caught in a particular method, the method-call stack is “unwound” and an attempt is made to catch the exception in the next enclosing try block. This process is called stack unwinding. Unwinding the method-call stack means that the method in which the exception was not caught terminates, all local variables in that method go out of scope and control returns to the statement that invoked that method. If a try block encloses that statement, an attempt is made to catch the exception. If a try block does not enclose that statement or the exception is not caught, stack unwinding occurs again. Figure 10.4 demonstrates stack unwinding, and the exception handler in main shows how to access the data in an exception object.4

4. If you execute this example using the command java UsingExceptions.java—which compiles the program in memory then runs it—this program’s output will differ from that of Fig. 10.4.

Stack Unwinding

In main, the try block (lines 6–8) calls method1 (declared at lines 30–32), which in turn calls method2 (declared at lines 35–37), which in turn calls method3 (declared at lines 40–42). The program then proceeds as follows:

  • Line 41 in method3 throws an Exception object—this is the throw point.

  • Because the throw statement is not enclosed in a try block, stack unwinding occurs. So, method3 terminates at line 41, then returns control to line 36—the statement in method2 that invoked method3.

  • Because no try block encloses line 36, stack unwinding occurs again. So, method2 terminates at line 36 and returns control to line 31—the statement in method1 that invoked method2.

  • Because no try block encloses line 31, stack unwinding occurs again. So, method1 terminates at line 31 and returns control to line 7—the statement in main that invoked method1.

  • The try block at lines 6–8 encloses this statement. The exception has not been handled, so the try block terminates, and the first matching catch block (lines 9–26) catches and processes the exception.

If there were no matching catch blocks, and the checked exception is not declared in each method that throws it, a compilation error would occur—main catches the exception so it does not have a throws clause.

Obtaining Data from an Exception Object

All exceptions derive from Throwable, which has a printStackTrace method that outputs the stack trace to the standard error stream. Often, this is helpful in testing and debugging. Class Throwable also provides a getStackTrace method that retrieves the stack-trace information that might be printed by printStackTrace. Class Throwable’s getMessage method (inherited by all Throwable subclasses) returns the descriptive string stored in an exception. Throwable method toString (also inherited by all Throwable subclasses) returns a String containing the name of the exception’s class and a descriptive message.

Java’s default exception handler runs if an exception is not caught, displaying the name of the exception, a descriptive message that indicates the problem that occurred and a complete execution stack trace. In an application with a single thread of execution, the application terminates. In an application with multiple threads, the thread that caused the exception terminates. We discuss multithreading in Chapter 18.

The catch handler in Fig. 10.4 (lines 9–26) demonstrates getMessage, printStack-Trace and getStackTrace. If we wanted to output the stack-trace information to streams other than the standard error stream, we could use the information returned from getStackTrace and output it to another stream or use one of the overloaded versions of printStackTrace. Sending data to other streams is discussed in Chapter 11.

Line 10 invokes the exception’s getMessage method to get the exception description. Line 11 invokes the exception’s printStackTrace method to output the stack trace that indicates where the exception occurred. Line 14 invokes the exception’s getStackTrace method to obtain the stack-trace information as an array of StackTraceElement objects for more detailed inspection. Lines 20–25 get each StackTraceElement in the array and invoke its methods getClassName, getFileName, getLineNumber and getMethodName to get the class name, filename, line number and method name, respectively, for that Stack-TraceElement. Each StackTraceElement represents one method call on the method-call stack.

The program’s output shows that the information printStackTrace displays follows the pattern:

Click here to view code image

className.methodName(fileName:lineNumber)

where className, methodName and fileName are the class, method and file in which the exception occurred, and lineNumber is where in the file the exception occurred. Method getStackTrace enables custom processing of the exception information. Compare the output of printStackTrace with the output created from the StackTraceElements to confirm that both contain the same stack-trace information.

Stack-Walking API

Throwable methods printStackTrace and getStackTrace each process the entire method-call stack. When debugging, this can be inefficient. For example, you may be interested only in stack frames corresponding to methods of a specific class. Java’s Stack-Walking API (class StackWalker in package java.lang) uses lambdas and streams (Chapter 14) to access method-call-stack information more efficiently. You can learn more about this API at:

https://openjdk.org/jeps/259

10.8 Chained Exceptions

 

Sometimes, a method responds to an exception by throwing a different exception type specific to the current application. If a catch block throws a new exception, the original exception’s information and stack trace are lost. Earlier Java versions provided no mechanism to wrap the original exception information with the new exception’s information to provide a complete stack trace showing where the original problem occurred, making debugging more difficult. Chained exceptions enable an exception object to maintain the complete stack-trace information from the original exception. Figure 10.5 demonstrates chained exceptions.

Program Flow of Control

The program has four methods—main (lines 5–12), method1 (lines 15–22), method2 (lines 25–32) and method3 (lines 35–37)—and operates as follows:

  • Line 7 in main’s try block calls method1. Line 17 in method1’s try block calls method2. Line 27 in method2’s try block calls method3.

  • In method3, line 36 throws a new Exception. Because line 36 is not in a try block, method3 terminates, and the exception is returned to line 27 in the calling method (method2).

  • Line 27 is in a try block, so the try block terminates, and the exception is caught at lines 29–31.

  • Line 30 in the catch block throws a new exception. We call the Exception constructor with two arguments, where the second represents the exception that was the original cause of the problem—every exception class has a constructor like this. In this program, the original exception occurred at line 36. Because an exception is thrown from the catch block, method2 terminates and returns the new exception to line 17 in method1.

  • Line 17 is in a try block, so the try block terminates, and the exception is caught at lines 19–21.

  • Line 20 in the catch block throws a new exception, using the exception that was caught as the constructor’s second argument. Because an exception is thrown from the catch block, method1 terminates and returns the new exception to line 7 in main.

  • The try block in main terminates, and the exception is caught at lines 9–11. Line 10 prints a stack trace containing all the information from the chained exceptions.

Throwable Method getCause

For any chained exception, you can get the Throwable that initially caused that exception by calling Throwable method getCause.

Program Output

In the program output:

  • the first three lines show the most recent exception thrown (i.e., the one from method1 at line 20),

  • the next four lines indicate the exception thrown from method2 at line 30, and

  • the last four lines represent the exception thrown from method3 at line 36.

As you read the output from bottom to top, it shows how many more chained exceptions remain.

10.9 Declaring Custom Exceptions

 

Most Java programmers use existing classes from the Java API, third-party vendors and freely available class libraries from sites like GitHub to build Java applications. The methods of those classes may throw appropriate exceptions when problems occur. You write code that processes these existing exceptions to make your programs more robust. If you build classes that other programmers will use, it’s often appropriate to declare your own exception classes specific to the problems that can occur when another programmer uses your classes. Associating each type of serious execution-time malfunction with an appropriately named Exception subclass improves program clarity.

Extending an Existing Exception Class

A new exception class must extend an existing one to ensure the new class can be used with the exception-handling mechanism. The new class’s name should end with “Exception” by convention. An exception class typically contains four constructors:

  • one that takes no arguments and passes a default error message String to the superclass constructor,

  • one that receives a customized error message as a String and passes it to the superclass constructor,

  • one that receives a customized error message as a String and a Throwable (for chaining exceptions) and passes both to the superclass constructor, and

  • one that receives a Throwable (for chaining exceptions) and passes it to the super-class constructor.

Use an Existing Exception Class if Possible

Most programmers will not need to declare their own exception classes. Before defining your own, study the Java API’s existing ones. If there is no appropriate existing class, try to extend a related exception class. For example, if you’re creating a new class to represent when a method attempts a division by zero, you might extend class ArithmeticException because division by zero occurs during arithmetic.

Choosing Whether Custom Exceptions Should be Checked or Unchecked

If the existing classes are not appropriate superclasses for your new exception class, decide whether your new class should be a checked or an unchecked exception class:

  • If clients should be required to handle the exception, the new exception class should be a checked exception that extends Exception but not RuntimeException. In this case, the client application should be able to reasonably recover from the exception.

  • If the client code can ignore the exception (i.e., the exception is an unchecked one), the new exception class should extend RuntimeException.

10.10 Preconditions and Postconditions

 

Programmers spend significant amounts of time maintaining and debugging code. To facilitate these tasks and to improve the overall design, you can specify the expected states before and after a method’s execution. These states are called preconditions and postconditions, respectively.

Preconditions

A precondition must be true when a method is invoked. Preconditions describe constraints on method parameters and any other expectations the method has about the current state of a program just before it begins executing. If the preconditions are not met, then the method’s behavior is undefined—it may throw an exception, proceed with an illegal value or attempt to recover from the error. You should not expect consistent behavior if the preconditions are not satisfied.

Postconditions

A postcondition is true after the method successfully returns. Postconditions describe constraints on the return value and any other side effects the method may have. When defining a method, you should document all postconditions so that others know what to expect when they call your method, and you should ensure that it honors all its postconditions if its preconditions are met.

Throwing Exceptions When Preconditions or Postconditions Are Not Met

When preconditions or postconditions are not met, methods typically throw exceptions. For example, examine String method charAt, which has one int parameter—an index in the String. Method charAt requires as a precondition that the index it receives is greater than or equal to zero and less than the String’s length. If the precondition is met, the postcondition states that the method will return the character at the index specified by its argument. Otherwise, charAt throws an IndexOutOfBoundsException. We trust that method charAt satisfies its postcondition, provided that we meet the precondition. We need not be concerned with the details of how the method actually retrieves the character at the index.

Documenting Preconditions or Postconditions

Typically, a method’s preconditions and postconditions are described as part of its specification. When designing your own methods, you typically state the preconditions and postconditions in a comment before the method declaration.

10.11 Assertions

 

As you implement and debug a class, it’s sometimes helpful to state conditions that should be true at a particular point in a method. These conditions, called assertions, help ensure a program’s validity by catching potential bugs and identifying possible logic errors during development. Preconditions and postconditions are two types of assertions. Preconditions are assertions about a program’s state when a method is invoked, and postconditions are assertions about its state after a method finishes.

The assert Statement

While assertions can be stated as comments to guide you during program development, Java includes two versions of the assert statement to validate assertions programmatically. The assert statement evaluates a boolean expression and, if false, throws an AssertionError (a subclass of Error). The first form of the assert statement is

assert expression;

which throws an AssertionError if expression is false. The second form is

Click here to view code image

assert expression1 : expression2;

which evaluates expression1 and throws an AssertionError with expression2 as the error message if expression1 is false.

Using assert

During development, you can use assertions to implement preconditions and postconditions programmatically or verify any other intermediate states that help ensure your code is working correctly.

Assertions are primarily for debugging and identifying logic errors in an application. They are ignored by default, so you must explicitly enable them when executing a program as follows—the -ea option stands for “enable assertions”:

java -ea AssertTest

Figure 10.6 demonstrates the assert statement. Line 9 prompts the user to enter a number between 0 and 10, then line 10 reads the number. Line 13 determines whether the user entered a number within the valid range. If the number is out of range, the assert statement reports an error; otherwise, the program proceeds normally. You should not use assert to indicate runtime problems in production code, as we do in Fig. 10.6 only for demonstration purposes. Production code should throw exceptions to indicate problems encountered during execution.

Do Not Catch AssertionErrors

AssertionErrors should be used only during program development to identify problems in your code. Do not catch them. Simply allow your program to terminate so you can then locate and fix the source of the problem to make your program more robust.

10.12 try-with-Resources Statement: Automatic Resource Deallocation

 

In early Java versions, you’d place resource-release code in a finally block to ensure that a resource was released, regardless of whether the corresponding try block that used the resource threw exceptions. The try-with-resources statement simplifies writing code in which you obtain one or more resources, use them in a try block and release them in a corresponding finally block. Most Java API classes representing resources that need to be released now implement the AutoCloseable interface and provide a close method. Objects of such classes may be used in a try-with-resources statement as follows:

Click here to view code image

try (var theObject = new ResourceClass()) {
   // Use theObject here. Resources automatically released when the
   // try block terminates successfully or due to an exception.
}
catch (Exception e) {
   // Catch exceptions that occur while using the resource.
}

where the ResourceClass in parentheses must implement AutoCloseable. The try-with-resources statement is the preferred way to manage AutoCloseable resources. The try block uses the ResourceClass object, then calls its close method to release the its resources when the block terminates successfully or due to an exception. The try-with-resources catch clause is optional. You can create multiple AutoCloseable objects in the parentheses following try by separating them with a semicolon (;). We’ll use the try-with-resources statement in several programs starting in Chapter 11, Files, I/O Streams, JSON Serialization & CSV Files.

try-with-Resources Can Use Effectively final Variables

If the compiler can infer that a local variable could have been declared final because the enclosing method never modifies it after it’s declared and initialized, then it’s effectively final. You can create an AutoCloseable object and assign it to a local variable that’s explicitly declared final or that’s effectively final. Then, you can use the variable in a try-with-resources statement that automatically releases the object’s resources:

Click here to view code image

var theObject = new ResourceClass();

try (theObject) {
   // Use theObject here. Resources automatically released when the
   // try block terminates successfully or due to an exception.
}
catch (Exception e) {
   // Catch exceptions that occur while using the resource.
}

As before, you can separate with a semicolon (;) multiple AutoCloseable objects in the parentheses following try. This simplifies the try-with-resources statement’s code, especially for cases in which the statement uses and releases multiple AutoCloseable objects.

Suppressed Exceptions

When an exception is thrown in a try-with-resources statement’s try block, the statement immediately closes the AutoCloseable resources specified in the try’s parentheses. If any exceptions occur while closing those resources, Java suppresses the new ones so the original exception can continue being processed. The suppressed exceptions are added to the original exception object. You can access the suppressed exception(s) via an exception object’s getSurpressed method (inherited from Throwable by all exception classes), which returns an array of the suppressed Throwable objects.

10.13 Unnamed Variables in catch Handlers

 

Java 22 introduced unnamed variables (_)5 for cases where a variable name is required but you do not need to use the variable. For example, Fig. 10.7 creates an array, then attempts to access an out-of-bounds element, which throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. A catch handler must specify a variable name after the exception type. However, if your catch handler does not require access to the exception object, you can use the unnamed variable _ in place of a variable name (line 10).

5. “JEP 456: Unnamed Variables & Patterns.” Accessed September 22, 2024. https://openjdk.org/jeps/456.

Unnamed Variables in record Patterns

You may also use unnamed variables in record patterns that decompose matching record objects in

  • pattern-matching instanceof expressions (Section 9.8.4) and

  • pattern-matching switch expressions (Section 8.20.1)

If a match requires only a subset of the record’s elements, the record pattern can use _ in place of the items you wish to ignore. For the complete list of other _ uses, visit

https://openjdk.org/jeps/456

10.14 Wrap-Up

In this chapter, you used exception handling via the try statement to deal with execution-time errors. You learned that exception handling enables you to remove error-handling code from the “main line” of the program’s execution, making your code easier to read. We showed how to use try blocks to enclose code that might throw exceptions and how to use catch blocks to deal with exceptions that arise. We also introduced multi-catch for processing several exceptions in the same catch handler.

You learned about the termination model of exception handling, in which program control does not return to the throw point after an exception is handled. We discussed checked vs. unchecked exceptions and how to specify with the throws clause the exceptions that a method might throw.

We showed that the finally block always executes, regardless of whether an exception occurs in the corresponding try block, making the finally block good for resource deallocation. You also learned how to re-throw exceptions. We showed how to obtain information about an exception using methods printStackTrace, getStackTrace and getMessage. We presented chained exceptions, which allow you to throw a more specific exception while maintaining the original exception and its stack trace information. Then, we showed how to create your own exception classes.

We introduced preconditions and postconditions to help programmers using your methods understand conditions that must be true when the method is called and when it returns, respectively. When preconditions and postconditions are not met, methods typically throw exceptions. We discussed the assert statement and how it can be used to help you debug your programs.

We introduced and the try-with-resources statement for automatically deallocating an AutoCloseable resource after it’s used in the try block. Finally, we demonstrated an unnamed variable (_) in a catch handler that did not need access to the exception it caught. In the next chapter, you’ll learn about file processing, including how persistent data is stored and retrieved.

11.1 Introduction

 

Data in memory is temporary. Files are used for data persistence—permanent data retention for data that should remain available after a program terminates. Computers store files on secondary storage devices, such as flash drives, and frequently today, in the cloud. This chapter explains how Java programs create and process files containing human-and-computer-readable data using some of Java’s extensive file-processing APIs and a popular free, open-source library. Another way to persist data is by using databases, which we discuss in Chapter 20, Accessing Databases with JDBC and SQLite.

We begin with Java’s architecture for handling files programmatically. Next, we explain that data can be stored in text or binary files, and discuss their differences. We demonstrate using NIO (short for new input/output) classes and interfaces to retrieve information about files and directories. Then, we use Formatter objects to write to text files and Scanner objects to read from them. We create and manipulate sequential text files and present several case studies that demonstrate transforming objects to and from popular data formats. For simplicity, several examples use type double for monetary amounts—recall that real applications should use BigDecimal for monetary amounts.

JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) and Invoking a Web Service

The first case study introduces JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)—a human-and-computer-readable text format. We use the popular Jackson open-source library to write objects’ JSON representations to a file (a process known as serialization), then read the JSON and recreate the objects (a process known as deserialization). In the second JSON case study, we use networking features from the Java API’s HttpClient, HttpRequest and HttpResponse classes (package java.net.http) to invoke an OpenWeatherMap.org web service that returns a city’s weather report in JSON format, then use Jackson to process the response and display the weather report.

Comma-Separated-Values (CSV) Files and Basic Data Analytics

The next two case studies introduce the CSV (comma separated values) file format and how to write and read CSV files using the Jackson open-source library. CSV is popular for datasets used in big data, data analytics, and data science, as well as artificial intelligence applications like natural language processing, machine learning, and deep learning.

A commonly used dataset for data-analytics beginners is the Titanic disaster dataset, which lists the passengers and whether they survived when the ship struck an iceberg and sank during its first voyage on April 10–15, 1912. This case study uses the Jackson library to read the dataset from a CSV file. Then, we view some of the data and perform basic data analytics.

Objects-Natural Security Case Study: RSA Public-Key Cryptography

We presented objects-natural case studies in Chapters 2–7 in which you conveniently worked with objects of existing Java API classes before you learned to develop custom classes in Chapter 8. In our final objects-natural case study, we continue emphasizing security and privacy by enhancing our private-key cryptography example from Section 7.9. We use RSA public-key cryptography to encrypt and decrypt the AES secret key. This enables secure transmission to an encrypted message’s recipient. Such encryption and decryption techniques are critical for securing data stored in files and transmitted over networks.

11.2 Files and Streams

 

Java views each file as a sequential stream of bytes:1

1. Java’s NIO APIs also include classes and interfaces that implement so-called channel-based architecture for high-performance I/O. These topics are beyond the scope of this book.

Every operating system provides a mechanism to determine the end of a file, such as an end-of-file marker or a count of the total bytes in the file that’s recorded in a system-maintained administrative data structure. A Java program processing a stream of bytes receives an indication from the operating system when it reaches the end of the stream—the program does not need to know how the underlying platform represents files or streams. In some cases, the end-of-file indication occurs as an exception. In others, the indication is a return value from a method invoked on a stream-processing object.

Byte-Based and Character-Based Streams

File streams can be used to input and output data as bytes or characters:

  • Byte-based streams output and input data in its binary format—an int is four bytes, a double is eight bytes, etc. Such streams are used for non-text data, such as images, videos or audio files. We’ll process binary data in Chapter 19, Building API-Based Java Generative AI Applications.

  • Character-based streams output and input text data as sequences of characters. Every character is two bytes, so the number of bytes for a given value depends on its number of characters. For example, the value 2000000000 (10 characters) requires 20 bytes, but the value 7 (one character) requires only two bytes.

Files manipulated with byte-based streams are binary files, while those manipulated with character-based streams are text files. Text files can be read by text editors, while binary files are read by programs that understand the file’s specific content. You can use a numeric value (e.g., 5) from a binary file directly in calculations. In contrast, the character '5' in a text file is just part of a String, like in the sentence "Sarah is 15 years old."

Standard Input, Standard Output and Standard Error Streams

A Java program opens a file by creating an object and associating a stream of bytes or characters with it. The object’s constructor interacts with the operating system to open the file. Java can also associate streams with different devices. When a Java program begins executing, it creates three stream objects that are associated with devices:

  • The System.in (standard input stream) object normally enables a program to obtain input from the keyboard.

  • The System.out (standard output stream) object normally enables a program to output data to the screen.

  • The System.err (standard error stream) object normally enables a program to output error messages to the screen.

These streams can be redirected via the Systemmethods setIn, setOutand setErr, respectively. For System.in, this enables the program to read bytes from a different source. For System.out and System.err, the output can be sent to a different location, such as a file on your system.

The java.io and java.nio Packages

Java programs perform stream-based processing with classes and interfaces from package java.io and the subpackages of java.nio. Other packages throughout the Java APIs also contain features based on those in the java.io and java.nio packages.

Character input and output can be performed with classes Scanner and Formatter, as you’ll see in Section 11.4. You’ve used Scanner extensively to input data from the keyboard. Scanner can also read data from a file. Class Formatter enables formatted data to be output to any text-based stream similar to System.out.printf. Appendix B, Formatted Output, presents the details of formatted output with printf. All these features can be used to format text files as well.

Another Type of Stream

Chapter 14, Functional Programming with Lambdas & Streams, introduces a type of stream used to process collections of elements (like arrays and ArrayLists) rather than the streams of bytes and characters we discuss in this chapter. Section 14.13 shows how to use lambdas and streams with a text file.

11.3 Using NIO Classes and Interfaces to Get File and Directory Information

 

Package java.nio.file provides features useful for retrieving information about files and directories:

  • Pathinterface—Objects of classes that implement Path represent the location of a file or directory. Path objects do not open files or provide any file-processing capabilities. Among its capabilities, the Path interface provides static methods to create Path objects representing file or directory locations.

  • Files class—This class provides static methods for common file and directory manipulations, such as copying files; creating and deleting files and directories; getting information about files and directories; reading the contents of files; getting objects that allow you to manipulate the contents of files and directories; and more.

  • DirectoryStream interface—Objects of classes that implement this interface enable a program to iterate through a directory’s contents.

Absolute vs. Relative Paths

A file or directory’s path specifies its location on your computer. The path includes some or all of the directories leading to the file or directory:

  • An absolute path specifies a complete location, starting with the root directory, that leads to a specific file or directory. Every file or directory on a particular disk drive or solid-state drive (SSD) has the same root directory in its path.

  • A relative path is “relative” to a directory—for example, a path relative to the directory in which the program began executing. In relative paths, dot (.) represents the current folder, and dot dot (..) represents the enclosing folder.

Example: Getting File and Directory Information

Figure 11.1 prompts the user to enter a file or directory name, then uses Path, Files and DirectoryStream to output metadata about that file or directory (also called a folder), including:

  • whether the file or folder exists,

  • its name,

  • whether it’s a file or folder,

  • whether its location is an absolute path,

  • when it was last modified,

  • its size,

  • its path and

  • its absolute path—if the user enters an absolute path, the path and absolute path will be the same.

For a folder, we also list its contents. In the first sample output, we entered the Path for the folder containing this chapter’s examples. In the second, we entered the Path for this example’s source-code file. In both cases, we specified absolute paths.

Line 13 prompts the user for a file or directory.2 Line 16 inputs the filename or directory name and passes it to Path static method of, which converts the String to a Path. Line 18 invokes Files static method exists, which receives a Path and determines whether it exists (either as a file or as a directory). If the name does not exist, line 44 displays a message containing the Path’s String representation followed by “does not exist.” Otherwise, lines 20–41 execute:

2. In Section 16.7, we’ll update this example with JavaFX FileChooser and DirectoryChooser dialogs that enable you to select a file or directory rather than entering it

  • Path method getFileName (line 20) gets the String name of the file or directory without any location information.

  • Files static method isDirectory (line 22) receives a Path and returns a boolean indicating whether that Path represents a directory.

  • Path method isAbsolute (line 24) returns a boolean indicating whether that Path represents an absolute path to a file or directory.

  • Files static method getLastModifiedTime (line 26) receives a Path and returns a FileTime (package java.nio.file.attribute) indicating when the file was last modified. The program outputs the FileTime’s default String representation.

  • Files static method size (line 27) receives a Path and returns a long representing the number of bytes in the file or directory. For directories, the value returned is platform-specific.

  • Path method toString (called implicitly at line 28) returns a String representing the Path.

  • Path method toAbsolutePath (line 29) converts the Path on which it’s called to an absolute path.

If the Path represents a directory (line 31), lines 35–36 use the Files class’s static method newDirectoryStream to get a DirectoryStream<Path> containing Path objects for the directory’s contents. DirectoryStream is a generic type like ArrayList. Lines 38–40 display the String representation of each Path in the DirectoryStream<Path>.

Once you’ve confirmed that a Path exists, the methods Fig. 11.1 demonstrates may still throw IOExceptions—we do not catch these checked exceptions in this program, so we added a throws clause to main (line 10). For example, the file or directory represented by the Path could be deleted from the system after the call to Files method exists and before the other statements in lines 20–41 execute. Industrial strength file- and directory-processing programs require extensive exception handling to deal with such possibilities.

Separator Characters

A separator character is used to separate directories and files in a path. On a Windows computer, the separator character is a backslash (\). On a Linux or macOS system, it’s a forward slash (/). Java processes both characters identically in a pathname.

When building Path objects, the Path method of can handle the separator characters for you. For example, the statement

Click here to view code image

Path documentsPath =
   Path.of(System.getProperty("user.home"), "Documents");

creates a Path object representing your user account’s Documents folder. The call

Click here to view code image

System.getProperty("user.home")

uses the System class’s getProperty method to get your user account’s folder (represented by "user.home"). On a Windows system, this would represent the path

Click here to view code image

c:\Users\YourAccount\Documents

and on macOS, this would represent the path

/Users/YourAccount/Documents

We’ll use this capability in subsequent examples.

11.4 Sequential Text Files

Next, we create and manipulate sequential files in which records3 are stored in order by the record-key field. We begin with text files, enabling the reader to quickly create and edit human-readable files. We discuss creating, writing data to, reading data from and updating sequential text files. We’ll use binary files to read and write images and audio files in Chapter 19, Building API-Based Java Generative AI Applications.

3. In this chapter, we use the term “record” to refer to records in a file. Many examples also use record classes. When we refer to a record class, we format the word “record” using a computer font.

11.4.1 Creating a Sequential Text File

Java imposes no structure on a file—notions such as records do not exist as part of the Java language. Therefore, you must structure files to meet the requirements of your programs. The following example shows how to impose a keyed record structure on a file.

The program in this section creates a simple sequential file that might be used in an accounts receivable system to keep track of the amounts owed to a company by its credit clients. For each client, the program obtains from the user an account number and the client’s name and balance (i.e., the amount the client owes the company for goods and services received). Each client’s data constitutes a record for that client. This program uses the account number as the record key—we will write the file’s records in account-number order. In a comprehensive accounts-receivable system (based on sequential files) that includes data input, a sorting capability would be provided so users could enter the records in any order. The records would then be sorted and written to the file.

Class CreateTextFile

Class CreateTextFile (Fig. 11.2) uses a Formatter to output formatted Strings, using the same formatting features as System.out.printf. We broke the program into parts for discussion purposes. Line 8 declares the record class Account to represent an Account’s accountNumber, name and balance—for this chapter’s examples, we use only last names.

List<Account> and List static Method of

Section 6.20 introduced the generic class ArrayList for creating dynamically resizable array-like data structures. As you’ll see in Chapter 12, Generic Collections, the generic List interface (package java.util) specifies the common features for lists of objects, like ArrayLists.

Many of this chapter’s examples use the same five Account objects without changing their data. For such cases, the List static method of creates and returns an immutable (unmodifiable) object that implements the List interface and contains the method’s arguments. Immutable means you cannot add objects to or remove objects from the List after you create it. The List’s element type is determined from of’s arguments. Lines 13–19 create a List<Account> containing the five Account objects we’ll write to the text file in this example.

Click here to view code image

10   public class CreateTextFile {
11      public static void main(String[] args) {
12         // account data to write to a text file
13         List<Account> accounts = List.of(
14            new Account(100, "Devi", 24.98),
15            new Account(200, "Taylor", 345.67),
16            new Account(300, "Huber", 0.00),
17            new Account(400, "Ito", -42.16),
18            new Account(500, "Lopez", 224.62)
19         );
20
Path to the clients.txt File

Lines 22–23 create a Path object representing the clients.txt file. This example writes the file into your user account’s Documents folder.

Click here to view code image

21         // Path to clients.txt in the user's Documents folder
22         Path filePath = Path.of(System.getProperty("user.home"),
23            "Documents", "clients.txt");
24
Using a Formatter to Write the Accounts to a File

A Formatter object can output to various locations, such as a command window or a file, as we do in this example. Line 26 creates the Formatter in the try-with-resources statement (introduced in Section 10.12). Recall that try-with-resources closes its resource(s) when the try block terminates successfully or due to an exception. This ensures we close the file when we no longer need it so other programs can use it. The Formatter constructor we use here takes one argument—a String containing the file’s location and name. We call the filePath object’s toString method to get its String representation. If you were to specify only the file’s name, the JVM would assume the file is in the directory from which you execute the program. For text files, we use the .txt file extension. If the file does not exist, the Formatter constructor will create it. If no exception occurs, the file is open for writing, and the Formatter object can be used to write data to the file.

Click here to view code image

25         // open clients.txt, output data to the file then close clients.txt
26         try (var output = new Formatter(filePath.toString())) {
27            // output each Account to file
28            for (var account : accounts) {
29               output.format("%d %s %.2f%n", account.accountNumber(),
30                  account.name(), account.balance());
31            }
32
33            System.out.printf(
34               "Text file created at: %s%n", filePath.toAbsolutePath());
35         }
36         catch (Exception e) {
37            System.err.printf(
38               "Error writing text file: %s%n", e.getMessage());
39         }
40      }
41   }
Text file created at: C:\Users\pauldeitel\Documents\clients.txt

If no exception occurs while opening the file, lines 28–31 output each Account’s data using Formatter’s format method, which works like System.out.printf but writes a formatted String to the Formatter object’s output destination (the file clients.txt). The format string "%d %s %.2f%n" indicates that the current record will be stored as an int (the account number) followed by a String (the name) and a double (the balance). We separate each piece of information from the next by a space and output the double value with two digits of precision.

When the try block terminates, the try-with-resources statement closes the Formatter and the underlying output file by calling Formatter method close. If a program does not explicitly call method close, the operating system will close the file when program execution terminates—an example of operating-system “termination housekeeping.” You should always explicitly close a file when it’s no longer needed.

Possible Exceptions

Line 36 catches any Exceptions that occur in the try block. There are several:

  • A SecurityException occurs if the user does not have permission to write data to the file opened in line 26.

  • A FileNotFoundException occurs if the file does not exist and a new file cannot be created or if there’s an error opening the file in line 26.

  • A FormatterClosedException occurs if the Formatter object is closed when you attempt to use it in lines 29–30 to write into a file.

For these exceptions, we display that there was an error writing the file and show the exception’s message.

Caution: Check Whether a File Exists Before Opening It for Writing

In general, you should use the features in Fig. 11.1 to check whether a file exists before you open it for output. Opening an existing file for output truncates its contents—all the data in the file is discarded.

Sample Output

This program’s output simply indicates that it wrote the Accounts into clients.txt. It does not show how the data records actually appear in the file. In Section 11.4.2, we present a program that reads the file and prints its contents to verify that the file was created successfully. Because this is a text file, you can also verify the information simply by opening the file in a text editor.

11.4.2 Reading Data from a Sequential Text File

We store data in files so we can retrieve it for processing when needed. In Fig. 11.3, we read the data sequentially from the file "clients.txt" created by the program of Fig. 11.2. Previously, we’ve used Scanners to input data from the user. Here, we use one to input each record from the file and display its contents.

The try-with-resources statement (line 13) opens the file for reading by creating a Scanner object. We pass a Path object to the constructor, which specifies that the Scanner object will read from the file "clients.txt" in the user’s Documents folder.

Lines 14–15 display headers for the columns in the program’s output. Lines 18–22 read and display the file’s content until end-of-file is reached—in which case, the hasNext method will return false at line 18. Lines 20–21 use Scanner methods nextInt, next and nextDouble to input an int (the account number), a String (the name) and a double (the balance). Each record is one line of text in the file.

The format string in line 20 left-aligns the account number and name and right-aligns the balance with two digits of precision. Each iteration of the loop inputs one line (record) from the text file. When the loop terminates and line 23 is reached, the try-with-resources statement implicitly calls the Scanner’s close method to close the Scanner and the file.

Potential Exceptions

Several exceptions can occur in the try block:

  • If the Scanner cannot open the file in line 14, an IOException occurs.

  • If the information in the file is not correctly formatted (e.g., there’s a name where there should be a balance), a InputMismatchException occurs when the record is input.

  • If the Scanner is closed before the data is input, an IllegalStateException occurs.

These exceptions are handled by lines 25–28.

11.4.3 Updating Sequential Files

The data in many sequential files cannot be modified without the risk of destroying other data in the file. For example, if you need to change the name “Pappas” to “Papadopoulou”, the old name cannot simply be overwritten, because the new name requires more space. The record for Pappas was written to the file as

300 Pappas 0.00

If you were to rewrite the record beginning at the same location in the file using the new name, the record would be

300 Papadopoulou 0.00

The new record is larger (has more characters) than the original record. “Papadopoulou” would overwrite the “0.00” in the current record, and the characters beyond the last “u” in “Papadopoulou” would overwrite the beginning of the next sequential record in the file.

The problem here is that fields in a text file—and hence records—can vary in size. For example, 7, 14, –117, 2074 and 27383 are all ints stored in the same number of bytes (4) internally, but they’re different-sized fields when written to a file as text. Therefore, you do not usually update records in a sequential file in place—instead, you rewrite the entire file. To make the preceding name change:

  • the records before 300 Pappas 0.00 would be copied to a new file,

  • the new record (which can be of a different size than the one it replaces) would be written and

  • the records after 300 Pappas 0.00 would be copied to the new file.

Rewriting the entire file is uneconomical to update just one record, but reasonable if a substantial number of records need to be updated.

11.5 Case Study: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Serialization

 

More and more computing today is done “in the cloud”—that is, distributed across the Internet. Many applications you use daily communicate over the Internet with cloud-based services that use massive clusters of computing resources (computers, processors, memory, storage, databases, etc.).

A service that provides access to itself over the Internet is known as a web service. Applications typically communicate with web services by sending and receiving JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) objects. JSON is a text-based, human- and computer-readable data-interchange format that represents objects as collections of name-value pairs. JSON has become the preferred data format for transmitting objects between platforms over the Internet. In this case study, we’ll explore using JSON in Java.

JSON Data Format

Each JSON object contains a comma-separated list of property names and values in curly braces. For example, the following name–value pairs might represent a client record:

Click here to view code image

{"accountNumber": 100, "name": "Devi", "balance": 24.98}

JSON also supports arrays as comma-separated values in square brackets. For example, the following represents a JSON array of numbers:

[100, 200, 300]

Values in JSON objects and arrays can be

  • strings in double quotes (like "Devi"),

  • numbers (like 100 or 24.98),

  • JSON Boolean values (represented as true or false),

  • null (to represent no value),

  • arrays of any valid JSON value and

  • other JSON objects containing values and arrays of the types mentioned above.

JSON arrays may contain elements of the same or different types.

Serialization

Converting an object into a format suitable for storage or transmission over the Internet is known as serialization. Similarly, reconstructing an object from serialized data is known as deserialization. JSON is just one of several serialization formats. Another common one is XML (eXtensible Markup Language). JSON is generally preferred for its simplicity (it’s less verbose than XML), ease of use, efficiency and widespread adoption.4,5,6,7

4. Hackr.io. “JSON vs XML in 2024: Comparing Features and Examples.” Accessed November 29, 2024. https://hackr.io/blog/json-vs-xml.

5. W3Schools. “JSON vs XML.” Accessed November 29, 2024. https://www.w3schools.com/js/js_json_xml.asp.

6. Imaginary Cloud. “JSON vs XML: Which One Is Faster and More Efficient?” Accessed November 29, 2024. https://www.imaginarycloud.com/blog/json-vs-xml.

7. Coursesity. “JSON vs XML Comparison: Which Is Better? [2024].” Accessed November 29, 2024. https://coursesity.com/blog/json-vs-xml/.

Serialization Security

Some programming languages (including Java) have serialization mechanisms that use a language-native format. Deserializing objects using these native formats is a source security issues. According to the Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP), these “can be repurposed for malicious effect when operating on untrusted data. Attacks against deserializers have been found to allow denial-of-service, access control, and remote code execution (RCE) attacks.” OWASP indicates that you can significantly reduce attack risk by avoiding language-native serialization formats in favor of “pure data” formats like JSON or XML.8

8. “Deserialization Cheat Sheet.” OWASP Cheat Sheet Series. Accessed November 11, 2024. https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Deserialization_Cheat_Sheet.html.

Jackson Open-Source Library

The Jackson open-source library9 is a popular Java library for converting objects to JSON and vice versa with minimal code. Jackson was initially developed as a JSON processing library but has since evolved into a multi-format data-processing library. Later in this chapter, we’ll also use it to process comma-separated value (CSV) files. You can access Jackson’s API documentation and download the library from the following links:

9. “Jackson Project Home @github.” Accessed November 11, 2024. https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson.

Click here to view code image

https://javadoc.io/doc/com.fasterxml.jackson.core/jackson-core/latest

https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson

For basic JSON and CSV processing with the Jackson library, you typically need the following Jackson library components:

  • jackson-core: Provides the core capabilities for parsing and generating JSON.

  • jackson-databind: Provides capabilities for converting Java objects to and from JSON.

  • jackson-annotations: Provides Jackson-specific annotations used to customize serialization and deserialization.

  • jackson-dataformat-csv: Provides additional capabilities for reading and writing CSV files.

For your convenience, we’ve included these components in the subfolder libs with this chapter’s examples. After discussing Fig. 11.4, we show the javac and java commands required to compile and run the Jackson-based examples.

Requirements for Serializable Classes

By default, Jackson serializes all of a record’s instance variables. For classes, Jackson requires get methods for each instance variable to serialize. When deserializing JSON to a record object, Jackson uses the record’s constructor to reconstruct the object. For other classes, it requires a default constructor and set methods to store each instance variable in the new object.

For macOS, change the semicolon (;) to a colon (:). The -cp option specifies the class-path, which indicates where the classes this program needs to compile can be found. The dot (.) indicates the current folder. Depending on your operating system, the semicolon (;) or colon (:) separates one location from another. The relative path ../libs/* specifies that the libs folder is up one level in the folder structure (i.e., in the ch11 folder containing this chapter’s examples). Finally, the * indicates that all the files in that folder should be added to the classpath. To run this example, use the following command on Windows:

11.5.2 Deserializing a List<Account>

Figure 11.5 reimplements Fig. 11.3 using JSON deserialization to create a List<Account> representing the account data in the file. For Jackson to recreate objects of regular Java classes in memory, it must have access to each class’s default or no-argument constructor. It will use that to create an object then use that object’s set methods to place the data into the object. For a record class, Jackson uses the autogenerated constructor.

Lines 22–23 use the ObjectMapper’s readValue method to deserialize the JSON data from the file in its first argument into a List<Account>. Jackson needs to know the type of data you want to convert (in this case, a List<Account>), which is the purpose of method readValue’s second argument:

Click here to view code image

new TypeReference<List<Account>>() {}

This uses Jackson’s TypeReference class (imported at line 3) to provide Jackson with the type information the ObjectMapper needs to deserialize complex generic types (such as a List<Account>), mapping the JSON data to the correct Java object structure. This expression creates an object of an anonymous inner class—a class with no name that you create “on-the-fly” to extend another class or implement an interface. Such a class exists only in the place where it’s written. In the preceding expression, TypeReference is an abstract class from the Jackson library that helps it understand generic types like List<Account>. The expression creates a new unnamed class that extends

TypeReference<List<Account>>

and immediately creates one object of this new unnamed class. Jackson uses this object to help it deserialize your data into a List<Account>. The anonymous inner class is similar to the following class declaration:

Click here to view code image

class MyTypeReference extends TypeReference<List<Account>> {
   // empty class body
}

Once the data is deserialized, we display it using the same format as in Fig. 11.3.
