11.6 Case Study: Processing a JSON Response from a Web Service

 

Section 1.8 introduced the Internet, the web, the cloud, web services and mashups. In this case-study, you’ll dive into the world of web services using Java’s built-in networking capabilities to invoke a web service and process the JSON results it returns. You’ll interact with an OpenWeatherMap free web service from

https://openweathermap.org/

to get the current weather report for a city of your choosing, which you’ll specify with the city name as a command-line argument to the application.

Web Services

The machine on which a web service resides is referred to as a web-service host. A web-service client application (in our case, a Java program) sends a web-service request over a network to the web-service host, which processes the request and returns a web-service response over the network to the client. This kind of distributed computing benefits systems in various ways. For example, an application without direct access to data on another system might be able to retrieve the data via a web service. Similarly, an application lacking the processing power to perform specific computations could use a web service to take advantage of another system’s superior resources.

Representational State Transfer (REST)

Most web services today use Representational State Transfer (REST) and are often called RESTful web services. In a RESTful web service, each function you can call is identified by a unique URL. URLs (Uniform Resource Locators) identify the locations of resources on the Internet, such as websites and web services. For example, https://deitel.com/ is the URL for the Deitel & Associates website. When a web server receives a request to a RESTful web service, it immediately knows what function to call on that server. RESTful web services can be called from programs, as you’ll do here, or directly from a web browser’s address bar by entering the appropriate URL.

OpenWeatherMap

OpenWeatherMap provides a free tier to several of its weather web services. Before using them, you must sign up for a free account at https://openweathermap.org/. They will send you an email to verify your account. Once you do, they’ll reply with an email that contains your free API key. You can also find this under the API Keys tab in your account when you log into the site.

You can view the variety of OpenWeatherMap APIs and their documentation at

Click here to view code image

https://openweathermap.org/api

Some are free, and some are available only to subscribers. With a free API key, you can access:

  • the Current Weather Data for a specified location, which we use in this case study,

  • the One Call API, which returns a combination of current and future weather data for a specified location, and

  • the 5-Day/3-Hour Forecast for a specified location.

Storing the API Key in an Environment Variable

The program in this section assumes you store your API key in a system environment variable named OPENWEATHERMAP_API_KEY. On Windows, perform the following steps to store your API key in an environment variable:

  1. Enter "environment" in the taskbar’s Search field.

  2. In the search results, select Edit the system environment variables.

  3. In the System Properties dialog, select or press the Environment Variables button.

  4. Under User variables, click New….

  5. Enter the Variable name OPENWEATHERMAP_API_KEY then, for the Variable value, paste in the API key provided by OpenWeatherMap.org.

  6. Click OK to save the environment variable, then click OK in the System Properties dialog to close it.

On macOS, perform the following steps to store your API key in an environment variable:

  1. Open Terminal.

  2. Open ~/.zshrc using a text editor (e.g., nano ~/.zshrc).

  3. Scroll to the end of the file and add the following line, replacing YourAPIKey with the API key provided by OpenWeatherMap.org:

    Click here to view code image

    export OPENWEATHERMAP_API_KEY="YourAPIKey"

  4. Save and close the file.

  5. Run the following command in the Terminal:

    source ~/.zshrc
JSON and Web Services

Many cloud-based services like OpenWeatherMap communicate with your applications via JSON objects. Figure 11.6 contains a sample JSON response from OpenWeatherMap’s Current Weather Data web service, which we formatted for readability. The items we highlighted in bold contain the information we’ll display in this example. We’ll direct Jackson to ignore the non-bold items.

Getting a Weather Report

Figure 11.7 interacts with OpenWeatherMap to get a weather report for the city the user specifies as a command-line argument to the program. You can compile this program as you did with the programs in Section 11.5. To get a weather report for Boston like the one in Fig. 11.6, you would execute the program on Windows with

Click here to view code image

java -cp ".;../libs/*" WeatherApp Boston

On macOS, replace the semicolon (;) with a colon (:). We broke the program into parts for discussion purposes.

record Classes for Deserializing the JSON Response

The record classes WeatherData (lines 18–25), Weather (lines 27–32) and Main (lines 34–40) mimic the structure of the JSON data we’ll extract from the web service response. The entire response in Fig. 11.6 represents the weather data for a city. Class WeatherData contains instance variables named for each top-level JSON key (Fig. 11.6, lines 6, 15, 34, 42 and 44) we use in this example. We’ve used the compile-time annotation @Override in previous chapters. Many libraries use runtime annotations to inject code into your programs and perform tasks for you. Line 18 above class WeatherData uses the Jackson runtime annotation @JsonIgnoreProperties to tell Jackson to ignore the rest of the top-level JSON fields from Fig. 11.6 that we do not use in this example.

Click here to view code image

17   // record classes for JSON mapping
18   @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
19   record WeatherData(
20      Weather[] weather,
21      long dt, // date and time
22      Main main,
23      int timezone,
24      String name
25   ) {}
26

The JSON keys dt, timezone and name are each single values that map to the corresponding WeatherData instance variables. The JSON key weather (Fig. 11.6, line 6) has as its value a JSON array of JSON objects—in Fig. 11.6, the array contains one JSON object. Similarly, the JSON key main (Fig. 11.6, line 15) has as its value a JSON object containing many name-value pairs. So, our WeatherData class declares instance variable weather as an array of Weather objects (defined in lines 27–32 below) and instance variable main as an object of class Main (defined in lines 34–40 below). We named these two classes based on the JSON keys they represent. Again, we do not use all the JSON name-value pairs, so both classes use the Jackson annotation @JsonIgnoreProperties to ignore the name-value pairs that do not match these classes’ instance variables.

Lines 63–70 construct a valid URL for requesting weather data from the OpenWeatherMap web service. URLEncoder method encode converts the city variable into a format safe for use in a URL—in case the command-line argument contains characters not allowed in URLs. Next, we insert the encodedCity into the URL, which specifies

The API endpoint is followed by ? and the options, each separated from the next by &.

65

Setting up the Web Service Request and Receiving the Response

To obtain the JSON response in Fig. 11.6, our application uses the HttpClient class (package java.net.http)10 to make a request to the OpenWeatherMap web service.

72         // use Java's HttpClient to make the request
73         HttpClient client = HttpClient.newHttpClient();
74
75         // build the request that HttpClient will use to
76         // invoke the OpenWeatherMap web service
77         HttpRequest request =
78            HttpRequest.newBuilder()
79               .uri(URI.create(apiUrl))
80               .GET()
81               .build();
82
83         // send the HTTP request and get the response
84         HttpResponse<String> response =
85            client.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
86
87         // check if the request was successful
88         if (response.statusCode() != 200) {
89            System.out.printf("Error: Received HTTP status %d\n",
90               response.statusCode());
91            System.exit(1);
92         }
93

Class HttpClient encapsulates the mechanisms to request information from web services and receive their responses. Line 73 calls the class’s HttpClient’s static method newHttpClient to get an HttpClient object. Next, lines 77–81 use a chained method call to build an HttpRequest:

  • Line 78 calls static method newBuilder to get an HttpRequest.Builder object for configuring the request.

  • Line 79 calls the builder’s uri method to specify where the web service resides on the Internet using the apiUrl created in lines 67–70. A Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) is a more general form of the Uniform Resource Locators (URLs) used to locate websites. URI method create converts the URL to a URI.

  • Line 80 uses the GET method to set the HTTP request method to GET, which indicates that the program will request data.

  • Line 81 calls the builder’s build method to create the HttpRequest object.

Next, lines 84–85 send the request using the HttpClient object’s send method:

  • The first argument is the HttpRequest.

  • The second argument uses the HttpResponse.BodyHandlers class’s ofString method to indicate that we expect the response to be a String.

The response is stored in an HttpResponse<String> object, which holds the status code that indicates whether the request was successful and, if so, the response content. Line 88 checks the status code—the status code 200 confirms the server processed the request successfully. Otherwise, the program prints an error message with the received status code and terminates. For more information on HTTP status codes, visit https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_HTTP_status_codes.

11.7 Case Study: Creating and Reading CSV Files

 

The CSV (comma-separated values) file format, which uses the .csv file extension, is popular for datasets used in big data, data analytics and data science, and in artificial intelligence applications like machine learning and deep learning. Here, we’ll demonstrate writing to and reading from a CSV file.

Datasets

There’s an enormous variety of free datasets available online. The OpenML machine learning resource site

https://openml.org

contains almost 6000 free datasets in CSV format. Other great sources of datasets include:

Click here to view code image

https://github.com/awesomedata/awesome-public-datasets
https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/articles/data.html

Also, many local and national governments publish free datasets. For example, as of December 2024, the U.S. government listed 25,515 CSV format datasets on data.gov:

Click here to view code image

https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/?res_format=CSV
account.csv

For our two examples, we’ll create the file clients.csv with the following data

accountNumber,name,balance
100,Devi,24.98
200,Taylor,345.67
300,Huber,0.0
400,Ito,-42.16
500,Lopez,224.62

then we’ll read that file. The first row of a CSV file typically contains column names. Each subsequent row contains one data record representing the values for those columns. This dataset has three columns representing an accountNumber, name and balance.

11.7.1 Creating a CSV File

Figure 11.8 reimplements Fig. 11.4 using CSV format.

Remember to add Jackson to the classpath when compiling and running this program. The primary differences in this example are Jackson’s CSV handling in lines 29–32 and 36–37:

  • Line 29 creates a CsvMapper object. This is similar to the ObjectMapper used for JSON but converts Java objects into CSV format and vice versa.

  • Lines 30–32 use chained method calls to build a CsvSchema for class Account. This defines the CSV file’s structure based on Account’s instance variables. The CsvSchema method schemaFor determines the schema from Account.class—a shorthand for a Java object that represents the Account class’s definition. Method withHeader specifies that the CSV file’s first line should contain Account’s instance variable names as column headers for the CSV records’ fields. By default, a CSV record’s fields are separated by commas, but Jackson allows you to customize this to use other separators.

  • An ObjectWriter writes the header and data to the CSV file. Line 36 creates an ObjectWriter configured with the CsvSchema from lines 30–32.

  • Finally, line 37 uses the ObjectWriter’s writeValue method to write the List of Accounts to the file at the specified path. This method serializes the accounts list into CSV format, producing a file with rows corresponding to each Account object and columns matching the fields in the schema.

11.7.2 Reading a CSV File

Figure 11.9 reimplements Fig. 11.5 to read the CSV data, then display it in the same format as Fig. 11.5. Remember to add Jackson to the classpath when compiling and running this program.

The primary differences in this example are Jackson’s CSV handling in lines 20, 24–26 and 31–35:

  • Line 20 creates a CsvMapper object that will convert CSV records into Java objects.

  • Lines 24–26 create a CsvSchema for the Account class. This schema defines how the columns in the CSV file correspond to the instance variables in an Account. As in Fig. 11.8, we indicate that the CSV file’s first row contains column headers. Jackson uses these to map the columns to the corresponding fields in the Account record object.

  • To read the CSV file, we use a MappingIterator. Lines 31–33 create a Mapping-Iterator<Account> using a chained method call. An “iterator” is an object that enables a program to iterate over a collection’s elements one by one. For example, an enhanced for loop uses an iterator to access each element in a collection, such as an ArrayList. The MappingIterator enables this program to access each record in the CSV file. CsvMapper’s readerFor method receives Account.class to indicate it will create Account objects. The with method provides the schema Jackson will use when deserializing the CSV records into Account objects. Finally, the readValues method indicates that the MappingIterator will read data from the file specified in its argument.

  • Line 35 calls the MappingIterator’s readAll method to iterate through all the records in the CSV file, reading them into a List<Account>. This makes it easy to work with all the CSV file’s data in memory.

Caution: Commas in CSV Data Fields

Be careful when working with strings containing embedded commas, such as the name "Flores, Silvio". If this name were accidentally stored as the two strings "Flores" and "Silvio", that CSV record would have four fields, not three. Programs that read CSV files typically expect every record to have the same number of fields; otherwise, problems occur.

Caution: Missing Commas and Extra Commas in CSV Files

Be careful when preparing and processing CSV files. For example, suppose your file is composed of records, each with four comma-separated int values, such as

100,85,77,9

If you accidentally omit one of these commas, as in

100,8577,9

then the record has only three fields, one with the invalid value 8577.

If you put two adjacent commas where only one is expected, as in

100,85,,77,9

then you have five fields rather than four, and one of the fields erroneously would be empty. Each of these comma-related errors could confuse programs trying to process the record.

11.8 Case Study: Reading and Analyzing a CSV File Containing the Titanic Disaster Dataset

 

The Titanic disaster dataset11 is one of the most commonly used datasets for data analytics beginners. It lists all the passengers and whether they survived when the ship Titanic struck an iceberg and sank during its first voyage of April 10–15, 1912. In this case, study, we’ll load the dataset, view some of its data and perform some basic data analytics.

11. “TitanicSurvival” dataset on https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets. Dataset authors: Frank E. Harrell, Jr., and Thomas Cason.

The dataset is available from numerous dataset repositories. We used the version from the Rdatasets repository at

Click here to view code image

https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/csv/carData/
   TitanicSurvival.csv

We placed this file in the same folder as the example’s code.

Getting to Know Your Data

In data analytics, you’ll often begin by getting to know your data. One way is to simply look at the raw data. If you open the TitanicSurvival.csv file in a text editor or spreadsheet application, you’ll see that the dataset contains 1,309 rows, each with five columns—often called features in data analytics. We ignore the first column containing the passenger’s names and use only the last four columns in this case study:

  • survived: "yes" or "no".

  • sex: "female" or "male".

  • age: The passenger’s age. Most ages are integers, but some children under 1 year of age have floating-point values, so we’ll process this column as double values.

  • passengerClass: "1st", "2nd" or "3rd" for first, second or third class, respectively.

To learn more about the dataset’s origins, visit

Click here to view code image

https://hbiostat.org/data/repo/titanic
Missing Data

Bad data values and missing values can significantly impact data analysis. The Titanic dataset is missing the ages for 263 passengers. These are represented as empty fields in the CSV file—that is, there is no data between the commas that delimit the age field in those records. In this example, when we produce descriptive statistics for the passengers’ ages, we’ll “clean” the data to filter out and ignore the missing values. In data science, preparing data for analysis is called data munging or data wrangling.

Some data scientists advise against any attempts to insert “reasonable values.” Instead, they advocate clearly marking missing data and leaving it up to a data analytics package to handle the issue. Others offer strong cautions.12

12. This footnote was abstracted from a comment sent to us July 20, 2018, by one of our Python textbook’s academic reviewers, Dr. Alison Sanchez of the University of San Diego School of Business. She commented: “Be cautious when mentioning ‘substituting reasonable values’ for missing or bad values. A stern warning: ‘Substituting’ values that increase statistical significance or give more ‘reasonable’ or ‘better’ results is not permitted. ‘Substituting’ data should not turn into ‘fudging’ data. The first rule students should learn is not to eliminate or change values that contradict their hypotheses. ‘Substituting reasonable values‘ does not mean students should feel free to change values to get the results they want.”

Loading the Dataset

Figure 11.10 loads the dataset and performs our analysis. We broke the program into parts for discussion purposes. Remember to add Jackson to the classpath when compiling and running this program.

record Class TitanicAnalysis for Storing Each Dataset Record

Jackson can read CSV records and create objects of a type you specify so you can conveniently access the record’s fields. Lines 13–19 declare the record class TitanicRecord, which has instance variables representing the four dataset columns we use in this example. As discussed previously, line 13 tells Jackson to ignore JSON name-value pairs that do not have a matching instance variable in class TitanicRecord.

Click here to view code image

11   public class TitanicAnalysis {
12      // record class representing the fields in each dataset row
13      @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
14      public record TitanicRecord(
15         String survived,
16         String sex,
17         String age,
18         String passengerClass
19      ) {}
20
Loading the Dataset

Lines 22 and 26 create the CsvMapper and CsvSchema we’ll use to configure Jackson to read the CSV file and convert each record to a TitanicRecord object. In this example, we use CsvSchema’s static emptySchema method to indicate that Jackson should automatically determine how to map the CSV records to TitanicRecords. At the end of this section, you’ll prompt genAIs, asking for the benefits and disadvantages of this approach. Lines 30–32 configure the MappingIterator that converts each record to a TitanicRecord object, then line 35 uses it to read all the CSV file’s records into a List<TitanicRecord>.

Extracting the Column Data into ArrayLists

Lines 38–41 create ArrayLists for each column. The loop at lines 44–58 populates each ArrayList with the corresponding column’s data. As we add each age to the age Array-List, we check whether it’s empty. If not, we convert it to a double and add it to the ArrayList; otherwise, we add the value Double.NaN (not a number) to indicate the missing value. You’ll learn in Chapter 12 that Java collections can store only objects and that doubles and ints are converted to their Double object and Integer object equivalents (and vice versa) automatically. As we add each passenger class to the pclass ArrayList, we convert it from the String "1st", "2nd" or "3rd" to the number 1, 2 or 3. We’ll use these as array indexes when summarizing the number of passengers in each class.

39         var sex = new ArrayList<String>();
40         var age = new ArrayList<Double>();
41         var pclass = new ArrayList<Integer>();

45            survived.add(record.survived());
46            sex.add(record.sex());
47            age.add(!record.age().isEmpty() ?

51                  case "1st" -> 1;

53                  case "3rd" -> 3;

Data Munging: Cleaning the Age Column for Calculating Descriptive Statistics

As part of getting to know a dataset, data scientists often use statistics to describe and summarize data. We’ll calculate several descriptive statistics for the age column, including the number of passengers for which we have ages, and the average, minimum, maximum and median age values. Before performing these calculations, we must remove NaN values, because a calculation that includes the value NaN produces NaN as the result. So, lines 80–85 create the ArrayList cleanAge containing only the values from age that are not NaN. Double method isNaN returns true if the value is NaN.

Click here to view code image

79         // clean the age column (remove NaN)
80         var cleanAge = new ArrayList<Double>();
81         for (Double value : age) {
82            if (!value.isNaN()) {
83               cleanAge.add(value);
84            }
85         }
86
Basic Descriptive Statistics for the Cleaned Age Column

Now, we can calculate the descriptive statistics. Line 88 sorts cleanAge, so we can determine the minimum, maximum and median values. When sort’s argument is null the ArrayList’s element type must implement the Comparable interface so sort can compare the elements to determine sort order—class Double implements Comparable. To count the number of people for which we have valid ages, we simply get cleanAge’s size (line 89). Lines 92–94 determine the median. If cleanAge’s size is even, the median is the average of the two middle elements (line 93); otherwise, it’s the middle element (line 94). Lines 97–103 calculate the average age.

Click here to view code image

87         // descriptive statistics for cleaned age column
88         cleanAge.sort(null); // helps determine min, max and median ages
89         int size = cleanAge.size();
90
91         // get median age
92         double medianAge = (size % 2 == 0) ?
93            (cleanAge.get(size / 2 - 1) + cleanAge.get(size / 2)) / 2.0 :
94            cleanAge.get(size / 2);
95
96         // calculate average of ages
97         double sum = 0.0;
98
99         for (double value : cleanAge) {
100           sum += value;
101        }
102
103        double averageAge = sum / size;
104

Lines 106–111 display the descriptive statistics. The ArrayList is sorted, so lines 109–110 call the ArrayList’s getFirst and getLast methods to get first and last elements, which contain the minimum and maximum values, respectively. The average and median are measures of central tendency. Each produces a single value that represents a “central” value in a set of values—a value that is, in some sense, typical of the others. For the 1046 people with valid ages, the average age was 29.88 years old. The youngest passenger (i.e., the minimum) was just over two months old (0.17 * 12 is 2.04), and the oldest (i.e., the maximum) was 80. The median age was 28.

11.9 Objects-Natural Security Case Study: RSA Public-Key Cryptography

 

In Section 7.9, you began learning about secret-key cryptography. The sender’s plaintext was encrypted with a secret key to form ciphertext. The receiver used the same secret key to decode the ciphertext, forming the original plaintext—this process is called symmetric encryption because the same key is used by both the sender and the recipient.

Public-Key Cryptography

A problem with secret-key cryptography is that the security of the ciphertext is only as good as the security of the secret key, and several copies of that key are “floating around.” In their paper “New Directions in Cryptography,”14 Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, introduced public-key cryptography to address the weakness of secret-key cryptography—the vulnerability of the secret key having to be known by both the sender and the recipient. They came up with the idea but not an implementation of the scheme.

14. “New Directions in Cryptography.” November 6, 1976. Accessed January 1, 2025. https://ee.stanford.edu/~hellman/publications/24.pdf.

RSA Public-Key Cryptography

Rivest, Shamir and Adelman were the first to publish a working implementation of public-key cryptography. The scheme, called RSA, bears the initials of their last names.15 RSA is one of the world’s most widely implemented public-key cryptography schemes.16 Because RSA can be slow,17 many organizations prefer to stick to faster private-key encryption, using RSA only to securely send the secret key. Such encryption and decryption techniques are critical for securing data stored in files and transmitted over networks.

15. R. Rivest; A. Shamir; L. Adleman (February 1978). “A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-Key Cryptosystems” (PDF). Communications of the ACM. 21 (2): 120–126. Accessed January 1, 2025. https://people.csail.mit.edu/rivest/Rsapaper.pdf.

16. Cobb, Michael. “RSA algorithm (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman).” Accessed January 1, 2025. https://searchsecurity.techtarget.com/definition/RSA.

17. “RSA (cryptosystem).” Accessed January 1, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem).

Historical Note

Clifford Cocks in the U.K. created a workable public-key scheme several years before the RSA paper was published,18 but his work was classified, so it was not revealed until about 20 years after RSA appeared. The company RSA Security held a patent on the RSA algorithm. In 2000, that patent was coming due for renewal—instead of renewing, they placed the algorithm into the public domain.19

18. “Clifford Cocks.” Accessed January 1, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Cocks.

19. “RSA Security Releases RSA Encryption Algorithm into Public Domain.” September 6, 2000. Accessed January 1, 2025. https://web.archive.org/web/20071120112201/http://www.rsa.com/press_release.aspx?id=261.

Enhanced Cryptography Demo

In this case study, we enhance our AES private-key encryption example to demonstrate how to securely encrypt the secret key using RSA public-key cryptography.20,21,22 In particular, we focus on how to generate:

  • the public key any sender can use to encrypt an AES secret key for transmission to a specific recipient, and

  • the private key only the specific recipient can use to decrypt the AES secret key.

20. “RSA (cryptosystem).” Accessed January 1, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem).

21. “RSA Algorithm.” Accessed January 1, 2025. https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_algorithm.

22. “PKCS #1: RSA Cryptography Specifications Version 2.2.” November 2016. Accessed January 1, 2025. https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8017.

Public-key cryptography is also called asymmetric-key cryptography because different keys are used for encryption and decryption. This technique is often used to transmit the secret keys used in symmetric encryption. RSA is based on sophisticated mathematics using enormous prime numbers consisting of hundreds of digits, but the Java cryptography APIs encapsulate this complexity, hiding it from you. Much of Fig. 11.11’s code is identical to the AES cryptography demo in Fig. 7.23, so we focus on the enhancements. We split the example into parts for discussion purposes.

Getting the Message to Encrypt and AES Encrypting It

Lines 20–35 perform the same tasks as in Section 7.9:

  • Input the plain text to encrypt,

  • input the secret key seed for reproducibility (again, for demo purposes only),

  • generate the secret key for AES encryption, and

  • use the secret key to AES encrypt the plain text.

Generating the RSA Public and Private Keys

Lines 38–45 generate an RSA key pair that we’ll use to simulate the secure transmission of an encrypted AES secret key:

  • Line 38 calls the KeyPairGenerator static method getInstance with the argument "RSA" to get a KeyPairGenerator object for RSA encryption.

  • Line 39 uses the KeyPairGenerator method initialize to set the key size to 2048 bits, as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) recommends23—this defines the encryption strength.

    23. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Recommendation for Key Management: Part 3 — Application-Specific Key Management Guidance. Special Publication 800-57 Part 3 Revision 1. Gaithersburg, MD: National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2015. https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-57Pt3r1.pdf.

  • Line 40 generates the RSA KeyPair by calling the KeyPairGenerator method generateKeyPair.

  • Lines 44–45 get the KeyPair’s PublicKey and a PrivateKey via KeyPair methods getPublic and getPrivate.

You share your PublicKey with anyone sending you encrypted data. You keep the Private-Key secret and use it to decrypt data encrypted with your PublicKey, ensuring that only the intended recipient (you) can read the message.

Click here to view code image

37            // generate RSA key pair -- normally done by message receiver
38            var keyPairGenerator = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("RSA");
39            keyPairGenerator.initialize(2048); // set key size to 2048 bits
40            KeyPair rsaKeyPair = keyPairGenerator.generateKeyPair();
41
42            // get RSA public and private keys -- recipient sends the
43            // public key to anyone who needs to send them something securely
44            PublicKey publicKey = rsaKeyPair.getPublic();
45            PrivateKey privateKey = rsaKeyPair.getPrivate();
46
Encrypting the AES Secret Key

Lines 49–50 use RSA to encrypt the AES SecretKey. Method encryptRSA (lines 117–130) takes the SecretKey’s byte array representation (secretKey.getEncoded()) and the RSA publicKey and uses the publicKey to encrypt the AES SecretKey—this ensures only the intended recipient can later decrypt it using their corresponding RSA private key. Encrypting the AES secret key allows it to be transmitted securely. For demo purposes, we display the encrypted AES SecretKey so you can confirm later that it was decrypted properly—your output will differ as the RSA publicKey was generated randomly. In real-world cryptography, we’d send the cipherText (line 34) and the encryptedAESKey to the recipient.

Decrypting the AES Secret Key

To decrypt the ciphertext, the recipient must first decrypt the AES secret key that was used to produce the ciphertext. Lines 55–56 call method decryptRSA (lines 133–148) to decrypt the AES SecretKey using RSA decryption. The method decryptRSA receives the encrypted AES key and the RSA private key—the only key that can decrypt data encrypted by the corresponding public key, ensuring the AES secret key’s security. This process ensures that only the intended recipient, who possesses the private key, can obtain the original AES key and read the encrypted message. For demonstration purposes, we display the decrypted AES secret key, so you can compare it to the one output by lines 30–31 and see that it was decrypted properly.

73      // Generate and return a SecretKey. Note: We are seeding a
74      // SecureRandom object for reproducibility so you get the same results
75      // we show in this program's output. Don't do this in production code.
76      public static SecretKey generateKey(String seed) throws Exception {
77         // get a secure random number generator
78         var random = SecureRandom.getInstance("SHA1PRNG");
79         random.setSeed(seed.getBytes()); // for demo reproducibility
80
81         // get an AES SecretKey generator
82         var keyGen = KeyGenerator.getInstance("AES");
83         keyGen.init(256, random); // set up for 256-bit keys
84         return keyGen.generateKey(); // generate and return new SecretKey
85      }

92         cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, secretKey); // configure to encrypt
93
94         // encrypt the byte[] representation of plaintext
95         byte[] encrypted = cipher.doFinal(plaintext.getBytes());
96
97         // Base64 encode encrypted as a ciphertext String and return
98         return Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(encrypted);
99      }
100
101     // decrypt an AES-encrypted String
102     public static String decrypt(
103        String ciphertext, SecretKey secretKey) throws Exception {
104
105        var cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES"); // get a Cipher object
106        cipher.init(Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE, secretKey); // configure to decrypt
107
108        // Base64 decode ciphertext to byte array
109        byte[] ciphertextBytes = Base64.getDecoder().decode(ciphertext);
110
111        // create plaintext String from ciphertextBytes and return it
112        return new String(cipher.doFinal(ciphertextBytes));
113     }
114
Encrypting the AES Secret Key Using RSA

Method encryptRSA (lines 117–130) encrypts a byte array using an RSA PublicKey:

  • Line 120 creates a Cipher object configured to use the RSA algorithm.

  • Line 123 initializes the Cipher object for encryption mode using the RSA public key. This ensures that only the recipient with the corresponding private key can decrypt the data.

  • Line 126 calls the Cipher object’s doFinal to encrypt the byte array data, which, in this case, is the AES secret key.

  • Finally, line 129 encodes the encrypted data as a Base64 String and returns a String representing the encrypted AES secret key.

This encrypted key can then be safely sent to the recipient along with the encrypted message, so they can use their RSA private key to decrypt the AES secret key and decrypt the message.

Click here to view code image

115     // encrypt data using RSA public key -- the result of this method
116     // would be sent to the AES encrypted message's receiver
117     public static String encryptRSA(byte[] data, PublicKey publicKey)
118        throws Exception {
119
120        var cipher = Cipher.getInstance("RSA"); // create RSA Cipher object
121
122        // initialize cipher in encryption mode with recipient's public key
123        cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, publicKey);
124
125        // encrypt data (the AES key) using the RSA public key
126        byte[] encryptedData = cipher.doFinal(data);
127
128        // Base64 encode the encrypted AES key
129        return Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(encryptedData);
130     }
131
Decrypting the AES Secret Key Using RSA

Method decryptRSA (lines 133–148) decrypts data using an RSA PrivateKey and returns the decrypted data as an AES SecretKey:

  • Line 136 creates a Cipher object configured for the RSA algorithm.

  • Line 139 initializes the Cipher object in decryption mode with the recipient’s PrivateKey—only this key can decrypt the data that was encrypted with the corresponding PublicKey.

  • Lines 142–143 decode the encrypted data from its Base64 String format to a byte array, then call the Cipher object’s doFinal to decrypt the array, resulting in the original AES secret key as a byte array.

  • Finally, the method converts this byte array to an AES SecretKey object, which the recipient can use to decrypt of the corresponding message. The Secret-KeySpec class is an implementation of the SecretKey interface.

This process ensures that only the intended recipient, who has the RSA PrivateKey, can decrypt and use the AES SecretKey.

Click here to view code image

132     // decrypt data using RSA private key and return the SecretKey
133     public static SecretKey decryptRSA(
134        String encryptedData, PrivateKey privateKey) throws Exception {
135
136        var cipher = Cipher.getInstance("RSA"); // create RSA Cipher object
137
138        // initialize cipher in decryption mode with recipient's private key
139        cipher.init(Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE, privateKey);
140
141        // decode the encrypted AES key from Base64 format and decrypt it
142        byte[] decryptedData =
143           cipher.doFinal(Base64.getDecoder().decode(encryptedData));
144
145        // convert decrypted byte array back to an AES SecretKey object
146        return new SecretKeySpec(
147           decryptedData, 0, decryptedData.length, "AES");
148     }
149  }

11.10 Wrap-Up

In this chapter, you created and manipulated persistent data on secondary storage devices. We began with Java’s file-handling architecture, explained that data can be stored in text or binary files, and discussed their differences. We demonstrated Java NIO classes and interfaces for retrieving information about files and directories. We discussed using Formatter objects to write to and Scanner objects to read from text files. We created and manipulated sequential text files.

Next, we presented several case studies on transforming objects to and from popular data formats. The first introduced the human-and-computer-readable JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) data format. We used the popular Java-based Jackson open-source library to serialize objects to a file in JSON format, then deserialized the JSON text from the file into objects in memory. The second JSON case study used Java’s HttpClient, HttpRequest and HttpResponse classes to invoke a free OpenWeatherMap.org web service that returned a city’s weather report in JSON format. Then, we used Jackson to process the response and display the weather report.

The next two case studies introduced the popular CSV (comma-separated-values) file format and how to write and read CSV files using the Jackson open-source library. Then, we used CSV reading capabilities to load the Titanic disaster dataset, which is commonly used to introduce basic data analytics.

Finally, we presented our last objects-natural case study. We enhanced Section 7.9’s private-key cryptography example by using RSA public-key cryptography to encrypt and decrypt the AES secret key, enabling secure transmission of the secret key to an encrypted message’s recipient. Such encryption and decryption techniques are critical for securing data stored in files and transmitted over networks. We’ll continue our discussions of persisting data in Chapter 20, Accessing Databases with JDBC and SQLite.

In the next chapter, we discuss the Java Collections Framework, which contains many predefined collection classes and interfaces for manipulating data in memory, like the ArrayList class (introduced in Section 6.20) and the List interface (introduced in Section 11.4.1).

Objectives

In this chapter, you’ll:

  • Learn what collections are.

  • Learn the type-wrapper classes that enable programs to process primitive data values as objects.

  • Understand the automatic boxing and unboxing that occurs between objects of the type-wrapper classes and their corresponding primitive types.

  • Use prebuilt generic data structures from the collections framework.

  • Use various algorithms of the Collections class to process collections.

  • Use iterators to traverse a collection.

  • Learn about factory methods for conveniently creating immutable Lists, Sets and Maps optimized for 0 to 10 elements.

12.1 Introduction

 

Section 6.20 introduced the generic ArrayList collection—a dynamically resizable array-like data structure that stores references to objects of the type you specify when you create the ArrayList. Here, we continue our discussion of the Java collections framework, which contains many other prebuilt generic data structures. Some examples of collections are the songs stored on a smartphone, a contacts list, the cards a player holds in a card game and the players on a sports team.

We discuss the collections-framework interfaces that declare the capabilities of each collection type, various classes that implement these interfaces, methods that process collection objects, and iterators that traverse collections. In Section 12.11, we introduce convenience factory methods that help you create small immutable collections. A factory method is typically a static method that builds and returns an object for you.

After reading Chapter 14, Functional Programming with Lambdas & Streams, you’ll be able to reimplement many of this chapter’s examples more concisely and elegantly, and in a way that makes them easier to parallelize to improve performance on multi-core systems. In Chapter 18, Concurrency: Platform Threads to Virtual Threads, you’ll learn how to improve performance on multi-core systems using Java’s concurrent collections and parallel stream operations.

Displaying Collections

In this chapter, we sometimes iterate over a collection using a loop to display its elements so we can introduce various collection methods. You can also print a collection’s String representation. Each Java collection provides a toString method that formats the collection’s data as a comma-delimited list in square brackets ([]) or curly braces ({}), depending on the collection’s type.

12.2 Collections Overview

 

A collection (also called a data structure) is an object that can hold references to other objects. Collections contain references to objects of any type that has the is-a relationship with the collection’s element type.

Java Collections Framework Interfaces

Sections 9.11–9.13 introduced interfaces. The collections framework’s interfaces declare the operations performed on various collection types. The following list contains some key collections-framework interfaces1—several implementations of these interfaces are provided within the framework, and you may also provide your own:

1. The complete list of collections-framework interfaces can be found at https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/util/package-summary.html#class-summary by clicking the Interfaces tab.

  • Collection is the collections hierarchy’s root interface. Interfaces Set, Queue and List extend Collection, which contains common collection manipulations, such as adding elements, removing elements, clearing an entire collection, comparing entire collections and converting a collection to an array. In addition, interface Collection provides a method that returns an Iterator object (Section 12.5.1) that a program can use to traverse a collection one element at a time. For the complete list of the Collection interface’s methods, visit:

    Click here to view code image

    https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/
    java/util/Collection.html

  • The Set interface specifies operations for a collection that does not allow duplicate elements. By default, there’s no guaranteed order for a Set’s elements. However, Java also provides Set implementations that maintain elements in their insertion order (the order you add them to the Set) or sorted order.

  • The List interface specifies operations for an ordered collection of elements that may contain duplicate elements. A List is “ordered” in that you can access its elements by index, like an array.

  • The Map interface specifies operations for a collection that associates keys to values and may not contain duplicate keys. Map does not derive from Collection. By default, there’s no guaranteed order for a Map’s key-value pairs. However, Java also provides Map implementations that maintain the key-value pairs in their insertion order (the order you add them to the Map) or sorted order by key.

  • The Queue interface specifies operations for a first-in, first-out collection that models a waiting line. Other orders can be specified.

Generic Collections

Collection, List, Set, Map and Queue are generic interfaces. Generics (like ArrayList in Section 6.20) enable you to specify the exact type stored in a collection and give you the benefits of compile-time type checking. The compiler issues error messages if you use inappropriate types in your generic collections. We discuss Java’s generics mechanisms in more detail in Chapter 13, Generic Classes and Methods: A Deeper Look.

Choosing a Collection

Before building your own data structures, consider using the interfaces and collections of the Java collections framework, which have been carefully tested and tuned to meet most application requirements. The documentation for each collection discusses its memory requirements and the performance characteristics of its methods for operations such as adding and removing elements, searching for elements, sorting elements and more. Chapter 22, Recursion and Big O, discusses a means for describing how hard an algorithm works to perform its task—based on how sensitive it is to the number of data items to be processed. After reading Chapter 22, you’ll better understand each collection’s performance characteristics described in the online documentation.

Declaring Parameters with Generic Interface Types

Generic interfaces are frequently used as parameter types to allow polymorphic processing of all objects that implement a given generic interface with the correct element type. For example, many Java collection classes have a constructor that takes a Collection argument, allowing a new collection to be populated with the elements of any existing collection with the correct element type. So, if you’re constructing an ArrayList<String>, any object that is a Collection<String> can be passed to the ArrayList<String>’s constructor.

Collections Class static Methods

Class Collections provides static convenience methods that search, sort and perform many other common operations on various collections. Section 12.6 discusses several of these Collections methods.

Generative AI

1 Prompt genAIs, asking how the Java compiler ensures that only objects of the correct type are added to a generic collection.

12.3 Type-Wrapper Classes

For each primitive type, the java.lang package contains a corresponding type-wrapper class—Boolean, Byte, Character, Double, Float, Integer, Long and Short. These enable programs to manipulate primitive-type values as immutable objects. Java collections cannot store primitive-type values directly, but they can manipulate objects of the type-wrapper classes. The Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float and Double numeric type-wrapper classes extend class Number. The type-wrapper classes are final, so you cannot extend them.

Unlike class types, primitive types cannot have methods. So, methods associated with a given primitive type are defined as static methods in the corresponding type-wrapper class. For example, class Integer contains the static method parseInt, which converts a String to an int value. The other type-wrapper classes have similar methods.

2 Prompt genAIs, asking why Java collections cannot store primitive-type values directly.

12.4 Boxing and Unboxing

Java can automatically convert between primitive-type values and type-wrapper objects when necessary:

  • A boxing conversion converts a primitive-type value to an object of the corresponding type-wrapper class.

  • An unboxing conversion converts an object of a type-wrapper class to its corresponding primitive-type value.

The following statement boxes the int value 10 by creating an Integer object containing the value 10 and assigning the object’s reference to integerObject:

Click here to view code image

Integer integerObject = 10; // boxes 10 to an Integer object

The following statement unboxes the int value 10 from the Integer object referenced by integerObject:

Click here to view code image

int value = integerObject; // unboxes 10 from integerObject

Many of our forthcoming examples use boxing and unboxing conversions to store primitive values in and retrieve them from collections.

12.5 Lists

A List (sometimes called a sequence) is a Collection of elements in sequence that may contain duplicate items. Like array indices, List indices start at 0. In addition to the methods inherited from Collection, List inherits interface Collection’s methods and provides additional methods for

  • manipulating elements via their indices,

  • manipulating a specified range of elements,

  • searching for elements and

  • obtaining a ListIterator to access elements.

For the complete list of methods, visit:

Click here to view code image

https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/
   util/List.html

Several Java Collections Framework classes implement List, including ArrayList (introduced in Section 6.20) and LinkedList:

  • An ArrayList provides a resizable array implementation. Inserting an element between existing ArrayList elements is inefficient. All elements after the new one must be moved out of the way, which is expensive for a large ArrayList.

  • A LinkedList enables efficient insertion or removal of elements anywhere in a list but is much less efficient than an ArrayList for jumping to an element at a specific index.

12.5.1 ArrayList and Iterator

Figure 12.1 uses an ArrayList to demonstrate several Collection capabilities using two ArrayList<String> objects. We broke the example into parts for discussion purposes.

Creating the ArrayLists and Adding Elements

Lines 11 and 19 declare and initialize String arrays colors and removeColors. Lines 12 and 20 create ArrayList<String> objects and assign their references to List<String> variables colorList and removeList—we’ll say more about declaring these variables using the List interface rather than the ArrayList class shortly. Recall that ArrayList is a generic class, so we specify a type argument (String) to indicate each list’s element type. Because you specify the type to store in a collection at compile time, generic collections provide compile-time type safety—the compiler catches attempts to use invalid types. For example, you cannot store String objects in a collection of Employees.

We use methods size and get here for demonstration purposes. Typically, lines 29–31 would be implemented with an enhanced for statement, as in lines 39–41. Working with Iterators

Method removeColors declares two Collection<String> parameters (lines 45–46)—any two Collections containing Strings can be passed as arguments. The method accesses the elements of the first Collection (allItems) via an Iterator. Line 48 calls Collection method iterator to get an Iterator<String> for allItems. The loop continues executing while Iterator method hasNext (line 51) returns true, indicating there are more elements in allItems to process.

Click here to view code image

44      // remove colors specified in itemsToRemove from allItems
45      private static void removeColors(Collection<String> allItems,
46         Collection<String> itemsToRemove) {
47
48         Iterator<String> iterator = allItems.iterator(); // get iterator
49
50         // loop while collection has items
51         while (iterator.hasNext()) {
52            if (itemsToRemove.contains(iterator.next())) {
53               iterator.remove(); // remove current element
54            }
55         }
56      }
57   }

The if condition in line 52 calls Iterator method next to obtain a reference to the next element in allItems, then uses Collection method contains to determine whether that element is in itemsToRemove. If so, line 53 calls Iterator method remove to remove allItems’ current element.

We declared method removeColors in this example to demonstrate working directly with Iterators. However, Collections method removeAll performs the same task. So, the call to removeColors in line 34 and its definition in lines 45–56 can be replaced with:

Click here to view code image

colorList.removeAll(removeList);

In Chapter 14, Functional Programming with Lambdas & Streams, we’ll demonstrate filtering, which enables you to produce a new collection containing only the elements that match the criteria you specify—the original collection remains unmodified in the spirit of immutability. In a genAI question in Chapter 14, we’ll ask you to prompt genAIs with Fig. 12.1’s code, asking them to refactor the code, improving it using techniques introduced in that chapter.

Iterator Invalidation

If a Collection is modified by one of its methods after creating an Iterator for it, the Iterator immediately becomes invalid—any subsequent operation performed with the iterator fails immediately, throwing a ConcurrentModificationException. This is known as failing fast—fail-fast iterators help ensure that a modifiable collection is not manipulated by multiple threads simultaneously, which could corrupt the data. In Chapter 18, Concurrency: Platform Threads to Virtual Threads, you’ll learn about the java.util.concurrent package’s concurrent collections that multiple concurrent threads can safely manipulate. Modifying the collection via the Iterator, however, does not invalidate it.

Referring to Collection Objects with Interface Variables

In this example, we refer to the ArrayLists using List variables. This makes our code more flexible and easier to modify. If we later determine that LinkedLists would be more appropriate, only the import statement at line 4 and the statements that created the ArrayList objects (lines 12 and 20) need to be modified. In general, when you create a collection object, refer to it with a variable of the corresponding collection interface type. Similarly, implementing method removeColors to receive Collection<String> parameters enables the method to be used with any object that implements Collection<String>.

Type Inference with the <> Notation

Lines 12 and 20 specify the ArrayList’s element type (String) in the variables’ types and object creation expressions. You can use type inferencing with the diamond notation <> in statements that declare and create generic type variables and objects. For example, line 12 can be written as:

Click here to view code image

List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();

The <> tells the compiler to infer the ArrayList’s element type from the type in angle brackets on the left of the declaration (that is, String). We’ll use this syntax as appropriate for the remaining examples in this chapter.

12.5.3 Views into Collections and Arrays Method asList

Arrays static method asList returns a List view of an array’s data, enabling you to use an array in code where a List is expected and, since a List is a Collection, also where a Collection is expected. For example, we can use a List view of an array to

  • initialize a new collection with the array’s elements by calling the new collection’s constructor that receives a Collection argument and

  • add all of an array’s elements to a Collection by calling Collection method addAll, which receives a Collection argument.

The next example creates a LinkedList and initializes it with a List view of an array. Any modifications made to the List view change the array’s elements, and any modifications made to the array’s elements change the List view. Recall that an array has a fixed size, so for a List view of an array, calling methods that change the List’s size by adding or removing elements results in UnsupportedOperationExceptions.

Viewing Arrays as Lists and Converting Lists to Arrays

Figure 12.3 uses Arrays method asList to view an array as a List and List method toArray to create an array from the contents of a LinkedList.

Line 9 constructs a LinkedList<String> containing the elements of array colors. Arrays method asList returns a List view of colors, which we pass to the LinkedList’s constructor to initialize it. This constructor receives a Collection as an argument—again, a List is a Collection. Line 11 calls LinkedList method addLast to append "red" to the list. Lines 12–13 call LinkedList method add to add "pink" as the last element and "green" as the element at index 3 (i.e., the fourth element). Method addLast works identically to the single-argument add method. Line 14 calls LinkedList method addFirst to add "cyan" as the new first item in the LinkedList. The add operations are permitted because they operate on the LinkedList object, not the view returned by asList. When we add "cyan" as the first element, "green" becomes the LinkedList’s fifth element.

Line 17 calls the List interface’s toArray method to get a String array from list. The array is a copy of the list’s elements—modifying the array’s contents does not alter the list. The array passed to toArray must have the element type that toArray should return. If the array’s number of elements exceeds the LinkedList’s, toArray copies the list’s elements into its array argument and returns that array. If the LinkedList has more elements than the array argument, toArray allocates a new array of the same type, then copies the list’s elements into the new array and returns it. So, passing a correctly sized array is more efficient because it avoids reallocation.

Possible toArray Logic Error

Passing an array that contains data as toArray’s argument can cause logic errors. If the array’s number of elements is smaller than the number of elements in the list on which toArray is called, a new array is allocated to store the list’s elements. If the array’s number of elements exceeds the list’s, the array’s elements (starting at index zero) are overwritten with the list’s elements. The first element of the remainder of the array is set to null to indicate the end of the list.

12.6 Collections Methods

Class Collections provides many prepackaged, high-performance algorithms for manipulating collection elements. The algorithms in the following table are static methods:

The methods sort, binarySearch, reverse, shuffle, fill and copy operate on Lists. Methods min, max, addAll, frequency and disjoint operate on Collections, so they support a wider range of collection objects than the List-specific methods. The Collections methods are polymorphic—each can operate on objects that implement specific interfaces, regardless of the underlying implementations.

12.6.1 Method sort

Method sort sorts the elements of a List. The elements’ type must implement interface Comparable. The order is determined by the natural order of the elements’ type as implemented by a compareTo method. For example, the natural order for numeric values is ascending order, and the natural order for Strings is based on their lexicographical ordering (Section 7.3). Method compareTo is declared in interface Comparable and is sometimes called the natural comparison method. The sort call may specify as a second argument an object that implements interface Comparator to specify an alternative ordering of the elements.

Sorting in Ascending Order

Figure 12.4 uses Collections method sort to order the elements of a List in ascending order (line 15). Line 12 creates a List of Strings. Lines 13 and 16 each use an implicit call to the list’s toString method to output the list contents as a comma-delimited list in square brackets ([ and ]).

Sorting in Descending Order

Figure 12.5 sorts the same list of strings used in Fig. 12.4 in descending order. The example introduces the Comparator interface to customize sorting a Collection’s elements. Line 16 calls Collections’s method sort to order the List in descending order. The static Collections method reverseOrder returns a Comparator object that orders the collection’s elements in reverse order. Because the collection being sorted is a List<String>, reverseOrder returns a Comparator<String>.

Sorting with a Custom Comparator

Figure 12.6 creates a custom class TimeComparator that implements interface Comparator to compare two Time2 objects. Recall that class Time2 (Fig. 8.14) represents times with hours, minutes and seconds.

Class TimeComparator (Fig. 12.6) implements generic interface Comparator, which has one type argument (in this case, Time2). A class that implements Comparator must declare a compare method that receives two arguments of the type to compare and returns

  • a negative integer if the first argument is less than the second,

  • 0 if the arguments are equal or

  • a positive integer if the first argument is greater than the second.

Method compare (lines 6–22) compares Time2 objects. Line 8 calculates the difference between their hours. If the hours are different (line 10), then we return this value:

  • If this value is positive, time1’s hour is greater than time2’s, and time1 is greater than time2.

  • If this value is negative, time1’s hour is less than time2’s, and time1 is less than time2.

If the hour difference is zero, the hours are the same, so we must test the minutes (lines 14–18) to determine which time is greater. If the minutes are the same, we must test the seconds (lines 20–21) to determine which time is greater.

Figure 12.7 sorts an ArrayList<Time2> object’s elements using our TimeComparator. Line 9 creates the ArrayList. Lines 11–15 create five Time2 objects and add them to the list. Line 21 calls method sort, passing it a TimeComparator object to customize the comparison (Fig. 12.6).

12.6.3 Methods reverse, fill, copy, max and min

Class Collections provides methods for reversing, filling and copying Lists:

  • Collections method reverse reverses the order of the elements in a List.

  • Collections method fill overwrites elements in a List with a specified value—for example, to reinitialize an existing List.

  • Collections method copy receives a destination List and a source List. Each element in the source is copied to the destination. The destination List must be at least as long as the source; otherwise, an IndexOutOfBoundsException occurs. If the destination List is longer, the elements not overwritten are unchanged.

Collections methods min and max operate on any Collection—min returns the smallest element, and max returns the largest. Both can be called with a Comparator object as a second argument to perform custom comparisons of objects, such as the TimeComparator in Fig. 12.7. Figure 12.9 demonstrates methods reverse, fill, copy, max and min.

Method reverse takes one List argument. Since list is a List view of the array letters, the array’s elements are now in reverse order. The reversed contents are output in lines 16–17.

Line 24 uses Collections method copy to copy list’s elements into copyList. Changes to copyList do not change letters because copyList is a separate List that’s not a List view of the array letters. Method copy requires two List arguments—the destination List and the source List.

Line 29 calls Collections method fill to place the character 'R' in each list element. Because list is a List view of the array letters, this operation changes each element in letters to 'R'. Method fill requires a List for the first argument and an object of the List’s element type for the second argument. In this case, the object is the boxed Character version of 'R'.

Lines 37–38 in method outputList call Collections methods max and min to find the largest and the smallest element of a Collection, respectively. Recall that interface List extends interface Collection, so a List is a Collection.

12.6.4 Method binarySearch

If you need to search for a key in a short List, simply iterating through the List’s elements is usually efficient. If you need to search for a key in a lengthy List, the high-speed binary search algorithm can be far more efficient. The static Collections method binarySearch implements the high-speed binary search algorithm. This method locates an object in a List that’s sorted in ascending order. If the object is found, binarySearch returns its index; otherwise, binarySearch returns a negative value. If multiple elements in the list match the search key, there’s no guarantee which one will be located first. Figure 12.10 uses binary-Search to search for various Strings in an ArrayList.

Line 13 initializes list with an ArrayList containing a copy of the elements in array colors. A precondition (Section 10.10) of Collections method binarySearch is that its List argument’s elements must be sorted in ascending order. Line 15 uses Collections method sort to sort the List, which is a time-consuming operation for large Lists. If binarySearch’s precondition is not met, its result is undefined—you’ll explore this issue with genAI momentarily. Line 16 outputs the sorted list. Lines 19–24 call method print-SearchResults (lines 28–40) to perform searches and output the results. Line 32 calls Collections method binarySearch to search list for the specified key, passing a List and the search key as arguments. Lines 34–39 output the search results. An overloaded version of binarySearch takes a Comparator object as its third argument, which specifies how binarySearch should compare the search key to the List’s elements.

12.7 Class PriorityQueue and Interface Queue

 

Recall that a queue is a collection representing a waiting line—typically, insertions are made at the back of a queue, and deletions are made from the front. This section demonstrates Java’s Queue interface and PriorityQueue class from package java.util. In Chapter 18, Concurrency: Platform Threads to Virtual Threads, we’ll use concurrent queues.

Interface Queue extends interface Collection and provides additional operations for inserting, removing and inspecting elements in a queue. Class PriorityQueue, which implements the Queue interface, orders elements by their natural ordering as specified by Comparable elements’ compareTo method or by a Comparator object supplied to the constructor.

Class PriorityQueue provides functionality that enables insertions in sorted order into the underlying data structure and deletions from the front of the underlying data structure. For PriorityQueues containing numeric values, the lowest value has the “highest” priority and will be removed from the PriorityQueue first.

PriorityQueue Operations

The common PriorityQueue operations are:

  • offer to insert an element at the appropriate location based on priority order,

  • poll to remove the highest-priority element of the priority queue (i.e., the head of the queue),

  • peek to get a reference to the highest-priority element of the priority queue (without removing that element),

  • clear to remove all elements in the priority queue and

  • size to get the number of elements in the priority queue.

Demonstrating PriorityQueue

Figure 12.12 demonstrates generic class PriorityQueue with a PriorityQueue<Double> (line 8). By default a PriorityQueue’s initial capacity is 11 elements. Class PriorityQueue provides several additional constructors. One of these takes an int and a Comparator object to create a PriorityQueue with the initial capacity specified by the int and the ordering by the Comparator.

Lines 11–13 use method offer to add elements to the priority queue. Method offer throws a NullPointerException if the program attempts to add a null object to the queue. The loop in lines 18–21 uses method isEmpty to determine whether the priority queue is empty (line 18). While there are more elements, line 19 uses PriorityQueue method peek to look at the highest-priority element in the queue for output (without actually removing it from the queue). Line 20 removes the highest-priority element in the queue with method poll, which returns the removed element.

12.8 Hash Tables

 

When a program creates objects, it may need to store and retrieve them efficiently. Storing and retrieving information with arrays is efficient if some aspect of your data matches a numerical key value (that is, the index) and if the keys are unique and tightly packed. If you have 100 employees with nine-digit Social Security numbers and you want to store and retrieve employee data by using the Social Security number as an array index, the task will require an array with approximately 900 million elements because nine-digit Social Security numbers must begin with 001–899 (excluding 666) as per the Social Security Administration’s website:

Click here to view code image

https://www.ssa.gov/employer/randomization.html

A program with such a large array could achieve high performance for storing and retrieving employee records by simply using the Social Security number as the array index. This is impractical for most applications that use Social Security numbers as keys.

Non-Integer and Sparsely-Spread Keys

Numerous applications have this problem—namely, that either the keys are of the wrong type (e.g., not positive integers usable as array subscripts) or they’re of the right type but sparsely spread over a vast range, such as Social Security numbers for a small company’s employees. What is needed is a high-speed scheme for converting keys—such as Social Security numbers, inventory part numbers and the like—into unique array indices over a modest-size array. Then, when an application needs to store a data item, the scheme can rapidly convert the application’s key into an array index (a process called hashing), and the item can be stored at that slot in the array. Retrieval is accomplished the same way: Once the application has a key for which it wants to retrieve the data, it simply applies the conversion to the key, producing the array index where the data is stored and retrieved.

Why the Term Hashing?

When we convert a key into an array index, we literally scramble the bits, forming a kind of “mishmashed,” or hashed, number. The number actually has no real significance beyond its usefulness in storing and retrieving particular data.

Hashing Collisions

A glitch in the scheme is called a collision, which occurs when two different keys “hash into” the same array element (or cell). We cannot store two values in the same space, so we need to find an alternative home for all values beyond the first that hash to the same array index. There are many schemes for doing this. One is to “hash again”—that is, to apply another hashing transformation to the previous hash result to provide the next candidate cell in the array. The hashing process is designed to distribute the values throughout the table, so hopefully, an available cell will be found with one or a few hashes.

Another scheme uses one hash to locate the first candidate cell. If that cell is occupied, adjacent cells are searched sequentially until an available cell is found. Retrieval works the same way: The key is hashed once to determine the initial location and check whether it contains the desired data. If it does, the search is finished; otherwise, successive cells are searched sequentially until the desired data is found. A popular solution to hash-table collisions is to have each table cell be a hash bucket—typically a list of all the key–value pairs that hash to that cell. This is the solution that Java’s HashMap class (Section 12.10) uses.

Load Factor and Performance

A hash table’s load factor affects the performance of hashing schemes. The load factor is the ratio of the hash table’s number of occupied cells to its total number of cells. The closer this ratio gets to 1.0, the greater the chance of collisions, which slow data insertion and retrieval.

A hash table’s load factor is a classic example of a memory-space/execution-time tradeoff: By increasing the load factor, we get better memory utilization, but the program runs slower due to increased hashing collisions. By decreasing the load factor, we get better program speed because of reduced hashing collisions, but we get poorer memory utilization because a larger portion of the hash table remains empty.

HashSet and HashMap Collections

Java’s HashSet and HashMap collections (presented in Sections 12.9–12.10) are implemented as hash tables “under the hood.” When you use those collections, you get the benefit of high-speed data storage and retrieval without having to build your own hash-table mechanisms—a classic example of software reuse. Class Object’s hashCode method is used to determine a key’s location in a Java hash-table-based collection.

Virtual Memory

Another interesting application of hashing is with virtual memory2 operating systems. Programs and data are maintained on massive secondary storage and brought into more limited primary memory (and even more limited and faster cache memory) to execute. The trick to running applications efficiently is to keep in primary memory (and cache memory) the portion of the program that needs to execute at a given time. Finding those program pieces in virtual memory involves searching the large data structures that define it. Hashing is often used for that purpose.

2. “Virtual Memory.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed September 24, 2024. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_memory.

12.9 Sets

 

A Set is a collection of unique elements (i.e., no duplicates). The collections framework contains several Set implementations, including HashSet and TreeSet:

  • A HashSet stores its elements (unordered) in a hash table—hash tables are presented in Section 12.8.

  • A TreeSet stores its elements (ordered) in a tree. Trees and their applications are discussed in upper-level computer science courses typically called Data Structures and Algorithms.

Figure 12.13 uses a HashSet to remove duplicate strings from a List. Recall that both List and Collection are generic types, so line 14 creates a List that contains String objects, and line 18 passes the collection to method printNonDuplicates (lines 22–33), which takes a Collection argument. Line 24 constructs a HashSet<String> from the Collection<String> argument. By definition, Sets do not contain duplicates, so when the HashSet is constructed, any duplicates in the Collection are ignored. Lines 28–30 output elements in the Set. We used a loop here to iterate through a HashSet’s elements, but we also could have used the HashSet’s String representation.

Sorted Sets

The collections framework also includes the SortedSet interface (which extends Set) for sets that maintain their elements in sorted order—either the elements’ natural order (e.g., numbers are in ascending order) or an order specified by a Comparator. Class TreeSet implements SortedSet. Figure 12.14 places Strings into a TreeSet. The Strings are sorted as they’re added to the TreeSet. This example also demonstrates range-view methods, which enable a program to view a portion of a collection.

Line 12 creates a TreeSet<String> containing the elements of array colors, then assigns the new TreeSet<String> to SortedSet<String> variable tree. Lines 26–27 call SortedSet methods first and last to get the smallest and largest elements of the set, respectively. Methods headSet and tailSet return views of the TreeSet’s data. Any changes made to the view modify the original TreeSet.

Method printSet (lines 31–37) accepts a SortedSet as an argument and prints it. Lines 32–34 print each element of the SortedSet. We used a loop here to iterate through a SortedSet’s elements, but we also could have displayed the SortedSet’s String representation. Note that the loop iterates through the SortedSet’s elements in sorted order.

12.10 Maps

 

Maps associate keys to values. The keys in a Map must be unique, but the associated values need not be. If a Map contains unique keys and unique values, it’s said to implement a oneto-one mapping. If only the keys are unique, the Map is said to implement a many-to-one mapping—many keys can map to one value.

Maps differ from Sets in that Maps contain keys and values, whereas Sets contain only values. Two classes that implement interface Map are HashMap and TreeMap:

  • HashMaps store elements in hash tables, and

  • TreeMaps store elements in trees.

This section uses a HashMap to store key–value pairs. Interface SortedMap extends Map and maintains its keys in sorted order—either the elements’ natural order or an order specified by a Comparator. Class TreeMap implements SortedMap.

Figure 12.15 uses a HashMap to count the number of occurrences of each word in a string. Line 12 creates an empty HashMap with a default initial capacity (16 elements) and a default load factor (0.75)—these defaults are built into the implementation of HashMap. When the number of occupied slots in the HashMap exceeds the capacity times the load factor, the capacity is doubled automatically.

HashMap is a generic class that takes two type arguments—the type of key (i.e., String) and the type of value (i.e., Integer). Recall that the type arguments passed to a generic class must be reference types, so the second type argument is Integer, not int.

Method createMap

Line 14 calls method createMap (lines 19–40), which uses a Map to store the number of occurrences of each word in the sentence. Line 22 obtains the user input, and line 25 tokenizes it. For each token, lines 28–39 convert the token to lowercase letters (line 29) for case-insensitive word counting, then call Map method containsKey (line 32) to determine whether the word is in the map (and thus has occurred previously in the string):

  • If the word exists in the map, line 33 uses Map method get to obtain the key’s associated value (the count) in the map. Line 34 increments that value and uses put to replace the key’s associated value with a boxed Integer version of the new count. Method put returns the key’s prior associated value, or null if the key was not in the map.

  • If the Map does not contain the word, line 37 uses Map method put to create a new entry, with the word as the key and an Integer object containing 1 as the value (1 is boxed).

Keys in Maps should be immutable objects. The key determines where a corresponding value is placed. Modifying a key after using it to insert a key–value pair could prevent a program from locating the key’s corresponding value later. In this chapter’s examples, we use Strings as keys because they’re immutable.

Method displayMap

Method displayMap (lines 43–58) displays all the entries in the map. It uses HashMap method keySet (line 44) to get a set of the keys. The keys have type String in the map, so keySet returns a Set<String>. Line 47 creates a TreeSet of the keys to store them in sorted order. Lines 52–54 access the map’s key–value pairs. Line 53 displays each key and its value using format specifier %-10s to left align each key and format specifier %10s to right align each value. The keys are displayed in ascending order. Line 57 calls Map method size to get the number of key–value pairs in the Map, and calls Map method isEmpty, which returns a boolean indicating whether the Map is empty.
