15.5 Tip Calculator Application: Intro to Event Handling

The Tip Calculator application calculates and displays a restaurant bill tip and total:

By default, the application calculates the total with a 15% tip. The following screen capture contains the GUI after you enter the amount 34.56 and click the Calculate Button:

You can specify a tip percentage from 0% to 30% by moving the Slider thumb—this updates the tip percentage. The following screen capture contains the GUI after the user moves the Slider’s thumb to change the tip percentage to 20%, then clicks Calculate:

In this section, you’ll build the Tip Calculator application using several JavaFX components and learn how to respond to user interactions with the GUI. You’ll begin by test-driving the application, using it to calculate 15% and 20% tips. Then, we’ll overview the technologies you’ll use to create the application. You’ll build the application’s GUI using the Scene Builder. Finally, we’ll present the complete Java code for the application and do a detailed code walkthrough.

15.5.1 Test-Driving the Tip Calculator

Let’s compile and run the application, which is located in the TipCalculator folder with this chapter’s examples. Class TipCalculator is the main application class.

Compiling the Tip Calculator Application

As we mentioned, JavaFX uses the Java Platform Module System (JPMS; Chapter 21) to organize its capabilities. To compile and run the Tip Calculator application, you must include two javac command-line JPMS options:

  • The --module-path option specifies where the JavaFX modules are located on your system—the PATH_TO_FX environment variable you created in this book’s Before You Begin section specifies the JavaFX modules’ location.

  • The --add-modules option specifies the JavaFX modules containing the capabilities required by the application. In this case, the javafx.controls module contains the JavaFX API features that define controls, such as Labels, TextFields, Buttons and Sliders, and the javafx.fxml module provides the capabilities we’ll use in the app to construct the GUI from the FXML file.

To compile the application, enter the following command in its entirety before pressing Enter:

Click here to view code image

javac --module-path pathToFX
   --add-modules javafx.controls,javafx.fxml *.java

replacing pathToFX with

  • $PATH_TO_FX if you are using macOS,

  • $env:PATH_TO_FX if you are using a PowerShell window on Microsoft Windows or

  • %PATH_TO_FX% if you are using a Command Prompt window on Microsoft Windows.

Running the Tip Calculator Application

To run the application, enter the following command in its entirety before pressing Enter:

Click here to view code image

java --module-path pathToFX
   --add-modules javafx.controls,javafx.fxml TipCalculator

The same --module-path and --add-modules options are required for both the javac and java commands.

Entering a Bill Total

Use your keyboard to enter the bill amount 34.56 into the Amount TextField, then click the Calculate Button. The Tip and Total TextFields contain the tip amount and the total bill for a 15% tip, as in:

Selecting a Custom Tip Percentage

Next, use the Slider to specify a custom tip percentage. Drag the Slider’s thumb until the percentage reads 20%. As you drag the thumb, the tip percentage in the Label to the Slider’s left updates continuously. By default, a Slider allows you to select floating-point values from 0.0 to 100.0, but this application restricts the Slider to whole numbers from 0 to 30. Click the Calculate Button to display the updated tip and total:

15.5.2 Technologies Overview

This section introduces the technologies you’ll use to build the Tip Calculator application.

Class Application

The class that launches a JavaFX application (which we’ll present in Section 15.5.4) is a subclass of Application (package javafx.application). When you execute the subclass:

  1. Method main calls class Application’s static launch method to begin executing the application.

  2. The launch method, in turn, causes the JavaFX runtime to create an object of the Application subclass and call its start method.

  3. The Application subclass’s start method creates the GUI, attaches it to a Scene and places it on the Stage that start receives as an argument.

Arranging JavaFX Components with a GridPane

Recall that layout containers arrange JavaFX components in a Scene. A GridPane (package javafx.scene.layout) arranges JavaFX components in a rectangular grid of rows and columns. This application uses a GridPane to arrange views into five rows and two columns:

Each cell in a GridPane can be empty or hold one or more JavaFX components, including layout containers that arrange other controls. Each component in a GridPane can span multiple rows or columns, though we did not use that capability in this GUI. When you drag a GridPane onto Scene Builder’s content panel, Scene Builder creates the GridPane with two columns and three rows by default. You can add and remove columns and rows as necessary. We’ll discuss other GridPane features as we present the GUI-building steps. To learn more about class GridPane, visit:

Click here to view code image

https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/layout/
   GridPane.html
Creating and Customizing the GUI with Scene Builder

In Section 15.5.3, you’ll create Labels, TextFields, a Slider and a Button:

  • A TextField (package javafx.scene.control) can accept text input from the user or display text. You’ll use one editable TextField to input the bill amount from the user and two uneditable TextFields to display the tip and total amounts.

  • A Slider (package javafx.scene.control) represents a value in the range 0.0–100.0 by default and allows the user to select a number in that range by moving the Slider’s thumb. You’ll customize the Slider so the user can choose a custom tip percentage only from the more limited integer range 0–30.

  • A Button (package javafx.scene.control) allows the user to initiate an action—in this application, clicking the Calculate Button calculates and displays the tip and total amounts.

Formatting Numbers as Locale-Specific Currency and Percentage Strings

You’ll use class NumberFormat (package java.text) to create locale-specific currency and percentage strings—an important part of internationalization.

Event Handling

A user interacts with an application’s GUI to indicate the tasks the application should perform. For example, when you write an e-mail, clicking the e-mail application’s Send button tells the application to send the e-mail to the specified recipient(s).

GUIs are event-driven. When the user interacts with a GUI component, the interaction—known as an event—drives the program to perform an action. Some common user interactions that cause an application to perform a task include

  • clicking a button,

  • entering text in a text field,

  • selecting an item from a menu,

  • minimizing, maximizing or closing a window,

  • pressing a mouse button and

  • moving the mouse.

The code that performs a task in response to an event is called an event handler, and the process of responding to events is known as event handling. Before an application can respond to an event for a particular control, you must:

  1. Define an event handler that implements an appropriate interface—known as an event-listener interface.

  2. Indicate that an object of that class should be notified when the event occurs— known as registering the event handler.

In this application, you’ll respond to two events—when the user moves the Slider’s thumb, the application will update the Label that displays the current tip percentage, and when the user clicks the Calculate Button, the application will calculate and display the tip and total bill amount.

We’ll demonstrate that for certain events—such as when the user clicks a Button—you can link a control to its event-handling method (that is, register the event handler) by using the Code section of Scene Builder’s Inspector window. In this case, JavaFX implements the event-listener interface for you and it calls the method you specify. For events that occur when the value of a control’s property changes, such as when the user moves a Slider’s thumb to change the Slider’s value, you must create the event handler entirely in code, as we’ll demonstrate.

Implementing Interface ChangeListener for Handling Slider Thumb Position Changes

You’ll implement interface ChangeListener (package javafx.beans.value) to respond when the user moves the Slider’s thumb. In particular, you’ll use the interface’s changed method to display the updated tip percentage as the user moves the Slider’s thumb. ChangeListener is a functional interface, so we’ll use a lambda to implement it.

Model-View-Controller (MVC) Architecture

JavaFX programs in which the GUI is implemented as FXML adhere to the Model-View-Controller (MVC) design pattern, which separates an application’s data (contained in the model) from the application’s GUI (the view) and the application’s processing logic (the controller).

The controller implements logic for processing user inputs. The model contains the program’s data, and the view presents the data stored in the model. When a user provides some input, the controller modifies the model with the given input. In the Tip Calculator, the model is the bill amount, the tip and the total. When the model changes, the controller updates the view to present the changed data.

In a JavaFX FXML application, a controller class defines instance variables for interacting with controls programmatically, as well as event-handling methods that respond to the user’s interactions. The controller class may also declare additional instance variables, static variables and methods that support the application’s operation. In a simple application like the Tip Calculator, the model and controller are often combined into a single class, as we’ll do in this example.

FXMLLoader Class

When a JavaFX FXML application begins executing, class FXMLLoader’s static method load reads the contents of the GUI’s FXML file into memory. Then, load performs the following actions:

  • Creates the scene graph containing the GUI’s layouts and controls and returns a Parent (package javafx.scene) reference to the scene graph’s root node.

  • Creates an instance of the controller class and initializes the controller’s instance variables for the components that will be manipulated programmatically.

  • Creates and registers the event handlers for any events specified in the FXML.

We’ll discuss these steps in more detail in Sections 15.5.4 and 15.5.5.

15.5.3 Building the Application’s GUI

In this section, we’ll present the precise steps for creating the Tip Calculator’s GUI.

fx:id Property Values for This Application’s Controls

If the controller class will manipulate a control or layout programmatically (as we’ll do with one Label, all the TextFields and the Slider), you must provide a name for that control or layout. In Section 15.5.4, you’ll declare Java variables for each such component in the FXML, and we’ll discuss how those variables are initialized for you. Each object’s name is specified via its fx:id property. You can set this property’s value by selecting a component in your scene, then expanding the Inspector window’s Code section—the fx:id property appears at the top of that section. The following diagram contains the fx:id properties of the Tip Calculator’s programmatically manipulated controls. Our naming convention is to use the control’s class name in the fx:id property. So, the fx:ids amountTextField, tipTextField and totalTextField each include the control’s class name—TextField:

Creating the TipCalculator.fxml File

As you did in Section 15.4.1, open Scene Builder to create a new empty FXML file. Then, select File > Save to display the Save As dialog:

  • specify the location in which to store the file (the same folder where you’ll store the application’s Java source code),

  • name the file TipCalculator.fxml and

  • click the Save button.

Step 1: Adding a GridPane

Drag a GridPane from the Library window’s Containers section onto Scene Builder’s content panel. By default, the GridPane contains two columns and three rows:

Step 2: Adding Rows to the GridPane

Recall that the application’s final GUI has two columns and five rows. Here, you’ll add two more rows. To add a row above or below an existing row:

  1. Right-click any row’s row number tab and select either Grid Pane > Add Row Above or Grid Pane > Add Row Below.

  2. Repeat this process to add another row.

After adding two rows, the GridPane should appear as follows:

You can use similar steps to add columns. You can delete a row or column by right-clicking the tab containing its row or column number and selecting Delete.

Step 3: Adding the Controls to the GridPane

You’ll now add the controls to the GridPane. When you drag a control onto the GridPane:

  • If the control has an fx:id in the following diagram, use the corresponding variable name to set the control’s fx:id property in the Inspector window’s Code section.

  • If the control displays text in the following diagram, use the corresponding text to set the control’s Text property in the Inspector window’s Properties section.

Perform the following steps to build the GUI:

  1. Adding the Labels. Drag Labels from the Library window’s Controls section into the first four rows of column 0 (the GridPane’s left column). As you add each, set its text.

  2. Adding the TextFields. Drag TextFields from the Library window’s Controls section into rows 0, 2 and 3 of column 1 (the GridPane’s right column).

  3. Adding a Slider. Drag a horizontal Slider from the Library window’s Controls section into row 1 of column 1.

  4. Adding a Button. Drag a Button from the Library window’s Controls section into row 4 of column 1. Change the Button’s text to Calculate. You can set the Button’s text by double-clicking it or by selecting the Button then setting its Text property in the Inspector window’s Properties section.

The GridPane should appear as follows:

Step 4: Sizing the GridPane to Fit Its Contents

When you begin designing a GUI by adding a layout, Scene Builder automatically sets the layout object’s Pref Width property to 600 and Pref Height property to 400, which is much larger than this GUI’s final width and height. For this application, we’d like the layout’s size to be computed based on the layout’s contents. To make this change:

  1. First, select the GridPane by clicking inside the GridPane, but not on any of the controls you’ve placed into its columns and rows. Sometimes, it’s easier to select the GridPane node in the Scene Builder Document window’s Hierarchy section in Scene Builder’s left column.

  2. In the Inspector’s Layout section, reset the Pref Width and Pref Height property values to their defaults (as you did in Section 15.4.6). This sets both properties’ values to USE_COMPUTED_SIZE, so the layout calculates its own size.

The layout now appears as follows:

Step 5: Right-Aligning GridPane Column 0’s Contents

A GridPane column’s contents are left-aligned by default. To right-align the contents of column 0, select it by clicking the tab at the top or bottom of the column, then in the Inspector’s Layout section, set the Halignment (horizontal alignment) property to RIGHT.

Step 6: Sizing the GridPane Columns to Fit Their Contents

By default, Scene Builder sets each GridPane column’s width to 100 pixels and each row’s height to 30 pixels to ensure that you can easily drag controls into the GridPane’s cells. In this application, we sized each column to fit its contents. To do so, select the column 0 by clicking the tab at the top or bottom of the column, then in the Inspector’s Layout section, reset the Pref Width property to its default size (that is, USE_COMPUTED_SIZE) to indicate that the column’s width should be based on its widest child—the Amount Label in this case. Repeat this process for column 1. The GridPane should appear as follows:

Step 7: Sizing the Button

By default, Scene Builder sets a Button’s width based on its text. For this application, we chose to make the Button the same width as the other controls in the GridPane’s right column. To do so, select the Button, then in the Inspector’s Layout section, set the Max Width property to MAX_VALUE. This causes the Button’s width to grow to fill the column’s width.

Previewing the GUI

Preview the GUI by selecting Preview > Show Preview in Window:

Notice that there’s no space between the Labels in the left column and the controls in the right column, nor is there space around the GridPane. By default, the Stage is sized to fit the Scene’s contents, so many of the controls touch the window’s borders. You’ll fix these issues in the next step.

Step 8: Configuring the GridPane’s Padding and Horizontal Gap Between Its Columns

The space between a node’s contents and its top, right, bottom and left edges is known as padding, which separates the contents from the node’s edges. Since the GridPane’s size determines the Stage’s window size, the GridPane’s padding separates its children from the window’s edges. To set the GridPane’s padding, select it, then in the Inspector’s Layout section, set the Padding property’s four values (which represent the TOP, RIGHT, BOTTOM and LEFT) to 14—a commonly used distance between a control’s edge and the Scene’s edge.

You can specify the default amount of space between a GridPane’s columns and rows with its Hgap (horizontal gap) and Vgap (vertical gap) properties, respectively. Because Scene Builder sets each GridPane row’s height to 30 pixels—which is greater than the heights of this application’s controls—there’s already some vertical space between the components. To specify the horizontal gap between the columns, select the GridPane in the Document window’s Hierarchy section, then in the Inspector’s Layout section, set the Hgap property to 8—a commonly used distance between controls. If you’d like to precisely control the vertical space between components, you can reset each row’s Pref Height to its default value, then set the GridPane’s Vgap property.

Step 9: Making the tipTextField and totalTextField Uneditable and Not Focusable

The tipTextField and totalTextField are used in this application only to display results, not receive text input. For this reason, they should not be interactive. You can enter text in a TextField only if it’s “in focus”—that is, it’s the control the user is interacting with. When you click an interactive control, it receives the focus. Similarly, when you press the Tab key, the focus transfers from the current focusable control to the next one— by default, this is the order in which the controls were added to the GUI. Interactive controls—such as TextFields, Sliders and Buttons—are focusable by default. Non-interactive controls—like Labels—are not focusable.

In this application, the tipTextField and totalTextField are neither editable nor focusable. To make these changes, select both TextFields, then in the Inspector’s Properties section uncheck the Editable and Focus Traversable properties. To select multiple controls at once, you can click the first (in the Document window’s Hierarchy section or in the content panel), then hold the Shift key and click each of the others.

Step 10: Setting the Slider’s Properties

To complete the GUI, you’ll now configure the Tip Calculator’s Slider. By default, a Slider’s range is 0.0 to 100.0, and its initial value is 0.0. This application allows only integer tip percentages in the range 0 to 30 with a default of 15. To make these changes, select the Slider, then in the Inspector’s Properties section, set the Slider’s Max property to 30 and the Value property to 15. We also set the Block Increment property to 5—this is the amount by which the Value property increases or decreases when the user clicks between an end of the Slider and the Slider’s thumb. Save the FXML file by selecting File > Save.

Though we set the Max, Value and Block Increment properties to integer values, the Slider still produces floating-point values as the user moves its thumb. In the application’s Java code, we’ll restrict the Slider’s values to integers when we respond to its events.

Previewing the Final Layout

You’ve now completed the Tip Calculator’s design. Select Preview > Show Preview in Window to view the final GUI:

When we discuss the TipCalculatorController class in Section 15.5.5, we’ll show how to specify the Calculate Button’s event handler in the FXML file.

Specifying the Controller Class’s Name

As we mentioned in Section 15.5.2, in a JavaFX FXML application, the application’s controller class typically defines instance variables for interacting with controls programmatically, as well as event-handling methods. To ensure that an object of the controller class is created when the application loads the FXML file at runtime, you must specify the controller class’s name in the FXML file:

  1. Expand the Scene Builder Document window’s Controller section—this is located below the Hierarchy section in the bottom-left corner of Scene Builder.

  2. In the Controller Class field, type TipCalculatorController—by convention, the controller class’s name starts with the same name as the FXML file (in this case, TipCalculator) and ends with Controller.

Specifying the Calculate Button’s Event-Handler Method Name

You can specify in the FXML file the names of the methods that handle the controls’ events. When you select a control, the Inspector window’s Code section shows all the events for which you can specify event handlers. When the user clicks a Button, the method in the On Action field is called. This method is defined in the controller class you specify in Scene Builder’s Controller window. Enter calculateButtonPressed in the Button’s On Action field.

Generating a Sample Controller Class

You can have Scene Builder generate the initial controller class containing the variables you’ll use to interact with controls programmatically and the empty Calculate Button event handler. Scene Builder calls this the “controller skeleton.” Select View > Show Sample Controller Skeleton to generate the skeleton:

Notice that the sample class has the class name you specified, a variable for each control that has an fx:id and an empty Calculate Button event handler. We’ll discuss the @FXML annotation in Section 15.5.5. To use this skeleton to create your controller class, click the Copy button, then paste the contents into a file named TipCalculatorController.java in the same folder as the TipCalculator.fxml file you created in this section.

15.5.4 TipCalculator Class

A simple JavaFX FXML-based application has two Java source-code files. For the Tip Calculator application, these are:

  • TipCalculator.java—This file contains the TipCalculator class (discussed in this section), which declares the main method that loads the FXML file to create the GUI and attaches the GUI to a Scene displayed on the application’s Stage.

  • TipCalculatorController.java—This file contains the controller class (discussed in Section 15.5.5), where you’ll specify the Slider and Button controls’ event handlers.

Figure 15.1 presents class TipCalculator. As we discussed in Section 15.5.2, the starting point for a JavaFX application is an Application subclass, so class TipCalculator extends Application (line 9). The main method calls class Application’s static launch method (line 23) to initialize the JavaFX runtime and to begin executing the application. This method causes the JavaFX runtime to create an object of the TipCalculator class and calls its start method (lines 10–19), passing the Stage object representing the window in which the application will be displayed. The JavaFX runtime creates the window.

Overridden Application Method start

Method start (lines 10–19) creates the GUI, attaches it to a Scene and places it on the Stage that method start receives as an argument. Lines 12–13 use class FXMLLoader’s static method load to create the GUI’s scene graph. This method:

  • Returns a Parent (package javafx.scene) reference to the scene graph’s root node—this is a reference to the GUI’s GridPane in this application.

  • Creates an object of the TipCalculatorController class that we specified in the FXML file.

  • Initializes the controller’s instance variables for the components that are manipulated programmatically.

  • Registers the event handlers specified in the FXML with the appropriate controls, enabling them to call their event handlers in response to user interactions.

We discuss the initialization of the controller’s instance variables and the registration of the event handlers in Section 15.5.5.

Creating the Scene

To display the GUI, you must attach it to a Scene, then attach the Scene to the Stage that method start receives as an argument. To attach the GUI to a Scene, line 15 creates a Scene, passing root (the scene graph’s root node) as an argument to the constructor. By default, the Scene’s size is determined by the size of the scene graph’s root node. Overloaded versions of the Scene constructor allow you to specify the Scene’s size and fill (a color, gradient or image), which appears in the Scene’s background. Line 16 uses Stage method setTitle to specify the text that appears in the Stage window’s title bar. Line 17 calls Stage method setScene to place the Scene onto the Stage. Finally, line 18 calls Stage method show to display the Stage window.

15.5.5 TipCalculatorController Class; Implementing an Event Handler with a Lambda

Figure 15.2 presents the TipCalculatorController class that responds to user interactions with the application’s Button and Slider. We split the class into pieces for discussion purposes. Lines 3–10 show the class’s import statements:

The classes and interfaces used by class TipCalculatorController include:

  • Class BigDecimal (line 3; introduced in Section 4.11) is used to perform precise monetary calculations. The RoundingMode enum of package java.math (line 4) is used to specify how BigDecimal values are rounded during calculations or when formatting floating-point numbers as Strings.

  • Class NumberFormat of package java.text (line 5) provides numeric formatting capabilities, such as locale-specific currency and percentage formats. For example, in the U.S. locale, the monetary value 34.95 is formatted as $34.95 and the percentage 15 is formatted as 15%. Class NumberFormat determines the locale of the system on which your application runs then formats currency amounts and percentages accordingly.

  • A Button’s event handler receives an ActionEvent object (line 6; package javafx.event) indicating which Button the user clicked. Many JavaFX controls support ActionEvents.

  • The annotation FXML (line 7; package javafx.fxml) is used in a JavaFX controller class’s code (as @FXML) to mark instance variables that should refer to JavaFX components in the GUI’s FXML file and methods that can respond to the events of JavaFX components in the GUI’s FXML file.

  • Package javafx.scene.control (lines 8–10) contains many JavaFX control classes, including Label, Slider and TextField.

TipCalculatorController’s static Variables and Instance Variables

Lines 14–35 declare class TipCalculatorController’s static and instance variables. The NumberFormat objects (lines 14–17) are used to format currency values and percentages, respectively. NumberFormat method getCurrencyInstance returns a NumberFormat object that formats values as currency using the default locale for the system on which the application is running. Similarly, NumberFormat method getPercentInstance returns a NumberFormat object that formats values as percentages using the system’s default locale. The BigDecimal object tipPercentage (line 19) stores the current tip percentage and is used in the tip calculation when the user clicks the Calculate Button.

@FXML Annotation

Recall from Section 15.5.3 that each control that this application manipulates in its Java source code needs an fx:id. Lines 22–35 declare the controller class’s corresponding instance variables. The @FXML annotation that precedes each declaration (lines 22, 25, 28, 31 and 34) indicates that the variable name can be used in the FXML file that describes the application’s GUI. The variable names that you specify in the controller class must precisely match the fx:id values you specified when building the GUI; otherwise, the FXMLLoader will throw a LoadException. When the FXMLLoader loads TipCalculator.fxml to create the GUI, it also initializes each of the controller’s instance variables declared with @FXML to ensure that they refer to the corresponding GUI components.

TipCalculatorController’s calculateButtonPressed Event Handler

Lines 38–53 declare TipCalculatorController’s calculateButtonPressed method, which is called when the user clicks the Calculate Button. The @FXML annotation (line 38) preceding the method indicates that this method can be used to specify a control’s event handler in the FXML file that describes the application’s GUI. For a control that generates an ActionEvent (as many JavaFX controls do), the event-handling method must return void and receive one ActionEvent parameter (line 39).

Click here to view code image

37      // calculates and displays the tip and total amounts
38      @FXML
39      private void calculateButtonPressed(ActionEvent event) {
40         try {
41            BigDecimal amount = new BigDecimal(amountTextField.getText());
42            BigDecimal tip = amount.multiply(tipPercentage);
43            BigDecimal total = amount.add(tip);
44
45            tipTextField.setText(currency.format(tip));
46            totalTextField.setText(currency.format(total));
47         }
48         catch (NumberFormatException ex) {
49            amountTextField.setText("Enter amount");
50            amountTextField.selectAll();
51            amountTextField.requestFocus();
52         }
53      }
54
Registering the Calculate Button’s Event Handler

When the FXMLLoader loads TipCalculator.fxml to create the GUI, it creates and registers an event handler for the Calculate Button’s ActionEvent. The event handler for this event must implement interface EventHandler<ActionEvent> (package javafx.event)—EventHandler is a generic interface containing a handle method that returns void and receives an ActionEvent parameter. This method, in turn, calls calculateButtonPressed when the user clicks the Calculate Button. FXMLLoader performs similar tasks for every event listener you specify via the Scene Builder Inspector window’s Code section.

Calculating and Displaying the Tip and Total Amounts

Lines 41–46 calculate and display the tip and total. Line 41 calls the amountTextField’s getText method to get the bill amount entered by the user. This String is passed to Big-Decimal’s constructor, which throws a NumberFormatException if its argument is not a number. In that case, line 49 calls amountTextField’s setText method to display "Enter amount" in the TextField. Line 50 calls amountTextField’s selectAll method to select the TextField’s text. Line 51 calls amountTextField’s requestFocus method to give the TextField the focus. Now, the user can enter a new value in the amountTextField without having to first select the text. TextField inherits methods getText, setText and selectAll from class TextInputControl (package javafx.scene.control) and method requestFocus from class Node (package javafx.scene).

If line 41 does not throw an exception, line 42 calculates the tip by calling method multiply to multiply the amount by the tipPercentage, and line 43 calculates the total by adding the tip to the bill amount. Next, lines 45 and 46 use the currency object’s format method to create currency-formatted Strings representing the tip and total amounts, which we display in tipTextField and totalTextField, respectively.

TipCalculatorController’s initialize Method

Lines 56–69 declare TipCalculatorController’s private initialize method. When present and annotated with @FXML, JavaFX will call this method to configure the controller before the GUI is displayed. Line 59 calls the currency object’s setRoundingMode method to specify that currency values should be rounded using the RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN (as discussed in Section 4.11).

60
61         // listener for changes to tipPercentageSlider's value
62         tipPercentageSlider.valueProperty().addListener(
63            (ov, oldValue, newValue) -> {
64               tipPercentage =
65                  BigDecimal.valueOf(newValue.intValue() / 100.0);
66               tipPercentageLabel.setText(percent.format(tipPercentage));
67            }
68         );
69      }
70   }
Using a Lambda for Event Handling

Each JavaFX control has properties. Some—such as a Slider’s value—can generate events when they change. For such events, you must manually register as the event handler an object that implements the ChangeListener interface (package javafx.beans.value).

ChangeListener is a generic type that’s specialized with the property’s type. The call to valueProperty (line 62) returns a DoubleProperty (package javax.beans.property) that represents the Slider’s value. A DoubleProperty is an ObservableValue<Number> that can notify listeners when a value changes. Each class that implements interface ObservableValue provides method addListener (called in lines 62–68) to register an event-handler that implements interface ChangeListener. For a Slider’s value, addListener’s argument is an object that implements ChangeListener<Number> because the Slider’s value is a numeric value.

ChangeListener is a generic functional interface, so we can conveniently implement it using a lambda (lines 63–67; introduced in Section 14.3). ChangeListener’s abstract changed method receives three arguments:

  • an ObservableValue<T>,

  • the old value of type T, and

  • the new value of type T.

Since the Slider’s addListener method expects a ChangeListener<Number> object, the compiler infers that T is Number for the lambda’s three parameters:

  • ov—the ObservableValue<Number> that changed,

  • oldValue—a Number containing the Slider’s old value before the event occurred and

  • newValue—a Number containing the Slider’s new value.

When the user moves the Slider’s thumb, lines 64–65 store the new tip percentage and line 66 updates the tipPercentageLabel.

15.6 Features Covered in the Other JavaFX Chapters

JavaFX is a robust GUI, graphics and multimedia technology. In Chapters 16 and 17, you’ll:

  • Learn additional JavaFX layouts and controls.

  • Handle other event types (such as MouseEvents).

  • Apply transformations (such as moving, rotating, scaling and skewing) and effects (such as drop shadows, blurs, reflection and lighting) to a scene graph’s nodes.

  • Use CSS to specify the look-and-feel of controls.

  • Use JavaFX properties and data binding to enable automatic updating of controls as corresponding data changes.

  • Access files and folders on disk using FileChooser and DirectoryChooser dialogs.

  • Use JavaFX graphics capabilities.

  • Perform JavaFX animations.

  • Use JavaFX multimedia capabilities to play audio and video.

15.7 Wrap-Up

In this chapter, we introduced JavaFX for creating graphical user interfaces (GUIs). We briefly discussed JavaFX’s benefits over the older AWT and Swing GUI technologies. We explored a JavaFX application window’s structure, including its stage, scene and various controls. We explained key JavaFX concepts such as using Scene Builder to create the FXML that declaratively specifies a GUI’s layout and controls, the Model-View-Controller (MVC) design pattern, and how a controller class responds to the events generated by users interacting with GUI controls.

We used two examples to introduce key JavaFX concepts. In the simple Welcome application, we used drag-and-drop visual programming techniques in Scene Builder to design a GUI consisting of a VBox layout container, a Label and an ImageView without writing any Java code.

In the Tip Calculator application, we used Scene Builder to create a more elaborate GUI consisting of Labels, TextFields, a Slider and a Button arranged in a GridPane layout container with multiple rows and columns. We used class FXMLLoader to read the FXML created in Scene Builder, create the corresponding GUI, create an instance of the controller class and attach the GUI controls to the controller class’s @FXML annotated fields and methods.

The Tip Calculator’s controller class responded to user interactions with the application’s Button and Slider controls and updated the GUI accordingly. We showed that some event handlers (such as the Button’s On Action handler) can be specified directly in Scene Builder as part of the FXML, but event handlers for changes to a control’s property values (such as the Slider’s value) must be implemented directly in the controller’s code. We used a lambda to implement the event handler that responded to the Slider’s value changes. Throughout the examples, we emphasized JavaFX best practices, such as proper spacing and alignment of GUI elements.

In the next chapter, you’ll learn more details of laying out nodes in a scene graph with various JavaFX layout panels so you can build more intricate GUIs. We’ll demonstrate additional JavaFX controls and event types. We’ll use CSS to style GUIs. We’ll customize a control’s display. You’ll also learn more about JavaFX properties and how to use data binding to automatically update elements in a GUI with new data.

16.1 Introduction

This chapter continues our JavaFX presentation. In this chapter, you’ll:

  • Use additional layouts (TitledPane, BorderPane and Pane) and controls (RadioButton and ListView).

  • Handle mouse and RadioButton events.

  • Set up event handlers that respond to property changes on controls (such as the value of a Slider).

16.2 Laying Out Nodes in a Scene Graph

 

A layout determines the size and positioning of nodes in the scene graph.

Node Size

In general, a node’s size should not be defined explicitly. Doing so often creates a design that looks pleasing when it loads but deteriorates as the application is resized or the content updates. In addition to width and height, most JavaFX nodes have additional properties that specify a node’s range of acceptable sizes as it’s laid out within its parent node:

  • The minWidth and minHeight properties specify a node’s minimum size in pixels.

  • The maxWidth and maxHeight properties specify a node’s maximum size in pixels.

  • The prefWidth and prefHeight properties specify a node’s preferred size that should be used by the layout in most cases.

Node Position and Layout Panes

A node’s position should be defined relative to its parent node and the other nodes in its parent. JavaFX layout panes are container nodes that arrange their child nodes in a scene graph relative to one another based on their sizes and positions. Child nodes are controls, other layout panes, shapes and more.

Most JavaFX layout panes use relative positioning—if a layout-pane node is resized, it adjusts its children’s sizes and positions accordingly, based on their preferred, minimum and maximum sizes. The following table describes each of the JavaFX layouts, including those presented in Chapter 15—these are defined in the packages javafx.scene.layout and javafx.scene.controls. In this chapter, we’ll use Pane, BorderPane, GridPane and VBox from the javafx.scene.layout package:

16.3 Painter Application: RadioButtons, Mouse Events and Shapes

In this section, you’ll create the following simple Painter application that allows you to drag the mouse to draw—you can compile and run each of this chapter’s applications using javac and java commands similar to those you saw in Section 15.5.1:

First, we’ll overview the technologies you’ll use, then we’ll discuss creating the application’s project and building its GUI. Finally, we’ll present the source code for its Painter and PainterController classes.

16.3.1 Technologies Overview

This section introduces the JavaFX features you’ll use in the Painter application.

RadioButtons and ToggleGroups

RadioButtons function as mutually exclusive options. You add multiple RadioButtons to a ToggleGroup to ensure that only one RadioButton in a given group is selected at a time. You’ll use JavaFX Scene Builder to specify each RadioButton’s ToggleGroup in FXML; however, you can also create a ToggleGroup programmatically, then use a RadioButton’s setToggleGroup method to specify its ToggleGroup. In fact, some programmers create entire JavaFX GUI’s programmatically without using FXML.

BorderPane Layout Container

A BorderPane layout container arranges controls into one or more of the five regions shown in the following diagram:

The top and bottom areas have the same width as the BorderPane. The left, center and right areas fill the vertical space between the top and bottom. Each area may contain only one control or one layout container—any layout container, in turn, may contain other controls, layouts and nodes. All the areas in a BorderPane are optional:

  • If the top or bottom area is empty, the left, center and right areas expand vertically to fill that area.

  • If the left or right area is empty, the center expands horizontally to fill that area.

TitledPane Layout Container

A TitledPane layout container displays a title at its top and is a collapsible panel containing a layout for other nodes. You’ll use TitledPanes to organize the application’s RadioButtons and to help the user understand the purpose of each RadioButton group.

JavaFX Shapes

The javafx.scene.shape package contains various classes for 2D and 3D shape nodes that can be displayed in a scene graph. In this application, you’ll programmatically create Circle objects as the user drags the mouse, then attach them to the application’s drawing area to display them in the scene graph.

Pane Layout Container

The drawing area will be a Pane layout. Each Circle object will be placed at an x-y coordinate measured from the Pane’s upper-left corner.

Mouse Event Handling

When you drag the mouse, the application’s controller responds by displaying a Circle in the currently selected color and pen size at the current mouse position in the Pane. JavaFX nodes support various mouse events, which are summarized in the following table:

For this application, you’ll configure the Pane’s onMouseDragged event handler. JavaFX also supports other types of input events. For example, for touchscreen devices, there are touch-oriented events, and for keyboards, there are key events. For a complete list of JavaFX node events, see the Node class’s properties that begin with the word “on” at:

Click here to view code image

https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/Node.html
Setting a Control’s User Data

Each JavaFX control has a setUserData method that receives an Object. You can use this to store any object you’d like to associate with that control. With each drawing-color RadioButton, we store the specific Color that the RadioButton represents. With each pen size RadioButton, we store an enum constant for the corresponding pen size. We use these objects when handling the RadioButton events.

16.3.2 Creating the Painter.fxml File

Create a folder on your system for this example’s files, then open Scene Builder and save the new FXML file as Painter.fxml. If you already have an FXML file open, you can also choose File > New to create a new FXML file, then save it.

16.3.3 Building the GUI

In this section, we’ll discuss the Painter application’s GUI. Rather than providing the exact steps as we did in Chapter 15, we’ll provide general instructions for building the GUI and focus on specific details for new concepts. As you build the GUI, keep in mind that it’s often easier to manipulate layouts and controls via Scene Builder’s Hierarchy section than directly in the stage design area.

fx:id Property Values for This Application’s Controls

The following diagram shows the fx:id properties of the Painter application’s programmatically manipulated controls. As you build the GUI, you should set the corresponding fx:id properties in the FXML document, as we discussed in Chapter 15:

Step 1: Adding a BorderPane as the Root Layout Node

Drag a BorderPane from the Scene Builder Library window’s Containers section onto the content panel.

Step 2: Configuring the BorderPane

Set the BorderPane’s Pref Width and Pref Height properties to 640 and 480. Recall that the stage’s size is determined based on the size of the root node in the FXML document. For the BorderPane, set the Padding property’s four values to 8 to inset it from the stage’s edges.

Step 3: Adding the Pane and VBox

Drag a Pane into the center area and a VBox into the BorderPane’s left area. As you drag over the BorderPane, Scene Builder shows the layout’s five regions and highlights the one where the item you’re dragging will appear when you release the mouse. Set the Pane’s fx:id to drawingAreaPane.

For the VBox, set its Spacing property (in the Inspector’s Layout section) to 8 to add some vertical space between the controls that you’ll place in this container. Set its right Margin property to 8 to add some horizontal spacing between the VBox and the Pane. Also, set its Max Height property to MAX_VALUE. This will enable the VBox to be as wide as it needs to be to accommodate its child nodes and occupy the full column height.

Reset the Pane’s Pref Width and Pref Height to their default USE_COMPUTED_SIZE values, and set its Max Width and Max Height to MAX_VALUE so that it occupies the entire width and height of the BorderPane’s center area. In the Pane’s JavaFX CSS category of the Inspector window’s Properties section, click the field below Style (initially empty) and select

-fx-background-color

so you can specify the Pane’s background color. In the field to its right, specify white.

Step 4: Adding the TitledPanes to the VBox

From the Library window’s Containers section, drag two TitledPane (empty) objects onto the VBox. For the first TitledPane, set its Text property to Drawing Color. For the second, set its Text property to Pen Size.

Step 5: Customizing the TitledPanes

Each TitledPane in the completed GUI contains multiple RadioButtons. We’ll use a VBox in each TitledPane to help arrange those controls. Drag a VBox onto each TitledPane. Set each VBox’s Spacing property to 8 and Pref Width and Pref Height to USE_COMPUTED_SIZE so the VBoxes will be sized based on their contents.

Step 6: Adding the RadioButtons to the VBox

From the Library window’s Controls section, drag four RadioButtons onto the VBox for the Drawing Color TitledPane and three RadioButtons onto the VBox for the Pen Size Titled-Pane. Configure their Text properties and fx:ids as shown previously. Next, select the blackRadioButton and ensure its Selected property is checked, then do the same for the mediumRadioButton.

Step 7: Specifying the ToggleGroups for the RadioButtons

Select all four RadioButtons in the first TitledPane’s VBox. In the Inspector’s Properties section, set the Toggle Group property to colorToggleGroup. When the application loads the FXML file at execution time, the FXMLLoader will create a ToggleGroup object by that name and associate these four RadioButtons with it to ensure that only one is selected at a time. Repeat this step for the three RadioButtons in the second TitledPane’s VBox, but set the Toggle Group property to sizeToggleGroup.

Step 8: Changing the TitledPanes’ Preferred Width and Height

For each TitledPane, set its Pref Width and Pref Height to USE_COMPUTED_SIZE so the TitledPanes will be sized based on their contents.

Step 9: Adding the Buttons

Add two Buttons below the TitledPanes, then configure their Text properties and fx:ids as shown previously. Set each Button’s Max Width property to MAX_VALUE so that they fill the VBox’s width.

Step 10: Setting the VBox’s Width

We want the VBox to be only as wide as required for the controls in that column. Select the VBox in the Document window’s Hierarchy section. Set its Min Width and Pref Width properties to USE_COMPUTED_SIZE, then set the Max Width to USE_PREF_SIZE to indicate that the maximum width should be the preferred width. Also, reset the Max Height to its default USE_COMPUTED_SIZE value. The GUI should now appear as shown at the beginning of this section.

Step 11: Specifying the Controller Class’s Name

As we mentioned in Section 15.5.2, in a JavaFX FXML application, the application’s controller class typically defines instance variables for interacting with controls programmatically, as well as event-handling methods. To ensure that an object of the controller class is created when the application loads the FXML file at runtime, specify the controller class’s name in the FXML file:

  1. Expand Scene Builder’s Controller window (located below the Hierarchy window).

  2. In the Controller Class field, type PainterController.

Step 12: Specifying the Event-Handler Method Names

Next, specify in the Inspector window’s Code section the names of the methods that will be called to handle specific events:

  • For the drawingAreaPane, go to the Code section’s Mouse heading and specify drawingAreaMouseDragged as the On Mouse Dragged event handler. This method will draw a circle in the specified color and size for each mouse-dragged event.

  • For the four Drawing Color RadioButtons, specify colorRadioButtonSelected as each RadioButton’s On Action event handler. This method will set the current drawing color based on the user’s selection.

  • For the three Pen Size RadioButtons, specify sizeRadioButtonSelected as each RadioButton’s On Action event handler. This method will set the current pen size based on the user’s selection.

  • For the Undo Button, specify undoButtonPressed as the On Action event handler. This method will remove the last circle the user drew on the screen.

  • For the Clear Button, specify clearButtonPressed as the On Action event handler. This method will clear the entire drawing.

Step 13: Generating a Sample Controller Class

As you saw in Section 15.5, Scene Builder generates the initial controller-class skeleton when you select View > Show Sample Controller Skeleton. You can copy this code into a PainterController.java file and store the file in the same folder as Painter.fxml. We show the completed PainterController class in Section 16.3.5.

16.3.4 Painter Subclass of Application

Figure 16.1 shows the Painter subclass of Application that launches the application. This class performs the same tasks described for the Tip Calculator application in Section 15.5.4.

16.3.5 PainterController Class

Figure 16.2 shows the final version of the PainterController class, which we broke into parts for discussion purposes. Recall from Chapter 15 that the controller class defines instance variables for interacting with controls programmatically, as well as event-handling methods. The controller class may also declare additional instance variables, static variables and methods that support the application’s operation.

PenSize enum

Lines 15–25 define the nested enum type PenSize, which specifies three pen sizes—SMALL, MEDIUM and LARGE. Each contains a radius that will be used when creating a Circle object to display in response to a mouse-drag event. Java allows you to declare classes, records, interfaces and enums as nested types inside other classes. Most previously presented types were top-level, not nested in other types. The PenSize enum is declared as a private nested type because it’s used only by the PainterController.

drawingAreaMouseDragged Event Handler

Lines 57–62 define drawingAreaMouseDragged, which responds to drag events in the drawingAreaPane. Each mouse event handler receives a MouseEvent parameter (package javafx.scene.input). When the event occurs, this parameter contains information about the event, such as its location, whether any mouse buttons were pressed, which node the user interacted with and more. You specified drawingAreaMouseDragged in Scene Builder as the drawingAreaPane’s On Mouse Dragged event handler.

Click here to view code image

56      // handles drawingArea's onMouseDragged MouseEvent
57      @FXML
58      private void drawingAreaMouseDragged(MouseEvent e) {
59         var newCircle = new Circle(e.getX(), e.getY(),
60            radius.getRadius(), brushColor);
61         drawingAreaPane.getChildren().add(newCircle);
62      }
63

Lines 59–60 create a new Circle object using its constructor that receives its center’s x-y coordinates, its radius and its Color. Next, line 61 attaches the new Circle to the drawingAreaPane. A layout’s getChildren method returns an ObservableList<Node> collection containing its child nodes. An ObservableList has methods for adding and removing elements. Line 61 uses the ObservableList’s add method to add a new Node to the drawingAreaPane—all JavaFX shapes inherit indirectly from class Node in the javafx.scene package. You’ll learn more about ObservableList later in this chapter.

colorRadioButtonSelected Event Handler

Method colorRadioButtonSelected (lines 65–70) responds to the ActionEvents of the Drawing Color RadioButtons, which occur when a new color RadioButton is selected. You specified this method in Scene Builder as the On Action event handler for all four Drawing Color RadioButtons. Lines 68–69 set the current drawing Color. ColorToggleGroup’s getSelectedToggle method returns the selected Toggle. RadioButton is one of several controls (others are RadioButtonMenuItem and ToggleButton) that implement interface Toggle. The Toggle’s getUserData method returns the user data Object we associated with the selected RadioButton in method initialize—for ColorToggleGroup’s RadioButtons, the Object is always a Color, so we cast the Object to a Color and assign it to brushColor.

Lines 81–89 define undoButtonPressed, which responds to an ActionEvent from the undoButton by removing the last Circle displayed. You specified this method in Scene Builder as the undoButton’s On Action event handler. To undo the last Circle, we remove the last child from the drawingAreaPane’s collection of child nodes. First, line 83 gets the number of elements in that collection. Then, if that’s greater than 0, line 87 removes the node at the last index in the collection.

Click here to view code image

80      // handles Undo Button's ActionEvents
81      @FXML
82      private void undoButtonPressed(ActionEvent event) {
83         int count = drawingAreaPane.getChildren().size();
84
85         // if there are any shapes, remove the last one added
86         if (count > 0) {
87            drawingAreaPane.getChildren().remove(count - 1);
88         }
89      }
90
clearButtonPressed Event Handler

16.4 Color Chooser Application: Property Bindings and Property Listeners

This section demonstrates property bindings and property listeners by building a Color Chooser application. The following diagram shows the result of using the Red and Green Sliders to create an opaque orange color:

The following diagram shows the result of using the Red, Green and Alpha Sliders to create a semitransparent orange color—notice that the semitransparent orange mixes with the color of the circle behind the colored square:

16.4.1 Technologies Overview

Let’s introduce the technologies you’ll use to build the Color Chooser.

RGBA Colors

The application uses the RGBA color model to display a rectangle of color based on the values of four Sliders. RGBA represents every color by its red, green and blue color values, each ranging from 0 to 255—0 denotes no color and 255 full color. For example, a color with a red value of 0 would contain no red component. The alpha value (A) ranges from 0.0 to 1.0 and represents a color’s opacity—0.0 is transparent, and 1.0 is opaque. The two colors in the previous sample outputs have the same RGB values, but the color displayed in Part (b) is semitransparent. You’ll create an RGBA Color object then use it to fill a Rectangle with that Color.

Properties of a Class

JavaFX uses properties extensively. A property is an instance of a class that implements JavaFX’s Property interface (package javafx.beans.property) and is accessed via set and get methods. In general, the pair of methods that define a read/write property have the form:

Click here to view code image

public final void setPropertyName(Type propertyName)
public final Type getPropertyName()

Typically, such methods manipulate a corresponding private instance variable with the same name as the property, but this is not required. For example, in a Time class, methods setHour and getHour together represent an hour property—they’d typically manipulate a private hour instance variable. If the property represents a boolean value, its get method name would begin with “is” rather than “get”—for example, ArrayList method isEmpty. Methods that define properties should be declared final to prevent subclasses from overriding the methods, which could lead to unexpected results in client code.

Property Bindings

JavaFX properties are implemented in a manner that makes them observable—when a property’s value changes, other objects can respond accordingly. This is similar to event handling. One way to respond to a property change is via a property binding, which enables a property of one object to be updated when a property of another object changes. You’ll use property bindings to update a TextField with the corresponding Slider’s current value when the user moves that Slider’s thumb. Property bindings are not limited to JavaFX controls. Package javafx.beans.property contains many classes that you can use to define bindable properties in your own classes.

Property Listeners

Property listeners are similar to property bindings. A property listener is an event handler that’s invoked when a property’s value changes. In the event handler, you can respond to the property change in a manner appropriate for your application. In this application, when a Slider’s value changes, a property listener will store the value in a corresponding instance variable, create a new Color based on the values of all four Sliders and set that Color as the fill color of a Rectangle object that displays the current color. For more information on properties, property bindings and property listeners, visit:

Click here to view code image

https://deitel.com/JavaFXPropertyBindingTutorial

16.4.2 Building the GUI

In this section, we’ll discuss the Color Chooser application’s GUI. Rather than providing the exact steps as we did in Chapter 15, we’ll provide general instructions for building the GUI and focus on specific details for new concepts. As you build the GUI, recall that it’s often easier to manipulate layouts and controls via the Scene Builder Document window’s Hierarchy section than directly in the stage design area. Before proceeding, open Scene Builder and create an FXML file named ColorChooser.fxml.

fx:id Property Values for This Application’s Controls

The following diagram shows the fx:id properties for the Color Chooser application’s pro-grammatically manipulated controls. You should set these controls’ fx:id properties in the FXML document, as you learned in Chapter 15.

Step 1: Adding a GridPane

Drag a GridPane from the Library window’s Containers section onto Scene Builder’s content panel.

Step 2: Configuring the GridPane

This application’s GridPane requires four rows and four columns. Use the techniques you’ve learned previously to add two columns and one row to the GridPane. Set the Grid-Pane’s Hgap and Padding properties to 8 to inset the GridPane from the stage’s edges and provide space between its columns.

Step 3: Adding the Controls

Using the previous diagram as a guide, add the Labels, Sliders, TextFields, a Circle and a Rectangle to the GridPane—Circle and Rectangle are located in the Scene Builder Library’s Shapes section. When adding the Circle and Rectangle, place both in the rightmost column’s first row, adding the Circle before the Rectangle so it will be behind the rectangle in the layout. Set the text of the Labels and TextFields as shown and set all the appropriate fx:id properties as you add each control.

Step 4: Configuring the Sliders

For the red, green and blue Sliders, set the Max properties to 255 (the maximum amount of a given color in the RGBA color scheme). For the alpha Slider, set its Max property to 1.0 (the maximum opacity in the RGBA color scheme).

Step 5: Configuring the TextFields

Set all of the TextField’s Pref Width properties to 50.

Step 6: Configuring the Rectangle

Set the Rectangle’s Width and Height properties to 100, then set its Row Span property to Remaining so it spans all four rows in that column.

Step 7: Configuring the Circle

Set the Circle’s Radius property to 40, then set its Row Span property to Remainder so it spans all four rows in that column.

Step 8: Configuring the Rows

Set all four rows’ Pref Height properties to USE_COMPUTED_SIZE so the rows are only as tall as their content.

Step 9: Configuring the Columns

Set all four columns’ Pref Width properties to USE_COMPUTED_SIZE so the columns are only as wide as their content. For the leftmost column, set the Halignment property to RIGHT. For the rightmost column, set the Halignment property to CENTER.

Step 10: Configuring the GridPane

Set the GridPane’s Pref Width and Pref Height properties to USE_COMPUTED_SIZE so it sizes itself based on its contents. Your GUI is now complete.

Step 11: Specifying the Controller Class’s Name

To ensure that an object of the controller class is created when the application loads the FXML file at runtime, specify ColorChooserController as the controller class’s name in the FXML file.

Instance Variables

Lines 13–27 declare the controller’s instance variables. The variables red, green, blue and alpha store the redSlider, greenSlider, blueSlider and alphaSlider current values. We use these to update the colorRectangle’s fill color when the user adjusts a Slider.

18      @FXML private TextField greenTextField;

20      @FXML private TextField alphaTextField;

22
23      // instance variables for managing
24      private int red = 0;

26      private int blue = 0;

Method initialize

Lines 29–66 define method initialize to complete the controller’s initialization after the FXMLLoader creates the GUI. In this application, initialize configures the property bindings and property listeners.

Click here to view code image

29      @FXML
30      private void initialize() {
31         // bind TextField values to corresponding Slider values
32         redTextField.textProperty().bind(
33            redSlider.valueProperty().asString("%.0f"));
34         greenTextField.textProperty().bind(
35            greenSlider.valueProperty().asString("%.0f"));
36         blueTextField.textProperty().bind(
37            blueSlider.valueProperty().asString("%.0f"));
38         alphaTextField.textProperty().bind(
39            alphaSlider.valueProperty().asString("%.2f"));
40
41         // listeners that set Rectangle's fill based on Slider changes
42         redSlider.valueProperty().addListener(
43            (ov, oldValue, newValue) -> {
44               red = newValue.intValue();
45               colorRectangle.setFill(Color.rgb(red, green, blue, alpha));
46            }
47         );
48         greenSlider.valueProperty().addListener(
49            (ov, oldValue, newValue) -> {
50               green = newValue.intValue();
51               colorRectangle.setFill(Color.rgb(red, green, blue, alpha));
52            }
53         );
54         blueSlider.valueProperty().addListener(
55            (ov, oldValue, newValue) -> {
56               blue = newValue.intValue();
57               colorRectangle.setFill(Color.rgb(red, green, blue, alpha));
58            }
59         );
60         alphaSlider.valueProperty().addListener(
61            (ov, oldValue, newValue) -> {
62               alpha = newValue.doubleValue();
63               colorRectangle.setFill(Color.rgb(red, green, blue, alpha));
64            }
65         );
66      }
67   }
Property-to-Property Bindings

Lines 32–39 set up property bindings between each Slider’s value and the corresponding TextField’s text so Slider changes update the corresponding TextField. Consider lines 32–33, which bind the redSlider’s valueProperty to the redTextField’s textProperty:

Click here to view code image

redTextField.textProperty().bind(
   redSlider.valueProperty().asString("%.0f"));

A TextField’s textProperty method returns its text property as a StringProperty (package javafx.beans.property). StringProperty method bind receives an ObservableValue as an argument. When its ObservableValue changes, the bound property updates. In this case, the ObservableValue is returned by

Click here to view code image

redSlider.valueProperty().asString("%.0f")

The Slider’s valueProperty method returns its value property as a DoubleProperty, which is an observable double value. However, the TextField’s text property must be bound to an observable String. So, we call the DoubleProperty method asString to get a StringBinding object—an ObservableValue that provides a String representation of the DoubleProperty. This version of asString receives a format-control String specifying the DoubleProperty’s String format.

Once you bind a TextField’s textProperty to a property of another control, the user may not edit the TextField, even though we did not disable its editable property in Scene Builder. In an end-of-chapter genAI exercise, you’ll investigate bidirectional property bindings, which would allow the TextField to remain editable by the user.

Property Listeners

You can register a property listener if you need to perform an arbitrary task when a property’s value changes. Lines 42–65 register property listeners for the Sliders’ value properties. Consider lines 42–47, which register the ChangeListener that handles changes to the redSlider’s value. As in Section 15.5, we implement the ChangeListener interface with a lambda. Each ChangeListener stores the newValue parameter’s int value in the corresponding ColorChooserController instance variable, then calls the colorRectangle’s setFill method to change its color, using Color method rgb to create the new Color object.

16.5 Cover Viewer Application: Data-Driven GUIs with JavaFX Collections

Often, an application needs to edit and display data. JavaFX provides a comprehensive model for allowing GUIs to interact with data. In this section, you’ll build the Cover Viewer application (shown in the following diagram), which binds a list of Book objects to a ListView. When the user selects an item in the ListView, the corresponding Book’s cover image is displayed in an ImageView.

16.5.1 Technologies Overview

This application uses a ListView control to display a list of book titles. Though you can individually add items to a ListView, this application binds an ObservableList object to the ListView. If you change an ObservableList’s elements, its observer (the ListView) will automatically be notified. Package javafx.collections defines ObservableList (which, similar to an ArrayList, implements the List interface) and other observable collection interfaces. The package also contains class FXCollections, which provides static methods for creating and manipulating observable collections. You’ll use a property listener to display the correct image when the user selects an item from the ListView. For this control, the property that changes is the selected item.

Before building the application, copy the images folder (which contains the large and small subfolders) from this chapter’s examples folder into the folder where you’ll save this application’s FXML file and the CoverViewer.java and CoverViewerController.java source-code files. Though you’ll use only the large images in this example, you’ll copy this application’s folder to create Section 16.6’s example, which uses both sets of images.

16.5.2 Building the GUI

In this section, we’ll discuss the Cover Viewer application’s GUI. Use Scene Builder to create a new FXML file and save it as CoverViewer.fxml.

fx:id Property Values for This Application’s Controls

  • Pref Width—200

For the ImageView, set the Fit Width and Fit Height properties to 370 and 480. To size the BorderPane based on its contents, set its Pref Width and Pref Height to USE_COMPUTED_SIZE. Also, set its Padding property to 8 to inset the BorderPane from the stage.

Listening for ListView Selection Changes

To synchronize the displayed book cover with the currently selected book, we listen for changes to the ListView’s selected item. By default, a ListView supports single selection—one item at a time may be selected. ListViews also support multiple selection. The ListView’s MultipleSelectionModel (a subclass of SelectionModel from package javafx.scene.control) manages the selection type. This object contains observable properties and various methods for manipulating the corresponding ListView’s items.

To respond to selection changes, you register a listener for the MultipleSelection-Model’s selectedItem property (lines 42–48). ListView method getSelectionModel returns a MultipleSelectionModel object. In this example, MultipleSelectionModel’s selectedItemProperty method returns a ReadOnlyObjectProperty<Book>, and the corresponding ChangeListener receives as its oldValue and newValue parameters the previously selected and newly selected Book objects, respectively.

Lines 45–46 use newValue’s large image path to initialize a new Image (package javafx.scene.image)—this loads the image from that path. We then pass the new Image to the coverImageView’s setImage method to display the Image.

16.6 Cover Viewer Application: Customizing ListView Cells

In the preceding example, the ListView displayed a Book’s String representation (its title). In this example, you’ll create a custom ListView cell factory to create cells that display each book as its thumbnail image and title using a VBox, an ImageView and a Label, as shown at the left side of the following screen capture:

16.6.1 Technologies Overview

ListCell Generic Class for Custom ListView Cell Formats

You saw in Section 16.5 that ListView cells display ListView items’ String representations by default. To create a custom cell format, you first define a subclass of the ListCell generic class (package javafx.scene.control) that specifies how to create a ListView cell. As the ListView displays items, it gets ListCells from its cell factory. You’ll use ListView’s setCellFactory method to replace the default cell factory with one that returns objects of your ListCell subclass. You’ll override this class’s updateItem method to specify the cells’ custom layout and contents.

Programmatically Creating Layouts and Controls

So far, you’ve created GUIs visually using JavaFX Scene Builder. In this application, you’ll also create a portion of the GUI programmatically. In fact, everything we’ve shown you in Scene Builder can also be accomplished directly in Java code. For this application, you’ll create and configure a custom ListView cell format using a VBox layout containing an ImageView and a Label.

16.6.2 Copying the CoverViewer Application

This application’s FXML layout and classes Book and CoverViewer are identical to those in Section 16.5, and the CoverViewerController class has only one new statement. For this example, we’ll show a new class that implements the custom ListView cell factory and CoverViewerController’s new statement. Rather than creating a new application from scratch, copy the CoverViewer application from the previous example into a new folder named CoverViewerCustomListView.

16.6.3 ImageTextCell Custom ListView Cell Layout

Class ImageTextCell (Fig. 16.7) defines the custom ListView cell layout for this version of the Cover Viewer application. We broke the class into parts for discussion purposes. The ImageTextCell class extends ListCell<Book> because it defines a customized presentation of a Book in a ListView cell. For the best ListView performance, it’s considered best practice to define the custom presentation’s controls as instance variables in the ListCell subclass and configure them in the subclass’s constructor. This minimizes the amount of work required in each call to method updateItem.

Constructor

The constructor (lines 17–29) configures the instance variables we use to build the custom presentation. Line 18 indicates that the VBox’s children should be centered. Lines 20–22 configure the ImageView and attach it to the VBox’s collection of children. Line 20 indicates that the ImageView should preserve the image’s aspect ratio, and line 21 indicates that the ImageView should be 100 pixels tall. Line 22 attaches the ImageView to the VBox.

Click here to view code image

16      // constructor configures VBox, ImageView and Label
17      public ImageTextCell() {
18         vbox.setAlignment(Pos.CENTER); // center VBox contents horizontally
19
20         thumbImageView.setPreserveRatio(true);
21         thumbImageView.setFitHeight(100.0); // thumbnail 100 pixels tall
22         vbox.getChildren().add(thumbImageView); // attach to Vbox
23
24         label.setWrapText(true); // wrap if text too wide to fit in label
25         label.setTextAlignment(TextAlignment.CENTER); // center text
26         vbox.getChildren().add(label); // attach to VBox
27
28         setPrefWidth(USE_PREF_SIZE); // use preferred size for cell width
29      }
30

Lines 24–26 configure the Label and attach it to the VBox’s collection of children. Line 24 indicates that the Label should wrap its text if it’s too wide to fit in the Label’s width, and line 25 indicates that the text should be centered in the Label. Line 26 attaches the Label to the VBox. Finally, line 28 indicates that the cell should use its preferred width, which is determined from the width of its parent ListView.

Method updateItem

Method updateItem (lines 32–46) configures the Label’s text and the ImageView’s Image, then displays the custom presentation in the ListView. The ListView’s cell factory calls this method when a ListView cell is required—when the ListView is first displayed and when ListView cells are about to scroll onto the screen. The method receives the Book to display and a boolean indicating whether the cell about to be created is empty. You must call the superclass’s updateItem method (line 35) to ensure the custom cells display correctly.

Click here to view code image

31      // called to configure each custom ListView cell
32      @Override
33      protected void updateItem(Book item, boolean empty) {
34         // required to ensure that cell displays properly
35         super.updateItem(item, empty)
36
37         if (empty || item == null) {
38            setGraphic(null); // don't display anything
39         }
40         else {
41            // set ImageView's thumbnail image
42            thumbImageView.setImage(new Image(item.thumbImage()));
43            label.setText(item.title()); // configure Label's text
44            setGraphic(vbox); // attach custom layout to ListView cell
45         }
46      }
47   }

If the cell is empty or the item parameter is null, then there is no Book to display and line 38 calls the ImageTextCell’s inherited setGraphic method with null. This method receives the Node that should be displayed in the cell. Any JavaFX Node can be provided, giving you tremendous flexibility for customizing a cell’s appearance.

If there is a Book to display, lines 40–45 configure the ImageTextCell’s Label and ImageView. Line 42 creates the Book’s Image object and sets it to display in the ImageView. Line 43 sets the Label’s text to the Book’s title. Finally, line 44 uses method setGraphic to set the ImageTextCell’s VBox as the custom cell’s presentation.

16.6.4 CoverViewerController Class

Once you’ve defined the custom cell layout, updating the CoverViewerController to use it requires setting the ListView’s cell factory. Insert the following code as the last statement in the CoverViewerController’s initialize method:

Click here to view code image

// set custom ListView cell factory
booksListView.setCellFactory(
   listView -> new ImageTextCell();
);

The argument to ListView method setCellFactory is an implementation of the functional interface CallBack (package javafx.util). This generic interface provides a call method that receives one argument and returns a value. In this case, we implement interface Callback with a lambda. Though we don’t use it here, the compiler will infer that the lambda’s parameter is a ListView<Book>. The parameter represents the ListView in which the custom cells will appear. The compiler also infers that the lambda’s return type is a ListCell<Book> object—an ImageTextCell is a ListCell<Book>. The lambda returns a new ImageTextCell object. Each time the ListView requires a new cell, the lambda is invoked to get a new ImageTextCell. Then the ImageTextCell’s updateItem method is called to create the custom cell presentation.
