16.7 FileChooser and DirectoryChooser Dialogs

 

JavaFX’s FileChooser and DirectoryChooser classes (package javafx.stage) are predefined dialogs that applications can display so users can select local system files and directories. To demonstrate these, we’ll enhance the file-and-directory processing example from Section 11.3. Sample screen captures are shown in the code discussion.

Creating the JavaFX GUI

The GUI (FileChooserTest.fxml) consists of a 600-by-400 BorderPane with the fx:id borderPane:

The BorderPane’s top contains a ToolBar layout (from the Scene Builder Library’s Containers section), which arranges its controls horizontally (by default) or vertically. Typically, you place ToolBars at your GUI’s edges, such as in a BorderPane’s top, right, bottom or left areas.

The BorderPane’s center contains a TextArea control with the fx:id textArea. We set the control’s Text property to "Select file or directory" and enabled its Wrap Text property to ensure that long lines of text wrap to the next line. If there are more lines of text to display than vertical lines in the TextArea, the control will show a vertical scrollbar. When Wrap Text is not enabled, the TextArea also shows a horizontal scrollbar if the text is too wide to display.

By default, the ToolBar you drag onto your layout has one Button. You can drag other controls onto the ToolBar and, if necessary, remove the default Button. We added a second Button. For the first Button, we set:

  • the Text property to "Select File",

  • the fx:id property to selectFileButton and

  • the On Action event handler to selectFileButtonPressed.

For the second Button, we set:

  • the Text property to "Select Directory",

  • the fx:id property to selectDirectoryButton and

  • the On Action event handler to selectDirectoryButtonPressed.

Finally, we specified FileChooserTestController as the FXML’s controller.

Class That Launches the Application

Figure 16.8 shows the FileChooserTest subclass of Application, which operates the same as the previous examples’ Application subclasses. The figure also shows the application’s initial GUI.

Controller Class

Class FileChooserTestController (Fig. 16.9) responds to the Buttons’ events. We broke the class into parts for discussion purposes. Lines 18–21 declare the variables for the controls with fx:ids in the FXML file.

Method selectFileButtonPressed

When the user presses the Select File button, method selectFileButtonPressed (lines 24–44) creates, configures and displays a FileChooser (shown in the first screen capture below the code). Line 28 sets the text displayed in the FileChooser’s title bar. Line 31 specifies the initial directory that should be opened when the FileChooser is displayed. Method setInitialDirectory receives a File object representing the directory’s location—"." represents the current folder from which the application was launched.

Click here to view code image

23   // handles selectFileButton's event
24   @FXML
25   private void selectFileButtonPressed(ActionEvent e) {
26      // configure dialog allowing selection of a file
27      var fileChooser = new FileChooser();
28      fileChooser.setTitle("Select File");
29
30      // display files in folder from which the application was launched
31      fileChooser.setInitialDirectory(new File("."));
32
33      // display the FileChooser
34      File file = fileChooser.showOpenDialog(
35         borderPane.getScene().getWindow());
36
37      // process selected Path or display a message
38      if (file != null) {
39         analyzePath(file.toPath());
40      }
41      else {
42         textArea.setText("Select file or directory");
43      }
44   }
45

Lines 34–35 display the FileChooser by calling its showOpenDialog method to display a dialog with an Open button for opening a file. This method receives as its argument a reference to the application’s Window. A non-null argument makes the FileChooser a modal dialog that prevents the user from interacting with the rest of the application until the dialog is dismissed—when the user selects a file or clicks Cancel. To obtain the application’s Window, we use the borderPane’s getScene method to get a reference to its parent Scene, then use the Scene’s getWindow method to get a reference to the Window containing the Scene.

Method showOpenDialog returns a File representing the selected file’s location, or null if the user clicks the Cancel button. If the File is not null, line 39 calls analyzePath to display the selected file’s information—File method toPath returns a Path object representing the location. Otherwise, line 42 displays a message in the TextArea telling the user to select a file or directory. The screen captures following method selectFileButtonPressed show the FileChooser dialog with the FileChooserTest.java file selected and the file’s information displayed in the application after the user presses the dialog’s Open button. FileChooser also has a showSaveDialog method that displays a dialog with a Save button for saving a file.

Method selectDirectoryButtonPressed

When the user presses the Select Directory button, method selectDirectoryButton-Pressed (lines 47–67) creates, configures and displays a DirectoryChooser.

Click here to view code image

54         directoryChooser.setInitialDirectory(new File("."));
55
56         // display the DirectoryChooser
57         File file = directoryChooser.showDialog(
58            borderPane.getScene().getWindow());
59
60         // process selected Path or display a message
61         if (file != null) {
62            analyzePath(file.toPath());
63         }
64         else {

66         }
67      }

The method performs the same tasks as method selectFileButtonPressed. The key difference is line 57, which calls DirectoryChooser method showDialog to display the dialog—there are not separate open and save dialogs for selecting folders. Method show-Dialog returns a File object representing the location of the selected directory, or null if the user clicks Cancel. If the File is not null, line 62 calls analyzePath to display information about the selected directory. Otherwise, line 65 displays a message in the TextArea telling the user to select a file or directory. The screen captures following method select-FileButtonPressed show the FileChooser dialog with the FileChooserTest directory selected and the directory’s information displayed in the application after the user presses the Open button.

Method analyzePath

Both event handlers call method analyzePath (lines 70–110) to determine whether a Path is a file or directory, display information about it and, if it’s a directory, list its contents.

Click here to view code image

69      // display information about file or directory user specifies
70      public void analyzePath(Path path) {
71         try {
72            // if the file or directory exists, display its info
73            if (path != null && Files.exists(path)) {
74               // gather file (or directory) information
75               var builder = new StringBuilder();
76               builder.append(String.format("%s:%n", path.getFileName()));
77               builder.append(String.format("%s a directory%n",
78                  Files.isDirectory(path) ? "Is" : "Is not"));
79               builder.append(String.format("%s an absolute path%n",
80                  path.isAbsolute() ? "Is" : "Is not"));
81               builder.append(String.format("Last modified: %s%n",
82                  Files.getLastModifiedTime(path)));
83               builder.append(String.format("Size: %s%n", Files.size(path)));
84               builder.append(String.format("Path: %s%n", path));
85               builder.append(String.format("Absolute path: %s%n",
86                  path.toAbsolutePath()));
87
88               if (Files.isDirectory(path)) { // output directory listing
89                  builder.append(String.format("%nDirectory contents:%n"));
90
91                  // object for iterating through a directory's contents
92                  DirectoryStream<Path> directoryStream =
93                     Files.newDirectoryStream(path);
94
95                  for (Path p : directoryStream) {
96                     builder.append(String.format("%s%n", p));
97                  }
98               }
99
100              // display file or directory info
101              textArea.setText(builder.toString());
102           }
103           else { // Path does not exist
104              textArea.setText("Path does not exist");
105           }
106        }
107        catch (IOException ioException) {
108           textArea.setText(ioException.toString());
109        }
110     }
111  }

16.8 Other JavaFX Capabilities and JavaFX Accessibility

 

This section overviews various additional JavaFX capabilities.

TableView and TreeTableView Controls

Section 16.5 demonstrated how to bind data to a ListView control. You often load such data from a database (Chapter 20, Accessing Databases with JDBC and SQLite). JavaFX’s TableView control (package javafx.scene.control) displays tabular data in rows and columns, and supports user interactions with that data. A TreeTableView control adds capabilities for hierarchical data with rows that can have child rows, such as a category and the items within that category.

Accessibility

JavaFX has accessibility features to help people with visual impairments use their devices. For example, the screen readers in various operating systems can speak screen text or text that you provide to help users with visual impairments understand the purpose of a control. Visually impaired users must enable their operating systems’ screen-reading capabilities. JavaFX controls also support:

  • GUI navigation via the keyboard—for example, the user can press the Tab key to jump from one control to the next. If a screen reader is enabled, as the user moves the focus from control to control, the screen reader will speak appropriate information about each control (discussed below).

  • A high-contrast mode to make controls more readable—as with screen readers, visually impaired users must enable this feature in their operating systems.

See your operating system’s documentation for information on enabling its screen reader and high-contrast mode.

Every JavaFX Node subclass also has the following accessibility-related properties:

  • accessibleTextProperty—A String that a screen reader speaks for a control. For example, a screen reader usually speaks the text displayed on a Button, but setting this property for a Button causes the screen reader to speak this property’s text instead. You can also set this property to provide accessibility text for controls that do not have text, such as ImageViews.

  • accessibleHelpProperty—A more detailed control description String than that provided by the accessibleTextProperty. This property’s text should help the user understand the purpose of the control in the context of your application.

  • accessibleRoleProperty—A value from the enum AccessibleRole (package javafx.scene). A screen reader uses this property value to determine the attributes and actions supported for a given control.

  • accessibleRoleDescriptionProperty—A String text description of a control that a screen reader typically speaks followed by the control’s contents (such as the text on a Button) or the value of the accessibleTextProperty.

In addition, you can add Labels to a GUI that describe other controls. In such cases, you should set each Label’s labelFor property to the specific control the Label describes. For example, a TextField in which the user can enter a phone number might be preceded by a Label containing the text "Phone Number". If the Label’s labelFor property references the TextField, then a screen reader will read the Label’s text as well when describing the TextField to the user.

Creating Custom JavaFX Controls

You can create custom controls by extending existing JavaFX control classes to customize them or by extending JavaFX’s Control class directly.

16.9 JavaFX Updates

 

This section overviews various JavaFX changes and enhancements.

Modularization

In Chapter 21, Java Platform Module System, we discuss Java’s module system in detail. JavaFX 9 and higher are modularized, enabling developers to bundle only the JavaFX modules their apps require. The key JavaFX modules are:

  • javafx.base—Contains the packages required by all JavaFX apps. All the other JavaFX modules depend on this one.

  • javafx.controls—Contains the packages for controls, layouts and charts, including the various controls shown in this chapter and Chapter 15.

  • javafx.fxml—Contains the packages for working with FXML, including the FXML features we demonstrated in this chapter and Chapter 15.

  • javafx.graphics—Contains the packages for working with graphics, animation, CSS (for styling nodes), text and more (Chapter 17, JavaFX Graphics and Multimedia).

  • javafx.media—Contains the packages for incorporating audio and video (Chapter 17, JavaFX Graphics and Multimedia).

  • javafx.swing—Contains the packages for integrating older Swing GUI components into JavaFX apps.

  • javafx.web—Contains the package for integrating web content.

Skinning APIs

Chapter 17 demonstrates formatting JavaFX Nodes using Cascading Style Sheets (CSS)— originally for styling web page elements. CSS specifies presentation (e.g., fonts, spacing, sizes, colors, positioning) separately from the GUI’s structure and content (layout containers, shapes, text, GUI components, etc.). If a JavaFX GUI’s presentation is determined entirely by a style sheet, you can swap in a new style sheet—sometimes called a skin—to change the GUI’s appearance. Each JavaFX control also has a skin class that determines its default appearance (located in package javafx.scene.control.skin). You can extend the appropriate skin class to customize the look-and-feel for a given type of control. You then create an object of your custom skin class and set it via a control’s setSkin method.

Subscription API

JavaFX 21 added the new Subscription API for adding and removing event listeners pro-grammatically. See https://deitel.com/javafp5 for a demonstration.

High-DPI Screen Support

JavaFX supports high DPI (dots-per-inch) screens on Windows, macOS and Linux, as well as capabilities to programmatically manipulate the scale at which JavaFX apps are rendered.

Updated GStreamer

JavaFX implements its audio and video multimedia capabilities using the open-source GStreamer framework (https://gstreamer.freedesktop.org). JavaFX 23 incorporates a more recent version of GStreamer with bug fixes and performance enhancements.

Updated WebKit

JavaFX’s WebView control enables you to embed web content in your JavaFX apps. It’s based on the open-source WebKit framework (https://www.webkit.org)—a web browser engine that supports loading and rendering web pages. JavaFX incorporates WebKit updates several times per year.

CSS Transitions

JavaFX 23 added support for CSS transitions, which allow smoother animations when CSS properties change. We’ll introduce CSS transitions in Section 17.7.

16.11 Wrap-Up

In this chapter, we continued our presentation of JavaFX. We discussed JavaFX layout panes in more detail and used BorderPane, TitledPane and Pane to arrange controls.

We discussed the many mouse events supported by JavaFX nodes and used the onMouseDragged event in a simple Painter application that displayed Circles as the user dragged the mouse across a Pane. We used ToggleGroups and RadioButtons to manage mutually exclusive options and set the user data Object for a control. When you selected a RadioButton, the Painter application obtained the selected RadioButton from the corresponding ToggleGroup, then accessed the RadioButton’s user data Object for convenient access to the Painter application’s selected color or pen size.

We discussed property binding and property listeners then used them to implement a Color Chooser application. You bound a TextField’s text to a Slider’s value to automatically update the TextField when the user moved the Slider’s thumb. You also used a property listener to allow the application’s controller to update a Rectangle’s color when a Slider’s value changed.

In the Cover Viewer application, we showed how to bind a JavaFX ObservableList collection to a ListView control to populate it with the collection’s elements. By default, each object in the collection was displayed as a String in the ListView. You configured a property listener to display an image in an ImageView when the user selected an item in the ListView. We then modified the Cover Viewer application to use a custom ListView cell factory that specified a custom layout for the ListView cells’ contents. We displayed FileChooser and DirectoryChooser dialogs so the user could select a file or directory.

Finally, we introduced several other JavaFX capabilities and recent changes, and discussed several JavaFX online resources. In the next chapter, we’ll demonstrate additional JavaFX features, including graphics, multimedia and customizing a GUI’s look-and-feel with JavaFX’s CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) capabilities.

17.1 Introduction

In this chapter, we continue our discussion of JavaFX from Chapters 15 and 16. Here, we present various JavaFX graphics and multimedia capabilities. You’ll:

  • Use Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) to customize the appearance of JavaFX nodes.

  • Customize fonts and font attributes used to display text.

  • Display two-dimensional shapes, including lines, rectangles, circles, ellipses, arcs, polylines, polygons and custom paths.

  • Apply transforms to Nodes, such as rotating a Node around a particular point, scaling, translating (moving) and more.

  • Display video and control its playback (e.g., play and pause).

  • Dynamically modify JavaFX Nodes with Transition and Timeline animations that change Node property values over time. As you’ll learn, built-in Transition animations change specific JavaFX Node properties (such as a Node’s stroke and fill colors), but Timeline animations can change any modifiable Node property.

  • Create frame-by-frame animations with an AnimationTimer.

  • Apply CSS transitions to a Node’s CSS properties.

  • Draw two-dimensional graphics on a Canvas Node.

  • Display three-dimensional shapes, including boxes, cylinders and spheres.

  • Get a brief introduction to FXGL for JavaFX game development.

This chapter does not include each example’s Application subclass because it performs the same tasks we discussed and demonstrated in Chapters 15 and 16. Some examples do not have controller classes because they display JavaFX controls or graphics only to demonstrate Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) capabilities.

17.2 Controlling Fonts with Cascading Style Sheets (CSS)

In Chapters 15–16, you built JavaFX GUIs using Scene Builder. You specified a particular JavaFX object’s appearance by selecting the object in Scene Builder then setting its property values in the Properties inspector. With this approach, if you want to change the GUI’s appearance, you must edit each object. This can be time-consuming and error-prone for more complex GUIs in which you want to make the same changes to multiple objects.

In this chapter, we format JavaFX objects using Cascading Style Sheets (CSS)—a technology typically used to style web page elements. A CSS style sheet specifies appearance details (fonts, spacing, sizes, colors, positioning, etc.) separately from the GUI’s structure and content (layout containers, shapes, text, GUI components, etc.) If a JavaFX GUI’s presentation is determined entirely by CSS rules, you update its appearance by swapping in a new style sheet.

In this section, you’ll use CSS to specify several Labels’ font properties and the VBox layout’s spacing and padding properties. You’ll place CSS rules that specify the font properties, spacing and padding in a separate file that ends with the .css filename extension, then reference that file from the FXML. You’ll observe that

  • before referencing the CSS file from the FXML, Scene Builder displays the GUI without styling and

  • after referencing the CSS file from the FXML, Scene Builder renders the GUI with the CSS rules applied to the appropriate objects.

For a complete reference containing

  • all the JavaFX CSS properties,

  • the JavaFX Node types to which the attributes can be applied, and

  • the allowed values for each attribute

visit:

Click here to view code image

https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-
   files/cssref.html

17.2.1 CSS That Styles the GUI

Figure 17.1 presents this app’s CSS rules specifying the VBox’s and Labels’ styles. We split the file into parts for discussion purposes. We use the shorthand “app” for “application” throughout this chapter.

.vbox CSS Rule—Style Class Selectors

Lines 4–7 define the .vbox CSS rule that will be applied to this app’s VBox object (lines 8–18 of Fig. 17.2).

Each CSS rule begins with a CSS selector which specifies the JavaFX objects that will be styled according to the rule. In this rule, .vbox is a style class selector. The CSS properties in this rule are applied to any JavaFX object that has a styleClass property with the value "vbox". In CSS, a style class selector begins with a dot (.) and is followed by its class name (not to be confused with a Java class). By convention, selector names typically have all lowercase letters, and multi-word names separate each word from the next with a dash (-).

Each CSS rule’s body is delimited by required braces ({}) containing the CSS properties applied to objects matching the CSS selector. JavaFX CSS property names begin with -fx- followed by the JavaFX object’s property name in all lowercase letters.1 So,

1. According to https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-files/cssref.html, JavaFX CSS properties are considered extensions to CSS, so JavaFX’s CSS property names begin with “-fx-” to ensure they have distinct names from their HTML CSS counterparts.

  • -fx-spacing (line 5) defines the value for a JavaFX object’s spacing property and

  • -fx-padding (line 6) defines the value for a JavaFX object’s padding property.

Each property value is specified to the right of a required colon (:). In this case, we set

  • -fx-spacing to 10 for 10 pixels of vertical space between objects in the VBox and

  • -fx-padding to 10 to separate the VBox’s contents from the VBox’s edges by 10 pixels at the top, right, bottom and left edges.

You also can specify the -fx-padding with four values separated by spaces. For example,

-fx-padding: 10 5 10 5

specifies 10 pixels for the top padding, 5 for the right, 10 for the bottom and 5 for the left. In Section 17.2.2, you’ll apply the .vbox CSS rule to the VBox object.

#label1 CSS Rule—ID Selectors

Lines 9–11 of Fig. 17.1 define the #label1 CSS rule that will be applied to the Label with the fx:id label1.

Click here to view code image

 9   #label1 {
10      -fx-font: bold 14pt Arial;
11   }
12

Selectors that begin with # are ID selectors—they’re applied to objects with the specified ID. In this case, the #label1 selector matches an object with the fx:id label1—that is, the Label object in line 12 of Fig. 17.2. The #label1 CSS rule

-fx-font: bold 14pt Arial;

sets an object’s font property so that a corresponding object displays its text in a bold, 14-point Arial font. The -fx-font property can specify all aspects of a font, including its style, weight, size and font family. The size and font family are required. There are also properties for each aspect of a font: -fx-font-style, -fx-font-weight, -fx-font-size and -fx-font-family. These are applied to a JavaFX object’s similarly named properties. For more information on CSS font attributes, visit

Click here to view code image

https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-
   files/cssref.html#typefont

For a complete list of CSS selector types and how you can combine them, visit

Click here to view code image

https://www.w3.org/TR/selectors-3/
#label2 CSS Rule

Lines 13–15 of Fig. 17.1 define the #label2 CSS rule that will be applied to the Label with the fx:id label2.

Click here to view code image

13   #label2 {
14      -fx-font: 16pt "Times New Roman";
15   }
16

The CSS property

Click here to view code image

-fx-font: 16pt "Times New Roman";

specifies only the required font size (16pt) and font family ("Times New Roman") components—font family names with multiple words must be enclosed in quotes ("").

#label3 CSS Rule

Lines 17–19 define the #label3 CSS rule that will be applied to the Label with the fx:id label3.

Click here to view code image

17   #label3 {
18      -fx-font: bold italic 16pt "Courier New";
19   }
20

The CSS property

Click here to view code image

-fx-font: bold italic 16pt "Courier New";

specifies all the font components—weight (bold), style (italic), size (16pt) and font family ("Courier New").

#label4 CSS Rule

Lines 21–24 define the #label4 CSS rule that will be applied to the Label with the fx:id label4.

21   #label4 {
22      -fx-font-size: 14pt;
23      -fx-underline: true;
24   }
25

The CSS property

-fx-font-size: 14pt;

specifies the font size 14pt—all other aspects of this Label’s font are inherited from the Label’s parent container. The CSS property

-fx-underline: true;

indicates that the text in the Label should be underlined—this property’s default value is false.

#label5 CSS Rule

Lines 26–28 define the #label5 CSS rule that will be applied to the Label with the fx:id label5 and set its font size to 14pt.

26   #label5 {
27      -fx-font-size: 14pt;
28   }
29
#label5 .text CSS Rule

Lines 30–32 define the #label5 .text CSS rule that will be applied to the Text object within the Label that has the fx:id value "label5".

Click here to view code image

30   #label5 .text {
31      -fx-strikethrough: true;
32   }

This selector combines an ID selector and a style class selector. Each Label contains a Text object with the CSS class .text. When applying this CSS rule, JavaFX first locates the object with the ID label5, then within that object, looks for a nested object that specifies the class text.

The CSS property

-fx-strikethrough: true;

indicates that the text in the Label should be displayed with a line through it—this property’s default value is false.

17.2.2 FXML That Defines the GUI—Introduction to XML Markup

Figure 17.2 presents FontCSS.fxml. The FontCSS app’s FXML GUI consists of a VBox layout element (lines 8–18) containing five Labels (lines 12–16). To create this in Scene Builder, drag five Labels onto the VBox. Configure their text as in Fig. 17.2(a) and set their fx:ids from top to bottom as label1, label2, label3, label4 and label5. All the Labels initially have the same appearance, and there’s no spacing between or around them.2

2. In many of this chapter’s examples, after creating a GUI in Scene Builder, we used a text editor to format the FXML, remove unnecessary properties that were inserted by Scene Builder and properties that we specified via CSS rules. The text editors in various popular IDEs also can be used to edit FXML. For this reason, when you build these examples from scratch, your FXML may differ from what’s presented in this chapter. You also can set a property to its default value in Scene Builder to remove it from the FXML.

XML Declaration

Each FXML document begins with an XML declaration (line 1), which must be the first line in the file and indicates that the document contains XML markup. For FXML documents, line 1 must appear as in Fig. 17.2. The XML declaration’s version attribute specifies the document’s XML syntax version (1.0). The encoding attribute specifies the document’s character format—XML documents typically contain Unicode characters in UTF-8 format.3 Scene Builder automatically inserts the XML declaration.

3. “UTF-8.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed September 26, 2024. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTF-8.

Attributes

Each XML attribute has the format

name="value"

The name and value are separated by =, and the value is placed in quotes (""). Multiple name=value pairs are separated by whitespace.

Comments

Lines 2–3 are XML comments. These are delimited by <!-- and --> and can be placed almost anywhere in an XML document. XML comments can span multiple lines. We added these XML comments to state the FXML document’s figure number, filename and purpose, as we typically do in our Java code.

FXML import Declarations

Lines 5–6 are FXML import declarations—delimited by <?import and ?>—specifying the fully qualified names of the JavaFX types used in the document. Scene Builder automatically inserts FXML import declarations based on the various JavaFX node types you add to the GUI.

Elements

XML documents contain elements specifying the document’s structure. Most elements are delimited by a start tag and an end tag:

  • A start tag consists of angle brackets (< and >) containing the element’s name followed by zero or more attributes. For example, the VBox element’s start tag (lines 8–10) has four attributes.

  • An end tag consists of the element name preceded by a forward slash (/) in angle brackets—for example, </VBox> in line 18.

An element’s start and end tags enclose the element’s contents. In this case, lines 11–17 declare other elements that describe the VBox’s contents. Every XML document must have exactly one root element containing the other elements. In Fig. 17.2, VBox is the root.

A layout element always contains a children element (lines 11–17) that, in turn, contains the child Nodes arranged by that layout. For a VBox, the children element’s child Nodes are listed in their display order from top to bottom. The elements in lines 12–16 represent the VBox’s five Labels. These are empty elements that use the shorthand start-tag-only notation:

<ElementName attributes />

in which the empty element’s start tag ends with /> rather than >. The empty element:

Click here to view code image

<Label fx:id="label1" text="Arial 14pt bold"/>

is equivalent to

Click here to view code image

<Label fx:id="label1" text="Arial 14pt bold">
</Label>

which does not have content between the start and end tags. Empty elements often have attributes (such as fx:id and text for each Label element).

XML Namespaces

In lines 9–10, the VBox attributes

Click here to view code image

xmlns="http://javafx.com/javafx/23"
xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1"

specify the XML namespaces used in FXML markup. An XML namespace specifies a collection of element and attribute names you can use in the document. The attribute

Click here to view code image

xmlns="http://javafx.com/javafx/23"

specifies the default namespace. FXML import declarations (like those in lines 5–6) add names to this namespace for use in the document. The attribute

Click here to view code image

xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1"

specifies JavaFX’s fx namespace. Elements and attributes from this namespace (such as the fx:id attribute) are used internally by the FXMLLoader class. For example, for each FXML element that specifies an fx:id, the FXMLLoader initializes a corresponding variable in the controller class. The fx: in fx:id is a namespace prefix that specifies the namespace (fx) that defines the attribute (id). Every element or attribute name in Fig. 17.2 that does not begin with fx: is part of the default namespace.

17.2.3 Referencing the CSS File from FXML

For the Labels to appear with the customized fonts, we must reference the FontCSS.css file from the FXML. This enables Scene Builder to apply the CSS rules to the GUI. To reference the CSS file:

  1. Select the VBox in the Scene Builder.

  2. In the Properties inspector, click the + button under the Stylesheets heading.

  3. In the dialog that appears, select the FontCSS.css file and click Open.

This adds the stylesheets attribute (line 8)

stylesheets="@FontCSS.css"

to the VBox’s opening tag (lines 8–10). The @ symbol—called the local resolution operator in FXML—indicates that FontCSS.css is located relative to the FXML file on disk. The CSS and FXML files must be in the same folder if no path information is specified.

17.2.4 Specifying the VBox’s Style Class

The preceding steps apply the font styles to the Labels based on their ID selectors but do not apply the spacing and padding to the VBox. For the VBox, we defined a CSS rule using a style class selector named .vbox. To apply this CSS rule to the VBox:

  1. Select the VBox in the Scene Builder.

  2. In the Properties inspector, under the Style Class heading, click the empty box and select vbox from the list of available selectors.

This adds the styleClass attribute

styleClass="vbox"

to the VBox’s opening tag (line 8). At this point, the GUI appears as in Fig. 17.2(b). You can now run the app to produce the output in Fig. 17.2(c).

17.2.5 Programmatically Loading CSS

In the FontCSS app, the FXML referenced the CSS style sheet directly (line 8). It’s also possible to load CSS files dynamically and add them to a Scene’s collection of style sheets. You might do this, for example, in an app that enables users to choose their preferred look-and-feel, such as a light background with dark text vs. a dark background with light text.

To load a stylesheet dynamically, add the following statement to the Application subclass’s start method:

Click here to view code image

scene.getStylesheets().add(
   FontCSS.class.getResource("FontCSS.css").toExternalForm());

In the preceding statement:

  • The notation FontCSS.class creates a Class object representing the FontCSS subclass of Application. This is equivalent to calling the method getClass(), which all classes inherit.

  • Class method getResource returns a URL representing the location of the file FontCSS.css. Method getResource looks for the file in the same location from which class FontCSS was loaded by the JVM.

  • URL method toExternalForm returns the URL’s String representation. This is passed to the add method of the Scene’s collection of style sheets to add the style sheet to the scene.

Method getStyleSheets returns an ObservableList object, which supports standard List methods, so you may also remove a stylesheet and clear all the stylesheets programmatically.

17.3 Displaying Two-Dimensional Shapes

JavaFX has two ways to draw shapes:

  • You can define Shape and Shape3D (package javafx.scene.shape) subclass objects, add them to a container in the JavaFX stage and manipulate them like other JavaFX Nodes.

  • You can add a Canvas object (package javafx.scene.canvas) to a container in the JavaFX stage, then draw on it using various GraphicsContext methods.

This section’s BasicShapes example displays Line, Rectangle, Circle, Ellipse and Arc Shapes. Like other Node types, you can drag these from the Scene Builder Library’s Shapes category onto the design area, then configure them via the Inspector’s Properties, Layout and Code sections. You can also create objects of any JavaFX Node type programmatically.

17.3.1 Defining Two-Dimensional Shapes with FXML

Figure 17.3 contains the completed FXML for the BasicShapes app, which references the BasicShapes.css file (line 13) that we present in Section 17.3.2. For this app, we used Scene Builder to drag two Lines, a Rectangle, a Circle, an Ellipse and an Arc onto a Pane layout, then configured their dimensions and positions.

Each property you can set in Scene Builder has a corresponding attribute in FXML. For example, the Pane object’s Pref Height property in Scene Builder corresponds to the prefHeight attribute (line 12) in FXML. When you build this GUI in Scene Builder, use the FXML attribute values in Fig. 17.3. As you drag each shape onto your design, Scene Builder automatically configures certain properties, such as the Fill and Stroke colors for the Rectangle, Circle, Ellipse and Arc. For each property that does not have a corresponding attribute in Fig. 17.3, you can remove the attribute by setting it to its default value in Scene Builder or by manually editing the FXML.

Lines 6–10 import the shape classes used in the FXML. We also specified fx:id values (lines 16 and 18) for the two Lines—we use these values in CSS rules with ID selectors to define separate styles for each Line. We removed the shapes’ fill, stroke and stroke-Type properties that Scene Builder autogenerated. The default fill for a shape is black. The default stroke is a one-pixel black line. The default strokeType is centered—based on the stroke’s thickness, half the thickness appears inside the shape’s bounds and half outside. You also may display a shape’s stroke entirely inside or outside the shape’s bounds. We specify the strokes and fills with the styles in Section 17.3.2.

Line Objects

Lines 16–17 and 18–19 define two Lines. Each connects two endpoints specified by the properties startX, startY, endX and endY. The x- and y-coordinates are measured from the top-left corner of the Pane, with x-coordinates increasing from left to right and y-coordinates increasing from top to bottom. If you specify a Line’s layoutX and layoutY properties, the startX, startY, endX and endY properties are measured from that point.

Rectangle Object

Lines 20–21 define a Rectangle object. A Rectangle is displayed based on its layoutX, layoutY, width and height properties:

  • A Rectangle’s upper-left corner is positioned at the coordinates specified by the layoutX and layoutY properties, which are inherited from class Node.

  • A Rectangle’s dimensions are specified by the width and height properties—in this case, they have the same value, so the Rectangle defines a square.

Circle Object

Lines 22–23 define a Circle object with its center at the point specified by the centerX and centerY properties. The radius property determines the Circle’s size (two times the radius) around its center point.

Ellipse Object

Lines 24–25 define an Ellipse object. Like a Circle, an Ellipse’s center is specified by the centerX and centerY properties. You also specify radiusX and radiusY properties that help determine the Ellipse’s width (left and right of the center point) and height (above and below the center point).

Arc Object

Lines 26–27 define an Arc object. Like an Ellipse, an Arc’s center is specified by the centerX and centerY properties, and the radiusX and radiusY properties determine the Arc’s width and height. For an Arc, you also specify:

  • length—The arc’s length in degrees (0–360). Positive values sweep counterclockwise.

  • startAngle—The angle in degrees at which the arc should begin.

  • type—How the arc should be closed. ROUND indicates that the starting and ending points of the arc should be connected to the center point by straight lines. You also may choose OPEN, which does not connect the start and end points, or CHORD, which connects the start and end points with a straight line.

17.3.2 CSS That Styles the Two-Dimensional Shapes

Figure 17.4 contains the CSS for the BasicShapes app. In this CSS file, we define two CSS rules with ID selectors (#line1 and #line2) to style the app’s two Line objects. The remaining rules use type selectors, which apply to all objects of a given type. You specify a type selector by using the JavaFX class name. We split the file into parts for discussion purposes.

Specifying Common Attributes for Various Objects

The CSS rule in lines 4–6 defines the -fx-stroke-width CSS property for all the shapes in the app—this property specifies the thickness of the Lines and the border thickness of all the other shapes:

We use CSS type selectors in a comma-separated list to apply this rule to multiple shapes. Line 4 indicates this should be applied to all objects of types Line, Rectangle, Circle, Ellipse and Arc.

Styling the First Line

The CSS rule in lines 8–10 sets the -fx-stroke to the solid color red for the Line with the fx:id "line1":

 8   #line1 {
 9       -fx-stroke: red;
10   }
11

This rule is in addition to the one at lines 4–6, which sets the stroke width for all the shapes in this app. When JavaFX renders an object, it combines all the CSS rules that apply to the object to determine its appearance. Colors may be specified as

  • named colors (such as "red", "green" and "blue"),

  • colors defined by their red, green, blue and alpha (transparency) components,

  • colors defined by their hue, saturation, brightness and alpha components,

and more. For details on all the ways to specify color in CSS, visit

Click here to view code image

https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-
   files/cssref.html#typecolor
Styling the Second Line

The CSS rule in lines 12–15 applies to the Line with the fx:id "line2".

Click here to view code image

12   #line2 {
13       -fx-stroke: rgba(0%, 50%, 0%, 0.5);
14       -fx-stroke-line-cap: round;
15   }
16

For this rule, we specified the -fx-stroke property’s color using the CSS function rgba, which defines a color based on its red, green, blue and alpha (transparency) components. We used the version of rgba that receives percentages from 0% to 100%, specifying the amount of red, green and blue in the color and a value from 0.0 (transparent) to 1.0 (opaque) for the alpha component. Line 13 produces a semitransparent green line. Notice the interaction between the two Lines’ colors at the intersection point in Fig. 17.3’s output windows. The -fx-stroke-line-cap CSS property (line 14) indicates that the ends of the Line should be rounded—the rounding effect is more noticeable with thicker strokes.

Styling the Rectangle

For Rectangles, Circles, Ellipses and Arcs, you can specify both the -fx-stroke for the shapes’ borders and the -fx-fill for the color or pattern that appears inside the shape. The rule in lines 17–22 uses a CSS type selector to indicate that all Rectangles should have red borders (line 18) and yellow fill (line 21).

17   Rectangle {
18      -fx-stroke: red;
19      -fx-arc-width: 50;
20      -fx-arc-height: 50;
21      -fx-fill: yellow;
22   }
23

Lines 19–20 define the Rectangle’s -fx-arc-width and -fx-arc-height properties. These specify the width and height of an ellipse that’s divided in half horizontally and vertically, then used to round the Rectangle’s corners. Because these properties have the same value (50) in this app, the four corners are each a quarter of a circle with a diameter of 50.

Styling the Circle

The CSS rule in lines 24–27 applies to all Circle objects.

Click here to view code image

24   Circle {
25      -fx-stroke: blue;
26      -fx-fill: radial-gradient(center 50% 50%, radius 60%, white, red);
27   }
28

Line 25 sets the Circle’s stroke to blue. Line 26 sets the Circle’s fill with a gradient—colors that transition gradually from one color to the next. You can transition between as many colors as you like and specify the points at which to change colors—such points are called color stops. You can use gradients for any property that specifies a color. In this case, we use the CSS function radial-gradient to create a gradient in which the color changes gradually from a center point outward. The fill

Click here to view code image

-fx-fill: radial-gradient(center 50% 50%, radius 60%, white, red);

indicates the gradient should begin from a center point at 50% 50%—the shape’s horizontal and vertical middle. The radius specifies the distance from the center at which an even mixture of the two colors appears. This radial gradient begins with white in the center and ends with red at the outer edge of the Circle’s fill. We’ll discuss a linear gradient momentarily.

Styling the Ellipse

The CSS rule in lines 29–32 applies to all Ellipse objects.

Click here to view code image

29   Ellipse {
30      -fx-stroke: green;
31      -fx-fill: image-pattern("yellowflowers.png");
32   }
33

Line 30 specifies that an Ellipse should have a green stroke. Line 31 specifies that the Ellipse’s fill should be the image in yellowflowers.png (located in this app’s folder). If you’re building this app from scratch, copy the image from the images folder with the chapter’s examples into the app’s folder. To specify an image as fill, you use the CSS function image-pattern.4

4. At the time of this writing, Scene Builder does not display a shape’s fill correctly if it’s specified with a CSS image-pattern. You must run the example to display the fill (Fig. 17.3(b)). We’ll post updates on the book’s web site: https://deitel.com/javafp5.

Styling the Arc

The CSS rule in lines 34–37 applies to all Arc objects.

Click here to view code image

34   Arc {
35      -fx-stroke: purple;
36      -fx-fill: linear-gradient(to right, cyan, white);
37   }

Line 35 specifies that an Arc should have a purple stroke. In this case, line 36

Click here to view code image

-fx-fill: linear-gradient(to right, cyan, white);

specifies that the Arc should be filled with a linear gradient—such gradients gradually transition from one color to the next horizontally, vertically or diagonally. You can transition between as many colors as you like and specify the points at which to change colors. To create a linear gradient, you use the CSS function linear-gradient. In this case,

to right

indicates that the gradient should start from the shape’s left edge and transition through colors to the shape’s right edge. We specified only two colors here—cyan at the left edge of the gradient and white at the right edge—but two or more colors can be specified in the comma-separated list. For more information on all the options for configuring radial gradients, linear gradients and image patterns, visit

Click here to view code image

https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-
   files/cssref.html#typepaint

17.4 Polylines, Polygons and Paths

Several JavaFX classes enable you to create custom shapes:

  • Polyline—draws a series of connected lines defined by a collection of points.

  • Polygon—draws a series of connected lines defined by a set of points and connects the last point to the first point.

  • Path—draws a series of connected PathElements by moving to a given point, then drawing lines, arcs and curves.

In the PolyShapes app, you select the shape to display by clicking a RadioButton in the left column. You specify a shape’s points by clicking throughout the AnchoredPane in which the shapes are displayed.

17.4.1 GUI and CSS

The following screen captures contain the PolyShapes app’s GUI. It’s similar to the Painter app in Section 16.3, so we show only the key GUI elements’ fx:id property values rather than the complete FXML. Each fx:id property value ends with the GUI element’s type.

In this GUI:

  • The three RadioButtons are in a ToggleGroup with the fx:id "toggleGroup". The Polyline RadioButton is Selected by default. We also set each RadioButton’s On Action event handler to shapeRadioButtonSelected.

  • We dragged a Polyline, a Polygon and a Path from the Scene Builder Library’s Shapes section onto the Pane that displays the shapes, and we set their fx:ids to polyline, polygon and path, respectively. We set each shape’s visible property to false by selecting the shape in Scene Builder then unchecking the Visible checkbox in the Properties inspector. We display only the shape with the selected RadioButton at runtime.

  • We set the Pane’s On Mouse Clicked event handler to drawingAreaMouseClicked.

  • We set the Clear Button’s On Action event handler to clearButtonPressed.

  • We set the controller class to PolyShapesController.

  • Finally, we edited the FXML to remove the Path object’s <elements> and the Polyline and Polygon objects’ <points>, as we’ll set these programmatically in response to the user’s mouse-click events.

The PolyShapes.css file defines the properties -fx-stroke, -fx-stroke-width and -fx-fill that are applied to all three shapes in this example. Each shape has a black, five-pixel outline and with red fill color:

Polyline, Polygon, Path {
   -fx-stroke: black;
   -fx-stroke-width: 5;
   -fx-fill: red;
}

17.4.2 PolyShapesController Class

Class PolyShapesController (Fig. 17.5) responds to this app’s user interactions. We split the code into parts for discussion purposes. The enum ShapeType (line 17) defines constants we use to determine which shape to display.

Lines 20–26 declare the variables corresponding to the GUI components and shapes with fx:ids in the FXML. The shapeType variable (line 29) stores whichever shape type is currently selected in the GUI’s RadioButtons. By default, the Polyline will be displayed. The sweepFlag variable will determine whether to draw an arc with a negative or positive sweep angle.

Click here to view code image

19      // instance variables that refer to GUI components
20      @FXML private RadioButton polylineRadioButton;
21      @FXML private RadioButton polygonRadioButton;
22      @FXML private RadioButton pathRadioButton;
23      @FXML private ToggleGroup toggleGroup;
24      @FXML private Polyline polyline;
25      @FXML private Polygon polygon;
26      @FXML private Path path;
27
28      // instance variables for managing state
29      private ShapeType shapeType = ShapeType.POLYLINE;
30      private boolean sweepFlag = true; // used with arcs in a Path
31
Method initialize

Recall from Section 16.3.1 that you can associate any Object with each JavaFX control via its setUserData method. For the shape RadioButtons in this app, method initialize (lines 33–41) stores the ShapeType that each RadioButton represents (lines 36–38). When handling the RadioButton events, we use these to set the shapeType instance variable. Line 40 calls method displayShape to display the currently selected shape (the Polyline by default). Initially, the shape is not visible because it has no points.

Click here to view code image

32      // set user data for the RadioButtons and display polyline object
33      @FXML
34      private void initialize() {
35         // user data on a control can be any Object
36         polylineRadioButton.setUserData(ShapeType.POLYLINE);
37         polygonRadioButton.setUserData(ShapeType.POLYGON);
38         pathRadioButton.setUserData(ShapeType.PATH);
39
40         displayShape(); // sets polyline's visibility to true when app loads
41      }
42
Method drawingAreaMouseClicked

When the user clicks the app’s Pane, method drawingAreaMouseClicked (lines 44–65) modifies all three shapes to incorporate the new point at which the user clicked.

Click here to view code image

43      // handles drawingArea's onMouseClicked event
44      @FXML
45      private void drawingAreaMouseClicked(MouseEvent e) {
46         polyline.getPoints().addAll(e.getX(), e.getY());
47         polygon.getPoints().addAll(e.getX(), e.getY());
48
49         // if path is empty, move to first click position and close path
50         if (path.getElements().isEmpty()) {
51            path.getElements().add(new MoveTo(e.getX(), e.getY()));
52            path.getElements().add(new ClosePath());
53         }
54         else { // insert a new path segment before the ClosePath element
55            // create an arc segment and insert it in the path
56            ArcTo arcTo = new ArcTo();
57            arcTo.setX(e.getX());
58            arcTo.setY(e.getY());
59            arcTo.setRadiusX(100.0);
60            arcTo.setRadiusY(100.0);
61            arcTo.setSweepFlag(sweepFlag);
62            sweepFlag = !sweepFlag;
63            path.getElements().add(path.getElements().size() - 1, arcTo);
64         }
65      }
66

Polylines and Polygons store their points as a collection of Doubles—the first two values represent the first point’s location, the next two represent the second point’s location, etc. Line 46 adds the new click point to the polyline object’s points collection by calling addAll with the MouseEvent’s x- and y-coordinate values. This adds the new point’s information to the end of the collection. Line 47 performs the same task for the polygon object.

Lines 50–64 manipulate the path object. A Path is represented by a collection of PathElements. The subclasses of PathElement used in this example are:

  • MoveTo—Moves to a specific position without drawing anything.

  • ArcTo—Draws an arc from the previous PathElement’s endpoint to the specified location. We’ll discuss this in more detail momentarily.

  • ClosePath—Closes the path by drawing a straight line from the last PathElement’s endpoint to the first PathElement start point.

Other PathElements not covered here include LineTo, HLineTo, VLineTo, CubicCurveTo and QuadCurveTo.

When the user clicks the Pane, line 50 checks whether the Path contains elements. If not, line 51 moves the path’s starting point to the mouse-click location by adding a MoveTo element to the path’s PathElements collection. Then, line 52 adds a new Close-Path element to complete the path. For each subsequent mouse-click event, lines 56–61 create an ArcTo element, and line 63 inserts it before the ClosePath element by calling the PathElements collection’s add method that receives an index as its first argument.

Lines 57–58 set the ArcTo element’s endpoint to the MouseEvent’s coordinates. The arc is drawn as a piece of an ellipse for which you specify the horizontal radius and vertical radius (lines 59–60). Line 61 sets the ArcTo’s sweepFlag, which determines whether the arc sweeps in the positive angle direction (true; counter-clockwise) or the negative angle direction (false; clockwise). By default, an ArcTo element is drawn as the shortest arc between the last PathElement’s endpoint and the point specified by the ArcTo element. To sweep the arc the long way around the ellipse, set the ArcTo’s largeArcFlag to true. For each mouse click, line 62 reverses the value of our controller class’s sweepFlag instance variable so that the ArcTo elements toggle between positive and negative angles for variety.

Method shapeRadioButtonSelected

When the user clicks a shape RadioButton, lines 71–72 set the controller’s shapeType instance variable, then line 73 calls method displayShape to display the selected shape. Try creating a Polyline of several points, then changing to the Polygon and Path to observe how the points are used in each shape.

Click here to view code image

67      // handles color RadioButton's ActionEvents
68      @FXML
69      private void shapeRadioButtonSelected(ActionEvent e) {
70         // user data for each color RadioButton is a ShapeType constant
71         shapeType =
72            (ShapeType) toggleGroup.getSelectedToggle().getUserData();
73         displayShape(); // display the currently selected shape
74      }
75
Method displayShape

Lines 78–80 in method displayShape set the visibility of the three shapes based on the current shapeType. The currently selected shape’s visibility is set to true to display the shape, and the other shapes’ visibility is set to false to hide those shapes.

Click here to view code image

76      // displays currently selected shape
77      private void displayShape() {
78         polyline.setVisible(shapeType == ShapeType.POLYLINE);
79         polygon.setVisible(shapeType == ShapeType.POLYGON);
80         path.setVisible(shapeType == ShapeType.PATH);
81      }
82
Method clearButtonPressed

When the user clicks the Clear Button, lines 86–87 in method clearButtonPressed clear the polyline’s and polygon’s collections of points, and line 88 clears the path’s collection of PathElements. The user can then begin drawing a new shape by clicking the Pane.

Click here to view code image

83      // resets each shape
84      @FXML
85      private void clearButtonPressed(ActionEvent event) {
86         polyline.getPoints().clear();
87         polygon.getPoints().clear();
88         path.getElements().clear();
89      }
90   }

17.5 Transforms

A transform can be applied to any UI element to reposition or reorient the element. The built-in JavaFX transforms are subclasses of Transform. Some of these subclasses include:

  • Translate—moves an object to a new location.

  • Rotate—rotates an object around a point and by a specified rotation angle.

  • Scale—scales an object’s size by the specified amounts.

The next example draws stars using the Polygon control and uses Rotate transforms to create a circle of randomly colored stars. This app’s FXML consists of an empty 300-by-300 Pane layout with the fx:id "pane". We also set the controller class to DrawStarsController. Figure 17.6 contains the app’s controller and a sample output.

Method initialize (lines 15–39) defines the stars, applies the transforms and attaches the stars to the app’s pane. Lines 18–20 define the ten x-y coordinates that form a star as a Double array. A Polygon’s collection of points is a generic collection, so you must use type Double rather than double—recall that primitive types cannot be used in Java generic collections. Each pair of values in the array represents a point’s x-y coordinates.

During each iteration of the loop, lines 25–36 create a Polygon using the points in the points array and apply a Rotate transform, resulting in a circle of Polygons. To generate each star’s random colors, we use a RandomGenerator to create three random values from 0–255 for the red, green and blue components of the color and one random value from 0.0–1.0 for the color’s alpha transparency value. We pass those values to class Color’s static rgb method to create a Color.

To apply a rotation to the new Polygon, we add a Rotate transform to its collection of Transforms (lines 35–36). Transform’s static method rotate (line 36) returns a Rotate object. The method’s first argument is the rotation angle. Each iteration of the loop assigns a new rotation-angle value by using the control variable multiplied by 20 as the rotate method’s first argument. The method’s next two arguments are the x-y coordinates of the point of rotation around which the Polygon rotates. The center of the circle of stars is the point (150, 150)—we rotated all 18 stars around that point. Adding each Polygon as a new child element of the pane object (line 37) allows the Polygon to be rendered on screen.

17.6 Playing Video with Media, MediaPlayer and MediaView

 

Many of today’s most popular apps are multimedia intensive. JavaFX provides audio and video multimedia capabilities via the javafx.scene.media package:

  • For simple audio playback, use class AudioClip.

  • For audio playback with more playback controls and for video playback, use classes Media, MediaPlayer and MediaView.

In this section, you’ll build a basic video player.5 We’ll explain Media, MediaPlayer and MediaView as we encounter them in this example’s controller class (Section 17.6.2). The video we use in this example is from NASA’s multimedia library6 and was downloaded from

Media Formats

JavaFX supports several video formats, but some are platform-specific. MPEG-4 video (also called MP4) is well-supported across platforms. If you find a video in a format that’s not supported, there are many free online video conversion tools you can use to convert a video file to another format, including:

controlsfx-11.2.1.jar

in this chapter’s examples folder. For convenience, place this file in your JavaFX SDK folder’s lib subfolder.

Compiling and Running the App with ControlsFX

To compile and run this app, you must include ControlsFX and the JavaFX media capabilities in the javac and java commands. Enter the entire following command, then press or select Enter to compile the code in the VideoPlayer folder:

   javafx.controls,javafx.fxml,javafx.media,org.controlsfx.controls
   *.java

Similarly, to run the app, enter the entire following command, then press or select Enter:

   javafx.controls,javafx.fxml,javafx.media,org.controlsfx.controls

Recall from Section 15.5 that you need to replace pathToFX with

17.6.1 VideoPlayer GUI

Figure 17.7 contains the completed VideoPlayer.fxml file and two sample screen captures of the running VideoPlayer app. The GUI’s layout is a BorderPane consisting of

  • a MediaView (from the Scene Builder Library’s Controls section) with the fx:id mediaView and

  • a ToolBar (from the Scene Builder Library’s Containers section) containing one Button with the fx:id playPauseButton and the text "Play". The controller method playPauseButtonPressed responds when the Button is pressed.

We placed the MediaView in the BorderPane’s center region (lines 25–27) so that it occupies all available space in the BorderPane, and we placed the ToolBar in the BorderPane’s bottom region (lines 15–24). By default, Scene Builder adds one Button to the ToolBar when you drag the ToolBar onto your layout. You can then add other controls to the ToolBar as necessary. We set the controller class to VideoPlayerController.

17.6.2 VideoPlayerController Class

Class VideoPlayerController (Fig. 17.8) configures video playback, responds to the MediaPlayer’s state changes and responds to the playPauseButton’s events. The controller uses classes Media, MediaPlayer and MediaView as follows:

  • A Media object specifies the location of the media to play and provides access to various information about the media, such as its duration, video dimensions and more.

  • A MediaPlayer object loads a Media object and controls its playback, transitioning through various states (ready, playing, paused, etc.) during loading and playback. You’ll use lambdas to define Runnables that respond to these state transitions.

  • A MediaView object is a Node in the scene graph that displays the Media being played by a given MediaPlayer object.

We split the code into parts for discussion purposes.

Instance Variables

Lines 17–19 declare the controller’s instance variables. When the app loads, mediaView (line 17) is assigned a reference to the MediaView object declared in the app’s FXML. The mediaPlayer variable (line 19) is configured in method initialize to load the video specified by a Media object and used by method playPauseButtonPressed (lines 67–77) to play and pause the video.

Click here to view code image

17   @FXML private MediaView mediaView;
18   @FXML private Button playPauseButton;
19   private MediaPlayer mediaPlayer;
20
Creating a Media Object Representing the Video to Play

Method initialize (lines 21–64) configures media playback, registers event handlers for MediaPlayer events and sets up a data binding to change the Button’s text to Play or Pause based on the MediaPlayer’s state. Lines 24–25 get a URL representing the location of the video file. The notation

VideoPlayerController.class

is a Class object representing the VideoPlayerController class. This is equivalent to calling the inherited method getClass(). Next, line 28 creates a Media object representing the video. The argument to the Media constructor is a String representing the video’s location, which we obtain with URL method toExternalForm. The URL String can represent a local file on your computer or can be a location on the web. The Media constructor throws various exceptions, including MediaExceptions if the media cannot be found or is not of a supported media format.

Click here to view code image

21      @FXML
22      private void initialize() {
23         // get URL of the video file
24         URL url = VideoPlayerController.class.getResource(
25            "A1Launch~medium.mp4");
26
27         // create a Media object for the specified URL
28         var media = new Media(url.toExternalForm());
29
30         // create a MediaPlayer to control Media playback
31         mediaPlayer = new MediaPlayer(media);
32
33         // specify which MediaPlayer to display in the MediaView
34         mediaView.setMediaPlayer(mediaPlayer);
35
36         // set handler to be called when the video completes playing
37         mediaPlayer.setOnEndOfMedia(() -> {
38            mediaPlayer.seek(Duration.ZERO);
39            mediaPlayer.pause();
40         });
41
42         // set handler that displays an ExceptionDialog if an error occurs
43         mediaPlayer.setOnError(() -> {
44            var dialog = new ExceptionDialog(mediaPlayer.getError());
45            dialog.showAndWait();
46         });
47
48         // set handler to resize mediaView to window size once ready to play
49         mediaPlayer.setOnReady(() -> {
50            DoubleProperty width = mediaView.fitWidthProperty();
51            DoubleProperty height = mediaView.fitHeightProperty();
52            width.bind(Bindings.selectDouble(
53               mediaView.sceneProperty(), "width"));
54            height.bind(Bindings.selectDouble(
55               mediaView.sceneProperty(), "height"));
56         });
57
58         // bind playPauseButton's text to the MediaPlayer's status
59         playPauseButton.textProperty().bind(Bindings.when(
60            mediaPlayer.statusProperty().isEqualTo(Status.PLAYING))
61                       .then("Pause")
62                       .otherwise("Play")
63         );
64      }
65
Creating a MediaPlayer Object to Load the Video and Control Playback

To load the video and prepare it for playback, you must associate it with a MediaPlayer object (line 31). Playing multiple videos requires a separate MediaPlayer for each Media object. However, a given Media object can be associated with multiple MediaPlayers. The MediaPlayer constructor throws

  • a NullPointerException if the Media is null or

  • a MediaException if a problem occurs while constructing the MediaPlayer.

Attaching the MediaPlayer Object to the MediaView to Display the Video

To display video, you must associate a MediaPlayer with a MediaView. When the MediaView already exists—e.g., when it’s created in FXML—you call the MediaView’s setMediaPlayer method (line 34) to perform this task. When creating a MediaView object programmatically, you can pass the MediaPlayer to the MediaView’s constructor. A MediaView is like any other Node in the scene graph, so you can apply CSS styles, transforms and animations (Sections 17.7–17.9) to it as well.

Configuring Event Handlers for MediaPlayer Events

A MediaPlayer transitions through various states. Common states include ready, playing and paused. For these and other states, you can execute a task as the MediaPlayer enters the corresponding state. In addition, you can specify tasks that execute when the end of media playback is reached or when an error occurs during playback. To perform a task for a given state, you specify an object that implements the Runnable interface (package java.lang). This interface contains a no-parameter run method that returns void.

Runnable is a functional interface that can be implemented using a lambda. For example, lines 37–40 call the MediaPlayer’s setOnEndOfMedia method, passing a lambda that executes when video playback completes. Line 38 calls MediaPlayer method seek to move to the beginning of the video, and line 39 pauses the video.

Lines 43–46 call the MediaPlayer’s setOnError method to specify a task to perform if the MediaPlayer enters the error state, indicating that an error occurred during playback. In this case, we display a ControlsFX ExceptionDialog containing the error message. Calling the ExceptionDialog’s showAndWait method indicates that the app must wait for the user to dismiss the dialog before continuing.

Binding the MediaView’s Size to the Scene’s Size

Lines 49–56 call the MediaPlayer’s setOnReady method to specify a task to perform if the MediaPlayer enters the ready state. We use property bindings to bind the MediaView’s width and height to the scene’s width and height so it resizes when the app’s window resizes. A Node’s sceneProperty returns an object of type ReadOnlyObjectProperty<Scene> you can use to access the Scene in which the Node is displayed. This object has many properties. To bind to its specific properties, you can use the methods of class Bindings (package javafx.beans.binding) to select the corresponding properties. The Scene’s width and height are each DoubleProperty objects. Bindings method selectDouble gets a reference to a DoubleProperty. The method’s first argument is the object that contains the property, and the second argument is the name of the property to which you’d like to bind.

Binding the Button’s Text to the MediaPlayer’s Status

Lines 59–63 bind the Button’s text to the MediaPlayer’s Status, so the text updates based on the current playback status. Button method textProperty returns the button’s text property, which we bind to the result of a condition configured using the Bindings method when. This method’s argument (line 60) gets the MediaPlayer’s status property and calls its isEqualTo method to compare the current status to Status.PLAYING. The when call returns a When object that specifies what to do based on the condition. If the condition is true, the Button’s text is set to "Pause" via the chained call .then("Pause"); otherwise, the Button’s text is set to "Play" via the chained call .otherwise("Play").

Method playPauseButtonPressed

The event handler playPauseButtonPressed (lines 67–77) toggles video playback. We get the MediaPlayer’s Status (line 69), then when the status is either Status.READY (ready to play) or Status.PAUSED (currently paused), line 72 calls the MediaPlayer’s play method; otherwise, line 75 sets calls the MediaPlayer’s pause method.

Click here to view code image

66      // toggle media playback and the text on the playPauseButton
67      @FXML
68      private void playPauseButtonPressed(ActionEvent e) {
69         Status status = mediaPlayer.getStatus();
70
71         if (status == Status.READY || status == Status.PAUSED) {
72            mediaPlayer.play();
73         }
74         else {
75            mediaPlayer.pause();
76         }
77      }
78   }

17.7 Transition Animations

Animations in JavaFX apps transition a Node’s property values from one value to another in a specified amount of time. Most properties of a Node can be animated. This section focuses on several of JavaFX’s predefined Transition animations from the javafx.animations package. By default, the subclasses that define Transition animations change the values of specific Node properties. For example, a FadeTransition changes the value of a Node’s opacity property (which specifies whether the Node is opaque or transparent) over time, whereas a PathTransition changes a Node’s location by moving it along a Path over time. Though we include sample screen captures for all the animation examples, the best way to experience each is to run the examples yourself.

17.7.1 TransitionAnimations.fxml

Figure 17.9 contains this app’s GUI and sample screen captures of it running. When you click the Button (lines 17–18), its startButtonPressed event handler in the app’s controller creates a sequence of Transition animations for the Rectangle (lines 15–16) and plays them. The Rectangle is styled with the following CSS from the file TransitionAnimations.css:

Rectangle {
   -fx-stroke-width: 10;
   -fx-stroke: red;
   -fx-arc-width: 50;
   -fx-arc-height: 50;
   -fx-fill: yellow;
}

which produces a rounded rectangle with a 10-pixel red border and yellow fill.

17.7.2 TransitionAnimationsController Class

Class TransitionAnimationsController (Fig. 17.10) defines the startButton’s event handler (lines 25–81). This event handler defines several animations that are played in sequence. We split the code—including the method startButtonPressed—into parts for discussion purposes.

FillTransition

Lines 28–33 configure a one-second FillTransition that changes a shape’s fill color.

Click here to view code image

24      // configure and start transition animations
25      @FXML
26      private void startButtonPressed(ActionEvent event) {
27         // transition that changes a shape's fill
28         var fillTransition = new FillTransition(Duration.seconds(1));
29         fillTransition.setToValue(Color.CYAN);
30         fillTransition.setCycleCount(2);
31
32         // each even cycle plays transition in reverse to restore original
33         fillTransition.setAutoReverse(true);
34

Line 29 specifies the color (CYAN) to which the fill will transition. Line 30 sets the animation’s cycle count to 2—this determines the transition’s number of iterations to perform over the specified duration. Line 33 specifies that the animation should automatically play itself in reverse once the initial transition is complete. For this animation, during the first cycle, the fill color changes from the original fill color to CYAN, and during the second cycle, the animation transitions back to the original fill color.

StrokeTransition

Lines 36–39 configure a one-second StrokeTransition that changes a shape’s stroke color.

Click here to view code image

35         // transition that changes a shape's stroke over time
36         var strokeTransition = new StrokeTransition(Duration.seconds(1));
37         strokeTransition.setToValue(Color.BLUE);
38         strokeTransition.setCycleCount(2);
39         strokeTransition.setAutoReverse(true);
40

Line 37 specifies the color (BLUE) to which the stroke will transition. Line 38 sets the animation’s cycle count to 2, and line 39 specifies that the animation should automatically play itself in reverse once the initial transition is complete. For this animation, the stroke color changes from the original stroke color to BLUE during the first cycle and transitions back to the original stroke color during the second cycle.

ParallelTransition

Lines 42–43 configure a ParallelTransition that performs multiple transitions at the same time (that is, in parallel).

Click here to view code image

41         // parallelizes multiple transitions
42         var parallelTransition =
43            new ParallelTransition(fillTransition, strokeTransition);
44

The ParallelTransition constructor receives a variable number of Transitions as a comma-separated list. In this case, the FillTransition and StrokeTransition will be performed in parallel on the app’s Rectangle.

FadeTransition

Lines 46–50 configure a one-second FadeTransition that changes a Node’s opacity.

Click here to view code image

45         // transition that changes a node's opacity over time
46         var fadeTransition = new FadeTransition(Duration.seconds(1));
47         fadeTransition.setFromValue(1.0); // opaque
48         fadeTransition.setToValue(0.0); // transparent
49         fadeTransition.setCycleCount(2);
50         fadeTransition.setAutoReverse(true);
51

Line 47 specifies the initial opacity—1.0 is fully opaque. Line 48 specifies the final opacity—0.0 is fully transparent. Once again, we set the cycle count to 2 and specified that the animation should auto-reverse itself.

RotateTransition

Lines 53–57 configure a one-second RotateTransition that rotates a Node.

Click here to view code image

52         // transition that rotates a node
53         var rotateTransition = new RotateTransition(Duration.seconds(1));
54         rotateTransition.setByAngle(360.0);
55         rotateTransition.setCycleCount(2);
56         rotateTransition.setInterpolator(Interpolator.EASE_BOTH);
57         rotateTransition.setAutoReverse(true);
58

You can rotate a Node by a specified number of degrees (line 54), or you can use other methods of class RotateTransition to specify a start angle and end angle. Each Transition animation uses an Interpolator to calculate new property values throughout the animation’s duration. The default is a LINEAR Interpolator, which evenly divides the property value changes over the animation’s duration. For the RotateTransition, line 56 uses the Interpolator EASE_BOTH, which changes the rotation slowly at first (known as “easing in”), speeds up the rotation in the middle of the animation, then slows the rotation again to complete the animation (known as “easing out”). For a list of Interpolators, visit

Click here to view code image

https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/animation/
   Interpolator.html
PathTransition

Lines 60–66 configure a two-second PathTransition that moves a node along a Path. The Path (lines 60–61) is specified as the second argument to the PathTransition constructor (lines 62–63). A LineTo object draws a straight line from the previous PathElement’s endpoint to the specified location. Line 65 specifies that this animation should use the Interpolator EASE_IN, which changes the position slowly at first before performing the animation at full speed.

Click here to view code image

59         // transition that moves a node along a Path
60         var path = new Path(new MoveTo(45, 45), new LineTo(45, 0),
61            new LineTo(90, 0), new LineTo(90, 90), new LineTo(0, 90));
62         var translateTransition =
63            new PathTransition(Duration.seconds(2), path);
64         translateTransition.setCycleCount(2);
65         translateTransition.setInterpolator(Interpolator.EASE_IN);
66         translateTransition.setAutoReverse(true);
67
ScaleTransition

Lines 69–74 configure a one-second ScaleTransition that changes a Node’s size. Lines 70–71 specify that the object will be scaled 75% larger along the x-axis (i.e., horizontally) and y-axis (i.e., vertically), respectively. Line 73 specifies that this animation should use the Interpolator EASE_OUT, which begins scaling the shape at full speed then slows down as the animation completes.

Click here to view code image

68         // transition that scales a shape to make it larger or smaller
69         var scaleTransition = new ScaleTransition(Duration.seconds(1));
70         scaleTransition.setByX(0.75);
71         scaleTransition.setByY(0.75);
72         scaleTransition.setCycleCount(2);
73         scaleTransition.setInterpolator(Interpolator.EASE_OUT);
74         scaleTransition.setAutoReverse(true);
75
SequentialTransition

Lines 77–79 configure a SequentialTransition that performs a sequence of transitions—as each completes, the next one begins executing. The SequentialTransition constructor receives the Node to which the sequence of animations will be applied, followed by a comma-separated list of Transitions to perform. In fact, every transition animation class has a constructor that enables you to specify a Node. For this example, we did not specify Nodes when creating the other transitions because they’re all applied to the Rectangle by the SequentialTransition. Every Transition has a play method (line 80) that begins the animation. Calling play on the SequentialTransition automatically calls play on each animation in the sequence.

Click here to view code image

76         // transition that applies a sequence of transitions to a node
77         var sequentialTransition = new SequentialTransition(
78            rectangle, parallelTransition, fadeTransition,
79            rotateTransition, translateTransition, scaleTransition);
80         sequentialTransition.play(); // play the transition
81      }
82   }
