17.8 Timeline Animations

 

Next, we’ll use a Timeline animation to bounce a Circle object around the app’s Pane over time. A Timeline animation can change any modifiable Node property. You specify how to change property values with one or more KeyFrame objects that the Timeline animation performs in sequence. For this app, we’ll specify a single KeyFrame that modifies a Circle’s location, then we’ll play that KeyFrame indefinitely.

TimelineAnimation.fxml

This app’s FXML (Fig. 17.11) defines a Circle object (lines 13–15) with the fx:id "c", a five-pixel black border and the fill color DODGERBLUE.

TimelineAnimationController.java

Class TimelineAnimationController’s (Fig. 17.12) initialize method (lines 20–43) configures then plays the Timeline animation. Lines 23–42 define the animation, line 41 specifies that the animation should cycle indefinitely (until the animation’s stop method is called), and line 42 plays the animation.

Creating the Timeline

The Timeline constructor used in lines 23–38 can receive a comma-separated list of Key-Frames as arguments—in this case, we pass one. Each KeyFrame issues an ActionEvent at a particular time in the animation. The app can respond to the event by changing a Node’s property values. The KeyFrame constructor used here specifies that, after ten milliseconds, the ActionEvent will occur. We set the Timeline’s cycle count to Timeline.INDEFINITE, so the Timeline will perform this KeyFrame every ten milliseconds. Lines 24–37 use a lambda to define the EventHandler for the KeyFrame’s ActionEvent. The lambda’s parameter (e) receives the ActionEvent.

KeyFrame’s EventHandler

The lambda uses class TimelineAnimationController’s instance variables dx and dy (declared and initialized at lines 15–16) to change the Circle’s x- and y-coordinates each time the KeyFrame plays. Lines 26–27 add these values to the Circle’s x- and y-coordinates. Next, lines 30–36 determine whether the Circle has collided with any of the Pane’s edges. If the Circle hits the left or right edge, line 31 multiplies dx’s value by -1 to reverse the Circle’s horizontal direction. If the Circle hits the top or bottom edge, line 35 multiplies dy’s value by -1 to reverse the Circle’s horizontal direction.

17.9 Frame-by-Frame Animation with AnimationTimer

 

A third way to implement JavaFX animations is via the javafx.animation package’s class AnimationTimer, which enables you to define frame-by-frame animations. You specify how your objects should move in a given frame. JavaFX aggregates all of the drawing operations and displays the frame. This can be used with objects in the scene graph or to draw shapes in a Canvas. JavaFX calls the handle method of every AnimationTimer before it draws an animation frame.

JavaFX tries to display animation frames at 60 frames per second for smooth animation. This frame rate varies based on the animation’s complexity, the processor speed and how busy the processor is at a given time. For this reason, method handle receives a time stamp in nanoseconds (billionths of a second) that you can use to determine the elapsed time since the last animation frame, then you can scale the movements of your objects accordingly. This enables you to define animations that operate at the same overall speed, regardless of the frame rate on a given device. We’ll discuss JavaFX performance issues in more detail in Chapter 18.

Figure 17.13 reimplements the animation in Fig. 17.12 using an AnimationTimer. The FXML is identical (other than the filename and controller class name). Much of the code is identical to Fig. 17.12, so we focus on the new features.

Extending abstract Class AnimationTimer Using an Anonymous Inner Class

Class AnimationTimer is an abstract class, so you must create a subclass. In this example, rather than defining an AnimationTimer subclass in a separate file, lines 21–44 create an anonymous inner class. Such a class does not have a name and is typically declared in a method. Lines 21–44 are one statement that

  • declares the AnimationTimer subclass,

  • immediately creates an object of that class and

  • assigns the new object’s reference to the AnimationTimer variable timer (line 21).

Since an anonymous inner class has no name, you must create an object of the class at the point where it’s declared, thus the keyword new in line 21. The parentheses in

new AnimationTimer()

call the anonymous class’s constructor. After the parentheses are the braces that delimit the anonymous class’s body (lines 21 and 44), which may contain field and method declarations like other classes. Lines 22–23 define the anonymous inner class’s instance variables:

  • Variable velocity is used as a multiplier to determine the distance moved in each animation frame. We discuss this momentarily.

  • Variable previousTime represents the time stamp (in nanoseconds) of the previous animation frame—this will be used to determine the elapsed time between frames. We initialized previousTime to System.nanoTime(), which returns the number of nanoseconds since the JVM launched the app. AnimationTimer’s handle method also receives as its argument the number of nanoseconds since the JVM launched the app.

Overriding AnimationTimer’s handle Method

Lines 26–43 override class AnimationTimer’s handle method, which specifies what to do during each animation frame:

  • Line 28 calculates the elapsedTime in seconds since the last animation frame. If method handle is called 60 times per second, the elapsed time between frames will be approximately 0.0167 seconds—that is, 1/60 of a second.

  • Line 29 stores the time stamp in previousTime for use in the next animation frame.

  • When we change the Circle’s layoutX and layoutY (lines 33–34), we multiply dx and dy by the scale (line 30). In Fig. 17.12, the Circle’s speed was determined by moving between one and five pixels along the x- and y-axes every 10 milliseconds—the larger the values, the faster the Circle moved. If we were to scale dx or dy by just elapsedTime, we’d move the Circle only small fractions of dx and dy during each frame—approximately 0.0167 seconds (1/60 of a second) to 0.083 seconds (5/60 of a second), based on their randomly chosen values. For this reason, we multiply the elapsedTime by the velocity (60) to scale the movement in each frame. This results in values that are approximately one to five pixels, as in Fig. 17.12.

After creating the AnimationTimer object, the controller class’s initialize method calls the AnimationTimer object’s start method (line 46) to begin animating the ball.

Anonymous Inner Class Notes

An anonymous inner class can access its top-level class’s instance variables, static variables and methods. In this example, the anonymous inner class uses the controller class’s instance variables dx and dy. An anonymous inner class has limited access to the local variables of the method in which it’s declared. It can access only the final or effectively final local variables declared in the enclosing method’s body.

17.10 CSS Transitions

 

Sections 17.2–17.3 introduced JavaFX CSS for styling JavaFX GUIs. JavaFX’s CSS support traditionally has focused on static Node styling. If you wanted to animate a Node property, you’d use the programmatically applied JavaFX transitions shown in Section 17.7. In web development, CSS transitions are widely used to create smooth animation effects. These are often applied in response to the user hovering the mouse cursor over a webpage element—that is, moving the mouse cursor into a webpage element’s bounds. When the user moves the mouse cursor outside the element’s bounds, the element typically returns to its original appearance. Some CSS hover transitions include:7,8,9

7. “CSS Transitions.” Accessed October 3, 2024. https://www.w3.org/TR/css-transitions-1/.

8. “Using CSS Transitions.” Accessed October 3, 2024. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_transitions/Using_CSS_transitions.

9. “Transitions.” Accessed October 3, 2024. https://web.dev/learn/css/transitions.

  • changing an element’s appearance to indicate it’s clickable,

  • scaling an element’s size (zooming) to draw attention to it,

  • changing an image (such as an icon) temporarily to show that an element is interactive,

  • highlighting menu items as the user moves the mouse cursor over them,

  • moving elements to grab a user’s attention,

  • changing an element’s rotation angle,

  • adding shadows to make an element appear as if it’s raised off the screen, and

  • fading an element in so it’s visible or out so it’s not visible.

Other events that can trigger transitions include when a control receives the focus or is pressed.

CSS Transitions in JavaFX 23

JavaFX 23 adds support for webpage-style CSS transitions,10 which you can apply to any Node property styled with JavaFX CSS properties. The CSS transitions execute automatically in response to events, like hovering the mouse cursor over a Node. For precise animation control, you can use the other animation techniques shown in Sections 17.7–17.9.

10. “JavaFX CSS Reference Guide—Transitions.” Accessed October 3, 2024. https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-files/cssref.html#introtransitions.

CSSTransition.fxml

To demonstrate CSS transitions, we’ll use an FXML GUI consisting of a Pane layout containing a rounded Rectangle (Fig. 17.14). Line 9 references the CSS stylesheet containing the Rectangle’s properties and the CSS transitions (presented in Fig. 17.15).

TransitionAnimations.fxml

Using CSS transitions, we’ll modify the Rectangle’s fill, stroke color, stroke width and rotation angle. The following screen captures show the transition progressions—they begin when the user hovers the mouse cursor over the Rectangle and transition back to the original state when the user moves the mouse outside the Rectangle’s bounds:

CSSTransition.css

Figure 17.15 contains this example’s CSS stylesheet. In the Rectangle CSS rule:

  • lines 4–9 specify the Rectangle’s initial styling, and

  • lines 10–12 specify the CSS transition settings (discussed momentarily).

The -fx-rotate property specifies the Rectangle’s rotation angle in degrees. The CSS rule in lines 15–20 specifies the values of the four CSS properties JavaFX will apply when the user hovers the mouse cursor over the Rectangle. The notation :hover is a CSS pseudo-class—JavaFX applies this rule only when the mouse cursor hovers over the Node that matches the rule.11 The CSS properties return to their original values in lines 4, 5, 8 and 9 when the user moves the mouse out of the Rectangle.

11. Visit the “Pseudo-classes” section of the JavaFX CSS reference at https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-files/cssref.html for other pseudo-classes that can trigger transitions.

Specifying the Transition Settings

The CSS transition-property (lines 10–11) specifies the Rectangle rule’s CSS properties that will participate in the CSS transition animation—in this case:

  • -fx-fill (the Rectangle’s fill color),

  • -fx-stroke (the Rectangle’s border color),

  • -fx-stroke-width (the Rectangle’s border thickness) and

  • -fx-rotate (the Node’s rotation angle in degrees).

The CSS transition-duration (line 12) specifies the transition animation’s duration (3s indicates three seconds).

When the user hovers the mouse over the Rectangle, JavaFX automatically applies a smooth animation for the properties listed in the transition-property. As with the Transition animations shown in Section 17.7, CSS animations interpolate between the properties’ original values (lines 4, 5, 8 and 9) and their new values (lines 16–19). All the CSS transitions for the properties listed in the transition-property (lines 10–11) are applied to the Rectangle in parallel. When the user moves the mouse cursor out of Rectangle’s bounds, JavaFX automatically applies smooth transition animations that return each property to its original value (lines 4, 5, 8 and 9).

Other JavaFX CSS Transition Properties

Each CSS transition has an associated transition-timing-function. By default, CSS transitions use the ease timing function, which begins the transition slowly (“easing in”), speeds up the transition in the middle then slows the transition at the end (“easing out”)— like Interpolator.EASE_BOTH in Fig. 17.10. You can customize the transition-timing-function by adding the property

Click here to view code image

transition-timing-function: value;

to the CSS rule that specifies the transition-property. For the list of timing functions, visit:

Click here to view code image

https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-
   files/cssref.html#typeeasingfunction

You may also delay the transition animation’s start by a specified time interval using the transition-delay property.

You can combine all the CSS transition properties into a single shorthand transition property of the form:

Click here to view code image

transition:
   property duration timing-function delay,
   …
   property duration timing-function delay;

in which you specify the property, duration, timing-function and delay for each CSS property that participates in the CSS transition. For example, we could write this example’s transition property as:

Click here to view code image

transition:
   -fx-fill 3.0s ease 0s,
   -fx-stroke 3.0s ease 0s,
   -fx-stroke-width 3.0s ease 0s,
   -fx-rotate 3.0s ease 0s;

The timing-function and delay shown here are the defaults, so we can exclude them, as in:

transition:
   -fx-fill 3.0s,
   -fx-stroke 3.0s,
   -fx-stroke-width 3.0s,
   -fx-rotate 3.0s;
JavaFX CSS Transition Notes

There are several cases in which JavaFX CSS transitions are ignored or canceled:12

12. “JavaFX CSS Reference Guide—Transitions.” Accessed October 3, 2024. https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-files/cssref.html#introtransitions.

  • your program sets the corresponding Node property programmatically,

  • the property is used in a data binding,

  • the corresponding node is not visible on the screen or

  • the node has been removed from the scene.

CSS Transition Resources

At the time of this writing, JavaFX CSS transitions are new, and there is little online documentation about them. However, they’re based directly on the CSS transitions used in web development. By studying discussions of the transitions used in web development, you can get ideas for how JavaFX CSS properties can be animated. In particular, the CSS Transition Generator at

Click here to view code image

https://dev.to/smpnjn/css-transition-generator-5de0

enables you to experiment with various transition settings and view the corresponding CSS. You can copy the settings into your JavaFX CSS stylesheets to apply the settings to JavaFX Nodes with similar CSS properties. For additional CSS transition information, visit:

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/css-transitions-1/

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_transitions/Using_CSS_transitions

  • https://www.w3schools.com/css/css3_transitions.asp

17.11 Drawing on a Canvas

 

So far, you’ve displayed and manipulated JavaFX two-dimensional shape objects in the JavaFX scene graph. This section demonstrates similar drawing capabilities using the javafx.scene.canvas package, which contains two classes:

  • Class Canvas is a subclass of Node in which you can draw graphics.

  • Class GraphicsContext performs drawing operations on a Canvas.

A GraphicsContext object supports the same drawing characteristics you’ve previously used with Shapes, but you set these characteristics, then draw the shapes programmatically. Figure 17.16 re-implements Section 17.3’s BasicShapes example to demonstrate Canvas capabilities, producing the following output:

You’ll use various JavaFX classes and enums from packages javafx.scene.image, javafx.scene.paint and javafx.scene.shape. JavaFX’s CSS capabilities use these behind the scenes to style Shapes. A Canvas is typically preferred for performance-oriented graphics, such as games with moving elements. We split the code (and specifically method initialize) into parts for discussion purposes.

Obtaining the GraphicsContext and Setting the Line Width for All Shapes

To draw on a Canvas, you first obtain its GraphicsContext by calling Canvas method getGraphicsContext2D (line 23).

Click here to view code image

20      // draw on the Canvas
21      @FXML
22      private void initialize() {
23         GraphicsContext gc = drawingCanvas.getGraphicsContext2D();
24         gc.setLineWidth(10); // set all stroke widths
25

When you set a GraphicsContext’s drawing characteristics, they’re applied (as appropriate) to all subsequent shapes you draw. For example, line 24 calls the GraphicsContext method setLineWidth to specify the line thickness (10). All subsequent GraphicsContext method calls that draw lines or shape borders will use this line-width setting. This is similar to the -fx-stroke-width CSS attribute we specified for all shapes in Section 17.3.

Drawing Lines

Lines 27–34 draw the red and green lines:

Click here to view code image

26         // draw red line
27         gc.setStroke(Color.RED);
28         gc.strokeLine(10, 10, 100, 100);
29
30         // draw green line
31         gc.setGlobalAlpha(0.5); // half transparent
32         gc.setLineCap(StrokeLineCap.ROUND);
33         gc.setStroke(Color.GREEN);
34         gc.strokeLine(100, 10, 10, 100);
35
36         gc.setGlobalAlpha(1.0); // reset alpha transparency
37

  • GraphicsContext’s setStroke method (lines 27 and 33) specifies the Paint object (package javafx.scene.paint) used to draw the line. This can be any of the Paint subclasses Color, ImagePattern, LinearGradient or RadialGradient (all from package javafx.scene.paint).

  • GraphicsContext’s strokeLine method (lines 28 and 34) draws a line using the current Paint object we set as the stroke. The four arguments are the x-y coordinates of the start and end points.

  • GraphicsContext’s setGlobalAlpha method (line 31) sets the alpha transparency of all subsequent shapes you draw. For the green line, we used 0.5, which is 50% transparent. After drawing the green line, we reset this to the default 1.0 (line 35) so subsequent shapes are fully opaque.

  • GraphicsContext’s setLineCap method (line 32) sets the line cap, like the CSS property -fx-stroke-line-cap in Section 17.3. This method’s argument is a constant from the enum StrokeLineCap (package javafx.scene.shape). Here, we round the line ends.

Drawing a Rounded Rectangle

Lines 39–42 draw a rounded rectangle with a red border and yellow fill:

Click here to view code image

38         // draw rounded rect with red border and yellow fill
39         gc.setStroke(Color.RED);
40         gc.setFill(Color.YELLOW);
41         gc.fillRoundRect(120, 10, 90, 90, 50, 50);
42         gc.strokeRoundRect(120, 10, 90, 90, 50, 50);
43

  • Line 38 sets the border color to Color.RED.

  • GraphicsContext’s setFill method (lines 40, 50, 56 and 66) specifies the Paint object that fills a shape. Here we fill the rectangle with Color.YELLOW.

  • GraphicsContext’s fillRoundRect method (line 41) draws a filled rectangle with rounded corners using the current Paint object as the fill. The first four arguments represent the rectangle’s upper-left x-coordinate, upper-left y-coordinate, width and height. The last two arguments specify the arc width and arc height for rounding the corners. These work identically to the CSS properties -fx-arc-width and -fx-arc-height properties in Section 17.3. GraphicsContext also provides a fillRect method that draws a rectangle without rounded corners.

  • GraphicsContext’s strokeRoundRect method (line 42) has the same arguments as method fillRoundRect but draws a hollow rectangle with rounded corners. GraphicsContext also provides a strokeRect method that draws a rectangle without rounded corners.

Drawing a Circle with a RadialGradient Fill

Lines 45–52 draw a circle with a blue border and a red-white, radial-gradient fill:

Click here to view code image

44         // draw circle with blue border and red/white radial gradient fill
45         gc.setStroke(Color.BLUE);
46         Stop[] stopsRadial =
47            {new Stop(0, Color.RED), new Stop(1, Color.WHITE)};
48         var radialGradient = new RadialGradient(0, 0, 0.5, 0.5,
49            0.6, true, CycleMethod.NO_CYCLE, stopsRadial);
50         gc.setFill(radialGradient);
51         gc.fillOval(230, 10, 90, 90);
52         gc.strokeOval(230, 10, 90, 90);
53

Line 45 sets the border color to Color.BLUE. Lines 46–49 configure the RadialGradient—these lines perform the same tasks as the CSS function radial-gradient in Section 17.3. Lines 46–47 create an array of Stop objects (package javafx.scene.paint) representing the color stops. Each has an offset from 0.0 to 1.0 (a percentage from the gradient’s start point) and a Color. Here, the Stops indicate that the radial gradient will transition from red at the gradient’s start point to white at its endpoint.

The RadialGradient constructor call in lines 48–49 creates a red-white radial gradient that starts with solid red at the shape’s center and transitions to white at 60% of the radial gradient’s radius. The constructor’s arguments are:

  • the focus angle, which specifies the direction of the radial gradient’s focal point from the gradient’s center,

  • the distance of the focal point as a percentage (0.0–1.0)—using 0 for both the focus angle and focal point indicates the gradient should begin from the oval’s center,

  • the center point’s x and y location as percentages (0.0–1.0) of the width and height for the shape being filled,

  • a boolean indicating whether the gradient should scale to fill its shape,

  • a constant from the CycleMethod enum (package javafx.scene.paint) indicating how the color stops are applied and

  • an array of Stop objects—this can also be a comma-separated list of Stops or a List<Stop> object.

Line 50 sets the fill to the new radialGradient, then lines 51–52 call GraphicsContext’s fillOval and strokeOval methods to draw a filled oval and a hollow oval, respectively. Each method receives as arguments the upper-left x-coordinate, upper-left y-coordinate, width and height of the rectangular area in which the oval should be drawn—known as a bounding box. Because the width and height are the same, these calls draw circles.

Drawing an Oval with an ImagePattern Fill

Lines 55–58 draw an oval with a green border and containing an image:

Click here to view code image

54         // draw ellipse with green border and image fill
55         gc.setStroke(Color.GREEN);
56         gc.setFill(new ImagePattern(new Image("yellowflowers.png")));
57         gc.fillOval(340, 10, 200, 90);
58         gc.strokeOval(340, 10, 200, 90);
59

  • Line 55 sets the border color to Color.GREEN.

  • Line 56 sets the fill to an ImagePattern—a subclass of Paint that loads an Image from the local system or from a URL specified as a String. ImagePattern is the class used by the CSS function image-pattern in Section 17.3.

  • Lines 57–58 draw a filled and a hollow oval.

Drawing an Arc with a LinearGradient Fill

Lines 61–68 draw an arc with a purple border and filled with a cyan-white linear gradient:

Click here to view code image

60         // draw arc with purple border and cyan/white linear gradient fill
61         gc.setStroke(Color.PURPLE);
62         Stop[] stopsLinear =
63            {new Stop(0, Color.CYAN), new Stop(1, Color.WHITE)};
64         var linearGradient = new LinearGradient(0, 0, 1, 0,
65            true, CycleMethod.NO_CYCLE, stopsLinear);
66         gc.setFill(linearGradient);
67         gc.fillArc(560, 10, 90, 90, 45, 270, ArcType.ROUND);
68         gc.strokeArc(560, 10, 90, 90, 45, 270, ArcType.ROUND);
69      }
70   }

  • Line 61 sets the border color to Color.PURPLE.

  • Lines 62–65 configure the LinearGradient—the class used by the CSS function linear-gradient in Section 17.3. The constructor’s first four arguments are the endpoint coordinates that represent the direction and angle of the gradient. If the x-coordinates are the same, the gradient is vertical. If the y-coordinates are the same, the gradient is horizontal. All other linear gradients follow a diagonal line. When these values are specified in the range 0.0 to 1.0, and the constructor’s fifth argument is true, the gradient is scaled to fill the shape. The next argument is the CycleMethod. The last argument is an array of Stop objects—again, this can be a comma-separated list of Stops or a List<Stop> object.

Lines 67–68 call GraphicsContext’s fillArc and strokeArc methods to draw a filled arc and a hollow arc, respectively. Each method receives as arguments:

  • the upper-left x-coordinate, upper-left y-coordinate, width and height of the rectangular area (that is, the bounding box) in which the oval should be drawn,

  • the start angle and sweep of the arc in degrees, and

  • a constant from the ArcType enum (package javafx.scene.shape)

Additional GraphicsContext Features

There are many additional GraphicsContext features, which you can explore at

Click here to view code image

https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/canvas/
   GraphicsContext.html

Some of the capabilities that we did not discuss here include:

  • Drawing and filling text—similar to the font features in Section 17.2.

  • Drawing and filling polylines, polygons and paths—similar to the corresponding Shape subclasses in Section 17.4.

  • Applying effects and transforms—similar to the transforms in Section 17.5.

  • Drawing images.

  • Manipulating the individual pixels of a drawing in a Canvas via a PixelWriter.

  • Saving and restoring graphics characteristics via the save and restore methods.

17.12 Three-Dimensional Shapes

 

We’ve demonstrated many two-dimensional graphics capabilities. JavaFX provides several three-dimensional shapes and corresponding capabilities. The three-dimensional shapes are subclasses of Shape3D from the package javafx.scene.shape. In this section, you’ll use Scene Builder to create a Box, a Cylinder and a Sphere and specify several of their properties. Then, in the app’s controller, you’ll create materials that apply color and images to the 3D shapes.13

13. At the time of this writing, 3D shapes are not rendering correctly on M-processor (ARM) Macs in Scene Builder or in the running app, and 3D shapes are not rendering at all on Windows 11 ARM. We’ll post updates to the book’s web page: https://deitel.com/javafp5.

FXML for the Box, Cylinder and Sphere

Figure 17.17 presents the completed FXML that we created with Scene Builder:

  • Lines 16–21 define the Box object.

  • Lines 22–27 define the Cylinder object.

  • Lines 28–29 define the Sphere object.

We dragged objects of these Shape3D subclasses from the Scene Builder Library’s Shapes section onto the design area and gave them the fx:id values box, cylinder and sphere, respectively. We also set the controller to ThreeDimensionalShapesController.

All three shapes are initially gray. The shading in Scene Builder comes from the scene’s default lighting. Though we do not use them here, package javafx.scene’s classes AmbientLight, PointLight, SpotLight and DirectionalLight can be used to add lighting effects. You can also use camera objects to view the scene from different angles and distances. The AmbientLight, PointLight and camera capabilities are located in the Scene Builder Library’s 3D section.

Box Properties

Configure the Box’s properties in the Scene Builder Inspector’s Layout section as follows:

  • Set Width, Height and Depth to 100, making a cube. The depth is measured along the z-axis, which runs perpendicular to your screen. When you move objects along the z-axis, they get bigger as they’re brought toward you and smaller as they’re moved away from you.

  • Set Layout X and Layout Y to 100 to specify the cube’s location.

  • Set Rotate to 30 to specify the rotation angle in degrees. Positive values rotate counter-clockwise.

  • For Rotation Axis, set the X, Y and Z values to 1 to indicate that the Rotate angle should be used to rotate the cube 30 degrees around each axis.

To observe how the Rotate angle and Rotation Axis values affect the Box’s rotation, set two of the three Rotation Axis values to 0, then change the Rotate angle.

Cylinder Properties

Configure the Cylinder’s properties in Scene Builder as follows:

  • Set Height to 100.0 and Radius to 50.

  • Set Layout X and Layout Y to 265 and 100, respectively.

  • Set Rotate to -45 to specify the rotation angle in degrees. Negative values rotate clockwise.

  • For Rotation Axis, set the X, Y and Z values to 1 to indicate that the Rotate angle should be applied to all three axes.

Sphere Properties

Configure the Sphere’s properties in Scene Builder as follows:

  • Set Radius to 60.

  • Set Layout X and Layout Y to 430 and 100, respectively.

ThreeDimensionalShapesController Class

Figure 17.18 presents this app’s controller and final output. The final shapes’ colors and images are created by applying so-called materials to the shapes. A PhongMaterial (package javafx.scene.paint) defines materials for 3D shapes. The name “Phong” is a 3D graphics term. Phong shading is a technique for applying color and shading to 3D surfaces. For more details on this technique, visit

Click here to view code image

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phong_shading
PhongMaterial for the Box

Lines 21–23 configure and set the Box object’s PhongMaterial. The setDiffuseColor method sets the color that’s applied to the Box’s surfaces (that is, sides). The scene’s lighting effects determine the shades of the color applied to each visible surface. These shades change based on the angle from which the light shines on the objects.

PhongMaterial for the Cylinder

Lines 26–28 configure and set the Cylinder object’s PhongMaterial. The setDiffuseMap method sets the Image applied to the Cylinder’s surfaces. Again, the scene’s lighting affects how the image is shaded on the surfaces. In the output, notice that the image is darker at the left and right edges (where less light reaches) and barely visible at the bottom (where almost no light reaches).

PhongMaterial for the Sphere

Lines 31–35 configure and set the Sphere object’s PhongMaterial. We set the diffuse color to red. The setSpecularColor method sets the color of a bright spot that makes a 3D shape appear shiny. The setSpecularPower method determines the intensity of that spot. Try experimenting with different specular powers to observe changes in the bright spot’s intensity.

17.13 FXGL: A Brief Intro to Game Programming with JavaFX

 

Gaming is one of the most popular and entertaining application-development areas. By 2027, the global gaming market is expected to grow to $363.2 billion dollars,14 with mobile games accounting for about one-third of the market.15

14. “Video Games–Worldwide.” Accessed September 30, 2024. https://www.statista.com/outlook/dmo/digital-media/video-games/worldwide.

15. “Mobile Games–Worldwide.” Accessed September 30, 2024. https://www.statista.com/outlook/dmo/digital-media/video-games/mobile-games/worldwide.

FXGL Overview

The open-source, cross-platform FXGL library16,17 adds powerful game-development capabilities to JavaFX. FXGL provides a framework for creating 2D games.18 It combines JavaFX’s capabilities with game-development features, including:

16. “FXGL.” Accessed September 30, 2024. https://github.com/AlmasB/FXGL.

17. “FXGL 11.” Accessed September 30, 2024. https://github.com/AlmasB/FXGL/wiki/FXGL-11.

18. Its 3D features are experimental at the time of this writing.

  • a physics engine for replicating real-world physics, including mass, density, friction, restitution (bounciness), gravity, force, velocity, acceleration and more,

  • collision detection,

  • sound effects, and

  • support for animations and sprites—images or series of images (often represented as one large image) used to add animations that move independently of a game’s background.19

19. Löw, Andrew. “What is a sprite?” Accessed October 4, 2024. https://www.codeandweb.com/knowledgebase/what-is-a-sprite.

FXGL encapsulates complex game-development tasks—such as rendering, player input handling, game-state management and scene transitions—so you can focus on game logic and design. It also supports advanced features like multiplayer capabilities and particle effects, which can be used to generate complex animations like smoke, fire, rain, snow, explosions and more.20 FXGL is cross-platform, so the games you create can run on various operating systems, including Windows, macOS and Linux.

20. “Particle System.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed October 4, 2024. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_system.

17.14 Wrap-Up

In this chapter, we completed our discussion of JavaFX that began in Chapters 15 and 16. Here, we presented various JavaFX graphics and multimedia capabilities. We used external Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) to customize the appearance of JavaFX Nodes, including Labels and objects of various Shape subclasses. We displayed two-dimensional shapes, including lines, rectangles, circles, ellipses, arcs, polylines, polygons and custom paths.

We applied a transform to a Node, rotating 18 Polygon objects around a specific point to create a circle of star shapes. We created a simple video player using class Media to specify the video’s location, class MediaPlayer to load the video and control its playback and class MediaView to display the video.

We animated Nodes with Transition and Timeline animations that change Node properties to new values over time. We used built-in Transition animations to change specific JavaFX Node properties (such as a Node’s stroke and fill colors, opacity, rotation angle and scale). We used Timeline animations with KeyFrames to bounce a Circle around a window, demonstrating that such animations can be used to change any modifiable Node property. We created frame-by-frame animations with AnimationTimer, and we applied JavaFX CSS transitions to a Node’s CSS properties.

Next, we presented various capabilities for drawing on a Canvas Node programmatically using a GraphicsContext object, which supported many of the same drawing characteristics and shapes as Shape Nodes. Finally, we demonstrated the three-dimensional shapes Box, Cylinder and Sphere, and used materials to apply color and images to them. For more information on JavaFX, visit

https://www.jfx-central.com/
https://foojay.io/today/category/javafx/

We briefly introduced FXGL for JavaFX game development.

18.1 Introduction

 

It would be nice if we could focus on performing only one task at a time and doing it well. That’s usually difficult to do in a complex world with so much happening simultaneously. This chapter presents Java’s capabilities for creating and managing multiple tasks. As we’ll demonstrate, this can significantly improve program performance and responsiveness.

Concurrency

When we say that two tasks operate concurrently, we mean they’re both making progress. Until the early 2000s, most computers had only a single processor. Operating systems on such computers executed tasks concurrently by rapidly switching between them, doing a small portion of each before moving on to the next, so all tasks keep progressing. For example, it’s common for personal computers to concurrently accept keyboard input, compile a program, send a file to a printer, receive electronic mail messages over a network and more. Since its inception, Java has supported concurrency.

Parallelism

When we say that two tasks operate in parallel, we mean they’re executing simultaneously. In this sense, parallelism is a subset of concurrency. The human body performs a great variety of operations in parallel. Respiration, blood circulation, digestion, thinking and walking, for example, can occur in parallel, as can all the senses—sight, hearing, touch, smell and taste. It’s believed that this parallelism is possible because the human brain is thought to contain billions of “processors.” Today’s multi-core CPUs have multiple processors that can perform tasks in parallel. A key difference between concurrency and parallelism is that code can execute concurrently by sharing a single core, whereas executing code in parallel requires multiple cores.

Java Concurrency

Java makes concurrency available to you through the language and APIs—we use only API concurrency features in this chapter. Java programs can have multiple threads of execution, each with its own method-call stack, allowing it to execute concurrently with other threads while sharing system resources such as processors, memory and file handles. This is called multithreading. The JVM creates threads to run programs and perform housekeeping tasks such as garbage collection.

A problem with single-threaded programs that can lead to poor responsiveness is that lengthy activities must complete before others can begin. In a multithreaded program, threads can be distributed across multiple cores (if available) so multiple tasks execute in parallel. This enables programs to operate more efficiently and optimize system resource use. Multithreading can also increase performance on single-processor systems—when one thread cannot proceed (because, for example, it’s waiting for the result of an I/O operation), another can use the processor.

Concurrent Programming Uses

We’ll discuss many applications of concurrent programming. For example, when streaming an audio or video over the Internet, the user may not want to wait until the entire audio or video downloads before starting the playback. To solve this problem, multiple threads can be used:

  • one to download the audio or video (later in the chapter, we’ll refer to this as a producer) and

  • another to play it (later in the chapter, we’ll refer to this as a consumer).

These threads proceed concurrently. To avoid choppy playback, an audio/video player synchronizes the threads’ actions (that is, coordinates them) so the player thread doesn’t begin playing until there’s enough audio or video in memory to keep the player thread busy. Producer and consumer threads share memory—we’ll demonstrate one of Java’s concurrent collections that automatically coordinates such threads to ensure correct execution.

Concurrent Programming Is Difficult

Writing multithreaded programs can be error-prone. Although the human mind can perform functions concurrently, jumping between parallel trains of conscious thought can be difficult.

To understand why multithreaded programs can be challenging to write and comprehend, try the following experiment: Open three books to page 1 and try reading the books concurrently. Read a few words from the first book, then a few from the second, then a few from the third, then loop back and read the next few words from the first book, and so on. After this experiment, you’ll appreciate many of the challenges of multithreading— switching between the books, reading briefly, remembering your place in each book, moving the book you’re reading closer so you can read it and pushing the books you’re not reading aside—and, amid all this chaos, trying to comprehend the content of the books!

The reading-multiple-books analogy is similar to context switching in multithreaded applications. To switch between threads, your system must pause one thread, save its state, load another thread’s state and resume that thread’s execution. This context switching affects performance due to the time spent managing threads instead of running code. Frequent context switching makes it harder to process information efficiently.

Use the Prebuilt Classes of the Concurrency APIs Whenever Possible

In programs requiring thread synchronization, most programmers should use the Java Concurrency APIs from package java.util.concurrent that manage synchronization for you, like ArrayBlockingQueue (Section 18.10). The concurrency API classes are

  • written by experts,

  • designed to be correct and operate efficiently,

  • have been thoroughly tested and debugged, and

  • help you avoid common traps and pitfalls.

Section 18.10.8 briefly overviews the Java Concurrency API’s other prebuilt concurrent collections.

Project Loom: Virtual Threads, Structured Concurrency and Scoped Values

In addition to several traditional concurrency and multithreading topics, this chapter focuses on Project Loom’s enhancements to Java’s threading model that provide simpler, lightweight virtual threads (finalized in Java 21). These require significantly less memory than Java’s traditional threads (known as platform threads), enabling applications to launch enormous numbers of concurrent virtual threads to meet the demands of today’s massively parallel applications. Project Loom also reduces the complexity of writing concurrent programs, making concurrency easier to use and get right.

We also introduce two emerging Project Loom technologies—structured concurrency and scoped values.1 Structured concurrency enables programmers to treat multiple threads as a single unit of work (a scope), making it easier to manage those threads, handle errors and reclaim resources no longer needed. Scoped values simplify data sharing among virtual threads in the same scope, reducing the need for complex thread-synchronization techniques. Scoped values become implicit arguments to every method called in a given structured concurrency scope.

1. At the time of this writing, structured concurrency and scoped values were preview features. Once they are finalized, we’ll post the updated examples on our blog at https://deitel.com/blog.

ThreadLocalRandom vs. RandomGenerator

Java’s regular random-number generators, like the one returned by

RandomGenerator.getDefault()

are not designed to be shared among multiple threads. They are not “thread-safe”—when multiple threads share a random-number generator, they can interfere with one another, making the generated values less random. Each thread that calls ThreadLocalRandom’s static method current receives its own RandomGenerator object. This prevents conflicts when parallelSetAll generates random numbers for multiple portions of an array in parallel.

18.4 Creating and Executing Platform Threads with the Executor Framework

 

In Sections 18.2–18.3, we used parallel methods of the Arrays class and parallel streams that automatically “figure out” how to take advantage of your system’s CPU cores to improve performance. You can also create your own custom concurrent tasks.

Creating Concurrent Tasks with the Runnable Interface

You implement the Runnable interface (of package java.lang) to specify a task that can execute concurrently with other tasks. You specify the code that performs your task by overriding the Runnable interface’s run method.

Executing Runnable Objects with an Executor

You execute a Runnable to perform its task, typically using an object that implements the Executor interface. This interface’s execute method receives a Runnable and executes it at some point in the future. When an Executor begins executing a Runnable, it assigns the Runnable to a Thread and calls the Runnable’s run method to perform the specified task. Any method called from a Runnable’s run method executes as part of that task’s Thread.

You obtain an Executor object by calling a static method of the Executors class (package java.util.concurrent). This class’s methods return objects that implement the ExecutorService interface (package java.util.concurrent), which extends Executor and declares additional methods for managing an Executor’s life cycle. ExecutorService objects are AutoCloseable, so you can use them with the try-with-resources statement.

Though it’s possible to create Threads explicitly, Executors have many advantages. For example, some Executors manage a group of platform threads called a thread pool and can reuse existing platform threads to eliminate the overhead of creating new ones for each task. Such Executors can improve performance for CPU-intensive tasks by optimizing the number of threads to ensure that the CPU’s cores stay busy.

Implementing the Runnable Interface

Let’s use a mechanical example to demonstrate creating and executing Runnable tasks. Class PrintTask (Fig. 18.3) implements Runnable (line 5)—each PrintTask can execute concurrently with other tasks. Variable sleepTime (line 8) stores a random integer value from 0 to 5000 milliseconds (line 15)—we did not use ThreadLocalRandom here, as the PrintTask constructor is always called from the main thread. Each thread running a Print-Task sleeps for the amount of time specified by sleepTime, then outputs its task’s name and a message indicating that it’s done sleeping.

A PrintTask executes when a thread calls its run method (lines 19–33). Lines 22–23 output a message indicating the task’s name and that it’s going to sleep for sleepTime milliseconds. Line 24 invokes Thread static method sleep to pause the thread for the specified amount of time. At this point, the thread loses the processor, and the operating system can allow another thread to execute. When the thread awakens, and the operating system eventually assigns it to a processor to continue executing, line 32 outputs a message indicating that the task is done sleeping, then method run terminates.

A Runnable’s run Method Must Catch InterruptedExceptions

The catch handler at lines 26–29 is required because method sleep might throw a checked InterruptedException if a sleeping thread’s interrupt method is called. Recall from Chapter 10 that when you override a method, the throws clause may contain only the same exception types or a subset of those declared in the original method’s throws clause. In the Runnable interface’s definition, method run does not have a throws clause, so we cannot add one in line 20. For this reason, you must catch InterruptedExceptions (and any other checked exceptions) in a Runnable’s run method.

When a thread is interrupted, it’s typically because another part of the program needs it to terminate—perhaps due to an error or another thread having already finished the required task. Every thread has a boolean interrupted status. A thread can periodically check this status by calling Thread static method isInterrupted. If this method returns true, the thread knows it has been interrupted and can decide how to terminate gracefully. When you catch an InterruptedException, the thread’s interrupted status is set to false, which could prevent the thread from terminating. For this reason, it’s considered good practice to set the thread’s interrupt status back to true in the catch handler to ensure that subsequent calls to isInterrupted return true. Line 28 obtains a reference to the currently executing Thread by calling Thread static method currentThread, then uses that Thread’s interrupt method to set the thread’s interrupted status to true.4

4. For detailed information on handling thread interruptions, read Chapter 7 of Java Concurrency in Practice by Brian Goetz, et al., Addison-Wesley Professional, 2006.

Executing PrintTasks Concurrently

Figure 18.4 uses an ExecutorService object to execute PrintTasks. Lines 8–10 create three PrintTasks to execute. Line 18 in the try-with-resources statement calls Executors static method newCachedThreadPool to obtain an ExecutorService that manages a cached thread pool. Such a thread pool executes each task by

  • using an existing platform Thread if one is available in the pool or

  • creating a new platform Thread if no existing ones are available to reuse.

When a task completes, the cached thread pool ExecutorService keeps the platform Thread for 60 seconds. If the program submits another task to the ExecutorService within that time, it reuses the cached Thread to execute that task, eliminating the overhead of creating a new platform thread (we say more about this overhead in Section 18.7). Otherwise, the ExecutorService terminates the Thread and removes it from the cache. Cached thread pools are typically used in programs that execute many short tasks.5

5. “Class Executors.” Accessed February 7, 2025. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/Executors.html#newCachedThreadPool().

Java maps each Thread in a cached thread pool to an operating system thread—the Java documentation refers to these as platform threads. Multi-core systems can schedule multiple platform threads (and the other programs running on your computer) on separate cores, enabling them to execute in parallel. Lines 20–22 use the cached thread pool to execute Runnables—in this case, PrintTasks—at some time in the future. Method execute returns immediately from each invocation—the program does not wait for each PrintTask to finish.

Waiting for Tasks to Complete Execution

After scheduling tasks to execute, you’ll typically want to wait for them to complete—for example, so you can use the tasks’ results, as we’ll do in later examples. When the try-with-resources statement completes execution (line 23), it calls the ExecutorService’s close method, which

  • calls ExecutorService method shutdown to prevent the ExecutorService from accepting new tasks then

  • calls ExecutorService method awaitTermination to wait for all the previously scheduled tasks to complete.

Main Thread

The code in main executes in the main thread, which is created by the JVM. The code in PrintTask’s run method (lines 19–33 of Fig. 18.3) executes sometime after each task is passed to the ExecutorService’s execute method (Fig. 18.4, lines 20–22).

Sample Outputs

Each task displays its name and sleep time then puts its thread to sleep. In most cases, the thread running the task with the shortest sleep time awakens first (though this is not guaranteed), then indicates it’s done sleeping and terminates. In sample outputs, note that the tasks did not go to sleep in the same order they were launched. This illustrates that we cannot predict the order in which the tasks will start executing, even if we know the order in which they were created and started. Similarly, we cannot predict when a thread that awakens from a sleep will be assigned to a processor to continue executing.

18.5 Project Loom Overview

 

Section 18.4 executed PrintTasks using resource-intensive platform threads. Each platform thread has its own default method-call stack size—typically one to two megabytes (depending on the hardware)6 to keep track of methods called by the task in that thread. The number of platform threads is limited not only by the amount of available memory but also by7

6. “The java Command.” Accessed February 9, 2025. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/specs/man/java.html.

7. Summary of responses from ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity to the prompt “What are the operating system limits for threads in an application?” https://chatgpt.com, https://claude.ai, https://gemini.google.com/app and https://perplexity.ai.

  • operating system limits on threads per process (i.e., per application) and

  • the overheads of scheduling and executing large numbers of concurrent tasks and sharing resources among those tasks.

These limitations make it difficult for developers to build scalable applications requiring thousands or even millions of concurrent tasks—like those that handle the enormous number of interactions between users and popular social media apps, such as YouTube, Face-book, WhatsApp, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, Reddit and X. In Java, such applications have typically required complex programming techniques and frameworks to reduce overhead and share limited resources.

Project Loom enhances Java with three new concurrency capabilities that simplify massively parallel application development:

  • virtual threads (Sections 18.6–18.7),8

  • structured concurrency (Section 18.8)9 and

  • scoped values (Section 18.8).10

8. “JEP 444: Virtual Threads.” Accessed February 9, 2025. https://openjdk.org/jeps/444.

9. “JEP 499: Structured Concurrency (Fourth Preview).” Accessed February 9, 2025. https://openjdk.org/jeps/499.

10. “JEP 487: Scoped Values (Fourth Preview).” Accessed February 9, 2025. https://openjdk.org/jeps/487.

As we’ll discuss in Section 18.6.1, virtual threads do not replace platform threads—they have different use-cases.

Virtual threads were finalized in Java 21. Structured concurrency and scoped values were preview features at the time of this writing. If our code examples require changes when the final structured concurrency and scoped values versions are released, we’ll post updates on our blog at https://deitel.com/blog.

Virtual Threads Have Significantly Less Overhead than Platform Threads

Virtual threads are lightweight and managed by the JVM, not the operating system. Rather than pre-allocating a large method-call stack, the JVM allocates a few-hundred-byte stack chunk for each virtual thread. This stack chunk grows and shrinks dynamically based on the virtual thread’s required number of method-call stack frames—possibly as few as one if the task performs all its work in one method’s body.11,12 Due to the low virtual-thread memory requirements, an application can create thousands or even millions of virtual threads without overwhelming system resources. Creating millions of platform threads would quickly exhaust system resources, possibly causing the program to crash with an OutOfMemoryError.

11. “JEP 444: Virtual Threads.” Accessed February 9, 2025. https://openjdk.org/jeps/444.

12. Goetz, Brian. “Virtual Threads: New Foundations for High-Scale Java Applications.” InfoQ, November 2, 2022. Accessed February 9, 2025. https://www.infoq.com/articles/java-virtual-threads/.

18.6 Creating and Executing Virtual Threads with the Executor Framework

Java provides several ways to execute tasks with virtual threads. Section 18.6.1 modifies Section 18.4’s PrintTask example to demonstrate an ExecutorService that creates a separate virtual thread for each task. Section 18.6.2 shows how to create Thread objects for virtual threads.

18.6.1 Launching Virtual Threads with a Thread-Per-Task Executor

A primary virtual threads use-case is for server software that handles massive numbers of concurrent requests where each spends most of its time blocked from continuing to execute until I/O requests complete, such as

  • web servers that respond to user requests by returning web pages to their web browsers or

  • application servers that return the results of database queries to applications.

Platform threads are more appropriate for CPU-intensive tasks, such as sorting and long-running calculations. Arrays method parallelSort uses platform threads to execute the subtasks that sort portions of an array.

As an example of massive numbers of concurrent requests, consider the social media site X.com. In December 2024, X had 4.6 billion visits, and each visitor viewed 12.35 pages on average.13 If we assume each page view requires one server request,14 there were approximately 56.81 billion requests (4.6 billion times 12.35) handled by X.com’s servers—about 21,200 requests per second. Lightweight virtual threads enable Java servers to handle huge numbers of concurrent requests like this with thread-per-request code—that is, creating a new virtual thread for each request.

13. Similarweb, “X.com Traffic Analytics & Market Share.” Accessed February 9, 2025. https://www.similarweb.com/website/x.com/#overview.

14. A request for web-based content often requires many sub-requests for items like images, videos and advertisements that a web browser renders in a web page.

Launching Virtual Threads with an ExecutorService

Figure 18.5 reuses Fig. 18.3’s PrintTask class and launches virtual threads. Line 18 of Fig. 18.5 calls the Executors class’s static newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor method to get an ExecutorService that launches a new virtual thread for each task you submit. Lines 20–22 call the ExecutorService’s execute method to launch each PrintTask.

Carriers, Mounting and Unmounting

A virtual thread’s carrier is the platform thread that runs the virtual thread. When the JVM schedules a virtual thread for execution, it mounts the virtual thread on a carrier. Then, the operating system is responsible for scheduling the carrier’s execution. The JVM unmounts a virtual thread from its carrier when it blocks for I/O, sleeps or completes its task. The runtime can then mount a different virtual thread on that carrier to efficiently use the system’s platform-thread resources.

Non-Daemon vs. Daemon Threads15

15. “Class Thread.” Accessed February 9, 2025. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Thread.html.

Platform threads may be non-daemon or daemon threads. A Java app runs while its non-daemon threads are still executing their tasks. Examples of non-daemon threads include:

  • the thread where the main method executes and

  • a JavaFX app’s event-handling thread.

A daemon thread typically performs background tasks that support a program’s execution. Examples of daemon threads include:

  • Java’s background garbage collector thread that reclaims unused objects from memory and

  • an “auto-save” background thread that watches for changes you make to a document and automatically saves them—a common feature in many apps that process files like documents, spreadsheets and more.

A Java app terminates if the only remaining threads are daemon threads.

Thread Defaults

By default, a platform thread is a non-daemon thread unless you

  • launch it from a daemon thread or

  • call setDaemon(true) on it to make it a daemon thread.

Every virtual thread is always a daemon thread.

Awaiting Virtual Thread Completion

If you want your program to remain running until its virtual threads’ tasks complete, you must prevent main from terminating. The try-with-resources statement and ExecutorService manage this for you. When the try-with-resources statement terminates, it automatically calls the ExecutorService’s close method, which, in turn, calls

  • the ExecutorService’s shutdown method to prevent the ExecutorService from accepting new tasks and

  • the ExecutorService’s awaitTermination method to wait for the ExecutorSer-vice’s previously launched tasks to complete execution.

18.6.2 Other Ways to Launch Virtual Threads

Thread Method startVirtualThread

Platform threads and virtual threads are each instances of the java.lang package’s Thread class, but a virtual thread is managed entirely by the JVM. If you need

  • more control over a virtual thread via class Thread’s methods or

  • a convenient way to launch a virtual thread without using an ExecutorService,

you can use class Thread’s static method startVirtualThread. This method receives a Runnable, launches a virtual thread to execute it and returns a reference to the virtual thread’s Thread object. For example, the following statement creates a virtual thread for the PrintTask object task1:

Click here to view code image

var virtualThread = Thread.startVirtualThread(task1);

In this case, if your program needs the task’s result, you must somehow wait for it to complete—typically by calling the Thread’s join method before main terminates, as in:

virtualThread.join();

Otherwise, main might terminate before the virtual thread executes its task.

Thread Method ofVirtual

When you need to specify virtual threads’ configuration options, you can use class Thread’s static method ofVirtual, which returns a Thread.Builder.OfVirtual object.16,17 This object uses the builder design pattern—a common technique for constructing complex objects step-by-step via chained method calls.18,19 The builder design pattern is handy for flexible object configuration—you call only the builder’s methods that add the options you need. Without this pattern, a Java class might require many overloaded constructors for each possible combination of options.

16. “Interface Thread.Builder.OfVirtual.” Accessed February 9, 2025. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Thread.Builder.OfVirtual.html.

17. Thread’s static method ofPlatform returns a Thread.Builder.OfPlatform object for similar creation and configuration of platform threads.

18. Bloch, Joshua. Effective Java. 3rd ed. Upper Saddle River, NJ: Addison-Wesley, 2018.

19. Kiwy, Frank. “Exploring Joshua Bloch’s Builder design pattern in Java.” May 28, 2021. Accessed February 9, 2025. https://blogs.oracle.com/javamagazine/post/exploring-joshua-blochs-builder-design-pattern-in-java.

A Thread.Builder.OfVirtual object enables you to specify several virtual thread options, including:

  • the virtual thread’s name,

  • a virtual thread’s name concatenated with a specified counter value—useful when launching multiple virtual threads to give each a unique name and

  • a method to call when an uncaught exception occurs in a virtual thread.

In the builder design pattern, you call a static method to get a builder object. Each subsequent method you call on the builder object adds a configuration option and returns a reference to the builder object so you can add more options. In the case of Thread.Builder.OfVirtual object, the last call in the chain is one of the following:

  • start creates a virtual thread to execute its Runnable argument, schedules the thread for execution and returns a reference to the corresponding Thread object.

  • factory returns a reference to a ThreadFactory that can create virtual threads with the settings specified in the previous calls to the builder object’s methods.

  • unstarted creates a virtual thread to execute its Runnable argument and returns a reference to the Thread object but does not start it. In this case, you must subsequently call the Thread’s start method to execute the virtual thread.

For example, assuming the variable id contains 1 and task is a Runnable object, the following chained method call would create a new virtual thread named "Task1", schedule the Runnable for execution and return a reference to the corresponding Thread object:

Thread thread =
   Thread.ofVirtual()
         .name("Task", id)
         .start(task);

Again, you must call thread.join() if you want to ensure the thread executes before the program terminates.

18.7 Profiling Platform vs. Virtual Threads20

20. This section’s example was inspired by Brian Goetz’s intro to virtual threads in the article “Virtual Threads: New Foundations for High-Scale Java Applications.” InfoQ, November 2, 2022. Accessed January 31, 2025. https://www.infoq.com/articles/java-virtual-threads/.

In real-world applications—such as social media web servers handling millions to billions of requests per month—efficiently performing large numbers of concurrent tasks is crucial. As we mentioned, platform threads have large memory overhead and map one-to-one to operating system threads, making applications that use them more complicated to scale for massive numbers of concurrent tasks. Virtual threads address this limitation by enabling millions of lightweight threads to run concurrently with minimal overhead. To demonstrate this, we’ll build an example that executes large numbers of tasks using platform and virtual threads.

18.7.1 Future and Callable Interfaces

Each task in the next example returns a result. Interface Runnable’s run method returns void, so it cannot return a value. Interface Callable (package java.util.concurrent) fixes this limitation—its call method returns a value representing a task’s result. Callables typically run concurrently with other Runnables and Callables. ExecutorService method submit executes its Callable argument and returns an object that implements the Future interface (package java.util.concurrent)—this represents the Callable’s result, which will be available at some point in the future. The Future interface’s get method returns the task’s result, possibly blocking the calling thread to wait until that result is available. The interface also provides methods that enable you to

  • cancel a Callable’s execution,

  • determine whether the Callable was canceled and

  • determine whether the Callable completed its task.

18.7.2 Threading Approaches We’ll Use

Figure 18.6 demonstrates virtual threads vs. platform threads handling large numbers of concurrent tasks that simulate blocking operations. The example submits tasks to three ExecutorService objects that manage the tasks with the following threading approaches:

  • a fixed thread pool of 1000 pre-allocated platform threads that are shared among all the submitted tasks,

  • a cached thread pool of platform threads that dynamically adjusts its number of threads based on demand and

  • a separate virtual thread per task—because virtual threads use minimal resources and are easy to create in large numbers, you should not pool them.21

21. “JEP 444: Virtual Threads.” Accessed February 9, 2025. https://openjdk.org/jeps/444.

We split the example into pieces for discussion purposes. Lines 3–9 import the classes and interfaces used in this example.

18.7.3 Launching and Timing Large Numbers of Concurrent Tasks

Method executeAndTimeThreads (lines 13–48) manages the process of launching and timing the execution of large numbers of concurrent tasks. For demo purposes, each task in this example sleeps for one second to simulate blocking, then calculates and returns the square of a long value. We sum these squared values and display them in the sample outputs. Method executeAndTimeThreads requires three arguments:

  • tasks—the number of concurrent tasks the method should execute,

  • threadType—a String description of the threading approach used and

  • executor—an ExecutorService implementation that creates the threads.

Click here to view code image

12      // execute and time threads; sum squares of 1 to number of tasks
13      private static void executeAndTimeThreads(int tasks,
14         String threadType, ExecutorService executor) throws Exception {
15         var clock = InstantSource.system(); // system clock for timing
16
17         // stores Futures for all the launched tasks
18         var futures = new ArrayList<Future<Long>>(tasks);
19
20         System.out.printf(
21            "Executing %d tasks on %s...%n", tasks, threadType);
22         var start = clock.instant();
23
24         // auto-closes the ExecutorService at the end of the try block;
25         // automatically waits for all tasks to complete
26         try (executor) {
27            // launch the number of tasks specified by tasks parameter
28            LongStream.rangeClosed(1, tasks).forEach(value ->
29               futures.add(executor.submit(() -> {
30                  Thread.sleep(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); // simulate blocking
31                  return value * value;
32               }))
33            );
34         }
35
36         // sum the results from the Futures
37         long sum = 0;
38         for (var future : futures) {
39            sum += future.get();
40         }
41
42         var end = clock.instant();
43
44         // display results
45         System.out.printf("Execution time: %.2f seconds%n",
46            Duration.between(start, end).toMillis() / 1000.0);
47         System.out.printf("Sum of squares 1-%d: %d%n%n", tasks, sum);
48      }
49

The method operates as follows:

  • Line 15 gets the system clock for the timing operations.

  • Line 18 creates an ArrayList to store Future objects for accessing each task’s results.

  • Lines 20–21 display the number of tasks being performed and the threading approach used in this call to executeAndTimeThreads.

  • Line 22 records the system time before launching any tasks.

  • Lines 26–34 are the try-with-resources statement in which we submit the tasks. We use a LongStream to count from 1 to tasks. For each value, we use the executor to submit a task—in this case, a lambda expression that implements the Callable interface, telling the thread to sleep for one second (to simulate a blocking), then returns the squared value. We store the Future<Long> returned by each call to submit in an ArrayList—we’ll use this to get all the tasks’ results later. When the stream finishes launching the tasks, control reaches the try-with-resources statement’s closing brace, automatically closing the executor and waiting for the launched tasks to complete execution.

  • When all the tasks complete, lines 37–40 total all the tasks’ results to determine the sum of the squares of the values from 1 through tasks.

  • Line 42 records the system time after the tasks and final calculation complete execution.

  • Lines 45–47 calculate and display the total execution time and final sum.

18.7.4 Testing the Threading Approaches

In the main method (lines 50–73):

  • Lines 52–55 ensure the program was launched with one command-line argument. This value represents the number of threads to create, so we convert it to an int (line 58).

  • Lines 61–63 invoke executeAndTimeThreads, passing the number of tasks to launch, a description of the kind of threading that will be used to execute tasks and an ExecutorService to launch the tasks. In this case, we use an ExecutorService that manages a fixed-size pool of 1000 platform threads. This thread pool can execute only 1000 tasks concurrently. Additional tasks must wait for executing tasks to complete before they can be assigned to threads in the pool.

  • Lines 66–68 invoke executeAndTimeThreads with an ExecutorService that manages a cached thread pool, which dynamically adjusts its number of threads based on demand.

  • Lines 71–72 invoke executeAndTimeThreads with an ExecutorService that creates a virtual thread per task.

Click here to view code image

50      public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
51         // check for proper command-line arguments
52         if (args.length != 1) {
53            System.out.println("Usage: PlatformAndVirtualThreads <count>");
54            System.exit(1);
55         }
56
57         // get number of threads to launch
58         final int TASKS = Integer.parseInt(args[0]);
59
60         // execute and time platform threads with fixed thread pool
61         executeAndTimeThreads(TASKS,
62            "Platform Threads (fixed pool of 1000 threads)",
63            Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1000));
64
65         // execute and time platform threads with cached thread pool
66         executeAndTimeThreads(TASKS,
67            "Platform Threads (cached thread pool)",
68            Executors.newCachedThreadPool());
69
70         // execute and time virtual threads

72            "Virtual Threads", Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor());
73      }
74   }

18.7.5 Performance Analysis

The following sample executions for 1,000, 5,000, 10,000 and 50,000 tasks were performed on a MacBook Pro with an M2 MAX processor with 96GB of RAM. Depending on your system configuration, you may not be able to execute as many tasks (possibly running out of memory for large numbers of tasks), or you may be able to execute even more than we demonstrate here. You can run the example with the following command

Click here to view code image

java PlatformAndVirtualThreads numberOfTasks

where numberOfTasks should be an integer representing the number of tasks to launch. The sample executions reveal interesting performance comparisons.

1,000 Tasks

There’s little difference in execution times for the three threading approaches for 1,000 tasks—virtual threads had a slight advantage. In this case, the throughput using a fixed pool of platform threads is about 962 tasks-per-second (1000 / 1.04), using a cached pool of platform threads is about 971 (1000 / 1.03) and using virtual threads is about 980 tasks-per-second (1000 / 1.02):

Click here to view code image

Executing 1000 tasks on Platform Threads (fixed pool of 1000 threads)...
Execution time: 1.04 seconds
Sum of squares 1-1000: 333833500

Executing 1000 tasks on Platform Threads (cached thread pool)...
Execution time: 1.03 seconds
Sum of squares 1-1000: 333833500

Executing 1000 tasks on Virtual Threads...
Execution time: 1.02 seconds
Sum of squares 1-1000: 333833500
5,000 Tasks

In the sample execution for 5,000 tasks, the fixed-thread pool’s throughput (986 tasks-per-second) is similar to that of 1,000—the number of tasks-per-second this pool can handle is limited by the fixed number of threads in the pool. There are not enough platform threads to handle all the tasks, so many tasks must wait until threads become available. The cached pool throughput increased to 3,759 tasks-per-second and the virtual threads throughput increased to 4,762 tasks-per-second. The cached pool of platform threads and the virtual threads scale better than the fixed pool of platform threads, with virtual threads again performing best.

Sum of squares 1-5000: 41679167500

Executing 5000 tasks on Platform Threads (cached thread pool)...
Execution time: 1.33 seconds
Sum of squares 1-5000: 41679167500

Executing 5000 tasks on Virtual Threads...
Execution time: 1.05 seconds
Sum of squares 1-5000: 41679167500
10,000 Tasks

The Oracle virtual threads documentation indicates that “if your application never has 10,000 virtual threads or more, it is unlikely to benefit from virtual threads.”22 In the sample execution for 10,000 tasks, the benefits of virtual threads for large numbers of blocking tasks become more apparent. The fixed pool’s throughput is 992 tasks-per-second—similar in scale to the throughput for 1,000 tasks and 5,000 tasks. The cached pool throughput increased to 7,518 tasks-per-second and the virtual threads throughput to 9,523 tasks-per-second. Again, the cached pool of platform threads and the virtual threads scale better, but the spread between the tasks-per-second of virtual threads and the cached pool of platform threads increased.

This enables applications with large numbers of blocking tasks to scale without the limitations of traditional platform threads.

18.8 Structured Concurrency and Scoped Values

 

This section introduces Project Loom’s two other key features—structured concurrency and scoped values:

  • Structured concurrency simplifies task management by enabling developers to treat groups of virtual threads performing related tasks as a single unit and program with them in a simple statement-by-statement sequential programming style. This makes the code more readable and easier to maintain, modify and debug. It also avoids more complex asynchronous programming techniques, such as reactive programming.23 Structured concurrency also simplifies resource management and error handling because those sequential statements can be placed in familiar try and try-with-resources statements.

  • Scoped values enable a task and its subtasks to share immutable data in a structured concurrency scope. They fix problems associated with ThreadLocal variables, introduced in Java almost three decades ago.24 Scoped values become implicit arguments to every method called from that structured concurrency scope.

23. The details of reactive programming are beyond this book’s scope. For some details on how virtual threads are better than reactive techniques, read: Goetz, Brian. “Virtual Threads: New Foundations for High-Scale Java Applications.” InfoQ, November 2, 2022. Accessed February 9, 2025. https://www.infoq.com/articles/java-virtual-threads/.

24. The details of ThreadLocal variables are beyond this book’s scope. For more information on how scoped values are better than ThreadLocal variables, visit https://openjdk.org/jeps/487 and see Generative AI Exercise 18.2.

Example Overview

To demonstrate structured concurrency and scoped values, let’s modify Section 11.6’s OpenWeatherMap web-services example that returns the current weather for a specified city. Recall that virtual threads are primarily used for large numbers of concurrent tasks that spend most of their time blocking—a web-service request blocks until its results are available or the request fails. Let’s assume we’d like to build an application in which each user can submit a request that specifies a city for which the user would like the current weather and the forecast for the next few days—these are separate OpenWeatherMap web-service requests. As in Section 11.6, we’ll use the Jackson library to parse the JSON responses for convenient access to the weather data.

For demo purposes, we’ll build this as a command-line app that simulates “requests” (the individual cities) as command-line arguments. We’ll use thread-per-request handling, launching a virtual thread for each request. That thread, in turn, will launch two subtasks in separate virtual threads so they may proceed concurrently:

  • one to invoke the OpenWeatherMap web service that returns the city’s current weather and

  • one to invoke the OpenWeatherMap web service that returns the city’s five-day forecast in three-hour increments.

If a subtask fails, we’ll consider that an error for which we’d like the overall request and its subtasks to terminate immediately—structured concurrency can do this automatically. In addition, the request and its subtasks require a shared piece of data—the city for which to get the weather. This information does not change for a particular request’s duration, so we’ll use a scoped value to share that immutable data between the virtual thread handling the request and its subtask virtual threads.

Compiling and Running This Example

Structured concurrency and scoped values were preview features at the time of this writing and some changes are expected before they become standard Java features. We’ll post updates on the book’s website at

https://deitel.com/javafp5

Until they become standard, you must enable them when compiling and running the code. This example also uses the Jackson open-source library located in the libs subfolder with this chapter’s examples. To compile the program on macOS, enter the command:

Click here to view code image

javac --enable-preview -source 23 -cp ".:../libs/*" WeatherApp.java

where

  • The --enable-preview option indicates that we use preview features.

  • The -source 23 option indicates that we’re compiling with Java 23.

These options can be removed once structured concurrency and scoped values are official Java features. On Windows, replace the forward slashes (/) with backslashes (\) and the colon (:) with a semicolon (;).

To run the code on macOS, enter the following command

Click here to view code image

java --enable-preview -cp ".:../libs/*" WeatherApp Boston \
   "New Orleans" "Los Angeles"

On Windows, replace the backslash (\) with a caret (^) if you’re using a Command Prompt window or a backtick (`) if you’re using a PowerShell window. Multiword city names must be enclosed in quotes (""); otherwise, each word is treated as a separate city.

The main method (lines 53–83) simulates a server that implements thread-per-request handling. The try-with-resources statement gets an ExecutorService for launching virtual threads (line 61). After launching a virtual thread for each request (i.e., city), this statement closes the ExecutorService and waits for all the launched virtual threads to complete. The loop in lines 62–81 uses the executor to launch a virtual thread for each city. The lambda expression in lines 66–79 defines a Runnable task:
