The getWeather method (lines 86–116) uses the CITY ScopedValue’s get method (line 89) to get the city to use in the task and subtasks launched from getWeather. The get method automatically accesses the scoped value in the ScopedValue.Carrier object associated with the current task. Lines 92–97 form the URLs for the two OpenWeatherMap web-service requests we’ll perform. Next, the try-with-resources statement (lines 100–115) creates a new StructuredTaskScope (line 100). For this example, we consider the task in method getWeather successful only if both web-service requests complete successfully. The expression in line 100

Click here to view code image

new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()

creates a StructuredTaskScope that shuts down on failure. If a subtask launched in this scope fails, the other subtasks will be interrupted so they can shut down. Lines 101–104 call StructuredTaskScope’s fork method to launch virtual threads that execute Callable tasks—implemented by the lambdas in lines 102 and 104. Each lambda calls our generic requestData method (discussed momentarily), passing the URL for the web-service request and the Class object (WeatherData.class or ForecastResponse.class) the Jackson library will use when extracting the data items we need from the JSON responses.

Method requestData returns an object of the appropriate record class (WeatherData or ForecastResponse) for each request. Each fork call returns an object that implements the StructuredTaskScope.Subtask interface, which we’ll use to access the subtasks’ results when they become available.

Click here to view code image

85      // use structured concurrency to request current weather and forecast
86      public static String getWeather() throws Exception {
87         // URL encode the city parameter
88         String encodedCity =
89            URLEncoder.encode(CITY.get(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
90
91         // construct API URLs
92         String currentWeatherUrl = String.format(
93            "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=%s" +
94            "&units=metric&appid=%s", encodedCity, API_KEY);
95         String forecastUrl = String.format(
96            "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/forecast?q=%s" +
97            "&units=metric&appid=%s", encodedCity, API_KEY);
98
99         // use StructuredTaskScope to manage concurrent tasks
100        try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) {
101           var currentWeatherTask = scope.fork(
102              () -> requestData(currentWeatherUrl, WeatherData.class));
103           var forecastTask = scope.fork(
104              () -> requestData(forecastUrl, ForecastResponse.class));
105
106           scope.join(); // waits for responses
107           scope.throwIfFailed(); // throws an exception if a task fails
108
109           // tasks completed successfully, retrieve results
110           WeatherData weatherData = currentWeatherTask.get();
111           ForecastResponse forecastResponse = forecastTask.get();
112
113           // format and return output
114           return formatWeatherOutput(weatherData, forecastResponse);
115        }
116     }
117

Line 106 calls StructuredTaskScope’s join method to wait for the two web-service requests to complete. If either fails, line 107 calls StructuredTaskScope’s throwIfFailed method to ensure the task’s exception can be handled. In this example, we handle it in main rather than in a catch handler following the try-with-resources statement. If both tasks complete successfully, lines 110–111 get the WeatherData or ForecastResponse objects by calling StructuredTaskScope.Subtask method get. Finally, line 114 calls method formatWeatherOutput to produce the weather report and returns the resulting String to main for display at lines 70–71.

requestData Method

The requestData method (lines 119–138) uses the techniques presented in Section 11.6 to

  • build an HttpRequest (lines 121–122),

  • submit the request via an HttpClient and wait for the response (lines 125–126),

  • check whether the response was successful (lines 123–133), and

  • deserialize the JSON data into a record object (line 137).

118     // generic method to retrieve JSON data from OpenWeatherMap API
119     private static <T> T requestData(String url, Class<T> type)
120        throws Exception {
121        // build the request to the OpenWeatherMap web service
122        HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
123           .uri(URI.create(url)).GET().build();
124
125        // send the HTTP request and get the response
126        HttpResponse<String> response = HTTP_CLIENT.send(request,
127           HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
128
129        // check if the request was successful; otherwise, throw Exception
130        if (response.statusCode() != 200) {
131           throw new Exception(String.format(
132              "Error: HTTP status %d\n", response.statusCode()));
133        }
134
135        // use Jackson library to deserialize the JSON response
136        // into the format specified by type
137        return new ObjectMapper().readValue(response.body(), type);
138     }

formatWeatherOutput Method

The formatWeatherOutput method (lines 141–174) receives the record objects containing the data from the two web-service requests then creates a formatted weather report:

  • Lines 145–146 get the current temperature and convert it from Celsius to Fahrenheit.

  • Lines 149–152 create a DateTimeFormatter configured to display the date and time in the format yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm.

  • Lines 155–164 use stream processing to convert the first 16 items in the Fore-castResponse’s List<ForecastEntry> into formatted text containing the date, time, weather description and temperature in both Celsius and Fahrenheit.

  • Lines 166–173 return the result of calling String method formatted on a format String implemented as a text block, inserting the city’s name, the current day’s weather description, the current Celsius and Fahrenheit temperatures and the forecastInfo from lines 155–164.

143
144        // current temperature

146        double tempF = (tempC * 9 / 5) + 32;

153

159              return String.format(
160                 "%s: %s; temp: %.1f C (%.1f F)",
161                 dateFormatter.format(Instant.ofEpochSecond(f.dt())),
162                 f.weather()[0].main(), tempCForecast, tempFForecast);
163           })
164           .collect(Collectors.joining("\n"));
165
166        return """
167           %s Weather: %s
168           Temperature: %.1f C (%.1f F)
169
170           Forecast:
171           %s""".formatted(weatherData.name(),
172              weatherData.weather()[0].description(),

18.9 Thread Synchronization Overview

 

When multiple threads share an object, and it’s modified by one or more of them, indeterminate results may occur unless access to the shared object is managed correctly:

  • If one thread is updating a shared object and another thread tries to update it at the same time, it’s uncertain which thread’s update takes effect.

  • Similarly, if one thread is updating a shared object and another thread tries to read it at the same time, it’s uncertain whether the reading thread will read the old value that’s no longer valid (known as a stale value) or the new one.

In such cases, the program’s behavior cannot be trusted. Sometimes the program will produce the correct results, and sometimes it won’t, and there won’t be any indication that the shared object was manipulated incorrectly.

The problem can be solved by giving only one thread at a time exclusive access to code that manipulates the shared object. During that time, other threads desiring to access the object are kept waiting. When the thread with exclusive access finishes manipulating the object, one of the waiting threads can proceed. This process, called thread synchronization, coordinates access to shared data by multiple concurrent threads. By synchronizing threads in this manner, you can ensure that each thread accessing a shared object excludes all other threads from doing so simultaneously—this is called mutual exclusion.

Java provides extensive mechanisms designed to ensure mutually exclusive access to shared mutable data, from low-level capabilities that enable developers to manage mutual exclusion to high-level ones in which the Java APIs handle mutual exclusion for you. One of the challenges of multithreaded programming is spotting the errors—they may occur so infrequently and unpredictably that a broken program does not produce incorrect results during testing, creating the illusion that the program is correct. For this reason, most developers should work with the predefined concurrent collections that handle thread synchronization for you. These collections are designed by Java concurrency experts to work correctly and perform optimally in applications that share mutable data.

Immutable Data

Thread synchronization is necessary only for shared mutable data—that is, data that may change during its lifetime. With shared immutable data that will not change, it’s impossible for a thread to read old or incorrect values due to another thread’s manipulation of that data.

When you share immutable data across threads, declare the corresponding data fields final to indicate that the variable’s values will not change after they’re initialized. This prevents accidental modification of the shared data, which could compromise thread safety. Labeling object references as final indicates that the reference will not change, but it does not guarantee that the referenced object is immutable—this depends entirely on the object’s properties. But, it’s still good practice to mark references that will not change as final.

As a good practice, declare data fields you do not expect to change as final. Primitive variables that are declared as final can safely be shared across threads. An object reference declared as final ensures that the object it refers to will be fully constructed and initialized before it’s used by the program, preventing the reference from pointing to another object.

18.10 Producer/Consumer Relationship with ArrayBlockingQueue

 

A common scenario in which multiple threads access shared mutable data is in a producer/consumer relationship:

  • The producer portion of a program generates data and stores it in a shared object, and

  • the consumer portion of the program reads data from the shared object and processes it.

Examples of Producer/Consumer Relationship

One example of a producer/consumer relationship is print spooling. Although a printer might not be available when you want to print from an application (i.e., the producer), you can still “complete” the print task, as the data is temporarily placed on disk until the printer becomes available. Similarly, when the printer (i.e., a consumer) is available, it doesn’t have to wait until a current user wants to print. The spooled print jobs can print when the printer becomes available. Another example of the producer/consumer relationship is an application that backs up data to a storage device—such as a solid-state drive (SSD)—by placing data in a fixed-size buffer, which is emptied as the storage device writes the data.

Generative AI

1 Prompt genAIs for real-world Java examples of producer/consumer relationships.

18.10.1 Synchronization and State Dependence

In a multithreaded producer/consumer relationship, a producer thread generates data and places it in a shared object called a buffer or a queue. A consumer thread reads data from the buffer. This relationship requires synchronization to ensure that values are produced and consumed properly to prevent data corruption:

  • Data can be lost or garbled if the producer places new data into the shared buffer before the consumer reads the previous data.

  • Also, data can be incorrectly duplicated if the consumer consumes data again before the producer produces the next value.

Operations on the buffer data shared by a producer and consumer thread are also state-dependent. As an example of state dependence, consider an electric vehicle. You can’t drive an electric vehicle if its battery is not charged, and you can’t charge an electric vehicle’s battery more, if it’s already fully charged. Similarly, a producer and consumer should proceed only if the buffer is in the correct state:

  • If the buffer is in a not-full state, the producer may produce.

  • If the buffer is in a not-empty state, the consumer may consume.

All operations that access the buffer must use synchronization to ensure that data is written to the buffer or read from the buffer only if the buffer is in the proper state:

  • If the producer attempts to write a new value into a full buffer, the producer thread must wait until there’s space to write the value.

  • If a consumer thread attempts to read a value from an empty buffer, the consumer must wait for new data to become available.

18.10.2 Class ArrayBlockingQueue

A reliable way to synchronize producers and consumers is to use classes that implement the synchronization for you. The java.util.concurrent package’s ArrayBlockingQueue class defines a fully implemented, thread-safe buffer class that implements the interface BlockingQueue. Among its methods, this interface declares:

  • method put to place an element at the tail of a BlockingQueue, waiting if the queue is full, and

  • method take to remove an element from the head of the BlockingQueue, waiting if the queue is empty.

These methods make class ArrayBlockingQueue a good choice for implementing a shared buffer. Because method put blocks until there’s room in the buffer to write data, and method take blocks until there’s new data to read:

  • the producer must produce a value first,

  • the consumer correctly consumes only after the producer writes a value, and

  • the producer correctly produces the next value (after the first) only after the consumer reads the previous (or first) value.

ArrayBlockingQueue stores the shared mutable data in an array, the size of which is specified as ArrayBlockingQueue’s constructor argument. An ArrayBlockingQueue is fixed in size and will not expand to accommodate extra elements.

18.10.3 Overview of the Producer/Consumer Example

Our next example (Figs. 18.8–18.10) implements a producer/consumer relationship with proper synchronization provided by a one-element ArrayBlockingQueue. The producer thread writes the numbers 1 through 10 into the shared ArrayBlockingQueue. The consumer thread reads this data from the shared ArrayBlockingQueue. Each value the producer thread writes must be consumed by the consumer thread exactly once. To help confirm this,

  • the producer thread will output each value it writes (produces) and add the values to a running total, and

  • the consumer thread will output each value it reads (consumes) and add the values to a running total.

If the producer writes each value from 1–10 exactly once and the consumer reads each value from 1–10 exactly once, each thread’s total of the values should be 55.

To further emphasize that the ArrayBlockingQueue provides the synchronization, the producer and consumer threads each sleep for random intervals of up to 3,000 milliseconds between attempting to write or read a value, respectively. As a result, we do not know when the producer thread will attempt to write a new value into the shared buffer or when the consumer thread will attempt to read what’s in the shared buffer. The program consists of the following interface and classes:

  • interface Buffer (Fig. 18.8),

  • class BlockingBuffer (Fig. 18.9) and

  • class BlockingBufferTest (Fig. 18.10).

18.10.4 Interface Buffer

Interface Buffer (Fig. 18.8) declares methods blockingPut (line 5) and blockingGet (line 8) that our BlockingBuffer class implements for a producer thread to place a value in the buffer and a consumer thread to retrieve a value from it, respectively. Methods blocking-Put and blockingGet will call ArrayBlockingQueue methods that throw InterruptedExceptions. They will also output text for pedagogic purposes, which is why this example declares interface Buffer rather than calling ArrayBlockingQueue methods directly. Interface Buffer’s methods list InterruptedException in their throws clauses so the exceptions can be returned to the producer or consumer threads calling Buffer’s methods.

18.10.5 Class BlockingBuffer

Class BlockingBuffer (Fig. 18.9) implements the Buffer interface and uses an object of class ArrayBlockingQueue to store one Integer (lines 7–8) and manage mutually exclusive access to it—we’ll say more about an ArrayBlockingQueue’s size at the end of this section. Because our BlockingBuffer class uses the thread-safe ArrayBlockingQueue class to manage all of its shared state (the shared buffer), BlockingBuffer is itself thread-safe, even though we have not implemented the synchronization ourselves.

Line 13 in method blockingPut calls the ArrayBlockingQueue object’s put method. If the ArrayBlockingQueue is full, the producer thread waits at line 13 until there’s room in the ArrayBlockingQueue to write the value. Line 21 in method blockingGet calls the ArrayBlockingQueue object’s take method. If the ArrayBlockingQueue is empty, the consumer thread waits at line 21 until there’s an element in the ArrayBlockingQueue to read. Lines 14–15 and 22–23 use the ArrayBlockingQueue size method to display the ArrayBlockingQueue’s current number of elements. In this example, when the size is 1, the buffer is full, and when it’s 0, the buffer is empty.

The ArrayBlockingQueue approach used in this example demonstrates encapsulated synchronization—the producer and consumer threads that call blockingPut and blockingGet to access the shared ArrayBlockingQueue (i.e., the buffer) are unaware that their writes and reads are synchronized. This is handled entirely by the ArrayBlockingQueue methods put and take.

18.10.6 Class BlockingBufferTest

Class BlockingBufferTest’s main method (Fig. 18.10) launches two virtual threads to execute a producer task that writes values into a shared BlockingBuffer and a consumer task that reads values from the same BlockingBuffer. We split class BlockingBufferTest into parts for discussion purposes. The tasks in this example are not CPU-intensive and block if they cannot perform their tasks, so line 10 creates an ExecutorService for virtual threads. Line 12 creates the shared BlockingBuffer object that both the producer and consumer tasks will access.

Producer Task

Lines 15–31 define the producer’s Runnable task as a lambda expression and launch its execution in a virtual thread. Each iteration of its loop (lines 18–27) invokes Thread method sleep (line 20) to place the producer’s virtual thread to sleep for a random time interval. When the thread awakens and begins executing again, line 21 passes the control variable count’s value to the buffer object’s blockingPut method to set the shared buffer’s value. Line 22 keeps a total of all the values produced so far so we can output that total when the producer finishes executing. When the loop completes, lines 29–30 output a message indicating that the producer finished executing and the total of all the values produced. The producer virtual thread terminates when the flow of control reaches the end of the lambda that defines its Runnable’s run method.

The consumer virtual thread terminates when the flow of control reaches the end of the lambda that defines its Runnable’s run method. The program terminates once both virtual threads in this program complete their tasks.

A Note Regarding BlockingBuffer’s Output Statements

There’s no guarantee that the outputs written by BlockingBuffer methods blockingPut and blockingGet will occur immediately after those methods’ corresponding calls to ArrayBlockingQueue’s put or take. So, in some executions, the outputs might appear out of order. Even if the outputs appear out of order, the ArrayBlockingQueue object properly synchronizes access to its data, as evidenced by the sums of values written by the producer and read by the consumer.

We Call Thread Method sleep Only for Demonstration Purposes

We call method sleep in the producer and consumer Runnables to emphasize that, in multithreaded programs, it’s unpredictable when each thread will perform its task and for how long it will perform the task when it has a processor. These thread-scheduling issues are usually beyond the control of Java developers.

We cannot make assumptions about the relative speeds of concurrent threads. Interactions that occur with the operating system, the network, the user and other components can cause the threads to operate at different and ever-changing speeds. When this happens, threads wait. When threads wait excessively, programs become less efficient, interactive programs become less responsive, and applications suffer longer delays.

18.10.7 Bounded Buffers

To minimize the waiting time for threads that share resources and operate at the same average speeds, we can implement a bounded buffer that provides a fixed number of buffer cells where the producer can place values and the consumer can retrieve those values. In fact, the ArrayBlockingQueue class is a bounded buffer.

With a bounded buffer, if the producer temporarily produces values faster than the consumer can consume them, the producer can write additional values into the extra buffer cells if any are available. This capability enables the producer to perform its task even though the consumer is not ready to retrieve the current value being produced. Similarly, if the consumer temporarily consumes faster than the producer produces new values, the consumer can read additional values (if there are any) from the buffer. This enables the consumer to keep busy even though the producer is not ready to produce additional values. An example of the producer/consumer relationship that uses a bounded buffer is video streaming, which we discussed in Section 18.1.

Even a bounded buffer is inappropriate if the producer and the consumer operate consistently at different speeds. If the consumer always executes faster than the producer, then a buffer containing one location is enough. If the producer always executes faster, only a buffer with an “infinite” number of locations would be able to absorb the extra production. However, if the producer and consumer execute at about the same average speed, a bounded buffer helps to smooth the effects of any occasional speeding up or slowing down in either thread’s execution.

The key to using a bounded buffer with a producer and consumer that operate at about the same speed is providing the buffer with enough locations to handle the anticipated “extra” production. If, over a period of time, we determine that the producer often produces as many as three more values than the consumer can consume, we can provide a buffer of at least three cells to handle the extra production. Making the buffer too small would cause threads to wait longer.

ArrayBlockingQueue can work with multiple producers and multiple consumers, ensuring each stored item is read only once. For example, a factory that produces its product very fast will need to have many more delivery trucks (i.e., consumers) to remove those products quickly from the warehousing area (i.e., the bounded buffer) so that the factory can continue to produce products at full capacity.

18.10.8 Other Concurrent Collections

In Chapter 12, we introduced various collections from the Java Collections API. The collections from the java.util.concurrent package are specifically designed and optimized for sharing collections among multiple threads. A few of the most commonly used are:

  • ArrayBlockingQueue (Fig. 18.9)—A fixed-size queue that supports the producer/consumer relationship—possibly with many producers and consumers.

  • ConcurrentHashMap—A hash-based map (similar to the HashMap introduced in Chapter 12) that allows an arbitrary number of reader and writer threads.

  • LinkedBlockingQueue—A blocking queue implemented as a linked list that can optionally be fixed in size.

The concurrent collections provide their own implementations of various stream-like operations. For example, ConcurrentHashMap has methods forEach, reduce and search, which are designed and optimized for concurrent collections shared among threads. 18.11 Multithreading in JavaFX

 

JavaFX apps present unique challenges for multithreaded programming. All JavaFX apps have one JavaFX application thread that handles interactions with the app’s controls, such as rendering them or processing user actions with them. All tasks that require interaction with the GUI are placed in an event queue and executed by the JavaFX application thread in first-in-first-out (FIFO) order.

JavaFX’s scene graph is not thread-safe—manipulating its nodes from multiple threads can lead to incorrect results that might corrupt the scene graph. To ensure thread safety in JavaFX you use a technique called thread confinement in which you ensure that programs manipulate the scene graph from only the JavaFX application thread, not by using thread synchronization techniques. Allowing just one thread at a time to access non-thread-safe objects eliminates the possibility of corruption due to multiple threads accessing these objects concurrently.

It’s acceptable to perform brief tasks on the JavaFX application thread—like calculating tips and totals in Chapter 15’s Tip Calculator app. However, lengthy tasks performed in the JavaFX application thread prevent it from rendering controls or responding to events until that task completes, making the GUI unresponsive and leading to a poor user experience. So, it’s preferable to handle long-running tasks in separate threads, freeing the JavaFX application thread to continue managing GUI interactions. Of course, you must update the GUI with the computation’s results from the JavaFX application thread rather than from the worker thread that performed the calculation.

Platform Method runLater

JavaFX provides multiple mechanisms for updating the GUI from other threads. One is to call the static method runLater of class Platform (package javafx.application). This method receives a Runnable and schedules it on the JavaFX application thread for execution in the future. Such Runnables should perform only small updates, such as changing the text on a Label, so the GUI remains responsive.

Class Task and Interface Worker

Long-running or compute-intensive tasks should be performed on separate worker threads, not the JavaFX application thread. Package javafx.concurrent provides interface Worker and classes Task and ScheduledService for this purpose:

  • The Worker interface is for a task that should execute using one or more separate threads.

  • The Task class provides a Worker implementation that enables you to perform a task (such as a long-running computation) in a worker thread and update the GUI from the JavaFX application thread based on the task’s results. Task implements several interfaces, including Runnable, so a Task object can be scheduled to execute in a separate thread. Class Task also provides methods that are guaranteed to update its properties in the JavaFX application thread—this enables programs to bind a Task’s properties to GUI controls for automatic updates. Once a Task completes, it cannot be restarted, so performing it again requires a new Task object. We’ll demonstrate Tasks in the next two examples.

  • The ScheduledService class provides a Worker implementation that creates and manages a Task. Unlike a Task, a ScheduledService can be reset and restarted. It can also be configured to automatically restart both after successful completion and if it fails due to an exception.

18.11.1 Performing Computations in a Worker Thread: Fibonacci Numbers

In the next example, the user enters a number n, and the program gets the nth Fibonacci number in the Fibonacci series,

0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, …

which begins with 0 and 1 and has the property that each subsequent value in the series is the sum of the previous two. In this example, we calculate the nth Fibonacci number using a CPU-intensive algorithm that we discuss thoroughly in Section 22.4, so we do not present its details here.

The algorithm is particularly time-consuming for large values of n, so we use a Task object to perform the calculation in a worker thread. The GUI also provides a separate set of components that displays the next Fibonacci number in the sequence each time the user presses (or selects) a Button. This set of components performs its short computation directly in the Java FX application thread. The program can produce up to the 92nd Fibonacci number—subsequent values are outside the range that can be represented by a long. Recall that you can use class BigInteger to represent arbitrarily large integer values.

Creating a Task

Class FibonacciTask (Fig. 18.11) extends Task<Long> (line 5) to perform the calculation in a worker thread. The instance variable n (line 6) represents the Fibonacci number to calculate. Overridden Task method call (lines 14–20) computes the nth Fibonacci number and returns the result. The Task’s type parameter, Long (line 5), determines method call’s return type (line 15). Inherited Task method updateMessage (called in lines 16 and 18) updates the Task’s message property in the JavaFX application thread. In Fig. 18.12, we’ll use this to bind a JavaFX control to FibonacciTask’s message property to display messages while the task is executing.

When the worker thread starts running, FibonacciTask’s call method begins executing. First, line 16 calls the inherited updateMessage method to update the FibonacciTask’s message property, indicating that the task is calculating. Next, line 17 invokes method fibonacci (lines 23–30) with instance variable n’s value as the argument. When fibonacci returns, line 18 updates FibonacciTask’s message property again to indicate that the calculation completed, then line 19 returns the result to the JavaFX application thread.

FibonacciNumbers GUI

The following screen captures demonstrate the app. We labeled the app’s GUI (defined in FibonacciNumbers.fxml) with its fx:ids in the third screen capture:

Here, we point out only the key elements and the event-handling methods we’ll implement in class FibonacciNumbersController (Fig. 18.12). For the complete layout details, open FibonacciNumbers.fxml in Scene Builder. The GUI’s primary layout is a VBox containing two TitledPanes. The controller class defines two event handlers:

  • goButtonPressed is called when the Go Button is pressed—this launches the worker thread to calculate a Fibonacci number recursively.

  • nextNumberButtonPressed is called when the Next Number Button is pressed—this calculates the next Fibonacci number in the sequence. Initially, the app displays the Fibonacci of 0 (which is 0).

We do not present the JavaFX Application subclass (located in FibonacciNumbers.java) because it performs the same tasks we’ve used previously to load the app’s FXML GUI and initialize the controller.

Class FibonacciNumbersController

Class FibonacciNumbersController (Fig. 18.12)—which we’ve split into parts for discussion purposes—handles events from two sets of controls:

  • The "With FibonacciTask" TitledPane provides controls that enable the user to enter a Fibonacci number to calculate and launch a FibonacciTask in a worker thread. Labels in this TitledPane display the FibonacciTask’s message property value as it’s updated and the final result of the FibonacciTask once it’s available.

  • The "Without FibonacciTask" TitledPane provides the Next Number Button that enables the user to calculate the next Fibonacci number in sequence. Labels in this TitledPane display the Fibonacci number being calculated ("Fibonacci of n") and the corresponding Fibonacci value.

Instance variables n1 and n2 (lines 20–21) contain the previous two Fibonacci numbers in the sequence and are initialized to 0 and 1, respectively. Instance variable number (initialized to 1 in line 22) keeps track of which Fibonacci value will be calculated and displayed next when the user presses (or selects) the Next Number Button. The first time this Button is pressed (or selected), the Fibonacci of 1 is displayed.

Method goButtonPressed

When the user presses (or selects) the Go Button, method goButtonPressed (lines 25–59) executes. Line 29 gets the value entered in the numberTextField and attempts to parse it as an integer. If this fails, lines 55–57 prompt the user to enter an integer, select the text in the numberTextField and give the numberTextField the focus so the user can immediately enter a new value in the numberTextField.

27         // get Fibonacci number to calculate

30

36

39               goButton.setDisable(true);

41            });

44            task.setOnSucceeded((succeededEvent) -> {
45               fibonacciLabel.setText(task.getValue().toString());
46               goButton.setDisable(false);
47            });
48
49            // launch the FibonacciTask
50            var executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1);
51            executor.execute(task); // start the task
52            executor.shutdown(); // prevent more tasks from being scheduled
53         }
54         catch (NumberFormatException e) {
55            numberTextField.setText("Enter an integer");
56            numberTextField.selectAll();

60

Line 32 creates a new FibonacciTask object, passing the constructor the user-entered value. Line 35 binds the messageLabel’s text property (a StringProperty) to the FibonacciTask’s message property (a ReadOnlyStringProperty). When FibonacciTask updates this property, the messageLabel displays the new value.

All Workers transition through various states. Class Task, an implementation of interface Worker, enables you to register listeners for several of these states:

  • Lines 38–41 use Task method setOnRunning to register a listener (implemented as a lambda) that’s invoked when the Task begins executing—that is, when the Task has been assigned a processor and its call method is invoked. In this case, we disable the goButton so the user cannot launch another FibonacciTask until the current one completes. Then, we clear the fibonacciLabel (so an old result is not displayed when a new FibonacciTask begins).

  • Lines 44–47 use Task method setOnSucceeded to register a listener (implemented as a lambda) that’s invoked when the Task successfully runs to completion. In this case, we call Task method getValue (from interface Worker) to get the result, which we convert to a String then display in the fibonacciLabel. Then, we enable the goButton so the user can start a new FibonacciTask.

You can also register listeners to be notified when a Task is canceled, failed to execute correctly or is scheduled for execution.

Finally, lines 50–52 use an ExecutorService to launch the FibonacciTask, which schedules it for execution in a separate worker thread. Method execute does not wait for the FibonacciTask to finish executing. It returns immediately, allowing the GUI to continue processing other events while the computation is performed. Line 52 ensures that no other tasks can be scheduled using the ExecutorService. We don’t use the ExecutorSer-vice’s AutoCloseable feature here, because it would block the JavaFX application thread from proceeding as it waits for the task to complete, freezing the GUI.

Method nextNumberButtonPressed

If the user presses (or selects) the Next Number Button, method nextNumberButtonPressed (lines 62–71) executes. Lines 65–66 update the nthLabel with the Fibonacci number, then update nthFibonacciLabel to display n2’s value. Next, lines 67–70 add the previous two Fibonacci numbers stored in n1 and n2 to determine the next number in the sequence (which will be displayed on the next call to nextNumberButtonPressed), update n1 and n2 to their new values and increment number.

Click here to view code image

61      // calculates next Fibonacci value
62      @FXML
63      void nextNumberButtonPressed(ActionEvent event) {
64         // display the next Fibonacci number
65         nthLabel.setText("Fibonacci of " + number + ": ");
66         nthFibonacciLabel.setText(String.valueOf(n2));
67         long temp = n1 + n2;
68         n1 = n2;
69         n2 = temp;
70         ++number;
71      }
72   }

The code for these calculations is in method nextNumberButtonPressed, so they’re performed on the JavaFX application thread. Handling such short computations in this thread does not cause the GUI to become unresponsive, as with the recursive algorithm for calculating the Fibonacci of a large number. Because the longer Fibonacci computation is performed in a separate worker thread, it’s possible to click the Next Number Button to get the next Fibonacci number while the recursive computation is still in progress.

18.11.2 Processing Intermediate Results: Sieve of Eratosthenes

Class Task provides additional methods and properties that enable you to update a GUI with a Task’s intermediate results as the Task continues executing in a Worker thread. The next example uses the following Task methods and properties:

  • The updateProgress method updates a Task’s progress property, which represents the percentage completion.

  • The updateValue method updates a Task’s value property, which holds each intermediate value.

Like updateMessage, updateProgress and updateValue are guaranteed to update the corresponding properties in the JavaFX application thread.

A Task to Find Prime Numbers

Figure 18.13 presents class PrimeCalculatorTask, which extends Task<Integer> to compute the first n prime numbers in a worker thread. In the FindPrimesController class (Fig. 18.14), we’ll bind this Task’s progress property to a ProgressBar control so the app can indicate the Task’s completion percentage. The controller also registers a listener for the value property’s changes—we’ll store each prime value in an ObservableList that’s bound to a ListView.

Constructor

The constructor (Fig. 18.13, lines 10–13) receives an int for the upper limit of the prime numbers to locate, creates the boolean array primes and initializes its elements to true.

Sieve of Eratosthenes

PrimeCalculatorTask uses the primes array and the Sieve of Eratosthenes algorithm to find all primes less than max. The Sieve of Eratosthenes takes a list of integers and, beginning with the first prime number, filters out all multiples of that prime. It then moves to the next prime, which will be the next number that’s not yet filtered out, and eliminates all of its multiples. It continues until the end of the list is reached and all non-primes have been filtered out. Algorithmically, we begin with element 2 of the boolean array and set the cells corresponding to all values that are multiples of 2 to false to indicate that they’re divisible by 2 and thus not prime. We then move to the next array element, check whether it’s true and, if so, set all of its multiples to false to indicate that they’re divisible by the current index. When the whole array has been traversed in this way, all indices that contain true are prime, as they have no divisors.

Overridden Task Method call

Task method call (lines 16–52) is invoked when the Task is executed. The method is protected because it’s meant to be overridden by a subclass, not called directly. In method call, the control variable i for the loop (lines 22–49) represents the current index for implementing the Sieve of Eratosthenes. Line 23 calls the inherited Task method isCan-celled to determine whether the user has clicked the Cancel button. If so, line 24 updates the Task’s message property, then line 25 returns 0 to terminate the Task immediately.

If the calculation isn’t canceled, line 29 puts the currently executing thread to sleep for 10 milliseconds. We discuss the reason for this shortly. Line 36 calls Task’s update-Progress method to update the progress property in the JavaFX application thread. The percentage completion is determined by dividing the method’s first argument by its second argument.

Next, line 38 tests whether the current primes element is true (and thus prime). If so, line 39 increments the count of prime numbers found so far and line 40 updates the Task’s message property with a String containing the count. Then, line 41 passes the index i to method updateValue, which updates Task’s value property in the JavaFX application thread—in the controller, we’ll process this intermediate result and display it in the GUI. When the entire array has been traversed, line 51 returns 0, which we ignore in the controller (line 53 of Fig. 18.14) because it is not a prime number.

Because the computation progresses quickly, publishing values often, updates can pile up on the JavaFX application thread, causing it to ignore some updates. This is why, for demonstration purposes, we put the worker thread to sleep for 10 milliseconds during each iteration of the loop. The calculation is slowed just enough to allow the JavaFX application thread to keep up with the updates and enable the GUI to remain responsive.

FindPrimes GUI

The following screen captures demonstrate the app. We labeled the app’s GUI (defined in FindPrimes.fxml) with its fx:ids in the third screen capture:

Here, we point out only the key elements and the event-handling methods we’ll implement in class FindPrimesController (Fig. 18.14). For the complete layout details, open FindPrimes.fxml in Scene Builder. The GUI’s primary layout is a BorderPane containing two ToolBars in the top and bottom areas. The controller class defines two event handlers:

  • getPrimesButtonPressed is called when the Get Primes Button is pressed. This launches the worker thread to find prime numbers less than the value input by the user.

  • cancelButtonPressed is called when the Cancel Button is pressed. This terminates the worker thread.

We do not present the JavaFX Application subclass (located in FindPrimes.java), because it performs the same tasks we’ve used previously to load the app’s FXML GUI and initialize the controller.

Class FindPrimesController

Class FindPrimesController (Fig. 18.14)—which we’ve split into parts for discussion purposes—creates an ObservableList<Integer> (lines 24–25) and binds it to the app’s primesListView (line 31). The controller also provides the event handlers for the Get Primes and Cancel Buttons.

Method getPrimesButtonPressed

When the user presses (or selects) the Get Primes Button, getPrimesButtonPressed (lines 35–84) creates a PrimeCalculatorTask (line 42) and configures various event listeners:

  • Line 45 binds the statusLabel’s text property to the task’s message property to update the statusLabel automatically as new primes are found.

  • Line 48 binds the progressBar’s progress property to the task’s progress property to update the progressBar automatically with the percentage of completion.

  • Lines 51–58 register a ChangeListener (using a lambda) that responds to the task’s value property changes. If the property’s newValue is not 0 (indicating the task terminated), line 54 adds it to the primes ObservableList<Integer>, which is bound to the primesListView to display the list’s elements. Next, lines 55–56 scroll the ListView to its last element so the latest prime number is on the screen.

  • Lines 62–72 register listeners for when the task begins running and when the task completes successfully. We use these to enable and disable the app’s Buttons based on the task’s state.

  • The long-running PrimeCalculatorTask sleeps between passing prime values to the JavaFX application thread for display in the ListView. Since this task is not CPU-bound, lines 75–77 launch a virtual thread to execute it, potentially enabling better use of your system’s CPU resources. Note that we do not wait for this thread to complete as we have for all of this chapter’s virtual thread examples. If the app were to wait here, the event handler would not terminate until the task completes, and the GUI would freeze, preventing other user interactions, such as canceling the task.

18.12 Wrap-Up

This chapter presented Java’s concurrency capabilities for enhancing performance on multi-core systems. You learned the differences between concurrent and parallel execution. We explained that Java makes concurrency available to you through the language and libraries, and we focused on high-level library features and creating threads to run tasks various ways. You learned that the JVM creates platform threads to run programs and perform housekeeping tasks, such as garbage collection.

We used the Arrays class’s sort and parallelSort methods to demonstrate the benefit of a parallel sorting algorithm on a multi-core processor, timing the operations with the Java Date/Time API. You learned that stream pipelines are easy to parallelize, enabling programs to benefit from enhanced performance on multi-core systems. To obtain a parallel stream, you invoked method parallel on an existing sequential stream.

We presented the Runnable interface for specifying a task that can execute concurrently with other tasks. This interface’s run method is invoked by the thread executing the task. Then we showed how to use the Executor interface to manage the execution of Runnable objects via a thread pool, which can reuse existing platform threads to eliminate the overhead of creating a new thread for each task and can improve performance by optimizing the number of threads to ensure that the processor stays busy.

We explored Project Loom’s virtual threads, structured concurrency and scoped values—significant enhancements to Java’s concurrency capabilities that address the limitations of traditional platform threads in applications requiring massive numbers of concurrent tasks that spend most of their time blocking. We discussed that virtual threads are lightweight and managed by the JVM rather than the operating system. We compared the initial memory requirements of virtual threads (only a few hundred bytes) and platform threads (one to two megabytes) and presented three ways to create and launch virtual threads. We did detailed performance comparisons, demonstrating how virtual threads significantly outperform platform threads when handling large numbers of concurrent I/O-bound tasks, enabling applications to efficiently manage thousands or millions of concurrent operations. In that example, we discussed the Callable and Future interfaces, which enable you to execute tasks that return results and obtain those results, respectively.

We discussed structured concurrency and scoped values—preview features at the time of this writing—in the context of a practical weather application example that uses Open-WeatherMap’s web services (introduced in Section 11.6). We demonstrated how these features simplify concurrent programming and resource management while making code easier to read, maintain and debug. We used StructuredTaskScope to treat related concurrent tasks as a single unit, enabling concurrent programming with straightforward sequential statements. We also used ScopedValue objects to share immutable data between tasks launched from the same structured concurrency scope.

You learned that when multiple threads share an object and one or more of them modify that object, indeterminate results may occur unless access to the shared object is managed properly. In an example of the producer/consumer relationship, we showed how to solve this problem via the built-in class ArrayBlockingQueue, which handles all the synchronization details for you.

We discussed the fact that JavaFX GUIs are not thread-safe, so all interactions with and modifications to the GUI must be performed in the JavaFX application thread. We also discussed the problems associated with performing long-running calculations in that thread. Then, we demonstrated how to use class Task to perform long-running calculations in worker threads but update the GUI in the JavaFX application thread. You learned how to use a Task’s properties to display the results of a Task in a GUI when the calculation completes and how to display intermediate results while the calculation is still in process.

In the next chapter, we build API-based Java generative AI applications. You’ll use OpenAI APIs to create apps that summarize text, analyze text for sentiment, create accessible descriptions of images, detect a text’s language and translate text among languages, generate Java code, perform named entity recognition on text and obtain structured JSON outputs, transcribe speech to text, synthesize speech from text, generate closed captions for a video and more.

Special Section: Generative AI Exercises

For each of the following questions, try multiple genAIs to determine which performs best. Always verify the results. Keep in mind that they sometimes make mistakes and even hallucinate, creating unreliable information.

18.1 (Best Practices and Common Pitfalls) Prompt genAIs for best practices and common pitfalls of Java multithreaded application development.

18.2 (ThreadLocal Variables vs. ScopedValues) Prompt genAIs, asking for a detailed comparison of the pros and cons of ThreadLocal variables vs. ScopedValues with code examples.

18.3 (Weather App Enhancement) Sometimes, a web service may not respond promptly. Prompt genAIs with the code from Section 18.8’s weather app, asking how to make each OpenWeatherMap request stop executing if it has not responded within a specified amount of time (known as “timing out”).

18.4 (Nested StructuredTaskScopes) Prompt genAIs for real-world examples of nested StructuredTaskScopes and a simple code example demonstrating how to create them.

18.5 (Exceptions in StructuredTaskScopes) Prompt genAIs for a detailed discussion of how exceptions are handled in StructuredTaskScopes.

18.6 (Custom StructuredTaskScopes) You can inherit from StructuredTaskScope to customize how their virtual threads are managed. Prompt genAIs to provide code examples demonstrating use-cases for custom StructuredTaskScopes.

18.7 (Limiting Concurrent Access By Virtual Threads to a Shared Resource) Prompt genAIs, asking how to limit the number of concurrent virtual threads accessing a resource.

18.8 (Java Flight Recorder) Prompt genAIs for an overview of Java Flight Recorder and how it can be used to debug multithreaded applications.

18.9 (Fork/Join Framework) Prompt genAIs for an overview of Java’s Fork/Join framework and how it’s used in parallel streams and the Arrays methods parallelSort and parallelSetAll.

18.10 (Uncaught Exceptions in Multithreaded Applications) Prompt genAIs, asking them to list cases where an uncaught exception does not terminate a Java program.

18.11 (Deadlock, Livelock and Indefinite Postponement) Three problems that can occur in systems that allow threads to wait (such as the producer/consumer relationship) are

  • deadlock—in which one or more threads will wait forever for an event that cannot occur,

  • livelock—in which threads remain active but keep retrying or adjusting in a way that prevents completion of their tasks and

  • indefinite postponement—in which one or more threads will be delayed for some unpredictably long time.

Prompt genAIs, asking them to discuss how to avoid deadlock, livelock and indefinite postponement in multithreaded Java programs.

18.12 (Bounded Buffer: A Real-World Example) Prompt genAIs to describe how a highway off-ramp onto a local road is a good example of a producer/consumer relationship with a bounded buffer and how the designers might choose the size of the off-ramp.

19.1 Introduction

 

So far, you’ve manually prompted genAIs via their web interfaces and compared and used their results. We did not show these prompts’ results. In this chapter, we program Java API-based genAI applications and show their outputs or play the generated audios and videos.

Multimodal GenAIs

When genAI chatbots were introduced, they received a text prompt and generated text or an image. Many are now multimodal—they can understand text, code, images, audio and video inputs and use them to generate mixed text, code, images, audio and video outputs.1,2,3 For example, you can prompt a genAI with an audio file containing speech and instructions, asking it to transcribe the speech into text, display the transcription, analyze its sentiment, translate it to another spoken language and synthesize speech in that other language.

OpenAI APIs

We’ll use the OpenAI APIs to build multimodal Java genAI applications. Companies like Google, Anthropic, Meta, Hugging Face and more also provide APIs.5 The OpenAI API does not have an official Java library, so we’ll use the free, open-source Simple-OpenAI library (discussed in Section 19.3) to interact with the OpenAI APIs and process their results. As you’ll see, prompts like those you’ve used throughout this book are essential to genAI API-based programming.

5. It’s expensive for companies like OpenAI, Google and Anthropic to train the models we access here via APIs. So, their web-based APIs are typically paid services. Some offer limited free tiers.

Generative AI APIs with Free Tiers

Google Gemini and Hugging Face have free tiers. For an overview these, visit:

  • Google Gemini pricing tiers: https://ai.google.dev/pricing

  • Hugging Face pricing tiers: https://huggingface.co/pricing

Hugging Face is an open-source platform specializing in natural language processing, providing pretrained language models (almost 1.5 million of them), datasets and tools for working with models. Meta offers its Llama 3 genAI models free for download to run locally. For more information, visit https://www.llama.com/. Meta’s Llama models are also available on Hugging Face.

Caution on Using Paid GenAI APIs

Generative AI services often charge based on usage, which can result in significant fees depending on request volume and task complexity. Review the pricing structures of paid APIs and monitor your usage to avoid unexpected charges. Free tiers typically have strict usage limits, so exceeding these can lead to substantial bills. Always check for available budgeting tools and cost management strategies the API services provide.6

19.2.4 OpenAI Developer API Key

You need a developer key to invoke OpenAI’s APIs. Perform the following steps to get one:

  1. Sign into your account at https://platform.openai.com/docs/overview.

  2. Press (or select) the Start building button in the page’s upper-right corner—after you create your first API key below, this button will change to a settings icon ().

  3. Fill in the Organization name and What best describes you? fields then press (or select) the Create organization button.

  4. In the Invite your team step, you can add email addresses for other team members. Press (or select) Continue.

  5. In the Make your first API call step, specify an API key name and a Project name, then press (or select) the Generate API Key button. (If you create additional API keys in the future, you’ll select API Keys the left column of your account’s settings page.)

  6. Press or select the Copy button to copy the alphanumeric key to the clipboard.

For security, you’ll store your API key in an environment variable on your system rather than embedding it in your code, as discussed below.

Storing the API Key in macOS

Perform the following steps to store your API key on macOS:

  1. Open Terminal.

  2. Open ~/.zshrc using a text editor (e.g., nano ~/.zshrc).

  3. Scroll to the end of the file and add the following line, replacing YourAPIKey with the lengthy alphanumeric API key you copied previously.

    Click here to view code image

    export OPENAI_API_KEY="YourAPIKey"

  4. Save and close the file.

  5. Run the following command in the Terminal:

    source ~/.zshrc
Storing the API Key on Windows

Perform the following steps to store your API key on Windows:

  1. In the taskbar’s Search field, enter SystemPropertiesAdvanced, and press or select Enter.

  2. In the System Properties dialog, press or select the Environment Variables… button.

  3. Under User variables, click New….

  4. Enter the Variable name as OPENAI_API_KEY and, for the Variable value, paste in the lengthy alphanumeric API key you copied previously.

  5. Click OK to save the environment variable, then click OK in the System Properties dialog to close it.

19.4 Text Generation Via Chat Completions

In this section, we present fully coded apps that interact with OpenAI’s "gpt-4o" model to request chat completions:

  • Section 19.4.1 performs text summarization—in two OpenAI API requests, we upload a Deitel video transcript and ask the chat API to return a summary abstract paragraph, followed by a list of the transcript’s key points. Text responses like these are known as chat completions.

  • Section 19.4.2 uses a chat-completion request to perform sentiment analysis—determining whether the Deitel video transcript is positive, neutral or negative. We also ask the genAI to explain how it came to its conclusion.

  • Section 19.4.3 asks OpenAI to describe images for accessibility. This multi-modal application uploads an image and requests a detailed image description. We get detailed descriptions of Section 4.3’s for-loop UML diagram and a scenic Aruba beach photo.

  • Section 19.4.4 uses chat-completion requests to translate text. OpenAI will auto-detect the text’s source language then translate the text to a specified target language. We translate text from English to Spanish and Japanese then translate the Spanish and Japanese text back to English.

  • Section 19.4.5 uses a chat-completion request to generate Java code for a simulation that summarizes 600,000,000 six-sided die rolls and displays the results. We then compile and execute the generated code.

  • Section 19.4.6 uses a chat-completion request to perform the natural language processing (NLP) task named-entity recognition (NER), which attempts to locate and categorize text mentions like dates, times, quantities, places, people, things, organizations, etc. This example demonstrates OpenAI’s ability to produce structured output in your application’s required format. To make the results easier to process, we provide the API with the exact JSON response format we wish to receive, then use the Jackson open-source library (Chapter 11) to process the result. NER is one of many natural language processing tasks OpenAI’s APIs can perform. Section 7.7 listed many common NLP tasks you could try.

19.4.1 Text Summarization

Text summarization is a natural language processing (NLP) task that analyzes a body of text and produces a shorter version containing the key ideas. This is useful for getting quick summaries of items like articles, academic papers, book chapters or sections, lengthy emails, reports, study materials, product reviews and more. Figure 19.1 summarizes a presentation transcript as

  • a summary abstract paragraph and

  • a key-points list.

The file transcript.txt in the ch19 examples folder’s resources subfolder contains the original presentation transcript. Many of this chapter’s examples use files from this folder, and those that generate audio, images and Java code write their results into files in the resources folder’s outputs subfolder. Throughout this chapter’s examples, we assume the book’s code is located in your user account’s Documents folder in the examples subfolder, as discussed in the Before You Begin section. If you placed them elsewhere, you must update the files paths we specify in the examples.

Compiling and Running this Chapter’s Examples

where SourceFile is the name of the Java source-code file for the example—in this section, TextSummarizationDemo.java. To run the code, enter the following command

Lines 19–31 call our OpenAIUtilities class’s static chat method (discussed in Section 19.9.5) to request an OpenAI chat completion that produces a summary abstract paragraph for the transcript loaded in line 15. 29               new Message("user", transcript)

Messages Passed to the OpenAI APIs

Many OpenAI API calls require messages consisting of a role and content. The role is "user", "system" or "assistant"—discussed momentarily. The content is typically

  • a prompt like you’d input via a genAI’s web interface or

  • data the API call will process.

In our code, we defined these messages using our OpenAIUtilities class’s nested record class Message (imported at line 4 and discussed in Section 19.9.3):

Click here to view code image

public record Message(String role, String content) {}

Several of our OpenAIUtilities class’s methods, including chat, receive List<Message> objects. Our chat method’s first argument specifies the OpenAI model to use to formulate a response—the "gpt-4o" model was one of OpenAI’s most up-to-date and powerful models at the time of this writing. Each item in the List<Message> passed as chat’s second argument is a Message object containing a role and content.

"system" Role

A message with the "system" role25 prompts the model with details to help it perform a task. The corresponding content typically explains what you want the model to do.26 For example, lines 21–28 define a text block describing how we’d like the model to summarize text. If you were asking the model to write Java code, you might tell it that it’s an expert in Java programming. Instructions like this give the model context to help it provide more relevant results.

25. “Messages and Roles.” Accessed February 25, 2025. https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/text-generation/#messages-and-roles.

26. OpenAI recently added "developer" messages that are specifically for use with OpenAI’s “reasoning models” (such as "o1" or "o3-mini). According to https://community.openai.com/t/how-is-developer-message-better-than-system-prompt/1062784/2, if you submit a "developer" message to the "gpt-4o" model (or another GPT model), it’s converted to a "system" message, and if you submit a "system" message to reasoning model, it’s converted to a "developer" message.

"user" Role

A message with the "user" role27 provides as its content a prompt for a task to perform or data the model requires to perform a task. You can supply multiple "system" and "user" messages—"system" messages are prioritized over "user" messages. Line 29 provides the data to summarize (transcript). If you’d like the model to generate code, the content would indicate what you’d like the code to do.

27. “Messages and Roles.” Accessed February 25, 2025. https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/text-generation/#messages-and-roles.

"assistant" Role

A message with the "assistant" role28 is typically used to provide examples to the model, such as showing it the exact format you want for a response. Unlike the ChatGPT web interface, the chat-completion API does not have memory, so it does not remember previous chat-completion requests. So, messages with the "assistant" role can also be used to supply a previous chat-completion response in a conversation your code is having with the genAI, giving it more context for the current request. For more details on prompt engineering and these roles, visit

28. “Messages and Roles.” Accessed February 25, 2025. https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/text-generation/#messages-and-roles.

Click here to view code image

https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/prompt-engineering

To extract key points from the transcript, we use class OpenAIUtilities’ chat method but lines 36–45 change the "system" prompt to ask OpenAI to generate a list of the top five key points from the original audio transcription. In our experience, the resulting key points are sometimes returned as a numbered list and sometimes as a bullet list, so we explicitly asked for a numbered list in this prompt.

19.4.2 Sentiment Analysis

Figure 19.2 analyzes the sentiment of the text in transcript.txt. This example uses our OpenAIUtilities class’s chat method with the "gpt-4o" model again, but lines 21–25 change the "system" prompt to ask for a chat completion that analyzes the sentiment of the original transcript and explains how the model came to its conclusion. The model’s response indicates that the transcript’s sentiment is neutral. It also broke its conclusion into segments, indicating:

  • the content is “Objective and Informative,”

  • the speaker has a “Lack of Personal Emotional Expression,”

  • the speaker maintains a “Balanced Tone” and

  • the speaker provides “Constructive and Supportive Notes,”

each with explanatory notes.

Markdown-Formatted Responses

The chat completion API often returns responses in markdown format, as it did when we ran this example. Markdown is a lightweight formatting language that uses text delimiters to indicate formatting instructions. Various code editors and IDEs can read markdown formatting delimiters and render the text in HTML (web-page) or other formats. The following are examples of markdown formatting that a markdown-enabled tool would format:

  • ``` delimits blocks of program code that should be formatted in a fixed-width code font,

  • ` delimits code words that should be formatted in a code font inside non-code paragraphs,

  • ** delimits text that should be formatted in bold for emphasis

  • numbers starting from 1, followed by a period and a space indicate items in a numbered list, and

  • items starting with a - followed by a space indicate a bullet in a bullet list.

The website markdownguide.org provides a Getting Started guide at

Click here to view code image

https://www.markdownguide.org/getting-started/

and an overview of markdown syntax at

Click here to view code image

https://www.markdownguide.org/basic-syntax/

To experiment with markdown, check out the free online markdown editor with side-by-side live content rendering at https://dillinger.io.

19.4.3 Accessible Image Descriptions

A key goal of the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) is to make the web accessible to everyone, regardless of their abilities. To that end, accessible image descriptions are vital for people who are blind or have low vision. As we’ll discuss in Section 19.9.7, method describeImage in our OpenAIUtilities class passes a "system" message to an OpenAI model indicating that the model is an expert in creating accessible descriptions of images per the W3C’s guidelines.29

examples/ch19/resources

For Section 4.3’s UML activity diagram:

The OpenAI API returned the following chat completion:

Click here to view code image

ACCESSIBLE DESCRIPTION OF A DIAGRAM
The image is a highly detailed diagram showing the flow of control within a
logical structure of a Java 'for' loop, using the Unified Modeling Language
(UML) Activity Diagram standards. This diagram visually represents the se-
quence and operations involved in executing a 'for' loop in Java, a common
programming language used for building applications.

### Visual Breakdown:
1. **Diagram Format:** The activity diagram is structured to use standard UML
elements such as nodes, activities, decision points, transitions, and annota-
tions for depicting the logical flow.

2. **For Loop Structure:**
   - **Initialization:** The diagram starts with an initial node, indicating
the start of the logical process. This initial node flows into an activity
node representing the 'for' loop's initialization section (e.g., int i = 0).
   - **Condition Checking:** The next activity depicts the condition that
must be met for the loop to execute. This is shown with a diamond-shaped de-
cision node. It checks if the loop condition is true (e.g., i < 10), indicat-
ing whether the loop should continue or terminate.

   - **Loop Body:** From the true branch of the decision node, the flow pro-
ceeds to an activity node representing the loop body where actions (e.g.,
logic or statements) are executed if the condition is satisfied. These ac-
tions are enclosed within a rectangular activity node.
   - **Iteration:** A control flow arrow then typically points from the loop
body back to a small circular node, symbolizing the iterative aspect of the
loop (e.g., i++), where loop control variables are updated.

   - **Re-checking Condition:** After updating, control returns to the deci-
sion node to re-evaluate the condition.

3. **End of Loop:** If the condition is no longer satisfied, the control flow
follows the false branch from the decision node, leading to a final node.
This terminal node represents the end of the loop operation.

4. **Annotations:** The diagram may include UML notes or text boxes that pro-
vide additional context or explanations at various stages of the loop for
clarity. These are depicted generally as small rectangles connected to the
relevant part of the diagram by dashed lines.

5. **Flow Arrows:** The flow of control is indicated with arrows that con-
nect nodes and activities, forming a clear path illustrating the iterative
process of the 'for' loop.

6. **Styling and Color:** The diagram would use distinct shapes for decision
nodes (diamond), activity nodes (rounded rectangles), and annotations to
avoid confusion and provide a clear visual means to follow the logic.

Overall, this diagram serves as a tool to understand the execution flow of a
'for' loop in Java, detailing the iterative process in a structured graphi-
cal format. Each component is meticulously laid out to ensure the entire
mechanism is visually and logically represented.

19.4.4 Language Detection and Translation

Inter-language translation is a challenging problem in natural language processing and AI. With AI advances in large language models, genAIs can translate between languages instantly. Natural language translation has a wide range of uses, including:30

30. ChatGPT response to “Provide common uses for natural language translation.” December 14, 2024. https://chatgpt.com.

  • Cross-language communication: Facilitating conversations between people speaking different languages.

  • Global business operations: Translating documents, websites and customer communications for international markets.

  • Tourism: Helping travelers communicate in foreign countries using.

  • Education: Enabling students and researchers to access academic content in different languages.

  • Healthcare: Assisting healthcare providers in understanding patients who speak different languages.

  • Diplomatic relations: Supporting negotiations and communications between countries, such as at the United Nations.

  • Entertainment: Translating subtitles, scripts and media for global audiences.

The program in Fig. 19.4 translates text among spoken languages. In the OpenAI APIs, translation is simply a chat request. Our OpenAIUtilities class’s translate method (called in lines 15, 20, 25 and 31; discussed in Section 19.9.8) is similar to the class’s chat method (Section 19.9.5), but translate sends a "system" message to the OpenAI model indicating that

  • it’s an expert in natural language translation, and

  • it should translate the text specified in our translate method’s second argument to the language specified in the third argument.

For this demonstration, we translate two English sentences to Spanish and Japanese, then translate the Spanish and Japanese versions back to English. Note that the final results had the same first sentence as the original English text, but the second sentences were different (though similar).

19.4.5 Code Generation

Generative AIs can write code in many programming languages, but their code quality can vary substantially from well-written, functioning code that does what your prompt described to code that does not work. So, thoroughly test and verify any code genAIs provide.

Figure 19.5 uses our OpenAIUtilities class’s chat method (lines 20–32) with the "gpt-4o" model, a "system" message (lines 22–23) telling the model it’s an expert Java programmer and a "user" message (lines 24–30) discussing the Java program the model should write. Recall from Section 19.4.2 that chat completions often return responses in markdown format, as in this program’s output, which includes Java code with an explanation of how it works. The program the Java code into RollDie.java so we can compile and run it later. Lines 38–40 extract the Java code from the response using a regular expression that matches all text between the markdown delimiters "```java", which begins a Java-code block and "```", which terminates a code block. The subexpression "(.*?)" captures all the text between the delimiters. Pattern.DOTALL enables the pattern to match multiple lines of text. Lines 43–48 write the code into RollDie.java—line 46 extracts the text that matched the pattern.31

31. Another approach would be to prompt the model to return only the Java code with no additional formatting so you can write it directly to a file.

Other AI Code Capabilities

In addition to writing programs from scratch in various programming languages, many genAIs can also perform coding tasks like:

  1. Generating code from diagrams/pseudocode—Convert UML diagrams or flowcharts to code or convert pseudocode to code.

  2. Improving performance—Improve speed, reduce memory use and parallelize.

  3. Debugging—Locate and fix compilation errors, runtime errors (exceptions) and logic errors.

  4. Refactoring—Simplify code, split code into smaller reusable methods and classes, rename code elements and extract repeated code into a method.

  5. Improving readability—Rename variables, methods and classes and tune existing comments.

  6. Code review—Check code for style, code smells,35 adherence to clean code guidelines,36 adherence to SOLID principles37,38 and adherence to latest idioms.

19.4.6 Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Structured Outputs

You’ve seen that generative AIs can determine what a text is about and summarize information. A key aspect of this is a natural language processing (NLP) task called named entity recognition (NER), which attempts to locate and categorize items like dates, times, quantities, places, people, things, organizations and more. Our next example demonstrates a chat request asking the model to perform NER on a body of text. We ask the model to use the OntoNotes Named Entity Tag Set.39 To make the results more convenient to process, we provide the OpenAI API with the exact JSON response format we wish to receive—known as structured output.

39. Linguistic Data Consortium, OntoNotes Release 5.0, LDC2013T19 (Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania, 2013). Accessed March 8, 2024. https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/LDC2013T19.

JSON Output for Named Entities

We’d like the chat-completion API to return its response in the JSON format shown below:

Click here to view code image

{
   "entities": [
      {
         "text": "Tim Berners-Lee",
         "tag: "PERSON"
      },
      {
         "text": "CERN",
         "tag: "ORG"
      },
      ...
   ]
}

This has one "entities" attribute in which the value is a JSON array of JSON objects. Each JSON object in the array contains

  • a "text" attribute representing a named entity identified by the model and

  • a "tag" attribute indicating that named entity’s type.

Calling Class OpenAIUtilities class’s chatWithStructuredOutput Method

Figure 19.6 uses our OpenAIUtilities class’s chatWithStructuredOutput method (Section 19.9.9) to analyze text in the file web.txt containing information about the World Wide Web from Chapter 1. This file is located in the resources subfolder with this chapter’s examples. Method chatWithStructuredOutput receives as arguments:

  • The OpenAI model to use ("gpt-4o" ),

  • a "system" message telling the model it’s an expert in named entity recognition and that it should return the results in the specified JSON format,

  • a "user" message containing the text in which to identify the named entities and

  • a Class object—OpenAIUtilities.NamedEntities.class (line 29) is used by the compiler to create a Class<OpenAIUtilities.NamedEntities> object that Simple-OpenAI will use to determine the JSON response format.

The method deserializes the model’s JSON response and returns a NamedEntities object containing a List<NamedEntity> called entities. Lines 37–38 get the List then use its forEach method to output each NamedEntity’s text and tag attributes. The classes NamedEntities and NamedEntity (discussed in Section 19.9.9) are nested record classes in class OpenAIUtilities.

The speech-to-text model can transcribe speech in many spoken languages. The text-to-speech models can produce speech in many languages using nine natural-sounding voices.

19.5.2 Text-to-Speech

A challenge in natural language processing (NLP) is that there are over 7000 natural languages worldwide.40 According to the CIA World Fact Book, the top 11 languages alone account for 44.5% of the world’s population.41 OpenAI’s Audio API can synthesize speech from text in nine voices ("alloy", "ash", "coral", "echo", "fable", "onyx", "nova", "sage" and "shimmer") across 57 languages. OpenAI’s text-to-speech documentation provides audio samples for each voice and lists the supported spoken languages:

19.6 Image Generation

 

Figure 19.9 uses the OpenAI Dall-E API to generate original images. Lines 18–19, 23–24 and 28–29 call class OpenAUtilities’s image method (Figure 19.9.12), which requires three arguments:
