The "dall-e-3" model currently supports images in the following resolutions:44

44. “Image generation.” Accessed February 25, 2025. https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/images.

  • 1024-by-1024 pixels (the default),

  • 1024-by-1792 pixels or

  • 1792-by-1024 pixels.

You may request images in standard or high-definition (HD) quality. HD images, which our image method requests, provide more detail but take longer to generate. The model returns the image in the PNG format, which is widely used on the web for its lossless compression and ability to represent millions of colors.45 With lossless compression, the image’s original information can be restored from its compressed representation.

45. “PNG.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 25, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PNG.

Sample Outputs

The Dall-E API generated the following images in response to this example’s prompts. Note the dramatically different looks—not just different colors and styles, but also the dogs’ faces and hair arrangements! In our experience, we get significantly different results each time we run this program.

How Does ChatGPT Ensure Images Are Original?

We prompted ChatGPT with “How do you ensure that the images Dall-E creates are original?” ChatGPT responded as follows:46 DALL-E generates images using machine learning models trained on large datasets of publicly available images and text, not by copying or manipulating existing images directly. Here's how originality is maintained:

46. ChatGPT in response to “How do you ensure that the images Dall-E creates are original?” October 14, 2024, https://chatgpt.com/.

  1. Generative Process: DALL-E uses a process called “diffusion,” where the model starts from random noise and iteratively refines it based on the given text prompt. This ensures that the output is generated from scratch each time. The model doesn’t retrieve or edit existing images but instead creates entirely new ones based on patterns it has learned from its training data.

  2. No Direct Copying: DALL-E doesn’t store specific images from its training data. It learns to understand relationships between textual descriptions and visual features, but the outputs are not replicas of any particular image in the dataset. As a result, the images it creates are novel combinations of visual elements that match the given prompts.

  3. Ethical Guidelines: The developers of DALL-E implement safeguards and policies to ensure the model adheres to ethical standards, such as not creating content that is offensive, harmful, or violates copyright. Additionally, it’s designed to avoid creating recognizable likenesses of specific individuals or copyrighted works, focusing instead on generating creative, original content.

  4. Diversity in Outputs: The same prompt can result in different images across multiple generations. This variability demonstrates that the images aren’t pre-generated or stored but are the result of a creative, generative process every time.

  5. Training Data: The model is trained on large, diverse datasets, which include publicly available images, but it doesn’t reproduce them. Instead, it learns high-level concepts and relationships between images and text, which it uses to create original art in response to new prompts.

If you’re concerned about originality and copyright, it’s always advisable to review the specific use cases for the generated images and consider any legal implications based on how the images will be used (e.g., commercial vs. personal use).

19.7 Video

This section presents an application that uses multiple OpenAI APIs to create closed captions for a video, demonstrates OpenAI’s Sora video generator and introduces several other powerful video genAIs.

19.7.1 Generating Video Closed Captions

Our next example is a multimodal application (speech, text and video playback) that:

  • uploads a video’s audio track,

  • transcribes it into a JSON format containing timestamps that can be used with the transcribed text to generate closed captions (also called subtitles), then

  • uses a chat-completion request to generate those closed captions in VTT (Video Text Track) format.47

47. “WebVTT.” Wikipedia. Last modified December 31, 2024. Accessed February 25, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebVTT.

The following screen captures contain a couple of this app’s generated captions overlaid on the original video.

Figure 19.10 call our OpenAIUtilities class’s speechToVTT method (lines 22–23; discussed in Section 19.9.13) to create the VTT captions corresponding to the audio in the file ImplicitClass.m4a. Currently, you cannot upload the video file directly to OpenAI to have it generate closed captions. However, you can perform the following steps, which we’ve implemented in the speechToVTT method:

  1. Use a tool like QuickTime on macOS or the cross-platform VLC Media Player (https://www.videolan.org/) to save the video’s audio track as an audio file.

  2. Pass the audio file to the "whisper-1" model to perform a transcription. In this example, speechToVTT explicitly asks the model to produce a verbose JSON formatted response, causing the model to return a collection of transcription segments. Each segment contains a piece of the transcription and the timestamps where that piece starts and ends in the audio file.

  3. Build a String containing the segments with their start and end timestamps.

  4. Submit a chat-completion request with the VTT format requirements, asking the chat API to generate captions in the VTT format for video players. We save this to a VTT file.

  5. Open the video in an application that supports closed captions and play it. For this example, we used the cross-platform VLC Media Player, which allows you to indicate where the VTT file is located. Like the other outputs in this chapter, we write the VTT file to the resources/outputs subfolder of this chapter’s examples folder.

Figure 19.10’s output contains a portion of the VTT-format closed caption text that was written to the standard output and to the file ImplicitClass.vtt.

19.8 Moderation

 

The OpenAI moderation API51 helps developers identify and filter potentially harmful or inappropriate text and image content. The "omni-moderation-latest" model evaluates text and image inputs for harassment, hate speech, violence, self-harm and sexually explicit content—several of these also have more specific subcategories. For each category and sub-category, the response contains:

51. OpenAI, “Moderation,” OpenAI Platform Documentation. Accessed February 26, 2025. https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/moderation.

  • a boolean indicating whether that category was detected and

  • a confidence score from 0 to 1—higher values indicate more offensive content.

For a list of the moderation API’s reporting categories, visit:

Click here to view code image

https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/moderation

Apps can use the results to ensure user safety and comply with ethical guidelines. For information on OpenAI’s usage policies and guidelines, visit:

Click here to view code image

https://openai.com/policies/usage-policies/
Demonstrating Moderation

Figure 19.11 presents a simple example of using the OpenAI moderation API. The program obtains a prompt from the user, then line 14 calls our OpenAIUtilities class’s static method checkPrompt (Section 19.9.14) to evaluate the prompt for offensive content using the moderation API. Method checkPrompt returns a Simple-OpenAI ModerationResult object. Line 16 calls its getFlagged method to check whether the prompt was flagged. If so, lines 21–46 show the individual moderation categories and their scores. Lines 21–22 get a ModerationResult.Category object containing the categories’ boolean values and a ModerationResult.CategoryScore object containing the categories scores. Both classes provide identically named get methods to obtain the boolean values and scores (called in lines 32–46).52

52. At the time of this writing (Simple-OpenAI version 3.18.0), both the Category and CategoryScore classes contain the misspelled method getViolencGraphic, which should be getViolenceGraphic. This bug was reported and slated to be fixed in the next Simple-OpenAI release.

19.9 Class OpenAIUtilities

In this chapter’s examples, we focused on each application’s genAI concepts, encapsulating the details of using the Simple-OpenAI library to interact with the OpenAI APIs in this section’s OpenAIUtilities class. We present this class’s methods and nested types in the order the examples used them. As discussed in Section 19.3.2, the libs subfolder with this chapter’s examples contains a JAR file containing the compiled OpenAIUtilities class. For those who wish to modify this class, we discuss the IntelliJ IDEA project we used to manage the class and its dependencies in our IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition test-drive at https://deitel.com/javafp5. We also provide the project with the chapter’s examples.

19.9.1 Builder Design Pattern

Section 18.6.2 introduced the builder design pattern—a common technique for constructing complex objects step-by-step via chained method calls. When working with the Simple-OpenAI Library, you’ll use this pattern to

  • create a SimpleOpenAI object for performing the interactions with the OpenAI APIs and

  • to formulate the OpenAI API requests.

Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Execution

In this chapter’s examples, the programs issue OpenAI API requests and await their entire responses before outputting the results. The Simple-OpenAI library supports asynchronous programming. When you submit a request, Simple-OpenAI returns a Completable-Future, which is a Future (Section 18.7.1) with additional capabilities. Some features of CompletableFuture include:

  • combining multiple asynchronous tasks then handling their results collectively when they become available,

  • providing “callback” methods that are called automatically to process results when a task completes and

  • more control over a task’s lifecycle, such as manually terminating a task.

Each method in our OpenAIUtilities class calls a CompletableFuture’s join method to synchronously await the results. For more information on CompletableFutures, visit:

Click here to view code image

https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs//api/java.base/java/
   util/concurrent/CompletableFuture.html
https://www.baeldung.com/java-completablefuture
https://dzone.com/articles/20-examples-of-using-javas-
   completablefuture

19.9.2 package and import Statements

Class OpenAIUtilities (Fig. 19.12) uses the Simple-OpenAI open-source library to interact with the OpenAI APIs. This class is defined in its own IntelliJ project as a library that we import into this chapter’s examples. We split the class into parts for discussion purposes. To enable our apps to use class OpenAIUtilities, they must be able to import the class from our custom library. For this reason, we placed this class OpenAIUtilities in the custom deitel.openai package by using a package statement (line 4), which must appear in a Java source-code file before any import statements. Lines 7–22 import the Simple-OpenAI library classes—we discuss each as we use it.

19.9.3 Nested record Class Message

The record class Message (line 37) groups an OpenAI role ("system", "user" or "assistant") and its corresponding content. We’ll turn each Message object into an object of a Simple-OpenAI class that represents a message with the specified role. Simple-OpenAI, in turn, will convert these to messages sent to OpenAI’s web services with our requests.

Click here to view code image

19.9.4 SimpleOpenAI Client Object

An object of the Simple-OpenAI library’s SimpleOpenAI class authenticates with OpenAI using your OPENAI_API_KEY and provides methods that invoke OpenAI’s web services. Lines 40–41:

  • call the SimpleOpenAI static method builder to get a SimpleOpenAIBuilder object for building a SimpleOpenAI that is authenticated to use the OpenAI APIs,

  • call the SimpleOpenAIBuilder’s apiKey method to specify our OPENAI_API_KEY, which we load from the environment variable you created in Section 19.2.4, then

  • call the SimpleOpenAIBuilder’s build method to create the SimpleOpenAI client object for interacting with the OpenAI APIs.

We store the resulting SimpleOpenAI object in a static class variable for use by all the OpenAIUtilities class’s methods.

Click here to view code image

41         .apiKey(System.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY")).build();

19.9.5 chat Method

OpenAIUtilities method chat (lines 44–59) receives the OpenAI model to use for a chat completion and a List<Message>, builds a chat request, uses it to invoke OpenAI’s chat-completion API53 and returns the chat response as a String.

53. OpenAI, Chat Completions API Reference, OpenAI Platform. Accessed February 25, 2025. https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat.

Click here to view code image

43      // perform a chat completion
44      public static String chat(String chatModel, List<Message> messages) {
45         // start building a ChatRequest
46         var chatRequest = ChatRequest.builder().model(chatModel);
47
48         // add messages to the ChatRequest
49         for (var currentMessage : makeChatMessages(messages)) {
50            chatRequest = chatRequest.message(currentMessage);
51         }
52
53         var request = chatRequest.build(); // complete building the request
54
55         // make the ChatRequest and get the Chat response
56         var chatResponse = openAI.chatCompletions().create(request).join();
57
58         return chatResponse.firstContent(); // return the response text
59      }
60

The method operates as follows:

  • Line 46 calls the Simple-OpenAI ChatRequest class’s static builder method to get a ChatRequestBuilder object for configuring a ChatRequest. We call this object’s method to add options to the request.

  • Next, line 46 calls the ChatRequestBuilder object’s model method to set the chat-completion model.

  • As discussed in Section 19.4.1, the OpenAI chat endpoint can receive "system", "user" and "assistant" messages. The Simple-OpenAI library represents these with the ChatMessage class, which has SystemMessage, DeveloperMessage, UserMessage, AssistantMessage subclasses. Lines 49–51 continue building the chat request by calling our makeChatMessages utility method (Section 19.9.6) to convert our chat method’s messages argument into a List<ChatMessage>. For each ChatMessage, line 50 calls the ChatRequestBuilder’s message method, which adds a ChatMessage to the request and returns the updated ChatRequest-Builder. We then assign the update builder to chatRequest.

  • When all the messages have been added, line 53 calls ChatRequestBuilder’s build method to finish building the ChatRequest.

  • Line 56 sends the request to OpenAI and awaits its response. First, we call the SimpleOpenAI object’s chatCompletions method to get a ChatCompletions object that encapsulates the details of invoking OpenAI’s chat-completion web service. We submit the request by calling the ChatCompletions object’s create method, passing request as the argument. Method create returns a CompletableFuture<Chat> from which we’ll obtain a Simple-OpenAI Chat object containing the response, once it’s available. Calling the CompletableFuture<Chat>’s join method causes the caller to wait for the completed response before proceeding.

  • Finally, line 58 calls the Chat object chatResponse’s firstContent method to get and return the String representing the completed chat response.

Mapping Simple-OpenAI Classes and Methods to OpenAI API Documentation

The Simple-OpenAI classes and method calls used in our chat method map to the options discussed in the Request body section of the OpenAI chat completion API documentation at

Click here to view code image

https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat/create

For example,

  • the model method call (line 46) specifies the value of the chat API’s model parameter and

  • each message call (line 50) adds a message to the chat API’s messages parameter.

A benefit of writing Simple-OpenAI code in an IDE like IntelliJ is that, as you enter code, the IDE can tell you the methods you can call and what their parameters are. We demonstrate this in our IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition test-drive at

https://deitel.com/javafp5

19.9.6 Helper Method makeChatMessages

Our helper method makeChatMessages (lines 63–77) converts a List<Message> into a List<ChatMessage> containing SystemMessage, UserMessage and AssistantMessage objects, based on each Message’s role ("system", "user" or "assistant"). The stream pipeline in lines 66–76 maps each Message object to the appropriate ChatMessage subclass object (lines 67–75). Line 76 converts these into a List, which makeChatMessages returns.

Click here to view code image

61      // utility method to convert our Message record objects into
62      // SystemMessage, UserMessage and AssistantMessage objects
63      private static List<ChatMessage> makeChatMessages(
64         List<Message> messages) {
65         // convert each Message record to a ChatMessage subclass object
66         return messages.stream()
67            .map(m -> switch(m.role().toLowerCase()) {
68               case "system" ->
69                  ChatMessage.SystemMessage.of(m.content());
70               case "user" -> ChatMessage.UserMessage.of(m.content());
71               case "assistant" ->
72                  ChatMessage.AssistantMessage.of(m.content());
73               default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException(
74                  "invalid role: " + m.role());
75            })
76            .toList();
77      }
78
Nested Classes

Classes SystemMessage, UserMessage and AssistantMessage are public static nested classes in class ChatMessage. A static nested class is defined inside another class and preceded by the static keyword. Such classes are often used when the nested class is closely related to its enclosing class. In this case, the nested classes are also ChatMessage subclasses. So, objects of these classes are valid wherever ChatMessages are required. Each of these nested subclasses has an of method that receives a String representing the message’s content and returns a new object of the corresponding ChatMessage subclass.

19.9.7 describeImage Method

OpenAIUtilities method describeImage (lines 80–104) uses the OpenAI chat API’s vision capabilities to create accessible image descriptions for people who are blind or have low vision. This method’s "system" message (lines 85–89) directs the chat API to adhere to the accessible image-description guidelines provided by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C).54 Method describeImage requires three arguments:

54. W3C Web Accessibility Initiative, “Images,” Web Accessibility Tutorials. Last modified February 8, 2022. Accessed February 25, 2025. https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/.

  • the chat model that should create the accessible image description,

  • a prompt that will be supplied as a "user" message to the chat model—used in Section 19.4.3 to provide the model with a brief description of an image—and

  • a Path to the image that will be uploaded.

OpenAI’s models can also receive the URL of an image to analyze, though we do not support that in our describeImage method.

Click here to view code image

79      // perform a chat completion
80      public static String describeImage(
81         String chatModel, String prompt, Path imagePath) {
82         // start building a ChatRequest for accessible image descriptions
83         var chatRequest = ChatRequest.builder()
84            .model(chatModel)
85            .message(ChatMessage.SystemMessage.of("""
86               You are an expert at creating accessible descriptions
87               of images per the World Wide Web Consortium's (W3C's)
88               guidelines. Given an image, explain it in detail for
89               people who are blind or have low vision."""))
90            .message(ChatMessage.UserMessage.of(
91               List.of(
92                  ContentPart.ContentPartText.of(prompt),
93                  ContentPart.ContentPartImageUrl.of(
94                     ContentPart.ContentPartImageUrl.ImageUrl.of(
95                        Base64Util.encode(imagePath.toString(),
96                           Base64Util.MediaType.IMAGE))))))
97            .build();
98
99         // make the ChatRequest and get the Chat response
100        var chatResponse =
101           openAI.chatCompletions().create(chatRequest).join();
102
103        return chatResponse.firstContent(); // return the response text
104     }
105

Method describeImage is similar to chat (Section 19.9.5). The key difference is in lines 90–96 of creating the ChatRequest. To analyze an image, the OpenAI chat API requires a JSON array of messages containing a text prompt and the URL of an image to analyze. If the image is a local file on your system, as in Section 19.4.3’s example, the URL must have the format:

Click here to view code image

"data:image/imageFormat ;base64, base64EncodedImageString"

where imageFormat in our example is png or jpeg, depending on which image we send, and base64EncodedImageString is a String containing the image’s Base64-encoded data (introduced in Section 7.9). Lines 90–96 create a JSON array of messages:

  • When you create a ChatMessage with a List as an argument, Simple-OpenAI converts the List to a JSON array—lines 91–96 create a List containing two Simple-OpenAI ContentParts, each representing a message in the JSON array.

  • The ContentPart nested class ContentPartText (line 92) creates a message for the required text prompt.

  • The ContentPart nested class ContentPartImageUrl (lines 93–96) creates a message containing the required Base64-encoded image. The Simple-OpenAI utility class Base64Util’s encode method (lines 95–96) receives as arguments the image’s location on your system and the kind of data being encoded—Base64Util.MediaType.IMAGE indicates the data is an image. The kind of data is embedded in the Base64 encoding so the OpenAI API can decode it correctly.

19.9.8 translate Method

OpenAIUtilities method translate (lines 107–122) uses the chat model specified in its first argument to translate the String in its second argument to the language in its third argument, then returns the translated String. Text translation is also accomplished via standard chat completions. Lines 111–116 build the ChatRequest:

  • The SystemMessage ("system" role) in lines 112–114 tells the chat model how to operate. In this case, the chat is a translation expert that will translate text to the targetlanguage.

  • The UserMessage ("user" role) in line 115 provides the text to translate.

Line 119 submits the request to OpenAI and awaits its response. Then, line 121 returns the result as a String.

Click here to view code image

106     // perform a chat completion for translation
107     public static String translate(
108        String chatModel, String textToTranslate, String targetLanguage) {
109
110        // build a ChatRequest to translate a String
111        var chatRequest = ChatRequest.builder().model(chatModel)
112           .message(ChatMessage.SystemMessage.of(String.format("""
113              You are an expert in natural language translation.
114              Translate the following text into %s.""", targetLanguage)))
115           .message(ChatMessage.UserMessage.of(textToTranslate))
116           .build();
117
118        // create and submit the ChatRequest and wait for the Chat response
119        Chat response = openAI.chatCompletions().create(chatRequest).join();
120
121        return response.firstContent(); // return the translation
122     }
123

19.9.9 chatWithStructuredOutput Method

As discussed in Section 19.4.6, OpenAI chat completions can return structured outputs containing data in the format you specify. This section discusses the record classes and method chatWithStructuredOutput we used in Section 19.4.6’s named entity recognition (NER) example.

record Classes NamedEntity and NamedEntities

Lines 126–127 define the record classes we used in our named entity recognition example (Section 19.4.6) to represent the structured output format:

  • Our NamedEntity record class represents one named entity as two Strings—the entity’s text and corresponding tag.

  • Our NamedEntities record class represents a List of NamedEntity objects.

Click here to view code image

124     // record classes to define the structure of a JSON response
125     // containing results of named entity recognition
126     public record NamedEntity(String text, String tag) {}
127     public record NamedEntities(List<NamedEntity> entities) {}
128
Method chatWithStructuredOutput

OpenAIUtilities method chatWithStructuredOutput (lines 131–160) is not specific to named entity recognition. It’s a generic method that receives as arguments:

  • the chat model that will process the chat request,

  • a List<Message> specifying the messages to pass in the chat request, and

  • a Class<T> representing the class that will be used to determine the structured output format. In Section 19.4.6, this argument was specified as

    Click here to view code image

    OpenAIUtilities.NamedEntities.class

    which the Java compiler converts to an object of type

    Click here to view code image

    Class<OpenAIUtilities.NamedEntities>

The chatWithStructuredOutput method returns an object of the class represented by the type parameter T—for Section 19.4.6’s example an OpenAIUtilities.NamedEntities object. When calling chatWithStructuredOutput, include a "system" message telling the chat request to return a JSON response in the “specified format” (determined by lines 134–138) and nothing else; otherwise, the chat response may nest your desired JSON response in a larger JSON object containing additional information.

Click here to view code image

129     // generic method that performs a chat completion and
130     // returns structured output
131     public static <T> T chatWithStructuredOutput(String chatModel,
132        List<Message> messages, Class<T> jsonStructure) throws Exception {
133        // set up JSON schema for structured output based on jsonStructure
134        var schema = ResponseFormat.jsonSchema(JsonSchema.builder()
135           .name(jsonStructure.getSimpleName()) // schema name
136           .schemaClass(jsonStructure) // schema Java class
137           .build()
138        );
139
140        // start building a ChatRequest that returns structured output
141        var chatRequest = ChatRequest.builder()
142           .model(chatModel)
143           .responseFormat(schema);
144
145        // add messages to the ChatRequest
146        for (var currentMessage : makeChatMessages(messages)) {
147           chatRequest = chatRequest.message(currentMessage);
148        }
149
150        var request = chatRequest.build(); // complete building the request
151
152        // make the ChatRequest and get the Chat response
153        Chat response = openAI.chatCompletions().create(request).join();
154
155        // ObjectMapper for deserializing JSON into a NamedEntities object
156        var mapper = new ObjectMapper();
157
158        // return the structured response
159        return mapper.readValue(response.firstContent(), jsonStructure);
160     }
161
Determining the Response Format

Section 19.4.6 presented sample JSON containing the expected response format. Lines 134–138 build a Simple-OpenAI ResponseFormat object representing the structured output format. ResponseFormat static method jsonSchema creates a ResponseFormat based on its argument—a Simple-OpenAI JsonSchema object. Lines 134–138, use a Simple-OpenAI JsonSchemaBuilder object to determine the JSON format:

  • Line 135 calls JsonSchemaBuilder method name to specify the class name to which the schema corresponds. Class method getSimpleName returns the unqualified class name of the class represented by the jsonStructure argument.

  • Line 136 calls JsonSchemaBuilder schemaClass method to infer the JSON structure we’d like to receive in the OpenAI chat response. Method schemaClass inspects its argument’s class, NamedEntities, to determine that it contains a List<NamedEntity> called entities. This will result in a key-value pair in the JSON response with the key "entities" and a JSON array as the value. It also infers from the List<NamedEntity> that each element in the JSON array contains the strings text and tag. So, each named entity will be represented as a JSON object with key-value pairs having the keys "text" and "tag".

  • Finally, line 137 builds the JsonSchema.

Setting Up the Chat Request

Lines 141–150 set up the chat request similarly to lines 46–53 of method chat. The key difference is adding the JsonSchema to the request by calling ChatRequestBuilder method responseFormat.

Executing the Request and Processing the Response

Line 153 issues the request using the same technique shown previously. Lines 156 and 159 use a Jackson library ObjectMapper to deserialize the JSON response (as discussed in Section 11.5.2) and return an object of the class represented by the generic type T. For the named entity recognition example in Section 19.4.6, chatWithStructuredOutput’s return value will be a NamedEntities object containing a List<NamedEntity>.

19.9.10 speechToText Method

OpenAIUtilities method speechToText (lines 163–174) gets a transcription of an audio file. It receives an OpenAI audio-transcription model and a String representing the file’s location, builds a Simple-OpenAI TranscriptionRequest (lines 165–168) to get the audio file’s transcription, uses the request to invoke OpenAI’s Audio API55 and returns a String containing the transcription:

55. OpenAI, Audio API Reference, OpenAI Platform. Accessed February 25, 2025, https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/audio.

  • Line 165 calls the TranscriptionRequest static method builder to get a TranscriptionRequestBuilder object for configuring the request.

  • Line 166 calls the TranscriptionRequestBuilder object’s file method to specify the audio file’s Path.

  • Line 167 calls the TranscriptionRequestBuilder object’s model method to specify the model that will transcribe the audio.

  • Line 168 calls the TranscriptionRequestBuilder object’s build method to create the TranscriptionRequest.

Click here to view code image

162     // convert audio to text transcription
163     public static String speechToText(String model, String audioPath) {
164        // build a TranscriptionRequest
165        var audioRequest = TranscriptionRequest.builder()
166           .file(Paths.get(audioPath))
167           .model(model)
168           .build();
169
170        // submit TranscriptionRequest and wait for Transcription
171        Transcription transcription =
172           openAI.audios().transcribe(audioRequest).join();
173        return transcription.getText(); // return transcription text
174     }
175

Lines 171–172 initiate the transcription request:

  • First, we call the SimpleOpenAI object’s audios method to get a Simple-OpenAI Audios object encapsulating the details of invoking OpenAI’s audio-transcription web service.

  • The Audios object’s transcribe method receives a TranscriptionRequest and returns a CompletableFuture<Transcription>, enabling the program to obtain the OpenAI response once it becomes available.

  • Again, the join method call tells the program not to continue until the complete response is received.

Line 173 returns the transcription.

19.9.11 textToSpeech Method

OpenAIUtilities method textToSpeech (lines 177–192) receives Strings representing an OpenAI speech-synthesis model, the text to synthesize into speech, the voice used to speak the text and the file in which to store the audio. It sends a speech-synthesis request to the OpenAI Audio API and writes the audio response into the specified file.

Click here to view code image

176     // synthesize speech from text
177     public static void textToSpeech(String model, String text,
178        String voice, String filename) throws Exception {
179        // build a SpeechRequest
180        var speechRequest = SpeechRequest.builder()
181           .model(model)
182           .input(text)
183           .voice(Voice.valueOf(voice.toUpperCase()))
184           .build();
185
186        // submit SpeechRequest and wait for audio, then save audio to file
187        try (var audioStream = openAI.audios().speak(speechRequest).join();
188             var audioFile = new FileOutputStream(filename)) {
189           audioFile.write(audioStream.readAllBytes());
190           System.out.printf("Wrote audio to %s%n", filename);
191        }
192     }
193

Lines 180–184 build a Simple-OpenAI SpeechRequest:

  • Line 180 calls the Simple-OpenAI SpeechRequest class’s static builder method to get a SpeechRequestBuilder object for configuring the SpeechRequest.

  • Line 181 calls the SpeechRequestBuilder object’s model method to set the text-to-speech model.

  • Line 182 calls the SpeechRequestBuilder object’s input method to specify the input to the model—that is, the text the model will synthesize into speech.

  • Line 183 calls the SpeechRequestBuilder object’s voice method to set the voice the text-to-speech model will use. The Voice enumeration provides constants for each currently supported voice. We use the enum’s valueOf method to get the correct constant based on our method’s voice argument.

  • Line 184 builds the SpeechRequest.

Lines 187–191 submit the SpeechRequest and write its response to the specified file:

  • As with audio transcription, we call the SimpleOpenAI object’s audios method to get a Simple-OpenAI Audios object, which also provides access to the OpenAI text-to-speech capabilities. The Audios object’s speak method (line 187) receives a SpeechRequest and returns a CompletableFuture<InputStream>, enabling the program to obtain the OpenAI response once it becomes available. We call join to await the complete response.

  • Next, line 188 creates a byte-based FileOutputStream that we’ll use to write the audio bytes into the specified file.

  • Line 189 calls the InputStream’s readAllBytes method to get the complete audio from the response, then writes the bytes into the file using FileOutputStream method write.

When the try-with-resources statement completes, both streams are closed automatically.

19.9.12 image Method

OpenAIUtilities static method image (lines 195–217) uses OpenAI’s image-generation API56 to generate an image based on a text prompt. The method receives the name of an image-generation model, a prompt describing the image to generate and a Path in which to store the generated image. The method then creates an image-generation request, uses it to invoke the image-generation API and stores the resulting image in the file specified by the Path argument.

56. OpenAI, Images API Reference, OpenAI Platform. Accessed February 25, 2025, https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/images.

Click here to view code image

194     // generate an image with Dall-E
195     public static void image(
196        String model, String prompt, Path imagePath) throws Exception {
197        // build an ImageRequest with the specified model and prompt
198        var imageRequest = ImageRequest.builder()
199           .model(model)
200           .prompt(prompt)
201           .quality(ImageRequest.Quality.HD)
202           .build();
203
204        // submit ImageRequest and wait for image
205        var imageResponse = openAI.images().create(imageRequest).join();
206
207        // get image's URL
208        String urlString = imageResponse.getFirst().getUrl();
209        URL url = URI.create(urlString).toURL();
210
211        // save image to PNG file
212        try (var inputStream = url.openStream()) {
213           Files.copy(inputStream, imagePath,
214              StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
215           System.out.printf("Wrote image to %s%n", imagePath);
216        }
217     }
218

Lines 198–202 build a Simple-OpenAI ImageRequest:

  • Line 198 calls the Simple-OpenAI ImageRequest class’s static builder method to get an ImageRequestBuilder object to configure the ImageRequest.

  • Line 199 calls the ImageRequestBuilder object’s model method to set the image-generation model.

  • Line 200 calls the ImageRequestBuilder object’s prompt method to specify the text prompt describing the image to generate.

  • Line 201 calls the ImageRequestBuilder object’s quality method to set the image quality to high definition (ImageRequest.Quality.HD)—the default is standard definition (STANDARD).

  • Line 202 builds the ImageRequest.

This image request produces one generated image (the default). You can request up to 10 images by calling the ImageRequestBuilder object’s n method (short for "number") with an integer argument.

Lines 205–216 submit the ImageRequest and write the generated image to the specified file:

  • Line 205 calls the SimpleOpenAI object’s images method to get a Simple-OpenAI Images object, which provides access to the OpenAI image-generation and editing capabilities. The Images object’s create method receives an ImageRequest and returns a CompletableFuture<List<Image>>, enabling the program to obtain the list of generated images. We call join to await the complete response.

  • Line 208 calls the List method getFirst to get the first (and in this case, only) Image, then calls the Image’s getUrl method to get a String URL representing the generated image on OpenAI’s servers.

  • Line 209 converts the String URL into a URL object.

  • Line 212 calls URL method openStream to get a byte-based InputStream from which we can read the image’s bytes.

  • Line 213–214 uses the Files class’s static method copy to read the bytes from the first argument’s InputStream and write them to the second argument’s Path.

The InputStream is closed when the try-with-resources statement completes.

19.9.13 speechToVTT Method

OpenAIUtilities static method speechToVTT (lines 220–263) receives an OpenAI audio-transcription model name and a Path to an audio file, then

  • uses a TranscriptionRequest to transcribe the audio into segments with timestamps,

  • uses a ChatRequest to format the transcription into WebVTT format (discussed in Section 19.7.1) for use as closed captions, and

  • returns the WebVTT-formatted transcription.

Click here to view code image

219     // convert audio track of a video into closed captions
220     public static String speechToVTT(String model, Path audioPath) {
221        // build a TranscriptionRequest that returns JSON containing the
222        // transcription segments and their start/end times
223        var audioRequest = TranscriptionRequest.builder()
224           .file(audioPath)
225           .model(model)
226           .responseFormat(AudioResponseFormat.VERBOSE_JSON)
227           .build();
228
229        // submit TranscriptionRequest and wait for Transcription
230        Transcription transcription =
231           openAI.audios().transcribe(audioRequest).join();
232
233        // get the transcript's segments
234        List<Transcription.Segment> segments = transcription.getSegments();
235
236        // create a String representation of the transcription's
237        // segments with their start and end times
238        String transcriptionText = segments.stream()
239           .map(segment -> String.format("Start: %f, End: %f, Text: %s",
240              segment.getStart(), segment.getEnd(), segment.getText()))
241           .collect(Collectors.joining("\n"));
242
243        // issue a chat request to convert the audio
244        // segment transcriptions into VTT format
245        var request = ChatRequest.builder()
246           .model("gpt-4o")
247           .message(ChatMessage.SystemMessage.of("""
248              You are a subtitle formatting assistant. Take the following
249              transcription data and format it into VTT (WebVTT) format.
250              Timestamps must have the hh:mm:ss.mmm format required by
251              WebVTT. Include the required WEBVTT header at beginning of
252              the file. Output the VTT content only."""))
253           .message(ChatMessage.UserMessage.of(transcriptionText))
254           .build();
255
256        // make the ChatRequest and get the response
257        var response = openAI.chatCompletions().create(request).join();
258
259        // remove markdown code-block delimiters (```) at beginning
260        // and end of response and return VTT-formatted captions
261        var captions = response.firstContent();
262        return captions.substring(3, captions.length() - 3);
263     }
264

The speechToVTT method operates as follows:

  • Lines 223–227 build an audio-transcription request, as shown previously. The key difference is in line 226 where we call TranscriptionRequestBuilder method responseFormat with AudioResponseFormat.VERBOSE_JSON as the argument. This tells the transcription model to return audio segments with time-stamps in JSON format. Simple-OpenAI converts the audio segments to objects of class Transcription.Segment that are stored in the Transcription response.

  • Lines 230–231 submit the TranscriptionRequest.

  • Line 234 gets a List<Transcription.Segment> by calling the Transcription’s getSegments method.

  • Lines 238–241 use a stream pipeline to map each Segment to a formatted String containing the Segment’s start time, end time and text, then collects these formatted Strings into a single String with each segment separated by a newline from the next.

  • Lines 245–257 build and execute a chat-completion request with a "system" message (lines 247–252) telling the model how to format the data supplied in the "user" message (line 253).

  • Finally, lines 261–262 get the content of the chat response. OpenAI returns the formatted response in markdown format, so line 262 removes the ``` delimiters before returning the WebVTT formatted transcription.

19.9.14 checkPrompt Method

Method checkPrompt (lines 266–276) uses the OpenAI moderation API to check its argument’s text for offensive content.

Click here to view code image

265     // send text to OpenAI moderation API to check for offensive content;
266     public static Moderation.ModerationResult checkPrompt(String prompt) {
267        // build a ModerationRequest
268        var moderationRequest = ModerationRequest.builder()
269           .model("omni-moderation-latest") // OpenAI recommended model
270           .input(List.of(prompt))
271           .build();
272
273        // submit the request and return the result
274        var result = openAI.moderations().create(moderationRequest).join();
275        return result.getResults().getFirst();
276     }
277  }

Lines 268–274 build then execute a Simple-OpenAI ModerationRequest:

  • Line 268 calls the Simple-OpenAI ModerationRequest class’s static builder method to get a ModerationRequestBuilder object to configure the request.

  • Line 269 calls the ModerationRequestBuilder object’s model method to set the image-generation model.

  • Line 270 calls the ModerationRequestBuilder object’s input method to specify a list of Strings to send to the moderation API. In this method, we send one prompt as input, but the List may contain multiple items, some of which can be URLs of online images or Base64-encoded images being uploaded from the user’s computer.

  • Line 271 builds the ImageRequest.

  • Line 274 calls the SimpleOpenAI object’s moderations method to get a Simple-OpenAI Moderations object, which provides access to the OpenAI moderation API. The Moderations object’s create method receives a ModerationRequest and returns a CompletableFuture<Moderation>, enabling the program to obtain the moderation results when they are available. We call join to await the complete response.

  • Line 275 gets the first ModerationResult from the List<ModerationResult> returned by Moderation method getResults. Each ModerationResult contains a boolean indicating whether the items was flagged for offensive content, a collection of categories with boolean values indicating which were flagged and a corresponding collection of scores from 0 (not offensive) to 1 (completely offensive). We extracted and displayed those results in Fig. 19.11.

19.10 Wrap-Up

In this chapter, we built API-based Java genAI applications that interacted with OpenAI's genAI models via the Simple-OpenAI Java library. We introduced the concept of multi-modal genAIs that process and generate text, images, audio and video content. You learned about several OpenAI genAI models for text generation, speech recognition, speech synthesis, image creation and moderation.

We discussed setting up a Java environment to work with OpenAI APIs using the Simple-OpenAI library. You learned how to obtain an OpenAI developer account, generate an API key and store it securely on your system. We mentioned an IntelliJ-based Maven project setup that simplifies dependency management and compilation of Java applications using the Simple-OpenAI Java library. More details on that project are provided in our IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition test-drive at

https://deitel.com/javafp5

We presented many genAI apps, starting with several text-based applications. You learned how to generate text using OpenAI’s chat-completion models and explored genAI text capabilities such as summarization, sentiment analysis, accessible image descriptions, language detection and translation, code generation and named entity recognition (NER). In the NER example, we demonstrated the OpenAI chat model’s ability to return structured JSON output.

We used OpenAI’s Whisper model to perform speech recognition, transcribing audio to text, and their TTS model to synthesize natural-sounding speech in multiple languages. We generated original images from text prompts using OpenAI’s Dall-E API. We discussed OpenAI’s Sora video generator, which did not have an API at the time of this writing, and introduced several other genAI video services. We used OpenAI’s moderation tools to analyze and filter harmful content in text and discussed that moderation can also be used for images.

In our OpenAIUtilities class discussion, we explored invoking OpenAI’s APIs using the free, open-source Simple-OpenAI library, which encapsulates the details of working with OpenAI’s web services. We discussed each of our OpenAIUtilities class’s static helper methods and nested classes that we used in our genAI applications. The next chapter introduces relational databases and Structured Query Language (SQL) then demonstrates using JDBC and SQL to interact with SQLite relational databases.

19.46 (Multimedia Tortoise and the Hare Race with JavaFX) In this exercise, you’ll recreate the classic race of the tortoise and the hare. You’ll use random-number generation to develop a simulation of this memorable event. Prompt genAIs to build a fun, animated JavaFX multimedia “extravaganza” in which the user can watch the race.

Our contenders begin the race at square 1 of 70 squares. Each square represents a possible position along the race course. The finish line is at square 70. The first contender to reach or pass square 70 is rewarded with a pail of fresh carrots and lettuce. The course weaves its way up a slippery mountain’s side, so occasionally the contenders lose ground.

A clock ticks once per second. With each tick, your program should adjust the animal’s positions according to the following rules:

The program should keep track of the positions of the animals (i.e., position numbers are 1–70). Start each animal at position 1 (the “starting gate”). If an animal slips left before square 1, move it back to square 1.

Generate the percentages in the preceding table by producing a random integer i in the range 1 ≤ i ≤ 10. For the tortoise, perform a “fast plod” when 1 ≤ i ≤ 5, a “slip” when 6 ≤ i ≤ 7 or a “slow plod” when 8 ≤ i ≤ 10. Use a similar technique to move the hare.

For use in your race, we’ve provided in the resources/race subfolder with this chapter’s examples the following audio clips and images:62

62. Other than the public-domain William Tell Overture, we created these audios and images. If you prefer, you could search the web for others or create your own. Be sure to comply with the license terms for any media you’ll use in your applications.

  • An audio recording we created of the “Call to Post” trumpet piece played at the beginning of a horse race.

  • A cannon-firing sound we created for our Cannon game.

  • An audio clip we created of an announcer saying, “And they’re off!” You could record yourself as the announcer saying this and other phrases to play throughout the race, such as “Tortoise pulls ahead!”, “Hare pulls ahead!”, “Down the stretch they come!”, etc.

  • A public-domain Wikimedia audio recording of the William Tell Overture63, which we have edited down to just the gallop portion (bada bump, bada bump, bada bump bump bump…) and placed in this chapter’s resources folder for you to play during the race.

    63. “File:Gioachino Rossini, William Tell Overture (military band version, 2000).ogg.” Accessed February 25, 2025. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gioachino_Rossini,_William_Tell_Overture_(military_band_version,_2000).ogg.

  • Two slightly different tortoise and two slightly different hare images we created:

Tell the genAI to toggle between these images to create simple animations of the animals running. You can see the animations by viewing the tortoise.gif and hare.gif animated GIF images provided in the resources/race subfolder. You can use our images or ask the genAIs to create their own. Tell the genAIs that the app should perform the following tasks:

  1. Before the race begins, play the trumpet audio of the “Call to Post,” signifying that the racers should take their mark. As the “Call to Post” plays, the tortoise and hare should appear from the screen’s left side and take their positions.

  2. Play the cannon sound to start the race, followed by the announcer saying, “And they’re off!” At this point, the race animation begins.

  3. Throughout the race, repeatedly play the provided William Tell Overture’s gallop portion in the background.

  4. As the tortoise and the hare move across the screen, toggle between each animal’s two images to make them appear to be running. The tortoise moves slower than the hare, so you may want to toggle between the tortoise’s two images slower than between the hare’s two images. When the hare arrogantly sleeps, stop toggling between its images.

  5. When the tortoise and hare are in the same position, display “OUCH!” for the tortoise biting the hare and optionally play a high-pitched “OUCH!” audio clip.

  6. If the tortoise wins, display “Tortoise wins!” and optionally play a “Tortoise wins!” audio clip followed by cheering. If the hare wins, display “Hare wins” and optionally play a “Hare wins” audio clip followed by booing. If the race ends in a tie, have the announcer say, “It’s a tie!”

  7. Play crowd cheering sounds, booing sounds and additional announcer commentary as appropriate throughout the race. Locate public-domain crowd sounds online, or ask genAIs to generate original sounds.

19.81 (Generative AI: Computer-Assisted Instruction) Prompt genAIs to develop a command-line computer-assisted instruction program to help elementary school students improve their arithmetic skills. The program should prompt the student to select both a difficulty level and a type of arithmetic problem to study. The difficulty level determines the size of the numbers used:

  • level 1 uses only single-digit numbers,

  • level 2 includes up to two-digit numbers,

  • and so on)

The problem type can be addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, or a random mix of all four.

The program should then generate a problem using a RandomGenerator object (or equivalent), display a question such as “How much is 6 times 7?” (adjusting the operation based on the selected type), and continue to ask the same question until the student provides the correct answer. When the student answers, the program should provide immediate feedback, selecting a response at random from a list of encouraging messages for a correct answer (e.g., “Very good!”, “Excellent!”, “Nice work!”, “Keep up the good work!”) or a list of prompts for an incorrect answer (e.g., “No. Please try again.”, “Wrong. Try once more.”, “Don't give up!”, “No. Keep trying.”).

The program should monitor the student's performance over a session of 10 questions, keeping count of correct and incorrect responses, and at the end, calculate the percentage of correct answers. Based on the results, if the student scores less than 75%, the program should display “Please ask your teacher for extra help.”, and if 75% or higher, it should congratulate the student with “Congratulations, you are ready to go to the next level!”. Finally, the program should reset itself so the user can begin a new session. Make the program multimodal, using the OpenAI chat, speech synthesis and speech recognition APIs.

19.82 (Law of Large Numbers with Coin Flipping: Static Visualization) Prompt genAIs to create a JavaFX app that demonstrates the Law of Large Numbers in action by flipping a coin 200 million times, displaying the results as a bar chart with one bar representing the number of heads and the other representing the number of tails.

Game Development

19.85 (SpotOn Game) The SpotOn game tests a user’s reflexes by requiring the user to click moving spots before they disappear:

The required images and sounds for this exercise are located in the resources folder with this chapter’s examples, though you can also use free images and sounds from many web-sites or create your own.

In this game, the spots shrink as they move, making them harder to click. The game begins on level one, and the user reaches each higher level by clicking ten spots. The higher the level, the faster the spots move—making the game increasingly challenging. When the user clicks a spot, the app plays a “hit” sound (hit.mp3), and the spot disappears. Points are awarded for each clicked spot—ten times the current level. Accuracy is important—any click that isn’t on a spot plays a “miss” sound (miss.mp3) and decreases the score by 15 times the current level. You can tune the rewards and penalties to make the game more interesting.

The user begins the game with three additional “lives,” which are displayed in the bottom-left corner of the app. If a spot disappears before the user clicks it, the app plays a “flushing” sound (disappear.mp3) sound, and the user loses a life. The user gains a life for reaching each new level, up to a maximum of seven lives. When no lives remain and a spot’s animation ends before the spot is clicked, the game ends and displays an Alert dialog (package javafx.scene.control).

Prompt genAIs to generate the SpotOn game app using JavaFX. They should define a Spot subclass of Circle that encapsulates a spot’s data and functionality. For each Spot the genAIs should:

  1. Fill its circle with a spot image (orange_spot.png or blue_spot.png).

  2. Provide random start and end points, and ensure that the Spot is completely within the Pane’s bounds.

  3. Provide an event handler that responds to a mouse click within a Spot’s bounds, which you can set via the inherited Node method setOnMouseClicked.

  4. To make each Spot move, use a ParallelTransition consisting of a Scale-Transition that reduces the size of a spot from its original size to 25% of its original size and a PathTransition that moves the spot from its start point to its end point. Register an event handler that executes when the ParallelTransition runs to completion—in this case, the user should lose a life because the spot was not clicked.

The genAIs should use a TimelineAnimation to create the five initial spots—one every half-second. After that, each subsequent spot should be created when the user successfully clicks a spot or when a spot completes its animation and has not been clicked. To check for clicks that miss a spot, register a mouse-click handler for the app’s Pane.

19.86 (Cannon Game) The Cannon game app challenges you to destroy nine targets before a ten-second time limit expires:

This game requires some two-dimensional analytic geometry and some basic trigonometry to determine the angle of the cannon. All of the required sounds for this exercise are located in the resources folder with this chapter’s examples, though you also can use free sounds from reputable websites or create your own.

The game consists of a cannon, a cannonball, nine targets and a blocker that defends the targets—the blocker cannot be destroyed. The blocker and each target move vertically at different speeds, reversing direction when they hit the Canvas’s top or bottom. You aim and fire the cannon by clicking the mouse—the cannon’s barrel then rotates to aim at the click point and fires the cannonball in a straight line in that direction.

You win by destroying all nine targets before time expires—if the timer reaches zero, you lose. When you destroy a target, the time remaining increases by a three-second time bonus. When you hit the blocker, the time remaining decreases by a three-second time penalty. When the game ends, the app displays an Alert dialog (package javafx.scene.control) indicating whether you won or lost, the number of shots fired and the elapsed time.

When you fire the cannon, the game plays a firing sound (cannon_fire.wav), and a cannonball begins moving from the cannon’s barrel toward the blocker and targets. When a cannonball hits a target, a glass-breaking sound (target_hit.wav) plays and that target disappears. When the cannonball hits the blocker, a hit sound (blocker_hit.wav) plays, and the cannonball bounces back toward the cannon.

Prompt genAIs to generate this game using a JavaFX Circles and Rectangles to represent the game elements and TransitionAnimations to move them. Class Shape provides static method intersect that can be used for collision detection based on the actual shapes (that is, a Circle for the cannonball and Rectangles for the blocker and targets). Tell the genAIs to consider defining classes that represent the various game elements.

Accessing Databases with JDBC and SQLite

Objectives

In this chapter, you’ll:

  • Learn relational database concepts.

  • Use Structured Query Language (SQL) and the SQLite command-line interface to retrieve data from and manipulate data in a SQLite database.

  • Use the JDBC API’s classes and interfaces to manipulate SQLite databases.

  • Use JDBC’s automatic JDBC driver discovery.

  • Display query results in a JavaFX TableView.

  • Bind query results to a TableView using JavaFX observable collections.

  • Sort and filter a TableView’s contents.

  • Create precompiled SQL statements with parameters via PreparedStatements.

  • Learn how transaction processing makes database applications more robust.

20.1 Introduction

 

In Chapter 11, we demonstrated sequential text-file processing, working with plain-text, JSON-format and CSV-format data. These are useful when most or all of a file’s data is to be processed. On the other hand, in transaction processing, it’s crucial to locate and possibly update an individual data item quickly.

A database is an integrated collection of data. A database management system (DBMS) provides mechanisms for storing and organizing data in a manner consistent with the database’s format. Database management systems allow for convenient access and storage of data without concern for the internal representation of databases.

Relational Database Management Systems and Structured Query Language

Many of today’s most popular database systems are relational databases (Section 20.2). Relational database management systems (RDBMSs) store data in tables and define relationships among the tables. SQL (Structured Query Language) is used almost universally with RDBMSs to manipulate data and perform queries, which request information that satisfies given criteria.1

1. The writing in this chapter assumes that SQL is pronounced as “see-quel.” Some prefer “ess que el.”

Popular Relational Database Management Systems

Popular open-source RDBMSs include SQLite, PostgreSQL, MariaDB and MySQL. These can be downloaded and used freely by anyone. All have support for Java. We’ll use SQLite, which comes bundled with macOS and many Linux distributions and can be downloaded and installed on Windows. Some popular proprietary RDBMSs include Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server and IBM Db2.

JDBC

Java programs use the JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) API to interact with databases. A JDBC driver enables programs to connect to a database in a particular DBMS and manipulate that database using the JDBC API. The JDBC API is portable—the same code can manipulate databases in various RDBMSs.

Most popular database management systems provide JDBC drivers or have JDBC drivers provided by third parties. This chapter introduces JDBC and uses it to manipulate SQLite databases. The techniques we demonstrate here can be used to manipulate other databases with JDBC drivers. You can get the SQLite JDBC driver from

Click here to view code image

https://github.com/xerial/sqlite-jdbc/releases

For your convenience, we included this driver in the libs folder of this chapter’s examples.

Generative AI

1 Prompt genAIs for the pros and cons of using databases vs. files for data storage in Java applications.

20.2 Relational Databases

 

A relational database is a logical table-based data representation that allows the data to be accessed without considering its physical structure. The following diagram contains a sample Employee table that might be used in a personnel system:

The table’s primary purpose is to store employees’ attributes. Tables are composed of rows, each describing a single entity. Here, each row represents one employee. Rows are composed of columns containing individual attribute values. The table above has six rows. The Number column represents the primary key—a column (or group of columns) with a unique value for each row. This guarantees that each row can be identified by its primary key. Examples of primary keys are social security numbers, employee ID numbers and part numbers in an inventory system—values in each are guaranteed to be unique. In this case, the rows are listed in ascending order by primary key, but they could be listed in descending order or no particular order at all.

Each column represents a different data attribute. Rows within a table are unique by primary key, but particular column values may be duplicated between rows. For example, three rows in the Employee table’s Department column contain number 413.

Selecting Data Subsets

Database users are often interested in different data and different relationships among the data. Most users require only subsets of the rows and columns. Queries specify which subsets of the data to select from a table. You use Structured Query Language (SQL) to define queries. For example, you might select data from the Employee table to determine where each department is located, presenting the data sorted in increasing order by department number, as in the following result. We’ll discuss SQL shortly.

Click here to view code image

Department     Location

413            New Jersey
611            Orlando
642            Los Angeles

20.3 Setting Up the SQLite RDBMS

 

SQLite and its command-line tools come bundled with macOS and Linux. Windows users can download SQLite and its tools from

Click here to view code image

https://www.sqlite.org/download.html

Under the heading Precompiled Binaries for Windows, download SQLite2 by selecting

2. Version 3470200 (for 3.47.2) was current at the time of this writing.

Click here to view code image

sqlite-tools-win-x64-3470200.zip

In your Downloads folder, right-click the ZIP file, select Extract All… then specify where to place the SQLite files. We placed the extracted files in our Downloads folder in the sub-folder named sqlite-tools-win-x64-3470200.

Add SQLite to the Windows Path Environment Variable

Next, add SQLite to the Path environment variable:

  1. Right-click the folder sqlite-tools-win-x64-3470200 and select Copy as path.

  2. In the taskbar’s Search field, enter SystemPropertiesAdvanced, and press or select Enter.

  3. In the System Properties dialog, select Environment Variables….

  4. Under System variables, select the Path variable, then select Edit….

  5. Select New, then paste in the path you copied in Step 1 and select OK to save the changes.

  6. Close the Environment Variables and System Properties dialogs.
