20.4 A books Database

 

This section presents a books database containing information about several of our books. We’ll set up the database in SQLite using the file books.sql provided in the ch20 examples folder. Then, we’ll introduce the database’s tables. We’ll use this database via SQLite’s command-line tools to introduce various database concepts, including operations that create, read, update and delete data—the so-called CRUD operations. As we introduce the tables, we’ll execute SQL queries that output each table’s contents.

Creating the books Database

In your command line, change to the ch20 examples folder. Create the books.db database using the sqlite3 command as follows:

  1. On macOS or in a Windows Command Prompt, enter the following command— the notation < provides the file books.sql as input to the sqlite3 command:

    sqlite3 books.db < books.sql

  2. In a Windows PowerShell, enter the following command to read books.sql then provide it as input to the sqlite3 command:

    Click here to view code image

    Get-Content books.sql | sqlite3.exe books.db

These commands do not display output at the command line if they successfully create the database.

Opening the books Database with the SQLite Command-Line Tools

Next, execute the following command to open the database in SQLite:

sqlite3 books.db

This launches the SQLite command-line tools and displays:

Click here to view code image

SQLite version 3.47.2 2024-12-07 20:39:59
Enter ".help" for usage hints.
sqlite>

As we introduce the database’s tables, we’ll execute commands here to list each table’s contents. To list the data in a column-based format, execute the following SQLite command:

sqlite> .mode column
sqlite>
authors Table

The database has three tables—authors, author_ISBN and titles. The authors table stores all the authors and has three columns:

  • id—The author’s unique ID number. This integer column is defined as autoincremented—for each row inserted in the table, SQLite increases the id value by 1 to ensure that each row has a unique value. This column is the table’s primary key.

  • first—The author’s first name (a string).

  • last—The author’s last name (a string).

Viewing the authors Table’s Contents

Let’s use a SQL query to view the authors table’s contents:

Click here to view code image

sqlite> SELECT * FROM authors;
id  first      last
--  ---------  ------
1   Paul       Deitel
2   Harvey     Deitel
3   Abbey      Deitel
4   Dan        Quirk
5   Alexander  Wald

SQLite executes the query and outputs its results. A SELECT query gets rows and columns from one or more tables in a database. The asterisk (*) wildcard in the query selects all the columns from the authors table. We’ll discuss SELECT queries in more detail shortly. Each SQL query you enter in the SQLite command-line tool must end with a semicolon (;). We show SQL keywords like SELECT and FROM in all capital letters by convention.

titles Table

The titles table stores all the books and has four columns:

  • isbn—The book’s ISBN (a string) is this table’s primary key. ISBN is an abbreviation for “International Standard Book Number,” a numbering scheme that publishers use to give every book a unique identification number.

  • title—The book’s title (a string).

  • edition—The book’s edition number (an integer).

  • copyright—The book’s copyright year (a string).

Use the following SQL query to list the titles table’s contents:

Click here to view code image

sqlite> SELECT * FROM titles;
isbn        title                              edition  copyright
----------  --------------------------------   -------  ---------
0135404673  Intro to Python for CS and DS      1        2020
0135224330  Python for Programmers             1        2019
0132151006  Internet & WWW How to Program      5        2012
0137598351  Java How to Program                12       2025
0137398395  C How to Program                   9        2022
0133406954  Visual Basic 2012 How to Program   6        2014
0134601548  Visual C# How to Program           6        2017
0136151574  Visual C++ How to Program          2        2008
0136905692  C++20 for Programmers              2        2023
0138092427  C++ How to Program                 11       2024
0134444302  Android How to Program             3        2017
0134289366  Android 6 for Programmers          3        2016
author_ISBN Table

The author_ISBN table uses the following columns to associate authors from the authors

table with their books in the titles table:

  • id—An author’s id (an integer).

  • isbn—The book’s ISBN (a string).

The id column is a foreign key, a column in this table that matches a primary-key column in another table—specifically, the authors table’s id column. The isbn column is also a foreign key that matches the titles table’s isbn primary-key column. A database might have many tables. A goal when designing a database is to minimize data duplication among the tables. To do this, each table represents a specific entity, and foreign keys help link the data in multiple tables. The primary keys and foreign keys are designated when you create the database tables (in our case, in the books.sql script).

Together, the id and isbn columns in this table form a composite primary key. Every row in this table uniquely matches one author to one book’s ISBN. This table contains many entries, so let’s use the SQL LIMIT keyword to restrict the results to the table’s first five rows—LIMIT is not a standard SQL keyword, so it’s not supported by all DBMSs:

Click here to view code image

sqlite> SELECT * FROM author_ISBN LIMIT 5;
id  isbn
--  ----------
1   0134289366
2   0134289366
5   0134289366
1   0135404673
2   0135404673

Every foreign-key value must appear as the primary-key value in a row of another table so the DBMS can ensure that the foreign-key value is valid. This is known as the Rule of Referential Integrity. For example, the DBMS ensures that the id value for a particular author_ISBN row is valid by checking that there is a row in the authors table with that id as the primary key.

Foreign keys also allow related data in multiple tables to be selected from those tables and combined—this is known as joining the data. There is a one-to-many relationship between a primary key and a corresponding foreign key:

  • one author can write many books, and

  • one book can be written by many authors.

So, a foreign key can appear many times in its table but only once (as the primary key) in another table. For example, in the books database, the ISBN 0134289366 appears in several author_ISBN rows because this book has several authors, but it appears only once as a primary key in titles.

Entity-Relationship (ER) Diagram

The following entity-relationship (ER) diagram for the books database illustrates the database’s tables and the relationships among them:

The first compartment in each box contains the table’s name, and the remaining compartments contain the table’s columns. The names in italics are primary keys. A table’s primary key uniquely identifies each row in the table. Every row must have a primary-key value, and that value must be unique in the table. This is known as the Rule of Entity Integrity. Again, for the author_ISBN table, the primary key is the combination of both columns— this is known as a composite primary key.

The lines connecting the tables represent the relationships among the tables. Consider the line between authors and author_ISBN. There’s a 1 on the authors end and an infinity symbol (∞)on the author_ISBN end. This indicates a one-to-many relationship. For each author in the authors table, there can be an arbitrary number of ISBNs for books written by that author in the author_ISBN table—that is, an author can write any number of books, so an author’s id can appear in multiple rows of the author_ISBN table. The relationship line links the id column in the authors table (where id is the primary key) to the id column in the author_ISBN table (where id is a foreign key). The line between the tables links the primary key to the matching foreign key.

The line between the titles and author_ISBN tables illustrates a one-to-many relationship—one book can be written by many authors. The line links the primary key isbn in table titles to the corresponding foreign key in table author_ISBN. The relationships in the entity-relationship diagram illustrate that the sole purpose of the author_ISBN table is to provide a many-to-many relationship between the authors and titles tables—an author can write many books, and a book can have many authors.

SQL Keywords

The following subsections continue our SQL presentation in the context of our books database, demonstrating SQL queries and statements using the SQL keywords in the following table. Other SQL keywords are beyond this text’s scope:

20.4.1 SELECT Queries

The previous section used SELECT statements and the * wildcard character to get all the columns from a table. Typically, you need only a subset of the columns. To retrieve only the specific columns you need, specify a comma-separated list of column names. For example, let’s retrieve only the columns first and last from the authors table:

Click here to view code image

sqlite> SELECT first, last FROM authors;
first      last
---------  ------
Paul       Deitel
Harvey     Deitel
Abbey      Deitel
Dan        Quirk
Alexander  Wald

20.4.2 WHERE Clause

You’ll often select rows in a database that satisfy specific selection criteria, especially in big data, where a database might contain millions or billions of rows. Only rows meeting the selection criteria are selected. SQL’s WHERE clause specifies a query’s selection criteria. Let’s select the title, edition and copyright for all books with copyright years greater than 2019. String values in SQL queries are delimited by single (') quotes, as in '2019':

Click here to view code image

sqlite> SELECT title, edition, copyright
   ...> FROM titles
   ...> WHERE copyright > '2019';
title                          edition   copyright
-----------------------------  -------   ---------
Intro to Python for CS and DS  1         2020
Java How to Program            12        2025
C How to Program               9         2022
C++20 for Programmers          2         2023
C++ How to Program             11        2024

You can enter lengthy SQL queries over several lines for readability. SQLite will not execute a query until you terminate it with a semicolon and press (or select) Enter. Before each line of the query after the first, SQLite displays the continuation prompt "...>" to indicate that the query is not complete.

Pattern Matching: Zero or More Characters

The WHERE clause may contain the operators <, >, <=, >=, =, <> (not equal) and LIKE. Operator LIKE is used for pattern matching—searching for strings that match a given pattern. A pattern containing the percent (%) wildcard character searches for strings with zero or more characters at the percent character’s position. For example, let’s locate all authors whose last name starts with the letter D:

Click here to view code image

sqlite> SELECT id, first, last
   ...> FROM authors
   ...> WHERE last LIKE 'D%';
id  first   last
--  ------  ------
1   Paul    Deitel
2   Harvey  Deitel
3   Abbey   Deitel
Pattern Matching: Any Character

An underscore (_) in the pattern string indicates a single wildcard character at that position. Let’s select the rows of all the authors whose last names start with any character, followed by the letter b, followed by any number of additional characters (specified by %):

Click here to view code image

sqlite> SELECT id, first, last
   ...> FROM authors
   ...> WHERE first LIKE '_b%';
id  first  last
--  -----  ------
3   Abbey  Deitel

20.4.3 ORDER BY Clause

The ORDER BY clause sorts a query’s results into ascending order (lowest to highest) or descending order (highest to lowest), specified with ASC and DESC, respectively. The default sorting order is ascending, so ASC is optional. Let’s sort the titles in ascending order:

Click here to view code image

sqlite> SELECT title FROM titles ORDER BY title ASC;
title
--------------------------------
Android 6 for Programmers
Android How to Program
C How to Program
C++ How to Program
C++20 for Programmers
Internet & WWW How to Program
Intro to Python for CS and DS
Java How to Program
Python for Programmers
Visual Basic 2012 How to Program
Visual C# How to Program
Visual C++ How to Program
Sorting By Multiple Columns

To sort by multiple columns, use a comma-separated list of column names after ORDER BY. Let’s sort author names by last, then first for any authors who have the same last name:

Click here to view code image

sqlite> SELECT id, first, last
   ...> FROM authors
   ...> ORDER BY last, first;
id  first      last
--  ---------  ------
3   Abbey      Deitel
2   Harvey     Deitel
1   Paul       Deitel
4   Dan        Quirk
5   Alexander  Wald

The sorting order can vary by column. Let’s sort the authors in descending order by last name and ascending order by first name for any authors who have the same last name:

Click here to view code image

sqlite> SELECT id, first, last
   ...> FROM authors
   ...> ORDER BY last DESC, first ASC;
id  first      last
--  ---------  ------
5   Alexander  Wald
4   Dan        Quirk
3   Abbey      Deitel
2   Harvey     Deitel
1   Paul       Deitel
Combining the WHERE and ORDER BY Clauses

The WHERE and ORDER BY clauses can be combined in one query. Let’s get the isbn, title, edition and copyright of each book in the titles table that has a title ending with 'How to Program' and sort them in ascending order by title.

Click here to view code image

sqlite> SELECT isbn, title, edition, copyright
   ...> FROM titles
   ...> WHERE title LIKE '%How to Program'
   ...> ORDER BY title;
isbn        title                              edition  copyright
----------  --------------------------------   -------  ---------
0134444302  Android How to Program             3        2017
0137398395  C How to Program                   9        2022
0138092427  C++ How to Program                 11       2024
0132151006  Internet & WWW How to Program      5        2012
0137598351  Java How to Program                12       2025
0133406954  Visual Basic 2012 How to Program   6        2014
0134601548  Visual C# How to Program           6        2017
0136151574  Visual C++ How to Program          2        2008

20.4.4 Merging Data from Multiple Tables with INNER JOIN

The books database’s author_ISBN table links authors to their corresponding titles. If we did not separate this information into individual tables, we’d need to include author information with each entry in the titles table, resulting in duplicate information for authors who wrote multiple books. You can merge data from multiple tables, referred to as joining the tables, with INNER JOIN. Let’s produce a list of authors accompanied by their books’ ISBNs. There are many results for this query, so we limited the results to the first five rows:

Click here to view code image

sqlite> SELECT first, last, isbn
   ...> FROM authors
   ...> INNER JOIN author_ISBN ON authors.id = author_ISBN.id
   ...> ORDER BY last, first LIMIT 5;
first   last    isbn
------  ------  ----------
Abbey   Deitel  0132151006
Abbey   Deitel  0133406954
Harvey  Deitel  0134289366
Harvey  Deitel  0135404673
Harvey  Deitel  0132151006

The INNER JOIN’s ON clause uses a primary-key column in one table and a foreign-key column in the other to determine which rows to merge from each table. This query merges the authors table’s first and last columns with the author_ISBN table’s isbn column, sorts the results in ascending order by last then first, and selects only the first five results.

The syntax authors.id (table_name.column_name) in the ON clause uses qualified name syntax—this is required if the columns have the same name in both tables. This syntax can be used in any SQL statement to distinguish columns in different tables that have the same name. In some systems, table names qualified with the database name can be used to perform cross-database queries. As always, the query can contain an ORDER BY clause.

20.4.5 INSERT INTO Statement

To this point, you’ve queried existing data. Sometimes, you’ll execute SQL statements that modify the database. The INSERT INTO statement inserts a row into a table. Let’s insert a new author named Mei-ling Liu into the authors table:

Click here to view code image

sqlite> INSERT INTO authors (first, last)
   ...> VALUES ('Mei-ling', 'Liu');

The SQL keywords INSERT INTO are followed by the table in which to insert the new row and a comma-separated list of column names in parentheses. The list of column names is followed by the SQL keyword VALUES and a comma-separated list of values in parentheses. The values provided must match the column names specified in order and type.

We do not specify a value for the id column because it’s an autoincremented column in the authors table—this was defined in the script books.sql that created the table. For every new row, SQLite assigns a unique id value that is the next value in the autoincremented sequence (i.e., 1, 2, 3, …). In this case, Mei-ling Liu is assigned id number 6. To confirm this, let’s query the authors table’s contents:

Click here to view code image

sqlite> SELECT id, first, last FROM authors;
id  first      last
--  ---------  ------
1   Paul       Deitel
2   Harvey     Deitel
3   Abbey      Deitel
4   Dan        Quirk
5   Alexander  Wald
6   Mei-ling   Liu
Note Regarding Strings That Contain Single Quotes

SQL delimits strings with single quotes ('). A string containing a single quote, such as O’Malley, must have two single quotes in the position where the single quote appears (e.g., 'O''Malley'). The first acts as an escape character for the second. Not escaping single-quote characters in a string that’s part of a SQL statement is a SQL syntax error.

20.4.6 UPDATE Statement

An UPDATE statement modifies existing values. Let’s assume that Mei-ling Liu’s last name is incorrect in the database and update it to 'Cai':

Click here to view code image

sqlite> UPDATE authors SET last='Cai'
   ...> WHERE last='Liu' AND first='Mei-ling';

The UPDATE keyword is followed by the table to update, the keyword SET and a comma-separated list of column_name = value pairs indicating the columns to change and their new values. The change will be applied to every row if you do not specify a WHERE clause. The WHERE clause in this query indicates that we should update only rows with the last name 'Liu' and the first name 'Mei-ling'.

Of course, multiple people could have the same first and last name. To make a change to only one row, use the row’s unique primary key in the WHERE clause. In this case, we could have specified:

WHERE id = 6

For statements that modify the database, you can use the SQLite changes function to check the number of rows that were modified. The following confirms that the UPDATE modified one row:

sqlite> SELECT changes();
changes()
---------
1

We also can confirm the update by listing the authors table’s contents:

Click here to view code image

sqlite> SELECT id, first, last FROM authors;
id  first      last
--  ---------  ------
1   Paul       Deitel
2   Harvey     Deitel
3   Abbey      Deitel
4   Dan        Quirk
5   Alexander  Wald
6   Mei-ling   Cai

20.4.7 DELETE FROM Statement

A DELETE FROM statement removes rows from a table. Let’s remove Mei-ling Cai from the authors table using her author ID:

Click here to view code image

sqlite> DELETE FROM authors WHERE id=6;

The optional WHERE clause determines which row(s) to delete. If WHERE is omitted, all the table’s rows are deleted. Here’s the authors table after the DELETE operation:

Click here to view code image

sqlite> SELECT id, first, last FROM authors;
id  first      last
--  ---------  ------
1   Paul       Deitel
2   Harvey     Deitel
3   Abbey      Deitel
4   Dan        Quirk
5   Alexander  Wald
Closing the Database and Exiting SQLite

When you’re done interacting with the database at the command line, execute the following command to close the database and exit the SQLite command-line tools.

sqlite> .exit

20.5 Connecting to and Querying a Database with JDBC

The example of Fig. 20.1 performs a simple query on the books database that retrieves the entire authors table and displays the data. The program illustrates connecting to the database, querying the database and processing the result. We broke the program into parts for discussion purposes. After compiling this program, you can run it with the following command, which adds the SQLite driver to the classpath—Windows users should replace the colon (:) with a semicolon (;) and the forward slashes (/) with backslashes (\):

Click here to view code image

java -cp ".:../libs/sqlite-jdbc-3.47.1.0.jar" DisplayAuthors

In this chapter’s code, we assume the book’s examples folder is located in your user account’s Documents folder, as discussed in the book’s Before You Begin section. If not, you must update lines 14–15 and similar lines in subsequent examples.

Lines 4–9 import the JDBC interfaces and classes from package java.sql used in this program. The main method connects to the books database, queries the database, displays the query result and closes the database connection. Line 17 declares a String constant for the database URL (also known as a connection string). This identifies the database to connect to and information about the protocol used by the JDBC driver (discussed shortly). Line 18 declares a String constant representing the SQL query that will select the id, first and last columns from the database’s authors table.

20.5.1 Automatic Driver Discovery

JDBC supports automatic driver discovery—it loads the database driver into memory for you. To ensure that the program can locate the driver class, you must include the class’s location in the program’s classpath3 when you execute the program, as shown in the java command above Fig. 20.1.

3. In a modularized application (Chapter 21, Java Platform Module System), you’d include the driver’s module on the module path.

20.5.2 Connecting to the Database

The JDBC interfaces we use in this example extend the AutoCloseable interface, so you can use objects that implement these interfaces with the try-with-resources statement (lines 21–48). Lines 22–24 create this example’s AutoCloseable objects, which are closed when the try block terminates (line 45) or if an exception occurs during the try block’s execution. Each object created in the parentheses following keyword try must be separated from the next by a semicolon (;).

Line 22 creates a Connection object that manages the connection between the Java program and the database. Connection objects enable programs to create SQL statements that manipulate databases. The program initializes connection with the result of a call to the DriverManager class’s static method getConnection. The method’s argument is a String specifying the database URL. This method attempts to connect to the database specified by its URL argument—if it cannot, it throws a SQLException.

The URL locates the database. In this chapter’s examples, the database is a file on the local computer in this chapter’s examples folder, but it could reside on a network. The JDBC URL begins with "jdbc:sqlite:", specifying:

  • the protocol for communication (jdbc) and

  • the subprotocol for communication (sqlite).

This is followed by the SQLite database file’s location (created in lines 14–15).

The subprotocol sqlite indicates that the program uses a SQlite-specific subprotocol to connect to the database. The following table lists the JDBC driver names and database URL formats of several popular RDBMSs:

Most database management systems require users to log in before accessing the database contents. DriverManager method getConnection is overloaded with versions that enable the program to supply the username and password to gain access.

20.5.3 Creating a Statement for Executing Queries

Line 23 of Fig. 20.1 invokes Connection method createStatement to obtain an object that implements interface Statement (package java.sql). You use a Statement object to submit SQL statements to the database.

20.5.4 Executing a Query

Line 24 uses the Statement object’s executeQuery method to submit a query that selects all the author information from the Authors table. This method returns an object that implements the ResultSet interface and contains the query results.

20.5.5 Processing a Query’s ResultSet

Lines 27–44 process the ResultSet.

Displaying the Column Names

Line 27 obtains the ResultSet’s ResultSetMetaData object (package java.sql). The metadata describes the ResultSet’s contents. Programs can use metadata programmatically to get information about the ResultSet’s column names and types. Line 28 uses ResultSetMetaData method getColumnCount to retrieve the number of columns in the ResultSet. Lines 33–35 display the column names. Metadata enables programs to process ResultSet contents dynamically when detailed information about the ResultSet is not known in advance.

Displaying Each Row’s Data

Lines 39–44 display the data in each ResultSet row. First, the program positions the ResultSet cursor (which points to the row being processed) to the first row. Method next (line 39) returns the boolean value true if it can position to the next row; otherwise, the method returns false to indicate there are no more results. Initially, a ResultSet cursor is positioned before the first row. A SQLException occurs if you access a ResultSet’s contents before positioning the ResultSet cursor to the first row with method next.

If the ResultSet has rows, lines 40–42 extract and display the current row’s columns. Each column can be extracted as a specific Java type—the ResultSetMetaData method getColumnType returns a constant from class Types (package java.sql) indicating a given column’s type. Programs can use these values in a switch statement to invoke ResultSet methods that return the column values as appropriate Java types. For example, if the column’s type is Types.INTEGER, ResultSet method getInt gets the column value as an int. For simplicity, this example treats each value as an Object. We retrieve each column value with ResultSet method getObject (line 41), then display the Object’s String representation. ResultSet get methods typically receive as an argument either a column number (as an int) or a column name (as a String) indicating which column’s value to obtain. Unlike array indices, ResultSet column numbers start at 1. Specifying column index 0 when obtaining values from a ResultSet causes a SQLException.

Accessing Columns By Column Number vs. Column Name

If a query specifies the exact columns to select from the database, the ResultSet contains the columns in the specified order. For this scenario, using the column number to obtain the column’s value is more efficient than using the column name. The column number provides direct access to the specified column. Using the column name requires a search of the column names to locate the appropriate column. However, using column names to obtain values from a ResultSet is less error-prone than obtaining values by column number—you don’t need to remember the column order. Also, your code does not have to change if the column order changes.

Closing the Database Resources

When line 45 is reached, the ResultSet, Statement and Connection objects’ close methods are called to close the corresponding resources. If you attempt to manipulate a ResultSet after closing the Statement that created it, a SQLException occurs—the ResultSet is discarded when the Statement is closed.

Each Statement object can open only one ResultSet object at a time. When a Statement returns a new ResultSet, the Statement closes the prior ResultSet. To use multiple ResultSets in parallel, separate Statement objects must return the ResultSets.

Class DisplayQueryResultsController (Fig. 20.2) responds to the GUI’s events and updates the GUI accordingly. Instance Variables and static Variables

Lines 22–23 define the instance variables for programmatically interacting with the GUI’s TextArea and TableView. Lines 26–28 define the JDBC URL for accessing the books.db database. Click here to view code image

Method submitQueryButtonPressed

When the user clicks the Submit Query Button, method submitQueryButtonPressed (lines 52–55) invokes method executeQuery, passing the text in queryTextArea.

Click here to view code image

51      // query the database and display results in TableView
52      @FXML
53      void submitQueryButtonPressed(ActionEvent event) {
54         executeQuery(queryTextArea.getText());
55      }
56
Method executeQuery

The executeQuery method (lines 59–114) queries the database, processes the results and dynamically updates the TableView to display the data. Line 60 uses the connection object to create a Statement. Line 61 uses the Statement to execute the SQL query and obtain a ResultSet containing the retrieved data. The Statement and ResultSet will be closed automatically when the program exits the try block. If a SQLException occurs during this process, it’s caught and displayed to the user using an Alert dialog (lines 110–113).

Click here to view code image

57      // performs the query and updates the ObservableList<Object>
58      // that the TableView uses to populate its rows and columns
59      private void executeQuery(String query) {
60         try (Statement statement = connection.createStatement();
61              ResultSet resultSet = statement.executeQuery(query)) {
62            tableView.getColumns().clear(); // remove current content
63
64            // create two-dimensional ObservableList for current ResultSet
65            ObservableList<ObservableList<Object>> data =
66               FXCollections.observableArrayList();
67
68            // use the ResultSetMetaData to get the column heads
69            // and set up the TableView's columns
70            ResultSetMetaData metaData = resultSet.getMetaData();
71            int columnCount = metaData.getColumnCount();
72
73            for (int i = 1; i <= columnCount; i++) {
74               // create a new TableColumn for each column in the ResultSet
75               var column = new TableColumn<ObservableList<Object>, Object>(
76                  metaData.getColumnName(i));
77
78               // map the column to the corresponding index in each row
79               final int columnIndex = i - 1;
80               column.setCellValueFactory(param ->
81                  new SimpleObjectProperty<>(
82                     param.getValue().get(columnIndex)));
83
84               // autoscale column width to divide space equally
85               column.prefWidthProperty().bind(
86                  tableView.widthProperty().divide(columnCount));
87
88               // add the column to the TableView
89               tableView.getColumns().add(column);
90            }
91
92            // populate the rows from the ResultSet
93            while (resultSet.next()) {
94               // create a new ObservableList to represent the row
95               ObservableList<Object> row =
96                  FXCollections.observableArrayList();
97
98               // populate the row with data from the ResultSet
99               for (int i = 1; i <= columnCount; i++) {
100                 row.add(resultSet.getObject(i));
101              }
102
103              // add the row to the data list
104              data.add(row);
105           }
106
107           // set the TableView's items to the ObservableList data
108           tableView.setItems(data);
109        }
110        catch (SQLException sqlException) {
111           displayAlert(AlertType.ERROR, "Query Error",
112              sqlException.getMessage());
113        }
114     }
115
Clearing the TableView and Getting the ResultSetMetaData

If the query is successful, the method processes the ResultSet. Line 62 removes any existing columns in the TableView to prepare to display the new query results. Lines 65–66 create the empty ObservableList data, which will hold each row of the query results as an ObservableList<Object>. Line 70 gets the ResultSetMetaData so we can get the number of columns (line 71) and the column names (line 76).

Setting Up the TableView’s TableColumns

Lines 73–90 set up the TableView’s TableColumns, which display the ResultSet’s data. Lines 75–76 create a new TableColumn object for each ResultSet column and set the TableColumn’s header to the corresponding ResultSet column’s name retrieved from the ResultSetMetaData. TableColumn is a generic class:

  • The first type argument—ObservableList<Object>—tells the TableColumn the data structure type that represents a row in the TableView.

  • The second type argument—Object—tells the TableColumn the data type each cell in the column displays.

For simplicity, we treat all the ResultSet data as type Object. The TableColumns will fill the cells with the Objects’ String representations.

Lines 79–82 bind each TableColumn’s cells to the ObservableLists representing the rows:

  • The columnIndex (line 79) determines the ObservableList index for a given TableColumn’s data—recall that ResultSets are indexed from 1, but ObservableLists are indexed from 0.

  • A TableView relies on observable properties to determine when to update its cells and what data to display. TableColumn method setCellValueFactory receives a lambda that describes how to retrieve a value for this column from its rows’ ObservableLists of data. The lambda’s parameter receives a TableView row and uses that object’s getValue method to get the ObservableList<Object> bound to that row—we’ll populate those from the ResultSet momentarily. We call the ObservableList’s get method to get the data at location columnIndex, then wrap this value in a SimpleObjectProperty—an observable property that stores an Object.

Lines 85–86 bind the column widths to the TableView’s width divided by the number of columns to scale the column widths to fit in the TableView. Line 89 adds the Table-Column to the TableView.

Populating the ObservableList data with the ResultSet

Lines 93–105 use the ResultSet’s data to populate the ObservableList data. Lines 95– 96 create an ObservableList<Object> to store the current row’s data. Lines 99–101 iterate through the ResultSet columns, adding each column’s value to row. Then, line 104 adds that row to the ObservableList data. After processing all the ResultSet rows, line 108 uses the TableView’s setItems method to bind the TableView to data, which automatically updates the displayed data.

Method displayAlert

When an exception occurs, the app calls method displayAlert (lines 117–123) to create and display an Alert dialog (package javafx.scene.control) containing a message. Line 119 creates the dialog, passing its AlertType to the constructor. The AlertType.ERROR constant displays a dialog with a red icon containing an X to indicate an error. Line 120 sets the title that appears in the dialog’s title bar. Line 121 sets the message that appears inside the dialog. Finally, line 122 calls Alert method showAndWait, which makes this a modal dialog. The user must close the dialog before interacting with the rest of the app.

Click here to view code image

116     // display an Alert dialog
117     private void displayAlert(
118        AlertType type, String title, String message) {
119        Alert alert = new Alert(type);
120        alert.setTitle(title);
121        alert.setContentText(message);
122        alert.showAndWait();
123     }
124  }

20.7 PreparedStatements

 

A PreparedStatement enables you to create compiled SQL statements that execute more efficiently than Statements, especially executing SQL statements multiple times. Prepared-Statements also can specify parameters, making them more flexible than Statements. You can execute the same query repeatedly with different parameter values. For example, in the books database, you might want to locate all book titles for an author with a specific last and first name, and you might want to execute that query for several authors. With a Prepared-Statement, that query is defined as:

Click here to view code image

PreparedStatement authorBooks = connection.prepareStatement("""
   SELECT last, first, title FROM authors
   INNER JOIN author_ISBN ON authors.id=author_ISBN.id
   INNER JOIN titles ON titles.isbn=author_ISBN.isbn
   WHERE last = ? AND first = ?""");

The question marks (?) in the SQL statement’s last line are placeholders for values passed to the database as part of the query. Before executing a PreparedStatement, the program must specify the values by using the PreparedStatement interface’s set methods.

Setting Parameter Values

For the preceding query, both parameters are Strings that can be set with Prepared-Statement method setString as follows:

Click here to view code image

authorBooks.setString(1, "Deitel");
authorBooks.setString(2, "Paul");

Method setString’s first argument represents the parameter number being set, and the second argument is that parameter’s value. Parameter numbers are counted from 1, starting with the first question mark (?). When the program executes the preceding Prepared-Statement with the parameter values set above, the SQL passed to the database is

Click here to view code image

SELECT last, first, title FROM authors
INNER JOIN author_ISBN ON authors.id=author_ISBN.id
INNER JOIN Titles ON titles.isbn=author_ISBN.isbn
WHERE last = 'Deitel' AND first = 'Paul'

Method setString automatically escapes String parameter values as necessary. For example, if the last name is O’Brien, the statement

Click here to view code image

authorBooks.setString(1, "O'Brien");

escapes the ' character in O’Brien by replacing it with two single-quote characters so the ' appears correctly in the database.

PreparedStatements Are More Secure

PreparedStatements help prevent SQL injection attacks,4 which typically occur in SQL statements that include improper user input. To avoid this security issue, use Prepared-Statements in which user input can be supplied only via parameters—each indicated with a question mark (?) in a PreparedStatement. Once you’ve created such a PreparedStatement, you can use its set methods to specify the user input as arguments for those parameters.

4. “SQL Injection.” Accessed January 13, 2025. https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/SQL_Injection.

Interface PreparedStatement provides set methods for each supported SQL type. Use the set method that matches the parameter’s SQL type in the database—SQLExceptions occur when a program attempts to convert a parameter value to an incorrect type.

20.7.1 AddressBook App That Uses PreparedStatements

We now present an AddressBook JavaFX app that enables you to browse existing entries, add new entries and search for entries with a last name that begins with the specified characters. Our addressbook SQLite database contains an addresses table with the columns id, first, last, email and phone. The column id is an auto-incremented identity column in the addresses table.

Creating the addressbook Database

In your command line, change to the fig20_03-05 folder. Create the addressbook.db database using the sqlite3 command as follows:

  1. On macOS or in a Windows Command Prompt, enter the following command:

    Click here to view code image

    sqlite3 addressbook.db < addressbook.sql

  2. In a Windows PowerShell, enter the following command to read books.sql then provide it as input to the sqlite3 command:

    Click here to view code image

    Get-Content addressbook.sql | sqlite3.exe addressbook.db

20.7.2 record Class Person

Our AddressBook app loads data into Person objects (Fig. 20.3). Each represents one entry in the addressbook database. The record class contains instance variables for the address ID, first name, last name, email address and phone number, as well as a custom toString method that returns the Person’s name in the format

last name, first name

We do not use the address ID in this example.

20.7.3 Class PersonQueries

Class PersonQueries (Fig. 20.4) manages the Address Book program’s database connection and creates the PreparedStatements for interacting with the database. We split the code into parts for discussion purposes. Lines 19–21 declare three PreparedStatement variables.

Creating PreparedStatements

The constructor (lines 24–47) connects to the database at line 26. Lines 29–30 invoke Connection method prepareStatement to create the PreparedStatement selectAll-People that selects all the rows in the addresses table and sorts them by last name, then by first name. Lines 34–36 create the PreparedStatement selectPeopleByLastName with a parameter. This statement uses the SQL LIKE operator to search the addresses table by last name. The ? character specifies the last-name parameter—the text we’ll set as this parameter’s value will end with a % symbol to locate entries for last names starting with the characters the user enters. Lines 39–42 create the PreparedStatement insertNewPerson with four parameters that represent the first name, last name, email address and phone number for a new entry. Again, notice the ? characters used to represent these parameters.

Click here to view code image

23      // constructor
24      public PersonQueries() {
25         try {
26            connection = DriverManager.getConnection(DATABASE_URL);
27
28            // create query that selects all entries in the AddressBook
29            selectAllPeople = connection.prepareStatement(
30               "SELECT * FROM addresses ORDER BY last, first");
31
32            // create query that selects entries with last names
33            // that begin with the specified characters
34            selectPeopleByLastName = connection.prepareStatement("""
35               SELECT * FROM addresses WHERE last LIKE ?
36               ORDER BY last, first""");
37
38            // create insert operation that adds a new entry to the database
39            insertNewPerson = connection.prepareStatement("""
40               INSERT INTO addresses (first, last, email, phone)
41               VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)""");
42         }
43         catch (SQLException sqlException) {
44            sqlException.printStackTrace();
45            System.exit(1);
46         }
47      }

20.8 Stored Procedures

Many database-management systems can store individual or sets of SQL statements in a database, so programs can invoke them. JDBC enables programs to invoke such stored procedures using objects that implement the CallableStatement interface, which can receive arguments specified by the methods inherited from interface PreparedStatement. In addition, CallableStatements can specify output parameters in which a stored procedure can place return values. The CallableStatement interface includes methods to specify which parameters in a stored procedure are output parameters. The interface also includes methods to obtain the values of output parameters returned from a stored procedure.

Although the syntax for creating stored procedures differs across database management systems, the interface CallableStatement provides a uniform interface for specifying input and output parameters for stored procedures and for invoking stored procedures.

According to the Java API documentation for interface CallableStatement, for maximum portability between database systems, programs should process the update counts (which indicate how many rows were updated) or ResultSets returned from a Callable-Statement before obtaining the values of any output parameters.

20.9 Transaction Processing

Many database applications require guarantees that a series of database insertions, updates and deletions are executed properly before the application continues processing the next database operation. For example, when you transfer money electronically between bank accounts, several factors determine if the transaction is successful. You begin by specifying the source account and the amount you wish to transfer from that account to a destination account. Next, you specify the destination account. The bank checks the source account to determine whether its funds are sufficient to complete the transfer. If so, the bank withdraws the specified amount and, if all goes well, deposits it into the destination account to complete the transfer. What happens if the transfer fails after the bank withdraws the money from the source account? In a proper banking system, the bank redeposits the money in the source account. How would you feel if the money was subtracted from your source account and the bank did not deposit the money in the destination account?

Transaction processing enables a program that interacts with a database to treat a database operation (or set of operations) as a single operation. Such an operation also is known as an atomic operation or a transaction. At the end of a transaction, a decision can be made either to commit the transaction or roll back the transaction. Committing the transaction finalizes the database operation(s); all insertions, updates and deletions performed as part of the transaction cannot be reversed without performing a new database operation. Rolling back the transaction leaves the database in its state prior to the database operation. This is useful when a portion of a transaction fails to complete properly. In our bank-account-transfer discussion, the transaction would be rolled back if the deposit could not be made into the destination account.

Java provides transaction processing via methods of interface Connection. Method setAutoCommit specifies whether each SQL statement commits after it completes (a true argument) or whether several SQL statements should be grouped as a transaction (a false argument). If the argument to setAutoCommit is false, the program must follow the last SQL statement in the transaction with a call to Connection method commit (to commit the changes to the database) or Connection method rollback (to return the database to its state prior to the transaction). Interface Connection also provides method getAutoCommit to determine the auto-commit state for the Connection.

20.10 Wrap-Up

This chapter introduced accessing and manipulating relational databases using JDBC. We presented the core concepts of relational databases, including their table, row and column structure, and the importance of primary and foreign keys in maintaining data integrity.

You created and configured SQLlite databases using predefined SQL scripts. We discussed the standard SQL language for querying and manipulating relational databases. We demonstrated the SQL commands SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE and the clauses WHERE, ORDER BY and INNER JOIN using the SQLite command-line tools in the context of a books database.

Next, we used JDBC to interact with SQLite databases from Java applications. We used class DriverManager to obtain a database Connection, and used it to create Statements containing queries that interacted with the database’s data. We then executed the Statements and processed their ResultSets. For each ResultSet, we used the ResultSetMetaData to get and display the column names in the query results.

The AddressBook app demonstrated CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations. We used PreparedStatements to create precompiled SQL statements that accept parameters, improving performance. We incorporated a JavaFX TableView into a GUI and bound a ResultSet to the TableView via JavaFX observable collections. We also discussed how PreparedStatements enhance security by preventing SQL injection attacks.

We discussed stored procedures and CallableStatements for encapsulating SQL logic within the database for reuse and efficiency. Finally, we discussed transaction processing, explaining how to group multiple database operations into one atomic transaction. You learned how to use a Connection to manage transactions, including committing changes to a database or rolling them back if errors occur.

In the next chapter, you’ll learn about the Java Platform Module System (JPMS), which helps developers at all levels be more productive as they build, maintain and evolve software systems, especially large systems.

Java Platform Module System

Objectives

In this chapter, you’ll:

  • Understand the motivation for modularity.

  • Review the Java Platform Module System JEPs and JSRs.

  • Create module declarations that specify module dependencies with requires and specify which packages a module makes available to other modules with exports.

  • Allow runtime reflection of types with open and opens.

  • Use services to loosely couple system components to make large-scale systems easier to develop and maintain.

  • Indicate that a module uses a service or provides a service implementation with the uses and provides…with directives, respectively.

  • Use the jdeps command to determine a module’s dependencies.

  • Migrate non-modularized code with unnamed and automatic modules.

  • Use Graphviz to create module graphs.

  • Learn how the runtime determines dependencies with the module resolver.

  • Use jlink to create smaller runtimes appropriate for resource-constrained devices.

21.1 Introduction1

1. We’d like to thank Brian Goetz, Alex Buckley, Alan Bateman, Lance Anderson, Mandy Chung and Paul Bakker for answering our questions and sharing insights when we wrote this chapter for Java 9 for Programmers.

 

This chapter introduces the Java Platform Module System (JPMS). Modularity—the result of Project Jigsaw2—helps developers at all levels be more productive as they build, maintain and evolve software systems, especially large systems.

2. “Project Jigsaw.” Accessed January 7, 2025. https://openjdk.org/projects/jigsaw/.

What is a Module?

Modularity adds a higher level of aggregation above packages. The key language element is the module—a uniquely named, reusable group of related packages, as well as resources (like images and other files) and a module declaration specifying:

  • the module’s name,

  • the module’s dependencies (that is, other modules this module depends on),

  • the packages it explicitly makes available to other modules (all other packages in the module are implicitly unavailable to other modules),

  • the services it offers,

  • the services it consumes, and

  • to what other modules it allows reflection.

History

The Java Platform was first released in 1995. Millions of developers use Java to build everything from small apps for resource-constrained devices—like those in the Internet of Things (IoT) and other embedded devices—to large-scale business-critical and mission-critical systems. Until Java 9, the Java platform was primarily a monolithic, one-size-fits-all solution.

Modularizing the Java Platform was challenging to implement and took many years. JSR 277: Java Module System was first proposed in 20053 for Java 7. This JSR was later superseded by JSR 376: Java Platform Module System and targeted for Java 8. The Java Platform was fully modularized in Java 9 and subsequently refined in Java 16 and 17.

3. “JSR 277: Java Module System.” Accessed January 7, 2025. https://jcp.org/en/jsr/detail?id=277.

Goals

According to JSR 376, the key goals of modularizing the Java Platform are:4

4. “JSR 376: Java Platform Module System.” Accessed January 7, 2025. https://jcp.org/en/jsr/detail?id=376.

  • Reliable configuration—Modularity provides mechanisms for explicitly declaring dependencies between modules in a manner recognized at compile time and execution time. The system can follow these dependencies to determine the subset of all modules required to support your app.

  • Strong encapsulation—The packages in a module are accessible to other modules only if the module explicitly “exports” them. Even then, another module cannot use those packages unless it explicitly states that it “requires” the other module’s capabilities. This improves platform security because fewer classes are accessible to potential attackers. Modularity helps you come up with cleaner, more logical designs.

  • Scalable Java Platform—Before JPMS, the Java Platform was a monolith consisting of massive numbers of packages, making it challenging to develop, maintain and evolve. It couldn’t be easily subsetted. The platform is now modularized into dozens of modules. You can create custom runtimes consisting of only modules you need for your apps or the devices you’re targeting. For example, if a device does not support GUIs, you could create a runtime that does not include the GUI modules, significantly reducing the runtime’s size.

  • Greater platform integrity—Before Java 9, it was possible to use many classes in the platform that were not meant for use by an app’s classes. With strong encapsulation, internal APIs are truly encapsulated and hidden from apps using the platform.

  • Improved performance—The JVM uses various optimization techniques to improve program performance.These techniques are more effective when the JVM knows in advance that required types are located only in specific modules.5

5. “JSR 376: Java Platform Module System.” Accessed January 7, 2025. https://jcp.org/en/jsr/detail?id=376.

With these goals in mind, many popular open-source Java libraries, including Jackson (Chapter 11) and JavaFX (Chapters 15–17), are now modularized.

Each module name is followed by an @ symbol and a version number. We used Java 23, so each module is followed by "@23". The 12 items in bold are platform-specific and not listed in the documentation’s modules overview at

Click here to view code image

https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/index.html

Java Enhancement Proposals (JEPs) and Java Specification Requests (JSRs) of Java Modularity

The preface introduced JEPs and JSRs. The following table contains the Java modularity JEPs and JSRs, many of which we cite these throughout the chapter.

Quick Tour of the Chapter

This chapter introduces key modularity concepts you’ll likely use when building large-scale systems. Some of the key topics presented in this chapter include:

  • Module declarations—These specify a module’s dependencies (with the requires directive), the packages a module makes available to other modules (with the exports directive), the services it offers (with the provides…with directive), the services it consumes (with the uses directive) and to what other modules it allows reflection (with the open modifier and the opens and opens…to directives).

  • Module-dependency graphs—We’ll create graphs that visualize the dependencies among modules. We’ll use the jdeps tool to create files that the open-source Graphviz tool (https://graphviz.org/) can convert into graphs.

  • Module resolver—We’ll discuss the steps the JVM’s module resolver performs to ensure a module’s dependencies are fulfilled.

  • jlink (the Java linker)—You’ll use jlink to create smaller custom runtimes then use them to execute apps. In fact, many of this book’s command-line apps can be executed on a custom runtime consisting only of the most fundamental JDK module—java.base—which includes core Java API packages, such as java.lang, java.io and java.util. All modules implicitly depend on java.base.

  • Reflection—Reflection enables Java code to look inside a class and access and use all its members (including its private ones) at execution time.7 These capabilities can still be used, despite JPMS’s strong encapsulation, but only with modules that explicitly allow it. We’ll specify that a module allows reflection with an open modifier and the opens and opens…to directives in a module declaration.

    7. The Java™ Tutorials, “Trail: The Reflection API.” Accessed January 7, 2025. https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/reflect/.

  • Migration—The Java platform has been used for almost three decades, so there’s enormous amounts of non-modularized legacy code. We’ll discuss how the unnamed module and automatic modules can help with migrating legacy code to JPMS. We’ll use the jdeps tool to determine code dependencies among modules and on internal APIs (which, for the most part, are now strongly encapsulated). Much legacy code will run without modification, but we explain some potential issues in Section 21.6.

  • Services and Service Providers—Substantial software systems that fulfill essential needs can live on for decades. During that time, change is the rule rather than the exception. In Section 9.13, we discussed tight coupling and loose coupling. It’s been proven that tight coupling makes it challenging to modify systems. We’ll create loosely coupled system components with service-provider interfaces and implementations, and the ServiceLoader class. We’ll also demonstrate the uses and provides…with directives in module declarations to indicate that a module uses a service or provides a service implementation, respectively.

We’ll present the preceding concepts using live-code examples with meaningful outputs, some code snippets, module graphs containing a module’s dependencies, and examples of module-related commands (like jlink and jdeps) and module-related options for other commands (like javac, java and jar). Some additional example-rich sources include:

  • Project Jigsaw: Module System Quick-Start Guide—https://openjdk.org/projects/jigsaw/quick-start.

  • Mak, Sander, and Paul Bakker. Java 9 Modularity: Patterns and Practices for Developing Maintainable Applications. Sebastopol, CA: O’Reilly Media, 2017.

  • Parlog, Nicolai. The Java Module System. Shelter Island, NY: Manning Publications, 2019.

A Terminology Note

Before Java 9, the Java Runtime Environment (JRE) was a separate software package that included the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) and other software for executing Java programs. With JPMS, the JRE is a proper subset of the Java Development Kit (JDK), which contains all the Java APIs and tools required to create and run Java programs. This chapter uses the terms Java Platform and Java SE Platform synonymously with the JDK.

21.2 Module Declarations

As we mentioned, a module must provide a module declaration specifying

  • the module’s dependencies,

  • the packages the module makes available to other modules,

  • and more.

The module declaration is defined in a file named module-info.java. Each module declaration begins with the keyword module, followed by a unique module name and a module body enclosed in braces, as in

module modulename {
   // module directives
}

The module declaration’s body can be empty or may contain module directives, including requires, exports, provides…with, uses and opens. As you’ll learn in Section 21.3.5, compiling the module declaration creates the module descriptor, which is stored in a file named module-info.class in the module’s root folder. Here we briefly introduce each module directive. We’ll present actual module declarations beginning in Section 21.3.3.

21.2.1 requires

A requires module directive specifies that this module depends on another module—this relationship is called a module dependency. Each module must explicitly state its dependencies. When module A requires module B, module A is said to read module B and module B is read by module A. To specify a dependency on another module, use requires, as in:

requires modulename;

Section 21.3.3 demonstrates a requires directive.8

8. There is also a requires static directive to indicate that a module is required at compile time, but optional at runtime. This is known as an optional dependency and is beyond this chapter’s scope.

21.2.2 requires transitive—Implied Readability

To specify a dependency on another module and to ensure that other modules reading your module also read that dependency—known as implied readability—use requires transitive as in:

Click here to view code image

requires transitive modulename;

Consider the following directive from the java.desktop module declaration:

requires transitive java.xml;

Any module that reads java.desktop also implicitly reads java.xml. For example, if a method from the java.desktop module returns a type from the java.xml module, code in modules that read java.desktop, becomes dependent on java.xml. Without the requires transitive directive in java.desktop’s module declaration, such dependent modules will not compile unless they explicitly read java.xml.

Java’s standard modules must grant implied readability in all cases like the one described here.9 Also, though a Java standard module may depend on non-standard modules, it must not grant implied readability to them—this ensures that code depending only on Java standard modules is portable across Java implementations.

9. Clark, Iris, and Mark Reinhold. “Java SE 9 (JSR 379).” March 6, 2017. Accessed January 7, 2025. https://cr.openjdk.org/~iris/se/9/java-se-9-pr-spec-01/java-se-9-spec.html#s7.

21.2.3 exports and exports…to

An exports module directive specifies one of the module’s packages whose public types (and their nested public and protected types) should be accessible to code in all other modules. An exports…to directive enables you to specify in a comma-separated list precisely which module’s or modules’ code can access the exported package—known as a qualified export. Section 21.4 demonstrates the exports directive.

21.2.4 uses

A uses module directive specifies a service used by this module—making the module a service consumer. A service is an object of a class that implements the interface or extends the abstract class specified in the uses directive. Section 21.9.3 demonstrates the uses directive.

21.2.5 provides…with

A provides…with module directive specifies that a module provides a service implementation—making the module a service provider. The provides part of the directive specifies an interface or abstract class listed in a module’s uses directive. The with part of the directive specifies the name of the class that implements the interface or extends the abstract class. Section 21.9.6 demonstrates the provides…with directive.

21.2.6 open, opens and opens…to10,11

10. Buckley, Alex. “JPMS: Modules in the Java Language and JVM.” February 23, 2017. Accessed January 7, 2025. https://cr.openjdk.org/~mr/jigsaw/spec/lang-vm.html.

11. Gosling, James, Bill Joy, Guy Steele, Gilad Bracha, Alex Buckley, Dan Smith, and Gavin Bierman. “Java Language Specification, Java SE 23 Edition,” Section 7.7. August 21, 2024. Accessed January 7, 2025. https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se23/jls23.pdf.

Before Java 9, reflection could be used at runtime to learn about all types in a package and all members of a type—even its private members—whether or not you wanted to allow this. So, nothing was truly encapsulated. JPMS provides strong encapsulation. By default, a type in a module is not accessible to other modules unless it’s a public type and you export its package—even then, reflection is still unavailable by default. You expose only the packages you want to expose, and you must explicitly allow reflection, if needed.

Allowing Runtime-Only Access to a Package

An opens module directive of the form

opens package

indicates that a specific package’s public types and their nested public and protected types are accessible to code in other modules at runtime only. Also, the types in the specified package and all of those types’ members are accessible via reflection.

Allowing Runtime-Only Access to a Package By Specific Modules

An opens…to module directive of the form

Click here to view code image

opens package to comma-separated-list-of-modules

indicates that a specific package’s public types and their nested public and protected types are accessible to code in the listed module(s) at runtime only. Also, the types in the specified package (and all of the types’ members) are accessible via reflection to code in the specified modules.

Allowing Runtime-Only Access to All Packages in a Module

If all the packages in a given module should be accessible at runtime and via reflection to all other modules, you may open the entire module, as in

open module modulename {
   // module directives
}
Reflection Defaults

A module with runtime reflective access to a package can use the package’s public types and their nested public and protected types. However, reflection allows access to all types in the opened package and all members within those types, including private members. For more information on using reflection to access all of a type’s members, visit

Click here to view code image

https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/reflect/
Dependency Injection

Reflection is commonly used with dependency injection. One example of this is an FXML-based JavaFX app, like those presented in Chapters 15–17. When an FXML app loads, the controller object and the GUI components on which it depends are dynamically created as follows:

  • First, because the app depends on a controller object that handles the GUI interactions, the FXMLLoader injects a controller object into the running app—that is, the FXMLLoader uses reflection to locate and load the controller class into memory and to create an object of that class.

  • Next, because the controller depends on the GUI components declared in FXML, the FXMLLoader creates the GUI-component objects and injects them into the controller object by assigning each to the controller object’s corresponding @FXML instance variable.

Once this process is complete, the controller can interact with the GUI and respond to its events. We’ll use the opens…to directive in Section 21.7.1 to allow the FXMLLoader to use reflection on a JavaFX app in a custom module.

21.2.7 Restricted Keywords

The keywords exports, module, open, opens, provides, requires, to, transitive, uses and with are restricted keywords. They’re keywords only in module declarations and may be used as identifiers anywhere else in your code. We mentioned in footnote 8 that there is also a requires static module directive. Of course, static is a regular keyword.

21.3 Modularized Welcome App

In this section, we create a simple Welcome app to demonstrate module fundamentals. We’ll:

  • create a class that resides in a module,

  • provide a module declaration,

  • compile the module declaration and the Welcome class into a module, and

  • run the class containing main in that module.

After covering these basics, we’ll also demonstrate:

  • packaging the Welcome app in a modular JAR file and

  • running the app from that JAR file.

21.3.1 Welcome App’s Structure

The app we present in this section consists of two .java files:

  • Welcome.java contains the Welcome app class, and

  • module-info.java contains the module declaration.

By convention, a modularized app has the following folder structure:

Click here to view code image

AppFolder
   src
      ModuleNameFolder
         PackageFolders
            JavaSourceCodeFiles
         module-info.java

For our Welcome app, which will be defined in the package com.deitel.welcome, the following diagram presents the folder structure:

The src folder stores all of the app’s source code. It contains the module’s root folder, which has the module’s name—com.deitel.welcome (we’ll discuss module naming momentarily). The module’s root folder contains nested folders representing the package’s directory structure—com/deitel/welcome—corresponding to the package com.deitel.welcome. This folder contains Welcome.java. The module’s root folder contains the required module declaration module-info.java.

Module Naming Conventions

Like package names, module names must be unique. To ensure unique package names, you typically begin the name with your organization’s Internet domain name in reverse order. Our domain name is deitel.com, so we begin our package names with com.deitel. Module names also use the reverse-domain-name convention. If multiple modules have the same name at compile time, a compilation error occurs. At runtime, if multiple modules have the same name an exception occurs.

This example uses the same name for the module and its contained package because there is only one package in the module. This is not required but is a common convention. In a modular app, Java maintains the module names separately from package names and any type names in those packages, so duplicate module and package names are allowed.

Modules group related packages. As such, the packages will often have commonality among portions of their names. For example, if a module contains the packages

Click here to view code image

com.deitel.sample.firstpackage;
com.deitel.sample.secondpackage;
com.deitel.sample.thirdpackage;

you’d typically name the module com.deitel.sample—the common portion of the package names. If there’s no common portion, choose a name representing the module’s purpose. For example, the java.base module contains core packages that are considered fundamental to Java apps (such as java.lang, java.io, java.time and java.util), and the java.sql module contains the packages required for interacting with databases via JDBC (such as java.sql and javax.sql). These are just two of the many standard modules listed in Section 21.1. The online documentation for each provides a complete list of its exported packages—for the java.base module, visit:

Click here to view code image

https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/module-
   summary.html
Listing the java.base Module’s Contents

You can use the java command’s --describe-modules option to display information from the java.base module’s descriptor, including its list of exported packages, as in:

Click here to view code image

java --describe-module java.base

The complete output of the preceding command lists lots of additional java.base module information. The following presents a portion of the remaining output with sample lines from each category of information.

Click here to view code image

...
uses java.util.spi.CalendarDataProvider
uses java.util.spi.CurrencyNameProvider
...

   with jdk.internal.jrtfs.JrtFileSystemProvider

The uses lines like

Click here to view code image

uses java.util.spi.CalendarDataProvider

indicate there are types in the java.base module’s packages which use objects that implement various service-provider interfaces. The provides…with

Click here to view code image

provides java.nio.file.spi.FileSystemProvider
   with jdk.internal.jrtfs.JrtFileSystemProvider

indicates that this module’s jdk.internal.jrtfs package contains a service-provider implementation class named JrtFileSystemProvider that implements the service-provider interface FileSystemProvider from package java.nio.file.spi. Section 21.9 presents a substantial example demonstrating that service-provider interfaces and implementations create loosely coupled system components for systems that are easier to develop, maintain and evolve than tightly coupled systems.

The qualified exports…to lines like

Click here to view code image

qualified exports com.sun.security.ntlm to java.security.sasl

indicate that the java.base module exports a given package (com.sun.security.ntlm) only to a specified module (java.security.sasl). The java.base module has many of these qualified exports. Packages listed in such exports may be read only by the designated modules in the comma-separated list after the to keyword. In the JDK, such qualified exports are used for packages containing JDK internal implementations of types that developers should not use.

The contains lines like

Click here to view code image

contains com.sun.crypto.provider

specify that the module contains packages that are not exported for use in other modules. Note that contains is not a directive like requires or exports that you can use in your modules. Rather, it’s information inserted by the compiler to indicate that a module contains the specified package. The JVM uses this information to improve performance when it loads classes from those packages at runtime.12

12. Brian Goetz, e-mail message to authors, March 16, 2017.

21.3.2 Class Welcome

Figure 21.1’s Welcome app simply displays a String at the command line. Types that will be placed in modules must be placed into a package using a package statement (line 3).

21.3.3 module-info.java

Figure 21.2 is the module declaration for the com.deitel.welcome module, which begins with the module keyword followed by the module’s name and braces that enclose the declaration’s body. This module declaration contains a requires module directive, indicating that the app depends on types defined in module java.base. All modules implicitly depend on java.base, so this requires directive may be omitted.

21.3.4 Module-Dependency Graph

The following diagram is the module-dependency graph for com.deitel.welcome, indicating that the module reads the standard module java.base. This dependency is indicated in the diagram with the arrow from com.deitel.welcome to java.base.

A module-dependency graph illustrates dependencies among observable modules— standard modules and any additional modules required by a given app or library module.13 The graph’s nodes are modules, and their dependencies are represented by directed edges (arrows) that connect the nodes. Some edges represent explicit dependencies on modules explicitly specified in a module declaration’s requires clauses (as we’ll present in Fig. 21.6). Some edges represent implicit dependencies in which one of the required modules, in turn, depends on other modules. The preceding graph was produced using the JDK’s jdeps tool and the free Graphviz visualization tool. We discuss how to use these tools to create module dependency graphs in Section 21.6.3.

13. Bateman, Alan, Alex Buckley, Jonathan Gibbons and Mark Reinhold. “JEP 261: Module System.” Updated August 19, 2024. Accessed January 7, 2025. https://openjdk.org/jeps/261.

21.3.5 Compiling a Module

The commands to compile modules and run modularized apps using the JDK’s tools are lengthy. Popular IDEs like JetBrains IntelliJ, the Eclipse IDE for Java Developers, Visual Studio Code and NetBeans have build tools that handle these commands for you.

For your convenience, the file CommandsForCopyPaste.txt in this chapter’s examples folder contains the commands to compile and run the examples. For readability, we split many commands into multiple lines, using platform-specific line-continuation characters. The commands throughout this chapter are presented in macOS format with the backslash (\) line-continuation character. Windows users would replace the backslashes with

  • carets (^) in Command Prompt windows or

  • back ticks (`) in PowerShell windows.

Compiling the Welcome App

To compile the Welcome app’s module, open a command window, use the cd command to change to this chapter’s WelcomeApp folder, then enter:

Click here to view code image

javac -d mods/com.deitel.welcome \
   src/com.deitel.welcome/module-info.java \
   src/com.deitel.welcome/com/deitel/welcome/Welcome.java

The -d option indicates that javac should place the compiled code in the specified folder.14 This example’s mods folder will contain a subfolder named com.deitel.welcome, representing the compiled module. The name mods is used by convention.

14. The “d” is short for “directory,” which is another name for a folder.

Welcome App’s Folder Structure After Compilation

If the code compiles, the WelcomeApp folder’s mods subfolder structure will be:

This is known as the exploded-module folder because the folders and .class files are not in a JAR (Java archive) file. A JAR is a collection of folders and files compressed into a single file, known as an archive. The exploded module’s structure parallels the app’s src folder structure described in Section 21.3.1. We’ll package the app as a JAR shortly. Exploded module folders and modular JAR files (Section 21.3.7) together are module artifacts. These can be placed on the module path—a list of module artifact locations— when compiling and executing modularized code.15,16

15. Reinhold, Mark. “The State of the Module System.” March 8, 2016. Accessed January 7, 2025. https://openjdk.org/projects/jigsaw/spec/sotms/#module-artifacts.

16. Bateman, Alan, Alex Buckley, Jonathan Gibbons and Mark Reinhold. “JEP 261: Module System.” Updated August 19, 2024. Accessed January 7, 2025. http://openjdk.java.net/jeps/261.

Listing the com.deitel.welcome Module’s Contents

You can use the java command’s --describe-module option to display information from the com.deitel.welcome module descriptor, as in:

Click here to view code image

java --module-path mods --describe-module com.deitel.welcome

The resulting output:

Click here to view code image

com.deitel.welcome file:///Users/pauldeitel/Documents/examples/ch21/
WelcomeApp/mods/com.deitel.welcome/
requires java.base
contains com.deitel.welcome

indicates that the module requires the standard module java.base and contains the package com.deitel.welcome. Though the module contains this package, it is not exported, so other modules cannot use our module’s contents. This example’s module declaration explicitly required java.base, as indicated by the following line in the preceding command’s output:

requires java.base

If the module declaration had implicitly required java.base, the previous command’s output would instead contain

requires java.base mandated

where mandated indicates the implicit dependence on java.base.

21.3.6 Running an App from a Module’s Exploded Folders

To run the Welcome app from the module’s exploded folders, use the following command (again, from the WelcomeApp folder):

Click here to view code image

java --module-path mods \
   --module com.deitel.welcome/com.deitel.welcome.Welcome

The --module-path option specifies the module path—in this case, the mods folder. The --module option specifies the module name and the fully qualified class name of the app’s entry point—a class containing main. The program executes and displays:

Click here to view code image

Welcome to the Java Platform Module System!

In the preceding command, --module-path can be abbreviated as -p and --module as -m.
