1 Prompt genAIs for the instructions to run modularized apps using your preferred IDE.

21.3.7 Packaging a Module into a Modular JAR File

The jar command can package an exploded module folder as a modular JAR file17 containing all the module’s files. You specify the JAR file on the module path when you run the app. If a module contains an app’s entry point, you can specify that class with the jar command’s --main-class option, as in:

17. Bateman, Alan, Alex Buckley, Jonathan Gibbons and Mark Reinhold. “JEP 261: Module System.” Updated August 19, 2024. Accessed January 7, 2025. http://openjdk.java.net/jeps/261.

Click here to view code image

jar --create --file jars/com.deitel.welcome.jar \
   --main-class com.deitel.welcome.Welcome \
   -C mods/com.deitel.welcome .

The options are as follows:

  • --create specifies that the command should create a new JAR file.

  • --file specifies the name of the JAR file and is followed by the name—in this case, the file com.deitel.welcome.jar will be created in the folder named jars, which must exist before running the jar command.

  • --main-class specifies the fully qualified name of the app’s entry point—a class that contains a main method.

  • -C specifies which folder contains the files that should be included in the JAR file and is followed by the files to include—the dot (.) indicates that all files in the folder should be included.

You can simplify the --create, --file and --main-class options in the preceding command with the shorthand notation -cfe, followed by the JAR file name and main class, as in:

Click here to view code image

jar -cfe jars/com.deitel.welcome.jar \
   com.deitel.welcome.Welcome \
   -C mods/com.deitel.welcome .
Confirming the Contents of a Module’s JAR File

After creating the JAR file, you can verify its contents as follows:

Click here to view code image

jar --describe-module --file jars/com.deitel.welcome.jar

which produces the following output for the com.deitel.welcome module:

Click here to view code image

com.deitel.welcome jar:file:///Users/pauldeitel/Documents/examples/ch21/
   WelcomeApp/jars/com.deitel.welcome.jar!/module-info.class
requires java.base
contains com.deitel.welcome
main-class com.deitel.welcome.Welcome

The output includes:

  • the module name (which it obtains from the JAR’s module-info.class file),

  • the modular JAR file’s location,

  • what modules this module requires (java.base),

  • what this module contains (the package com.deitel.welcome), and

  • the main-class that executes when you run the app from this modular JAR file.

21.3.8 Running the Welcome App from a Modular JAR File

Once you place an app in a modular JAR file for which you’ve specified the entry point, you can execute the app as follows:

Click here to view code image

java --module-path jars -m com.deitel.welcome

or

Click here to view code image

java -p jars -m com.deitel.welcome

The program executes and displays:

Click here to view code image

Welcome to the Java Platform Module System!

If you did not specify the entry point when creating the JAR, you may still run the app by specifying the module name and fully qualified class name, as in:

Click here to view code image

java --module-path jars \
   -m com.deitel.welcome/com.deitel.welcome.Welcome

or

Click here to view code image

java -p jars -m com.deitel.welcome/com.deitel.welcome.Welcome

21.3.9 Aside: Classpath vs. Module Path

Before Java 9, the compiler and runtime located types via the classpath—a list of folders and library archive files containing compiled Java classes. In early Java versions, the class-path was defined by a combination of a CLASSPATH environment variable, extensions placed in a special JRE subfolder and options provided to the javac and java commands.

Because types could be loaded from several locations, the order in which they were searched resulted in brittle apps. For example, many years ago, one of the authors installed a Java app from a third-party vendor on his system. The app’s installer placed an old version of a Java library into the JRE’s extensions folder. Several Java apps on his system depended on a newer library version with additional types and enhanced versions of the library’s older types. Because classes in the JRE’s extensions folder were loaded before other classes on the classpath,18 the apps that depended on the newer library version stopped working, failing at runtime with NoClassDefFoundErrors and NoSuchMethodErrors—sometimes long after the apps began executing.

18. “Understanding Extension Class Loading.” Accessed December 15, 2024. https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/ext/basics/load.html.

The reliable configuration provided by modules and module descriptors helps eliminate many such runtime classpath problems. A module’s dependencies are resolved as an app launches. Section 21.8.4 presents the steps the JRE’s module resolver performs at launch time.

The module path may contain only one of each module and every package may be defined in only one module. If two or more modules have the same name or export the same packages, the runtime immediately terminates.

21.4 Creating and Using a Custom Module

To demonstrate a module that depends on a custom module, let’s reorganize an earlier, non-modularized example. We’ll declare Section 8.7’s Time1 and Time1Test classes in separate modules, then use Time1 from the module containing Time1Test. To make Time1 available to Time1Test, we’ll

  • export Time1’s package from its custom module and

  • require the module containing Time1 from the module containing Time1Test.

The following diagram contains the src folder structure for the app’s two modules.

21.4.1 Exporting a Package for Use in Other Modules

Every class in a module must be declared in a package. So, we added the package statement in line 3 (Fig. 21.3) to Fig. 8.10’s Time1.java.

com.deitel.timelibrary Module Declaration

In Fig. 21.4’s module declaration, line 4 exports the module’s com.deitel.timelibrary package. This package’s public class Time1 (and other public classes, if any) can be used by any module that reads the com.deitel.timelibrary module, as long as the module can be found on the module path (Section 21.4.3).

21.4.2 Using a Class from a Package in Another Module

The app’s entry point—class Time1Test (originally declared in Fig. 8.11)—also must be packaged for placement in a module (line 3 of Fig. 21.5). In addition, class Time1Test manipulates an object of class Time1, which is declared in a different package. So, line 5 imports the com.deitel.timelibrary package’s Time1 class.

com.deitel.timetest Module Declaration

Time1 is located in a package of the com.deitel.timelibrary module, so the module containing class Time1Test (com.deitel.timetest) must declare its dependency on the com.deitel.timelibrary module. The module declaration (Fig. 21.6) indicates this dependency with line 4’s requires directive. Due to JPMS’s strong encapsulation and reliable configuration features, this app needs both the exports directive in Fig. 21.4 and the requires directive in Fig. 21.6 for class Time1Test to import and use class Time1.

com.deitel.timetest Module-dependency Graph

The following Time1Test app module-dependency graph indicates that the module com.deitel.timetest reads (depend on) the custom module com.deitel.timelibrary and the standard module java.base.

21.4.3 Compiling and Running the Example

You must compile both modules before running this app. The com.deitel.timelibrary module must be compiled first because com.deitel.timetest depends on it. IDEs and other build tools (like Ant, Gradle and Maven) typically can deal with order-of-compilation issues like this for you.

Compiling Module com.deitel.timelibrary

To compile the com.deitel.timelibrary module, open a command window, use the cd command to change to this chapter’s TimeApp folder on your system, then enter:

Click here to view code image

javac -d mods/com.deitel.timelibrary \
   src/com.deitel.timelibrary/module-info.java \
   src/com.deitel.timelibrary/com/deitel/timelibrary/Time1.java
Compiling Module com.deitel.timetest

Next, to compile the com.deitel.timetest module, enter:

Click here to view code image

javac --module-path mods -d mods/com.deitel.timetest \
   src/com.deitel.timetest/module-info.java \
   src/com.deitel.timetest/com/deitel/timetest/Time1Test.java

Here, we added the option --module-path to indicate that the mods folder contains modules on which the com.deitel.timetest module depends—in this case, we previously compiled the com.deitel.timelibrary module into the mods folder.

Running the Example

Finally, to run this example, enter:

Click here to view code image

java --module-path mods \
   -m com.deitel.timetest/com.deitel.timetest.Time1Test

In this command:

  • the option --module-path indicates where the app’s modules are located, and

  • the option -m specifies which class should be used as the app’s entry point—that is, a class containing the main method that the JVM calls to launch the app.

For the main class, note that you must specify its module name followed by a slash and its fully qualified class name because the class is now in a package contained in a module. The program’s output is as follows:

Click here to view code image

After time object is created
Universal time: 00:00:00
Standard time: 12:00:00 AM

After calling setTime
Universal time: 13:27:06
Standard time: 1:27:06 PM

Exception: hour, minute and/or second was out of range

After calling setTime with invalid values
Universal time: 13:27:06
Standard time: 1:27:06 PM

21.4.4 Packaging the App into Modular JAR Files

In this section, we’ll package each app into a modular JAR file then run the app. To package com.deitel.timelibrary into a modular JAR file, enter:

Click here to view code image

jar --create -f jars/com.deitel.timelibrary.jar \
   -C mods/com.deitel.timelibrary .

To package com.deitel.timetest into a modular JAR file, enter:

Click here to view code image

jar --create -f jars/com.deitel.timetest.jar \
   --main-class com.deitel.timetest.Time1Test \
   -C mods/com.deitel.timetest .
Running the App from a Modular JAR File

Once you place an app in a modular JAR file for which you’ve specified the main class, you can execute the app as follows:

Click here to view code image

java --module-path jars -m com.deitel.timetest

The program executes and displays the same output as in Section 21.4.3.

21.4.5 Strong Encapsulation and Accessibility

Before modules, you could use any public class you imported into your code. Whether you could access the class’s members was determined by how they were declared—public, protected, package access or private (as described in Chapter 8). Due to modules’ strong encapsulation, public types in a module are no longer accessible to your code by default. So, public does not necessarily mean “available to all”:

  • If a module exports a package, the public types in that package are accessible to any module that reads the package’s module.

  • If a module exports a package to a specific module (via exports…to), the public types in that package are accessible only to the specific module and only if that module reads the package’s module.

  • If a module does not export a package, the public types in that package are accessible only within the module itself.

Once you have access to a type in another module, the normal rules of public, protected, package access and private apply.

Compilation Error When Attempting to Use an Inaccessible Type

The project TimeAppMissingExports in this chapter’s ExamplesShowingErrors folder demonstrates that explicitly named modules have strong encapsulation and do not export packages unless you explicitly list them in exports directives. In this project, we removed the exports directive from the com.deitel.timelibrary’s module declaration then recompiled the module. Next, we compiled the com.deitel.timelibrary module then tried to recompile the com.deitel.timetest module. The compiler produced the following error message, which indicates that the package com.deitel.timelibrary is not exported and thus is inaccessible:

Click here to view code image

src/com.deitel.timetest/com/deitel/timetest/Time1Test.java:5: error: package
com.deitel.timelibrary is not visible
import com.deitel.timelibrary.Time1;
          ^
   (package com.deitel.timelibrary is declared in module com.deitel.timeli-
brary, which does not export it)
1 error

When a requires dependency is not fulfilled by an exports clause in another module a compilation error occurs.

21.5 Module-Dependency Graphs: A Deeper Look

Let’s continue our discussion of module graphs and present the errors that occur if a module directly or indirectly requires itself—known as a cycle.

21.5.1 java.sql

Consider the following modulegraphtest module that depends on the java.sql module:

module modulegraphtest {
   requires java.sql;
}

The following diagram is the module-dependency graph for modulegraphtest:

The diagram illustrates that modulegraphtest depends directly on modules java.sql and java.base. Modules java.logging, java.transaction.xa and java.xml are included in the graph because java.sql depends on them—thus, modulegraphtest also depends on them indirectly. The java.sql module’s module-info.java declares these modules with the following requires transitive statements:

Click here to view code image

requires transitive java.logging;
requires transitive java.transaction.xa;
requires transitive java.xml;

So, modules that depend on java.sql also have access to these modules. Of course, all the modules in the graph point to java.base because it’s required by all Java modules.

21.5.2 java.se

Figure 21.7 presents the significantly more complex java.se module’s dependency graph. This aggregator module specifies via requires transitive all the modules necessary to support Java Standard Edition (SE) apps. We rotated the graph 90° for readability.

21.5.3 Error: Module Graph with a Cycle

A module is not allowed to directly or indirectly reference itself. Doing so would result in a cycle when computing the module’s dependency graph. A compilation error occurs if a module graph contains a cycle.

A Module That (Incorrectly) Requires Itself

Consider the following module declaration in which the module requires itself:

module mymodule {
   requires mymodule;
}

If you were to compile this declaration, the following error would occur, indicating a cycle in the module’s dependencies:

Click here to view code image

module-info.java:2: error: cyclic dependence involving mymodule
   requires mymodule;
            ^
1 error
Two Modules That (Incorrectly) Require One Another

Similarly, consider the project CircularDependency containing two modules—module1 and module2—with the structure in the following diagram:

If the module declarations for these two modules indicate that each module requires the other, as in

module module1 {
   exports package1;
   requires module2;
}

and

module module2 {
   exports package2;
   requires module1;
}

then, when you compile these modules

Click here to view code image

javac --module-source-path src \
   --module-path mods -d mods \
   src/module1/module-info.java \
   src/module1/package1/Class1.java \
   src/module2/module-info.java \
   src/module2/package2/Class2.java

the compiler again issues an error indicating a cycle in the module dependencies:

Click here to view code image

src/module1/module-info.java:9: error: cyclic dependence involving module2
   requires module2;
            ^
src/module2/module-info.java:9: error: cyclic dependence involving module1
   requires module1;
            ^
2 errors
Modules in a Cycle Are Really “One Thing”

Ultimately, all the modules in a cycle are really one module—not separate modules.19 When we were writing this chapter for Java How to Program, 11/e, a friend who worked for a large organization indicated that the organization had multiple large pre-Java-9 JAR files. Initially they thought they’d make each JAR a separate module. Their JARs were so interdependent that they combined them into a single module. This kind of interdependency is what leads to cycles in your design. Ideally, when you modularize a previously monolithic system, you want to break that system into separate modules that are easier to maintain and secure. This can pose significant refactoring challenges in large code bases.

19. Alex Buckley, e-mail message to authors, March 24, 2017.

21.6 Migrating Code to Modules

 

Many non-modularized apps will run using the modularized JDK. In fact, most programs presented in this book were not modularized and ran without issue. Technically, all programs are compiled and executed using the module system. Java strongly encapsulates types that are not exported by modules, so it’s possible some older apps will fail to compile in Java 9 and beyond because types that were accessible to them before Java 9 no longer are. For example, there are pre-Java-9 internal APIs that were meant only for use in the JDK but were used by developers in their apps and libraries. Most of these internal APIs have been replaced with proper publicly accessible capabilities, so the internal APIs are no longer exported and thus are inaccessible.20

20. Reinhold, Mark. “JEP 260: Encapsulate Most Internal APIs.” Updated April 28, 2024. Accessed January 7, 2025. https://openjdk.org/jeps/260.

Strong Encapsulation Is Now the Default

As we’ve mentioned, JPMS enables strong encapsulation. Code that is not exported cannot be accessed by other modules. Java versions 9–15 allowed some flexibility with respect to internal APIs to give developers time to migrate their code to JPMS. Since Java 16 and Java 17, strong encapsulation is the default.21 If you have older code that uses such internal APIs directly or indirectly, it will fail to compile.

21. Buckley, Alex and Mark Reinhold, “JEP 396: Strongly Encapsulate JDK Internals by Default.” Updated April 28, 2024. Accessed December 17, 2024. https://openjdk.org/jeps/396.

Checking Your Code’s Dependencies

You can use the jdeps tool (Section 21.6.3) to check your code’s dependencies. The jdeps option --jdk-internals specifically identifies uses of JDK internal APIs in code. For each internal API that jdeps locates, it suggests an appropriate replacement.

21.6.1 Unnamed Module

Technically, Java requires all code to be placed in modules. When you execute code that’s not in a module, the code is loaded from the classpath and placed in the unnamed module. This is why we can run some non-modularized code in the modularized JDK but without the benefits of strong encapsulation and explicit module dependencies.

The unnamed module:

  • implicitly exports all of its packages, and

  • implicitly reads all other modules.

There’s no way to refer to an unnamed module in a requires directive from a named module, so a named module cannot depend on an unnamed module.

21.6.2 Automatic Modules

There are enormous numbers of preexisting libraries that you can use in your apps. Some are modularized and some are not. To facilitate migration, you can add any library’s JAR file to an app’s module path then use the packages in that JAR. When you do, the JAR file implicitly becomes an automatic module and can be specified in a module declaration’s requires directives. An automatic module:

  • implicitly exports all of its packages—so any module that reads the automatic module (including the unnamed module) has access to the public types in the automatic module’s packages.

  • implicitly reads (requires) all other modules, including other automatic modules and the unnamed module—so an automatic module has access to all the public types exposed by the system’s other modules.

Automatic Module Names Derived from JAR File Names

An automatic module’s name is derived from its file name. If the JAR’s file name minus the .jar extension is a valid Java identifier, it becomes its automatic module name. Otherwise:

  • Characters that are not allowed in Java identifiers are replaced with dots (.).

  • If there are multiple consecutive dots, they are replaced with a single dot.

  • If there are dots at the beginning or end of the remaining name, they’re removed.

21.6.3 jdeps Tool for Java Dependency Analysis

Another tool to help you prepare to modularize your code is the jdeps command. It enables you determine a type’s class and package dependencies. Given that 28.8% of Java developers were still using Java 8 in 2024,22 a key use of jdeps is to help those developers locate dependencies on internal APIs that are now strongly encapsulated. To determine whether a class has any such dependencies, use the following command on your compiled class:

22. New Relic, “2024 State of the Java Ecosystem,” April 2024. Accessed December 15, 2024. https://newrelic.com/resources/report/2024-state-of-the-java-ecosystem.

Click here to view code image

jdeps --jdk-internals YourClassName.class

or if you have many compiled classes in a JAR file, use:

Click here to view code image

jdeps --jdk-internals YourJARName.jar

If this command does not produce output, then your class or set of classes does not depend on JDK internal APIs that are no longer accessible.

Determining the Modules You Need

A key aspect of modularization is the ability to create more compact Java runtimes that provide only the modules your app requires. When you’re preparing to create custom runtimes, you can use jdeps to discover your app’s module dependencies so you know which ones to include in your custom runtime. For example, this chapter’s Welcome app depends only on java.base. We can confirm that by executing the following command from the WelcomeApp folder, which checks the com.deitel.welcome module’s dependencies:

Click here to view code image

jdeps --module-path jars -m com.deitel.welcome

This produces the following output containing the packages and modules the app uses— we removed some horizontal spacing in this command’s output to make it more readable:

Click here to view code image

com.deitel.welcome
 [file:///Users/pauldeitel/Documents/examples/ch21/WelcomeApp/jars/
   com.deitel.welcome.jar]
   requires java.base (@23)
com.deitel.welcome -> java.base
   com.deitel.welcome -> java.io        java.base
   com.deitel.welcome -> java.lang      java.base

The output indicates that our module com.deitel.welcome depends on the java.base module, and that our module specifically uses types from the java.base module’s java.io and java.lang packages. The preceding command may also be written as

Click here to view code image

jdeps jars/com.deitel.welcome.jar

In addition, you can use jdeps on a specific .class file, as in:

Click here to view code image

jdeps mods/com.deitel.welcome/com/deitel/welcome/Welcome.class

which produces

Click here to view code image

Welcome.class -> java.base
   com.deitel.welcome -> java.io       java.base
   com.deitel.welcome -> java.lang     java.base
Verbose jdeps Output

If you’d like more details, you can specify the -v (verbose) option as in:

Click here to view code image

jdeps -v jars/com.deitel.welcome.jar

which produces:

Click here to view code image

com.deitel.welcome
 [file:///Users/pauldeitel/Documents/examples/ch21/WelcomeApp/jars/
   com.deitel.welcome.jar]
   requires java.base (@23)
com.deitel.welcome -> java.base
   com.deitel.welcome.Welcome -> java.io.PrintStream      java.base
   com.deitel.welcome.Welcome -> java.lang.Object         java.base
   com.deitel.welcome.Welcome -> java.lang.String         java.base
   com.deitel.welcome.Welcome -> java.lang.System         java.base

This lists precisely which packages, types and modules the app uses. Knowing that the app requires only java.base, we can then use jlink to create a custom runtime containing only that module, which we’ll do in Section 21.8.

Using jdeps to Produce DOT Files for Graphing Tools

You can use graphing tools—such as Graphviz (https://www.graphviz.org/)—to produce module-dependency graphs using the DOT graph description language,23 which specifies a graph’s nodes and edges. The jdeps tool can create DOT (.dot) files with the --dot-output option, as in:

23. “DOT (graph description language).” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified November 12, 2024. Accessed December 15, 2024. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DOT_(graph_description_language).

Click here to view code image

jdeps --dot-output . jars/com.deitel.welcome.jar

This produces two .dot files24 in the current folder (.):

24. The .dot extension is also used by Microsoft Word document templates. On systems with Microsoft Word installed, open the jdeps-produced .dot files directly from a text editor.

  • summary.dot—the description of module com.deitel.welcome’s dependencies.

  • com.deitel.welcome.dot—the description of module com.deitel.welcome’s specific package dependencies.

After installing Graphviz, we executed the following command to visualize summary.dot:

Click here to view code image

dot -Tpng summary.dot -Gdpi=600 -Nfontname="Open Sans" \
   -Nshape=box -o WelcomeApp.png

  • -Tpng specifies the image should be in the popular PNG image format commonly used on the web.

  • -Gdpi specifies the image resolution—600 dots-per-inch.

  • -Nfontname option enables you to choose a font for the nodes’ text.

  • -Nshape specifies the nodes’ shape—box produces rectangles rather than the default ovals.

  • -o is followed by the image’s filename.

21.7 Resources in Modules

 

When the types in a module require resources—such as images, videos, XML documents and more—those resources should be packaged with the module to ensure that they’re available when the module’s types are used at execution time. This is known as resource encapsulation.25 In this section, we’ll migrate our non-modularized JavaFX VideoPlayer example from Section 17.6 into a module that also encapsulates the app’s resources—the FXML file that describes the GUI and its video file that will be loaded and played at execution time. By convention, resources typically are placed in a folder named res.

25. Mark Reinhold, “Java Platform Module System Requirements.” April 1, 2015. Accessed January 7, 2025. https://openjdk.org/projects/jigsaw/spec/reqs/#resource-encapsulation.

Recall that the original VideoPlayer example consisted of the following files all in Chapter 17’s VideoPlayer folder:

  • VideoPlayer.xml—The FXML file that describes the app’s GUI.

  • VideoPlayer.java—The Application subclass that begins the app’s execution.

  • VideoPlayerController.java—The controller class that responds to the GUIs events and loads the video.

  • A1Launch~medium.mp4—The NASA video26 that the app loads and plays.

    26. For NASA’s terms of use, visit https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/

  • controlsfx-11.2.1.jar—The ControlsFX library containing the dialog class ExceptionDialog. We display an ExceptionDialog if the MediaPlayer encounters any errors.

Reorganizing for Modularization

For this example, we reorganized the files into the following folder structure to support modules.

Notice the following about the structure:

  • The files VideoPlayer.fxml and A1Launch~medium.mp4, which are not Java source code files, are located in the module directory’s res folder. These files will be read from the module’s res folder when the app executes.

  • As required for modularization, we placed the VideoPlayer and VideoPlayer-Controller classes in a package—the folder structure com/deitel/videoplayer corresponds to the package com.deitel.videoplayer.

  • As required, we created a module-info.java file in the module’s root folder.

In addition, we placed controlsfx-11.2.1.jar in the VideoPlayer folder’s mods subfolder.

Code Changes for Modularization

We made several code changes to the VideoPlayer application for modularization. In VideoPlayer.fxml, we modified the controller class’s name to use its fully qualified name

Click here to view code image

com.deitel.videoplayer.VideoPlayerController

so that the FXMLLoader can find the controller class. In VideoPlayer.java, we changed "VideoPlayer.fxml" to "/res/VideoPlayer.fxml" to indicate that the FXML file is located in the module’s res subfolder. We also added the package statement

Click here to view code image

package com.deitel.videoplayer;

In VideoPlayerController.java, we changed "A1Launch~medium.mp4" to

"/res/A1Launch~medium.mp4"

to indicate that the video file is located in the module’s res folder. We also added the package statement

Click here to view code image

package com.deitel.videoplayer;

The rest of the code is identical to what we presented in Section 17.6.

21.7.1 Requiring Multiple Modules

Module com.deitel.videoplayer’s declaration (Fig. 21.8) indicates that it requires javafx.controls, javafx.fxml, javafx.media and org.controlsfx.controls. The module exports package com.deitel.videoplayer (line 9), because class VideoPlayer-Controller is used by class FXMLLoader (module javafx.fxml) when it creates the controller object and the app’s GUI.

21.7.2 Opening a Module for Reflection

In Fig. 21.8, the opens…to directive (line 10) indicates that the accessible types in the package com.deitel.videoplayer should be available via reflection at runtime to types in the javafx.fxml module. As we discussed in Section 21.2.6, this enables the FXMLLoader to locate and load class VideoPlayerController. The FXMLLoader creates a VideoPlayer-Controller object and injects into it references to the GUIs components created from the app’s FXML file. For one module to open a package to another module, that package must first be exported (possibly as a qualified export using exports…to).

21.7.3 Compiling the Module

To compile the com.deitel.videoplayer module, enter:

Click here to view code image

javac --module-path "$PATH_TO_FX":mods \
   -d mods/com.deitel.videoplayer \
   src/com.deitel.videoplayer/module-info.java \
   src/com.deitel.videoplayer/com/deitel/videoplayer/*.java

We included the --module-path option to specify where the JavaFX modules are ("$PATH_TO_FX") and where controlsfx-11.2.1.jar is (mods).

Copying the Resource Files into the Module

Though some IDEs and build tools will automatically put the module’s resources into the compiled module, the preceding javac command does not. Once you’ve compiled the module, copy the res folder from this project’s src/com.deitel.videoplayer folder into the mods/com.deitel.videoplayer folder.

21.7.4 Running a Modularized App

To execute class VideoPlayer from the com.deitel.videoplayer module, enter:

Click here to view code image

java --module-path "$PATH_TO_FX":mods \
   -m com.deitel.videoplayer/com.deitel.videoplayer.VideoPlayer

Here is the app executing on macOS:

21.7.5 Module-Dependency Graph

The following diagram is the com.deitel.videoplayer module-dependency graph:

We produced this diagram using the following jdeps command to create summary.dot— the --recursive option indicates that jdeps should analyze all the runtime dependencies of the specified module:

Click here to view code image

jdeps --module-path "$PATH_TO_FX":mods --dot-output . \
   --recursive --module com.deitel.videoplayer

We then used Graphviz to visualize it:

Click here to view code image

21.8 Creating Custom Runtimes with jlink

Before JPMS, every Java SE program required the entire Java runtime to execute, even if the program used only a small portion of the Java platform’s capabilities. The jlink command enables you to create custom runtime images.27 In a custom runtime, you can include only what’s necessary for a given app or set of apps to execute. This is particularly useful for executing large numbers of Java runtimes in cloud-based architectures, where you pay for all the storage, memory and processor resources you use. It’s also useful for smaller capacity devices. If your app requires only packages from the java.base module, you can create a runtime containing just that module. In fact, such a runtime can execute most of this book’s text-only, command-line examples.

27. Denise, Jean-Francois. “JEP 282: jlink: The Java Linker.” Updated May 19, 2017. Accessed January 7, 2025. https://openjdk.org/jeps/282.

21.8.1 Custom Runtime Containing Only java.base

For this example, change to the WelcomeApp folder—after creating the custom runtime, you’ll execute the Welcome app using it. The following command creates a runtime containing only the module java.base:

Click here to view code image

jlink --module-path "$JAVA_HOME/jmods" --add-modules java.base \
   --output javabaseruntime

The commands options are as follows:

  • --module-path specifies one or more folders in which to locate modules to include in the runtime—in this case, the JDK’s jmods folder, which contains the JDK’s modules. Place "$JAVA_HOME" in quotes in case the path to the JDK on your system contains spaces.

  • --add-modules specifies which modules to include in the runtime—in this case, just java.base.

  • --output specifies the folder (javabaseruntime) in which the runtime’s contents are placed. This folder will be a subfolder of the one in which you execute the preceding command (unless you specify additional path information). If the folder already exists, an error occurs.

This runtime can execute an app that depends only on types from the packages in module java.base, including many of this book’s command-line apps.

Note Regarding the JAVA_HOME Environment Variable

The JAVA_HOME environment variable must refer to the JDK’s installation folder on your system. If you installed the JDK using the instructions in our Before You Begin section that follows the preface, the installer set up the JAVA_HOME environment variable for you. You may need to set up this environment variable yourself if you used a different Java distribution.

Executing the Welcome App Using This Custom Runtime

To run the app with the custom runtime, execute:

Click here to view code image

javabaseruntime/bin/java --module-path mods \

When executing the custom runtime’s java command, use / to separate folder names on macOS and \ to separate the folder names on Windows. The preceding command produces the following output:

java.logging@23
java.sql@23
java.transaction.xa@23
java.xml@23

To create a custom runtime containing only the modules com.deitel.welcome and its dependencies (in this case, java.base), change to the WelcomeApp folder, then use the following command:

On macOS, the path-separator character for lists of folders is a colon (:). The Windows version of this command is located in the file CommandsForCopyPaste.txt with this chapter’s examples. For the list of modules included in the custom runtime, on macOS use:

(use backslashes on Windows), which produces the following list of modules:

java.base@23

21.8.4 Using the Module Resolver on a Custom Runtime

When you run a modularized app, the JVM’s module resolver determines which modules are required at execution time and ensures their dependencies are satisfied—this is known as the transitive closure of those modules. To locate modules, the module resolver looks at the observable modules—those built into the runtime (like java.base) and those located on the module path. The runtime throws a java.lang.module.FindException if a required module cannot be found.

For a given app and runtime, you can view the steps the module resolver follows to determine module dependencies and ensure that the required modules are available to the program. To do so, include the --show-module-resolution option28 in the java command, as in the following command (use backslashes on Windows):

28. Bateman, Alan, Alex Buckley, Jonathan Gibbons and Mark Reinhold. “JEP 261: Module System.” Updated August 19, 2024. Accessed January 7, 2025. https://openjdk.org/jeps/261.

Click here to view code image

welcomeruntime/bin/java --show-module-resolution -m com.deitel.welcome

This uses the custom welcomeruntime’s java command to display the resolver’s steps for locating modules, followed by the program’s output:

Click here to view code image

root com.deitel.welcome jrt:/com.deitel.welcome
Welcome to the Java Platform Module System!

In the Welcome app’s module-resolution process, the resolver first locates the app’s initial module—com.deitel.welcome—containing the app’s entry point. The resolver refers to this as the root module—the root node in the module-dependency graph. Then, the resolver looks for other module dependencies. The Welcome app’s only other dependency is the java.base module. Since all modules depend on this, it’s not listed in the output.

Adding the --show-module-resolution option to the java command for the Video-Player app (Section 21.7) produces a substantial output, a portion of which is shown below:

Click here to view code image

root com.deitel.videoplayer file:///Users/pauldeitel/Documents/examples/ch21/
   VideoPlayer/mods/com.deitel.videoplayer/
com.deitel.videoplayer requires javafx.media file:///Users/pauldeitel/
   Downloads/javafx-sdk-23.0.1/lib/javafx.media.jar
com.deitel.videoplayer requires javafx.controls file:///Users/pauldeitel/
   Downloads/javafx-sdk-23.0.1/lib/javafx.controls.jar
com.deitel.videoplayer requires javafx.fxml file:///Users/pauldeitel/
   Downloads/javafx-sdk-23.0.1/lib/javafx.fxml.jar
com.deitel.videoplayer requires org.controlsfx.controls file:///Users/
   pauldeitel/Documents/examples/ch21/VideoPlayer/mods/controlsfx.jar
javafx.media requires javafx.base file:///Users/pauldeitel/Downloads/
   javafx-sdk-23.0.1/lib/javafx.base.jar
javafx.media requires javafx.graphics file:///Users/pauldeitel/Downloads/
   javafx-sdk-23.0.1/lib/javafx.graphics.jar
javafx.controls requires javafx.base file:///Users/pauldeitel/Downloads/
   javafx-sdk-23.0.1/lib/javafx.base.jar
javafx.controls requires javafx.graphics file:///Users/pauldeitel/Downloads/
   javafx-sdk-23.0.1/lib/javafx.graphics.jar
...

After resolving the root module com.deitel.videoplayer, the module resolver looks at each module the root requires, then each module those modules require, and so on, essentially building the module graph shown in Section 21.7.5. If the module resolver finds all the required modules, the program executes. Otherwise, the module resolver throws a java.lang.module.FindException and the program terminates.

21.9 Services and ServiceLoader

 

Section 9.13 discussed “programming to an interface, not an implementation” to create loosely coupled objects. In this section, we discuss services and the ServiceLoader class, which help you create loosely coupled system components, making large-scale systems easier to develop and maintain.

MathTutor App

We’ll create a MathTutor app consisting of three modules. The app supports various types of randomly generated math problems. Rather than hard-coding these into the app, we’ll load math problems through a service-provider interface that describes how to obtain math problems. We’ll then define two service-provider implementation classes that implement this interface—one for addition problems and one for multiplication problems. We’ll load and use objects of these service-provider implementation classes at runtime. The following diagram contains the completed three-module app structure:

MathTutor App’s Modules

Module com.deitel.mathtutor aggregates two related packages:

  • com.deitel.mathtutor: This package contains class MathTutor—a command-line app that displays random math problems to the user, inputs the user’s responses and displays whether each response is correct or incorrect.

  • com.deitel.mathtutor.spi: This package contains the service-provider interface ProblemProvider and its supporting abstract class Problem, representing a math problem. MathTutor uses ProblemProviders to obtain Problem objects.

Module com.deitel.additionprovider contains a package of the same name in which we declare class AdditionProblemProvider. This implementation of the service-provider interface ProblemProvider generates random addition Problems.

Module com.deitel.multiplicationprovider contains a package of the same name in which we declare class MultiplicationProblemProvider. This implementation of the service-provider interface ProblemProvider generates random multiplication Problems.

How We’ll Demonstrate the App

We’ll run the MathTutor app several times:

  • First, we’ll run it without placing the service-provider implementation modules on the module path to demonstrate what happens when no service providers are found at runtime.

  • Next, we’ll “plug in” the com.deitel.additionprovider module on the module path, then re-run the app to demonstrate that we can obtain Problems from an AdditionProblemProvider.

  • Finally, we’ll “plug in” both modules com.deitel.additionprovider and com.deitel.multiplicationprovider on the module path, then re-run the app to demonstrate that we’re able to obtain addition and multiplication Problems from the AdditionProblemProvider and the MultiplicationProblemProvider.

Plug-in Architecture

The MathTutor app is easy to extend via this “plug-in” architecture. Simply create a module containing a ProblemProvider implementation, then add it to the module path when you run the app. This architecture also makes the app more configurable—you can choose which modules to include on the module path when you execute the app.

Reliable Configuration

The mechanisms for creating loosely coupled systems like the MathTutor app have been used extensively in Java since its early versions. A key concept in JPMS—which also applies to modules in general—is reliable configuration. For the MathTutor app to be able to display Problems to the user, it must be able to locate and load ProblemProvider implementations. As you’ll learn, module declarations enable you to specify the service-provider interfaces a module uses and whether a module contains types that implement those interfaces.

21.9.1 Service-Provider Interface

The package com.deitel.mathtutor.spi contains the com.deitel.mathtutor module’s service-provider interface ProblemProvider and the supporting abstract class Problem. The final component of this package’s name—spi—is commonly used in packages that declare one or more service-provider interfaces. The ProblemProvider interface (Fig. 21.9) declares the abstract getProblem method (line 6), which returns a Problem.

The abstract Problem class (Fig. 21.10) provides the common features of this exam-ple’s math problems. Each has two int operands and an int result as well as a String representing the operation—the MathTutor displays this String with each math problem it presents to the user. Class Problem’s abstract method getResult is overridden in each service-provider implementation’s concrete Problem subclass.

21.9.2 Loading and Consuming Service Providers

Class MathTutor (Fig. 21.11) is the app’s entry point. It provides the logic to locate and load ProblemProvider implementations then use them to generate math problems. We split the MathTutor class into parts for discussion purposes.

Using ServiceLoader to Locate Service Providers

Lines 19–20 create a ServiceLoader (package java.util) that loads ProblemProvider implementations.

Click here to view code image

18         // get a service loader for ProblemProviders
19         ServiceLoader<ProblemProvider> serviceLoader =
20            ServiceLoader.load(ProblemProvider.class);
21

ServiceLoader’s static load method receives as its argument the Class object representing the service-provider interface’s type—the compiler automatically creates an object of type Class<ProblemProvider> from the class literal ProblemProvider.class. Method load returns a ServiceLoader<ProblemProvider> that dynamically discovers and loads ProblemProvider implementations available on the module path.

There are several ways to get service-provider implementations from a Service-Loader. Lines 23–24 obtain a List of the available service-provider implementations using ServiceLoader’s stream method.

Click here to view code image

22         // get the list of service providers
23         List<Provider<ProblemProvider>> providersList =
24            serviceLoader.stream().collect(Collectors.toList());
25
26         // check whether there are any providers
27         if (providersList.isEmpty()) {
28            System.out.println(
29               "Terminating MathTutor: No problem providers found.");
30            return;
31         }
32

This returns a Stream<Provider<ProblemProvider>> representing all available Problem-Provider implementations, if any. Interface Provider (imported at line 8) is a nested type of class ServiceLoader. For each available ProblemProvider implementation, the stream contains one Provider<ProblemProvider> object. Line 24 uses Stream’s collect method and the predefined Collector defined by Collectors.toList to get the List containing all the available implementations. If that List is empty (line 27) the program displays an appropriate message and terminates.

Using a Service-Provider Interface

If the List contains any service-provider implementations, lines 36–46 use them to display one math problem at a time to the user. Lines 38–39 randomly select one object from the providersList, then invoke that object’s get method to obtain its ProblemProvider. Line 42 then gets a Problem from that ProblemProvider. Note the loose coupling. The MathTutor app does not explicitly mention the ProblemProvider implementation classes AdditionProblemProvider and MultiplicationProblemProvider.

Click here to view code image

33         boolean shouldContinue = true;
34         var random = RandomGenerator.getDefault();
35
36         do {
37            // choose a ProblemProvider at random
38            ProblemProvider provider =
39               providersList.get(random.nextInt(providersList.size())).get();
40
41            // get the Problem
42            Problem problem = provider.getProblem();
43
44            // display the problem to the user
45            showProblem(problem);
46         } while (playAgain());
47      }
48
49      // show the math problem to the user
50      private static void showProblem(Problem problem) {
51         var problemStatement = String.format("%nWhat is %d %s %d? ",
52            problem.getLeftOperand(), problem.getOperation(),
53            problem.getRightOperand());
54
55         // display problem and get answer from user
56         System.out.printf(problemStatement);
57         int answer = input.nextInt();
58
59         while (answer != problem.getResult()) {
60            System.out.println("Incorrect. Please try again.");
61            System.out.printf(problemStatement);
62            answer = input.nextInt();
63         }
64
65         System.out.println("Correct!");
66      }
67
68      // play again?
69      private static boolean playAgain() {
70         System.out.printf("%nTry another? y to continue, n to terminate: ");
71         String response = input.next();
72
73         return response.toLowerCase().startsWith("y");
74      }
75   }

21.9.3 uses Module Directive and Service Consumers

Figure 21.12 contains the com.deitel.mathtutor module declaration. This module exports the com.deitel.mathtutor.spi package containing the service-provider interface ProblemProvider and its supporting Problem class, enabling modules that implement ProblemProvider to access those types. The new feature in this declaration is the uses module directive (line 6), indicating that code in the com.deitel.mathtutor module uses ProblemProvider objects. Such a module is a service consumer.

For the MathTutor to consume ProblemProviders, the ServiceLoader must be able to locate and load their implementations dynamically using Java’s reflection capabilities. When you run this app, the module resolver will note from the module descriptor (the compiled version of module-info.java) that this module uses ProblemProvider implementations and thus is dependent on such providers. The module resolver will search the modules on the module path looking for any that provide ProblemProvider implementations. If it finds any, it will add them to the module-dependency graph.

21.9.4 Running the App with No Service Providers

To compile the com.deitel.mathtutor module, enter:

Click here to view code image

   src/com.deitel.mathtutor/module-info.java \
   src/com.deitel.mathtutor/com/deitel/mathtutor/MathTutor.java \
   src/com.deitel.mathtutor/com/deitel/mathtutor/spi/*.java

Next, run the app with no ProblemProvider implementations on the module path by using the following java command, which places only the com.deitel.mathtutor module on the module path:

Click here to view code image

21.9.5 Implementing a Service Provider

Next, let’s create class AdditionProblemProvider (Fig. 21.13), which implements the ProblemProvider service-provider interface (line 10). Package com.deitel.addition-provider will be placed in module com.deitel.additionprovider (Section 21.9.6). We import interface ProblemProvider and class Problem from the com.deitel.mathtutor module’s exported com.deitel.mathtutor.spi package (lines 7–8). When MathTutor calls an AdditionProblemProvider’s getProblem method (lines 14–23), the method creates an object of an anonymous inner class (Section 11.5.2) that’s extends Problem (lines 16–22), passing to Problem’s constructor two random int operands and the String "+" to represent the arithmetic operation. Lines 18–21 override Problem’s getResult method, which adds the left and right operands and returns their sum.

21.9.6 provides…with Module Directive and Declaring a Service Provider

Figure 21.14 contains the com.deitel.additionprovider module declaration. Note that this module requires the module com.deitel.mathtutor. Recall from Fig. 21.12 that this module exports the package com.deitel.mathtutor.spi containing the types used in class AdditionProblemProvider.

The new feature in this module declaration is the provides…with module directive, indicating that the com.deitel.additionprovider module is a service provider. The provides keyword (line 6) is followed by the fully qualified name of an interface or abstract class that another module specified in a uses module directive. The with keyword (line 7) is followed by the name of a concrete class that implements the interface or extends the abstract class. Lines 6–7 specify that this module

  • provides an implementation of the ProblemProvider interface declared in the com.deitel.mathtutor module’s com.deitel.mathtutor.spi package

  • with the AdditionProblemProvider class, which is declared in this module’s com.deitel.additionprovider package.

21.10 Wrap-Up

This chapter presented the Java Platform Module System (JPMS) and discussed its role in creating more maintainable and secure Java applications. You learned that modules are uniquely named, reusable groups of related packages and resources. You used module declarations in module-info.java files to specify a module’s name, dependencies, exported packages, services and reflection permissions.

You learned that all modules implicitly depend on java.base, which contains fundamental packages required by all Java application. You created module declarations using:

  • requires directives for specifying dependencies,

  • exports and exports…to directives for making packages available to other modules,

  • the open modifier and the opens and opens…to directives for controlling reflection access,

  • uses for consuming services and

  • provides...with for implementing services.

You explored how module declarations enforce strong encapsulation, ensuring that only explicitly exported packages are accessible to other modules.

We built modular applications and used the Graphviz tool to visualize their dependencies in module-dependency graphs. You used the jdeps tool to analyze module dependencies and learned how the module resolver ensures dependencies are fulfilled at runtime. You used jlink to create custom runtime images containing only the modules an application needs, making Java more suitable for resource-constrained and cloud environments.

We discussed migrating existing code to modules using unnamed modules and automatic modules and how to use jdeps to check whether legacy code uses internal APIs that are now strongly encapsulated. We presented services, service providers and using the class ServiceLoader to create loosely coupled system components that make large-scale applications easier to develop and maintain. We then presented a MathTutor application in which we implemented service-provider interfaces and created multiple service providers, demonstrating how JPMS enables plug-in architectures and extensible applications. This foundation in JPMS prepared you to build modern Java applications that are more secure, maintainable, and efficient. In the next chapter, we discuss miscellaneous additional Java topics.

22.1 Introduction

In this chapter, we concentrate on some key aspects of computer science thinking that go beyond programming fundamentals, including a focus on performance issues. We begin with a treatment of recursive methods that call themselves. We’ll show examples and compare recursive programming to iterative programming. We’ll indicate where each might be preferable. We also introduce Big O notation, which concisely classifies algorithms by how hard they have to work to get the job done. Big O helps you compare the efficiency of algorithms.

22.2 Recursion Concepts

Recursive problem-solving approaches have several elements in common. When a recursive method is called to solve a problem, it can solve only the simplest case(s) or base case(s). If the method is called with a base case, it returns a result. If the method is called with a more complex problem, it divides the problem into two conceptual pieces—a piece that the method knows how to do and a piece that it does not know how to do. To make recursion feasible, the latter piece must resemble the original problem but be a slightly simpler or smaller version. Because this new problem resembles the original problem, the method calls a fresh copy of itself to work on the smaller problem—this is referred to as a recursive call and is also called the recursion step. The recursion step typically includes a return statement because its result will be combined with the portion of the problem the method knew how to solve to form a result that will be passed back to the original caller. Separating the problem into two smaller portions is a form of the divide-and-conquer approach.

The recursion step executes while the original method call is still active (i.e., it has not finished executing). It can result in many more recursive calls as the method divides each new subproblem into two conceptual pieces. For the recursion to eventually terminate, each time the method calls itself with a simpler version of the original problem, the sequence of smaller and smaller problems must converge on a base case. When the method recognizes the base case, it returns a result to the previous copy of the method. A sequence of returns ensues until the original method call returns the final result to the caller. We’ll illustrate this process with a concrete example in Section 22.3.

22.3 Recursion Example: Factorials

 

Let’s write a recursive program to perform a popular mathematical calculation. Consider the factorial of a positive integer n, written n! (pronounced “n factorial”), which is the product

n · (n – 1) · (n – 2) · … · 1

with 1! equal to 1 and 0! defined to be 1. For example, 5! is the product 5 · 4 · 3 · 2 · 1, which is equal to 120.

The factorial of an integer number (where number ≥ 0) can be calculated iteratively (nonrecursively) using a for statement as follows:

Click here to view code image

factorial = 1;

for (int counter = number; counter >= 1; --counter) {
   factorial *= counter;
}

A recursive declaration of the factorial calculation for integers greater than 1 is arrived at by observing the following relationship:

n! = n · (n – 1)!

For example, 5! is clearly equal to 5 · 4!, as shown by the following equations:

5! = 5 ·  4 · 3 · 2 · 1
5! = 5 · (4 · 3 · 2 · 1)
5! = 5 · (4!)

The evaluation of 5! would proceed as shown in the following diagram. Part (a) contains the succession of recursive calls that proceed until 1! (the base case) is evaluated as 1, which terminates the recursion. Part (b) contains the values returned from each recursive call to its caller until the final value is calculated and returned.

Implementing a Recursive Factorial Function

Figure 22.1 recursively calculates the factorials of 0–10 then 20, 30 and 40. The recursive method factorial (lines 7–15) first determines whether a terminating condition (line 8) is true. If so, factorial returns BigInteger.ONE, no further recursion is necessary, and the method returns. (A precondition of calling method factorial in this example is that its argument must be nonnegative.) If number is greater than 1, lines 12–13 express the problem as the product of BigInteger.valueOf(number) and a recursive call to method factorial evaluating the factorial of number - 1, which is a slightly smaller problem than the original calculation, factorial(number). The loop in lines 19–21 calls the factorial function for the values from 0 through 10. Lines 24–25 call method factorial for the values 20, 30 and 40. Note that factorial values grow quickly.

Factorial Values Grow Quickly

Method factorial receives an int and returns a BigInteger object (introduced in Section 3.12). The method produces large values so quickly that type long does not help us compute many factorial values before reaching its maximum value. Type long can store values from –9,223,372,036,854,775,808 to 9,223,372,036,854,775,807—a maximum of 19 decimal digits (which can represent integers in the quintillions). The factorial of 20 is a 19-digit number, and the subsequent values have significantly more than 19 digits.

Indirect Recursion

A recursive function may call another function, which may, in turn, make a call back to the recursive function. This is known as an indirect recursive call. For example, function A calls function B, which makes a call back to function A. This is still recursion because the second call to function A is made while the first call to function A is still active—that is, the first call to function A has not yet finished executing and has not returned to function A’s original caller because it’s waiting for function B to return a result.

Stack Overflow and Infinite Recursion

A computer’s memory is finite, so only a certain amount of memory can store activation records on the function-call stack. If more recursive function calls occur than can have their activation records stored on the stack, a fatal error known as stack overflow occurs.1 This typically results from infinite recursion, which can be caused by omitting the test for the base case or incorrectly writing the recursion step so it does not converge on the base case. Infinite recursion is analogous to an infinite loop in an iterative solution.

22.4 Recursion Example: Fibonacci Series

 

The Fibonacci series,

Click here to view code image

0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, …

begins with 0 and 1 and has the property that each subsequent Fibonacci number is the sum of the previous two. This series occurs in nature and describes a form of spiral. The ratio of successive Fibonacci numbers converges on a constant value of 1.618…, a number that has been called the golden ratio or the golden mean. Humans tend to find the golden mean aesthetically pleasing. Architects often design windows, rooms and buildings whose length and width are in the ratio of the golden mean. Postcards are often designed with a golden-mean length-to-width ratio.

Recursive Fibonacci Definition

The Fibonacci series may be defined recursively as follows:

Click here to view code image

fibonacci(0) = 0
fibonacci(1) = 1
fibonacci(n) = fibonacci(n – 1) + fibonacci(n – 2)

with two base cases—fibonacci(0) is defined as 0, and fibonacci(1) is defined as 1.

Implementing the Recursive Fibonacci Algorithm

Figure 22.2 recursively calculates the ith Fibonacci number, using method fibonacci (lines 9–18). Method main (lines 20–26) tests fibonacci, displaying the Fibonacci values of 0–40. The variable counter (line 22) indicates which Fibonacci number to calculate in each loop iteration. Fibonacci numbers become large quickly (though not as quickly as factorials), so we use BigInteger as the parameter type and the return type of the fibonacci method.

The call to method fibonacci (line 24) from main is not a recursive call, but all subsequent calls to fibonacci from lines 15–16 are recursive because the calls are initiated by method fibonacci. Each time fibonacci is called, it immediately tests for the base cases—number equal to 0 or number equal to 1 (lines 10–11). We use BigInteger constants ZERO and ONE to represent 0 and 1, respectively. If the condition in lines 10–11 is true, fibonacci simply returns number, because fibonacci(0) is 0 and fibonacci(1) is 1. Interestingly, if number is greater than 1, the recursion step generates two recursive calls (lines 15–16), each for a slightly smaller problem than the original call to fibonacci. Lines 15–16 use BigInteger methods add and subtract to help implement the recursive step. We also use a constant of type BigInteger named TWO (defined at line 6).

Analyzing the Calls to Method Fibonacci

The following diagram presents how function fibonacci evaluates fibonacci(3):

  • At the diagram’s bottom, we’re left with the values 1, 0 and 1—the results of evaluating the base cases.

  • The first two return values (from left to right), 1 and 0, are returned as the values for the calls fibonacci(1) and fibonacci(0).

  • The sum 1 plus 0 is returned as fibonacci(2)’s value. This is added to the result (1) of the rightmost call to fibonacci(1), producing the value 2.

This final value is then returned as fibonacci(3)’s value.

This diagram raises some interesting issues about the order in which Java compilers evaluate the operands of operators. This order differs from that in which operators are applied to their operands—namely, the order dictated by the operator precedence rules. From the diagram, it appears that while fibonacci(3) is being evaluated, two recursive calls will be made—fibonacci(2) and fibonacci(1). But in what order will they be made? The Java language specifies that the operands’ order of evaluation is left to right. Thus, the call fibonacci(2) is made first and fibonacci(1) second.

Complexity Issues

A word of caution is in order about recursive programs like the one we use here to generate Fibonacci numbers. Each invocation of the fibonacci function that does not match one of the base cases (0 or 1) results in two more recursive calls to the fibonacci function. Hence, this set of recursive calls rapidly gets out of hand. Calculating the Fibonacci value of 20 with the recursive implementation requires 21,891 calls to the fibonacci function; calculating the Fibonacci value of 30 requires 2,692,537 calls!

As you try to calculate larger Fibonacci values, you’ll notice that each consecutive Fibonacci number you calculate results in a substantial increase in calculation time and in the number of calls to the fibonacci function. For example, the Fibonacci value of 31 requires 4,356,617 calls, and the Fibonacci value of 32 requires 7,049,155 calls! The number of calls to fibonacci increases quickly—1,664,080 more calls between Fibonacci values of 30 and 31 and 2,692,538 more calls between Fibonacci values of 31 and 32! The difference in the number of calls made between Fibonacci values of 31 and 32 is more than 1.5 times the difference in the number of calls for Fibonacci values between 30 and 31. Problems of this nature can humble even the world’s most powerful computers.

In the field of complexity theory, computer scientists study how hard algorithms work to complete their tasks—that is, how many operations do they perform? We introduce various complexity issues in Section 22.9.

Avoid Fibonacci-style recursion that results in an exponential “explosion” of method calls taking a lot of time and consuming a lot of memory on the function-call stack. Iterative solutions in these cases are much more efficient.

22.5 Recursion vs. Iteration

 

We’ve studied methodso calculate factorials and Fibonacci values. Each can easily be implemented recursively or iteratively. Let’s compare the two approaches and discuss why you might choose each approach in a particular situation.

To illustrate the differences between iteration and recursion, let’s examine an iterative factorial calculation (Fig. 22.3, lines 11–13). Here, we use an iteration statement rather than a selection statement (Fig. 22.1, lines 8–14). Both solutions use a termination test. In the recursive solution (Fig. 22.1), line 8 tests for the base case. In Fig. 22.3’s iterative solution, line 11 tests the loop-continuation condition—if the test fails, the loop terminates. Finally, instead of producing smaller versions of the original problem, the iterative solution uses a counter-controlled loop.

Comparing Iteration and Recursion

Both iteration and recursion are based on a control statement: Iteration uses an iteration statement (e.g., for, while or do…while), whereas recursion uses a selection statement (e.g., if, if…else or switch):

  • Both involve iteration: Iteration explicitly uses an iteration statement, whereas recursion achieves iteration through repeated method calls.

  • Both involve a termination test: Iteration terminates when the loop-continuation condition fails, whereas recursion terminates when a base case is reached.

  • Iteration with counter-controlled iteration and recursion both gradually approach termination: Iteration keeps modifying a counter until it assumes a value that makes the loop-continuation condition fail, whereas recursion keeps producing smaller versions of the original problem until the base case is reached.

  • Both can occur infinitely: An infinite loop occurs with iteration if the loop-continuation test never becomes false, whereas infinite recursion occurs if the recursion step does not reduce the problem in a manner that converges on the base case or if the base case is not tested. This results in stack overflow, and the program terminates abruptly (that is, crashes).

Negatives of Recursion

Recursion has many negatives. It repeatedly invokes the mechanism, and consequently the overhead, of method calls. This iteration can be expensive in terms of both processor time and memory space. Each recursive call causes another copy of the method (actually, only the method’s variables, stored in the stack frame) to be created. This set of copies can consume considerable memory space. Since iteration occurs in a method, repeated method calls and their memory overhead are avoided.

When to Choose Recursion vs. Iteration

Any problem that can be solved recursively can be solved iteratively and vice versa. A recursive approach is preferred over an iterative approach when the recursive approach more naturally mirrors the problem and results in a program that’s easier to understand and debug. A recursive approach can often be implemented with fewer lines of code. Another reason to choose a recursive approach is that an iterative one might not be apparent. When performance is crucial, you might want to try various iterative and recursive approaches to determine which achieves your goal.

22.6 Towers of Hanoi

Earlier in this chapter, we studied methods that can be implemented recursively or iteratively. Now, we present a problem whose recursive solution demonstrates the elegance of recursion and whose iterative solution may not be as apparent.

The Towers of Hanoi is one of the classic recursion problems. Legend has it that in a temple in the Far East, priests are attempting to move a stack of golden disks from one diamond peg to another:

The initial stack has 64 disks threaded onto one peg and arranged from bottom to top by decreasing size. The priests are attempting to move the stack from one peg to another under the constraints that exactly one disk is moved at a time and at no time may a larger disk be placed above a smaller disk. Three pegs are provided, one being used for temporarily holding disks. Supposedly, the world will end when the priests complete their tasks, so we have little incentive to facilitate their efforts.

Let’s assume the priests are attempting to move the disks from peg 1 to peg 3. We wish to develop an algorithm that prints the precise sequence of peg-to-peg disk transfers.

If we try to find an iterative solution, we’ll likely find ourselves hopelessly “knotted up” in managing the disks. Instead, attacking this problem recursively yields an intuitive solution. Moving n disks can be viewed in terms of moving only n – 1 disks (hence the recursion) as follows:

  1. Move n – 1 disks from peg 1 to peg 2, using peg 3 as a temporary holding area.

  2. Move the last disk (the largest) from peg 1 to peg 3.

  3. Move n – 1 disks from peg 2 to peg 3, using peg 1 as a temporary holding area.

The process ends when the last task involves moving the n = 1 disk (i.e., the base case). This task is accomplished simply by moving the disk without using a temporary holding area.

In Fig. 22.4, method solveTowers (lines 5–22) solves the Towers of Hanoi, given the total number of disks (we’ll call the method for the case with 3 disks), the starting peg, the ending peg, and the temporary holding peg as parameters.

The base case (lines 8–11) occurs when only one disk needs to be moved from the starting peg to the ending peg. The recursion step (lines 15–21) moves disks - 1 disks (line 15) from the first peg (sourcePeg) to the temporary holding peg (tempPeg). When all but one of the disks have been moved to the temporary peg, line 18 moves the largest disk from the start peg to the destination peg. Line 21 finishes the rest of the moves by calling the method solveTowers to recursively move disks - 1 disks from the temporary peg (tempPeg) to the destination peg (destinationPeg), this time using the first peg (sourcePeg) as the temporary peg. Line 31 in main calls the recursive solveTowers method, which outputs the steps to the command prompt.

22.7 Fractals

A fractal is a geometric figure generated from a pattern repeated recursively. The figure is modified by recursively applying the pattern to each segment of the original figure. Although such figures had been studied before the 20th century, the mathematician Benoit Mandelbrot in the 1970s introduced the term “fractal,” along with the specifics of how a fractal is created and the practical applications of fractals. Mandelbrot’s fractal geometry provides mathematical models for many complex forms found in nature, such as mountains, clouds and coastlines. Fractals have many uses in mathematics and science. They can be used to better understand systems or patterns that appear in nature (e.g., ecosystems), in the human body (e.g., in the folds of the brain), or in the universe (e.g., galaxy clusters). Not all fractals resemble objects in nature. Drawing fractals has become a popular art form. Fractals have a self-similar property—when subdivided into parts, each resembles a reduced-size copy of the whole. Many fractals yield an exact copy of the original when a portion of the fractal is magnified—such a fractal is said to be strictly self-similar.

22.7.1 Koch Curve Fractal

As an example, let’s look at the strictly self-similar Koch Curve fractal—formed by removing the middle third of each line in the drawing and replacing it with two lines that form a point, such that if the middle third of the original line remained, an equilateral triangle would be formed;

Formulas for creating fractals often involve removing all or part of the previous fractal image. This pattern has already been determined for this fractal. We focus here on using those formulas in a recursive solution.

We start with a straight line in Part (a) and apply the pattern, creating a triangle from the middle third, as in Part (b). We then apply the pattern to each straight line, resulting in Part (c). Each time the pattern is applied, we say that the fractal is at a new level or depth— sometimes, the term order is also used. Fractals can be displayed at many levels—for example, a fractal at level 3 has had three iterations of the pattern applied (Part (d)). After only a few iterations, this fractal begins to look like a portion of a snowflake, as in Parts (e) and (f). Since this is a strictly self-similar fractal, each portion contains an exact copy of the fractal. For example, in Part (f), we’ve highlighted a portion of the fractal with a dashed box. If the image in this box were increased in size, it would look exactly like the entire fractal of part (e).

The Koch Snowflake fractal is similar to the Koch Curve but begins with a triangle rather than a line. The same pattern is applied to each side of the triangle, resulting in an image resembling an enclosed snowflake.

22.7.2 (Optional) Case Study: Lo Feather Fractal

We now demonstrate using recursion to draw fractals by writing a program to create a strictly self-similar fractal. We call this the “Lo feather fractal,” named for Sin Han Lo, a Deitel & Associates, Inc. colleague who created it. The fractal will eventually resemble one-half of a feather. The base case, or fractal level of 0, begins as a line between two points, A and B, as in the following diagram:

To create the next higher level, we find the midpoint (C) of the line. To calculate the location of point C, use the following formula:

xC = (xA + xB) / 2;
yC = (yA + yB) / 2;

The x and y to the left of each letter refer to the x-coordinate and y-coordinate of that point, respectively. For example, xA refers to the x-coordinate of point A, while yC refers to the y-coordinate of point C. Our diagrams denote the point by its letter, followed by two numbers representing the x- and y-coordinates.

To create this fractal, we must find a point D that lies to the left of segment AC and creates an isosceles right triangle ADC. To calculate point D’s location, use the formulas:

Click here to view code image

xD = xA + (xC - xA) / 2 - (yC - yA) / 2;
yD = yA + (yC - yA) / 2 + (xC - xA) / 2;

We now move from level 0 to level 1 as follows: First, add points C and D, as in the following diagram:

Then, remove the original line and add segments DA, DC and DB. The remaining lines will curve at an angle, causing our fractal to look like a feather.

For the next level, this algorithm is repeated on each of the three lines in level 1. For each line, the formulas above are applied, where the former point D is now considered to be point A, while the other end of each line is considered to be point B. The following diagram contains the line from level 0 (now a dashed line) and the three added lines from level 1:

We’ve changed point D to be point A, and the original points A, C and B to B1, B2 and B3, respectively. The preceding formulas have been used to find the new points C and D on each line. These points are also numbered 1–3 to track which point is associated with each line. For example, points C1 and D1 represent points C and D associated with the line formed from points A to B1.

To achieve level 2, the three lines in the preceding diagram are removed and replaced with new lines from the C and D points just added. The following diagram contains the new lines (the lines from level 2 are dashed lines for your convenience):

The following diagram contains level 2 without the dashed lines from level 1. Once this process has been repeated several times, the fractal will begin to look like one-half of a feather (peek ahead to Fig. 22.5 to see the fractal at various stages):

22.8 Recursive Backtracking

Our recursive methods all have a similar architecture—if the base case is reached, return a result; if not, make one or more recursive calls. This section explores a more complex recursive technique that finds a path through a maze, returning true if there’s a possible solution. The solution involves moving through the maze one step at a time, where moves can be made by going down, right, up or left (diagonal moves are prohibited). From the current location in the maze (starting with the entry point), the following steps are taken: For each possible direction, the move is made in that direction, and a recursive call is made to solve the remainder of the maze from the new location. When a dead end is reached (i.e., we cannot take any more steps forward without hitting a wall), we back up to the previous location and try to go in a different direction. If no other direction can be taken, we back up again. This process continues until we find a point in the maze where a move can be made in another direction. Once such a location is found, we move in the new direction and continue with another recursive call to solve the rest of the maze.

To back up to the previous location in the maze, our recursive method simply returns false, moving up the method-call chain to the previous recursive call (which references the previous location in the maze). Using recursion to return to an earlier decision point is known as recursive backtracking. If one set of recursive calls does not result in a solution to the problem, the program backs up to the previous decision point and makes a different decision, often resulting in another set of recursive calls. In this example, the previous decision point is the previous location in the maze, and the decision to be made is the direction the next move should take. One direction has led to a dead end, so the search continues with a different direction. The recursive backtracking solution to the maze problem uses recursion to return only partway up the method-call chain then try a different direction. If the backtracking reaches the entry location of the maze and the paths in all directions have been attempted, the maze does not have a solution.
