22.9 Big O Notation

One way to describe an algorithm’s effort is with Big O notation, which indicates how hard an algorithm may have to work to solve a problem. The Big O for searching and sorting algorithms depends mainly on how many data elements there are. We use Big O to describe various sorting algorithms’ worst-case run times.

22.9.1 O(1) Algorithms

Suppose an algorithm tests whether an array’s first element is equal to its second. If the array has 10 elements, this algorithm requires one comparison. If the array has 1,000 elements, the algorithm still requires one comparison. In fact, the algorithm is completely independent of the array’s number of elements. This algorithm is said to have constant run time, which we represent in Big O notation as O(1) and pronounce “order 1.” An O(1) algorithm does not necessarily require only one comparison. O(1) means that the number of comparisons is constant—it does not grow as the array size increases. An algorithm that tests whether the first array element is equal to any of the next three elements is still O(1), even though it requires three comparisons.

22.9.2 O(n) Algorithms

An algorithm that tests whether an array’s first element is equal to any of the array’s other elements requires at most n – 1 comparisons, where n is the array’s number of elements. If the array has 10 elements, this algorithm requires up to nine comparisons. If the array has 1,000 elements, this algorithm requires up to 999 comparisons.

As n grows, the n in the expression n – 1 “dominates,” so subtracting 1 becomes inconsequential. Big O is designed to highlight these dominant terms and ignore those that become unimportant as n grows. For this reason, an algorithm that requires n –1 comparisons is said to be O(n). An O(n) algorithm is referred to as having a linear run time. O(n) is often pronounced “on the order of n” or just “order n.”

22.9.3 O(n2) Algorithms

Suppose an algorithm tests whether any array element is duplicated elsewhere in the array. The algorithm compares the first element with all of the array’s other elements. It then compares the second element with all of the array’s other elements except the first—the second was already compared to the first. Then, the algorithm compares the third element with all the other elements except the first two. Ultimately, this algorithm makes a total of (n – 1) + (n – 2) + … + 2 + 1 or n2/2 – n/2 comparisons. As n increases, the n2 term dominates, and the n term becomes inconsequential. Big O notation highlights the n2 term, leaving n2/2. Constant factors (such as 1/2) are omitted in Big O notation.

Big O is concerned with how an algorithm’s run time grows in relation to the number of items processed. Suppose an algorithm requires n2 comparisons. With four elements, the algorithm will require 16 comparisons; with eight elements, the algorithm will require 64 comparisons. With this algorithm, doubling the number of elements quadruples the number of comparisons. Consider a similar algorithm requiring n2/2 comparisons. With four elements, the algorithm will require eight comparisons; with eight elements, the algorithm will require 32 comparisons. Again, doubling the number of elements quadruples the number of comparisons. Both algorithms grow as the square of n, so Big O ignores the constant and both algorithms are considered to be O(n2). This is called quadratic run time and pronounced “on the order of n-squared” or simply “order n-squared.”

When n is small, O(n2) algorithms (running on today’s billion-operations-per-second personal computers) will not noticeably affect performance. But as n grows, you’ll start to notice the performance degradation. An O(n2) algorithm running on a million-element array would require a trillion “operations,” where each could require several machine instructions. This could require a few hours to execute. A billion-element array would require a quintillion operations, a number so large that the algorithm could take decades! O(n2) algorithms are often easy to write. We’ll also present an algorithm with a more favorable Big O measure. Efficient algorithms require clever coding and more work to create. Their superior performance can be worth the extra effort, especially as n gets large.

2 Prompt genAIs, asking for real-world examples of how Big O affects application performance.

22.10 Common Big O Notations

The following table lists various common Big O categories and several values for n to highlight the differences in the growth rates. If you interpret the values in the table as seconds of calculation, you can easily see why O(n2) algorithms should be avoided!

22.11 Wrap-Up

In this chapter, you created recursive methods that call themselves. You divided each problem into two conceptual pieces—the base case that the method knows how to do and the recursion step that is a slightly smaller version of the original problem and is performed by a recursive method call. We presented some popular recursion examples, including calculating factorials and producing values in the Fibonacci series. We discussed the order in which recursive method calls are pushed on or popped off the program-execution stack. Next, we compared recursive and iterative approaches. We used recursion to solve more complex problems—the Towers of Hanoi and displaying fractals. We discussed recursive backtracking—a technique for solving problems that involves backing up through recursive calls to try different possible solutions.

This concludes Java for Programmers with Generative AI, 5/e. We hope you’ve found this modern computer programming presentation informative and entertaining. We wish you great success!

Self-Review Exercises with Answers

A.1 Introduction

 

Instructors have indicated a preference in introductory programming courses for languages with REPLs (read-evaluate-print loops). Java’s JShell provides a rich REPL experience. Third parties have built JShell and related interactive-development tools into major IDEs like IntelliJ, Eclipse, NetBeans and others.

What is JShell?

What’s the magic? It’s simple. JShell provides a fast and friendly environment that lets you quickly explore, discover and experiment with Java language features and its extensive libraries. REPLs like the one in JShell have been around for decades. In the 1960s, one of the earliest REPLs made convenient interactive development possible in the LISP programming language. Students of that era, like one of your authors, Harvey Deitel, found it fast and fun to use.

JShell replaces the editing, compiling and executing cycle with its read-evaluate-print loop. Rather than complete programs, you write JShell commands and Java code snippets. When you enter a snippet, JShell immediately reads it, evaluates it and prints the results that help you observe the effects of your code. Then, it loops to perform this process again for the next snippet. As you work through the scores of examples and exercises, you’ll learn how JShell and its instant feedback keep your attention, enhance your performance, and speed the learning and software development processes.

Code Comes Alive

As you know, we emphasize the value of the live-code teaching approach in our books, focusing on complete, working programs. JShell brings this to the individual snippet level. Your code literally comes alive as you enter each line. Of course, you’ll still make occasional errors as you enter your snippets. JShell reports compilation errors to you on a snippet-by-snippet basis. You can use this capability, for example, to test common programming errors and observe the errors as they occur.

Kinds of Snippets

Snippets can be expressions, individual statements, multi-line statements and larger entities, like methods and classes. JShell supports all but a few Java features, but there are some differences designed to facilitate JShell’s explore–discover–experiment capabilities. In JShell, methods do not need to be in classes, expressions and statements do not need to be in methods, and you do not need a main method (other differences are in Section A.13). Eliminating this infrastructure saves you considerable time, especially compared to the lengthy repeated edit, compile and execute cycles of complete programs. And because JShell automatically displays the results of evaluating your expressions and statements, you do not need as many print statements as we use throughout this book’s traditional Java code examples.

Discovery with Auto-Completion

We include a detailed treatment of auto-completion—a key discovery feature that speeds the coding process. After you enter a portion of a name (class, method, variable, etc.) and press (or select) the Tab key, JShell completes the name for you or provides a list of all possible names that begin with what you’ve entered so far. You can then easily display method parameters and the documentation that describes those methods.

Rapid Prototyping

Professional developers commonly use JShell for experimentation and rapid prototyping but not full-out software development. Once you create and test a small chunk of code, you can paste it into your larger project.

How This Appendix Is Organized

This appendix is optional. For those who want to use JShell, the appendix is designed as a series of units, paced to specific earlier chapters. Each unit begins with a statement like “This section may be read after studying Chapter 2.” So you’d start by reading through Chapter 2, then read this appendix’s corresponding section—and similarly for subsequent chapters.

Chapter 2 JShell Self-Review Exercises with Answers

As you work through this appendix, execute each snippet and command in JShell to confirm that the features work as advertised. Sections A.2–A.3 are designed to be read after Chapter 2. Once you read these sections, we recommend doing the dozens of self-review exercises at the end of this appendix. JShell encourages you to “learn by doing,” so the exercises have you write and test code snippets that exercise many of Chapter 2’s Java features. The self-review exercises are small and to the point, and each is followed immediately by its answer to help you quickly get comfortable with JShell’s capabilities.

A.2 Introduction to JShell

[This section may be read after studying Chapter 2, Intro to Java Programming.]

In Chapter 2, to create a Java application, you

  1. created a class containing a main method,

  2. declared in main the statements to execute when you run the program,

  3. compiled the program and fixed any compilation errors that occurred—his step had to be repeated until the program compiled without errors, and

  4. ran the program to observe the results.

By automatically compiling and executing code as you complete each expression or statement, JShell eliminates the overhead of

  • creating a class containing the code you wish to test,

  • compiling the class and

  • executing the class.

Instead, you can focus on interactively discovering and experimenting with Java’s language and API features. If you enter code that does not compile, JShell immediately reports the errors. You can then use JShell’s editing features to quickly fix and re-execute the code.

A.2.1 Starting a JShell Session

To start a JShell session, execute the jshell command in your system’s command line:

  • On Microsoft Windows, open a Command Prompt or PowerShell window.

  • On macOS, open a Terminal window.

This starts a new JShell session, displaying the following message and the jshell> prompt:

Click here to view code image

| Welcome to JShell -- Version 23
| For an introduction type: /help intro

jshell>

The first line above indicates that you’re using Version 23 of the JDK. JShell precedes informational messages with vertical bars (|). You are now ready to enter Java code or JShell commands.

A.2.2 Executing Statements

[As you work through this appendix, enter the same code and JShell commands that we present in each jshell> prompt to ensure that your outputs will match ours.]

JShell has two input types:

  • Java code, which the JShell documentation refers to as snippets and

  • JShell commands.

In this section and Section A.2.3, we begin with Java code snippets. Subsequent sections introduce JShell commands.

You can enter any expression or statement at the jshell> prompt, then press (or select) Enter to execute the code and observe its results immediately. Consider the program of Fig. 2.1, which we list again in Fig. A.1. To demonstrate how System.out.println works, this program required many lines of code and comments, which you had to write, compile and execute. Even without the comments, five code lines were still needed (lines 4 and 6–9).

In JShell, you can execute the statement in line 7 without creating all the infrastructure of class Welcome1 and its main method:

Click here to view code image

jshell> System.out.println("Welcome to Java Programming!")
Welcome to Java Programming!

jshell>

In this case, JShell displays the snippet’s command-line output below the initial jshell> prompt and the statement you entered. Per our convention, we use bold for user inputs.

We did not enter the statement’s semicolon (;). JShell adds terminating semicolons only for standalone statements.1 For example, if the statement is inside braces ({ and }), you must include the semicolon.

1. Not requiring semicolons is one example of how JShell reinterprets standard Java for convenient interactive use. We discuss several of these throughout the appendix and summarize them in Section A.13.

The blank line before the second jshell> prompt results from the newline displayed by method println and a separate newline that JShell always displays before each jshell> prompt. Using print rather than println eliminates the blank line:

Click here to view code image

jshell> System.out.print("Welcome to Java Programming!")
Welcome to Java Programming!
jshell>

JShell keeps track of everything you enter, which can be useful for re-executing prior statements and modifying statements to update the tasks they perform.

A.2.3 Declaring Variables Explicitly

Almost anything you can declare in a typical Java source-code file can also be declared in JShell (Section A.13 discusses some of the features you cannot use). For example, you can explicitly declare a variable as follows:

jshell> int number1
number1 ==> 0

jshell>

When you enter a variable declaration, JShell displays the variable’s name (in this case, number1) followed by ==> (which means “has the value”) and the variable’s initial value (0). If you do not specify an initial value explicitly, the variable is initialized to its type’s default value—in this case, 0 for an int variable.

A variable can be initialized in its declaration—let’s redeclare number1:

jshell> int number1 = 30
number1 ==> 30

jshell>

JShell displays

number1 ==> 30

to indicate that number1 now has the value 30. When you declare a new variable with the same name as another variable in the current JShell session, JShell replaces the first declaration with the new one.2 Because number1 was declared previously, we could have simply assigned number1 a value, as in

2. Redeclaring an existing variable is another example of how JShell reinterprets standard Java for interactive use. This behavior differs from how the Java compiler handles a new declaration of an existing variable—such a “double declaration” generates a compilation error.

jshell> number1 = 45
number1 ==> 45

jshell>
Compilation Errors in JShell

You must declare variables before using them in JShell. The following declaration of int variable sum attempts to use a variable named number2 that we have not yet declared, so JShell reports a compilation error, indicating that the compiler was unable to find a variable named number2:

Click here to view code image

jshell> int sum = number1 + number2
|  Error:
|  cannot find symbol
|    symbol:   variable number2
|  int sum = number1 + number2;
|                      ^-----^

jshell>

The error message uses the notation ^-----^ to highlight the error in the statement. No error is reported for the previously declared variable number1. This snippet has a compilation error, so it’s invalid. However, JShell still maintains the snippet as part of the JShell session’s history, which includes valid snippets, invalid snippets and the commands you’ve entered. As you’ll soon learn, you can recall this invalid snippet and execute it again later. JShell’s /history command displays the current session’s history—that is, everything you’ve entered:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /history

System.out.println("Welcome to Java Programming!")
System.out.print("Welcome to Java Programming!")
int number1
int number1 = 30
number1 = 45
int sum = number1 + number2
/history

jshell>
Fixing the Error

JShell makes it easy to fix a prior error and re-execute a snippet. Let’s fix the preceding error by first declaring number2 with the value 72:

jshell> int number2 = 72
number2 ==> 72

jshell>

Subsequent snippets can now use number2—in a moment, you’ll re-execute the snippet that declared and initialized sum with number1 + number2.

Recalling and Re-executing a Previous Snippet

Now that number1 and number2 are declared, we can declare the int variable sum. You can use the up and down arrow keys to navigate backward and forward through the snippets and JShell commands you’ve entered previously. Rather than re-entering sum’s declaration, you can press (or select) the up arrow key three times to recall the declaration that failed previously. JShell recalls your prior inputs in reverse order—the last snippet or command you entered is recalled first. So, the first time you press (or select) the up arrow key, the following appears at the jshell> prompt:

jshell> int number2 = 72

The second time you press (or select) the up arrow key, the /history command appears:

jshell> /history

The third time you press (or select) the up arrow key, sum’s prior declaration appears:

Click here to view code image

jshell> int sum = number1 + number2

Now you can press (or select) Enter to re-execute the snippet that declares and initializes sum:

Click here to view code image

jshell> int sum = number1 + number2
sum ==> 117

jshell>

JShell adds the values of number1 (45) and number2 (72), stores the result in the new sum variable, then outputs sum’s value (117).

A.2.4 Listing and Executing Prior Snippets

You can view a list of all previous valid Java code snippets with JShell’s /list command—JShell displays the snippets in the order you entered them:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /list

   1 : System.out.println("Welcome to Java Programming!")
   2 : System.out.print("Welcome to Java Programming!")
   4 : int number1 = 30;
   5 : number1 = 45
   6 : int number2 = 72;
   7 : int sum = number1 + number2;

jshell>

Each valid snippet is identified by a sequential snippet ID. The snippet with ID 3 is missing above because we replaced that original variable-declaration snippet

int number1

with the one that has the ID 4 in the preceding /list. The /list command does not display everything that /history does. As you recall, if you omit a terminating semicolon, JShell inserts it for you behind the scenes. When you execute /list, only the declarations (snippets 4, 6 and 7) include the semicolons that JShell inserted. Snippet 1 above is just an expression. If we enter it with a terminating semicolon, it’s an expression statement.

Executing Snippets By ID Number

You can execute any prior snippet by entering /id, where id is the snippet’s ID. For example, when you enter /1:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /1
System.out.println("Welcome to Java Programming!")
Welcome to Java Programming!

jshell>

JShell displays the current session’s snippet with the ID 1, executes it and displays the result.

Re-executing Several Individual Snippets or Snippet Ranges

You can also re-execute more than one statement at a time. For example, the following would re-execute the range of snippets from start through end, inclusive:

/start-end

and the following would re-execute separate individual snippets or snippet ranges:

/id1 id2 id3 …

In this case, the IDs can be can be individual snippet IDs or ID ranges.

Re-executing the Last Snippet

To re-execute the previous snippet, use /!:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /!
System.out.println("Welcome to Java Programming!")
Welcome to Java Programming!

jshell>

JShell assigns an ID to every valid snippet you execute, so even though

Click here to view code image

System.out.println("Welcome to Java Programming!")

already exists in this session as snippet 1, JShell creates a new snippet with the next ID in sequence (in this case, 8 and 9 for the last two snippets). The /list command’s output confirms that snippets 1, 8 and 9 are identical:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /list

   1 : System.out.println("Welcome to Java Programming!")
   2 : System.out.print("Welcome to Java Programming!")
   4 : int number1 = 30;
   5 : number1 = 45
   6 : int number2 = 72;
   7 : int sum = number1 + number2;
   8 : System.out.println("Welcome to Java Programming!")
   9 : System.out.println("Welcome to Java Programming!")

jshell>

A.2.5 Evaluating Expressions and Declaring Variables Implicitly

When you enter an expression in JShell, it evaluates the expression, implicitly creates a variable and assigns the expression’s value to the variable. Implicit variables are named $#, where # is the new snippet’s ID.3 For example:

jshell> 11 + 5
$10 ==> 16

jshell>

3. Implicitly declared variables are another example of how JShell reinterprets standard Java for interactive use. In regular Java programs, you must explicitly declare every variable.

evaluates the expression 11 + 5 and assigns the resulting value (16) to the implicitly declared variable $10 because there were nine prior valid snippets (even though one was deleted because we redeclared the variable number1). JShell infers the type of $10 as int because the expression 11 + 5 adds two int values, producing an int. Expressions may also include one or more method calls. The list of snippets is now:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /list

   1 : System.out.println("Welcome to Java Programming!")
   2 : System.out.print("Welcome to Java Programming!")
   4 : int number1 = 30;
   5 : number1 = 45
   6 : int number2 = 72;
   7 : int sum = number1 + number2;
   8 : System.out.println("Welcome to Java Programming!")
   9 : System.out.println("Welcome to Java Programming!")
  10 : 11 + 5

jshell>

Note that the implicitly declared variable $10 appears in the list simply as 10 without the $.

A.2.6 Using Implicitly Declared Variables

You can use implicitly declared variables in expressions. For example, the following assigns to the existing variable sum the result of adding number1 (45) and $10 (16):

jshell> sum = number1 + $10
sum ==> 61

jshell>

The list of snippets is now:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /list

   1 : System.out.println("Welcome to Java Programming!")
   2 : System.out.print("Welcome to Java Programming!")
   4 : int number1 = 30;
   5 : number1 = 45
   6 : int number2 = 72;
   7 : int sum = number1 + number2;
   8 : System.out.println("Welcome to Java Programming!")
   9 : System.out.println("Welcome to Java Programming!")
  10 : 11 + 5
  11 : sum = number1 + $10

jshell>

A.2.7 Viewing a Variable’s Value

You can view a variable’s value at any time by entering its name and pressing Enter:

jshell> sum
sum ==> 61

jshell>

Doing this does not create another implicitly declared variable.

A.2.8 Resetting a JShell Session

You can remove all prior code from a JShell session by entering the /reset command:

jshell> /reset
|  Resetting state.

jshell> /list

jshell>

The subsequent /list command has no output, confirming that all prior snippets were removed. Messages displayed by JShell, such as

| Resetting state.

are helpful when you’re becoming familiar with JShell. In Section A.11.5, we’ll demonstrate how you can change the JShell feedback mode, making it more or less verbose.

A.2.9 Writing Multiline Statements

Next, let’s enter an if statement that determines whether 45 is less than 72. First, store 45 and 72 in implicitly declared variables, as in:

jshell> 45
$1 ==> 45

jshell> 72
$2 ==> 72

jshell>

Next, begin entering the if statement:

jshell> if ($1 < $2) {
   ...>     _

JShell knows the if statement is incomplete because we entered the opening left brace but did not provide a body or a closing right brace. So, JShell displays the continuation prompt ...> at which you can enter more of the control statement. It also indents the second line four spaces. We used an underscore above to indicate where the cursor currently resides.4 The following completes and evaluates the if statement:

4. Java programmers commonly use four-space indents.

Click here to view code image

jshell> if ($1 < $2) {
   ...>     System.out.printf("%d < %d%n", $1, $2);
   ...> }
45 < 72

jshell>

The second continuation prompt appeared because the if statement was still missing its closing right brace (}). When you enter the closing brace, JShell automatically aligns it under the "i" in the "if" keyword. The statement-terminating semicolon (;) at the end of the System.out.printf statement in the if’s body is required. JShell assigns each multiline code snippet—such as an if statement—one snippet ID. The list of snippets is now:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /list

   1 : 45
   2 : 72
   3 : if ($1 < $2) {
          System.out.printf("%d < %d%n", $1, $2);
       }

jshell>

A.2.10 Editing Code Snippets

 

Sometimes you might want to create a new snippet based on an existing one in the current JShell session. For example, suppose you want to create an if statement that determines whether $1 is greater than $2. The statement that performs this task

Click here to view code image

if ($1 > $2) {
   System.out.printf("%d > %d%n", $1, $2);
}

is nearly identical to the if statement in Section A.2.9, so it would be easier to edit the existing statement rather than enter the new one from scratch. When you edit a snippet, JShell saves the edited version as a new snippet with the next snippet ID in sequence.

Editing a Single-Line Snippet

To edit a snippet:

  • locate it with the up-arrow key,

  • use the arrow keys to navigate to the location in the snippet requiring changes,

  • make your changes within the snippet, then

  • press (or select) Enter to evaluate it.

Section A.12 lists keyboard shortcuts that can help you edit snippets.

Editing a Multiline Snippet

For a larger multiline snippet—such as an if statement—you can also edit the entire snippet by using JShell’s /edit command to open the snippet in the JShell Edit Pad. The command

/edit

opens JShell Edit Pad and displays all valid code snippets you’ve entered so far. To edit a specific snippet, include the snippet ID, as in

/edit id

So, the command:

/edit 3

displays the if statement from Section A.2.9 in JShell Edit Pad:

You can also edit groups and ranges of snippets, as discussed in Section A.2.4. JShell Edit Pad does not display snippet IDs. This window is modal—that is, while it’s open, you cannot enter code snippets or commands at the JShell prompt until you dismiss the JShell Edit Pad window.

JShell Edit Pad supports only basic editing capabilities. You can:

  • click to insert the cursor at a specific position to begin entering text,

  • move the cursor via the arrow keys on your keyboard,

  • drag the mouse to select text,

  • use the Delete (Backspace) key to delete text,

  • cut, copy and paste text using your operating system’s keyboard shortcuts, and

  • enter text, including new snippets separate from the one(s) you’re editing.

In the first and second lines of the if statement, select each less than operator (<) and change it to a greater than (>) operator, then click Accept to create a new if statement containing the edited code. When you click Accept, JShell also immediately evaluates the new if statement and displays its results (if any)—$1 (45) is not greater than $2 (72), so the System.out.printf statement does not execute.5

5. We could have made this an if…else statement to output something when the condition is false but this section is meant to be used with Chapter 2 where we introduce only the single-selection if statement.

If you want to return immediately to the JShell prompt, rather than clicking Accept, you could click Exit to execute the edited snippet and close JShell Edit Pad. Clicking Cancel closes JShell Edit Pad and discards any changes you made since the last time you clicked Accept or since JShell Edit Pad was launched, if you have not yet clicked Accept.

When you change or create multiple snippets, then click Accept or Exit, JShell compares the JShell Edit Pad contents with the previously saved snippets. It then executes every modified or new snippet.

Adding a New Snippet Via JShell Edit Pad

To demonstrate that JShell Edit Pad does, in fact, execute snippets immediately when you click Accept, let’s change $1’s value to 100 by entering the following statement after the if statement in JShell Edit Pad:

$1 = 100

and clicking Accept:

Each time you modify a variable’s value, JShell immediately displays the variable’s name and new value:

jshell> /edit 3
$1 ==> 100

Click Exit to close JShell Edit Pad and return to the jshell> prompt.

The following lists the current snippets—notice that each multiline if statement has only one ID:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /list

   1 : 45
   2 : 72
   3 : if ($1 < $2) {
          System.out.printf("%d < %d%n", $1, $2);
       }
   4 : if ($1 > $2) {
          System.out.printf("%d > %d%n", $1, $2);
       }
   5 : $1 = 100

jshell>
Executing the New if Statement Again

The following re-executes the new if statement (ID 4) with the updated $1 value:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /4
if ($1 > $2) {
   System.out.printf("%d > %d%n", $1, $2);
}
100 > 72

jshell>

The condition $1 > $2 is now true, so the if statement’s body executes. The list of snippets is now

Click here to view code image

jshell> /list

   1 : 45
   2 : 72
   3 : if ($1 < $2) {
          System.out.printf("%d < %d%n", $1, $2);
       }
   4 : if ($1 > $2) {
          System.out.printf("%d > %d%n", $1, $2);
       }
   5 : $1 = 100
   6 : if ($1 > $2) {
          System.out.printf("%d > %d%n", $1, $2);
       }

jshell>

A.2.11 Exiting JShell

To terminate the current JShell session, use the /exit command or enter the keyboard shortcut Ctrl + d (or control + d).

A.3 Command-Line Input in JShell

 

[This section may be read after studying Chapter 2, Intro to Java Programming, and the preceding sections in this appendix.]

In Chapter 2, we performed command-line input using a Scanner object:

Click here to view code image

Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);

System.out.print("Enter first integer: ");
int number1 = input.nextInt();

We created a Scanner, prompted the user for input, then used Scanner method nextInt to read a value. Recall that the program then waited for you to enter an integer and press (or select) Enter before proceeding to the next statement. The on-screen interaction appeared as follows:

Enter first integer: 45

This section demonstrates what that interaction looks like in JShell.

Creating a Scanner

Start a new JShell session or /reset the current one, then create a Scanner object:

Click here to view code image

jshell> Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in)
input ==> java.util.Scanner[delimiters=\p{javaWhitespace}+] ...
\E][infinity string=\Q∞\E]

jshell>

You do not need to import Scanner. JShell automatically imports the java.util package and several others—Section A.9 presents the complete list. When you create an object, JShell displays its text representation. The notation to the right of input ==> is the Scanner’s text representation (which you can simply ignore).

Prompting for Input and Reading a Value

Next, prompt the user for input:

Click here to view code image

jshell> System.out.print("Enter first integer: ")
Enter first integer:
jshell>

The statement’s output is displayed immediately, followed by the next jshell> prompt. Now enter the input statement:

Click here to view code image

jshell> int number1 = input.nextInt()
_

At this point, JShell waits for your input. The input cursor is positioned below the jshell> prompt and snippet you just entered—indicated by the underscore (_) above— rather than next to the prompt "Enter first integer:" as it was in Chapter 2. Now enter an integer and press (or select) Enter to assign it to number1—the last snippet’s execution is now complete, so the next jshell> prompt appears.:

Click here to view code image

jshell> int number1 = input.nextInt()
45
number1 ==> 45

jshell>

Though you can use Scanner for command-line input in JShell, it’s awkward, and in most cases, unnecessary. The goal of the preceding interactions was to store an int in the variable number1. You can accomplish that in JShell with the simple assignment

jshell> int number1 = 45
number1 ==> 45

jshell>

So, you’ll typically use assignments, rather than command-line input in JShell.

A.4 Declaring and Using Classes

[This section may be read after studying Chapter 8, Real-World Modeling with Custom Classes.]

Section A.2 demonstrated basic JShell features. Here, we create a class and manipulate an object of a class. We’ll use the version of class Account presented in Fig. 8.1.

A.4.1 Creating a Class in JShell

Start a new JShell session (or /reset the current one), then declare class Account—we ignored the comments from Fig. 8.1:

Click here to view code image

jshell> public class Account {
   ...>    private String name;
   ...>
   ...>    public void setName(String name) {
   ...>       this.name = name;
   ...>    }
   ...>
   ...>    public String getName() {
   ...>       return name;
   ...>    }
   ...> }
|  created class Account

jshell>

JShell recognizes when you enter the class’s closing brace—then displays

| created class Account

and issues the next jshell> prompt. Note that the semicolons throughout class Account’s body are required.

To save time, rather than entering a class’s code, you can load an existing source code file into JShell, as we demonstrate in Section A.4.6. Though you can specify access modifiers like public on your classes (and other types), JShell ignores all access modifiers on the top-level types—that is, types that are not nested in other types.

Viewing Declared Classes

To view the names of the classes you’ve declared so far, enter the /types command:6

jshell> /types
|    class Account

jshell>

6. /types displays all types you declare, including classes, records, interfaces and enums.

A.4.2 Explicitly Declaring Reference-Type Variables

The following creates the Account variable account:

jshell> Account account
account ==> null

jshell>

The default value of a reference-type variable is null.

A.4.3 Creating Objects

You can create new objects. The following creates an Account variable named account and initializes it with a new object:

Click here to view code image

jshell> account = new Account()
account ==> Account@2d928643

jshell>

The strange notation

Account@2d928643

is the default text representation of the new Account object. If a class provides a custom toString method, the text representation it returns will be output instead. The value after the @ symbol is the object’s hashcode.

Declaring an Implicit Account Variable Initialized with an Account Object

If you create an object with only the expression new Account(), JShell assigns the object to an implicit variable of type Account, as in:

jshell> new Account()
$4 ==> Account@49993335

jshell>

Note that this object’s hashcode (49993335) differs from the prior Account object’s hash-code (2d928643)—these typically are different, but that’s not guaranteed.

Viewing Declared Variables

You can view all the variables you’ve declared so far with the JShell /vars command:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /vars
|    Account account = Account@2d928643
|    Account $4 = Account@49993335

jshell>

For each variable, JShell outputs the type and variable name followed by an equal sign and the variable’s text representation.

A.4.4 Manipulating Objects

Once you have an object, you can call its methods. In fact, you already did this with the System.out object by calling its println, print and printf methods in earlier snippets.

The following sets the account object’s name:

Click here to view code image

jshell> account.setName("Amanda")

jshell>

The method setName has the return type void, so it does not return a value, and no additional output appears in JShell.

The following gets the account object’s name:

jshell> account.getName()
$6 ==> "Amanda"

jshell>

Method getName returns a String. When you invoke a method that returns a value, JShell stores the value in an implicitly declared variable. In this case, $6’s type is inferred to be String. Of course, you could have assigned the result of the preceding method call to an explicitly declared variable.

Using the Return Value of a Method in a Statement

If you invoke a method as part of a larger statement, the return value is used in that statement, rather than stored. For example, the following uses println to display the account object’s name:

Click here to view code image

jshell> System.out.println(account.getName())
Amanda

jshell>

A.4.5 Creating a Meaningful Variable Name for an Expression

You can give a meaningful variable name to a value JShell previously assigned to an implicit variable. For example, with the following snippet recalled

jshell> account.getName()

Enter

Shift + Tab, v

This notation means you should press (or select) both the Shift and Tab keys together, then release those keys and press (or select) v. JShell infers the expression’s type and begins a variable declaration for you—account.getName() returns a String, so JShell inserts String and an equal sign (=) before the expression, as in

Click here to view code image

jshell> account.getName()
jshell> String _= account.getName()

JShell also positions the cursor (indicated by the _ above) immediately before the = so you can simply enter the variable name, as in

Click here to view code image

jshell> String name = account.getName()
name ==> "Amanda"

jshell>

When you press (or select) Enter, JShell evaluates the new snippet and stores the value in the specified variable.

A.4.6 Saving and Opening Code-Snippet Files

You can save a session’s valid code snippets to a file, which you can load into a JShell session as needed.

Saving Snippets to a File

To save just the valid snippets, use the /save command, as in:

/save filename

By default, the file is created in the folder from which you launched JShell. To store the file in a different location, specify the complete path of the file.

Loading Snippets from a File

Once you save your snippets, they can be reloaded with the /open command:

/open filename

which executes each snippet in the file.

Using /open to Load Java Source-Code Files

You can also open existing Java source code files using /open. For example, let’s assume you’d like to experiment with class Account from Fig. 8.1 (as you did in Section A.4.1). Rather than entering its code into JShell, you can save time by loading the class from the source file Account.java. In a command window, you’d change to the folder containing Account.java, execute JShell, then use the following command to load the class declaration into JShell:

/open Account.java

To load a file from another folder, you can specify the file’s full pathname. Section A.9 demonstrates how to use existing compiled classes in JShell.

A.5 Discovery with JShell Auto-Completion

[This section may be read after studying Section 2.8.]

JShell can help you write code. When you partially enter the name of an existing class, variable or method then press (or select) the Tab key, JShell does one of the following:

  • If no other name matches what you’ve entered so far, JShell enters the rest of the name for you.

  • If there are multiple names that begin with the same letters, JShell displays a list of those names to help you decide what to enter next—then you can enter the next letter(s) and press (or select) Tab again to complete the name.

  • If no names match what you entered so far, JShell does nothing, and your operating system’s alert sound plays as feedback.

Auto-completion is typically an IDE feature, but with JShell, it’s IDE-independent.

A.5.1 Auto-Completing Identifiers

Start a new JShell session or reset your current one. Then execute the following snippet to define the String variable greeting and initialize it to "hello":

Click here to view code image

jshell> String greeting = "hello"

The only variable declared so far that begins with lowercase "g" is greeting—auto-completion is case-sensitive. If you enter "g" at the jshell> prompt:

jshell> g

then press (or select) Tab, JShell auto-completes the name:

jshell> greeting

If you then enter a dot:

jshell> greeting.

then press (or select) Tab, JShell does not know what method you want to call, so it displays a list of everything—in this case, all the methods—that can appear to the right of the dot:

Click here to view code image

jshell> greeting.
charAt(                 chars()                 codePointAt(
codePointBefore(        codePointCount(         codePoints()
compareTo(              compareToIgnoreCase(    concat(
contains(               contentEquals(          describeConstable()
endsWith(               equals(                 equalsIgnoreCase(
formatted(              getBytes(               getChars(
getClass()              hashCode()              indent(
indexOf(                intern()                isBlank()
isEmpty()               lastIndexOf(            length()
lines()                 matches(                notify()
notifyAll()             offsetByCodePoints(     regionMatches(
repeat(                 replace(                replaceAll(
replaceFirst(           resolveConstantDesc(    split(
splitWithDelimiters(    startsWith(             strip()
stripIndent()           stripLeading()          stripTrailing()
subSequence(            substring(              toCharArray()
toLowerCase(            toString()              toUpperCase(
transform(              translateEscapes()      trim()
wait(

jshell> greeting.

and follows the list with a new jshell> prompt that includes what you’ve entered so far. The list includes the methods declared in class String and several Object methods that all Java classes have (discussed in Chapter 9). In the list of method names

  • those followed by "()" are methods that do not require arguments and

  • those followed only by "(" are methods that either require at least one argument or are overloaded methods that can be called with different numbers and/or types of arguments (discussed in Section 5.7).

Let’s assume you want to use String’s endsWith method to check whether greeting starts with "o". There’s only one method that begins with "en", so you can enter en then Tab to auto-complete endsWith:

jshell> greeting.endsWith(

JShell automatically inserts the method call’s opening left parenthesis. Now you can complete the snippet as in:

Click here to view code image

jshell> greeting.endsWith("o")
$2 ==> true

jshell>

A.5.2 Auto-Completing JShell Commands

Auto-completion also works for JShell commands. If you enter / then press (or select) Tab, JShell displays the list of JShell commands:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /
/!          /?          /drop       /edit     /env       /exit
/help       /history    /imports    /list     /methods   /open
/reload     /reset      /save       /set      /types     /vars

<press tab again to see synopsis>
jshell> /

If you then enter h and press (or select) Tab, JShell displays only the commands that start with /h:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /h
/help       /history

<press tab again to see synopsis>
jshell> /h

Finally, if you enter "i" and press (or select) Tab, JShell auto-completes /history. Similarly, if you enter /l then press (or select) Tab, JShell auto-completes the command as /list because only that command starts with /l.

A.6 Exploring a Class’s Members and Viewing Documentation

[This section may be read after studying Chapter 5, Methods.]

The preceding section introduced basic auto-completion capabilities. When using JShell for experimentation and discovery, you’ll often want to learn more about a class before using it. In this section, we’ll explore class Math to demonstrate how to view:

  • the parameters required by a method so that you can call it correctly

  • the documentation for a method

  • the documentation for a field of a class

  • the documentation for a class, and

  • the list of overloads for a given method.

Start a new JShell session or /reset the current one.

A.6.1 Listing Class Math’s static Members

As discussed in Chapter 5, class Math contains only static members—static methods for various mathematical calculations and the static constants PI, E and TAU. To view a complete list, start a new JShell session, then enter "Math." and press (or select) Tab:

Click here to view code image

jshell> Math.
<press tab again to see all possible completions; total possible
completions: 103>
jshell> Math.

Because there are so many possible completions, JShell asks you to press Tab again to see all possible completions. Once you do, it displays—only 62 of the 103 completions are displayed because many of class Math’s methods are overloaded:

Click here to view code image

jshell> Math.
E                  IEEEremainder(     PI                TAU
abs(               absExact(          acos(             addExact(
asin(              atan(              atan2(            cbrt(
ceil(              ceilDiv(           ceilDivExact(     ceilMod(
clamp(             class              copySign(         cos(
cosh(              decrementExact(    divideExact(      exp(
expm1(             floor(             floorDiv(         floorDivExact(
floorMod(          fma(               getExponent(      hypot(
incrementExact(    log(               log10(            log1p(
max(               min(               multiplyExact(    multiplyFull(
multiplyHigh(      negateExact(       nextAfter(        nextDown(
nextUp(            pow(               random()          rint(
round(             scalb(             signum(           sin(
sinh(              sqrt(              subtractExact(    tan(
tanh(              toDegrees(         toIntExact(       toRadians(
ulp(                unsignedMultiplyHigh(
jshell> Math.

Again, JShell auto-completion displays everything that can appear to the right of the dot (.). Here, we entered a class name and a dot (.), so JShell displays only the class’s static members. The names that are not followed by any parentheses (E, PI and TAU) are the class’s static variables. All the other names are the class’s static methods:

  • Any method names followed by ()—only random in this case—do not require arguments.

  • Any method names followed by only an opening left parenthesis, (, require at least one argument or are overloaded.

You can easily view the value of constants like PI and E:

jshell> Math.PI
$1 ==> 3.141592653589793

jshell> Math.E
$2 ==> 2.718281828459045

jshell>

A.6.2 Viewing a Method’s Parameters

Let’s assume you wish to test Math’s pow method but do not know the required parameters.

You can enter

Math.p

then press (or select) Tab to auto-complete the name pow:

jshell> Math.pow(

No other methods begin with "pow", so JShell inserts the left parenthesis to indicate the beginning of a method call. Next, you can press (or select) Tab to view the method’s parameters:

Click here to view code image

jshell> Math.pow(
$1   $2

Signatures:
double Math.pow(double a, double b)

<press tab again to see documentation>
jshell> Math.pow(

JShell displays

  • variables in the current session ($1 and $2) that could be used as pow’s arguments,

  • the method’s return type, name and complete parameter list, indicating that the method requires two double parameters,

  • "<press tab again to see documentation>", and

  • the next jshell> prompt containing what you’ve entered so far.

A.6.3 Viewing a Method’s Documentation

JShell integrates the Java API documentation so you can view documentation conveniently in JShell rather than using a separate web browser. Suppose you’d like to learn more about pow before completing your code snippet. You can press (or select) Tab again to view the method’s Java documentation (known as its javadoc). We cut out some of the documentation text and replaced it with an ellipsis (…) to save space—try the steps in your own JShell session to observe the complete text:

Click here to view code image

jshell> Math.pow(
double Math.pow(double a, double b)
Returns the value of the first argument raised to the power of the
second argument. Special cases:
  * If the second argument is positive or negative zero, then the result
is 1.0.
...
<press tab again to see next page>
jshell> Math.pow(

For lengthy documentation, JShell displays part of it followed by the message:

Click here to view code image

<press tab again to see next page>

You can press (or select) Tab to view the next page of documentation. The next jshell> prompt contains the portion of the snippet you’ve entered so far.

A.6.4 Viewing a public Field’s Documentation

You can use the Tab feature to learn more about a class’s public fields. For example, if you enter Math.PI followed by Tab, JShell displays

Click here to view code image

jshell> Math.PI
Signatures:
Math.PI:double

<press tab again to see documentation>

which includes Math.PI’s type and indicates that you can use Tab again to view the documentation. Doing so displays:

Click here to view code image

jshell> Math.PI
Math.PI:double
The double value that is closer than any other to pi (π), the ratio of
the circumference of a circle to its diameter.
jshell> Math.PI

and the next jshell> prompt contains the portion of the snippet you’ve entered so far.

A.6.5 Viewing a Class’s Documentation

You can also enter a class name then Tab to view the class’s fully qualified name. For example, entering Math then Tab outputs:

Click here to view code image

jshell> Math
Math         MathContext

Signatures:
java.lang.Math

<press tab again to see documentation>
jshell> Math

indicating that class Math is in the package java.lang. Entering Tab again contains the beginning of the class’s documentation:

Click here to view code image

jshell> Math
java.lang.Math
The class Math contains methods for performing basic numeric operations
such as the elementary exponential, logarithm, square root, and
trigonometric functions.
...

<press tab again to see next page>
jshell> Math

In this case, there is more documentation to view, so you can press (or select) Tab to view it. Whether or not you view the remaining documentation, the jshell> prompt contains the portion of the snippet you’ve entered so far.

A.6.6 Viewing Method Overloads

Many classes have overloaded methods. When you press (or select) Tab to view an overloaded method’s parameters, JShell displays the complete list of overloads with the parameters for every overload. For example, method Math.abs has four overloads:

Click here to view code image

jshell> Math.abs(
$1   $2

Signatures:
int Math.abs(int a)
long Math.abs(long a)
float Math.abs(float a)
double Math.abs(double a)

<press tab again to see documentation>
jshell> Math.abs(

When you press (or select) Tab again to view the documentation, JShell outputs the first overload’s documentation:

Click here to view code image

jshell> Math.abs(
int Math.abs(int a)
Returns the absolute value of an int value.If the argument is not
negative, the argument is returned. If the argument is negative, the
negation of the argument is returned.
...

<press tab again to see next page>

You can then press (or select) Tab to view the documentation for the next overload in the list. Again, whether or not you view the remaining documentation, the jshell> prompt contains the portion of the snippet you’ve entered so far.

A.6.7 Exploring Members of a Specific Object

The exploration features in Sections A.6.1–A.6.6 also apply to the members of a specific object. Let’s start a new session then create and explore a String object:

Click here to view code image

jshell> String dayName = "Monday"
dayName ==> "Monday"

jshell>

To view the dayName object’s methods, enter "dayName." and press (or select) Tab:

Click here to view code image

jshell> dayName.

codePointBefore(          codePointCount(        codePoints()

contains(                 contentEquals(         describeConstable()
endsWith(                 equals(                equalsIgnoreCase(

getClass()                hashCode()             indent(

replaceFirst(             resolveConstantDesc(   split(

Exploring toUpperCase

Let’s investigate the toUpperCase method. Continue by entering "toU" and pressing Tab to auto-complete its name:

jshell> dayName.toUpperCase(

Then, enter Tab to view the method’s parameters:

Click here to view code image

jshell> dayName.toUpperCase(
Signatures:
String String.toUpperCase(Locale locale)
String String.toUpperCase()

<press tab again to see documentation>
jshell> dayName.toUpperCase(

This method has two overloads. You can now use Tab to read about each overload or choose the one you wish to use by specifying the appropriate arguments (if any). In this case, we’ll use the no-argument version to create a new String containing MONDAY, so we simply enter the closing right parenthesis of the method call and press (or select) Enter:

jshell> dayName.toUpperCase()
$2 ==> "MONDAY"

jshell>
Exploring substring

Let’s assume you want to create the new String "DAY"—a subset of the implicit variable $2’s characters. For this purpose, class String provides the overloaded method substring. First, enter "$2.subs" and press (or select) Tab to auto-complete the method’s name:

jshell> $2.substring(

Next, use Tab to view the method’s overloads:

Click here to view code image

jshell> $2.substring(
Signatures:
String String.substring(int beginIndex)
String String.substring(int beginIndex, int endIndex)

<press tab again to see documentation>
jshell> $2.substring(

Next, use Tab again to view the first overload’s documentation:

Click here to view code image

jshell> $2.substring(

...
<press tab again to see next page>

The documentation indicates that this overload of the method enables you to obtain a substring starting from a specific character index (that is, position) and continuing through the end of the String. The first character in the String is at index 0. This is the version of the method we wish to use to obtain "DAY" from "MONDAY", so we can return to our code snippet at the jshell> prompt:

jshell> $2.substring(

jshell> $2.substring(3)

jshell>

A.7 Declaring Methods

[This section may be read after studying Chapter 5, Methods, and the preceding portions of this appendix.]

You can use JShell to prototype methods. For example, let’s assume we’d like to write code that displays the cubes of the values from 1 through 10. For the purpose of this discussion, we’re going to define two methods:

  • Method displayCubes will iterate 10 times, calling method cube each time.

  • Method cube will receive one int value and return the cube of that value.

A.7.1 Forward Referencing an Undeclared Method—Declaring Method displayCubes

Let’s begin with method displayCubes. Start a new JShell session or /reset the current one, then enter the following method declaration:

Click here to view code image

void displayCubes() {
   for (int i = 1; i <= 10; ++i) {
      System.out.printf("Cube of %d is %d%n", i, cube(i));
   }
}

When you complete the method declaration, JShell displays:

Click here to view code image

| created method displayCubes(), however, it cannot be invoked until
method cube(int) is declared

jshell>

After you enter the method body’s opening left brace, JShell displays continuation prompts (...>) before each subsequent line until you complete the method declaration by entering its closing right brace. Also, although JShell says "created method display-Cubes()", it indicates that you cannot call this method until "cube(int) is declared". This is not fatal in JShell—it recognizes that displayCubes depends on an undeclared method (cube)—this is known as forward referencing an undeclared method. Once you define cube, you can call displayCubes.

A.7.2 Declaring a Previously Undeclared Method

Next, let’s declare method cube but purposely make a logic error by returning the square rather than the cube of its argument:

jshell> int cube(int x) {
   ...>    return x * x;
   ...> }
|  created method cube(int)

jshell>

At this point, you can use JShell’s /methods command to list the methods declared in the current JShell session:

jshell> /methods
|    void displayCubes()
|    int cube(int)

jshell>

A.7.3 Testing cube and Replacing Its Declaration

Now that method cube is declared, let’s test it with the argument 2:

jshell> cube(2)
$3 ==> 4

jshell>

Based on how the method is currently implemented, it returns the 4 (that is, 2 * 2). However, the method’s purpose was to calculate the cube of its argument, so the result should have been 8 (2 * 2 * 2). You can edit cube’s snippet to correct the problem. Let’s edit the snippet directly in JShell rather than in JShell Edit Pad. Use the up arrow three times to redisplay cube’s definition:

jshell> int cube(int x) {
   ...>    return x * x;
   ...> }

Then use the arrow keys to move the cursor to the semicolon and edit the statement so the method appears as follows, then press (or select) Enter:

jshell> int cube(int x) {
   ...>   return x * x * x;
   ...> }
|  modified method cube(int)

jshell>

JShell confirms that method cube was modified.

A.7.4 Testing Updated Method cube and Method displayCubes

Now that method cube is properly declared, let’s test it again with the arguments 2 and 10:

jshell> cube(2)
$5 ==> 8

jshell> cube(10)
$6 ==> 1000

jshell>

The method properly returns the cubes of 2 (that is, 8) and 10 (that is, 1000) and stores the results in the implicit variables $5 and $6.

Now, let’s test displayCubes. If you enter "di" and press (or select) Tab, JShell auto-completes the name, including the parentheses of the method call, because displayCubes receives no parameters. The following contains results of the call:

jshell> displayCubes()
Cube of 1 is 1
Cube of 2 is 8
Cube of 3 is 27
Cube of 4 is 64
Cube of 5 is 125
Cube of 6 is 216
Cube of 7 is 343
Cube of 8 is 512
Cube of 9 is 729
Cube of 10 is 1000

jshell>

A.8 Exceptions

[This section may be read after studying Chapter 6 and the preceding sections of this appendix.]

In Section 6.11, we introduced Java’s exception-handling mechanism, demonstrating how to catch an exception that occurred when we attempted to use an out-of-bounds array index. In JShell, catching exceptions is not required—it automatically catches each exception and displays information about it, then displays the next JShell prompt, so you can continue your session. This is particularly important for checked exceptions (Section 10.5) that must be caught in regular Java programs. As you know, catching an exception requires wrapping the code in a try…catch statement. By automatically, catching all exceptions, JShell makes it easier for you to experiment with methods that throw checked exceptions.

In the following new JShell session, we declare an array of int values then demonstrate both valid and invalid array-access expressions:

Click here to view code image

jshell> int[] values = {10, 20, 30}
values ==> int[3] { 10, 20, 30 }

jshell> values[1]
$2 ==> 20

jshell> values[10]
|  Exception java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 10 out of
bounds for length 3
|        at (#3:1)

jshell>

The snippet values[10] attempts to access an out-of-bounds element—recall that this results in an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Even though we did not wrap the code in a try…catch, JShell catches the exception and displays its String representation. This includes the exception’s type and an error message (in this case, the invalid index 10), followed by a stack trace indicating where the problem occurred. The notation

|      at (#3:1)

indicates that the exception occurred at line 1 of the code snippet with the ID 3. Section 5.10 discussed the method-call stack. A stack trace indicates the methods that were on the method-call stack at the time the exception occurred. A typical stack trace contains several "at" lines like the one output here—one per stack frame. After displaying the stack trace, the next jshell> prompt appears. Chapter 10 discusses stack traces in detail.

A.9 Importing Classes and Adding Packages to the CLASSPATH

 

[This section may be read after studying Chapter 11, Files, I/O Streams, JSON Serialization & CSV Files, and the preceding sections of this appendix.]

JShell is helpful for experimenting with classes and class libraries before using them in your programs. You can import types from Java’s API and third-party libraries that you add to JShell’s classpath and module path. Several packages are so commonly used by Java developers that JShell automatically imports them for you. You can change this with JShell’s

/set start

command, which we present in Section A.11.

Viewing the Imported Packages

For this section, we assume you started jshell from the ch11 examples folder. The JShell /imports command lists the current session’s import declarations. The following packages are auto-imported when you begin a new JShell session:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /imports
|    import java.io.*
|    import java.math.*
|    import java.net.*
|    import java.nio.file.*
|    import java.util.*
|    import java.util.concurrent.*
|    import java.util.function.*
|    import java.util.prefs.*
|    import java.util.regex.*
|    import java.util.stream.*

jshell>

The java.lang package’s contents are always available in JShell, just as in any Java source-code file.

Adding Packages to the Class Path

You can also import your own or third-party packages to experiment with them in JShell. JShell’s /env -class-path command adds packages to JShell’s CLASSPATH, which tells JShell where additional packages are located.7 You can then use import declarations to experiment with the packages’ contents in JShell.

7. JShell also provides the options -module-path and -add-modules to add modules so you can import packages from them.

Using Jackson in JShell

In Chapter 11, we introduced the Jackson open-source library for serializing objects to JSON format. Here, we’ll add it to JShell’s CLASSPATH, then serialize an object to a JSON String in JShell. If you have an open JShell session, use /exit to terminate it. Then, change directories to the ch11 examples folder and start a new JShell session.

Adding the Location of a Package to the CLASSPATH

The ch11 folder’s libs subfolder contains the Jackson library components we used in Chapter 11. The following command adds this package to the CLASSPATH on Windows—ensure that you type the entire classpath without spaces:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /env -class-path libs/jackson-core-2.18.1.jar;libs/jackson-
databind-2.18.1.jar;libs/jackson-annotations-2.18.1.jar
|  Setting new options and restoring state.

jshell>

If you use macOS, replace the semicolons (;) with colons (:). The .jar (Java archive) files are ZIP files containing compiled Jackson library Java code. We use relative paths to the libs folder here. You can also specify absolute paths.

Importing a Class from the Package

Now, you can import ObjectMapper for use in JShell. The following demonstrates importing the ObjectMapper class and the complete list of imports in the current session:

Click here to view code image

jshell> import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
jshell> /imports
|    import java.io.*
|    import java.math.*
|    import java.net.*
|    import java.nio.file.*
|    import java.util.*
|    import java.util.concurrent.*
|    import java.util.function.*
|    import java.util.prefs.*
|    import java.util.regex.*
|    import java.util.stream.*
|    import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper

jshell>
Creating a List<Account> to Serialize as JSON

Let’s create a List<Account> to serialize in JShell:

Click here to view code image

jshell> record Account(int accountNumber, String name, double balance) {}
|  created record Account

jshell> List<Account> accounts = List.of(
   ...>    new Account(100, "Devi", 24.98),
   ...>    new Account(200, "Taylor", 345.67));
accounts ==> [Account[accountNumber=100, name=Devi, balance=24 ...
e=Taylor, balance=345.67]]

jshell>
Using the Imported ObjectMapper Class

Finally, you can use class ObjectMapper. Below, we create an ObjectMapper and demonstrate that JShell’s auto-complete capability can display the list of available methods. There are 247 autocomplete options, so we show just a few below and use an ellipsis to indicate there are more:

Click here to view code image

jshell> var mapper = new ObjectMapper();
mapper ==> com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper@7e5afaa6

jshell> mapper.
<press tab again to see all possible completions; total possible
completions: 247>
jshell> mapper.
acceptJsonFormatVisitor(             activateDefaultTyping(
activateDefaultTypingAsProperty(     addHandler(
addMixIn(                            addMixInAnnotations(
...
jshell> mapper.

Next, we use ObjectMapper’s writerWithDefaultPrettyPrinter method to get an ObjectWriter that outputs JSON text with indentation for better readability:

Click here to view code image

jshell> var prettyWriter = mapper.writerWithDefaultPrettyPrinter()
prettyWriter ==> com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectWriter@57d7f8ca

jshell>

Finally, we use the ObjectWriter’s writeValueAsString method to get accounts’ JSON representation and display the returned String:

Click here to view code image

jshell> System.out.println(prettyWriter.writeValueAsString(accounts))
[ {
  "accountNumber" : 100,
  "name" : "Devi",
  "balance" : 24.98
}, {
  "accountNumber" : 200,
  "name" : "Taylor",
  "balance" : 345.67
} ]

jshell>

A.10 Using an External Editor

 

Section A.2.10 demonstrated JShell Edit Pad for editing code snippets. This tool provides only simple editing functionality. Many programmers prefer to use more powerful text editors. You can specify your preferred text editor using JShell’s /set editor command. For example, the JShell command

Click here to view code image

jshell> /set editor notepad.exe
|  Editor set to: notepad.exe

jshell>

sets notepad.exe as the snippet editor for the current JShell session. The /set editor command’s argument is operating-system-specific. For example, on macOS, you can use the built-in nano text editor with the command

/set editor nano
Editing Snippets with a Custom Text Editor

When you’re using a custom editor, each time you save snippet edits JShell immediately re-evaluates any snippets that have changed and outputs their results (but not the snippets themselves) in the JShell output.

Retaining the Editor Setting

You can retain your editor setting for future JShell sessions as follows:

Click here to view code image

/set editor -retain commandToLaunchYourEditor
Restoring the JShell Edit Pad As the Default Editor

If you do not retain your custom editor, subsequent JShell sessions will use JShell Edit Pad. If you do retain the custom editor, you can restore JShell Edit Pad as the default with

/set editor -retain -default

A.11 Summary of JShell Commands

The following table contains the basic JShell commands. Many of these commands have been presented throughout this appendix. Others are discussed in this section.

A.11.1 Getting Help in JShell

JShell’s help documentation is incorporated directly via the /help or /? commands—/? is simply a shorthand for /help. For a quick introduction to JShell, enter:

/help intro

To display JShell’s list of commands, enter

/help

For more information on a given command’s options, enter

/help command

For example

/help /list

displays the /list command’s more detailed help documentation. Similarly

/help /set start

displays more detailed help documentation for the /set command’s start option. For a list of the shortcut key combinations in JShell, enter

/help shortcuts

A.11.2 /edit Command: Additional Features

We’ve discussed using /edit to load all valid snippets, a snippet with a specified ID or a method with a specified name into JShell Edit Pad. You can specify the identifier for any variable, method or type declaration you’d like to edit. For example, if the current JShell session contains the declaration of a class named Account, the following loads that class into JShell Edit Pad:

/edit Account

A.11.3 /reload Command

JShell’s /reload command can re-execute all valid snippets in the current session. Consider the session from Sections A.2.9–A.2.10:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /list

   1 : 45
   2 : 72
   3 : if ($1 < $2) {
          System.out.printf("%d < %d%n", $1, $2);
       }
   4 : if ($1 > $2) {
          System.out.printf("%d > %d%n", $1, $2);
       }
   5 : $1 = 100;
   6 : if ($1 > $2) {
          System.out.printf("%d > %d%n", $1, $2);
       }

jshell>

The following reloads that session one snippet at a time:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /reload
|  Restarting and restoring state.
-: 45
-: 72
-: if ($1 < $2) {
      System.out.printf("%d < %d%n", $1, $2);
   }
45 < 72
-: if ($1 > $2) {
      System.out.printf("%d > %d%n", $1, $2);
   }
-: $1 = 100
-: if ($1 > $2) {
      System.out.printf("%d > %d%n", $1, $2);
   }
100 > 72

jshell>

Each reloaded snippet is preceded by -: and in the case of the if statements, the output (if any) appears immediately following each if statement. If you prefer not to list the snippets as they reload, you can use the /reload command’s -quiet option:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /reload -quiet
|  Restarting and restoring state.
45 < 72
100 > 72

jshell>

In this case, only the results of output statements are displayed. Then, you can view the snippets that were reloaded with the /list command.

A.11.4 /drop Command

You can eliminate a snippet from the current session with JShell’s /drop command followed by a snippet ID or an identifier. The following new JShell session declares a variable x and a method cube, then drops x via its snippet ID and drops cube via its identifier:

Click here to view code image

jshell> int x = 10
x ==> 10

jshell> int cube(int y) {return y * y * y;}
|  created method cube(int)

jshell> /list

   1 : int x = 10;
   2 : int cube(int y) {return y * y * y;}

jshell> /drop 1
|  dropped variable x

jshell> /drop cube
|  dropped method cube(int)

jshell> /list

jshell>

A.11.5 Feedback Modes

JShell has several feedback modes that determine what gets displayed after each interaction. To change the feedback mode, use JShell’s /set feedback command:

/set feedback mode

where mode is concise, normal (the default), silent or verbose. All of the prior JShell interactions in this appendix used the normal mode.

Feedback Mode verbose

Below is a new JShell session in which we used verbose mode, which developers new to Java might prefer:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /set feedback verbose
|  Feedback mode: verbose

jshell> int x = 10
x ==> 10
|  created variable x : int

jshell> int cube(int y) {return y * y * y;}
|  created method cube(int)

jshell> cube(x)
$3 ==> 1000
|  created scratch variable $3 : int

jshell> x = 5
x ==> 5
|  assigned to x : int

jshell> cube(x)
$5 ==> 125
|  created scratch variable $5 : int

jshell>

Notice the additional feedback indicating that

  • variable x was created,

  • method cube was created,

  • scratch variable $3 was created on the first call to cube,

  • an int was assigned to the variable x, and

  • scratch variable $5 was created on the second call to cube.

Feedback Mode concise

Next, we /reset the session then set the feedback mode to concise and repeat the preceding session:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /set feedback concise
jshell> int x = 10
jshell> int cube(int y) {return y * y * y;}
jshell> cube(x)
$3 ==> 1000
jshell> x = 5
jshell> cube(x)
$5 ==> 125
jshell>

Note that the only feedback displayed is the result of each call to cube. If an error occurs, its feedback also will be displayed.

Feedback Mode silent

Finally, we /reset the session then set the feedback mode to silent and repeat the preceding session:

Click here to view code image

jshell> /set feedback silent
-> int x = 10
-> int cube(int y) {return y * y * y;}
-> cube(x)
-> x = 5
-> cube(x)
-> /set feedback normal
|  Feedback mode: normal

jshell>

In this case, the jshell> prompt becomes -> and only error feedback will be displayed. You might use this mode if you’ve copied code from a Java source file and want to paste it into JShell, but do not want feedback for each line.

A.11.6 Other JShell Features Configurable with /set

So far, we’ve demonstrated the /set command’s capabilities for setting an external snippet editor and setting feedback modes. The /set command provides extensive capabilities for creating custom feedback modes via the commands:

  • /set mode

  • /set prompt

  • /set truncation

  • /set format

The /set mode command creates a user-defined custom feedback mode. Then, you can use the other three commands to customize all aspects of JShell’s feedback. The details of these commands are beyond the scope of this appendix. JShell’s help documentation for each of the preceding commands contains more information.

Customizing JShell Startup

Section A.9 listed the set of common packages JShell imports at the start of each session. Using JShell’s /set start command

/set start filename

you can provide a file of Java snippets and JShell commands that will be used in the current session when it restarts due to a /reset or /reload command. You can also remove all startup snippets with

/set start -none

or return to the default startup snippets with

/set start -default

In all three cases, the setting applies only to the current session unless you also include the -retain option. For example, the following command indicates that all subsequent JShell sessions should load the specified file of startup snippets and commands:

/set start -retain filename

You can restore the defaults for future sessions with

/set start -retain -default

A.12 Keyboard Shortcuts for Snippet Editing

In addition to the commands in Fig. A.11, JShell supports many keyboard shortcuts for editing code, such as quickly jumping to the beginning or end of a line or jumping between words in a line. The following table contains some of the shortcuts available.

A.13 How JShell Reinterprets Java for Interactive Use

In JShell:

  • A main method is not required.

  • Semicolons are not required on standalone statements.

  • Variables do not need to be declared in classes or in methods.

  • Methods do not need to be declared inside a class’s body.

  • Statements do not need to be written inside methods.

  • Redeclaring a variable, method or type drops the prior declaration and replaces it with the new one, whereas the Java compiler typically would report an error.

  • You do not need to catch exceptions, though you can if you need to test exception handling.

  • JShell ignores top-level access modifiers (public, private, protected, static, final)—only abstract (Chapter 9) is allowed as a class modifier.

  • The synchronized keyword (Chapter 18, Concurrency: Platform Threads to Virtual Threads) is ignored.

  • package statements and module statements are not allowed.

A.14 IDE JShell Support

Many Java IDEs include JShell support, including IntelliJ IDEA, the Eclipse IDE for Java Developers, NetBeans and Visual Studio Code. Each handles opening JShell and running code snippets in its own way. Some include code syntax coloring and handle name auto-completion differently.

Generative AI

1 Prompt genAIs for a step-by-step tutorial on using JShell in your preferred IDE. Ask them to explain the key differences between JShell in your IDE vs. JShell at the command line.

A.15 Wrap-Up

In this appendix, you used JShell—Java’s interactive REPL for exploration, discovery and experimentation. We started a JShell session and worked with various types of code snippets, including statements, variables, expressions, methods and classes—all without having to declare a class containing a main method to execute the code.

You listed the valid snippets in the current session, and recalled and executed prior snippets and commands using the up and down arrow keys. You also learned that you can list the current session’s variables, methods, types and imports. We cleared the current JShell session to remove all existing snippets and saved snippets to a file then reloaded them.

We demonstrated JShell’s auto-completion capabilities for code and commands, explored a class’s members and displayed documentation directly in JShell. We explored class Math, demonstrating how to list its static members, how to view a method’s parameters and overloads, view a method’s documentation and view a public field’s documentation. We also explored the methods of a String object.

You declared methods and forward referenced an undeclared method that you declared later in the session, then learned that you could go back and execute the first method. We also replaced a method declaration with a new method—in fact, you can replace any declaration of a variable, method or type.

We demonstrated that JShell catches all exceptions and simply displays a stack trace followed by the next jshell> prompt, so you can continue the session. You imported an existing compiled class from a package, then used that class in a JShell session.

Next, we summarized and demonstrated various other JShell commands. We configured a custom snippet editor, viewed JShell’s help documentation, reloaded a session, dropped snippets from a session, configured feedback modes and more. We listed some additional keyboard shortcuts for editing the current snippet at the jshell> prompt. Finally, we discussed how JShell reinterprets Java for interactive use and mentioned IDE support for JShell.

Self-Review Exercises with Answers

We encourage you to use JShell to do Exercises A.1–A.43 after reading Sections A.2–A.3. We’ve included the answers for all these exercises to help you get comfortable with JShell quickly.
